<!-- generated from skills/product-requirements/scope-control/SKILL.md -->

# scope-control

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D1 Product & Requirements (PR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://projeric.com/blogs/scope-management/moscow-prioritization ; https://resources.rework.com/libraries/project-management/moscow-prioritization
- **Depends on:** requirements-writing
- **Feeds into:** roadmapping, user-stories

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a release or iteration has a fixed timeframe and more candidate work than capacity; a scope document is being written, re-triaged, or changed mid-flight; public copy is about to describe what the release includes.
- **Do NOT use when:** there is no requirements list yet (use requirements-writing first), or the question is long-term sequencing rather than this release's boundary (use roadmapping).

## Rules

1. **PR-141 — Four classes, always.** Every scope document classifies every candidate item as Must, Should, Could, or Won't have (this time), per DSDM/MoSCoW. An item with no class is not in scope and not out of scope — it is undecided, and undecided items never reach build or copy.
2. **PR-142 — Non-empty Won't-have list.** The scope document contains a Won't have (this time) section with at least one named item. A boundary that excludes nothing bounds nothing.
3. **PR-143 — Every Must traces to an objective.** Each Must have carries a link to the stated project objective it serves. A Must with no objective is demoted to Should pending review.
4. **PR-144 — Must effort capped at ~60%.** Must haves total no more than about 60% of the timeframe's estimated effort, measured by effort, not by item count, so Should and Could items act as contingency.
5. **PR-145 — Over-cap Musts force re-triage.** If estimated Must effort exceeds ~60% of capacity, re-triage happens before build starts. Proceeding anyway is a defect, not enthusiasm — unless the release records an explicit override, mirroring PR-224 in unit-economics: the override note states that the cap is exceeded, the reason, and the contingency risk accepted. An unrecorded over-cap is still a defect.
6. **PR-146 — Fixed de-scope order.** When the timeframe is threatened, items are cut in the agreed order: Could first, then Should. Musts and the date hold unless the release is re-baselined under PR-147.
7. **PR-147 — Changes displace or re-baseline.** A scope change enters only by displacing equal estimated effort from a lower class, or by a recorded re-baseline of the release (new date or new capacity) approved by the decider named in the document.
8. **PR-148 — Every change is logged.** Each scope change records the item, the decider, the date, and what it displaced. An unlogged change is treated as never approved.
9. **PR-149 — Public copy mirrors Must and Should only.** Marketing pages, changelogs, and sales material may describe Must and Should items as included. Could items are never presented as included, and Won't-have items are never presented at all.
10. **PR-150 — Owner and review date.** The scope document names one owner and a review date. A scope document past its review date cannot authorize new commitments until re-reviewed.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PR-071 — Unscoped feature in public copy.** Banned: describing a feature in marketing copy, a changelog, or a sales deck when the scope document classes it Could or Won't have (this time). Defeats: DET-CON-004. Bad: the landing page lists "SSO login — included in Pro" while the scope document has SSO under Won't have (this time). Instead: copy is written from the Must and Should classes only (PR-149). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-072 — Dated promise for unvalidated scope.** Banned: attaching a launch date or "coming soon" announcement to any item that is not a Must have with acceptance criteria attached. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: a banner reads "AI reports launch March 1" for an item classed Could with no criteria written. Instead: announce only Must items, and only with the release's own date. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-073 — Silent scope absorption.** Banned: adding an item to the build without a change-log entry naming the decider and the displaced item. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: a stakeholder asks in chat for CSV export, it gets built, and the help center and the pricing page end up describing different feature sets. Instead: log the change under PR-148 before build starts. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-074 — Promising a scope item as an operational commitment.** Banned: copy that commits the business to an ongoing service (support hours, uptime, response times) that no scope item or policy funds. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the pricing page promises "24/7 support" while the release scope contains no support staffing item at all. Instead: the promise is scoped and funded first, or the copy is cut. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PR-071 — Won't-have presence check.** Verifies: PR-141, PR-142. Check (automated): `sed -n "/won't have/I,/^## /p" scope.md | grep -q "^- "` — the Won't have section must contain at least one list item. Pass: command exits 0. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-072 — Must effort-share computation.** Verifies: PR-144, PR-145. Check (automated): export the requirements table to CSV (columns: item,class,effort) and run `awk -F, '$2=="Must"{m+=$3} {t+=$3} END {print m/t}' requirements.csv`. Pass: output ≤ 0.60. Fail: block shipment until re-triage is recorded. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-073 — Must-to-objective trace check.** Verifies: PR-143. Check (automated): every row classed Must in the requirements table has a non-empty objective column; a script or spreadsheet filter for `class=Must AND objective=""` must return zero rows. Pass: zero rows. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-074 — Change-log audit.** Verifies: PR-147, PR-148. Check (manual): diff the current scope document against its previous version; every added or reclassed item must have a matching change-log entry with decider, date, and displaced item. Pass: zero unexplained diffs. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-075 — Copy-to-scope sweep.** Verifies: PR-149. Check (manual): list every feature named in the release's public copy; each must appear in the scope document as Must or Should. Pass: zero features sourced from Could or Won't have. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Priority by loudness.** The class of an item quietly tracks who asked most recently or most seniorly, while the document still shows the old classes. Catch it by comparing the change log against who requested each reclass.
- **Contingency spent twice.** The same Should item is named as the buffer for two different Must overruns. Catch it by listing, for each Must, which contingency covers it — duplicates mean the buffer does not exist.
- **Shadow scope in tickets.** Work enters through the issue tracker without ever touching the scope document, so the document stays clean and wrong. Catch it by sampling closed tickets each iteration and checking each against the scope classes.
- **Won't-have amnesia.** An item classed Won't have (this time) reappears next release with no record that it was ever excluded, so its earlier rejection reasoning is lost. Catch it by carrying the Won't-have list forward into the next scope document as the starting draft.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The boundary that excluded nothing](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects PR-142.
- [Example 2 — Ninety percent Must](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects PR-144, PR-145.
- [Example 3 — The chat-request feature](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects PR-148.

## Recall anchors

- Four classes or it is not a scope document.
- A boundary that excludes nothing bounds nothing.
- Musts ≤ ~60% of effort — the rest is contingency.
- Changes displace, or the release is re-baselined. Never both silently.
- Public copy mirrors Must and Should only.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every candidate item carries a MoSCoW class (PR-141).
- [ ] Won't have (this time) section exists and is non-empty (PR-142, G-PR-071).
- [ ] Every Must links to a stated objective (PR-143, G-PR-073).
- [ ] Must effort share computed and ≤ ~60% (PR-144, G-PR-072).
- [ ] De-scope order (Could, then Should) written in the document (PR-146).
- [ ] Every change since the last version is logged with decider, date, and displacement (PR-148, G-PR-074).
- [ ] Public copy checked against Must/Should classes only (PR-149, G-PR-075).
- [ ] Owner and review date present and current (PR-150).

<!-- generated from skills/product-requirements/unit-economics/SKILL.md -->

# unit-economics

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D1 Product & Requirements (PR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.forentrepreneurs.com/ltv-cac/ ; https://www.construx.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/CxWhitePaper_ConeOfUncertainty.pdf
- **Depends on:** product-metrics, pricing-monetization
- **Feeds into:** scope-control, roadmapping

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** judging whether an acquisition motion or business model can work; computing or publishing CAC, LTV, their ratio, or payback; producing a cost or effort estimate for a project, feature, or plan.
- **Do NOT use when:** the acquisition motion does not exist yet and the honest output is "directional only" (say so and stop), or the numbers are published marketing metrics rather than economics (use product-metrics).

## Rules

1. **PR-221 — CAC is fully loaded.** CAC = (all sales + marketing cost for the period) ÷ (new customers acquired in the same period). "All" includes salaries, commissions, tools, agencies, and content production — never media spend alone.
2. **PR-222 — LTV is margin-based.** LTV = average revenue per account × gross margin ÷ churn rate, with revenue, margin, and churn stated for the same cohort and period. Revenue-based LTV is never reported as LTV.
3. **PR-223 — Payback uses gross profit.** CAC payback (months) = CAC ÷ monthly gross profit per customer. Ratio and payback are always reported together; either one alone hides the cash problem or the value problem.
4. **PR-224 — Heuristics are heuristics.** LTV:CAC above 3 and payback under 12 months are viability heuristics (Skok), recorded as defaults with an explicit override note when a project departs from them — never applied as universal pass/fail laws to non-SaaS models.
5. **PR-225 — No ratio before a repeatable motion.** LTV:CAC is not computed as a decision number until a repeatable acquisition motion exists. Figures computed earlier are labeled "directional" wherever they appear and cannot anchor commitments.
6. **PR-226 — Estimates are ranges with a method.** Every estimate states a range, the named assumptions, and the method used (analogy, decomposition, or parametric). A single-point estimate with none of these fails review.
7. **PR-227 — Estimate, target, commitment are separate.** The estimate (what the work is expected to take), the target (what the business wants), and the commitment (what was promised externally) are three distinct numbers, recorded separately and never silently merged.
8. **PR-228 — Estimate vs. actual is logged.** Every completed item records its estimate and its actual. A team with no such history states in writing that its estimates are uncalibrated guesses.
9. **PR-229 — Cohort before aggregate.** Economics are computed per cohort or segment first. A blended figure that hides a losing segment is a reporting defect, and the losing segment is reported, not averaged away.
10. **PR-230 — Cone position is stated.** Early estimates name their position on McConnell's Cone of Uncertainty (an initial-concept estimate can run 0.25x–4x the actual) and narrow only as named decisions and decomposition reduce the uncertainty.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PR-111 — Media-only CAC.** Banned: computing CAC from advertising spend alone, excluding salaries, commissions, tools, and agency cost. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: a report states "CAC: $45" from $9,000 of ad spend over 200 customers, while the same period carried $27,000 of salaries, commissions, tools, and agency fees — the real CAC is $180, and every downstream decision inherits the false figure. Instead: fully load the numerator under PR-221. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-112 — Revenue LTV labeled as LTV.** Banned: dividing revenue per account by churn and presenting the result as LTV without applying gross margin. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "LTV: $4,000" from $120/month ÷ 3% churn, when 75% gross margin makes the margin-based LTV $3,000 — and the published 4.0 ratio is really 3.0. Instead: apply margin under PR-222 and show both inputs. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-113 — Single-point estimate.** Banned: quoting one number ("$80k, three months") with no range, no assumptions, and no method. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: a client plan commits to "the migration will cost $80,000" at concept stage — inside the Cone's 0.25x–4x band, the honest statement is a range roughly four times wide in each direction, and the single point becomes a promise nobody derived. Instead: estimate under PR-226 and PR-230. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-114 — Blended ratio hiding a losing segment.** Banned: publishing one blended LTV:CAC while a named segment's ratio is below 1 and undisclosed. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the board deck reports a blended 3.4 while the self-serve segment runs at 0.8 and consumes half the spend; the fact sheet and the deck end up telling different stories about the same business. Instead: report per-cohort figures first (PR-229). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PR-111 — Formula audit.** Verifies: PR-221, PR-222, PR-223. Check (automated): recompute CAC, LTV, ratio, and payback from the raw inputs with a script or spreadsheet and diff against the reported figures (tolerance: rounding only). Pass: all four recomputed values match the report. Fail: block shipment of the report. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-112 — Estimate-record check.** Verifies: PR-226, PR-227, PR-230. Check (automated): every estimate record contains the fields range-low, range-high, method, assumptions, cone-position, and separate estimate/target/commitment values; a field-presence scan over the estimates file returns zero incomplete records. Pass: zero incomplete records. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-113 — Cohort disclosure check.** Verifies: PR-229. Check (automated): any document reporting a blended LTV, CAC, or ratio must also contain a per-cohort table; `grep -ci "cohort" report.md` ≥ 1 wherever a blended figure appears, and each cohort row shows its own ratio. Pass: blended figures never appear without the cohort table. Fail: warn; the table is added before the figures are used in a decision. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-114 — Calibration log review.** Verifies: PR-228. Check (manual): open the estimate-vs-actual log; the last five completed items have both numbers recorded, or the document states that the team is uncalibrated. Pass: log current or the uncalibrated statement present. Fail: warn. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Precision from nowhere.** A ratio quoted to two decimals ("3.47") whose inputs are a founder's guesses. Catch it by asking for the raw inputs; if they cannot be produced, the decimals are decoration and the figure is directional at best (PR-225).
- **Churn shopping.** Trying monthly, quarterly, and annualized churn and publishing whichever makes LTV largest. Catch it by requiring the churn definition to be written next to the LTV figure and identical across documents.
- **Estimate amnesia.** Each new estimate is produced fresh, with no reference to how the last three estimates performed. Catch it with the calibration log (G-PR-114): an estimate that does not cite the team's historical error range is starting over.
- **Heuristic lawyering.** Treating "above 3" as proof of health while payback stretches past two years, or killing a viable non-SaaS model for missing a SaaS heuristic. Catch it against PR-223 and PR-224: ratio and payback travel together, and overrides are recorded, not smuggled.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The $45 CAC](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects PR-221.
- [Example 2 — Revenue LTV in disguise](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects PR-222.
- [Example 3 — The $80,000 promise](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects PR-226, PR-230.

## Recall anchors

- CAC is fully loaded or it is fiction.
- LTV is margin-based, or it is revenue wearing a costume.
- Ratio and payback travel together.
- Estimates are ranges with assumptions; single points are promises.
- Cohort before aggregate — blends hide losers.

## Checklist

- [ ] CAC numerator includes salaries, commissions, tools, agencies, content (PR-221, G-PR-111).
- [ ] LTV computed from margin, with revenue, margin, and churn stated (PR-222).
- [ ] Payback reported alongside the ratio (PR-223).
- [ ] Heuristic departures recorded as overrides, not hidden (PR-224).
- [ ] Pre-motion figures labeled "directional" (PR-225).
- [ ] Every estimate carries range, method, assumptions, cone position (PR-226, PR-230, G-PR-112).
- [ ] Estimate, target, and commitment recorded as three numbers (PR-227).
- [ ] Estimate-vs-actual log current for the last completed items (PR-228, G-PR-114).
- [ ] Cohort table present wherever a blended figure appears (PR-229, G-PR-113).

# user-research

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D1 Product & Requirements (PR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Nielsen Norman Group, "Personas Make Users Memorable for Product Team Members" — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/persona/ ; Torres, Opportunity Solution Tree — https://www.chameleon.io/blog/opportunity-solution-tree
- **Depends on:** discovery
- **Feeds into:** personas-jtbd, requirements-writing

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** evidence about users must be gathered, recorded, or cited — before personas are built, before a segment claim is made, before a requirement claims user backing.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what to build next (that is discovery working from this evidence) or how a claim may be published (that is fact-sheet and real-content). Do not run "research" whose only source is the team's own opinion.

## Rules

1. **PR-021 — Findings before interpretations.** The research file writes findings (what was observed) separately from interpretations (what the team concludes). The two are never merged into a single statement.
2. **PR-022 — Every study is fully attributed.** Each study entry records method, participant count, participant source, and dates. An entry missing any of the four is incomplete and cannot be cited.
3. **PR-023 — Real segment only.** Participants come from the actual target segment. Team members, friends, and other builders never count as user evidence.
4. **PR-024 — No claim without a citation.** No persona, segment claim, or "users want X" statement exists without a cited finding ID behind it.
5. **PR-025 — Sample limits are stated.** Every study states who was not reached and what the sample cannot support; the limit is part of the finding.
6. **PR-026 — Context travels with quotes.** Every quote or observation keeps its context (task, moment, segment). A decontextualized quote is not evidence.
7. **PR-027 — Staleness is enforced.** Research past its stated refresh date is marked STALE in the file and cannot justify new commitments until refreshed.
8. **PR-028 — Triangulation for load-bearing claims.** A claim that a persona or requirement depends on is corroborated by a second source type (survey, support tickets, or analytics alongside interviews).
9. **PR-029 — Raw records are kept.** The notes or recordings the method allows are stored with the study, so any finding can be re-checked against its source.
10. **PR-030 — Supplied-material honesty.** When research is built from user-supplied material rather than studies the team ran, the file says so and names the material; anything inferred from it is labeled an inference.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PR-011 — The uncited "users want".** Banned: any "users want / need / prefer X" statement in a research artifact with no finding ID behind it. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: the findings file states "Users want a mobile app" and no study exists. Instead: cite the finding ("F-07: 6 of 9 dispatchers exported reports to phone spreadsheets during the March study") or delete the claim. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-012 — Invented participants.** Banned: participant counts, quotes, or studies that were never run. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "We interviewed 20 users" when the team read three support tickets. Instead: record what actually happened ("3 support tickets, March export, supplied by the user"). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-013 — Colleague-as-user.** Banned: counting team members, friends, or role-play sessions as research participants. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "Tested with 8 users" — the 8 were coworkers from the same office. Instead: recruit from the target segment, or label the session an internal review, not research. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-014 — Stale research presented as current.** Banned: citing research past its refresh date as justification for a new commitment without showing the date and the STALE mark. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: a 14-month-old pricing study cited in this quarter's roadmap with no date shown. Instead: show the date and the STALE mark, or refresh the study first. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PR-011 — Study-field completeness.** Verifies: PR-022. Check: automated — run a template check over the research file confirming every study entry has non-empty method, participant count/source, and date fields. Pass: 100% of entries complete. Fail: block citation of the incomplete studies. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-012 — Persona traceability.** Verifies: PR-024. Check: automated — run a script confirming every persona in the persona file cites at least one finding ID that exists in the research file. Pass: 100% of citations resolve. Fail: block persona sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-013 — Claim citation audit.** Verifies: PR-024, PR-028. Check: manual — sample 5 load-bearing claims in downstream artifacts; each must resolve to a finding, and load-bearing claims to two source types. Pass: 5 of 5 resolve. Fail: warn; a repeat failure blocks handoff. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-014 — Staleness sweep.** Verifies: PR-027. Check: automated — compare each study's refresh date against today's date and flag overdue studies STALE in the file. Pass: no overdue study remains unmarked. Fail: warn, and mark before any further citation. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Findings–interpretation blend.** "Users struggled with the export and clearly need a wizard" — observation and prescription in one breath. Catch it: prescriptions belong in the interpretation section; if a finding contains a feature name, it is blended.
- **Quote mining.** One vivid quote carries an entire segment claim. Catch it: ask for the count behind the quote; if the answer is one participant, the claim shrinks to match.
- **Convenience-sample laundering.** Participants were whoever replied to a forum post, then described in the file as "our users." Catch it: compare the participant source field against the segment definition, word by word.
- **Refresh-date drift.** Refresh dates get quietly extended instead of studies being re-run. Catch it: diff the file history; a changed refresh date with no new study attached is the tell.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A complete study entry](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PR-022.
- [Example 2 — Separating a finding from its interpretation](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PR-021.
- [Example 3 — A claim that carries its citation and its limits](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PR-024, PR-025.

## Recall anchors

- Findings and interpretations live in separate sections.
- Method, count, source, date — or it did not happen.
- No claim without a finding ID.
- Who was not reached is part of the finding.
- Stale research is marked, never silently reused.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every study entry has method, participant count/source, and dates (G-PR-011).
- [ ] Findings and interpretations are in separate sections (PR-021).
- [ ] No participant comes from outside the target segment (PR-023).
- [ ] Every downstream claim sampled resolves to a finding ID (G-PR-013).
- [ ] Each study states who was not reached (PR-025).
- [ ] No overdue study is unmarked STALE (G-PR-014).
- [ ] Supplied material is named as supplied, with inferences labeled (PR-030).

# user-stories

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D1 Product & Requirements (PR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Mike Cohn / Mountain Goat Software, "What Makes a Good User Story?" (INVEST) — https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/user-stories/good-user-stories
- **Depends on:** personas-jtbd, requirements-writing
- **Feeds into:** acceptance-criteria, scope-control

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** validated needs and requirements must become iteration-sized work items a team can build and confirm; a backlog is being refined.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work has no user-visible benefit (label it a task under PR-084), or the need behind the item has not been validated (return to discovery). Do not use story format to give technical work borrowed legitimacy.

## Rules

1. **PR-081 — Template is mandatory.** Every story reads: "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]." All three parts are present and non-empty.
2. **PR-082 — The role is a named persona.** The role names a persona or segment from the persona set. Bare "user" is allowed only when the capability serves every segment identically, and the story states that reason on its face.
3. **PR-083 — The benefit clause is real.** The "so that" states an outcome the role values. A clause that restates the capability ("so that I can use the feature") fails.
4. **PR-084 — Tasks are labeled tasks.** Work with no user-visible benefit — endpoints, migrations, refactors — is labeled a task and planned as one. It never wears story format.
5. **PR-085 — One iteration maximum.** A story too big to finish in one iteration is split before estimation, along workflow steps or business rules — never along technical layers.
6. **PR-086 — No story without criteria.** A story enters build only with at least one linked acceptance criterion (see acceptance-criteria).
7. **PR-087 — The conversation is recorded.** Decisions from the story conversation (card–conversation–confirmation) are written on the story before build. An unrecorded agreement does not exist.
8. **PR-088 — Splits keep value whole.** Each story produced by a split still delivers a complete, usable slice of value to its role. A split producing a fragment nobody can use is re-split.
9. **PR-089 — Stories trace upward.** Each story links to its parent opportunity ID or requirement ID, which must resolve.
10. **PR-090 — INVEST is a diagnostic, not a score.** Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable are checked at refinement; a failing letter triggers a fix or a recorded exception — never a points chase.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PR-041 — The bare-user story.** Banned: "As a user…" where segments differ in need, permission, or outcome. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "As a user, I want to export reports" — only dispatchers may export; drivers must not, and the story hides the rule. Instead: "As a dispatch lead, I want to export the filtered order list, so that I can send month-end totals to finance." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-042 — The disguised task.** Banned: technical work dressed as a story to borrow its legitimacy. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "As a user, I want an API endpoint for bulk import, so that the system has an endpoint." Instead: label it a task, link it to the story it enables, and plan it as engineering work. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PR-043 — The benefit-less story.** Banned: a story with no "so that" clause, or a clause that restates the capability. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "As a manager, I want a dashboard so that I can see the dashboard." Instead: "As a dispatch lead, I want late orders flagged on one screen, so that I can reassign drivers before customers call." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PR-044 — The epic in story's clothing.** Banned: estimating or scheduling, as a single story, work that cannot finish in one iteration. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "As a dispatcher, I want full reporting" enters the sprint and is still "in progress" three iterations later, its behavior never defined. Instead: split along the workflow (view late orders → export totals → schedule recurring sends) and estimate the pieces. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PR-041 — Story template lint.** Verifies: PR-081, PR-082, PR-083. Check: automated — run a regex over every story confirming the "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" shape, and that the role matches a persona name or carries the all-segments note. Pass: 100% of stories conform. Fail: block refinement sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-042 — Criteria linkage.** Verifies: PR-086. Check: automated — run a tracker query confirming no story in "in build" status has zero linked acceptance criteria. Pass: zero violations. Fail: block the status change until criteria are attached. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-043 — Split review.** Verifies: PR-085, PR-088. Check: manual — every story estimated above the team's one-iteration threshold shows its split, and each child story delivers usable value on its own. The review also judges each story's benefit clause: a benefit that merely repeats the capability text (a semantic judgment no lint can make) is sent back for rewriting. Pass: all oversized stories are split into whole-value pieces and no benefit clause repeats its capability. Fail: block estimation. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PR-044 — Traceability spot check.** Verifies: PR-089. Check: automated — run a script confirming every story carries an opportunity or requirement ID that resolves in its source file. Pass: 100% resolve. Fail: warn, and fix before build. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Story as mini-spec.** The card carries paragraphs of solution detail, killing the conversation it exists to start. Catch it: if the card text is longer than the recorded conversation notes, the card became the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing.** "Build the database part" written as a story. Catch it: ask who can use the finished slice; if the answer is "nobody yet," re-split vertically along the workflow.
- **Persona name-dropping.** The story names a persona, but the benefit is the business's, not the persona's. Catch it: read the benefit clause aloud from the persona's seat; if the persona would not say it, rewrite.
- **Solution-first wording.** The capability names the implementation ("I want a modal dialog…") instead of the outcome sought. Catch it: replace the named widget with its purpose; if the story collapses, it was a design instruction, not a story.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Replacing the bare "user" with a named persona](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PR-082.
- [Example 2 — Relabeling a disguised task](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PR-084.
- [Example 3 — Splitting an epic along the workflow](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PR-085, PR-088.

## Recall anchors

- As a named persona, I want a capability, so that a real benefit.
- No benefit clause, no story.
- Tasks are tasks — label them honestly.
- Split along the workflow, never along the layers.
- No criteria, no build.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every story passes the template lint (G-PR-041).
- [ ] Every role is a named persona or carries the all-segments reason (PR-082).
- [ ] Every benefit clause states an outcome, not the capability restated (PR-083).
- [ ] Technical work is labeled as tasks, not stories (PR-084).
- [ ] No story in build has zero acceptance criteria (G-PR-042).
- [ ] Oversized stories are split into whole-value pieces (G-PR-043).
- [ ] Every story traces to an opportunity or requirement ID (G-PR-044).

## Department D2 — architecture

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/adr-writing/SKILL.md -->

# adr-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** MADR — Markdown Architectural Decision Records (template and guidance) — https://adr.github.io/madr/
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: an ADR is written from the decision itself, as made with the user against the codebase at hand; it consumes no other skill's output. The recorded decisions feed stack-selection, system-design, and decision-logs.
- **Feeds into:** stack-selection, system-design, decision-logs

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a significant, hard-to-reverse decision is being made — stack components, tenancy model, API paradigm, pattern adoption, data ownership — or an existing decision is being revisited or reversed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the choice is trivially reversible or purely local (a variable name, a file layout inside one module); record those in code review and move on. Do not use an ADR as the design document itself — the design lives in ARCHITECTURE.md or the contract, and the ADR links to it.

## Rules

1. **AR-241 — One file per decision.** Each record is its own MADR file in `docs/decisions/`, numbered `NNNN-title.md`; a file deciding two questions is split.
2. **AR-242 — Full MADR sections.** Every record carries: title, status, context and problem statement, decision drivers, considered options, decision outcome, and consequences.
3. **AR-243 — At least two considered options.** The rejected alternative and the reason it lost are mandatory. An ADR with one option is incomplete: the rejected option is the record's most valuable content.
4. **AR-244 — At least one negative consequence.** Consequences include at least one negative or cost. An all-positive consequences section means the trade-off was not examined, and the record is sent back.
5. **AR-245 — Immutable once accepted.** An accepted ADR is never edited to change its decision. A change of mind is a new ADR that supersedes the old one, linked in both directions.
6. **AR-246 — Status is maintained.** When a decision is reversed, the old record's status becomes "superseded by NNNN" in the same commit as the new ADR. The folder never holds two contradictory "accepted" records on the same question.
7. **AR-247 — Titles state the decision.** The title is the decision in a sentence — "Use PostgreSQL for the primary store" — not the topic, "Database discussion."
8. **AR-248 — Written with the work.** The ADR lands in the same change as the work it governs, while the alternatives are still genuinely remembered, not reconstructed weeks later.
9. **AR-249 — Decisions, not designs.** The ADR records the choice and its reasoning; the full design lives in ARCHITECTURE.md or the contract, and the ADR links to it instead of copying it.
10. **AR-250 — Every significant decision gets one.** If reversing the choice would cost more than a day's work, it needs an ADR: stack components, tenancy model, paradigm, pattern adoptions, data ownership.
11. **AR-251 — Drivers before options.** Decision drivers and selection criteria are recorded before options are scored against them; criteria written after the winner is known are rationalization.
12. **AR-252 — Links resolve.** Supersedes and superseded-by links, and every referenced diagram, contract, and ADR, point at files that exist.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-121 — The silent swap.** Banned: changing a settled, ADR-backed decision with no new ADR recording the change. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: the accepted ADR says PostgreSQL; a pull request quietly moves the project to MongoDB because a tutorial used it, and six months later nobody can reconstruct why the database changed. Instead: write the superseding ADR with the new decision's drivers and rejected alternatives, and update the old record's status in the same commit. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-122 — Editing history.** Banned: modifying an accepted ADR's decision, options, or consequences in place. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: after the chosen vendor raises prices, the ADR's consequences section is quietly rewritten to remove the cost warning it originally carried, so the decision looks better than it was. Instead: leave the record untouched; write a new ADR that supersedes it and states what changed. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-123 — The all-positive record.** Banned: a consequences section listing only benefits. Defeats: DET-CODE-021. Bad: "Consequences: faster development, happier team, modern stack" — a record that narrates approval instead of explaining a trade-off, useless to the reader who must later decide whether to reverse it. Instead: name at least one real cost (operational burden, lock-in, a capability given up) and who bears it. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-124 — Topic titles.** Banned: titling an ADR with its subject area instead of its decision. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: `0007-database-discussion.md` — the title tells a future reader nothing about what was decided, and the decisions folder becomes unsearchable. Instead: `0007-use-postgresql-for-the-primary-store.md`. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-121 — ADR lint.** Verifies: AR-242, AR-243, AR-245, AR-252. Check: automated — a script over `docs/decisions/` asserts every file parses, carries a status from the allowed set (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded by NNNN), has a considered-options section with at least two options, and that superseded records link to an existing successor. Pass: zero violations. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-122 — Manifest cross-check.** Verifies: AR-250. Check: automated — every top-level dependency in the project's manifest maps to an ADR (by name or tag match). Pass: every major dependency has a record. Fail: block the dependency addition until its ADR exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-123 — Reconstruction test.** Verifies: AR-243, AR-244. Check: manual — sample one ADR and confirm a reader who was not present can reconstruct why the choice was made, including what was given up, without interviewing the author. Pass: the reader's summary matches the decision's actual drivers. Fail: warn; the record is expanded before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-124 — Contradiction scan.** Verifies: AR-246. Check: manual — at each release, scan the accepted ADRs for two records deciding the same question differently. Pass: no contradictory pair marked accepted. Fail: block release until one is superseded. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The ADR graveyard.** Records are written for trivial choices while significant ones go unrecorded, because writing was easier for the small ones. Catch it: sort by consequence — if the folder's biggest file decides a CSS framework and the database has no record, the practice is inverted.
- **Retroactive rationalization.** The ADR is written weeks after the decision, inventing alternatives that were never genuinely considered. Catch it: compare the ADR's commit date with the work it governs (AR-248); a long gap with suspiciously complete options is the tell.
- **The mega-ADR.** One file decides the stack, the topology, and the tenancy model at once, so none of them can be superseded independently. Catch it: count the decisions in the file; more than one means split it.
- **Status rot.** Superseded decisions still read "accepted" because nobody updated them, and a new team member follows a dead decision in good faith. Catch it: the contradiction scan (G-AR-124) exists precisely for this; a folder never scanned is rotting.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The single-option ADR, completed](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-243.
- [Example 2 — A reversal done as a superseding pair](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-245, AR-246.
- [Example 3 — Topic title and brochure consequences, fixed](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-247, AR-244.

## Recall anchors

- One file, one decision, at least two options.
- The rejected alternative is the most valuable part.
- Every record names a cost.
- Accepted records are immutable; reversal means a new ADR.
- The title is the decision, not the topic.

## Checklist

- [ ] The record is one MADR file, titled with the decision (AR-241, AR-247).
- [ ] Considered options number at least two, with the loser's reason stated (AR-243).
- [ ] Consequences include at least one negative or cost (AR-244).
- [ ] Decision drivers were recorded before options were scored (AR-251).
- [ ] ADR lint passes over `docs/decisions/` (G-AR-121).
- [ ] If this reverses a decision, the old record's status is updated in the same commit (AR-246).
- [ ] The ADR links to the design instead of copying it, and all links resolve (AR-249, AR-252).

# api-architecture

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Zalando RESTful API Guidelines — https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/ ; Google API design and compatibility rules — https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/compatibility/ ; Lint and diff tooling survey — https://apidog.com/blog/open-source-cli-tools-api-design/
- **Depends on:** system-design, domain-driven-design
- **Feeds into:** api-versioning, api-documentation, api-paradigms

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing a new HTTP API or a new resource surface on an existing one; reviewing an OpenAPI draft before implementation; settling naming, error, pagination, or idempotency conventions for a service.
- **Do NOT use when:** the interface is not resource-oriented HTTP (api-paradigms decides the paradigm first), the question is only how an accepted design evolves (api-versioning), or the work is documenting an existing contract (api-documentation).

**House profile (applies to this skill, api-versioning, and api-documentation — one style, no mixing):** Zalando-based. Resource names are plural nouns; property names are `snake_case`; custom actions are sub-resources (e.g., `POST /orders/{id}/cancellations`); errors use the Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) everywhere; collections paginate with cursors; the major version sits in the path segment (`/v1/…`); deprecations are signaled with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers.

## Rules

1. **AR-061 — Contract first.** The OpenAPI document is drafted and reviewed before implementation, and is written or updated in the same change as any API behavior change. Code that changes behavior without touching the contract is incomplete.
2. **AR-062 — Resources from the domain.** Resources and their relationships are identified from the domain model, with stable identifiers. An endpoint that cannot name its resource is a design smell to resolve, not to route around.
3. **AR-063 — One error format.** Every endpoint returns errors in the house Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`). Per-endpoint error shapes are a blocking defect.
4. **AR-064 — Every list paginates.** Every list endpoint paginates (cursor preferred) and states its ordering in the contract. An unbounded list response is forbidden.
5. **AR-065 — Filtering and sorting are first-version features.** Collection endpoints define their filter and sort parameters in the first version, per the house profile; bolting them on later is a breaking-change risk, not a plan.
6. **AR-066 — Mutations state their idempotency story.** Every mutating endpoint is one of: a safe/idempotent method by semantics, protected by an idempotency key, or explicitly documented as non-idempotent with a retry warning. Silence on idempotency is a defect.
7. **AR-067 — Names follow the house profile.** Resource names are plural nouns; verbs appear only as named sub-resource actions (`/orders/{id}/cancellations`); property names are `snake_case`. No endpoint invents its own convention.
8. **AR-068 — Auth is in the contract.** Every operation declares its security requirement in the OpenAPI document (scheme and, where applicable, scope). An operation with no declared security is treated as an oversight, not as public-by-default.
9. **AR-069 — One profile, applied uniformly.** The house profile named in this skill is the only style guide for the API. Where the profile is silent, the gap is resolved once, recorded, and applied everywhere — never per endpoint.
10. **AR-070 — Breaking changes leave this skill.** Any change the compatibility list classifies as breaking is routed to api-versioning (major bump plus deprecation window); it never ships quietly inside an existing version.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-031 — Per-endpoint error shapes.** Banned: each endpoint inventing its own error body. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: `GET /orders` fails with `{"error": "nope"}`, `POST /orders` with `{"message": ..., "code": 7}`, and `GET /invoices` with a plain-text 500; every client writes three error parsers. Instead: the house Problem Details body (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) from every endpoint (AR-063). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-032 — The unbounded list.** Banned: a list endpoint that returns the whole collection. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: `GET /customers` returns all 40,000 customer records in one response because "it's an internal tool for now." Instead: cursor pagination with a stated ordering and a default and maximum page size, in the first version (AR-064). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-033 — Verbs as resources.** Banned: endpoints named for actions instead of resources (`/createOrder`, `/getInvoices`, `/deleteUser`). Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: the API surface is 30 POST endpoints with verb names; HTTP methods and resources carry no meaning and every client hardcodes RPC-style paths. Instead: plural-noun resources with HTTP methods for the standard operations and sub-resource actions for the rest (`POST /orders`, `POST /orders/{id}/cancellations`) (AR-067). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-034 — Code-first drift.** Banned: shipping an API behavior change while the OpenAPI document stays untouched. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: a field is renamed in the service to fix a bug; the contract, the generated docs, and the partner's client all keep the old name until production traffic fails. Instead: the contract is edited in the same change, reviewed as the contract, and the diff gate in api-versioning classifies the rename as breaking (AR-061). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-031 — OpenAPI lint.** Verifies: AR-063, AR-064, AR-067, AR-068. Check: automated — CI runs Spectral (or Redocly CLI) with the house ruleset against the OpenAPI file: operationIds and descriptions present, error responses use the Problem Details schema, list operations declare pagination parameters, property names match `snake_case`. The linter version is pinned in the repo; if the sandbox cannot run it, the fallback is the documented manual ruleset walk, recorded in progress.md. Pass: zero lint errors. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-032 — Contract tests.** Verifies: AR-061, AR-063. Check: automated — contract tests generated from the OpenAPI document run against the implementation in CI and assert status codes, response shapes, and the error format on failure paths. Pass: all contract tests green. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-033 — Spec-diff design review.** Verifies: AR-062, AR-066, AR-069. Check: manual — before implementation starts, a reviewer reads the OpenAPI diff: resources trace to the domain model, every mutation states its idempotency story, and every deviation from the house profile is recorded as a profile decision. Pass: no unresolved findings. Fail: block implementation. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The chat-message contract.** Endpoint behavior agreed in prose messages and never written into the OpenAPI document. Catch it: if a consumer's question can only be answered from a chat thread, AR-061 was skipped and the contract does not exist.
- **Pagination as a retrofit.** "We'll add pagination when it gets slow." Catch it: any list endpoint without a cursor in v1 is a future breaking change already scheduled (AR-064).
- **The god resource.** One resource (`/things`) absorbing unrelated concepts because naming the real resources took effort. Catch it: if a resource's fields fall into two groups that are never read together, there are two resources (AR-062).
- **Profile à la carte.** snake_case on one endpoint, camelCase on the next; errors in Problem Details here, ad-hoc JSON there — each locally defensible. Catch it: run G-AR-031 and read two endpoints side by side; uniformity is the profile's whole value (AR-069).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — One error format replacing per-endpoint shapes](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-063.
- [Example 2 — Cursor pagination replacing an unbounded list](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-064.
- [Example 3 — Verb endpoints remodeled as resources](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-067.

## Recall anchors

- Contract first, code second — same change, every time.
- One error format: Problem Details, everywhere.
- Every list paginates; every mutation states its idempotency story.
- Plural nouns, snake_case, sub-resource actions — the house profile.
- Breaking change? Stop — api-versioning owns it.

## Checklist

- [ ] The OpenAPI document was drafted or updated in the same change as the behavior (AR-061).
- [ ] OpenAPI lint passes with the house ruleset (G-AR-031).
- [ ] Contract tests run against the implementation and pass (G-AR-032).
- [ ] Every error response uses the Problem Details format (AR-063).
- [ ] Every list endpoint paginates with a stated ordering (AR-064).
- [ ] Every mutating endpoint states its idempotency story (AR-066).
- [ ] Every operation declares its security requirement (AR-068).
- [ ] Names follow the house profile with no per-endpoint exceptions (AR-067, AR-069).

# api-documentation

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 ; Redocly CLI lint and bundle in the docs pipeline (tooling survey) — https://apidog.com/blog/open-source-cli-tools-api-design/
- **Depends on:** api-architecture, api-versioning
- **Feeds into:** api-versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** producing or repairing an API's reference documentation; setting up docs generation from the OpenAPI document; auditing published docs against the running API.
- **Do NOT use when:** the contract itself is still being designed (api-architecture) or does not exist — documentation cannot be generated from a contract that was never written. Do not use this skill to hand-write a reference that duplicates the spec.

**House profile (shared with api-architecture and api-versioning):** the reference is generated from the OpenAPI document; errors are documented in the shared Problem Details format (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`); property names in examples are `snake_case`; each version's docs publish under its own path segment and stay reachable for the version's whole lifetime.

## Rules

1. **AR-101 — Generated, never hand-maintained.** The reference documentation is generated from the OpenAPI document. Paths, schemas, and status codes are never edited by hand in a parallel document.
2. **AR-102 — The spec is the boundary.** If it is not in the OpenAPI document, it is not documented; if it is in the document, it renders in the reference. Side wikis are never the source of truth.
3. **AR-103 — Errors are documented for every endpoint.** Every operation documents its error responses in the shared Problem Details format. A "TODO: document errors" note shipped as final is a blocking defect.
4. **AR-104 — Examples are real and executed.** Examples are real requests with realistic, non-sensitive data, and every example payload is verified by executing it against a running instance — fields, types, and required values accepted by the real API, not checked by eye.
5. **AR-105 — Authentication is a complete flow.** Auth is documented as a walkthrough: obtain the credential, send it, its expiry and refresh behavior, and the failure response. "Use your API key" is not documentation.
6. **AR-106 — Humans write only the layer generation cannot.** Human-written docs are limited to the authentication walkthrough, one runnable example per endpoint group, the error catalog, and the changelog. Everything else is generated.
7. **AR-107 — Docs version with the API.** Documentation publishes with the API version it describes, under that version's path; older versions' docs stay reachable for the whole deprecation window defined by api-versioning.
8. **AR-108 — Changelog in the same change.** Each release updates the docs changelog in the same change as the contract change. A contract change without its changelog entry is incomplete.
9. **AR-109 — No sensitive data in examples.** Example payloads never contain real credentials, tokens, personal data, or production identifiers — realistic shape, synthetic values.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-051 — "TODO: document errors" shipped as final.** Banned: publishing documentation with error sections left as TODOs or omitted. Defeats: DET-CODE-011. Bad: the reference lists 24 endpoints; 19 have no error responses documented, and the other five say "TODO: document errors". The first integrator discovers the error contract in production. Instead: every operation documents its Problem Details error responses before the docs publish (AR-103). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-052 — The parallel hand-written wiki.** Banned: a hand-maintained wiki or doc page that restates paths, fields, or status codes from the spec. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Bad: the wiki says `POST /orders` returns 200 with a `total` field; the spec and the service say 201 with `total_price`. Integrators trust whichever they found first. Instead: generate the reference from the OpenAPI document and delete the restated pages, keeping only the human layer (AR-101, AR-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-053 — The example the API rejects.** Banned: an example payload the real API would refuse — wrong field names, wrong types, missing required values. Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Bad: the quickstart example posts `{"amount": "10.00"}` as a string and omits the required `currency`; copy-pasting it returns 422, and the docs' credibility goes with it. Instead: execute every example against a running instance in CI and fix the example or the API until it passes (AR-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-054 — Documented endpoints that do not exist.** Banned: reference entries for endpoints the service does not route. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: the docs describe `GET /reports/monthly`, generated from a spec draft; the endpoint was never built and returns 404. Instead: the docs are generated from the shipped spec and the example-execution gate proves every documented path responds (AR-102, AR-104). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-051 — Example execution.** Verifies: AR-104, AR-109. Check: automated — CI executes every documented example request (at minimum three per endpoint group, all of them where the suite is small) against a staging instance and asserts the documented status code and response shape. Pass: every executed example matches its documentation. Fail: block docs publication. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-052 — Documentation lint.** Verifies: AR-102, AR-103, AR-105. Check: automated — Spectral/Redocly rules over the OpenAPI document require a description and at least one example on every operation, a Problem Details error response on every operation, and a declared security scheme; the string "TODO" anywhere in the document fails the build. Pass: zero lint errors. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-053 — Docs-to-routes diff.** Verifies: AR-101, AR-102. Check: automated — a script compares the paths in the published OpenAPI document against the running service's route table. Pass: zero documented-but-unrouted paths and zero routed-but-undocumented public paths. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Screenshot documentation.** Request and response examples pasted as images — unsearchable, uncopyable, and stale the moment the API moves. Catch it: if an example cannot be pasted into a terminal, it is not an example (AR-104).
- **The marketing reference.** A reference page written as sales copy, with adjectives where the parameter tables should be. Catch it: a reader should be able to build a client from the page alone; if they still have questions a spec field would answer, the page is a brochure.
- **Changelog as commit dump.** The docs changelog generated raw from commit messages, full of "fix stuff" and merge noise. Catch it: changelog entries are written for consumers — what changed, whether it breaks, what to do (AR-108).
- **One-version docs.** Publishing new docs over the old URL while the old API version is still inside its deprecation window. Catch it: if a v1 consumer can no longer reach v1 docs, AR-107 was broken to save a deploy step.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Replacing "TODO: document errors" with the error catalog](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-103.
- [Example 2 — An executed example replacing one the API rejects](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-104.
- [Example 3 — Retiring a hand-written wiki for a generated reference](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-101, AR-106.

## Recall anchors

- Generated from the spec — never hand-maintained in parallel.
- Not in the OpenAPI document? Not documented.
- Every example is executed, not eyeballed.
- Errors are documented for every endpoint, in Problem Details.
- Docs version with the API; old versions stay reachable.

## Checklist

- [ ] The reference is generated from the current OpenAPI document (AR-101).
- [ ] Every operation documents its error responses; no TODOs remain (G-AR-052).
- [ ] Every documented example executes successfully against a running instance (G-AR-051).
- [ ] Authentication is documented as a complete flow, including failure (AR-105).
- [ ] The docs-to-routes diff shows zero mismatches (G-AR-053).
- [ ] The changelog entry landed in the same change as the contract (AR-108).
- [ ] Examples contain synthetic values only — no real credentials or personal data (AR-109).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/api-paradigms/SKILL.md -->

# api-paradigms

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** GraphQL Specification, October 2021 edition — https://spec.graphql.org/October2021/ ; OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 ; AsyncAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.1.0
- **Depends on:** api-architecture, system-design
- **Feeds into:** event-driven, api-documentation

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** choosing the interface paradigm for a new surface (REST, GraphQL, gRPC, event-based, end-to-end-typed RPC), or reviewing whether an existing surface is on the wrong paradigm.
- **Do NOT use when:** the paradigm is already settled and the work is designing within it (api-architecture for REST), or the question is how events themselves are specified once an event-based interface is chosen (event-driven).

## Rules

1. **AR-121 — The choice is an ADR naming the interaction shape.** Every paradigm adoption is recorded in an ADR that names the interaction shape driving it: resource CRUD, client-shaped reads, streaming, or fan-out facts. A paradigm with no stated shape has no justification.
2. **AR-122 — REST is the default.** REST over HTTP+JSON is the default for resource CRUD and for all public APIs. Any other paradigm carries the burden of proof in its ADR.
3. **AR-123 — GraphQL must earn its place.** GraphQL is adopted only when multiple client types need divergent, client-shaped reads over a richly connected graph — and the ADR names those clients and the reads.
4. **AR-124 — GraphQL ships with cost controls.** A GraphQL API ships with query depth and complexity limits and a field deprecation policy (`@deprecated` in the schema). An unbounded public GraphQL endpoint is a defect.
5. **AR-125 — gRPC stays internal by default.** gRPC fits internal service-to-service calls needing strict contracts and streaming performance. Exposing gRPC to public consumers requires an explicit ADR overruling this default.
6. **AR-126 — Events are for facts with independent consumers.** An event-based interface is chosen when multiple consumers react independently to facts. If one producer secretly depends on one specific consumer executing, it is a command, not an event — model it as one.
7. **AR-127 — Typed RPC stays inside one codebase.** tRPC-style end-to-end-typed RPC is acceptable only inside a single TypeScript codebase with no external consumers. The moment an outside client appears, a contract-first paradigm replaces it.
8. **AR-128 — No paradigm hides a modeling problem.** If the resources cannot be named, no paradigm fixes it. Unnameable resources send the work back to domain modeling, not to a more flexible query language.
9. **AR-129 — Every paradigm has its contract artifact.** Each paradigm in use keeps its contract in the repo: OpenAPI for REST, the SDL for GraphQL, `.proto` for gRPC, AsyncAPI for events. No contract artifact, no interface.
10. **AR-130 — Public surfaces get the boring paradigm.** Public consumers get the most boring paradigm that fits (REST first). Internal novelty never leaks into the public surface.
11. **AR-131 — Mixed paradigms are justified per surface.** Mixing paradigms is allowed; each surface's choice is justified by its own interaction shape in its own ADR. One paradigm's justification never covers another surface by association.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-061 — The unbounded public GraphQL endpoint.** Banned: exposing GraphQL publicly with no query depth or complexity limits. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: the public schema accepts arbitrarily nested queries; one recursive query from a curious client pins the resolvers and takes the API down for everyone. Instead: ship depth and complexity limits, and persisted queries where clients are known, before the endpoint is public (AR-124). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-062 — Paradigm by fashion.** Banned: adopting a paradigm with no ADR and no named interaction shape. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: the new public API is GraphQL "because the frontend lead prefers it"; the API is plain CRUD for one web client, and the team now owns schema governance it never needed. Instead: write the ADR naming the interaction shape, or take the REST default (AR-121, AR-122). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-063 — The contractless interface.** Banned: an interface in production with no contract artifact in the repo. Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Bad: a gRPC service ships with the `.proto` file living only in one developer's generated code; consumers reverse-engineer the wire format and break on every regeneration. Instead: commit the contract artifact — OpenAPI, SDL, `.proto`, or AsyncAPI — as the interface's source of truth (AR-129). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-064 — Flexibility as a modeling shortcut.** Banned: choosing GraphQL or generic RPC to avoid naming the domain's resources. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: the team cannot agree on what an "order" is, so the API becomes a generic query surface over the database tables; the disagreement is now encoded in every client's queries instead of resolved in the model. Instead: return to domain modeling until the resources can be named, then pick the paradigm (AR-128). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-061 — Contract artifact validation.** Verifies: AR-129. Check: automated — CI validates whichever artifacts exist: OpenAPI lint for REST, GraphQL SDL validation against the spec's type-system rules, `protoc` compilation for gRPC, AsyncAPI validation for events. Pass: every artifact validates. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-062 — GraphQL limits check.** Verifies: AR-124. Check: automated — if a GraphQL schema exists, a script confirms the server configuration sets a maximum query depth and a complexity limit, and the schema's deprecations use `@deprecated`. Pass: both limits configured. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-063 — ADR-to-traffic review.** Verifies: AR-121, AR-123, AR-131. Check: manual — for each paradigm in use, read its ADR and compare the stated interaction shape with the API's actual dominant traffic (logs or analytics). Pass: every paradigm's stated shape matches its real traffic. Fail: warn and open a re-evaluation ADR. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Paradigm tourism.** Each new service picks a different paradigm because each author wanted to try one. Catch it: list the surfaces and their paradigms; if the count of paradigms approaches the count of services, AR-131's per-surface justification has become a rubber stamp.
- **REST in name only.** A "REST API" that is verb-named POST endpoints over HTTP — RPC wearing REST's clothes, gaining none of its properties. Catch it: if removing the HTTP method names changes nothing about how clients call it, send it to api-architecture for remodeling.
- **The internal leak.** An internal convenience (gRPC streaming, typed RPC) exposed publicly because "it already works." Catch it: check AR-130 — public consumers inherit your internal constraints and cannot be migrated when you change your mind.
- **Events as hidden commands.** A producer that blocks, retries, or alarms until one specific consumer processes its "event." Catch it: if the producer cares which consumer acts, it issued a command; model the dependency honestly (AR-126).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — GraphQL proposed for plain CRUD, REST chosen instead](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-122, AR-123.
- [Example 2 — Cost controls added to a public GraphQL API](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-124.
- [Example 3 — Splitting a leaked internal paradigm from the public surface](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-125, AR-130.

## Recall anchors

- Name the interaction shape, or take the REST default.
- GraphQL earns its place — and ships with cost controls.
- gRPC internal, events for facts, typed RPC inside one codebase.
- No contract artifact, no interface.
- Public consumers get the boring paradigm.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every paradigm in use has an ADR naming its interaction shape (AR-121).
- [ ] Public surfaces use REST unless an ADR proves another paradigm (AR-122, AR-130).
- [ ] GraphQL, where used, has depth/complexity limits and a deprecation policy (G-AR-062).
- [ ] Every interface has its contract artifact in the repo, validating in CI (G-AR-061).
- [ ] Event-based surfaces carry facts for independent consumers, not hidden commands (AR-126).
- [ ] Typed RPC, where used, has no external consumers (AR-127).
- [ ] Each mixed-paradigm surface is justified by its own ADR (AR-131).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/api-versioning/SKILL.md -->

# api-versioning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — https://semver.org/ ; Google, "Compatibility" (breaking vs non-breaking change lists) — https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/compatibility/ ; Breaking-change gate design — https://www.api-contract-testing.com/api-contract-fundamentals-tool-selection/breaking-change-detection/
- **Depends on:** api-architecture
- **Feeds into:** api-documentation

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an API change must be classified as breaking or safe; a major version is being introduced; a version is being deprecated or removed; a consumer asks what a version number promises.
- **Do NOT use when:** the API does not exist yet (api-architecture designs v1), or the version in question is a library/package version with no API consumers — though the same semver rules are a sound default there too.

**House profile (shared with api-architecture and api-documentation):** the major version sits in the path segment (`/v1/…`) and nowhere else; deprecations are signaled with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers plus a changelog entry; within a major version only backward-compatible changes ship.

## Rules

1. **AR-081 — Breaking is an enumerated list, not a feeling.** Removing or renaming a field, method, or enum value; changing a field's type; changing a resource name format; or changing visible behavior is breaking. Adding interfaces, methods, fields, or enum values is safe. The classification follows the list, never intuition.
2. **AR-082 — Unlisted means breaking.** A change the list does not cover is treated as breaking until a recorded ruling says otherwise. The benefit of the doubt goes to consumers.
3. **AR-083 — Additive only within a major version.** Inside a major version, only backward-compatible changes ship: additive fields, new endpoints, new enum values where consumers tolerate unknowns. Anything else waits for the next major.
4. **AR-084 — Breaking under the same major is release-blocking.** A breaking change that reaches a release under the existing major version is a release-blocking defect, however small it looks.
5. **AR-085 — Every version has a changelog.** Each version carries a changelog entry connecting the version to its changes. "Latest" is never the only nameable version of the API.
6. **AR-086 — Deprecation needs three artifacts first.** Before a deprecation window starts, all three exist: the sunset date, the migration path, and the consumer notification (docs plus `Deprecation`/`Sunset` headers). A window announced without them has not started.
7. **AR-087 — Removal waits for the date and the check.** The old version is removed only after the announced sunset date has passed and a consumer check shows no remaining traffic (or named consumers who accepted the cutoff in writing).
8. **AR-088 — Consumers must tolerate unknowns.** The contract states that consumers ignore unknown fields and enum values. This obligation is what makes additive changes safe, and it is written down, not assumed.
9. **AR-089 — One placement, never mixed.** The version identifier lives in the path segment for public HTTP APIs, per the house profile. Header-based and query-parameter versioning never appear in the same API.
10. **AR-090 — Old and new run side by side.** During a deprecation window both major versions are deployed and supported; a flag-day cutover, where the old version dies the moment the new one ships, is forbidden for public APIs.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-041 — The quiet breaking change.** Banned: shipping a breaking change under the same major version. Defeats: DET-INF-026. Bad: `GET /v1/orders` renames `total_price` to `grand_total` in a "minor" release; every v1 client breaks on deploy day and the version number's promise turns out to be worthless. Instead: ship the rename in `/v2/`, run both side by side, and deprecate v1 with the full artifact set (AR-084, AR-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-042 — The random version bump.** Banned: version numbers bumped without a change classification behind them. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: the API jumps from 1.0 to 3.0 for a typo fix in a description, then stays at 3.0 through a field removal; consumers can infer nothing from any number. Instead: classify the change against the enumerated list first (AR-081); the bump follows the classification — patch for safe fixes, major for breaking changes. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-043 — The silent removal.** Banned: removing a deprecated version with no sunset date, no migration path, or no consumer notification. Defeats: DET-INF-028. Bad: `/v1/` starts returning 404 one Monday morning; the changelog says nothing, the headers said nothing, and two partners learn about it from their own error alerts. Instead: publish the sunset date, the migration path, and the notification first; remove only after the date and the consumer check (AR-086, AR-087). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-044 — Mixed version placement.** Banned: version identifiers in more than one location in the same API. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: most endpoints are `/v1/…`, newer ones take `?version=2`, and one partner API versions by header; nobody can state the API's versioning scheme in one sentence. Instead: path segment only, per the house profile, for every endpoint (AR-089). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-041 — Breaking-change diff.** Verifies: AR-081, AR-083, AR-084. Check: automated — CI runs `oasdiff breaking <last-shipped-spec> <new-spec>`; any breaking finding fails the build unless the change also bumps the major version and lands with an ADR recording the approved break. The tool is pinned in the repo; if it cannot run in the sandbox, the fallback is a manual field-by-field diff against the compatibility list, recorded in progress.md. Pass: no unapproved breaking findings. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-042 — Deprecation artifact check.** Verifies: AR-086, AR-087. Check: automated — for any version marked deprecated, a script confirms the changelog contains its sunset date and migration link, and a probe of the running service confirms responses carry `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers. Pass: all three artifacts present. Fail: block the deprecation announcement. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-043 — Runtime version matches the tag.** Verifies: AR-085, AR-089. Check: automated — query the deployed service's metadata/health endpoint and compare its reported API version with the release tag and the path segments it serves. Pass: exact match. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Semver as marketing.** Major bumps timed to launches ("Version 5 is here!") rather than to compatibility. Catch it: ask what broke; if nothing did, the number is a press release, not a version (AR-081).
- **The permanent beta.** An API kept at `v0` or "beta" for years so breaking changes need no window. Catch it: a public API with real consumers is a versioned API, whatever its label says; apply AR-086 when it changes.
- **Deprecation by blog post.** The sunset is announced in a blog post or a sales email but never in the changelog or the response headers consumers actually see. Catch it: run G-AR-042; if the artifacts are not where consumers look, the window has not started.
- **Tolerance assumed, not contracted.** Additive changes shipped as "safe" while nothing obliges consumers to ignore unknown fields — and one strict-parser client breaks on every new field. Catch it: if AR-088's sentence is not in the contract, the change is not yet safe.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A field rename shipped as v2, not as a quiet v1 break](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-084.
- [Example 2 — A complete deprecation package for retiring v1](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-086, AR-087.
- [Example 3 — Unifying mixed version placement on the path segment](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-089.

## Recall anchors

- Breaking is a list, not a feeling; unlisted means breaking.
- Additive only, inside a major version.
- Deprecation = sunset date + migration path + notification, before the window.
- Removal waits for the date and the consumer check.
- Path segment, one placement, never mixed.

## Checklist

- [ ] The change is classified against the enumerated compatibility list (AR-081).
- [ ] The breaking-change diff passes, or the break is approved with a major bump and an ADR (G-AR-041).
- [ ] The version has a changelog entry connecting it to its changes (AR-085).
- [ ] The contract states consumers must ignore unknown fields and enum values (AR-088).
- [ ] Any deprecation has its sunset date, migration path, and notification in place (G-AR-042).
- [ ] Old and new majors run side by side for the whole window (AR-090).
- [ ] The deployed version matches the release tag (G-AR-043).
