# architecture-patterns

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microservices.io pattern language (Saga, CQRS, event sourcing, transactional outbox, database per service) — https://microservices.io/ ; Fowler, "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?" — https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html
- **Depends on:** system-design, adr-writing
- **Feeds into:** api-architecture, event-driven, domain-driven-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a distributed-systems or structural pattern (Saga, CQRS, event sourcing, transactional outbox, database per service, and their kin) is proposed for a project, or an existing design claims a pattern that needs auditing.
- **Do NOT use when:** the choice is a routine local design decision with no cross-component consequences — record it in code and move on. Do not use this skill to pick libraries or frameworks; that is stack-selection.

## Rules

1. **AR-161 — Named catalog only.** Patterns are selected from a named catalog (the microservices.io pattern language, Fowler's pattern writings) and cited by their catalog name; invented pattern names are not adopted.
2. **AR-162 — Problem before pattern.** No pattern is adopted without a stated problem it solves in this project. "For scale" without a load figure is not a problem statement.
3. **AR-163 — Four-part adoption record.** Before adoption, the ADR fills in all four parts from the catalog entry: the problem, the forces, the solution shape, and the consequences for this project.
4. **AR-164 — The hard part is the deliverable.** Adopting Saga requires named compensating transactions; CQRS requires the read-model synchronization design; event sourcing requires the event store and replay procedure. The label without the mechanism is not an adoption.
5. **AR-165 — No decorative infrastructure.** A queue or broker in the diagram while all interactions remain synchronous request/response is decoration and fails review.
6. **AR-166 — Consequences accepted in writing.** Every adoption records the consequences it accepts — eventual-consistency window, operational components added, new failure modes — in the ADR.
7. **AR-167 — Simplest variant first.** Prefer choreography before orchestration for short sagas and a single read model before multiple. The ADR records what measured change would trigger the complex variant.
8. **AR-168 — One pattern at a time.** Patterns are adopted incrementally, each behind its own ADR; a big-bang re-architecture introducing several at once is not approved.
9. **AR-169 — Default composition.** The default for a typical web application is a modular monolith with feature modules. A distributed composition must cite the requirement that forces it.
10. **AR-170 — Exit cost noted.** Every adoption records what removing or replacing the pattern would cost, so the decision can be revisited honestly.
11. **AR-171 — The mechanism must exist in code.** A pattern claimed in ARCHITECTURE.md must have its mechanism findable in the codebase — the outbox table, the compensating handlers, the read model. A claim without a mechanism is marked false.
12. **AR-172 — Module boundaries are enforced.** Modules and contexts expose public interfaces; cross-module imports of internals are forbidden and checked mechanically.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-081 — Pattern adopted "for scale".** Banned: adopting a distributed pattern with no stated problem and no load figure behind it. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: a three-user internal tool is split into six services with a saga "because it will need to scale," and every deploy now takes an afternoon. Instead: state the problem the pattern solves here, with the number that proves it, or stay with the modular monolith. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-082 — Decorative broker.** Banned: installing a queue or broker while every interaction stays synchronous request/response. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: RabbitMQ runs in production, the architecture page says "event-driven," and the only producer sends messages that a consumer immediately answers while the HTTP request blocks waiting. Instead: either adopt a named event pattern with its contract and consumers, or remove the broker and the claim. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-083 — Saga without compensations.** Banned: claiming the Saga pattern with no compensating transaction defined for each step. Defeats: DET-CODE-006. Bad: the checkout saga reserves stock, charges the card, then fails at shipping — and nothing releases the stock or refunds the charge, because the compensations were "phase two." Instead: name and implement the compensation for every step before the saga ships; a step with no compensation is a step the saga may not take. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-084 — Reach-around imports.** Banned: one module importing another module's internal files, bypassing its public interface. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: the billing module imports `orders/internal/pricing.ts` directly, so the orders team cannot refactor pricing without breaking billing. Instead: consume the module's published interface, or propose the missing capability as part of that interface. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-081 — Pattern audit.** Verifies: AR-164, AR-171. Check: manual — for each pattern claimed in ARCHITECTURE.md, find its mechanism in code (outbox table, compensating handlers, read model) or mark the claim false. Pass: every claimed pattern has a mechanism. Fail: block release until the mechanism exists or the claim is removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-082 — Dependency-rule check.** Verifies: AR-172. Check: automated — CI lint rules forbid cross-module imports except through public interfaces. Pass: lint exits 0. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-083 — Adoption record completeness.** Verifies: AR-162, AR-163, AR-166, AR-170. Check: manual — each adopted pattern's ADR contains the problem with its evidence, the forces, the accepted consequences, and the exit cost. Pass: all four parts present for every adopted pattern. Fail: block adoption. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-084 — Simplicity review.** Verifies: AR-167, AR-169. Check: manual — for each adoption of Saga, CQRS, or event sourcing, confirm the ADR states why the simpler default was insufficient and what trigger would justify the complex variant. Pass: both statements present. Fail: warn; the adoption proceeds only with the trigger recorded. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Pattern bingo.** CQRS, event sourcing, and a saga all appear in a CRUD application whose hardest query is a filtered list. Catch it: count the patterns; each one should be able to name the problem that forced it, and most CRUD apps force none.
- **Resume-driven architecture.** Technologies chosen because the builder wants to learn them, with the project paying the tuition. Catch it: the ADR's forces section talks about the team's growth, not the project's constraints.
- **The distributed monolith.** Services split by technical layer, deployed together, chatting synchronously on every request — distribution's costs with none of its benefits. Catch it: if all services must deploy in lockstep to work, it is a monolith with network calls.
- **Cargo-cult topology.** Copying a hyperscaler's architecture at three orders of magnitude less load. Catch it: compare the design's load figures with the figures in the case study it imitates.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — "For scale" becomes a forcing-requirement test](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-162, AR-169.
- [Example 2 — The decorative queue, made real or removed](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-165.
- [Example 3 — A saga adoption with its compensations named](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-164.

## Recall anchors

- Problem before pattern, always.
- The hard part is the deliverable, not the label.
- A broker with only synchronous calls is decoration.
- Simplest variant first; record the trigger for the complex one.
- If the mechanism is not in the code, the pattern is not in the system.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every adopted pattern is cited by its catalog name (AR-161).
- [ ] Every adoption's ADR states the problem, with the load figure or evidence behind it (AR-162).
- [ ] Compensations, read-model sync, or replay procedure are named for Saga, CQRS, or event sourcing adoptions (AR-164).
- [ ] Accepted consequences and exit cost are recorded per adoption (AR-166, AR-170).
- [ ] Pattern audit passed: every claimed pattern's mechanism found in code (G-AR-081).
- [ ] Dependency-rule lint exits 0 (G-AR-082).
- [ ] The simplest variant is in place, with the complex variant's trigger recorded (AR-167).

# c4-diagrams

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** C4 model, notation and diagram guidance — https://c4model.com/
- **Depends on:** system-design
- **Feeds into:** adr-writing, api-architecture

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** architecture needs to be communicated or reviewed — a new system context or container view, a container whose internals are non-obvious, or a diagram that has drifted from the system it describes.
- **Do NOT use when:** there is no architecture decision to communicate yet (system-design comes first), or the audience needs the API surface rather than the structure (api-documentation). Do not produce a Level 3 component diagram for a container whose internals are a standard framework layout.

## Rules

1. **AR-021 — Produce only the levels the audience needs.** Level 1 (system context) and Level 2 (containers) are the default set. Level 3 (components) is drawn only where a container's internal structure is non-obvious. Level 4 (code) is generated by tools or omitted.
2. **AR-022 — Every element is typed.** Each element is declared as a person, software system, container, or component, and each container states its technology. An untyped box is incomplete.
3. **AR-023 — Every relationship is labeled.** Each line carries the interaction and its protocol or format ("Places orders via HTTPS/JSON"). An unlabeled line fails review.
4. **AR-024 — Stores and queues are containers.** Data stores and queues appear as first-class containers in Level 2, never as annotations, footnotes, or icons attached to another box.
5. **AR-025 — Diagrams live as code.** Diagram sources (Structurizr DSL, PlantUML, or Mermaid) are kept in the repo and reviewed like code, so they diff in pull requests. A pasted image with no source in the repo is not a diagram of record.
6. **AR-026 — One view per diagram, with a legend.** Each diagram serves one audience and one level, and carries a legend for its element types. Two audiences are never merged into one picture.
7. **AR-027 — No generic labels.** Element names name the actual thing ("Orders API", "PostgreSQL — orders store"). "Frontend / Backend / Database" as the whole model is an automatic fail.
8. **AR-028 — External systems show direction and mode.** Every external system is drawn with the direction of each integration and whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.
9. **AR-029 — Diagrams change with the architecture.** A diagram is updated in the same change that alters the architecture it depicts, and the ADR for that change links the updated diagram. A diagram known to be stale is a defect, not a backlog item.
10. **AR-030 — Context shows people and systems only.** The Level 1 diagram shows the system as one box, its users, and the external systems it touches — no internal containers leak into the context view.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-011 — The all-in-one mega-diagram.** Banned: one picture mixing context, containers, components, and code-level classes for every audience at once. Defeats: DET-CODE-016. Bad: a single wall-chart diagram with 60 boxes from "User" down to individual classes; every reader gives up and the diagram is never updated again. Instead: separate Level 1, 2, and (where earned) 3 diagrams, one view each, each with a legend (AR-021, AR-026). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-012 — Generic-label model.** Banned: a diagram whose elements are named only "Frontend", "Backend", "Database". Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: the container diagram for a system that actually runs a web app, a worker, two stores, and a queue is three generic boxes. Instead: name each element for the real unit it represents, with its technology (AR-027). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-013 — The stale diagram.** Banned: leaving a diagram unchanged in a change that alters the architecture it depicts. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the payments container is replaced by a third-party checkout, the code ships, and the container diagram still shows the old in-house payments service for two releases. Instead: update the diagram source in the same pull request, and link it from the ADR (AR-029). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-014 — Image-only diagram.** Banned: a diagram that exists only as an exported PNG or a slide screenshot, with no source in the repo. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: the context diagram is a screenshot in a slide deck; nobody can diff it, review it, or update it without redrawing from scratch. Instead: commit the Structurizr/PlantUML/Mermaid source and let the image be a build artifact (AR-025). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-011 — Diagram render check.** Verifies: AR-025. Check: automated — CI renders every diagram source with the pinned renderer (e.g., the project's locked Mermaid CLI or PlantUML jar) and fails on a non-zero exit; if the sandbox cannot run the renderer, the fallback is a manual render in the project's documented tool, recorded in progress.md. Pass: every source renders. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-012 — Label lint.** Verifies: AR-023, AR-027. Check: automated — grep the diagram sources for elements named exactly "Frontend", "Backend", or "Database" and for relationship lines with empty labels. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-013 — Element-to-deployment diff.** Verifies: AR-024, AR-028, AR-029. Check: manual — each release, diff the container diagram element by element against the deployment config: every deployable, store, and queue appears, and every external system shows direction and sync/async mode. Pass: zero differences. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Legend-free notation.** Boxes, cylinders, and dashed lines used with no legend, so each reader invents a meaning. Catch it: if you cannot point at the legend while explaining a line style, AR-026 was skipped.
- **The database as decoration.** A cylinder icon dangling off the application box, unnamed and untyped. Catch it: every store should be answerable to "which container, which technology, who writes to it" (AR-024).
- **Level inflation.** A Level 3 component diagram for a container that is a standard CRUD module, drawn to make the work look substantial. Catch it: ask what decision the diagram informs; if none, delete the level (AR-021).
- **Arrow soup.** So many unlabeled crossing lines that the flows cannot be followed. Catch it: pick any line and state its interaction and protocol aloud; if you cannot, the labels are missing, not implied (AR-023).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Splitting a mega-diagram into C4 levels](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-021, AR-026.
- [Example 2 — Naming and typing a generic container diagram](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-024, AR-027.
- [Example 3 — Updating a diagram in the same change as the architecture](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-029.

## Recall anchors

- Levels 1 and 2 by default; Level 3 only where it earns its keep.
- Typed elements, labeled lines, legend on every view.
- Stores and queues are containers, not decorations.
- Diagrams are code in the repo — they diff or they rot.
- Architecture changed? The diagram changes in the same pull request.

## Checklist

- [ ] Only the needed C4 levels exist, one view per diagram, each with a legend (AR-021, AR-026).
- [ ] Every element is typed and named for the real unit, with its technology (AR-022, AR-027).
- [ ] Every relationship line states the interaction and protocol (AR-023).
- [ ] Data stores and queues are first-class containers (AR-024).
- [ ] Diagram sources render cleanly in CI, or the manual fallback is recorded (G-AR-011).
- [ ] The release diff against the deployment config shows zero differences (G-AR-013).
- [ ] External systems show direction and sync/async mode (AR-028).

# data-architecture

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** MongoDB Manual, data modeling (embed vs reference by access pattern) — http://mongodocs.github.io/core/data-modeling-introduction.html ; Database-per-service and data ownership patterns — https://microservices.io/
- **Depends on:** system-design, requirements-writing
- **Feeds into:** schema-design, tenant-isolation, migrations

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project needs its data model designed or changed: choosing structures for a relational or document store, deciding embed vs reference, placing data ownership across services, or reviewing a schema before migrations are written.
- **Do NOT use when:** the model already exists and the task is writing or reviewing the migrations themselves — go to migrations and schema-design instead. Do not use this skill to tune individual queries in a settled schema; that is query-performance.

## Rules

1. **AR-141 — Access patterns first.** List the reads and writes each main screen and job performs before choosing any structure; a schema designed from nouns alone is sent back.
2. **AR-142 — Every entity maps.** Every entity in the requirements maps to a schema object, and every relationship is declared as a foreign key, a reference, or an explicit documented decision to denormalize with its consistency cost stated.
3. **AR-143 — Typed facts, typed columns.** Dates, money, enums, and statuses use typed columns, never strings. Money is integer minor units or a decimal type, never float.
4. **AR-144 — One writable home per fact.** The same fact has exactly one writable home; copies are read models with a named synchronization mechanism and a stated staleness bound.
5. **AR-145 — Index from named queries.** Every query used by a main screen is backed by an index, proven with the database's explain-plan tool, not assumed.
6. **AR-146 — Embed vs reference is decided per relationship.** Embed what is read together and owned together; reference what is shared or independently growing. The decision is recorded for each relationship, not defaulted for the whole store.
7. **AR-147 — One owner per store.** Cross-service data is owned by one service; other services hold references or replicated read models, never shared write access to another service's tables.
8. **AR-148 — Migrations only.** Schema evolution happens only through versioned migrations; manual edits to a live schema are forbidden.
9. **AR-149 — Tenant key from the first migration.** In any multitenant design, tenant-owned tables carry the tenant key from the first migration; retrofitting it later is treated as a redesign, not a migration.
10. **AR-150 — Constraints live in the database.** Integrity invariants (non-null, uniqueness, referential integrity, value ranges) are enforced by database constraints, not by application code alone.
11. **AR-151 — Denormalization is a documented decision.** Every denormalized field names its source of truth and the path that keeps it current; an undocumented copy is a defect.
12. **AR-152 — Every migration has a way back.** Each migration is reversible, or ships with a documented forward-fix procedure; an irreversible migration with neither is not merged.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-071 — Stringly-typed facts.** Banned: storing dates, money, enums, or statuses as free-text strings. Defeats: DET-CODE-025. Bad: `orders.status` is a VARCHAR holding 'paid', 'Paid', and 'PAID' from different code paths, and the revenue report silently misses two of the three. Instead: an enum or lookup type with a check constraint, and money as integer minor units. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-072 — Two writable homes for one fact.** Banned: the same fact stored in two places, both writable, updated by different code. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Bad: the customer's email lives in `users` and `billing_customers`; support updates one, invoices go to the other. Instead: one owning table; the second consumer gets a read model with a named sync mechanism. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-073 — Shared write access across services.** Banned: one service writing directly into another service's tables. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: the reporting service runs `UPDATE orders SET ...` during its nightly job, bypassing every invariant the orders service enforces. Instead: call the owning service's API, consume its events, or build a replicated read model. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-074 — Unbounded, unindexed main-screen query.** Banned: a query behind a main screen with no index support and no row limit. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: the admin order list runs `SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC` over two million rows on every page load. Instead: an index on the sort/filter columns, cursor pagination, and explain-plan evidence attached to the change. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-071 — Migration build check.** Verifies: AR-142, AR-148. Check: automated — CI applies all migrations to an empty database and diffs the resulting schema against the declared model. Pass: migrations apply cleanly and the diff is empty. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-072 — Explain-plan evidence.** Verifies: AR-145. Check: automated — the test harness runs EXPLAIN for each named main-screen query against a production-shaped dataset. Pass: every query uses its intended index; no sequential scan over a large table. Fail: block the schema change until the index exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-073 — Duplicate-fact audit.** Verifies: AR-144, AR-151. Check: manual — pick three core facts and trace each to its single writable home, naming the sync mechanism for every copy found. Pass: 3 of 3 facts have exactly one writable home. Fail: block release until the duplicate is demoted to a read model. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-074 — Tenant-key schema check (citation).** Verifies: AR-149. Check: automated — this requirement is verified by the canonical tenant-key schema check, G-AR-092 in multitenancy-saas (every tenant-owned table carries a non-null tenant key with a leading index); run that gate for the full procedure and pass criteria. Single-tenant projects record the exemption in ARCHITECTURE.md. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Noun-per-table modeling.** One generic table per requirement noun, with JSON blob columns absorbing every attribute nobody modeled. Catch it: ask for the access-pattern list; if it does not exist, the tables came from nouns.
- **Index astrology.** Indexes added "just in case," with no named query behind them, bloating writes while the slow query still scans. Catch it: every index should name the query it serves; an index that cannot is removed.
- **The temporary shared database.** Services coupled through one schema "until we split later," with the split never scheduled. Catch it: count the services writing to one schema; more than one means the shortcut became the architecture.
- **Premature sharding.** Data split across nodes or databases before any measured bottleneck exists. Catch it: ask for the load figure that forced the split; "future scale" without a number is the tell.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Typing a status and a price](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-143.
- [Example 2 — One writable home for the customer email](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-144.
- [Example 3 — Embed vs reference, decided per relationship](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-146.

## Recall anchors

- Access patterns first, nouns last.
- Every fact has one writable home.
- Typed facts get typed columns; money is never float.
- Indexes are proven with explain plans, not assumed.
- Evolution happens only through migrations.

## Checklist

- [ ] The access-pattern list exists and every main screen and job is on it (AR-141).
- [ ] Every requirement entity maps to a schema object; every relationship is declared (AR-142).
- [ ] No stringly-typed dates, money, enums, or statuses; money is integer minor units or decimal (AR-143).
- [ ] Duplicate-fact audit passed: 3 of 3 core facts traced to one writable home (G-AR-073).
- [ ] Explain-plan evidence attached for every named main-screen query (G-AR-072).
- [ ] Tenant-owned tables carry the tenant key from the first migration, or the single-tenant exemption is recorded (AR-149).
- [ ] Every migration is reversible or carries a forward-fix procedure (AR-152).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/domain-driven-design/SKILL.md -->

# domain-driven-design

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Eric Evans, *Domain-Driven Design Reference* (definitions of bounded context, aggregate, ubiquitous language) — https://www.domainlanguage.com/ ; Pattern context for how DDD boundaries interact with data ownership and sagas — https://microservices.io/
- **Depends on:** requirements-writing, system-design
- **Feeds into:** data-architecture, api-architecture, schema-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a domain is complex enough that its language and consistency rules drive the design: finding bounded contexts, drawing aggregates around invariants, building the ubiquitous language, or mapping how contexts integrate.
- **Do NOT use when:** the area is plain CRUD over one table with no invariants worth the name — model it as a simple CRUD module (AR-228) and spend the effort elsewhere. Do not use this skill as a naming ceremony for a design already fixed; the language work comes first or not at all.

## Rules

1. **AR-221 — Language first.** The ubiquitous language is built from domain conversations and the requirements before tactical modeling starts; one term has one meaning inside a context.
2. **AR-222 — Contexts are recorded.** Every bounded context has a name, a one-paragraph responsibility, its context-map relationships, and an owning module or service, recorded in ARCHITECTURE.md. A context that exists only in a slide is not a context.
3. **AR-223 — Boundaries follow language shifts.** Where the same word changes meaning (an "order" in sales is not an "order" in fulfillment), that shift marks a context boundary.
4. **AR-224 — Aggregates follow invariants.** If two objects must be consistent in the same transaction, they belong to one aggregate; if not, they reference each other by identity and accept eventual consistency.
5. **AR-225 — References by identity across aggregates.** Code never reaches through one aggregate's object graph into another's internals; cross-aggregate references are by ID.
6. **AR-226 — Declared cross-context mechanisms only.** Contexts communicate through the mechanism the context map declares (API, events, anti-corruption layer). Direct reads of another context's tables are forbidden.
7. **AR-227 — The glossary is testable.** Type, field, and endpoint names inside a context use its glossary terms verbatim; a synonym introduced in code is a defect.
8. **AR-228 — Honest CRUD.** An area that is CRUD over one table is modeled and named as a simple CRUD module, not dressed in tactical DDD vocabulary it does not use.
9. **AR-229 — Inferred terms are flagged.** When no domain expert is available, the glossary is derived from the requirements and fact sheet, and every inferred term is marked UNVERIFIED until a domain source confirms it.
10. **AR-230 — Domain events mark real state changes.** Events crossing a context boundary are named from the domain language for state changes that actually happened (see event-driven), not for technical row mutations.
11. **AR-231 — Invariants are enforced in one transaction.** For every named invariant, one aggregate enforces it atomically; an invariant checked in one transaction and applied in another is unenforced.
12. **AR-232 — Anti-corruption layer at hostile boundaries.** Integration with a legacy or external model goes through an anti-corruption layer that translates it into this context's language; foreign terms never leak inward.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-111 — Reading another context's tables.** Banned: one bounded context querying another context's database tables directly. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Bad: the fulfillment module joins the sales schema's `orders` table, absorbing sales' pricing rules into its own queries; when sales remodels, fulfillment breaks without a single shared contract changing. Instead: consume the sales context's published API or events, through an anti-corruption layer if its model is foreign. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-112 — Synonym drift.** Banned: introducing a code name that differs from the glossary term for the same concept. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: the glossary says "customer," the API exposes `/clients`, the schema has `buyer_id`, and every cross-team conversation needs a translation table. Instead: rename the code to the glossary term — `customer` everywhere in this context — and treat the rename as a defect fix, not a refactor. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-113 — Tactical theater.** Banned: wrapping plain CRUD in aggregates, repositories, and domain services that add no invariant or language value. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: a settings page backed by one table ships with a `SettingsAggregate`, a repository interface with one implementation, and a domain service that copies fields — three files where one module sufficed. Instead: model it as an honest CRUD module and reserve tactical patterns for contexts with real invariants. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AR-114 — Invariant split across transactions.** Banned: checking a consistency invariant in one transaction and applying the change in another. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: "never oversell the last seat" is checked by a read, then the booking is written a moment later; two concurrent requests both pass the check and the seat sells twice. Instead: enforce the invariant inside the aggregate's transaction — the seat inventory aggregate decrements and rejects atomically. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-111 — Glossary cross-check.** Verifies: AR-227. Check: manual — sample type and field names from the codebase and API schemas and match each against the context glossaries. Pass: every sampled name is a glossary term used verbatim. Fail: warn; each synonym found is filed as a defect. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-112 — Context dependency check.** Verifies: AR-226. Check: automated — CI module-dependency rules fail the build when one context imports another context's internals or connects to its tables. Pass: the check exits 0. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-113 — Invariant trace.** Verifies: AR-224, AR-231. Check: manual — pick one named invariant and find the aggregate that enforces it, in a single transaction, in code. Pass: the enforcing aggregate and transaction are identified. Fail: block release until the invariant has an owner. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-114 — Context record completeness.** Verifies: AR-222. Check: automated — a script over ARCHITECTURE.md asserts every context section carries a name, responsibility paragraph, context-map relationships, and an owning module. Pass: all four fields present for every context. Fail: block merge of the architecture change. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **One context for everything.** A single "domain model" spans sales and fulfillment, and the colliding meanings of its terms are resolved in hallway conversations. Catch it: find a term the glossary defines twice, differently; that is an unmarked boundary.
- **The slide-deck glossary.** The ubiquitous language lives in a presentation while the code evolves its own dialect. Catch it: the glossary is not in the repo, or its last edit predates the last three schema changes.
- **The aggregate of everything.** One giant aggregate serializes all writes through itself because "everything must be consistent." Catch it: measure contention — if unrelated operations queue behind one aggregate, its boundary followed the diagram, not the invariants.
- **Row-mutation events.** Boundary events named `RowUpdated` or `RecordChanged` expose the storage model instead of the domain. Catch it: read the event names aloud to a domain speaker; if they cannot say what happened in the business, the names are technical, not domain.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — One word, two contexts](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-223.
- [Example 2 — The cross-context table read, replaced](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-226.
- [Example 3 — The oversold seat, fixed at the aggregate](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-224, AR-231.

## Recall anchors

- One term, one meaning, per context.
- A word changing meaning marks a boundary.
- Aggregates follow invariants, not diagrams.
- Contexts talk through the map's declared mechanisms only.
- Plain CRUD is modeled as plain CRUD.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every bounded context is recorded with name, responsibility, relationships, and owner (AR-222).
- [ ] The glossary lives in the repo and inferred terms are marked UNVERIFIED (AR-229).
- [ ] Glossary cross-check passed on sampled code and schema names (G-AR-111).
- [ ] Context dependency check exits 0 in CI (G-AR-112).
- [ ] One named invariant was traced to the aggregate enforcing it in a single transaction (G-AR-113).
- [ ] Cross-context integrations use the context map's declared mechanisms, with an ACL where the model is foreign (AR-226, AR-232).
- [ ] CRUD-only areas are named and modeled as CRUD modules (AR-228).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/event-driven/SKILL.md -->

# event-driven

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Fowler, "What do you mean by 'Event-Driven'?" — https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html ; AsyncAPI Specification 3.1.0 — https://www.asyncapi.com/docs/reference/specification/v3.1.0 ; CloudEvents (CNCF envelope attributes) — http://cloudevents.io/ ; Zalando event guidelines (events as interface, compatibility, no sensitive personal data) — https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/
- **Depends on:** architecture-patterns, api-architecture, adr-writing
- **Feeds into:** queues-jobs, notifications, realtime

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** components communicate through events or messages: introducing a broker or stream, defining an event type, making consumers reliable, or auditing an existing event flow for coupling and correctness.
- **Do NOT use when:** a synchronous call is the honest shape of the interaction (the caller needs the answer to proceed) — use api-architecture and make the call. Do not use this skill to justify a broker for a system with no independent consumers; that is the decorative-infrastructure failure in architecture-patterns.

## Rules

1. **AR-201 — Name the pattern first.** Choose and record which pattern applies — event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing, or CQRS — before building; the four have different consistency and coupling consequences and are not interchangeable.
2. **AR-202 — Events are facts.** Events are named in the past tense (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentFailed`) and state something that already happened; an event is never a command a producer secretly depends on one specific consumer executing.
3. **AR-203 — Every event is a contract.** Each event type has an entry in the AsyncAPI document, a versioned payload schema, a named owner, and a list of known consumers.
4. **AR-204 — CloudEvents envelope.** Every event carries the standard envelope attributes — `specversion`, `id`, `source`, `type` — so events stay routable and deduplicatable across brokers and vendors.
5. **AR-205 — Publication is atomic.** Events are published atomically with the business write (transactional outbox or an event store). Writing to the database and then publishing as a separate step is a defect.
6. **AR-206 — Consumers are idempotent.** A consumer deduplicates on event `id` and `source` and produces the same effect whether an event arrives once or five times.
7. **AR-207 — Ordering scope is stated.** Each stream declares its ordering scope (per aggregate or per key, via partitioning), and consumers tolerate out-of-order delivery within that scope.
8. **AR-208 — Poison messages go to a dead-letter queue.** After bounded retries, a failing message lands in a DLQ with an alert. Infinite retry and silent dropping are both forbidden.
9. **AR-209 — Minimum payload.** Payloads carry only the data the chosen pattern requires. Full entity snapshots under event-carried state transfer require an explicit ADR, and events never carry sensitive personal data beyond need.
10. **AR-210 — A replay procedure exists.** Every stream documents how a consumer rebuilds state or reprocesses from a chosen point, and the procedure is exercised before it is needed in an incident.
11. **AR-211 — Schema evolution is compatibility-checked.** New payload schema versions are checked against the previous version under the compatibility rules (additive changes safe; removals and retypes breaking) before deployment.
12. **AR-212 — Consumers fail independently.** A producer keeps working while any consumer is down, and when the consumer returns, the backlog drains with no duplicate effects applied.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-101 — A command in event's clothing.** Banned: naming or using an event as an imperative command that one named consumer is expected to execute. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: the checkout service publishes `SendWelcomeEmail` and its success metric assumes the email service "event consumer" ran — the producer is coupled to a specific consumer's behavior while pretending to be decoupled. Instead: publish the fact (`UserRegistered`) and let the email service decide, as a known consumer, to send the email. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-102 — Dual-write publication.** Banned: writing to the database and publishing the event as two uncoordinated steps. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: the handler commits the order, then calls the broker; the process crashes between the two and the order exists with no event — downstream systems never learn of it, and nothing detects the gap. Instead: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and let a relay publish from the outbox. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-103 — Swallowed poison messages.** Banned: a consumer catching all exceptions, acknowledging the message, and moving on with no record. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Bad: a malformed event fails parsing, the catch block logs nothing, the message is acked, and 4,000 orders silently never reach fulfillment. Instead: bounded retries, then the dead-letter queue with an alert and the payload preserved for inspection. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-104 — Unversioned payload changed in place.** Banned: changing a published event's payload shape without a new schema version and compatibility check. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: `amount` is renamed to `amount_minor` in the producer on Friday; every consumer built against the old shape fails or, worse, reads a missing field as zero. Instead: add the new field, keep the old one through the deprecation window, and bump the schema version with a compatibility check in CI. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AR-101 — Contract and compatibility check.** Verifies: AR-203, AR-211. Check: automated — the AsyncAPI document validates in CI, and each new payload schema is compatibility-checked against its previous version. Pass: validation exits 0 and no unapproved breaking schema change. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-102 — Replay and duplicate-delivery test.** Verifies: AR-206, AR-210. Check: automated — recorded events are replayed against consumers in CI, with each event delivered twice. Pass: final state equals the single-delivery state; no duplicate effects. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-103 — Consumer-outage test.** Verifies: AR-212. Check: mechanized manual — in staging, disable one consumer, run normal producer traffic, then restore the consumer. Pass: producers are unaffected while it is down, and the backlog drains afterward with no duplicates applied. Fail: block release until the consumer is decoupled. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-104 — Outbox path check.** Verifies: AR-205. Check: automated — search the codebase for direct broker-publish calls outside the outbox relay module. Pass: none found; all publication flows through the outbox. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Event spaghetti.** Events trigger events trigger events, and no inventory exists, so nobody can say what happens when an order is placed. Catch it: pick one business action and trace its full event chain from the AsyncAPI document alone; if the trace needs the code, the inventory failed.
- **Request/reply in disguise.** A producer publishes an "event" and blocks waiting for a response event, rebuilding synchronous coupling with worse tooling. Catch it: any producer that cannot finish its transaction without a consumer's answer is a call, not an event.
- **The snapshot firehose.** Full entity snapshots published on every field change "just in case," coupling every consumer to the producer's entire schema and leaking personal data into the stream. Catch it: compare payload contents against the minimum-payload rule; fields no consumer reads are removed.
- **Retry as error handling.** Failures are met with longer retry loops instead of a DLQ and an alert, so poison messages surface only when users complain. Catch it: find the DLQ and its alert; if either is missing, retries are the error handling.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — `SendWelcomeEmail` becomes `UserRegistered`](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-202.
- [Example 2 — Dual write becomes a transactional outbox](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-205.
- [Example 3 — The poison message gets a DLQ, not a loop](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-208, AR-206.

## Recall anchors

- Name the pattern before building anything.
- Events are facts in the past tense, never commands.
- Publish atomically: outbox or event store, never dual write.
- Consumers deduplicate, tolerate disorder, and dead-letter poison.
- A consumer down must never take the producer with it.

## Checklist

- [ ] The pattern (notification, state transfer, event sourcing, CQRS) is named and recorded (AR-201).
- [ ] Every event type has an AsyncAPI entry, a versioned schema, an owner, and known consumers (AR-203).
- [ ] Every event carries the CloudEvents envelope attributes (AR-204).
- [ ] Outbox path check passes: no direct broker publishes outside the relay (G-AR-104).
- [ ] Replay test passes with duplicate delivery producing no duplicate effects (G-AR-102).
- [ ] Consumer-outage test passed in staging within the current release cycle (G-AR-103).
- [ ] Every stream has a DLQ with an alert and a documented replay procedure (AR-208, AR-210).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/multitenancy-saas/SKILL.md -->

# multitenancy-saas

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microsoft Learn, multitenancy and Azure SQL Database (tenancy models, row-level security, noisy neighbor) — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/service/sql-database ; Microsoft Learn, multitenancy tenancy models for Cosmos DB — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/multi-tenancy-vector-search
- **Depends on:** system-design, data-architecture, backend-auth
- **Feeds into:** tenant-isolation, schema-design, subscriptions

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product serves more than one customer organization or consumer from one deployment and the isolation model must be chosen, implemented, or audited — tenancy model selection, tenant context handling, provisioning, per-tenant operations.
- **Do NOT use when:** the product is single-tenant by design — say so in ARCHITECTURE.md and stop. Do not use this skill for the database-level implementation of row-level security itself; that is tenant-isolation and schema-design, working from the model chosen here. Data-level isolation enforcement and its review — tenant scoping across tables, queries, jobs, and cache keys — belongs to tenant-isolation (D5); this skill owns only the model-level choice and audit.

## Rules

1. **AR-181 — Tenant is defined first.** State what a tenant is (customer organization, individual consumer, or sub-unit) before choosing any model; the definition drives isolation, billing, and data-sovereignty requirements.
2. **AR-182 — Model per layer, named from the catalog.** Choose per layer from the named models — shared schema with tenant key (pool), schema/database per tenant (silo), or hybrid (bridge) — and record the choice in an ADR citing the isolation, compliance, and cost trade-offs.
3. **AR-183 — Context is established at the edge.** Tenant context is resolved once, at the request boundary, from the authenticated principal or the subdomain, and propagated. Code never accepts a tenant ID from an unauthenticated request body.
4. **AR-184 — Every path is scoped.** Every query path — API, admin, reporting, export, and background jobs — is scoped by tenant. An unscoped path is a blocker defect.
5. **AR-185 — Isolation is platform-enforced.** Scoping is applied automatically (ORM filter, row-level security, middleware), never by each developer remembering a filter per query.
6. **AR-186 — Tenant key on every tenant-owned table.** The key is non-null, present from the first migration, and leads the index used by tenant-scoped queries.
7. **AR-187 — Per-tenant operations are designed.** Backup and restore granularity, data export, and tenant deletion (including legal erasure) are specified for the chosen model before the first tenant onboards.
8. **AR-188 — Provisioning is automated.** New tenants are created by an automated, tested procedure. Manual database edits are not a provisioning path.
9. **AR-189 — Noisy-neighbor controls are part of the model.** Per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and per-tenant usage observability ship with the design, not after the first incident.
10. **AR-190 — Hybrid placements are enumerated.** In a bridge model, a tenant catalog records which tenant lives in which store; routing reads the catalog, never a hardcoded list in code.
11. **AR-191 — Async work carries tenant context.** Background jobs and event consumers receive and propagate tenant context; work that arrives without it fails closed rather than running unscoped.
12. **AR-192 — Isolation is tested, not assumed.** The cross-tenant test suite is part of the design deliverable, and it runs in CI from the first tenant onward.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-091 — Tenant ID from the request body.** Banned: resolving the tenant from a client-supplied value in an unauthenticated request. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Bad: `POST /invoices` accepts `tenant_id` in the JSON body, so any caller can read and write any tenant's invoices by changing one field. Instead: resolve the tenant from the authenticated principal (or the subdomain, verified against the session) at the edge and ignore body-supplied tenant values entirely. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-092 — Isolation by developer memory.** Banned: tenant scoping that depends on each query's author remembering to add the filter. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Bad: most queries carry `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, the new reporting query does not, and one tenant's dashboard shows everyone's revenue. Instead: enforce scoping in the platform layer — row-level security or an ORM-level automatic filter — so an unscoped query returns nothing rather than everything. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-093 — Manual provisioning.** Banned: creating a tenant by hand-editing the production database. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: onboarding a customer means an engineer runs remembered SQL inserts at midnight; one missed row leaves the tenant half-created with no error anywhere. Instead: a scripted, tested provisioning procedure that creates the tenant atomically and is exercised in staging on every release. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-094 — Unbounded shared tenants.** Banned: shared compute and storage with no per-tenant rate limit or quota. Defeats: DET-INF-023. Bad: one tenant's import job saturates the worker pool for six hours while every other tenant's requests time out. Instead: per-tenant rate limits and quotas at the edge and in the job queue, with per-tenant usage visible on a dashboard. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-091 — Cross-tenant test suite.** Verifies: AR-184, AR-192. Check: automated — authenticate as tenant A and attempt reads, writes, and exports against tenant B's known resource IDs through every interface class (API, export, report, job trigger). Pass: every attempt returns 403 or 404 and writes nothing. Fail: block release; a single cross-tenant success is a P0 defect. Recorded in: progress.md. Execution: this gate is specified here and executed by D8 (QA & Testing) in its test harness, with auth fixtures owned by D4/D7 and tenant data fixtures owned by D5.
- **G-AR-092 — Tenant-key schema check.** Verifies: AR-186. Check: automated — script asserts every table flagged tenant-owned has a non-null tenant key column and an index leading with it. Pass: zero violations. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md. Execution: this gate is specified here (canonical — data-architecture G-AR-074 cites it) and executed by D8 (QA & Testing), with schema fixtures owned by D5.
- **G-AR-093 — Provisioning drill.** Verifies: AR-188. Check: automated — run the provisioning procedure in staging, then verify the new tenant can sign in, sees an empty workspace, and appears in the tenant catalog. Pass: tenant fully created with no manual step. Fail: block the release that changed provisioning. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-094 — Noisy-neighbor review.** Verifies: AR-189. Check: manual — confirm per-tenant rate limits and quotas are configured and per-tenant usage metrics are visible on an operations dashboard. Pass: limits configured and metrics visible for every tenant. Fail: warn; schedule the fix before onboarding the next tenant. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Tenant_id sprinkling.** The column is added to the obvious tables while exports, search indexes, and file storage stay unscoped. Catch it: list every place tenant data can leave the system and check each one for scoping.
- **The god admin.** An internal admin console bypasses tenant scoping "temporarily" and becomes the largest cross-tenant surface in the product. Catch it: admin paths appear in the cross-tenant test suite like any other interface.
- **Silo sprawl.** Database-per-tenant adopted for a handful of tenants with no automation, until migrations and backups become per-tenant manual chores. Catch it: if provisioning and migration are not scripted, the silo model was chosen without its operating cost.
- **Untraceable usage.** Shared-everything metering means no tenant's consumption can be attributed, and invoices are assembled by hand. Catch it: pick one tenant and produce its usage for last month from the system alone; if a human had to estimate, metering failed.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Tenant context from the edge, not the body](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-183.
- [Example 2 — The unscoped export, scoped and tested](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-184.
- [Example 3 — Provisioning as a tested procedure](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-188.

## Recall anchors

- Define the tenant before choosing the model.
- Context comes from the edge, never from the body.
- Every path is scoped — admin, exports, and jobs included.
- Isolation is enforced by the platform, not by memory.
- Provisioning is a procedure, not a person with SQL access.

## Checklist

- [ ] The tenant definition is written down and the per-layer model is chosen in an ADR (AR-181, AR-182).
- [ ] Tenant context is resolved once at the edge from the authenticated principal or subdomain (AR-183).
- [ ] Cross-tenant test suite passes: every cross-tenant attempt returns 403/404 and writes nothing (G-AR-091).
- [ ] Tenant-key schema check passes on every tenant-owned table (G-AR-092).
- [ ] Backup/restore granularity, export, and tenant deletion are specified for the model (AR-187).
- [ ] Provisioning drill passes in staging with no manual step (G-AR-093).
- [ ] Per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and usage metrics are in place (AR-189).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/stack-selection/SKILL.md -->

# stack-selection

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** MADR template and guidance — https://adr.github.io/madr/ ; Twelve-Factor config and portability constraints — https://12factor.net/config
- **Depends on:** requirements-writing, system-design
- **Feeds into:** adr-writing, system-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** choosing or replacing a language, framework, database, queue, or any component the project will depend on for its lifetime; re-evaluating a settled stack decision.
- **Do NOT use when:** the component is already settled by an accepted ADR and nothing material has changed (build on it), or the choice is a leaf utility inside one module with no architectural reach (decide locally, note it in the pull request).

## Rules

1. **AR-041 — Criteria before candidates.** The selection criteria are written down before any candidate is named: requirements fit, data-model fit, team skill, ecosystem maturity and maintenance health, license, operational cost, hosting constraints, exit cost.
2. **AR-042 — Same table for every candidate.** Each candidate is scored against the same criteria in one comparison table. A candidate evaluated on criteria the others were spared is re-evaluated.
3. **AR-043 — Every adoption is an ADR.** No stack component is adopted without an ADR in MADR format whose status is "accepted", naming at least one seriously considered alternative and why it lost.
4. **AR-044 — Popularity is not a criterion.** "Popular", "trending", and "used at a big company" never appear as selection criteria or as a candidate's scored advantage.
5. **AR-045 — Versions agree everywhere.** Versions named in the ADR, the README stack list, and any prose must match the dependency manifest exactly. A mismatch is a defect.
6. **AR-046 — Pin in the same change.** Exact versions are pinned in the dependency manifest in the same change that adopts the component; "install latest" is not a pin.
7. **AR-047 — Disqualifiers are recorded.** A candidate with no maintenance activity, a license conflict with the project's license, or no production hosting path on the target platform is disqualified, and the disqualification is written in the ADR — not silently dropped from the table.
8. **AR-048 — Downsides are accepted on record.** The ADR states the chosen component's accepted downsides (the criteria where it scored worst). An ADR claiming no downsides is incomplete.
9. **AR-049 — Exit cost is assessed.** For data stores and platforms, the ADR states what leaving would cost: data export path, proprietary features in use, and contract or ecosystem lock-in.
10. **AR-050 — Changes supersede, never swap silently.** Replacing a settled component requires a new ADR that supersedes the old one and links both ways. Editing the manifest alone is forbidden.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-021 — Fashion adoption.** Banned: adopting a component because it is fashionable, with no criteria table and no ADR. Defeats: DET-CODE-024. Bad: the README announces a stack copied from a conference talk — a database the team has never operated, chosen before anyone listed the project's actual queries. Instead: write the criteria, score at least two candidates in one table, and record the choice as an ADR (AR-041, AR-043). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-022 — Version drift between prose and manifest.** Banned: a version named in the README or ADR that differs from the dependency manifest. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: the README says "PostgreSQL 16", the ADR says 15, and the deployment manifest pins 14; the team debugs behavior that only exists in one of them. Instead: the manifest is the single source; prose is regenerated or corrected to match it (AR-045). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-023 — The silent swap.** Banned: replacing a settled stack component by editing the manifest, with no superseding ADR. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: the queue library is swapped over a weekend; the old ADR still says "accepted", and the next incident review reconstructs the rationale from chat logs. Instead: a new ADR supersedes the old one, links both ways, and lands in the same change (AR-050). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-024 — The unmaintained dependency.** Banned: adopting a component with no maintenance activity or an unresolved license conflict without recording the risk. Defeats: DET-INF-025. Bad: a charting library unmaintained for years, with a known unpatched vulnerability, is added because its demo looked good. Instead: disqualify it in the ADR with the reason recorded, or accept the risk explicitly with a mitigation (AR-047). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-021 — Manifest-to-ADR coverage (citation).** Verifies: AR-043. Check: automated — this requirement is verified by the canonical manifest cross-check, G-AR-122 in adr-writing (every top-level manifest dependency maps to an ADR by name or tag match); run that gate for the full procedure and pass criteria. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-022 — Version agreement.** Verifies: AR-045, AR-046. Check: automated — a script extracts version strings from the README stack list and the ADRs and compares them with the manifest's pinned versions. Pass: zero mismatches and zero unpinned top-level dependencies. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-023 — Criteria predates decision.** Verifies: AR-041, AR-042, AR-048. Check: manual — in git history, confirm the criteria table exists at or before the commit that records the decision, the table scores every candidate on the same criteria, and the ADR names a rejected alternative and accepted downsides. Pass: all three hold. Fail: block stack sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Criteria written to fit the winner.** The criteria table appears after the choice and, miraculously, the favorite wins every row. Catch it: compare the table's first commit date with the decision date (G-AR-023); criteria that postdate the choice are advocacy, not evaluation.
- **The phantom alternative.** The ADR names a "considered alternative" that was never seriously evaluated — one line, no scores. Catch it: the alternative must appear in the same comparison table with real scores (AR-042), or the ADR is incomplete.
- **Benchmark theater.** Candidates ranked by a synthetic benchmark that resembles no workload the project has. Catch it: ask which stated criterion the benchmark measures; if it maps to none of AR-041's list, it is decoration.
- **Stack sprawl by accretion.** A second database, queue, or framework added for one feature without an ADR, because "it's just for this." Catch it: run G-AR-021; every top-level dependency without an ADR is sprawl made visible.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — From a fashionable pick to a criteria-based decision](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-041, AR-043.
- [Example 2 — Repairing version drift between README, ADR, and manifest](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-045.
- [Example 3 — Replacing a settled component with a superseding ADR](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-050.

## Recall anchors

- Criteria first, candidates second — always in that order.
- No ADR with a rejected alternative, no adoption.
- Popularity is not a criterion.
- The manifest is the only version that counts.
- A swap without a superseding ADR is a silent swap.

## Checklist

- [ ] Criteria were written before candidates were named (AR-041).
- [ ] Every candidate is scored in one table against the same criteria (AR-042).
- [ ] The ADR is accepted, names a rejected alternative, and states accepted downsides (AR-043, AR-048).
- [ ] Manifest-to-ADR coverage is 100% (G-AR-021).
- [ ] Versions in prose match the manifest exactly; everything is pinned (G-AR-022).
- [ ] Disqualified candidates are recorded with their disqualifier (AR-047).
- [ ] Exit cost is stated for stores and platforms (AR-049).

<!-- generated from skills/architecture/system-design/SKILL.md -->

# system-design

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D2 Architecture & System Design (AR)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** C4 model — https://c4model.com/ ; Pattern language for distributed designs — https://microservices.io/
- **Depends on:** requirements-writing, stack-selection
- **Feeds into:** c4-diagrams, adr-writing, data-architecture

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a new system or a major subsystem is being designed; the container topology, data ownership, or failure behavior of an existing system is being changed; a design review is requested.
- **Do NOT use when:** the change fits inside one existing container without new cross-boundary calls (build it and update the diagram via c4-diagrams instead), or when the open question is which stack to build on (stack-selection comes first).

## Rules

1. **AR-001 — Containers are real.** Every container in the design corresponds to a deployable unit, data store, or external system that exists in the repo or infrastructure config. Aspirational boxes are deleted or marked as future work outside the diagram.
2. **AR-002 — Every arrow is labeled.** Each relationship between containers carries a protocol or format label (HTTPS/JSON, gRPC, AMQP, SQL). An unlabeled arrow fails review.
3. **AR-003 — Failure behavior per call.** For every cross-container call, the design states the timeout, the retry policy, and what the caller does when the callee is down. A call missing any of the three is incomplete.
4. **AR-004 — Monolith by default.** The default topology is a modular monolith. A distributed design must cite, in an ADR, the requirement that forces it (independent scaling, team autonomy, isolation) — "future scale" without a load figure does not qualify.
5. **AR-005 — One writer per store.** Each data store has exactly one owning container that writes to it. Other containers read through the owner's interface or a replicated read model, never by writing directly.
6. **AR-006 — Quality attributes first.** Decomposition starts from the stated quality attributes (scale, latency, consistency, availability, tenancy), each with a target figure where one exists. A design that names components before attributes is sent back.
7. **AR-007 — Failure in the same pass.** Timeouts, retries, backpressure, and degradation are designed in the same pass as the happy path for every flow, not retrofitted after the first outage.
8. **AR-008 — Decisions become ADRs when made.** Each significant choice in the design (topology, ownership, protocol, consistency model) gets an ADR at the moment it is made, not reconstructed at the end of the project.
9. **AR-009 — Revisit on attribute change.** The design is revisited when a quality attribute changes (a new tenancy requirement, a 10× load target), not on a calendar schedule. The triggering change is named in the review note.
10. **AR-010 — External systems are explicit.** Every external system on the diagram is named, with the direction of the integration, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous, and who owns the relationship.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AR-001 — The generic three-box diagram.** Banned: a design whose whole model is boxes labeled "Frontend", "Backend", "Database" with unlabeled arrows. Defeats: DET-CODE-008. Bad: ARCHITECTURE.md contains one diagram, three boxes, no actors, no protocols; nobody can tell what calls what. Instead: a C4 container diagram with typed elements, named protocols on every arrow, and data stores as first-class containers (AR-001, AR-002). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-002 — Aspirational containers.** Banned: containers in the design that exist in no deployable unit, data store, or infrastructure config. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the diagram shows a "Recommendations Service" and a "Search Cluster"; the repo deploys one application and one PostgreSQL database. Instead: draw what exists; put the recommendations box in a clearly marked future-work note outside the diagram. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-003 — Distribution without a forcing requirement.** Banned: splitting the system into services with no ADR citing the requirement that forces distribution. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: six microservices for a CRUD application with one developer and no independent scaling need, chosen "so it can scale later." Instead: a modular monolith with module boundaries, plus an ADR naming the load or isolation figure that would trigger a split (AR-004). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AR-004 — Shared writable database.** Banned: two or more containers writing directly to the same tables. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: the billing worker and the web app both UPDATE the orders table; a race between them corrupts an order total. Instead: one owning writer; the other container calls the owner's interface or consumes its events (AR-005). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AR-001 — Container-to-deployable walk.** Verifies: AR-001, AR-010. Check: manual — walk the container diagram element by element against the repo's deployable units and infrastructure config; every element must match a real unit, store, or named external system, and every relationship line in the diagram source must carry a protocol label (checked here, by eye, because label syntax differs across diagram formats). Pass: zero unmatched elements and zero unlabeled relationships. Fail: block design approval. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-002 — Design document completeness.** Verifies: AR-002, AR-008. Check: automated — a script confirms ARCHITECTURE.md contains a container section and that every ADR file it references exists under `docs/decisions/`. Pass: script exits 0. Fail: block design approval. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-003 — Failure-behavior review.** Verifies: AR-003, AR-007. Check: manual — for each cross-container call in the design, point at the row stating its timeout, retry policy, and callee-down behavior. Pass: every call has all three. Fail: block design approval. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AR-004 — Data-ownership audit.** Verifies: AR-005. Check: manual — list every store in the design and its owning writer; confirm no second container writes to it directly. Pass: exactly one writer per store. Fail: block design approval. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Resume-driven topology.** The design mirrors whatever architecture is fashionable this year rather than the stated quality attributes. Catch it: ask which attribute each split serves; a split nobody can tie to AR-006's list is fashion, not design.
- **The happy-path sketch.** Flows are drawn only for success; timeouts and partial failure are "implementation details." Catch it: pick the busiest arrow and ask what happens at 10× load and when the callee hangs — if the design is silent, AR-007 was skipped.
- **Design by reconstruction.** ADRs written at project end from memory, with alternatives nobody actually considered. Catch it: check the ADR dates against the git history of the code they govern; a cluster of same-day ADRs for month-old decisions is reconstruction.
- **The invisible external system.** A third-party API the system depends on appears nowhere in the design because "it's just an SDK call." Catch it: grep the dependency manifest for HTTP clients and SaaS SDKs and match each against the diagram (AR-010).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — From three generic boxes to a real container design](examples/example-1.md) — corrects AR-001, AR-002.
- [Example 2 — Adding failure behavior to a happy-path design](examples/example-2.md) — corrects AR-003, AR-007.
- [Example 3 — Microservices by default, corrected to a modular monolith](examples/example-3.md) — corrects AR-004.

## Recall anchors

- Start from quality attributes, not components.
- Every container is real; every arrow is labeled.
- Timeout, retry, callee-down — for every call.
- Monolith by default; distribution needs a forcing requirement.
- One writer per store, always.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every container matches a deployable unit, store, or named external system (G-AR-001).
- [ ] Every arrow carries a protocol or format label (AR-002).
- [ ] Every cross-container call states timeout, retry policy, and callee-down behavior (G-AR-003).
- [ ] Data ownership is drawn: exactly one writer per store (G-AR-004).
- [ ] A distributed topology, if any, cites its forcing requirement in an ADR (AR-004).
- [ ] Each significant decision has an ADR written when it was made (AR-008).
- [ ] External systems are named with direction and sync/async marked (AR-010).

## Department D3 — frontend

# client-routing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D3 Frontend, Design & Motion (FE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** React Router data-router guide (loaders, error boundaries) — https://micropyramid.com/blog/react-router-for-navigation/ ; inherited Web Craft Pro Max rules R-5.2-3, R-10.1-4 and cure CD-06, mapped in docs/WCPM_MAPPING.md
- **Depends on:** frontend-core, data-fetching
- **Feeds into:** ui-states, frontend-state

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or changing the route structure of a single-page app or hybrid site — defining routes, navigation, guards, deep links, or the 404 view.
- **Do NOT use when:** the site is a set of plain server-rendered pages with no client router (the server framework's routing and frontend-core apply), or the question is what data a route loads (data-fetching owns fetching; this skill owns the URL and navigation contract).

## Rules

1. **FE-221 — Every meaningful view has a real URL.** If a user would bookmark it, share it, or return to it, it is a route — not a component swapped by local state.
2. **FE-222 — No state-flag navigation.** Refresh, deep link, and the back/forward buttons must all land on the correct view. A view reachable only by clicking from another view is a defect.
3. **FE-223 — Loaders fetch before render, errors stay local.** Routes load their data in route loaders (or the framework equivalent) and each route carries an error boundary, so a failed route renders its error view inside the layout instead of crashing the app shell.
4. **FE-224 — Unknown paths render the designed 404.** A catch-all route shows the product's 404 view with a path back into the product (inherited cure CD-06: design the 404 and error pages). A blank screen on a bad URL is a defect.
5. **FE-225 — Guards are UX only.** A route guard may redirect an unauthenticated user to login, but protected data is authorized by the API on every request, never by the router. Hiding a route is not protecting it.
6. **FE-226 — Crawlable links for indexable pages.** Navigation to public pages uses plain `<a href>` links to indexable canonical URLs — no JavaScript-only navigation for indexable pages (inherited R-5.2-3).
7. **FE-227 — One canonical URL per public page.** Every public page carries a canonical URL that returns 200 and does not redirect (inherited R-10.1-4; gate G-SCH-02).
8. **FE-228 — Navigation manages scroll and focus.** On navigation, scroll is restored on back/forward and reset on new views, and focus moves to the new view's heading or main region so keyboard and screen-reader users start at the top of the new content, not stranded mid-page.
9. **FE-229 — No full-page reloads inside the SPA.** In-app navigation uses the router's link component; a full document reload between app views breaks FE-222's back/forward and scroll contract.
10. **FE-230 — Route changes are announced.** The document title updates on every route change, and route transitions expose the loading state owned by ui-states — a silent, frozen screen during navigation is a missing state, not a fast load.

## BAN list

- **BAN-FE-111 — State-flag navigation.** Banned: switching views with a state variable (`const [page, setPage] = useState('home')`) instead of routes. Defeats: DET-UX-014. Bad: the settings view exists only as `page === 'settings'`; refreshing on it returns to home and the URL never changes. Instead: define a route per view and navigate with the router. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-112 — Blank screen on an unknown URL.** Banned: a route table with no catch-all, so an unmatched path renders an empty shell. Defeats: DET-UX-010 (see also DET-VIS-032). Bad: `/setings` (typo) renders the header, the footer, and nothing between. Instead: a catch-all route rendering the designed 404 view (FE-224). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-113 — JavaScript-only navigation for indexable pages.** Banned: `<div onClick>` or button handlers as the only way to reach a public page. Defeats: DET-UX-002. Bad: product pages reachable only through a clickable card div; crawlers, middle-click, and open-in-new-tab all fail. Instead: real anchor links to canonical URLs (inherited R-5.2-3). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-FE-114 — Router guard as the authorization boundary.** Banned: treating a client-side guard as protection for data the API serves without its own check. Defeats: DET-FAKE-002 (see also DET-VIS-032). Bad: `/admin` is hidden by a guard, but `GET /api/admin/users` answers any authenticated session. Instead: the guard redirects for UX; the API authorizes every request (FE-225). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-FE-111 — Cold-load and traversal pass.** Verifies: FE-221, FE-222, FE-224. Check: automated — Playwright: cold-load a nested route directly in a fresh tab and assert the correct view renders; traverse five views using link navigation plus back/forward and assert each lands correctly; load a nonsense URL and assert the designed 404 view appears. Pass: all assertions green. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-FE-112 — Refresh sweep.** Verifies: FE-222. Check: manual — refresh the browser on every route in the route table during QA; each must return the same view with its data. Pass: every route survives refresh. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-FE-113 — Authorization boundary probe.** Verifies: FE-225. Check: automated — request each guarded route's API endpoints with no credentials and with a non-privileged session (e.g. `curl -i https://<host>/api/admin/users`); assert 401/403 and no protected payload in any response. Pass: no endpoint leaks data. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-FE-114 — Focus and scroll check.** Verifies: FE-228, FE-230. Check: manual browser verification — navigate by keyboard through three views; after each navigation, focus sits on the new view's heading/main region, the title has changed, and back returns the previous scroll position. Pass: all three behaviors observed. Fail: warn, fix before release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The modal-as-route.** A "page" implemented as a full-screen modal over home: no URL, no back button, lost on refresh. Catch it: if closing it is the only way back, it should have been a route.
- **Redirect chains as architecture.** Legacy paths bouncing through two or three redirects to reach the real view. Catch it: follow every published URL; more than one hop is rework, and it breaks FE-227's canonical rule.
- **The guard forest.** Authorization logic smeared across a dozen route guards with slightly different conditions. Catch it: if two guards disagree about the same role, the rule belongs in one place — and the API check (FE-225) is the one that counts.
- **Query-string views.** Distinct views distinguished only by `?tab=` or `?view=` parameters that the router ignores, so links share one history entry. Catch it: if two "views" highlight different nav items but share a path, they are routes wearing a disguise.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — State-flag navigation replaced by real routes](examples/example-1.md) — corrects FE-222.
- [Example 2 — Missing catch-all replaced by a designed 404 route](examples/example-2.md) — corrects FE-224.
- [Example 3 — Guard-only protection replaced by guard plus API authorization](examples/example-3.md) — corrects FE-225.

## Recall anchors

- If a user would bookmark it, it is a route.
- Refresh, deep link, back button — all three must land correctly.
- Guards redirect; APIs authorize.
- Unknown path = designed 404, never a blank screen.
- Navigation moves focus and updates the title.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every meaningful view has its own route and URL (FE-221).
- [ ] Playwright cold-load/traversal/404 pass is green (G-FE-111).
- [ ] Refresh sweep done on every route (G-FE-112).
- [ ] API probe confirms no guarded data leaks (G-FE-113).
- [ ] Public navigation uses real anchor links to canonical URLs (FE-226, FE-227).
- [ ] Focus, title, and scroll behavior verified by keyboard (G-FE-114).
