# data-quality

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Datadog, "Implement dbt data quality checks with dbt-expectations" — https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/dbt-data-quality-testing/
- **Depends on:** schema-design, etl-pipelines, data-ingestion
- **Feeds into:** data-warehousing, pipeline-orchestration, seed-data

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** datasets need executable quality assertions — uniqueness, not-null, accepted values, referential integrity, range, freshness, row counts, business rules — declared, run, and enforced as pipeline gates.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is application-level input validation at a user boundary (use validation in D4), or a one-off exploratory analysis. Quality checks guard datasets that other people and systems build on; exploration guards itself.

## Rules

1. **DB-381 — Keys are always tested.** Every primary key carries unique and not-null tests; every foreign key carries a relationships test. No exceptions, no tolerance.
2. **DB-382 — Every boundary has a check.** Every pipeline layer boundary (raw → cleaned → modeled) has at least one row-count or freshness check on each dataset that crosses it.
3. **DB-383 — Failure fails the run.** A failing check fails the run with a non-zero exit and an alert naming the dataset and the check. A check that cannot fail a run is a report, not a gate.
4. **DB-384 — Results are stored and trended.** Check results are persisted per run and reviewed as a trend. A check's history is part of the dataset's record, not console output.
5. **DB-385 — Money paths have business-rule checks.** Every money path carries an arithmetic business-rule check (e.g. order totals equal the sum of their line items), in addition to structural tests.
6. **DB-386 — Tolerance is written and bounded.** A `mostly`-style tolerance is permitted only on noisy real-world columns, with the threshold written next to the check and a reason. Integrity rules — keys, references, money sums — get zero tolerance, always.
7. **DB-387 — Checks live with the model.** Checks are declared next to the model or dataset they guard, in the same repository, and run in CI and in the pipeline. A check defined only in a dashboard tool guards nothing upstream.
8. **DB-388 — Sudden perfection is investigated.** A check that has always passed and keeps passing unchanged after a source change is investigated, not celebrated: the likeliest explanations are a broken check or a disconnected dataset.
9. **DB-389 — The suite is proven against faults.** Before a check suite is trusted, it is run against a fixture with injected faults (a duplicate key, an orphaned foreign key) and must catch them. An unproven suite is assumed decorative.
10. **DB-390 — Every check set has an owner.** Each dataset's checks name an owner who receives the failure alert and owns the fix-or-quarantine decision.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-191 — Warning-only gates.** Banned: configuring quality checks to warn and exit zero, so failures never stop a run. Defeats: DET-INF-002. Bad: the dbt suite is set to `severity: warn` across the project "temporarily"; duplicates land in the warehouse for a month while every pipeline run reports success with warnings nobody reads. Instead: checks fail the run with a non-zero exit (DB-383); a deliberate exception is one check, time-boxed, with an owner — never the project default. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-192 — Tolerance on integrity.** Banned: applying a `mostly`-style tolerance threshold to key, reference, or money checks so a known fraction of violations passes. Defeats: DET-CODE-012. Bad: the orders primary-key test is set to pass at 99% uniqueness "because the source is messy"; the 1% duplicates are double-counted revenue. Instead: integrity checks get zero tolerance (DB-386); messy sources are fixed at ingestion quarantine, not averaged away at the gate. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-193 — The unreconciled money path.** Banned: shipping a money dataset with structural tests only and no business-rule check tying its totals to their components. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Bad: order totals are tested not-null and unique while a transformation bug drops a line item from 4% of orders; every structural test passes and the money is wrong. Instead: the money path carries an arithmetic check — totals equal line-item sums — that fails the run on any mismatch (DB-385). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-194 — Disposable check results.** Banned: running checks without persisting their results, or deleting failure history when it becomes embarrassing. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: check output exists only in CI console logs that expire in 14 days; when finance questions a figure from last quarter, there is no record of what the checks said at the time. Instead: results are stored per run and trended (DB-384), retained with the dataset's record. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DB-191 — Suite gate wiring.** Verifies: DB-383, DB-387. Check: automated — the check suite (`dbt build` or the project's checkpoint command) is wired into CI and into the orchestrator's promotion steps, and a deliberately failing test model in a scratch schema makes both runs exit non-zero. Pass: both runs fail on the planted failure. Fail: block; a suite that cannot fail a run is re-wired before anything ships. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-192 — Negative test.** Verifies: DB-389, DB-381. Check: automated — inject a duplicate primary key and an orphaned foreign key into a staging fixture and run the suite. Pass: the suite catches both faults and names the datasets. Fail: block; the suite is fixed and re-proven before it is trusted as a gate. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-193 — Coverage scan.** Verifies: DB-381, DB-382, DB-385. Check: automated — scan model and check declarations and assert every primary key has unique + not-null tests, every foreign key has a relationships test, every layer boundary has a row-count or freshness check, and every money dataset has a business-rule check. Pass: zero gaps. Fail: block the dataset's promotion. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-194 — Results retention check.** Verifies: DB-384, DB-390. Check: automated — query the check-results store and assert results exist for every scheduled run in the retention window and every dataset's check set names an owner. Pass: complete history and owners. Fail: block until result persistence and ownership are in place. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Tolerance creep.** A noisy column's threshold is loosened a little at every failure until the check is decorative. Catch it: threshold changes are reviewed like code and the history is trended (DB-384, DB-386); three loosenings in a row is a source problem, not a threshold problem.
- **Happy-path suites.** Checks cover the columns everyone already trusts and skip the messy joins where corruption actually happens. Catch it: the coverage scan (G-DB-193) counts checks per dataset, and the money and join-heavy datasets are checked first, not last.
- **Alert fatigue farming.** So many flaky checks fire that the team reflexively acknowledges and ignores them. Catch it: a check that fires without a real defect is itself a defect — it is fixed, re-scoped, or removed with a record, never left to cry wolf (DB-390).
- **Snapshot amnesia.** Results are stored but never looked at, so a slow degradation — rising null rates, shrinking row counts — crosses no threshold and surprises everyone at once. Catch it: trends are reviewed on a schedule (DB-384); a check whose trend nobody has opened in a month is flagged in the review.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Warning-only checks made into a real gate](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-383.
- [Example 2 — Key and relationship tests that catch injected faults](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-381.
- [Example 3 — A money path reconciled by a business-rule check](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-385.

## Recall anchors

- Keys and references get tests, always, at zero tolerance.
- A check that cannot fail the run is a report, not a gate.
- Money totals tie to their line items or the run stops.
- Tolerance is written next to the check, with a reason.
- Prove the suite against injected faults before trusting it.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every primary key has unique + not-null tests; every foreign key a relationships test (G-DB-193).
- [ ] Every layer boundary has a row-count or freshness check (DB-382).
- [ ] A planted failure makes CI and the pipeline exit non-zero (G-DB-191).
- [ ] The suite catches an injected duplicate key and orphaned foreign key (G-DB-192).
- [ ] Money datasets carry an arithmetic business-rule check (DB-385).
- [ ] Tolerances exist only on noisy columns, written with thresholds and reasons (DB-386).
- [ ] Check results are persisted, trended, and owned (G-DB-194).

# data-warehousing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Cloud documentation, "BigQuery overview" — https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/introduction?hl=vi
- **Depends on:** etl-pipelines, data-ingestion, schema-design
- **Feeds into:** data-quality, revenue-analytics, dashboards

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** reporting, dashboards, or analysis need data from operational systems — the analytical store, its models, metric definitions, and load discipline are being designed or changed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the query is part of serving a user request (that is the operational database's job, via data-access), or the "report" is a one-off operational lookup. A warehouse is never a reporting skin over the production primary.

## Rules

1. **DB-301 — The primary is not a reporting backend.** No dashboard, report, or analyst query runs against the production primary. Analytical reads run against the warehouse (or a replica explicitly provisioned for reporting, per read-replicas).
2. **DB-302 — One metric, one definition.** Every headline metric has exactly one definition, in one named model in the warehouse. Every consumer references that model; a metric re-implemented inside a dashboard is a defect.
3. **DB-303 — Loads are idempotent.** Warehouse loads are scheduled, monitored, and idempotent: re-running a day's load produces the same warehouse state, verified by row counts or checksums.
4. **DB-304 — PII is minimized on entry.** Personally identifiable data entering the warehouse is limited to what a named analysis needs, and access is controlled per dataset. The warehouse is not a full photocopy of the user table.
5. **DB-305 — Schemas are code.** Warehouse schemas and models are versioned code in the repository. A change made in a console or UI that is not in the repo does not exist and will be overwritten.
6. **DB-306 — The warehouse is a separate store.** Analytical data lives in a separate analytical store (columnar storage with storage/compute separation, e.g. BigQuery's model), loaded on a schedule from operational sources — not in extra tables on the production database.
7. **DB-307 — Freshness is stated and alerted.** Every warehouse dataset names its expected freshness (load cadence plus maximum lag). A load that misses its window alerts before a stakeholder finds a stale dashboard.
8. **DB-308 — Metric changes are migrations.** Changing a headline metric's definition updates the one owning model, records the change and its effective date, and re-points or re-checks every consumer. Silent redefinition is forbidden.
9. **DB-309 — Models, not raw dumps.** Consumers query modeled fact and dimension tables (or curated wide tables), not raw operational copies. Raw landings exist for reload and audit; they are not a reporting interface.
10. **DB-310 — Reconciliation runs on a schedule.** A headline metric computed in the warehouse is reconciled against the source system within a stated per-metric tolerance, on a schedule, and the result is recorded. A tolerance is a number written next to the check, not "close enough".

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-151 — Dashboards on the primary.** Banned: pointing a reporting tool or dashboard at the production primary database. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: the Monday revenue dashboard runs full-table aggregations on the primary at peak traffic; checkout latency triples while the report renders. Instead: load the data into the warehouse on a schedule (DB-306) and point the dashboard there. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-152 — The CSV warehouse.** Banned: a manually exported file (a nightly CSV emailed or shared around) serving as the analytical store. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: finance downloads a spreadsheet export each morning, edits two columns by hand, and circulates it as "the warehouse"; no one can reproduce last month's figures. Instead: a scheduled, idempotent pipeline load into the warehouse, with models as code (DB-303, DB-305). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-153 — A metric per dashboard.** Banned: defining the same business metric independently inside multiple dashboards, queries, or reports. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Bad: "revenue" excludes refunds in the sales dashboard and includes them in the finance dashboard; the two figures disagree in the same meeting. Instead: one definition in one named model that every consumer references (DB-302). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-154 — Console-edited models.** Banned: changing warehouse tables, views, or models directly in the provider console without the change existing as reviewed code. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: an analyst "fixes" a view in the console during an incident; the next pipeline deploy overwrites it and the fix vanishes with no record. Instead: every warehouse change is a code change in the repository, deployed by the pipeline (DB-305). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-151 — Primary protection check.** Verifies: DB-301. Check: automated — scan the production primary's query log for the reporting window and assert zero connections or queries from reporting tools and dashboard service accounts. Pass: zero reporting queries on the primary. Fail: block the release and move the consumer to the warehouse. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-152 — Reconciliation check.** Verifies: DB-310, DB-302. Check: automated — on schedule, compute a headline metric (e.g. yesterday's order count and revenue) in the warehouse and in the source system; assert the difference is within the tolerance recorded for that metric. Pass: within tolerance. Fail: alert and block promotion of the affected dataset until explained. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-153 — Idempotent reload test.** Verifies: DB-303. Check: automated — in staging, run one day's load twice and assert the destination row counts and checksums are identical after both runs. Pass: identical state. Fail: block until the load merges or replaces partitions instead of appending. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-154 — Schema-as-code diff.** Verifies: DB-305. Check: automated — export the warehouse's live schema/model definitions and diff against the repository's model code. Pass: zero differences. Fail: block; the drift is either committed as reviewed code or reverted. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Tolerance creep.** Each reconciliation failure is resolved by widening the tolerance a little, until the check cannot fail. Catch it: the tolerance history is part of the check's record (DB-310); a widened tolerance needs the same review as a metric change.
- **The PII photocopy.** The warehouse ingests entire user tables "because storage is cheap", including fields no analysis uses. Catch it: every PII column in the warehouse names the analysis that needs it (DB-304); an unnamed column is dropped.
- **Load and pray.** Loads run on a schedule but nothing watches them; the first sign of a three-day-old dashboard is a stakeholder complaint. Catch it: every dataset has a stated freshness and an alert on breach (DB-307); a dataset without one is unfinished.
- **Shadow metrics.** A team's spreadsheet quietly becomes the number executives quote, diverging from the warehouse model. Catch it: reconcile quoted figures back to the one owning model (DB-302); a figure with no model behind it is withdrawn.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A dashboard moved off the production primary](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-301.
- [Example 2 — Two revenues reconciled to one definition](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-302.
- [Example 3 — A load that duplicated on re-run, made idempotent](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-303.

## Recall anchors

- The primary serves users; the warehouse serves questions.
- One metric, one definition, one model.
- Re-running a load changes nothing.
- Warehouse schemas are code or they do not exist.
- Reconciliation has a number, and the number is written down.

## Checklist

- [ ] No reporting consumer connects to the production primary (G-DB-151).
- [ ] Every headline metric resolves to one named model (DB-302).
- [ ] Re-running a day's load leaves identical counts and checksums (G-DB-153).
- [ ] Live warehouse schema diffs clean against the repo models (G-DB-154).
- [ ] Every dataset states its freshness and alerts on breach (DB-307).
- [ ] PII in the warehouse is minimized and access-controlled per dataset (DB-304).
- [ ] Reconciliation runs on schedule within the recorded tolerance (G-DB-152).

---

# etl-pipelines

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Apache Airflow documentation, "Concepts" — https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/2.0.0/concepts.html
- **Depends on:** data-ingestion, pipeline-orchestration, schema-design
- **Feeds into:** data-warehousing, data-quality

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** data is moved and transformed between systems in stages — landing raw data, cleaning it, and modeling it for a warehouse or another consumer — or an existing pipeline's load semantics are changing.
- **Do NOT use when:** the movement is a one-off manual export (that is an incident waiting to be repeated; build the pipeline), or the "pipeline" is application request traffic (that is data-access and api-building). Ingestion contracts with sources belong to data-ingestion; scheduling belongs to pipeline-orchestration.

## Rules

1. **DB-321 — Raw is immutable.** Raw ingested data is never edited in place. Corrections happen in transformation, producing new cleaned output; the raw landing stays exactly as received.
2. **DB-322 — Every run is parameterized.** Each pipeline run is parameterized by date or window, so any single day can be re-run on demand. A run that only works for "today" is unfinished.
3. **DB-323 — Loads are idempotent.** Loads merge/upsert by key or replace whole partitions. Retries, re-runs, and backfills converge to the same destination state instead of duplicating rows.
4. **DB-324 — Partial loads publish nothing.** A failed transformation publishes no output: transforms write to a staging table and swap atomically, or load inside a transaction. Downstream never sees half a window.
5. **DB-325 — Transformations are reviewed code.** Every transformation is code in the repository, changed through the same review as application code. Editing transformation logic in production is forbidden.
6. **DB-326 — Quality gates sit between layers.** Data-quality checks run at each layer boundary (raw → cleaned → modeled). A dataset is promoted only when its checks pass; the checks are data-quality's, the placement is this skill's.
7. **DB-327 — Every dataset has an owner and lineage.** Each dataset names its owner and its source systems, written down where the pipeline is defined. An unowned dataset is a defect.
8. **DB-328 — Layers promote in one direction.** Data flows raw → cleaned → modeled. Consumers read the furthest layer they need; nothing reaches back and patches an earlier layer from a later one.
9. **DB-329 — Backfill is the same code path.** Backfilling a historical window runs the identical transformation and load code as a scheduled run, with the window as its parameter. There is no separate hand-written backfill procedure.
10. **DB-330 — Failures name themselves.** A failed run alerts with the dataset, the window, and the failing stage. "The pipeline failed" with no dataset or window is not an alert.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-161 — Editing raw in place.** Banned: updating or deleting rows in the raw landing zone to "fix" bad source data. Defeats: DET-INF-026. Bad: a malformed currency code is corrected with an `UPDATE` directly on the raw table; a month later nobody can tell what the source actually sent, and the audit trail is gone. Instead: leave raw untouched and correct the value in the transformation, where the rule is visible and re-runnable (DB-321). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-162 — The silent partial load.** Banned: a transformation that fails partway but lets downstream consume whatever was written before the failure. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Bad: the nightly transform dies at row 800,000 of 1M; the exception is caught and logged, the DAG reports success, and dashboards show a day that is 20% short. Instead: stage the output and swap atomically on success only (DB-324); a failed run publishes nothing and alerts (DB-330). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-163 — Production-edited transforms.** Banned: changing transformation SQL or code directly in the production environment. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: an engineer hot-fixes a join in the production scheduler's UI; the change is in no repository, the next deploy from code silently reverts it, and the figures change back overnight. Instead: the fix goes through the repository and the normal deploy, like any code change (DB-325). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-164 — Hard-coded windows.** Banned: transformation code with literal dates or "yesterday" baked in so no other window can be processed. Defeats: DET-CODE-009. Bad: the load script contains `WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-01'`; after an outage, the missed three days cannot be backfilled without editing code in production. Instead: the window is a run parameter supplied by the orchestrator (DB-322), and backfill uses the same code path (DB-329). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-161 — Failure-injection test.** Verifies: DB-324, DB-330. Check: automated — in staging, kill a transformation mid-run and assert (a) no partial output is visible in the destination layer, (b) an alert fires naming dataset and window, (c) the retry completes the full window. Pass: all three hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-162 — Idempotency test.** Verifies: DB-323, DB-329. Check: automated — run the same window twice through the full pipeline and assert destination row counts and checksums are identical after the second run. Pass: identical state. Fail: block until the load merges or replaces instead of appending. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-163 — Raw immutability check.** Verifies: DB-321. Check: automated — the pipeline's database role is denied UPDATE/DELETE on raw tables (permission assertion), and a checksum sample of raw partitions matches their landing checksums. Pass: writes are denied and checksums match. Fail: block; raw is restored from the source landing and the offending write path is removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-164 — Layer-gate presence scan.** Verifies: DB-326, DB-327. Check: automated — scan the pipeline definitions and assert every layer promotion step references at least one data-quality check and every dataset declares an owner and its sources. Pass: no promotion step without a check, no dataset without an owner. Fail: block the pipeline's release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The notebook transform.** The real transformation logic lives in an analyst's notebook or a BI tool's custom SQL, while the "pipeline" only moves files. Catch it: ask where a transformation change would be reviewed; if the answer is not the repository, the logic is in the wrong place (DB-325).
- **Silent success.** A run reports success while processing zero rows because the source was empty or the filter excluded everything. Catch it: layer-boundary checks include row-count expectations (DB-326); a zero-row promotion is a failure until a human confirms the source was truly empty.
- **Copy-paste pipelines.** Each new source gets a cloned pipeline with small edits, and the clones drift apart over months. Catch it: diff two pipelines for the same shape of job; shared stages that differ are one parameterized pipeline waiting to be written (DB-322).
- **Backfill by hand.** A missed window is repaired with one-off SQL run manually against production. Catch it: any production data write outside the pipeline's own code path is the tell; backfill is a run with a window parameter (DB-329), not a hand operation.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — An append load that duplicated on retry, replaced with a merge](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-323.
- [Example 2 — A partial load made atomic with staging and swap](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-324.
- [Example 3 — A hard-coded date replaced with a window parameter](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-322.

## Recall anchors

- Raw is read-only; corrections live in transformation.
- Any window can be re-run; no window is special.
- A failed transform publishes nothing.
- Transformations are code, reviewed like code.
- Retries converge; they never duplicate.

## Checklist

- [ ] Raw tables deny writes to the pipeline role and checksum clean (G-DB-163).
- [ ] Running the same window twice leaves identical counts and checksums (G-DB-162).
- [ ] Killing a transform mid-run publishes nothing and alerts with dataset + window (G-DB-161).
- [ ] Every layer promotion is gated by a data-quality check (G-DB-164).
- [ ] Every dataset names an owner and its source systems (DB-327).
- [ ] No literal dates or windows exist in transformation code (DB-322).
- [ ] Backfill runs the same code path as the scheduled run (DB-329).

# indexing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PostgreSQL documentation, "Text Search Functions and Operators" (GIN on `tsvector`) — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/10/functions-textsearch.html ; pgvector documentation (HNSW index construction) — https://access.crunchydata.com/documentation/pgvector/0.8.3/pdf/pgvector.pdf
- **Depends on:** schema-design, migrations, query-performance
- **Feeds into:** query-performance, search-engines, data-access

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing indexes for new query patterns, reviewing why a query cannot use an existing index, auditing index bloat, or adding an index to a table that already holds production data.
- **Do NOT use when:** the query itself is malformed (fix it under query-performance first) or the table is small enough that a sequential scan is the planner's correct choice. Do not use it to paper over a schema that models the domain wrong.

## Rules

1. **DB-161 — Indexes come from the query log.** Every index is designed from an actual, named query pattern. Speculative indexes "for later" are not created.
2. **DB-162 — Foreign keys and tenant columns are indexed.** Every foreign key column and every column used in tenant scoping carries an index, by default, from the migration that creates the table.
3. **DB-163 — Composite order follows the query.** Equality columns come first, the range or sort column last. An index whose leftmost column no query filters on is dead weight and is fixed or dropped.
4. **DB-164 — Cover hot read paths.** Where a hot query's columns fit, build a covering index with `INCLUDE` so the planner can answer with an index-only scan and skip heap fetches.
5. **DB-165 — Partial indexes for hot subsets.** When the hot set is a small, stable slice (for example `status = 'active'`), index the slice, not the table.
6. **DB-166 — The index type matches the operator.** B-tree for equality/range/order; GIN for `tsvector` full-text and JSONB containment; GiST or HNSW where the operator (similarity, geometry) demands it. A mismatch means the index is silently unused.
7. **DB-167 — Usage is audited on a schedule.** `pg_stat_user_indexes` is reviewed per release; indexes with no scans are dropped through a migration, with the audit recorded.
8. **DB-168 — Large-table indexes are built concurrently.** `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (or the engine equivalent) outside a transaction block, and the resulting index size is recorded.
9. **DB-169 — Every index names its query.** The migration or SCHEMA.md states which query each index serves. An index nobody can attribute is a removal candidate.
10. **DB-170 — Write cost is counted.** Every index taxes every insert and update on its table. An index no read uses is removed, never kept "just in case".

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-081 — Index-on-every-column.** Banned: adding indexes speculatively across a table's columns "for performance" without a query behind each one. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: a migration indexes all fourteen columns of `orders`; write throughput drops and none of the new indexes is ever scanned. Instead: index from the query log, one named query per index (DB-161, DB-169). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-082 — The unusable composite.** Banned: a composite index whose column order no real query can use leftmost, shipped as if the query were indexed. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: `INDEX (created_at, tenant_id)` while every query filters `tenant_id` first; the planner ignores it and the team believes tenant queries are covered. Instead: equality columns first — `INDEX (tenant_id, created_at)` — and prove use with `EXPLAIN`. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-083 — The fossil index.** Banned: leaving an index with zero recorded scans in place release after release. Defeats: DET-CODE-002. Bad: `idx_orders_legacy_ref` has no scans in a year of `pg_stat_user_indexes` history and still taxes every insert. Instead: audit per release and drop unused indexes through a migration (DB-167). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DB-084 — The locking index build.** Banned: building an index on a large production table with a plain in-transaction `CREATE INDEX` that blocks writes for the duration. Defeats: DET-INF-018. Bad: a migration runs `CREATE INDEX` on the 40-million-row `events` table inside the deploy transaction; writes queue for half an hour. Instead: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` outside a transaction block (DB-168). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-081 — Hot-query plan assertions.** Verifies: DB-161, DB-163, DB-164. Check: automated — CI runs `EXPLAIN` for each registered hot query against a seeded production-shaped fixture; the plan must show `Index Scan` or `Index Only Scan`, never `Seq Scan` on the large table. Pass: all registered queries use an index. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-082 — FK and tenant index coverage.** Verifies: DB-162. Check: automated — a catalog query against `pg_catalog` lists every foreign key column and tenant-scoping column lacking a supporting index. Pass: the list is empty. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-083 — Unused-index report.** Verifies: DB-167, DB-170. Check: automated report, human sign-off — per release, dump indexes with zero scans from `pg_stat_user_indexes`; each is dropped by migration or kept with a written reason. Pass: report reviewed and dispositions recorded. Fail: warn. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-084 — Concurrent-build check.** Verifies: DB-168. Check: automated — scan new migrations for `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` on tables above the project's large-table threshold. Pass: no matches. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Index as apology.** An index is added instead of fixing the query's shape, and both the bad query and the write tax survive. Catch it: ask which rule of query-performance was checked before the index was proposed.
- **Duplicate twins.** Two indexes cover the same columns in slightly different orders and both are kept because nobody knows which one matters. Catch it: the usage audit names a survivor; the other goes.
- **The console index.** An index created by hand in a production console during an incident, never written into a migration — the next environment simply lacks it. Catch it: diff the production catalog against the migration-built schema.
- **Statistics blindness.** A good index is declared useless because stale statistics steer the planner away from it. Catch it: check `ANALYZE` freshness before judging any index (DB-150).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Composite index reordered so the query can use it](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-163.
- [Example 2 — Covering index with INCLUDE reaching an index-only scan](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-164.
- [Example 3 — Fossil index found by audit and dropped by migration](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-167.

## Recall anchors

- No query, no index.
- Equality first, range last — or the planner walks past.
- Cover the hot path and skip the heap.
- Every index taxes every write; unused means dropped.
- Large tables get concurrent builds, never locking ones.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every new index names the query it serves (DB-169).
- [ ] All foreign key and tenant-scoping columns are indexed (DB-162, G-DB-082).
- [ ] Registered hot queries show index scans in CI plan assertions (G-DB-081).
- [ ] Composite column order matches the queries: equality first, range last (DB-163).
- [ ] Indexes on large tables are built concurrently, size recorded (DB-168, G-DB-084).
- [ ] The unused-index report was reviewed this release and dispositions recorded (G-DB-083).

# migrations

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Ruby on Rails Guides, "Active Record Migrations" — https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v7.1.3/active_record_migrations.html ; Prisma documentation, "Seeding" (migration workflows) — https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v6/prisma-migrate/workflows/seeding
- **Depends on:** schema-design
- **Feeds into:** ci-cd, rollback, deployment-strategies, seed-data

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** changing any database schema in any environment — adding or dropping tables, columns, constraints, or indexes — and when reviewing how a schema change will deploy and roll back.
- **Do NOT use when:** designing the target schema itself (use schema-design), moving data between systems (use etl-pipelines / data-ingestion), or changing only seed/reference content (use seed-data).

## Rules

1. **DB-121 — Versioned files, tracked application.** Every schema change is a versioned, ordered migration file in the repository. A runner applies them in order and records applied versions in a tracking table, so every environment converges to the same schema by construction.
2. **DB-122 — Applied migrations are immutable.** A migration that has run anywhere is never edited. A correction, however small, is a new migration. History that can be rewritten cannot be trusted.
3. **DB-123 — Reversible, or honestly irreversible.** Every migration is reversible (auto-reversed `change`-style or an explicit up/down pair). Where reversal is genuinely impossible, the migration says so in its header and names the recovery procedure that replaces rollback.
4. **DB-124 — Expand and contract.** Risky changes (renames, type changes, splits) run across deploys: add the new shape, backfill, dual-write or switch reads, then drop the old shape in a later deploy. No single deploy both changes the shape and depends on the new shape.
5. **DB-125 — Backfills are jobs, not migrations.** Data backfills on large tables run as separate, resumable, batched jobs. A schema migration never carries a full-table data rewrite.
6. **DB-126 — Concurrent index builds.** Indexes on large production tables are built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (or the engine equivalent), outside a transaction block where the engine requires it.
7. **DB-127 — Know your engine's DDL transactions.** Migrations use transactional DDL where the engine supports it (PostgreSQL does; MySQL largely does not). On engines without it, each migration is written so a mid-migration failure leaves a state a re-run can finish.
8. **DB-128 — The full set runs from empty in CI.** Every change runs the complete migration set against an empty database in CI. A migration that fails from empty fails the build, however well it worked on the author's machine.
9. **DB-129 — The schema file is generated.** The committed schema file/structure dump is regenerated by the migration run. It is never hand-edited; a diff between the dump and a fresh run's output is a defect (see G-DB-061).
10. **DB-130 — Down is tested, not assumed.** CI tests rollback as well as roll-forward: apply all migrations, roll back the latest, re-apply it. An untested down path is an untested promise (subject to DB-123's documented exceptions).

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-061 — Console cowboy DDL.** Banned: applying schema changes to production by hand in a SQL console or GUI, outside the migration runner. Defeats: DET-INF-018. Bad: during an outage someone runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN discount numeric` in a console; the fix works, no file records it, and the next deploy's migration fails against a schema nobody recognizes. Instead: write the migration, let the runner apply it, and let the tracking table be the record. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-062 — Editing an applied migration.** Banned: modifying a migration file after it has been applied in any environment, to "fix" it in place. Defeats: DET-INF-018. Bad: a developer corrects last week's migration; environments that already ran the original keep the old shape, new environments get the new one, and the tracking tables all claim the same version. Instead: leave the applied file untouched and ship a corrective migration (DB-122). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-063 — ORM auto-sync in production.** Banned: enabling schema auto-synchronization (`synchronize: true` and equivalents) against a production database, letting the ORM diff and alter the live schema at boot. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Bad: a renamed model field boots in production, the ORM drops the "unknown" column and its data, and creates an empty one with the new name. Instead: auto-sync stays off outside disposable development databases; production changes are migrations only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-064 — The in-migration backfill.** Banned: rewriting or backfilling a large table inside the schema migration that deploys with the release. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: the deploy migration runs `UPDATE sessions SET ...` over 40 million rows, holds its lock for the entire deploy window, and the release times out half-applied. Instead: ship the schema change, then run the backfill as a separate resumable batched job (DB-125). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DB-065 — The hand-edited schema dump.** Banned: editing the committed schema file/structure dump by hand so it matches a local database. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the dump now describes a schema no migration sequence produces; the declared state and the real state have drifted, and every future diff is noise. Instead: fix the migration, re-run, and commit the regenerated dump (DB-129). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DB-061 — Reversibility and diff test.** Verifies: DB-121, DB-123, DB-129. Check: automated — CI runs all migrations from an empty database, diffs the resulting schema against the committed schema file, rolls back the last migration, and re-applies it cleanly. Pass: diff is empty and the rollback/re-apply cycle succeeds. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-062 — Immutability check.** Verifies: DB-122. Check: automated — CI diffs the change against the release tag and fails if any migration file older than the newest is modified. Pass: no applied migration touched. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-063 — From-empty build.** Verifies: DB-128. Check: automated — on every change, CI applies the complete migration set to a fresh empty database and runs the application's boot check. Pass: full set applies and the app boots. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-064 — Concurrent-index check.** Verifies: DB-126. Check: automated grep plus review — migration files that add an index to an existing table must use `CONCURRENTLY` (or carry the documented small-table exception); a plain `CREATE INDEX` on an existing table fails the check. Pass: zero findings. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The mega-migration.** A month of schema changes lands in one file: unreviewable, unrollbackable, and guaranteed to conflict. Catch it: if the migration needs a table of contents, it should have been five migrations.
- **Down-migration theater.** Down methods exist but drop everything, do nothing, or have simply never been executed. Catch it: G-DB-061 runs them; a down path nobody has run is a rumor.
- **The deploy-day surprise.** The migration is written and merged but first executed against production-shaped data during the release itself. Catch it: DB-128's from-empty run plus one run against a production-sized snapshot in staging, before release day.
- **Environment archaeology.** Staging works because of a manual fix from March that exists in no file, and nobody remembers applying it. Catch it: rebuild the environment from migrations alone; whatever breaks was archaeology.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Expand-and-contract column rename](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-124.
- [Example 2 — A reversible migration pair](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-123.
- [Example 3 — Building an index without locking the table](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-126.

## Recall anchors

- Applied migrations are history: corrections are new migrations.
- Expand, backfill, switch, contract — never change and depend in one deploy.
- Backfills are resumable jobs, not migration steps.
- If CI cannot run it from empty, production should not run it at all.
- The schema dump is an output, never an input.

## Checklist

- [ ] The change is a versioned migration file; the runner and tracking table apply it (DB-121).
- [ ] No applied migration was edited (DB-122, G-DB-062).
- [ ] The migration is reversible, or declares itself irreversible with a named recovery procedure (DB-123).
- [ ] Renames/type changes follow expand-and-contract across deploys (DB-124).
- [ ] Any backfill is a separate resumable job, not part of the migration (DB-125).
- [ ] Indexes on large tables are built concurrently (DB-126, G-DB-064).
- [ ] From-empty CI run, schema diff, and rollback/re-apply all pass (DB-128, DB-130, G-DB-061, G-DB-063).

# nosql-patterns

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** pgvector documentation (the counter-pattern: specialized data staying inside Postgres when it fits) — https://access.crunchydata.com/documentation/pgvector/0.8.3/pdf/pgvector.pdf
- **Depends on:** schema-design, data-architecture
- **Feeds into:** data-access, search-engines, vector-db

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a named access pattern is a poor fit for the relational model (document-shaped reads, key-value lookups, wide-column time series, graph traversal), or when reviewing an existing NoSQL data model.
- **Do NOT use when:** the data is relational in shape and Postgres serves it — the relational default stands (use schema-design and sql-fundamentals). Do not reach for this skill because NoSQL feels simpler; simplicity is decided per access pattern, not per project.

## Rules

1. **DB-041 — Patterns before model.** The access patterns are listed, in writing, before any data model is drawn. NoSQL is chosen only for a named pattern the relational model serves badly; "flexible schema" is not a pattern.
2. **DB-042 — Every pattern has a model entry.** Each listed pattern maps to a concrete document shape and query. A pattern with no model entry does not ship; it is remodeled, moved to the relational store, or cut.
3. **DB-043 — Embed together, reference shared.** Data read together is embedded in one document. Data that is shared between documents or grows without bound is referenced, not embedded.
4. **DB-044 — Growth is capped by design.** Every document has a stated maximum size/growth shape. Unbounded arrays and ever-growing embedded lists are forbidden.
5. **DB-045 — One source of truth per field.** Every duplicated field names its single source of truth and a written update strategy (fan-out on write, reconciliation job, or accepted staleness with a stated bound).
6. **DB-046 — Invariants get machinery.** A rule spanning multiple documents is enforced by the engine's transaction support or by an explicit reconciliation job with an owner and a schedule. It is never enforced by hope.
7. **DB-047 — Validation is on.** Schema validation rules (e.g. JSON Schema validators) are enabled on every collection that accepts writes, covering required fields and types.
8. **DB-048 — The exit note exists.** The design document states what would trigger re-evaluating the relational default (a new cross-document pattern, a reporting need, a scale ceiling), so the choice stays a decision instead of becoming an accident.
9. **DB-049 — Postgres first for special data.** Embeddings, JSON documents, and full-text search that fit inside PostgreSQL (pgvector, JSONB, `tsvector`) stay there unless a named need — scale, filtering, analyzer support — says otherwise.
10. **DB-050 — Cross-document joins are a smell.** A read that must reassemble many documents in application code on a hot path means the model is wrong for that pattern: remodel around the pattern or move that pattern to the relational store.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-021 — Engine chosen with no pattern list.** Banned: adopting a NoSQL store because it is "flexible," "fast," or "what the tutorial used," with no written access-pattern list behind the choice. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: the team picks a document store for an order system whose main reads are joins across customers, orders, and payments; the app re-implements joins by hand for a year. Instead: list the patterns first (DB-041); if they are relational, the relational default stands. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DB-022 — Unbounded embedded growth.** Banned: embedding an ever-growing array inside a document (all comments inside the post, all events inside the user). Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: a popular post's document grows past the engine's document size limit and writes start failing in production. Instead: reference the growing side from its own collection and keep a capped preview/count on the parent. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DB-023 — Cross-document invariants by hope.** Banned: maintaining a rule that spans documents (stock decrement + order creation, balance transfer between accounts) with no transaction and no reconciliation job. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: the order document is written, the stock update fails silently, and inventory is wrong forever with no process that would ever notice. Instead: use the engine's multi-document transaction, or a reconciliation job that compares the two sides and repairs drift on a schedule. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-024 — Duplication with no owner.** Banned: copying a field into other documents with no named source of truth and no update strategy. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Bad: `displayName` is copied into 10,000 order documents; a user renames themselves and every historical and current screen disagrees about who they are. Instead: name the source document, and write down how copies are updated or why their staleness is acceptable. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DB-025 — Validation disabled on a writable collection.** Banned: a collection that accepts writes with schema validation off or absent, so any shape can be stored. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Bad: one buggy deploy writes orders missing `total` for a weekend; every downstream read crashes or silently skips them. Instead: enable the validator with required fields and types before the collection accepts traffic. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-021 — Access-pattern coverage check.** Verifies: DB-041, DB-042. Check: manual review against the profiler — each pattern in the design document maps to a query in the repository, and the staging profiler/slow-query log shows no full collection scan serving a listed pattern. Pass: every pattern covered, no collection scans. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-022 — Validator presence check.** Verifies: DB-047. Check: automated — a script queries the database metadata (e.g. `listCollections` with options) and asserts every writable collection carries a validator. Pass: all collections validated. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-023 — Document-growth test.** Verifies: DB-044. Check: automated — an integration test appends the design's stated maximum number of children to a parent document and asserts the document stays under the design cap (with margin to the engine limit). Pass: size under cap at maximum stated growth. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-024 — Reconciliation drill.** Verifies: DB-045, DB-046. Check: automated in staging — run each reconciliation job and assert its drift report is empty; deliberately corrupt one duplicated field and assert the job detects it. Pass: clean report plus detection of the planted drift. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Relational cosplay.** Documents are normalized into tiny pieces and the application re-joins everything on every read — the costs of both models, the benefits of neither. Catch it: count the queries per screen; if a screen needs five round trips to assemble, the model fights the patterns.
- **The junk-drawer document.** Every new feature adds fields to the user document until it is a schema-free attic. Catch it: list the document's fields and ask which access pattern each one serves; orphans get their own home.
- **The eventual-consistency shrug.** Stale duplicated data is waved away as "NoSQL being NoSQL," with no update strategy and no staleness bound. Catch it: for each duplicated field, ask "how does this become right again?" — silence is the finding.
- **Scale theater.** A clustered, sharded deployment is built for a dataset that fits comfortably in one PostgreSQL instance. Catch it: state the data volume and the read/write rates; if they fit the relational default, the burden of proof is on the cluster.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Modeling from the pattern list](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-041, DB-043.
- [Example 2 — Capping document growth](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-044.
- [Example 3 — A duplicated field with a source of truth](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-045.

## Recall anchors

- Patterns first; the model is the answer to the pattern list.
- Embed what is read together; reference what is shared or unbounded.
- Every duplicated field has one named source of truth.
- Cross-document invariants get transactions or reconciliation — never hope.
- If it fits in Postgres, it starts in Postgres.

## Checklist

- [ ] The access-pattern list exists and every pattern maps to a modeled query (DB-041, DB-042, G-DB-021).
- [ ] Every document shape has a stated growth cap, tested at the cap (DB-044, G-DB-023).
- [ ] Every duplicated field names its source of truth and update strategy (DB-045).
- [ ] Every cross-document invariant uses a transaction or a reconciliation job (DB-046, G-DB-024).
- [ ] Validators are enabled on all writable collections (DB-047, G-DB-022).
- [ ] The exit note states what would trigger re-evaluating the relational default (DB-048).

<!-- generated from skills/database/pipeline-orchestration/SKILL.md -->

# pipeline-orchestration

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Apache Airflow documentation, "Concepts" — https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/2.0.0/concepts.html
- **Depends on:** ci-cd, monitoring, alerting
- **Feeds into:** etl-pipelines, data-ingestion, backup-recovery

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** pipelines need scheduling, dependencies, retries, and backfills under one system of record — an orchestrator (Apache Airflow's model: workflows as code-defined DAGs, tasks with explicit states) is being adopted or its discipline tightened.
- **Do NOT use when:** the job is application request handling or a CI build (use ci-cd). Orchestration owns data-pipeline time: when things run, in what order, and what happens when they fail.

## Rules

1. **DB-361 — Everything runs under the orchestrator.** No production pipeline runs on a bare cron entry or a manually started script outside the orchestrator. If it moves production data on a schedule, it is a DAG.
2. **DB-362 — Every task declares its contract.** Each task declares: schedule, dependencies, retry count and backoff, timeout, and alert target. A task missing any of the five is not production-ready.
3. **DB-363 — Tasks are idempotent.** A task retried or re-run for the same window produces the same result as one clean run. Orchestration retries are only safe because the tasks underneath converge (etl-pipelines owns the load semantics; this skill owns the assumption).
4. **DB-364 — Freshness SLAs alert first.** Every pipeline has a freshness SLA. A breach alerts the pipeline's owner before consumers notice stale data.
5. **DB-365 — Backfill is first-class.** Backfilling a historical range uses the same DAG and the same code path as scheduled runs, with the range as a parameter — never a side script.
6. **DB-366 — DAGs are versioned code.** Orchestrator configuration and DAG code live in the repository and change through review, like application code. The running system is deployed from the repo, never edited in place.
7. **DB-367 — Run history is kept.** Run state and logs are retained long enough to audit the most recent failure of every pipeline without asking anyone what happened.
8. **DB-368 — Final failure reaches a human.** When retries are exhausted, the failure alerts a named target — a person or a monitored channel. A failure recorded only in a log file has alerted nobody.
9. **DB-369 — Dependencies are explicit, never timed.** Task ordering is declared as dependencies in the DAG. Sequencing by cron offsets ("job B starts 20 minutes after job A usually finishes") is forbidden.
10. **DB-370 — One place shows every pipeline's health.** The orchestrator's UI or API shows every pipeline's last successful run, and that view is checked on a schedule against each pipeline's window.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-181 — The bare-cron pipeline.** Banned: a production data pipeline scheduled by a standalone cron entry outside the orchestrator. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: three cron lines on one server move the billing data nightly; the server is rebuilt, the crontab is not restored, and the data silently stops for a week. Instead: the pipeline is a DAG under the orchestrator with declared retries and alerts (DB-361, DB-362). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-182 — The silent failure.** Banned: a pipeline whose final failure notifies nobody — no alert target, or an alert sent where no one reads it. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: the DAG fails on Friday night; the failure sits in the orchestrator's log, dashboards go stale, and the team learns about it from a customer on Monday. Instead: exhausted retries alert a named, monitored target (DB-368), and freshness SLAs alert before consumers notice (DB-364). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-183 — The unbounded task.** Banned: a task with no timeout and no retry policy, free to hang forever or to fail permanently on its first error. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: a task deadlocks against the source database at 02:00 and is still "running" at noon, blocking every downstream task while the DAG looks merely slow. Instead: every task declares a timeout and a retry count with backoff (DB-362); a hang becomes a failure, and a failure becomes an alert. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-184 — The server-edited DAG.** Banned: editing DAG code or orchestrator configuration directly on the production server. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: an engineer patches a schedule in the live DAG file during an incident; the next deployment from the repository silently reverts it and the incident recurs. Instead: the change goes through the repository and the normal deploy (DB-366). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-181 — Freshness audit.** Verifies: DB-364, DB-370. Check: automated — query the orchestrator's API and assert every production pipeline shows a last successful run within its schedule window plus its freshness SLA. Pass: all pipelines inside their windows. Fail: alert the owning team and block the pipeline's next promotion until the gap is explained. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-182 — Kill test.** Verifies: DB-362, DB-368, DB-363. Check: automated — in staging, terminate a running task and assert (a) it retries per its declared policy, (b) exhausting retries fires the alert to the named target, (c) no partial output is published downstream. Pass: all three hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-183 — Declaration scan.** Verifies: DB-362, DB-369. Check: automated — lint the DAG definitions and assert every task declares schedule, dependencies, retry count/backoff, timeout, and alert target, and that no dependency is expressed as a time offset. Pass: zero tasks missing a field, zero timed dependencies. Fail: block the DAG's release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-184 — Cron census.** Verifies: DB-361. Check: automated — scan production hosts' crontabs and scheduler configurations for data-pipeline jobs and diff against the orchestrator's DAG list. Pass: zero pipeline jobs outside the orchestrator. Fail: block; the stray job is migrated into a DAG before it runs again. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Cron lasagna.** Wrapper scripts call wrapper scripts that call the real job, each layer added during some past incident. Catch it: trace one pipeline's invocation from schedule to code; more than one hop outside the orchestrator means the layers are hiding the real entry point (DB-361).
- **The retry storm.** Retries are immediate and frequent, so a struggling source system is hammered by its own consumers until it falls over. Catch it: retry declarations show backoff (DB-362); a retry policy with no delay is a denial-of-service plan against your own source.
- **Green but stale.** Every DAG run succeeds, yet the data is old because an upstream source quietly delivered nothing. Catch it: freshness is measured on the data's arrival, not on the run's exit code (DB-364); success with zero new records is a signal, not a pass.
- **The unmonitored mailbox.** Alerts technically exist but go to a distribution list nobody reads. Catch it: name the human or channel that acknowledges the alert (DB-368) and test it in the kill test (G-DB-182); an unacknowledged test alert fails the gate.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A cron chain replaced with a declared DAG](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-361.
- [Example 2 — A silent failure wired to a named alert target](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-368.
- [Example 3 — A hand-run backfill replaced with a first-class backfill](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-365.

## Recall anchors

- If it moves production data on a schedule, it is a DAG.
- Every task declares five things: schedule, dependencies, retries, timeout, alert.
- Dependencies are declared, never timed.
- Exhausted retries reach a human, not a log file.
- Backfill is a run with a range, not a side script.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every production pipeline appears in the orchestrator; the cron census is clean (G-DB-184).
- [ ] Every task declares schedule, dependencies, retries/backoff, timeout, alert target (G-DB-183).
- [ ] The kill test retries, alerts a named target, and publishes nothing partial (G-DB-182).
- [ ] Every pipeline's last success is inside its freshness window (G-DB-181).
- [ ] DAG code and configuration diff clean against the repository (DB-366).
- [ ] Run state and logs are retained through the last failure of every pipeline (DB-367).
- [ ] Backfill of a test range runs the same DAG as the schedule (DB-365).

<!-- generated from skills/database/query-performance/SKILL.md -->

# query-performance

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PostgreSQL documentation — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/10/functions-textsearch.html ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md Part 3, *Caching* and *Search* (EXPLAIN-based Verify lines)
- **Depends on:** schema-design, data-access, indexing
- **Feeds into:** indexing, read-replicas, caching

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an endpoint or job is slow, a slow-query report lands, a hot query is being written or changed, or a release needs its latency budget defended with evidence.
- **Do NOT use when:** the schema itself is wrong for the access pattern (fix it with schema-design first), or the slowness is in application code with no database involvement. Do not use it to justify engine tuning before the queries themselves are fixed.

## Rules

1. **DB-141 — Measure first.** Optimization starts from the database's own evidence — `pg_stat_statements` rankings or the slow-query log — never from a guess about which query is slow.
2. **DB-142 — Before/after plans or it didn't happen.** Every optimization records a before and after `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` plus timing, run on production-shaped data (comparable row counts and distribution), not on an empty development database.
3. **DB-143 — Hot paths carry a latency budget.** Each registered hot query has a stated budget; a change that regresses a hot query past its budget fails review.
4. **DB-144 — Keyset pagination on large lists.** Pagination over large or unbounded result sets is cursor/keyset-based on a stable sort key. Deep `OFFSET` is a defect, not a style choice.
5. **DB-145 — Name the columns.** `SELECT` lists name the columns the caller needs. Over-fetching wide rows (especially text/blob columns) is a performance bug.
6. **DB-146 — Slow-query logging is on in production.** It runs with a stated threshold, and the top offenders are reviewed on a schedule; the review is recorded, not remembered.
7. **DB-147 — Fix in order.** Missing index → wrong join or ordering → N+1 → over-fetching → engine tuning, in that order. Engine parameters are touched only after the query-level causes are exhausted.
8. **DB-148 — No N+1.** Collection loads are eager or batched. List endpoints prove it with a query-count assertion, not by inspection.
9. **DB-149 — Compute in the database.** Aggregates, filters, and sorts that the database can do are done by the database, not by fetching rows and computing in application memory.
10. **DB-150 — Keep statistics honest.** When plans degrade without a query change, check `ANALYZE`/autovacuum health before blaming the query or the index.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-071 — Deep OFFSET pagination.** Banned: paging large lists with `LIMIT n OFFSET <large>` so cost grows with page depth. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: the orders API serves page 500 with `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000`, scanning and discarding ten thousand rows per request. Instead: keyset pagination on the sort key (`WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-072 — The unmeasured "optimization".** Banned: merging a change described as a performance fix with no plan or timing evidence behind it. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: a pull request titled "optimize dashboard query" rewrites the SQL, shows no `EXPLAIN`, and the sequential scan ships anyway. Instead: attach before/after `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output on production-shaped data, or do not call it an optimization. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-073 — The hot query with no plan test.** Banned: changing a registered hot query without a plan assertion in CI that would catch a sequential scan. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Bad: the checkout query is rewritten during a refactor; nothing fails, and it scans the full orders table in production. Instead: register the query and assert its plan in CI against a seeded fixture. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-074 — Diagnostic logging left on in production.** Banned: shipping per-query `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` or full query logging in production code paths. Defeats: DET-CODE-029. Bad: every production query is logged with its plan, flooding the log store and adding latency to every write. Instead: threshold-based slow-query logging with sampling; full plans are captured in staging or in a bounded diagnostic window. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DB-071 — Plan assertion suite.** Verifies: DB-142, DB-143. Check: automated — CI runs `EXPLAIN` for every registered hot query against a seeded production-shaped fixture and fails if the plan shows a sequential scan on the large table or exceeds the query's stated budget. Pass: all registered queries pass. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-072 — Query-count tests.** Verifies: DB-148. Check: automated — integration tests on list endpoints assert the number of executed queries stays at the registered maximum as fixture size doubles. Pass: counts flat. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-073 — Evidence check on performance changes.** Verifies: DB-141, DB-142. Check: manual review — every change claiming a performance improvement carries before/after plan output and timings on production-shaped data. Pass: evidence present and shows the claimed improvement. Fail: warn and return the change for measurement. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-074 — Slow-log review record.** Verifies: DB-146. Check: manual — the scheduled review of the production slow-query log's top offenders exists in the project record with dispositions (fixed, accepted, escalated). Pass: review current within its schedule window. Fail: warn. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Empty-database tuning.** The plan "looks instant" against twelve rows, so the query ships and meets production volume for the first time live. Catch it: demand the fixture's row count next to every plan you review.
- **Index-first reflex.** An index is added before anyone reads the plan, and the real cause — a bad join — survives untouched. Catch it: DB-147's order is a sequence, not a menu.
- **The one-query hero.** The single worst query is optimized while the endpoint still fires two hundred small ones. Catch it: check the endpoint's query count, not just its slowest member.
- **Tuning as camouflage.** `work_mem` and buffer settings creep up release after release while the queries stay wrong. Catch it: any engine-parameter change must name the query-level causes already ruled out.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Sequential scan to index scan, with evidence](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-142.
- [Example 2 — Deep OFFSET replaced by keyset pagination](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-144.
- [Example 3 — N+1 loop replaced by one batched load](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-148.

## Recall anchors

- Measure from the database's own statistics, not from suspicion.
- No before/after plan, no optimization claim.
- Keyset pages; OFFSET depth is a defect.
- Name columns; the database computes, the app does not fetch-and-filter.
- Fix queries in order; tune the engine last.

## Checklist

- [ ] Slow-query evidence (pg_stat_statements or slow log) identified the target queries (DB-141).
- [ ] Before/after `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` recorded on production-shaped data (DB-142).
- [ ] Plan assertion suite passes for every registered hot query (G-DB-071).
- [ ] List endpoints pass their query-count assertions (G-DB-072).
- [ ] Large lists use keyset pagination; no deep `OFFSET` remains (DB-144).
- [ ] Production slow-query logging is on with a threshold, and the last review is recorded (DB-146, G-DB-074).

<!-- generated from skills/database/read-replicas/SKILL.md -->

# read-replicas

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D5 Databases & Data (DB)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** AWS documentation, "Working with DB instance read replicas" — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md Part 11, *Read replicas and read scaling*
- **Depends on:** data-access, schema-design, backup-recovery
- **Feeds into:** data-warehousing, query-performance, caching

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** read load threatens the primary, reporting or feed traffic needs isolation, or an existing replica setup needs its routing, lag, and failover made honest.
- **Do NOT use when:** the real problem is a few bad queries (fix them under query-performance first), or the workload is write-bound — replicas scale reads only. Never present a replica as a backup; backup-recovery owns recovery.

## Rules

1. **DB-221 — The primary takes writes and read-your-own-write.** Anything that must see its own just-committed write reads from the primary. Replicas serve reads that tolerate staleness.
2. **DB-222 — Routing is named, never global.** Each query or service declares its target (primary or replica) explicitly. A blanket "reads go to replicas" default is forbidden.
3. **DB-223 — Consistency-critical reads are pinned.** Checkout, permissions, and balances always read from the primary, and the pinned list is written down.
4. **DB-224 — Every replica read states its staleness tolerance.** Each replica-routed read documents how old its data may be and still be correct for that feature.
5. **DB-225 — Lag is measured continuously.** Replication lag (in seconds and bytes) is a monitored metric with a stated alert threshold, not a quantity discovered through user complaints.
6. **DB-226 — Excess lag triggers a declared fallback.** When lag passes the threshold, affected reads fall back to the primary or the feature degrades explicitly — it never silently serves unbounded staleness.
7. **DB-227 — Promotion is rehearsed.** Replica promotion and failover are documented runbook steps that have been practiced, not improvised during an outage.
8. **DB-228 — Endpoints are configuration.** Primary and replica connection strings are separate, injected configuration. Code never hardcodes a host.
9. **DB-229 — A replica is not read scaling until reads flow.** Provisioning a replica changes nothing by itself; routing must exist and be verified in query logs before scaling is claimed.
10. **DB-230 — Heavy read traffic leaves the primary.** Dashboards, reports, and feeds read from a replica or the warehouse, never from the primary at peak load.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DB-111 — The decorative replica.** Banned: provisioning a replica, routing nothing to it, and reporting read scaling as delivered. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: the replica's connection string sits unused in config while the launch notes claim "read scaling in place" and the primary still takes every read. Instead: route the named, staleness-tolerant reads and verify replica traffic in its query log (DB-229). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-112 — Checkout reading its own write from a replica.** Banned: sending a read-your-own-write flow to an asynchronously replicated copy. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: the order is written to the primary, the confirmation page reads the replica, lag shows an empty cart, and the customer pays twice. Instead: pin read-your-own-write flows to the primary (DB-221, DB-223). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-113 — The hardcoded replica host.** Banned: writing a replica hostname or address as a literal in application code. Defeats: DET-INF-007. Bad: a reporting service embeds the replica's hostname; after failover it silently queries a demoted, stale node for a week. Instead: separate injected configuration per endpoint (DB-228). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DB-114 — Unmonitored lag.** Banned: running replicas with no lag metric and no threshold. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: during a campaign, lag grows to several minutes; users see stale prices, support fields the complaints, and nobody was alerted. Instead: continuous lag measurement with an alert threshold and a declared fallback (DB-225, DB-226). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DB-111 — Routing audit.** Verifies: DB-222, DB-223, DB-224. Check: review — the pinned-primary list covers every named consistency-critical flow, and every replica-routed read carries a written staleness tolerance. Pass: both lists complete. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-112 — Lag visibility test.** Verifies: DB-225. Check: automated — in staging, write a sentinel record on the primary and measure time-to-visible on the replica. Pass: visibility time is under the stated tolerance and the lag metric reports it. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-113 — Fallback drill.** Verifies: DB-226. Check: automated — in staging, force replica lag beyond the threshold (paused replay or load) and assert affected reads fall back to the primary or degrade explicitly. Pass: fallback engages and no read serves staleness past its tolerance. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DB-114 — Replica traffic check.** Verifies: DB-221, DB-229. Check: automated — production query logs show the routed read traffic actually executing on the replica. Pass: replica read volume matches the routing table. Fail: warn; a replica with zero routed reads fails the next release review. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Replica as backup.** The replica is listed as the disaster-recovery plan, although it replicates deletions and corruption with the same fidelity as data. Catch it: recovery belongs to backup-recovery; a replica is a performance tool.
- **Failover by folklore.** Promotion steps live in a chat thread from the last incident. Catch it: if the runbook cannot be followed by whoever is on call, DB-227 is unmet.
- **Lag by anecdote.** "It feels instant in testing" substitutes for a metric, right up until a traffic spike makes it minutes. Catch it: no threshold on a dashboard means no threshold at all.
- **Split by framework magic.** A library's automatic read/write splitting routes a permissions check to a replica because nobody declared the exception. Catch it: DB-222 — routing is named per flow, never inherited from a default.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Empty-cart confirmation fixed by pinning to the primary](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DB-223.
- [Example 2 — Decorative replica replaced by named, verified routing](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DB-229.
- [Example 3 — Unbounded staleness replaced by a tolerance and a fallback](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DB-224, DB-226.

## Recall anchors

- Writes and read-your-own-write go to the primary. Always.
- Routing is named per flow; there is no global replica default.
- Every replica read carries a written staleness tolerance.
- Lag is a metric with a threshold and a fallback, not a surprise.
- No routed reads, no read scaling — a replica alone changes nothing.

## Checklist

- [ ] The pinned-primary list covers checkout, permissions, and balances (DB-223, G-DB-111).
- [ ] Every replica-routed read has a documented staleness tolerance (DB-224).
- [ ] Lag is monitored with an alert threshold, and the visibility test passes (DB-225, G-DB-112).
- [ ] The fallback drill passes with lag forced past the threshold (G-DB-113).
- [ ] Replica query logs show the routed traffic actually arriving (G-DB-114).
- [ ] Promotion steps are in the runbook and have been rehearsed (DB-227).
