<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/incident-response/SKILL.md -->

# incident-response

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.pagerduty.com/ops-guides/incident-response-guide/different-roles ; https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/
- **Depends on:** alerting, monitoring, rollback
- **Feeds into:** postmortem-writing, reliability, status-communications

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Setting up or auditing how a production service responds to outages and major failures — on-call rotation, severity levels, incident command, runbooks, user communication, and postmortems.
- **Do NOT use when:** Defining the alerts and dashboards that detect failure — that is alerting and monitoring. Executing the technical act of reverting a release — that is rollback; this skill decides when to call it and who coordinates.

## Rules

1. **DO-281 — A named on-call rotation exists, with at least two escalation levels.** The current week's primary and escalation responders are named people in the paging tool or a committed rotation file — never "the team" — and any responder can state who is on call right now without asking. In single-operator mode (DO-293), the two levels read as a named primary plus a named escalation contact.
2. **DO-282 — Severity levels and declaration rights are written down before the first incident.** The document defines each severity by user impact, states who may declare an incident at each level, and names the response each level triggers; nobody negotiates definitions during an outage.
3. **DO-283 — Every major incident has exactly one Incident Commander.** The IC coordinates, assigns all repair work to named responders, and owns the communication cadence; the IC does not personally fix anything while commanding. (Single-operator mode sequences the two roles in one person instead — DO-293.)
4. **DO-284 — A scribe keeps the timeline from declaration.** From the moment an incident is declared, the scribe records timestamped events — detection, declaration, decisions, mitigations, resolution — in the incident record, not from memory afterward. (In single-operator mode the operator keeps the timeline — DO-293.)
5. **DO-285 — The runbook covers the top failure modes with exact commands.** Each entry names the symptom, the exact commands or console steps to mitigate, and the escalation trigger; the runbook lives at a recorded path the on-call can open at 3 a.m. — a chat thread is not a runbook.
6. **DO-286 — Mitigate first, diagnose second.** Under outage pressure the default first move is rollback, restore, or failover to a known-good state; root-cause debugging happens after service is restored, unless mitigation is demonstrably impossible and the IC records why.
7. **DO-287 — One voice speaks for the incident.** All status updates come from the IC or a named liaison, on a cadence stated in the first update, and the cadence is kept even when the update is "still investigating."
8. **DO-288 — The user-facing channel is prepared before it is needed.** A status page or equivalent comms channel exists, is linked from the product, and has a pre-written first-update template; for a major incident the first user-facing update goes out within the time the severity definition states.
9. **DO-289 — Every significant incident closes with a blameless postmortem.** The postmortem contains the timeline, the root cause stated as a system property, and follow-up actions each with an owner and a due date; it names no person as a cause.
10. **DO-290 — Postmortem actions are tracked to completion like features.** Each action lives in the same tracker as product work, with its owner and due date visible, and overdue actions surface in the regular review until closed.
11. **DO-291 — The paging path is proven, not assumed.** Alerts for downtime and SLO burn route to the current rotation, and a test alert is fired and acknowledged by the named responder on a regular cadence and after every rotation or tooling change.
12. **DO-292 — The process is rehearsed.** A game day or tabletop drill runs the declaration, command, communication, and postmortem steps on a stated cadence, and the drill's gaps are filed as follow-up actions under DO-290.
13. **DO-293 — Single-operator mode is a named variant, never a silent deletion.** Where one operator runs the service, the rotation is the named operator as primary plus the project owner or user as the escalation contact (level 2). The operator acts as Incident Commander and fixer in sequence — declare, then mitigate, then communicate — and keeps the timeline contemporaneously in the incident record in place of a separate scribe, so DO-284 is satisfied by the operator's own timestamped entries. Every other rule in this skill applies unchanged; the multi-person form above remains the general case wherever more than one responder exists.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-141 — "Contact the developer" as the response path.** Banned: the only documented response to an outage is a person's name, a chat handle, or "contact the developer if something breaks." Defeats: DET-INF-029. Bad: the README's operations section reads "If the site goes down, message Alex." Instead: publish a rotation with at least two escalation levels — in single-operator mode (DO-293), a named primary plus a named escalation contact — and a runbook, so the response survives any one person being unreachable. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-142 — Alerts that reach nobody.** Banned: alert rules fire into an unmonitored channel, a departed member's inbox, or a dashboard nobody opens, with no named on-call owner. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: downtime alerts post to a Slack channel muted by the whole team, and the last test alert was never acknowledged. Instead: route alerts to the paging tool against the named rotation and prove receipt with a test alert. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-143 — Users learn from social media.** Banned: no status page or comms channel exists, so users discover outages from complaints and rumors while the team stays silent. Defeats: DET-INF-028. Bad: during a two-hour outage the product, help center, and social accounts say nothing; users announce the outage first. Instead: prepare the status channel and first-update template in advance and post on the stated cadence from declaration. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DO-144 — Debugging forward while a rollback sits unused.** Banned: responders spend the outage hunting root cause in production while a tested rollback or restore path exists and is not executed. Defeats: DET-INF-017. Bad: ninety minutes of live log-diving during a full outage, then the rollback that fixed it in four minutes. Instead: the IC orders mitigation first (rollback, restore, failover) and diagnosis moves to after service is restored. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-145 — A person named as root cause.** Banned: a postmortem that attributes the incident to an individual's mistake, or no postmortem at all for a significant incident. Defeats: DET-INF-029. Bad: the review concludes "root cause: Sam deployed a bad config" and closes with no system change. Instead: state the root cause as the system property that let one action cause an outage, and file tracked follow-ups with owners and dates. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-141 — On-call inspection (automated).** Verifies: DO-281, DO-282, DO-293. Check: query the paging tool's API (or parse the committed rotation file) for the current week and confirm a named primary plus at least one escalation level, and confirm the severity/declaration document exists at its recorded path. Pass: a named primary plus at least one named escalation level for the current week — in single-operator mode, a named primary plus a named escalation contact (DO-293) — and the severity document present. Fail: block shipment — the service has no response path. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-142 — Paging-path test (automated).** Verifies: DO-291. Check: fire a test alert through the production alert route and confirm the currently named primary acknowledges it within the response time the severity definition states; log the drill timestamp. Pass: acknowledged in time by the named responder. Fail: block shipment until the route is fixed and the test passes. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-143 — Runbook coverage scan (automated).** Verifies: DO-285. Check: open the runbook at its recorded path; for each of the top failure modes confirm an entry containing a symptom and at least one exact command or console step; `grep -in "tbd\|todo\|someone should" <runbook>` returns no hits. Pass: every top failure mode has an actionable entry and no placeholder text. Fail: warn, and complete the runbook before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-144 — Last-incident audit (manual).** Verifies: DO-283, DO-284, DO-289, DO-290. Check: open the most recent significant incident's record; it must name the IC, contain a timestamped timeline kept during the incident, and link a postmortem whose every follow-up action has an owner and a due date in the work tracker. Pass: all four elements present. Fail: warn, and complete the record before the next incident review. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-145 — Status-channel readiness check (manual).** Verifies: DO-287, DO-288. Check: open the status page or comms channel from the product's public links; confirm it exists, that a first-update template is stored with it, and that the last drill or real incident posted its first update within the stated time. Pass: channel reachable, template present, first-update time on record. Fail: warn, and prepare the channel before the next major release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **War-room sprawl.** Five responders post competing updates across three chat channels and nobody can say what the current state is; catch it by asking who the IC is — if two people answer, there is none.
- **Timeline from memory.** The incident record is written two days later from scrollback and recollection, with times rounded and decisions missing; catch it by comparing the record's timestamps against the alert log.
- **Postmortem as paperwork.** The review is written, applauded, and filed while its actions quietly expire unowned; catch it by listing postmortem actions older than their due dates at the regular review.
- **Everything is SEV-1, or nothing is.** Severities are declared by adrenaline instead of the written user-impact definitions, so escalation either always fires or never does; catch it by sampling past incidents against the definitions.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Declaring and commanding an incident](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-282, DO-283.
- [Example 2 — Mitigate first at 3 a.m.](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-285, DO-286.
- [Example 3 — A blameless postmortem with tracked actions](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-289, DO-290.

## Recall anchors

- Mitigate first, diagnose second — rollback beats log-diving under outage pressure.
- One incident, one commander, one voice.
- If the timeline is written from memory, it is fiction.
- A chat message is not a runbook.
- Postmortems blame systems; actions have owners and dates.

## Checklist

- [ ] Current week's rotation names a primary and at least one escalation level (DO-281).
- [ ] Severity levels and who may declare are written and linked from the runbook (DO-282).
- [ ] The last major incident record names one IC and a scribe-kept timeline (DO-283, DO-284).
- [ ] Runbook covers the top failure modes with exact commands and no placeholder text (DO-285).
- [ ] A test alert was acknowledged by the named primary within the stated response time (DO-291).
- [ ] Status channel exists, is linked from the product, and holds a first-update template (DO-288).
- [ ] The last postmortem is blameless and every action has an owner and due date in the tracker (DO-289, DO-290).
- [ ] The last drill or game day is dated, and its gaps are filed as tracked actions (DO-292).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/infrastructure-as-code/SKILL.md -->

# infrastructure-as-code

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language ; https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: authored from the infrastructure the project needs and the live cloud state, inspected directly; it is the record, not a consumer of another skill's output. Feeds ci-cd, deployment-strategies, kubernetes, hosting, cloud-costs.
- **Feeds into:** ci-cd, deployment-strategies, kubernetes, hosting, cloud-costs

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** creating, changing, or auditing any durable infrastructure — compute, network, load balancers, DNS, storage, IAM — or when a project has console-built infrastructure with no code record.
- **Do NOT use when:** the change is application code or data (use the owning D4/D5 skill); for a fully managed platform, apply this skill to the platform's committed config files, which are its IaC of record.

## Rules

1. **DO-101 — Everything durable is declared.** All durable infrastructure (compute, network, DNS, storage, IAM) is declared in code — Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, or a managed platform's committed config files — in the project repo or a named companion deployment repo; nothing durable exists only in a console.
2. **DO-102 — Plan before apply.** Every change follows change → `plan` output attached to the PR showing exactly what will be created, modified, or destroyed → review → apply from CI; no change is applied without a reviewed plan.
3. **DO-103 — Remote, locked state.** State is stored remotely with locking and access control; local state files are never the source of truth for a shared environment.
4. **DO-104 — State is never hand-edited or committed with secrets.** State files are never edited by hand, never committed to version control containing credentials, and are themselves backed up so a lost state file does not orphan the infrastructure.
5. **DO-105 — Drift is a fail.** A scheduled or PR-triggered read-only `plan` against live state that reports changes nobody proposed is a failed check and a finding to resolve, not a curiosity to note and ignore.
6. **DO-106 — Console changes are emergencies.** A change made directly in a console is permitted only to stop an active incident and is back-ported into code the same day, with the back-port verified by a clean plan.
7. **DO-107 — Modules stamped per environment.** Environments are stamped from the same versioned modules with different variable values; per-environment copy-paste forks of the same resources are not maintained.
8. **DO-108 — Check before declaring "no IaC."** Before recording that a project has no IaC, check companion deployment repos and non-Terraform declarative systems (orchestration manifests, provisioning playbooks, platform config files); the test is declaration plus convergent application, not the tool brand.
9. **DO-109 — Destroy is a reviewed operation.** `destroy` and any plan containing resource deletions pass the same plan-and-review gate as creation, with the deletion list read line by line before approval.
10. **DO-110 — Providers and modules are pinned.** Provider and module versions are pinned to exact versions in the configuration; unpinned sources that float to latest on the next init are not used for shared environments.
11. **DO-111 — Fresh-environment build is proven.** The code can build a working environment from empty: applying it into a fresh account or namespace and passing smoke checks is demonstrated at least once per major module change.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-051 — Console-only infrastructure.** Banned: durable servers, networks, or DNS created by clicking in a console with no corresponding declaration in code. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the production VPC and its security groups exist only in the account owner's console session; nobody can reproduce or audit them. Instead: declare the resources in Terraform (or the platform's committed config) and import the existing resources so plan converges. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-052 — Generated-but-never-applied IaC.** Banned: shipping a generated `main.tf` that was never planned or applied while the real environment was hand-built separately. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the repo's Terraform describes the demo stack; production was built by hand and has diverged silently for months. Instead: run `plan` against the real environment, import or reconcile every difference, and apply from CI so the code and the environment are the same thing. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-053 — State committed with secrets.** Banned: committing a state file (or any IaC artifact) containing credentials or secret attribute values to version control. Defeats: DET-INF-005. Bad: `terraform.tfstate` with plaintext database passwords is pushed to the project repo. Instead: move state to a remote, access-controlled backend, add state files to `.gitignore`, and rotate every secret the committed file exposed. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-054 — Unexplained drift waved through.** Banned: seeing a non-empty unscheduled `plan` and applying or ignoring it without identifying what changed and why. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: the nightly plan shows a security group rule nobody added; the team applies anyway to "make it green." Instead: stop, identify the out-of-band change from the plan diff, and either back-port it into code the same day or revert it through code. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DO-051 — Drift check.** Verifies: DO-105, DO-106. Check: CI runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` (read-only) on every infrastructure PR and on a nightly schedule. Pass: exit code 0 (no changes) or the plan diff matches the PR's stated intent exactly. Fail: block the change and open a drift finding. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-052 — No state or secrets in the repo.** Verifies: DO-103, DO-104. Check: `git ls-files | grep -E '\.tfstate' ; grep -rn 'password\|secret_key' --include='*.tfstate' .` returns nothing, and the backend configuration block names a remote backend with locking. Pass: no state files tracked and a remote locked backend is configured. Fail: block shipment until state is migrated and exposed secrets are rotated. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-053 — Fresh-environment build test.** Verifies: DO-101, DO-111. Check: apply the code into an empty account or namespace (`terraform apply` in the sandbox target), then run the project's smoke checks against the new environment. Pass: apply completes with no manual console steps and smoke checks pass. Fail: block release of the module change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-054 — Declaration coverage review.** Verifies: DO-101, DO-108. Check: list the live environment's durable resources from the provider console/API and reconcile the list against the code and any companion deployment repo, item by item. Pass: every durable resource traces to a declaration. Fail: block shipment; undeclared resources are imported or removed. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Tutorial-shaped infrastructure.** The configuration is a copied provider tutorial with the tutorial's example names, CIDR blocks, and placeholder values still in it; catch it by searching for example values and resources nobody on the project can explain.
- **One mega-module.** Every resource for every environment lives in a single root module with hundreds of resources, so every plan is unreadable and every apply touches everything; catch it when a one-line change produces a plan nobody can review.
- **Variables in name only.** A module claims to be reusable but hardcodes region, instance size, and names in the resource bodies, so "stamping a new environment" means editing the module; catch it by diffing what a second environment would actually change.
- **Import-and-forget.** Existing resources were imported once to make the first plan green, but the generated configuration was never cleaned up or reviewed, so the code records attributes nobody chose; catch it by reading imported blocks for provider-default filler.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Console-built network declared and imported](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-101.
- [Example 2 — Drift found and back-ported](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-105.
- [Example 3 — State moved to a remote locked backend](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-103.

## Recall anchors

- If it is not in code, it does not exist — it is a rumor with an IP address.
- Plan is the review; apply is just the signature.
- Drift is a finding, never a shrug.
- Console changes are emergencies: back-port the same day or revert.
- State is the map to everything — remote, locked, backed up, never hand-edited.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every durable resource in the live environment traces to a declaration in code (DO-101, G-DO-054).
- [ ] The latest change shipped with a reviewed `plan` attached to its PR (DO-102).
- [ ] State is remote, locked, access-controlled, and backed up; no state file is tracked in the repo (DO-103, DO-104, G-DO-052).
- [ ] The most recent scheduled drift check is clean or its findings are resolved (DO-105, G-DO-051).
- [ ] Any console change from an incident was back-ported the same day (DO-106).
- [ ] All environments are stamped from the same versioned modules with different variables (DO-107).
- [ ] Provider and module versions are pinned exactly (DO-110).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/kubernetes/SKILL.md -->

# kubernetes

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/ ; https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/
- **Depends on:** containers, infrastructure-as-code
- **Feeds into:** deployment-strategies, scaling, reliability, rollback

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the workload has multiple services or a real scaling/failover requirement that justifies a cluster, and workloads are declared as manifests or Helm charts in Git and applied by the pipeline.
- **Do NOT use when:** the project is a single-service app with no scaling or failover need — use a managed platform or a VPS via the hosting or servers-vps skill instead; cluster ceremony for a one-service app is a finding, not an achievement.

## Rules

1. **DO-081 — Adoption test first.** Before any manifest is written, record in the project docs why Kubernetes is required (multiple services, real scaling, or failover need) and why a platform or VPS cannot meet it; no recorded justification, no cluster.
2. **DO-082 — Manifests are the source of truth.** Every workload is declared in manifests or Helm charts committed to Git and applied by the pipeline; no workload exists only in cluster state.
3. **DO-083 — Requests and limits on every container.** Every container in every workload sets CPU and memory requests and limits, sized from observed usage in staging or production metrics, not guessed.
4. **DO-084 — No BestEffort pods in production.** A pod with no requests and no limits is rejected at review; BestEffort pods are evicted first under pressure and are not a production posture.
5. **DO-085 — Readiness checks dependencies.** The readiness probe fails when a required dependency (database, cache, downstream API) is unreachable, so the pod leaves the Service endpoints until it can actually serve.
6. **DO-086 — Liveness checks only the process itself.** The liveness probe tests that the process is alive and able to make progress, never a downstream dependency; a dependency outage must drain pods via readiness, not restart-loop them via liveness.
7. **DO-087 — Slow starters get a startup probe.** A container that cannot answer its liveness probe during boot declares a startup probe, so liveness checks stay disabled until startup completes.
8. **DO-088 — Stateless tiers run at least two replicas.** Every stateless production workload sets `replicas: 2` or more, spread across nodes or zones with pod anti-affinity or topology spread constraints, behind a Service.
9. **DO-089 — State lives outside the pods.** Databases and durable state run in managed stores or replicated operators; a stateless tier never reads or writes state stored inside its own pods.
10. **DO-090 — Rollout history is retained.** Deployments keep enough revision history (`revisionHistoryLimit` ≥ 2) that `kubectl rollout undo` can return to the previous version at any time.
11. **DO-091 — No hand-edits to live objects.** `kubectl edit`, `kubectl patch`, and console changes to live objects are emergency-only and are back-ported into the committed manifests the same day.
12. **DO-092 — Images referenced by digest or pinned tag.** Workloads reference images by digest or a specific version tag, never `latest`, so the running version is identifiable and reproducible.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-041 — BestEffort production pod.** Banned: a production workload whose containers declare no resource requests or limits. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: a Deployment manifest with no `resources:` block at all, relying on node leftovers. Instead: set requests and limits on every container, sized from observed usage, before the workload ships. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-042 — Dependency-checking liveness probe.** Banned: a liveness probe that calls a database, cache, or downstream API. Defeats: DET-INF-020. Bad: `livenessProbe` hitting `/healthz` that returns 500 whenever Postgres is down, restarting every pod during a database outage. Instead: make liveness check only the process itself and move the dependency check into the readiness probe. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-043 — Single-replica stateless tier.** Banned: a production stateless workload running one replica as its only copy behind the Service. Defeats: DET-INF-019. Bad: `replicas: 1` on the only web tier, so one pod kill or node failure takes the site down. Instead: run at least two replicas spread across failure domains behind the Service. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-044 — Cluster state edited by hand.** Banned: changing live objects with `kubectl edit` or a console and leaving the committed manifests unchanged. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: an engineer raises a replica count live during an incident and the repo still says the old value, so the next pipeline apply silently reverts it. Instead: back-port every emergency live change into the manifests in Git the same day. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-041 — Manifest validity and resource lint.** Verifies: DO-082, DO-083, DO-084, DO-092. Check: `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f k8s/` succeeds, and a script over the manifests confirms every container has requests, limits, and a digest or pinned-tag image (no `latest`). Pass: dry-run clean and zero containers missing resources or using `latest`. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-042 — Probe behavior drill.** Verifies: DO-085, DO-086, DO-087. Check: in staging, stop a required dependency; the workload's readiness fails and pods drain from the Service, while liveness does not restart any pod. Pass: traffic stops, zero restarts during the outage, pods return when the dependency recovers. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-043 — Kill-one-pod drill.** Verifies: DO-088, DO-089. Check: `kubectl delete pod` on one replica of each stateless tier while sending requests; the Service keeps responding with no user-visible errors. Pass: no failed requests during the kill. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-044 — Drift and rollback check.** Verifies: DO-090, DO-091. Check: diff live objects against the committed manifests (`kubectl diff -f k8s/` shows no unexplained changes) and run `kubectl rollout undo` on one Deployment in staging to prove the previous revision restores. Pass: no unexplained drift and the undo succeeds. Fail: warn and reconcile before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Cluster for one container.** A full Kubernetes setup serving a single small app that a platform or VPS would host for a few dollars — catch it at the adoption test (DO-081) before any manifest exists.
- **Requests copied from a tutorial.** Resource values pasted from a blog post instead of measured usage; they pass the lint gate but starve or waste in production — compare against staging metrics at review.
- **Probes on a static path.** Readiness and liveness both hitting `/` and returning 200 while dependencies are dead; the homepage being up is not the service being able to serve — trace what the probe handler actually touches.
- **Helm values drift.** The chart is in Git but the real values live in a `--set` command in someone's shell history, so no one can reproduce the release — values belong in committed values files.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Probes that drain instead of restart-loop](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-085, DO-086.
- [Example 2 — Resources and replicas on a stateless tier](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-083, DO-088.
- [Example 3 — Emergency live edit back-ported to Git](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-091.

## Recall anchors

- No recorded need, no cluster.
- No requests, no autoscaling — and first to be evicted.
- Readiness checks dependencies; liveness never does.
- Two replicas minimum, state outside the pods.
- If it is not in Git, it does not exist.

## Checklist

- [ ] Adoption justification recorded, naming why a platform or VPS cannot meet the need (DO-081).
- [ ] Every container sets requests and limits from observed usage; no BestEffort pods (DO-083, DO-084).
- [ ] Readiness checks dependencies; liveness checks only the process; slow starters have startup probes (DO-085–DO-087).
- [ ] Stateless tiers run ≥2 replicas across failure domains; state lives outside the pods (DO-088, DO-089).
- [ ] Revision history retained and `kubectl rollout undo` proven in staging (DO-090).
- [ ] Live objects match committed manifests; any emergency edit back-ported same day (DO-091).
- [ ] All images referenced by digest or pinned tag, never `latest` (DO-092).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/preview-environments/SKILL.md -->

# preview-environments

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.Netlify.com/site-deploys/create-deploys ; https://vercel.com/docs/v1/features/repositories/
- **Depends on:** ci-cd
- **Feeds into:** deployment-strategies

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** A project has pull requests that need reviewable, running builds — platform-native previews (Vercel/Netlify Deploy Previews) or a pipeline-spun namespace/stack per PR.
- **Do NOT use when:** The change is production release mechanics (use deployment-strategies) or the pipeline itself is missing (build ci-cd first); a preview is never a substitute for staging-for-approval.

## Rules

1. **DO-021 — One preview per pull request, created automatically.** Opening or updating a PR creates or refreshes exactly one preview environment and posts its URL on the PR; no preview is created by hand.
2. **DO-022 — Previews never touch production data.** Each preview uses its own database (or schema/namespace) seeded with non-production data; the preview's database host must differ from the production host.
3. **DO-023 — Previews never hold production credentials.** Preview environments receive a separate, least-privilege secret set; no production API key, token, or password is present in the preview's environment variables.
4. **DO-024 — Same artifact path as production.** The preview is built by the same pipeline and artifact path that produces staging and production builds; previews are never built by a local script or a divergent build command.
5. **DO-025 — Config differs by values, never by code path.** Preview and production run the same code; every behavioral difference comes from environment variable values, with no preview-only branches, flags hardcoded on, or conditional build steps.
6. **DO-026 — Teardown is automatic.** Merging or closing the PR destroys its preview — app, database, and DNS/subdomain — within the documented teardown window recorded in the project config.
7. **DO-027 — Preview count and age are capped and visible.** A maximum number of live previews and a maximum age (TTL) are set in config; a scheduled sweep lists live previews and tears down any that exceed either limit.
8. **DO-028 — The preview serves the PR's commit.** The preview response identifies the commit it serves (build metadata endpoint, header, or footer injected at build time) and that SHA equals the PR head SHA.
9. **DO-029 — Previews are not publicly discoverable.** Every preview response carries `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` (or access control); no preview URL is linked from production pages or sitemaps.
10. **DO-030 — Debug surfaces stay off in previews.** Debug mode, verbose error pages, and admin/test endpoints are disabled in preview config exactly as in production config.
11. **DO-031 — The preview URL is the unit of review.** Reviewers verify the change on the preview URL, and the PR records which preview URL and commit SHA were reviewed before merge.
12. **DO-032 — Preview failures block like CI failures.** A failed preview build or a preview serving the wrong commit is a red status on the PR, treated as a stop, not background noise.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-011 — Preview wired to the production database.** Banned: a preview environment whose `DATABASE_URL` (or equivalent) resolves to the production database host. Defeats: DET-INF-003. Bad: the PR preview for a billing change reads and writes the live `orders` table during review. Instead: provision a per-preview database seeded with synthetic data and point the preview at it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-012 — Production secrets copied into preview config.** Banned: reusing production API keys, tokens, or passwords as preview environment values "to make it work." Defeats: DET-INF-003. Bad: the preview deploy carries the live payment provider secret key, so a test checkout charges real cards. Instead: issue separate sandbox/test-mode credentials scoped to the preview only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-013 — Preview built outside the pipeline.** Banned: building or updating a preview by hand — local build, FTP upload, or SSH rebuild — instead of the CI artifact path. Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: a developer runs a deploy script from a laptop so the preview shows code that exists in no commit. Instead: let the pipeline build the PR's commit and deploy that artifact to the preview. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-014 — The immortal preview.** Banned: a preview left running indefinitely after its PR merged or closed, kept "just in case" as an unofficial second site. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: forty stale preview subdomains from closed PRs still serve old builds on the shared quota. Instead: tear the preview down automatically on merge/close and sweep for orphans past the TTL. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-011 — Preview serves the PR commit (automated).** Verifies: DO-021, DO-028. Check: open a test PR, wait for the preview comment, then run `curl -s <preview-url>/.well-known/build-info.json` (or the project's build-metadata path) and compare its `commit` field to the PR head SHA. Pass: HTTP 200 and the SHAs match exactly. Fail: block merge until the preview rebuilds. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-012 — Preview isolation audit (automated).** Verifies: DO-022, DO-023. Check: script reads the preview environment's resolved config and asserts its database host differs from the production host and none of the production secret values appear in the preview value set. Pass: zero matches on both assertions. Fail: block the preview, rotate any exposed production secret. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-013 — Teardown on close (automated).** Verifies: DO-026, DO-027. Check: close the test PR, then poll the preview URL every 60 seconds; it must return 404/410 (or fail DNS) within the documented teardown window. Pass: preview unreachable inside the window. Fail: raise a teardown defect and run the orphan sweep. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-014 — Review evidence on the PR.** Verifies: DO-029, DO-031. Check: before merge, confirm the PR thread contains the preview URL, the reviewed commit SHA, and a reviewer note; fetch the preview URL and confirm the `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` header is present. Pass: all three items present and the header is set. Fail: hold the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Preview theater.** A preview URL is posted on every PR but nobody opens it; review happens from screenshots in chat. Catch it: the PR has no recorded preview URL/SHA review note (G-DO-014 fails).
- **The golden preview.** One long-lived "preview" branch environment is hand-tuned until it no longer matches what the pipeline would build. Catch it: its build predates the current pipeline config or its env values were edited in a console.
- **Seed-data cosplay.** The preview database is a copied production snapshot with names lightly renamed — real user data in disguise. Catch it: row counts and email domains match production patterns instead of the synthetic seed set.
- **Quota blindness.** Previews multiply silently until the platform's build minutes or preview cap stop all deploys, including production. Catch it: no dashboard or sweep output shows live preview count and age.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Preview database isolation](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-022.
- [Example 2 — Pipeline-built preview](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-024.
- [Example 3 — Automatic teardown](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-026.

## Recall anchors

- One PR, one preview, posted automatically.
- Never production data, never production secrets.
- Same artifact path as production — values differ, code does not.
- Merge or close means teardown.
- The preview URL and its SHA are the unit of review.

## Checklist

- [ ] Opening a test PR produced a preview URL on the PR (DO-021).
- [ ] Preview database host differs from production and holds only synthetic seed data (DO-022).
- [ ] No production secret value appears in the preview environment (DO-023, G-DO-012).
- [ ] Preview was built by the pipeline from the PR head commit, and its build metadata shows that SHA (DO-024, DO-028, G-DO-011).
- [ ] Preview responses carry `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` and debug surfaces are off (DO-029, DO-030).
- [ ] Closing the test PR removed the preview within the documented window (DO-026, G-DO-013).
- [ ] Live preview count and oldest age are within the configured caps (DO-027).
- [ ] The PR records the preview URL and commit SHA that were reviewed (DO-031, G-DO-014).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/reliability/SKILL.md -->

# reliability

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/welcome.html
- **Depends on:** backup-recovery, monitoring, rollback
- **Feeds into:** incident-response, scaling, cloud-costs

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Setting or auditing a production service's reliability system — SLOs and error budgets, golden-signal monitoring, burn-rate alerting, backup and restore assurance, and the disaster-recovery plan.
- **Do NOT use when:** Executing backups or restore jobs themselves — that is backup-recovery (this skill verifies placement, cadence, and evidence). Running an incident in progress — that is incident-response. Choosing replica counts and autoscaling ceilings — that is scaling.

## Rules

1. **DO-261 — Every production service has a written SLO.** The SLO names the SLI (the exact measured ratio, e.g., successful requests / total requests), the target percentage, and the rolling window; it lives in the project's reliability register, not in a slide deck. A service with no SLO has no reliability standard.
2. **DO-262 — The error budget gates release pace.** Remaining budget is computed from the SLI and displayed where the team plans work; when the budget for the window is exhausted, feature releases pause and reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers. The pause is a rule, not a negotiation held during an outage.
3. **DO-263 — Golden signals are monitored for every production service.** Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation each have a dashboard or recorded query per service; a signal with no query behind it counts as unmonitored.
4. **DO-264 — Paging alerts fire on error-budget burn rate.** Alerts use multi-window burn-rate thresholds against the SLO (per the SRE Workbook method), not raw cause metrics; alert rule files pass `promtool check rules` (or the platform equivalent) in CI.
5. **DO-265 — Every paging alert is symptom-based, actionable, and carries a runbook link.** If the on-call cannot act on it, it is deleted or demoted to a ticket; the alert annotation links the runbook section that handles it.
6. **DO-266 — Every alert routes to a named responder path.** Each paging alert terminates at a named on-call rotation — for a single operator, the operator plus a stated escalation contact — and the routing is test-fired after any change. An alert that lands in a channel nobody watches is no alert.
7. **DO-267 — An independent external probe watches the public URL.** The probe runs outside the hosting provider's failure domain, checks the public URL on a stated interval, and pages through the same path as internal alerts, so detection survives the host dying.
8. **DO-268 — Backups live outside the primary failure domain.** Backup storage sits in a different account, region, or provider than the primary data; this skill verifies the placement on the quarterly review (execution is owned by backup-recovery).
9. **DO-269 — Restores are rehearsed on a written cadence, with timings recorded.** Each drill records the date, the backup restored, the measured duration, and the operator; a backup with no drill record inside its cadence window counts as untested.
10. **DO-270 — Every service names RTO and RPO targets and a DR strategy tier.** The chosen tier — backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active — is written next to the targets it can actually meet; the tier is chosen deliberately, not inherited from a tutorial default.
11. **DO-271 — Disaster recovery is a game day, not a document.** Failover is executed on the recorded cadence and the measured RTO/RPO are filed against the DO-270 targets; a plan that has never been run is a hypothesis and is labeled as one.
12. **DO-272 — Reliability is reviewed quarterly against evidence.** The review checks: SLO inventory current, budget status per service, last restore drill date and duration, last DR game day date and measured RTO/RPO, and a sample of alerts for runbook linkage. Findings go into progress.md with owners.
13. **DO-273 — The project's reliability posture is declared, with a promotion trigger.** Project docs state the posture (validation on free tiers, with the specific rules waived named; or production, all rules apply) and the event that forces promotion — first real user, first payment, or first promised availability commitment, whichever comes first.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-131 — Backup declared done with no restore test.** Banned: marking backup work complete, or reporting a service as protected, when no restore drill record exists inside the cadence window. Defeats: DET-INF-009. Bad: the launch checklist says "Backups: enabled ✓" and nobody has ever restored one. Instead: run a restore drill, record date and measured duration, and only then report the service as protected. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-132 — Backups inside the primary failure domain.** Banned: the only copy of the backups lives in the same account, region, or provider failure domain as the primary data. Defeats: DET-INF-010. Bad: nightly database dumps are stored on a bucket in the same cloud account whose compromise or outage would take the primary down too. Instead: replicate backups to a separate account, region, or provider and verify the placement at the quarterly review. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-133 — Alerts that reach nobody.** Banned: paging rules whose notifications terminate in an unmonitored inbox, a muted channel, or a rotation with no named responder. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: burn-rate alerts post to a chat channel the team muted during a noisy week and never unmuted. Instead: route alerts to the named on-call path and test-fire after every routing change. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-134 — In-host monitoring as the only detection.** Banned: relying solely on monitoring that runs on the same host or provider as the service, with no independent external probe. Defeats: DET-INF-028. Bad: when the VPS dies, its own monitoring dies with it and the outage is discovered from user complaints hours later. Instead: run an external probe on the public URL from outside the provider, paging through the same path as internal alerts. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-135 — Golden-signal blind spot.** Banned: shipping a production service with no recorded query or dashboard for one or more of latency, traffic, errors, or saturation. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the team can see CPU on the host but has no error-rate or latency view, so a slow-burn failure is invisible until the budget is gone. Instead: record a query or dashboard per golden signal per service before launch, and re-check the inventory at the quarterly review. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-131 — SLO inventory audit (automated).** Verifies: DO-261, DO-273. Check: for each service in the deploy manifest, grep the reliability register for its SLO entry — `for s in $(cat deploy/services.txt); do grep -q "^## $s" docs/reliability.md || echo "MISSING $s"; done`. Pass: no MISSING lines; every production service has an SLI, target, and window on record. Fail: block shipment until the register covers every service. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-132 — Alert rule lint (automated).** Verifies: DO-264. Check: run `promtool check rules alerts/*.yml` (or the platform's rule validator) as a CI step. Pass: exit code 0. Fail: block merge until the burn-rate rules validate. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-133 — Runbook link check (automated).** Verifies: DO-265. Check: script extracts every runbook URL from the alert rule annotations and requests each (`curl -sfI <url>`); report any non-2xx/3xx response. Pass: 100% of paging alerts link a reachable runbook. Fail: block shipment; fix the link or demote the alert. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-134 — Restore drill currency (manual).** Verifies: DO-269, DO-270. Check: open the drill log and confirm the latest entry for each production data store is dated inside its cadence window and its measured duration is at or under the service's RTO target. Pass: every store has a current, in-target drill. Fail: block any "protected" claim for that service and schedule the drill before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-135 — External probe page test (manual).** Verifies: DO-266, DO-267. Check: in staging (or a maintenance window), make the public URL fail and confirm the external probe pages the named responder path; record the time from failure to page. Pass: page arrives through the production routing within the probe interval plus one minute. Fail: block shipment — detection that dies with the host is not detection. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Alert wallpaper.** Dozens of cause-based alerts (CPU, disk, connection counts) fire on every deploy until the channel is ignored in practice; catch it by listing alerts that fired in the last 30 days with no action taken — each one is a deletion or demotion candidate.
- **SLO theater.** A target like 99.99% copied from a blog post with no SLI query behind it; catch it by asking for the query that computes the SLI — if none exists, the SLO is decoration and the budget math is fiction.
- **Budget amnesia.** The error budget is exhausted, but feature releases continue at full pace because nobody looked at the number during planning; catch it by putting remaining budget at the top of the planning agenda, not in a dashboard nobody opens.
- **Drill deferral.** The restore drill and the DR game day are always scheduled for "next quarter," so the plan ages untested while the system drifts; catch it by checking drill dates at the quarterly review — a date that keeps moving is a finding, not a schedule.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — An SLO that can gate a release](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-261, DO-262.
- [Example 2 — A burn-rate alert with a runbook](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-264, DO-265.
- [Example 3 — A restore drill on record](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-268, DO-269, DO-270.

## Recall anchors

- No SLO, no standard: an unmeasured service is an unkept promise.
- The error budget is the release valve — when it is spent, features wait.
- Alerts page symptoms and link runbooks; causes get tickets.
- Detection must survive the host: probe from outside.
- An unrestored backup is a hope, not a backup.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every production service has an SLO entry with SLI, target, and window (DO-261).
- [ ] Remaining error budget is computed and visible where work is planned (DO-262).
- [ ] All four golden signals have a dashboard or recorded query per service (DO-263).
- [ ] Paging alerts are burn-rate based and the rule files pass lint in CI (DO-264).
- [ ] Every paging alert is actionable and links a reachable runbook (DO-265, G-DO-133).
- [ ] Alerts route to a named responder path and were test-fired after the last change (DO-266).
- [ ] An external probe watches the public URL and pages through the production path (DO-267, G-DO-135).
- [ ] Latest restore drill per data store is in-cadence and within RTO; RTO/RPO and DR tier are on record (DO-269, DO-270).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/rollback/SKILL.md -->

# rollback

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Kubernetes Docs, "Deployment" (rolling back a Deployment) — https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/
- **Depends on:** deployment-strategies, ci-cd
- **Feeds into:** incident-response, reliability

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** preparing a release so it can be reversed, responding to a bad deploy, or checking that the return path to the last good version actually exists and has been rehearsed.
- **Do NOT use when:** choosing the promotion pattern itself (deployment-strategies owns that; this skill owns reversing it), or when the failure is data loss rather than a bad release (D5 backup-recovery owns restore).

## Rules

1. **DO-301 — The rollback action is written before the release ships.** The runbook names the exact command or console step that restores the previous version (for example `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`), before merge. A rollback step first named during the incident does not count.
2. **DO-302 — The previous version stays deployable.** Artifacts are immutable and versioned; the prior artifact (image digest, platform build, or blue/green idle environment) is retained and redeployable until the new version clears its observation window.
3. **DO-303 — Rollback is the default first response to a bad deploy.** When a release breaches its abort thresholds, roll back first and diagnose second. Fix-forward is the exception and needs a written justification in the incident record.
4. **DO-304 — Flagged releases roll back by flag flip first.** If the change shipped behind a feature flag, the first rollback action is flipping the flag off — seconds, no redeploy. Artifact rollback follows only if the flag flip does not clear the fault.
5. **DO-305 — Data changes expand and contract.** A migration never drops or renames a column/table in the same release that stops using the old shape; the contract step ships at least one release later, so the old code runs against the new schema throughout the rollback window.
6. **DO-306 — Every migration has a down path or a documented exception.** Each migration ships with a reversal, or with a written forward-fix plan recorded as an explicit exception in the release checklist. "Irreversible, undocumented" blocks the release.
7. **DO-307 — The live version is always knowable.** Deploy records map production → artifact digest → commit SHA, so the rollback target (the previous record) is identified from the record, not from memory.
8. **DO-308 — Rollback is drilled and timed.** On a set cadence, staging runs the drill: deploy a deliberately broken version, execute the documented rollback, and record the time for the previous version to serve healthy traffic against a stated target (for example 5 minutes).
9. **DO-309 — Rollback triggers are named in advance.** The release record names the metric thresholds and the person/role authorized to call a rollback, matching the abort conditions set by deployment-strategies. No threshold, no release.
10. **DO-310 — Recovery is verified, not assumed.** After rollback, the restored version passes its health check and a key-route smoke test before the incident is declared mitigated; the result is recorded with the rollback timestamp.
11. **DO-311 — Rollback preserves the evidence.** Logs, deploy records, and the bad artifact are kept after rollback; the faulty release is never deleted before the postmortem has what it needs.
12. **DO-312 — A rolled-back release does not re-ship unchanged.** The same artifact is not promoted again until the fault is fixed and the fix is visible as a new version with its own deploy record.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-151 — In-place overwrite deploy.** Banned: the deploy copies new files over the live release, leaving no previous artifact to return to. Defeats: DET-INF-017. Bad: deploy script runs `rsync -a build/ /var/www/app/` and the rollback plan reads "redeploy from main and hope." Instead: deploy each release as a new immutable, versioned artifact and switch traffic to it, keeping the previous artifact live-capable. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-152 — Destructive migration in the retiring release.** Banned: dropping or renaming a schema element in the same release that stops reading/writing the old shape. Defeats: DET-INF-018. Bad: release 1.4 removes all reads of `users.name_old` and its migration runs `DROP COLUMN name_old`, so rolling back to 1.3 breaks against the new schema. Instead: expand in 1.4 (add the new shape, dual-write), contract in 1.5 or later once 1.3 is no longer a rollback target. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-153 — Migration with no down path and no exception.** Banned: a migration file with no reversal and no documented forward-fix plan. Defeats: DET-INF-018. Bad: `migrations/0042_add_billing.sql` exists only as an `up` script applied by hand in a SQL console, with nothing recorded about what ran on production. Instead: ship the migration through the pipeline with a down script, or record the forward-fix exception in the release checklist before merge. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-154 — Tearing down the return path at deploy time.** Banned: deleting the previous artifact, draining the idle blue/green environment, or pruning rollout history as part of the same action that ships the new version. Defeats: DET-INF-017. Bad: the deploy job ends with `docker image prune -a`, removing the last good image minutes after the new one starts. Instead: retain the previous version until the observation window closes and the release is declared good. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DO-151 — Staging rollback drill.** Verifies: DO-301, DO-302, DO-308. Check: in staging, deploy a deliberately broken version, then execute the exact rollback command written in the runbook (for example `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`) and time it; confirm both revisions appear in rollout/deploy history. Pass: previous version serves healthy traffic within the stated target time. Fail: block shipment of the release process until the drill passes. Before a staging environment is provisioned, this gate's disposition is a recorded provisioning waiver per the §6.3 protocol; it unblocks when a staging environment is provisioned and the drill can run against a deployed release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-152 — Deploy-record and retention audit.** Verifies: DO-302, DO-307. Check: script reads the last deploy record, resolves production → artifact digest → commit SHA, and confirms the previous artifact still exists in the registry/platform (`docker manifest inspect <image>@<previous-digest>` or platform build list). Pass: record resolves and previous artifact is present. Fail: block the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-153 — Migration down-path check.** Verifies: DO-305, DO-306. Check: CI step lists migration files added by the change and fails unless each has a matching down/reversal file or an exception entry in the release checklist. Pass: every new migration has a down path or a recorded exception. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-154 — Runbook rollback-step check.** Verifies: DO-301, DO-309. Check: grep the runbook/release checklist for the release's rollback command and named abort thresholds before the production deploy job runs. Pass: exact command and thresholds present. Fail: block the deploy. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Rollback theater.** A rollback paragraph exists in the wiki but has never been executed; the first real attempt happens during an outage and discovers the old artifact is gone. Catch it: no drill record in the last cadence window means the path is unproven, whatever the document says.
- **Half rollback.** Code returns to the previous version while config, flags, or schema stay in the new state, leaving a combination no version was tested in. Catch it: the rollback record must list every layer touched (artifact, flag, config, schema) and its end state.
- **Silent rollback.** The operator rolls back and tells nobody; monitoring "recovers," users see inconsistent behavior, and the postmortem never happens. Catch it: a rollback with no incident/status entry in the deploy record is a process failure even when it works.
- **Rollback amnesia.** Nobody records why the release was rolled back, so the same fault is rediscovered from scratch next release. Catch it: the deploy record for the bad version must carry the fault summary before it is closed.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Runbook rollback step written before release](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-301.
- [Example 2 — Expand-and-contract instead of a destructive migration](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-305.
- [Example 3 — Flag flip as the first rollback action](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-304.

## Recall anchors

- Rollback is a repoint to a kept artifact, never a forward fix under pressure.
- If the rollback step is not written before the release, it does not exist.
- Flag flip first; artifact rollback second.
- Expand now, contract next release — the old code must run on the new schema.
- A rollback that was never drilled is a hope, not a plan.

## Checklist

- [ ] Runbook names the exact rollback command for this release (DO-301).
- [ ] Previous artifact retained and confirmed present in the registry/platform (DO-302).
- [ ] Abort thresholds and the authorized rollback caller are in the release record (DO-309).
- [ ] Flagged changes list the flag flip as the first rollback action (DO-304).
- [ ] Every new migration has a down path or a recorded exception (DO-306).
- [ ] No schema element is dropped or renamed in the release that retires its use (DO-305).
- [ ] Last staging rollback drill passed within its target time (DO-308).
- [ ] Deploy record maps production → artifact digest → commit SHA (DO-307).

<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/scaling/SKILL.md -->

# scaling

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
- **Depends on:** containers, kubernetes
- **Feeds into:** reliability, cloud-costs

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a production workload needs defined scaling behavior — resource sizing, autoscaling, saturation alerting, or a documented capacity ceiling — before a launch, a traffic event, or in response to observed saturation.
- **Do NOT use when:** the service has no production traffic yet and no launch is scheduled — record the single-instance ceiling under the hosting or servers-vps skill and revisit at launch; speculative autoscaling for an unused service is ceremony, not capacity.

## Rules

1. **DO-241 — Scale from measurements, not forecasts.** Every scaling decision cites a golden-signal measurement (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) from the monitoring dashboards; a change justified only by an expected traffic guess is not approved.
2. **DO-242 — Requests and limits on every workload.** Every production container declares CPU and memory requests and limits, sized from observed p95 usage in staging or production metrics, never copied from a tutorial or left unset.
3. **DO-243 — Saturation alerts fire before exhaustion.** Alerts exist for each resource that can saturate the service — CPU, memory, disk, connection pools, queue depth — with thresholds set below the exhaustion point, so the page arrives while headroom remains.
4. **DO-244 — Stateless tiers scale horizontally.** Stateless workloads scale by adding replicas behind a load balancer or an autoscaler (HPA or platform equivalent) that measures utilization against the declared requests; no request means no autoscaling signal.
5. **DO-245 — The autoscaling ceiling is a deliberate number.** Every autoscaler sets a maximum replica count, recorded with the cost reasoning behind it; the ceiling is a budget decision owned with the cloud-costs skill, not a default left at the platform maximum.
6. **DO-246 — Stateful tiers scale on their own path.** Databases and stateful services scale by managed replication, read replicas, or connection management chosen with D5; adding stateless app replicas against a saturated single database is not a scaling action.
7. **DO-247 — Load-test before the traffic event.** Before any launch, campaign, or seasonal peak, a load test runs in staging and the tested ceiling — sustained throughput with p95 latency inside the service's target — is recorded as a number in the project docs.
8. **DO-248 — Scale-down is designed, not accidental.** Autoscalers declare a stabilization window and connections drain gracefully on replica removal; replica counts oscillating up and down within minutes are treated as a defect and fixed before production reliance.
9. **DO-249 — Sizing is reviewed after change.** Requests, limits, and ceilings are re-checked against observed usage after every load test and after any material traffic-pattern change; the review and its outcome are recorded.
10. **DO-250 — A single server still states its ceiling.** A workload on one VPS or a non-autoscaling platform documents its capacity ceiling (the load-test number or the measured saturation point) and carries saturation monitoring; having neither an autoscaler nor a stated ceiling is a fail.
11. **DO-251 — Every scaling change leaves a record.** Each change to replica counts, ceilings, requests, or limits is logged with the date and the measurement that motivated it, so capacity history is auditable.
12. **DO-252 — Autoscaler behavior is proven end to end.** Before production relies on an autoscaler, a staging run drives load up and down and observes scale-up to the ceiling and scale-down without flapping; unobserved autoscaler configuration is untested configuration.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-121 — Workload with no resources declared.** Banned: a production container with no CPU or memory requests or limits. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: a Deployment manifest with no `resources:` block, sized by whatever the node happens to have left. Instead: declare requests and limits sized from observed p95 usage on every container before the workload ships. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-122 — Unbounded autoscaler.** Banned: an autoscaler with no maximum replica count, or a maximum left at the platform default without a recorded cost decision. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: an HPA with `maxReplicas: 500` copied from a template on a service whose tested ceiling needs 6 replicas, turning a traffic spike or a retry storm into an unbounded bill. Instead: set the ceiling from the load-test result and the budget, and record the reasoning with the cloud-costs skill. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-123 — Capacity by forecast.** Banned: provisioning or promising capacity for a launch or traffic event from an estimate alone, with no load test behind the number. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: "Expect 10,000 launch-day users, so run 20 replicas" with no staging test showing what one replica sustains. Instead: load-test in staging, record the tested ceiling, and size replica counts from that number. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-124 — CPU-only saturation view.** Banned: judging scaling need from CPU alone while the service's real bottleneck — memory, disk, connection pool, or queue depth — is unmonitored. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: a dashboard charting CPU at 40% while the database connection pool sits exhausted and requests queue. Instead: monitor all four golden signals with saturation tracked for the resource that actually limits the service. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-121 — Resource and ceiling audit.** Verifies: DO-242, DO-245. Check: script over the production manifests or platform config confirms every container carries a `resources:` block and every autoscaler declares both a minimum and a maximum replica count. Pass: 100% of workloads have resources and no autoscaler is unbounded. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-122 — Load test report on file.** Verifies: DO-247, DO-252. Check: a load test report (k6, Locust, or platform equivalent) from staging is filed in the project docs, stating sustained throughput, p95 latency at that throughput, and the tested ceiling. Pass: the report exists and the ceiling is a recorded number. Fail: block the launch or traffic event. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-123 — Autoscaler end-to-end observation.** Verifies: DO-244, DO-248. Check: in staging, drive load until the autoscaler adds replicas, hold, then remove load and watch scale-down. Pass: replicas rise to at most the ceiling under load and drain without oscillation after load stops. Fail: block production reliance on the autoscaler. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-124 — Saturation alert coverage.** Verifies: DO-243, DO-250. Check: list the alerting rules for the service and confirm CPU, memory, disk, and the service's bottleneck resource (connections or queue depth) each have a threshold below exhaustion; fire one test alert. Pass: every listed resource alerts and the test alert reaches the on-call path. Fail: warn and fix before the next traffic event. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Bigger-box reflex.** Answering every slowdown by moving to a larger instance without identifying which resource saturates; the bottleneck moves with the box and the bill arrives first — find the saturating signal (DO-241) before spending.
- **Average-based sizing.** Requests sized from mean CPU or memory, so ordinary peaks exceed them and pods throttle or OOM at the busiest moment — size from p95 and compare against staging metrics at review.
- **Replicas in front of a saturated database.** Doubling the web tier while the single-writer database is the constraint; latency gets worse as contention grows — check stateful saturation (DO-246) before touching stateless counts.
- **Set-and-forget autoscaler.** An HPA shipped once and never re-observed after traffic patterns, instance types, or the app itself changed — the DO-249 review exists because last year's ceiling is a stale number.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Requests and limits sized from p95 usage](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-242.
- [Example 2 — Autoscaler with a ceiling and a stabilization window](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-245, DO-248.
- [Example 3 — Load test before a launch event](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-247.

## Recall anchors

- Scale from measurements, never from forecasts.
- No requests, no autoscaling — and no headroom.
- Every autoscaler has a ceiling, and the ceiling is a cost decision.
- Load-test before the event; the tested ceiling is a recorded number.
- Scale-down is designed: stabilize, drain, never flap.

## Checklist

- [ ] Golden-signal dashboards reviewed and the motivating measurement cited for this scaling change (DO-241).
- [ ] Every production container sets requests and limits from observed p95 usage (DO-242).
- [ ] Saturation alerts exist below exhaustion for CPU, memory, disk, and the bottleneck resource (DO-243).
- [ ] Autoscalers declare a maximum replica count with the cost reasoning recorded (DO-245, G-DO-121).
- [ ] Stateful saturation checked with D5 before stateless replica counts change (DO-246).
- [ ] Load test report filed with the tested ceiling as a recorded number (DO-247, G-DO-122).
- [ ] Autoscaler observed end to end in staging: scale-up to the ceiling, scale-down without flapping (DO-248, DO-252, G-DO-123).
- [ ] Single-server workloads state a documented capacity ceiling with saturation monitoring (DO-250).
