<!-- generated from skills/devops-deployment/servers-vps/SKILL.md -->

# servers-vps

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP, "Logging Cheat Sheet" (exposure guidance cited by DET-INF-021/022) — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md Part 4, Infrastructure/Hosting elements
- **Depends on:** infrastructure-as-code, domains-dns
- **Feeds into:** deployment-strategies, reliability, rollback

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a single virtual private server (or a small fixed set of them) hosts production: provisioning, hardening, patching, deploying to, and eventually replacing that host.
- **Do NOT use when:** the workload runs on a managed platform or Kubernetes — use hosting or kubernetes instead. Do not use a VPS as an excuse to skip the discipline those platforms enforce automatically; the VPS operator supplies it by hand.

## Rules

1. **DO-121 — Scripted provisioning.** The server is provisioned by a script or playbook committed to the repo, never by remembered console clicks. Every package, user, and config file on the box traces to that script.
2. **DO-122 — Hardening before first deploy.** Before any application deploys: directory listing off, version banners suppressed, default pages and default vhosts removed, unused services stopped and disabled (DET-INF-022).
3. **DO-123 — No public admin surfaces.** Debug endpoints, admin panels, and status pages are never reachable on the public interface; admin access sits behind authentication plus a network restriction (VPN, allowlist, or localhost-only binding) (DET-INF-021).
4. **DO-124 — Reverse proxy terminates TLS.** The application sits behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, or equivalent) that terminates TLS and forwards to the app on a loopback or private port; the app port is not exposed publicly.
5. **DO-125 — Patching is scheduled and recorded.** OS and package updates run on a written cadence (at least monthly, security updates sooner), and each run is logged with its date in the ops record. A box with no patch record is a finding (DET-INF-025).
6. **DO-126 — Deploys land as artifacts.** A deploy installs a built artifact — a container image or a versioned release directory — never an in-place edit of files on the live server (DET-INF-004).
7. **DO-127 — Previous release stays switchable.** Releases live in versioned directories with a symlink (or proxy target) selecting the live one; the previous release remains on disk so rollback is a symlink flip, not a rebuild (DET-INF-017).
8. **DO-128 — Logs ship off the box.** Application and system logs stream or rotate to storage outside the server. Logs that exist only on the box are lost with it and fill its disk until then (DET-INF-013).
9. **DO-129 — Saturation has an alert and a ceiling.** Disk, memory, and CPU usage are monitored with an alert before exhaustion — disk at 80% at the latest — and the server's capacity ceiling is written in the project docs (DET-INF-027).
10. **DO-130 — Only required ports are open.** The firewall defaults to deny; the open-port list matches the architecture document exactly, and any port not in the document is closed in the same change that discovers it.
11. **DO-131 — Key-only, named access.** SSH password authentication and direct root login are disabled; each operator logs in with a named account and an individual key, and elevation is via sudo.
12. **DO-132 — The server is replaceable.** Everything needed to rebuild the host — provisioning script, config, deploy procedure, restore steps — lives in the repo, and a rebuild from those files alone is drilled before the server is trusted (G-DO-063).

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-061 — In-place live edits.** Banned: editing application code or config directly on the production server to "fix it quickly". Defeats: DET-INF-004. Bad: an operator SSHs in and patches a template file with a text editor; the fix exists on no other machine and vanishes at the next deploy. Instead: change the source in the repo, build a new artifact, and deploy it as a new release. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-062 — Default configuration shipped.** Banned: leaving the stock server page, default vhost, version banners, or directory listing live in production. Defeats: DET-INF-022. Bad: the domain's default vhost still serves the web server's welcome page and announces its exact version in response headers. Instead: apply the DO-122 hardening baseline before the first deploy and re-check it after every server change. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-063 — Public admin surface.** Banned: an admin panel, debug endpoint, or metrics page reachable from the public internet protected by nothing more than its own login form. Defeats: DET-INF-021. Bad: `/admin` answers on the public domain and takes password guesses at full speed. Instead: bind admin surfaces to localhost or a VPN interface, or put them behind an IP allowlist, with authentication on top. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-064 — The never-patched box.** Banned: a production server with no patch cadence and no patch record since provisioning. Defeats: DET-INF-025. Bad: the VPS has run 14 months; nobody can say which security updates it has or has not received. Instead: schedule the patch cadence, log every run with its date, and treat a stale log as a release blocker. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-061 — Port reconciliation scan.** Verifies: DO-122, DO-130. Check: automated — run `nmap -Pn --top-ports 1000 <host>` (full-range `-p-` at setup) from an external machine and diff the open ports against the architecture document's port list. Pass: the two lists are identical. Fail: block the release; close or document every extra port. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-062 — Banner and listing probe.** Verifies: DO-122, DO-123. Check: automated — `curl -sI https://<domain>/` shows no server version banner, `curl -s https://<domain>/assets/` returns 403 or 404 (never a listing), and each admin/debug path returns 403, 404, or a network refusal from a non-allowlisted address. Pass: all three probes behave as stated. Fail: block the release until the baseline is applied. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-063 — Rebuild drill.** Verifies: DO-121, DO-132. Check: manual, timed — provision a fresh VPS using only the repo's scripts, deploy the current release, restore data per the documented steps, and run the smoke tests. Pass: the rebuilt server serves the application correctly with no step taken from memory or from the old box. Fail: the server is not yet replaceable; fix the scripts and repeat. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-064 — Patch record audit.** Verifies: DO-125. Check: automated — read the last entry date in the ops patch log and compare it against the written cadence. Pass: the last recorded patch run is within one cadence interval of today. Fail: warn the operator; two consecutive misses block the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The pet server.** Nobody dares reboot or rebuild the box because nobody knows what state lives only on it. Catch it: if the rebuild drill (G-DO-063) has never been run, the server is a pet by definition.
- **The orphaned test vhost.** A staging or test vhost from an early experiment still answers on the same box, unpatched and unmonitored, sharing the production IP. Catch it: list every vhost and service the provisioning script does not create; each one is removed or adopted into the script.
- **Monitoring that lives on the box.** The uptime check and the disk alert run on the server they watch, so a dead or full server reports nothing. Catch it: monitoring and log storage must be reachable and intact while the server is powered off.
- **Tribal-knowledge operations.** Restart commands, deploy quirks, and "watch out for" steps live in one operator's memory or chat history. Catch it: any step performed during an incident that is not in the repo's runbook is added to it before the incident is closed.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — An in-place hotfix replaced by an artifact deploy](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DO-126.
- [Example 2 — A default server configuration hardened before launch](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DO-122.
- [Example 3 — A public admin panel moved behind a network restriction](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DO-123.

## Recall anchors

- The server is replaceable; the repo is the server.
- Harden before the first deploy, not after the first incident.
- Artifacts in, symlink flips — never edits on the live box.
- Admin is never public; patches are never unrecorded.
- Logs and monitoring live somewhere the server's death cannot reach.

## Checklist

- [ ] Provisioning script in the repo reproduces the server with no manual steps (DO-121, G-DO-063).
- [ ] Hardening baseline applied: no default pages, banners, listings, or unused services (DO-122).
- [ ] Port scan output matches the architecture document exactly (G-DO-061).
- [ ] Admin and debug surfaces unreachable from a non-allowlisted address (DO-123, G-DO-062).
- [ ] Current deploy is an artifact in a versioned release directory; previous release still switchable (DO-126, DO-127).
- [ ] Patch log's last entry is within one cadence interval (DO-125, G-DO-064).
- [ ] Logs ship off the box and the disk alert fires at or before 80% (DO-128, DO-129).
- [ ] SSH is key-only with root login disabled and named operator accounts (DO-131).

# ssl-certificates

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D6 DevOps & Deployment (DO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Mozilla, "Server Side TLS" — https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS ; OWASP, "Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet" — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Protection_Cheat_Sheet.html
- **Depends on:** domains-dns, hosting
- **Feeds into:** cdn-strategy, reliability

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** any service becomes reachable over a network — first HTTPS setup, a new domain or subdomain goes live, a certificate is issued or replaced, TLS settings change, or a scan flags the TLS configuration.
- **Do NOT use when:** the service is local-only or reachable solely inside a private network with no public route (record that fact in the project notes instead). Do not hand-edit cipher suites outside a maintained profile — that is this skill's configuration step, not improvisation.

## Rules

1. **DO-221 — HTTPS everywhere, automated.** Every public hostname serves a valid certificate obtained through provider-managed issuance or an ACME client (Let's Encrypt via Certbot/acme.sh). A certificate installed by hand-upload with no renewal path does not satisfy this rule.
2. **DO-222 — Redirect all HTTP.** Every route, including API routes, answers plain HTTP with a 301 redirect to the same path over HTTPS. No route serves content or accepts credentials over HTTP.
3. **DO-223 — HSTS after stability.** HSTS is enabled only after HTTPS has been verified working on every route; the header is present on HTTPS responses once enabled and is never enabled as part of the first, untested TLS change.
4. **DO-224 — Mozilla Intermediate profile.** The server TLS configuration follows the Mozilla Intermediate profile: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, with the profile's cipher list. Deviations are listed in the project notes with a reason.
5. **DO-225 — Legacy protocols need an expiry.** TLS 1.0/1.1 or a legacy cipher may be enabled only for a named legacy client need, with a documented exception and an expiry date in the project notes. An exception without a date is removed.
6. **DO-226 — Renewal runs unattended.** Renewal is scheduled (ACME client timer or provider auto-renew) and a post-renewal hook reloads or restarts the server so the renewed certificate is actually served, not just stored on disk.
7. **DO-227 — Renewal is proven by dry-run.** `certbot renew --dry-run` (or the provider equivalent) passes at initial setup and after any server, DNS, or web-server change. An untested renewal is treated as no renewal.
8. **DO-228 — Expiry alert is the backstop.** An expiry monitor alerts at least 30 days before the served certificate's not-after date. The alert exists to catch automation failure; it is never the renewal mechanism itself.
9. **DO-229 — Zero mixed content.** No page served over HTTPS references an `http://` asset, script, stylesheet, or API endpoint. Asset URLs are HTTPS or scheme-relative behind the TLS terminator.
10. **DO-230 — Challenge type is chosen deliberately.** Wildcard certificates use DNS-01; per-host certificates use HTTP-01 or the web-server plugin. The chosen challenge and its credential (DNS API token scope) are recorded in the project notes.
11. **DO-231 — Full chain served.** The server presents the complete certificate chain (leaf plus intermediates); a scan or `openssl s_client -showcerts` shows no missing-intermediate error on any client.
12. **DO-232 — Scan after every TLS change.** An external scan (SSL Labs or `testssl.sh`) runs at launch and after any TLS configuration change; the grade and enabled protocol list are recorded in progress.md.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DO-111 — Manual certificate with calendar renewal.** Banned: a certificate installed once by hand (one-off Certbot run or uploaded commercial cert) with renewal left to memory or a calendar reminder. Defeats: DET-INF-016. Bad: the launch checklist says "renew cert in March" and no ACME timer or managed renewal exists. Instead: issue through an ACME client or provider-managed certificate with unattended renewal, a reload hook, and a dry-run proof. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-112 — HTTP left serving.** Banned: the site answers on plain HTTP without a redirect, or login/API routes accept HTTP. Defeats: DET-INF-014. Bad: `curl -sI http://example.com/login` returns 200 and the login form posts over HTTP. Instead: 301-redirect every HTTP route to its HTTPS equivalent and verify no route serves over HTTP. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-113 — Legacy TLS shipped unexamined.** Banned: default server TLS settings from an old base image or tutorial shipped as-is, leaving TLS 1.0/1.1 or obsolete ciphers enabled with no documented exception. Defeats: DET-INF-015. Bad: `testssl.sh` lists TLS 1.0 and 3DES as enabled and nobody can say why. Instead: apply the Mozilla Intermediate profile; keep any legacy protocol only as a dated, documented exception. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DO-114 — Hardcoded http:// references.** Banned: `http://` asset, script, or API URLs hardcoded in pages or configuration served over HTTPS. Defeats: DET-INF-015. Bad: the HTTPS homepage loads `http://cdn.example.com/app.js`, triggering mixed-content warnings. Instead: use the HTTPS URL (or scheme-relative URL behind the terminator) for every referenced resource. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-DO-111 — External TLS scan.** Verifies: DO-224, DO-225, DO-231, DO-232. Check: run `testssl.sh <domain>` (or the SSL Labs scan) at launch and after any TLS change. Pass: TLS 1.2/1.3 only (any legacy protocol matches a dated exception in the project notes), full chain presented, grade and protocol list recorded. Fail: block shipment until the configuration matches the Mozilla Intermediate profile. Before a production environment is provisioned, this gate's disposition is a recorded provisioning waiver per the §6.3 protocol; it unblocks when a production domain is provisioned and the deployed service is reachable over public TLS. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-112 — Redirect and HSTS probe (automated).** Verifies: DO-222, DO-223. Check: `curl -sI http://<domain>` and `curl -sI http://<domain>/login` return 301 to the `https://` URL; `curl -sI https://<domain>` shows the `Strict-Transport-Security` header once HTTPS is stable. Pass: every probed route redirects and the header is present. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-113 — Renewal proof.** Verifies: DO-221, DO-226, DO-227. Check: `certbot renew --dry-run` (or provider equivalent) exits 0, and the renewal timer/managed setting plus reload hook are shown in the server configuration. Pass: dry-run succeeds and the unattended renewal path is visible. Fail: block shipment — an unproven renewal is an unscheduled outage. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DO-114 — Expiry and mixed-content check (automated).** Verifies: DO-228, DO-229. Check: `echo | openssl s_client -connect <domain>:443 -servername <domain> 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate` shows more than 30 days remaining, an expiry alert rule exists at the 30-day threshold, and a crawl of key pages (browser console or `grep -r "http://" templates/`) finds zero `http://` resource references. Pass: all three conditions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Expiry-alert complacency.** The 30-day alert exists, so nobody checks whether auto-renewal actually works — until the alert fires during a holiday. Catch it: the dry-run gate (G-DO-113) is the mechanism check; the alert is only the backstop.
- **Cert renewed, server stale.** Renewal succeeds on disk but the web server keeps serving the old certificate because no reload hook runs. Catch it: after any renewal change, compare the served certificate's dates against the on-disk certificate.
- **HSTS on day one.** HSTS is enabled in the same change that first turns on HTTPS, locking in a misconfiguration before a single route is verified. Catch it: HSTS ships only in a later change, after the redirect probe passes.
- **Wildcard by default.** A wildcard certificate is issued because it was convenient, widening the blast radius of one private key across every subdomain. Catch it: per-host certificates are the default; a wildcard needs the DNS-01 decision recorded under DO-230.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Manual cert and calendar renewal](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DO-221, DO-226, DO-227.
- [Example 2 — HTTP left serving beside HTTPS](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DO-222, DO-223.
- [Example 3 — Tutorial TLS defaults and an http:// script](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DO-224, DO-229.

## Recall anchors

- Automate issuance and renewal; the expiry alert is the backstop, not the mechanism.
- Redirect every HTTP route — APIs and logins included.
- Mozilla Intermediate: TLS 1.2+ only; legacy needs a dated exception.
- Renewal is proven by dry-run, or it does not exist.
- Zero `http://` references on an HTTPS page.

## Checklist

- [ ] Certificate is provider-managed or ACME-issued, with unattended renewal and a reload hook (DO-221, DO-226).
- [ ] `certbot renew --dry-run` (or provider equivalent) passes and is re-run after server changes (DO-227).
- [ ] Every HTTP route 301-redirects to HTTPS; HSTS enabled only after HTTPS verified stable (DO-222, DO-223).
- [ ] Configuration matches the Mozilla Intermediate profile; any legacy protocol has a dated exception (DO-224, DO-225).
- [ ] Expiry alert set at 30 days and served certificate shows more than 30 days remaining (DO-228).
- [ ] No `http://` asset or API references on HTTPS pages (DO-229).
- [ ] Challenge type (DNS-01 for wildcards, HTTP-01/plugin per host) recorded in the project notes (DO-230).
- [ ] External scan grade and protocol list recorded in progress.md after the latest TLS change (DO-232).

## Department D7 — security

<!-- generated from skills/security/api-security/SKILL.md -->

# api-security

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D7 Security (SE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), https://orca.security/resources/blog/owasp-api-security-top-10/
- **Depends on:** owasp, session-security, auth-hardening
- **Feeds into:** security-audit, penetration-testing

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing, building, or reviewing any HTTP API endpoint — authentication, authorization, serialization, quotas, outbound fetching, or third-party API consumption.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work is the login/session lifecycle itself (use auth-hardening and session-security) or a general web vulnerability pass with no API surface (use owasp).

## Rules

1. **SE-041 — Authenticate every request on the server.** Every endpoint not on an explicit, documented public allowlist rejects requests without a valid credential, verified server-side; a check that exists only in the UI is not authentication.
2. **SE-042 — Authorize every object access against ownership (API1/BOLA).** An object ID in a request is a claim, not a permission: the server resolves the object's owner from the authenticated principal and returns 403/404 when they do not match.
3. **SE-043 — Authorize every function by role (API5/BFLA).** Privileged endpoints (admin, billing, moderation, export) check the caller's role server-side on every request, independent of what the client chose to render.
4. **SE-044 — Filter properties in both directions (API3/BOPLA).** Responses pass through an explicit field-allowlist serializer; writes bind only to a request DTO of writable fields, so extra submitted properties are ignored or rejected — never mass-assigned.
5. **SE-045 — Cap resource consumption per endpoint (API4).** Every list endpoint enforces a maximum page size, every endpoint a request-body size limit and a timeout, and every API key a quota; no endpoint runs unbounded.
6. **SE-046 — Protect sensitive business flows from automation (API6).** Signup, login-adjacent, checkout, coupon, OTP, and password-reset flows carry per-account and per-IP rate limits or equivalent anti-automation controls at the edge.
7. **SE-047 — Constrain server-side fetching of user-supplied URLs (API7/SSRF).** Outbound fetches go to allowlisted hosts only, deny private, loopback, and link-local ranges, re-validate the target after every redirect, and never attach internal credentials.
8. **SE-048 — Keep a complete, owned API inventory (API9).** Every deployed version and endpoint appears in the inventory with an owner and a retirement date; an undocumented live endpoint is treated as an incident, not a backlog item.
9. **SE-049 — Validate third-party API data as untrusted input (API10).** Responses consumed from external APIs are schema-validated and range-checked before use or storage, exactly like user input.
10. **SE-050 — Scope, expire, and rotate API keys and tokens.** Each key carries the least privilege it needs, an expiry, and a tested rotation path; keys are issued per consumer, never shared across services.
11. **SE-051 — Ship an authorization test matrix.** Automated tests cover each role × each protected endpoint with own, foreign, and missing credentials, including cross-tenant ID swaps, and run in CI on every change.
12. **SE-052 — Return safe errors and log authorization failures.** Error responses expose no stack traces, internal IDs, or existence oracles beyond the status code; every denied object or function access is logged with principal, endpoint, and object ID.

## BAN list

- **BAN-SE-021 — Trusting client-supplied identity or ownership.** Banned: authorizing from a request-supplied `userId`, `ownerId`, or `isAdmin` field. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Bad: `if (req.body.isAdmin) { deleteUser(...) }`. Instead: derive the principal and object ownership from the verified server-side session or token. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-022 — Returning the stored record as the response.** Banned: serializing the ORM/database object directly to the client. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Bad: `res.json(user)` exposing `passwordHash` and `internalNotes`. Instead: pass every response through an explicit field-allowlist serializer. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-023 — Shipping an API secret in a client bundle.** Banned: embedding private, service-role, or signing keys in browser or mobile code, including "public" environment variables. Defeats: DET-INF-006. Bad: a service-role key in a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable. Instead: keep the secret server-side and let the client call a scoped backend endpoint. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-024 — Unbounded collection endpoints.** Banned: list, search, or export endpoints with no maximum result size, timeout, or quota. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Bad: `GET /orders` returns every row to any authenticated key. Instead: enforce a maximum page size, a timeout, and a per-key quota on every collection endpoint. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-025 — Unrestricted fetching of user-supplied URLs.** Banned: server-side fetch of a caller-provided URL with no allowlist or network restriction. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Bad: `await fetch(req.body.webhookUrl)` reaching `http://169.254.169.254/`. Instead: allowlist hosts, deny private/loopback/link-local ranges, and re-validate after redirects. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-SE-021 — Authorization matrix suite.** Verifies: SE-041, SE-042, SE-043, SE-051. Check: run the API authorization test suite in CI (`pytest tests/api/test_authz_matrix.py` or the project's equivalent), covering each role × endpoint with own, foreign, and missing credentials. Pass: every foreign or unauthenticated case returns 401/403 and leaks no record data. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-022 — API inventory diff.** Verifies: SE-048. Check: export the live route listing from the framework and diff it against the documented inventory in CI (`diff <(list-routes) docs/api-inventory.md`). Pass: zero undocumented or unowned routes. Fail: block shipment until the inventory or the deployment is corrected. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-023 — Client bundle secret scan.** Verifies: SE-050. Check: scan the built client assets in CI (`gitleaks detect --source dist/client` or a grep for key/secret patterns over the bundle). Pass: no private key, token, or secret pattern found. Fail: block shipment and rotate any exposed credential. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-024 — API scan plus SSRF probe.** Verifies: SE-044, SE-047, SE-052. Check: run a ZAP API scan against the OpenAPI definition in CI (`zap-api-scan.py -t openapi.yaml -f openapi`), then manually submit a link-local URL (`http://169.254.169.254/`) to every user-URL fetch feature. Pass: no high-severity scan alerts and every SSRF probe is rejected. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Scanner-clean complacency.** The automated scan passes, so the API is declared secure — while BOLA stays untested because no scanner can judge ownership. Catch it: if the authorization matrix (G-SE-021) does not exist, the scan result proves nothing about authorization.
- **Happy-path-only security tests.** Tests cover the owner using their own data and stop there; no foreign-ID, lower-role, or missing-credential case exists. Catch it: count the negative cases in the suite — zero negative cases means zero authorization testing.
- **Shadow API versions.** `/v1` stays deployed and reachable after `/v2` launches, unpatched and absent from the inventory. Catch it: probe old version prefixes at every release and reconcile against the inventory.
- **Allowlist drift.** The SSRF or CORS allowlist grows by one-off exceptions until it includes internal or wildcard hosts. Catch it: review allowlist diffs like code, with an owner and an expiry on every exception.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Object access scoped to the owner](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects SE-042.
- [Example 2 — Allowlist serializer instead of the raw record](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects SE-044.
- [Example 3 — SSRF-safe server-side fetch](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects SE-047.

## Recall anchors

- An ID in the request is a claim, not a permission.
- Scanners cannot judge authorization — the role × endpoint matrix can.
- Serialize by allowlist, in both directions.
- Every deployed endpoint is inventoried and owned, or it is an incident.
- Cap every endpoint: page size, body size, timeout, quota.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every non-public endpoint authenticates server-side (SE-041).
- [ ] Object access resolves ownership from the principal, never the request body (SE-042).
- [ ] Response serializers and request DTOs are explicit allowlists (SE-044).
- [ ] Page-size, body-size, timeout, and quota caps exist on all endpoints (SE-045).
- [ ] User-supplied URL fetches are allowlisted and private-range-denied (SE-047).
- [ ] Live routes diff clean against the API inventory (G-SE-022).
- [ ] Authorization matrix suite passes in CI, including cross-tenant swaps (G-SE-021).
- [ ] Built client bundles scan clean for secrets (G-SE-023).

<!-- generated from skills/security/auth-hardening/SKILL.md -->

# auth-hardening

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D7 Security (SE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** NIST SP 800-63B Rev. 4, https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html ; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, "Authentication Cheat Sheet", https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
- **Depends on:** session-security, encryption
- **Feeds into:** api-security, backend-auth, security-audit

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Building or reviewing login, registration, password reset, MFA enrolment, or any privilege-change flow (role grant, email change, MFA reset).
- **Do NOT use when:** The question is token/session mechanics after login (use session-security), object-level authorization on API endpoints (use api-security), or password storage primitives in isolation (use encryption for the KDF parameters).

## Rules

1. **SE-061 — Password length policy.** Require at least 15 characters for single-factor passwords and at least 8 when MFA is also required; accept at least 64 characters; impose no composition rules (no forced symbol/uppercase mixes) per NIST SP 800-63B Rev. 4.
2. **SE-062 — Breached-password screening.** Screen every password at set and reset against a blocklist of known-breached and commonly used passwords; reject matches with a message that names the reason class, not the matched entry.
3. **SE-063 — No scheduled rotation, no hints.** Never force periodic password expiry absent evidence of compromise, never offer password hints, and never use knowledge-based recovery ("security questions").
4. **SE-064 — Paste and managers allowed.** Login and registration fields permit paste, autofill, and password-manager use; no `onpaste` blocking, no `autocomplete` suppression on credential fields.
5. **SE-065 — Strictest rate limits on auth.** Login, reset, and MFA-verification endpoints carry the strictest rate limits in the product, keyed on account identifier plus source IP — never on a client-supplied header alone (defeats DET-INF-023).
6. **SE-066 — Progressive delay, not silent failure.** After repeated failures, apply progressive delays and, at a defined threshold, a temporary lock or step-up challenge; the limit values live in config, not scattered constants.
7. **SE-067 — Generic failure responses.** Login and recovery responses never reveal whether an account exists: identical message, status, and response shape for "no such account" and "wrong password"; flatten obvious timing differences where feasible.
8. **SE-068 — Passwords hashed with a password KDF.** Store passwords only as Argon2id hashes (first choice), or scrypt/bcrypt/PBKDF2 at current OWASP parameters; never plaintext, never reversible encryption, never a fast general-purpose hash.
9. **SE-069 — MFA offered, pushed for privilege.** Offer MFA to every account — TOTP or WebAuthn/passkeys preferred over SMS — and require it (or a recorded exception) for admin and other privileged roles.
10. **SE-070 — Recovery as strong as login.** Reset tokens are single-use, short-lived, and unguessable; a successful reset invalidates existing sessions and notifies the account holder out-of-band; the reset endpoint never confirms whether the email is registered.
11. **SE-071 — Re-authentication for privilege changes.** Role grants, email changes, password changes, and MFA resets require the current password or an active MFA factor, and each notifies the account holder through a channel they already control.
12. **SE-072 — Auth events logged and alerted.** Log every authentication event — success, failure, reset requested/completed, MFA enrolment/change, lockout — with account, IP, and timestamp, and alert on anomaly patterns (failure bursts, impossible travel, stuffing signatures).

## BAN list

- **BAN-SE-031 — Any-password or test-mode login.** Banned: a login path that accepts any password, a fixed test password, or a backdoor bypass flag in shipped code. Defeats: DET-FAKE-001. Bad: `if (password === "test123" || user) { createSession(user) }` left in production. Instead: verify the submitted password against the stored KDF hash on every login, with no alternate success path. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-032 — Reset flow that fakes or leaks.** Banned: a password-reset flow that reports success without issuing a real single-use token, or whose response reveals whether the account exists. Defeats: DET-FAKE-020. Bad: "No account for that email" on the reset form, or a reset link that never expires and can be replayed. Instead: always return the same neutral confirmation, issue a single-use short-lived token, and expire it on first use. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-033 — Client-trusted privilege flags.** Banned: accepting role or privilege state (`isAdmin`, `role`) from the request body, a cookie, or any client-controlled value. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: `if (req.body.isAdmin) grantAdmin()`. Instead: read the role from the server-side account record on every privileged request and re-check it at the endpoint. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-034 — Unlimited auth attempts.** Banned: login, reset, or MFA endpoints with no rate limit, lockout, or progressive delay. Defeats: DET-INF-023. Bad: a `/login` route reachable at full request speed from a single IP indefinitely. Instead: enforce per-account and per-IP limits with progressive delays on the auth endpoints, stricter than any other route class. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-035 — Plaintext or fast-hash password storage.** Banned: storing passwords in plaintext, reversibly encrypted, or hashed with MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 or another fast general-purpose hash. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: a `users` table column holding `sha256(password)`. Instead: store an Argon2id (or approved KDF) hash with a per-password salt generated by the KDF. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-SE-031 — Auth abuse test pack.** Verifies: SE-065, SE-066, SE-067, SE-070. Check: run the scripted abuse suite against staging — a credential-stuffing burst (100 rapid attempts), a reset-token replay, a reset token used after expiry, and enumeration probes against login and reset. Pass: burst is throttled or locked by the configured threshold, replayed and expired tokens are rejected, and enumeration probes return indistinguishable responses. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-032 — NIST policy conformance assertion.** Verifies: SE-061, SE-062, SE-063, SE-064. Check: automated config assertion against the live auth configuration — minimum length ≥15 (single-factor) / ≥8 (with MFA), maximum length ≥64, composition rules off, forced rotation off, breached-password screening on, paste allowed. Pass: every assertion matches. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-033 — Password storage audit.** Verifies: SE-068. Check: `grep -RInE "md5\(|sha1\(|sha256\(.*password|password.*plaintext" src/` plus a schema inspection confirming the credential column stores KDF output (Argon2id/scrypt/bcrypt/PBKDF2 identifier prefix). Pass: zero fast-hash or plaintext hits and a recognised KDF format in stored credentials. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-034 — Privilege-change drill.** Verifies: SE-069, SE-071, SE-072. Check: manual drill on staging — grant a role, change an account email, and reset MFA, each first without re-authentication, then with it. Pass: every change is refused without re-authentication, succeeds with it, produces a holder notification, and appears in the auth event log. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-channel provision (pre-provisioning): where the operator has no email or SMS channel available, the holder notifications are delivered to a local simulated channel — a captured test inbox or an SMS double — and the drill otherwise runs unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, a drill with notification delivery over a real channel remains required before public launch, and simulated delivery must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).

## Anti-patterns

- **Lockout as a denial-of-service gift.** Hard permanent lockouts let an attacker disable any account by failing logins as them; catch it by checking that throttling pairs per-account limits with per-IP limits and a recovery path that does not depend on the locked factor.
- **Security theatre policy.** Composition rules and 30-day rotation that push users to `Password1!` and sticky notes while the minimum length stays at 8; catch it by reading the policy as an attacker — length and blocklist do the work, rituals do not.
- **MFA bolted onto login only.** MFA enforced at sign-in but absent from recovery and MFA-reset flows, so the weakest path bypasses it; catch it by walking every path that ends in an authenticated session and checking each one demands the same assurance.
- **Helpful error messages.** Distinct "user not found" / "wrong password" / "account locked" responses written for support convenience; catch it by diffing the three responses byte-for-byte in a test account sweep.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Password policy rewritten to NIST 800-63B](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects SE-061, SE-062, SE-063.
- [Example 2 — Login endpoint gains throttling and generic errors](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects SE-065, SE-066, SE-067.
- [Example 3 — Reset and privilege-change flow made real](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects SE-070, SE-071.

## Recall anchors

- Length and blocklist beat composition rules and rotation rituals.
- The strictest rate limits in the product belong on auth endpoints.
- Never reveal whether the account exists — anywhere, including reset.
- Recovery is part of login's strength, not an exception to it.
- Privilege changes re-authenticate and notify, every time.

## Checklist

- [ ] Password policy matches SE-061/SE-063 and passes the G-SE-032 config assertion.
- [ ] Breached-password screening is active at set and reset (SE-062).
- [ ] Auth endpoints are rate-limited per account + IP with progressive delay (SE-065, SE-066; G-SE-031 passes).
- [ ] Login and reset responses are indistinguishable for existing vs. non-existing accounts (SE-067).
- [ ] Stored credentials are KDF hashes only (SE-068; G-SE-033 passes).
- [ ] MFA is offered to all accounts and required for privileged roles (SE-069).
- [ ] Reset tokens are single-use and short-lived, sessions invalidated on reset (SE-070).
- [ ] Privilege changes re-authenticate, notify the holder, and are logged (SE-071, SE-072; G-SE-034 passes).

<!-- generated from skills/security/content-moderation/SKILL.md -->

# content-moderation

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D7 Security (SE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.tspa.org/curriculum/ts-curriculum/content-moderation-simulation/
- **Depends on:** auth-hardening, audit-trails (D14)
- **Feeds into:** security-audit, compliance-audit (D14)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product accepts user-generated content, user profiles, messages, reviews, or uploads — anywhere a user can report content or an account, or the platform must act on abuse, spam, or illegal content.
- **Do NOT use when:** the site has no user content at all (a static marketing page needs no moderation system); for the legal determination of jurisdiction-specific duties (NCMEC reporting, EU DSA notice-and-action) — implement the technical controls here and route the legal call to D14 privacy-laws / compliance-audit.

## Rules

1. **SE-261 — Policy exists in two forms.** Publish a user-readable policy and keep an internal enforcement guide with a worked example per clause; every enforcement decision cites a clause that exists in both.
2. **SE-262 — Reporting reaches a staffed queue.** Every content item and every account exposes an in-product report action; a submitted report creates a queue row with category, reporter, target, and timestamp, and each priority tier has a written response target.
3. **SE-263 — Automation queues, humans decide the top of the ladder.** Automated detection (spam filters, hash-matching, classifiers) may enqueue, label, and reduce visibility; it never issues a ban or a mass removal without a human decision.
4. **SE-264 — The queue is priority-tiered.** Imminent-harm and illegal-content reports are tier 1 and reviewed before all other tiers; tier order and per-tier review targets are written in the enforcement guide, not improvised per shift.
5. **SE-265 — Enforcement follows the ladder.** Actions escalate in order — label, reduce visibility, remove, suspend, ban — and the chosen rung is proportionate to the clause violated and the account's history; skipping rungs requires a recorded reason.
6. **SE-266 — Every action is logged.** Each enforcement action records actor, policy clause, evidence reference, and timestamp in an append-only log; an action with no log entry is treated as not defensible and is reverted on discovery.
7. **SE-267 — Appeals reach a different reviewer.** Every enforcement notice includes a working appeal path; where staffing allows, the appeal is decided by a reviewer other than the original decision-maker, and the appeal outcome is logged against the original action.
8. **SE-268 — Illegal content is a hard lane, not a policy choice.** Known-CSAM hash matches and credible imminent-harm reports bypass normal tiers: content is preserved for reporting, access is restricted immediately, and escalation follows the runbook; the jurisdiction-specific reporting duty itself is confirmed with D14, never improvised.
9. **SE-269 — Moderation tooling is least-privilege and admin-only.** Queue access is granted per role, enforced server-side on every moderation endpoint, and no moderation route is reachable outside the authenticated admin surface.
10. **SE-270 — Moderator welfare is designed in.** Graphic content is blurred by default with a warning before reveal, queue tooling never autoplays media, and exposure rotation for tier-1 reviewers is defined in the enforcement guide.
11. **SE-271 — Report categories map 1:1 to policy clauses.** Every category offered in the report UI names a clause in the public policy; a category with no clause, or a clause with no category, blocks release until reconciled.
12. **SE-272 — Accountability is measured, not asserted.** The action log produces, per period: report volume by tier, median time-to-first-review per tier against target, and appeal overturn rate; these figures are reviewed on a set cadence and guide fixes are filed from them.

**Minimal tier.** A small product with user content (a single community surface, one moderator role, low report volume) runs the minimal tier of this skill instead of the full operation: an in-product report action on every content item and account (SE-262), one queue with two priorities — the illegal/imminent-harm hard lane (SE-268), which is never simplified away, and everything else under a single written response target — a public policy whose clauses the report categories map to (SE-271), an enforcement ladder with an appeal path, least-privilege admin-only queue access (SE-269), and the action log (SE-272, reduced to report volume and time-to-first-review until volume justifies per-tier reporting). The full tier — priority tiers with per-tier targets (SE-264), moderator-welfare rotation (SE-270), per-tier SLA reporting (G-SE-133) — applies when report volume or reviewer headcount makes a single queue and a single target unworkable, and the tier in force is recorded in the enforcement guide.

## BAN list

- **BAN-SE-131 — Report button that submits nowhere.** Banned: a report control that opens a mailto link, posts to an unmonitored inbox, or returns success without writing a queue row. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Bad: the Report button calls `POST /reports`, whose handler sends an email to reports@ and discards the payload. Instead: the handler inserts a queue row (category, target, reporter, timestamp) and returns the row's tracking ID. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-132 — Moderation actions that don't persist.** Banned: queue UI that marks an item "resolved" or "actioned" in local state while writing nothing to the database or action log. Defeats: DET-FAKE-010. Bad: clicking Remove hides the post in the moderator's browser; a reload shows it live again and no log entry exists. Instead: the action commits the state change and its log entry in one transaction, and the UI renders the persisted result. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-133 — Staged review notifications.** Banned: telling a reporter or an author "your report was reviewed" / "action was taken" on a timer or on submission, independent of any actual decision. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Bad: the intake endpoint immediately emails the reporter "We've reviewed your report" before the item enters the queue. Instead: notifications are emitted only by the decision event, and state the actual outcome and the appeal path. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-134 — Moderator role enforced only in the UI.** Banned: hiding moderation controls from non-moderators in the client while the moderation endpoints accept any authenticated (or unauthenticated) request. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: `/api/moderation/ban` checks only that a session cookie exists because the button is admin-only in the frontend. Instead: every moderation endpoint verifies the moderator role server-side and returns 403 otherwise. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-135 — Intake that swallows failures and reports success.** Banned: a report or appeal handler that catches a queue-write or storage error, logs nothing, and still returns a success response. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Bad: `try { await queue.insert(report) } catch { /* ignore */ }` followed by `201 Report received`. Instead: a failed insert returns an error to the user, raises an alert, and the report is never acknowledged as received. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-SE-131 — End-to-end report drill.** Verifies: SE-262, SE-266, SE-267. Check: automated workflow test — file a test report through the public UI, trace it to a queue row, a decision, and an appeal, asserting a log entry exists at each step. Pass: all four records exist and link to each other. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-132 — Persistence and role test.** Verifies: SE-269, BAN-SE-132, BAN-SE-134. Check: automated API test — perform a removal as a moderator, reload the target from the database and assert the removal and its log entry persisted; repeat the same call as a regular user. Pass: state persisted; non-moderator call returns 403. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-133 — Queue SLA report.** Verifies: SE-264, SE-272. Check: automated query over the action log for the last 30 days computing median time-to-first-review per priority tier, compared against the targets in the enforcement guide. Pass: every tier at or under target, or a filed remediation note per breached tier. Fail: warn and escalate to the department lead. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-134 — Policy-coverage check.** Verifies: SE-261, SE-271. Check: manual checklist — list every report category in the shipped UI and trace each to a clause in the public policy and an example in the enforcement guide; list every ladder rung and confirm it is reachable in the queue UI. Pass: zero unmapped categories, clauses, or rungs. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Keyword-list theater.** The "moderation system" is an ever-growing banned-word list with no queue, clauses, or metrics. Catch it: ask where a report goes and what the overturn rate is — if neither exists, there is no system.
- **Shadow queue.** Moderators coordinate actions in chat or DMs and apply them without queue entries, so the log shows a fraction of real enforcement. Catch it: sample live enforcement outcomes and try to find their log entries.
- **Rubber-stamp appeals.** Appeals are decided by the original decision-maker in bulk with near-zero overturns and no reasons recorded. Catch it: check the appeal log for reviewer identity and overturn rate before calling the appeal path real.
- **Policy drift.** The team's actual practice evolves (new violation types, new shortcuts) while the public policy and enforcement guide stay frozen. Catch it: compare the last month's cited clauses against the published policy text.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Report intake that reaches a queue](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects SE-262 (BAN-SE-131).
- [Example 2 — Classifier flag without an auto-ban](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects SE-263.
- [Example 3 — Logged enforcement with a real appeal](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects SE-266, SE-267.

## Recall anchors

- A report button that reaches no staffed queue is a defect, not a feature.
- Automation queues and labels; humans decide bans and mass removals.
- No log entry, no enforcement — unlogged actions get reverted.
- Illegal content is a hard legal lane: preserve, restrict, escalate, let D14 make the legal call.
- Every report category names a public policy clause, or it does not ship.

## Checklist

- [ ] Public policy and internal enforcement guide both exist, with an example per clause (SE-261).
- [ ] Report drill passed end to end: report → queue → decision → appeal, all logged (G-SE-131).
- [ ] Moderation endpoints reject non-moderators server-side with 403 (SE-269).
- [ ] No automated filter can ban or mass-remove without a human decision (SE-263).
- [ ] Median time-to-first-review per tier is within target or has a remediation note (G-SE-133).
- [ ] Every UI report category traces to a public policy clause (G-SE-134).
- [ ] Graphic content is blurred by default in the queue; no autoplay (SE-270).
- [ ] Appeal overturn rate and tier volumes were produced from the action log this period (SE-272).

<!-- generated from skills/security/dependency-safety/SKILL.md -->

# dependency-safety

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D7 Security (SE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://osv.dev/ ; https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: it works from the project's own manifests, lockfiles, and published vulnerability advisories — primary sources read directly, not another skill's output. Its hygiene rules feed supply-chain.
- **Feeds into:** supply-chain

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** adding, updating, or removing a dependency; setting up CI for a project; preparing a release; triaging a vulnerability alert; choosing or pinning a base image.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is how the release artifact itself was built, signed, or provenance-attested — that is supply-chain. License legality beyond a compatibility flag is D14 licensing.

## Rules

1. **SE-101 — The lockfile is the build input.** A lockfile pinning every direct and transitive version is committed, and CI installs from it with the frozen/locked mode of the stack (`npm ci`, `pip install --require-hashes`, or equivalent). A build that resolves versions at install time fails this rule by definition.
2. **SE-102 — One SBOM per release.** CI generates an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) from the shipped manifest for every release and stores it with the release artifacts.
3. **SE-103 — Scanning runs in CI and on a schedule.** A vulnerability scanner (OSV-Scanner, `npm audit`, `pip-audit`, or the stack equivalent) runs on every change and on a recurring schedule against the last released manifest; a scheduled run that finds a new critical opens an alert, not just a log line.
4. **SE-104 — Reachable criticals and highs block release.** A critical or high vulnerability in a reachable dependency stops the release until fixed. An unreachable or disputed finding is exempted only by a written, dated analysis (for example a VEX note) naming the finding, the reachability reasoning, and a review-by date.
5. **SE-105 — Update automation is on.** Dependabot, Renovate, or the platform equivalent is configured for every manifest and base image in the repo; security fixes are fast-tracked as individual PRs, routine updates are batched on a stated cadence, and opened update PRs are merged or explicitly rejected — never left to rot.
6. **SE-106 — New dependencies pass an adoption check.** Before a dependency is added, the PR records: it is actively maintained, its license is compatible (flag conflicts to D14 licensing), and it is actually needed over the standard library or an existing dependency.
7. **SE-107 — Install scripts are code execution.** The install/postinstall scripts of a new or updated dependency are read before merge, exactly as its library code would be; an unread install script blocks the merge.
8. **SE-108 — Abandoned and lookalike packages are rejected at adoption.** A package with no maintenance activity, or whose name is a lookalike of a popular package, is not adopted; if it is already in the tree, it gets a replacement plan or a dated risk acceptance under SE-104's format.
9. **SE-109 — Scanners run against what ships.** Scanning covers the production manifest and the final built image, not only the development tree; a green dev-tree scan is not evidence about the shipped artifact.
10. **SE-110 — Base images are pinned and rebuilt on a cadence.** Base images are pinned by digest, rebuilt on a stated cadence so OS patches flow in, and the rebuild is verified by a scan of the new image before it replaces the old one.
11. **SE-111 — The manifest stays coherent.** Every manifest entry is imported or used by the build, every import resolves to a manifest entry, and no version range is a wildcard or `latest`; removals prune the entry in the same change.
12. **SE-112 — Suppressions expire.** Every scanner suppression carries the finding ID, the justification, and an expiry date; expired suppressions fail CI until re-justified or fixed. There are no permanent global ignores.

## BAN list

- **BAN-SE-051 — Floating versions or a missing lockfile.** Banned: a manifest with `*`/`latest` ranges, or CI installing without a committed lockfile. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `"express": "*"` in package.json and CI running plain `npm install`. Instead: pin exact versions, commit the lockfile, and install in CI with `npm ci`. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-052 — Muting a critical or high finding without analysis.** Banned: adding a CVE to a scanner ignore list with no written reachability analysis. Defeats: DET-INF-025. Bad: `.osv-scanner.toml` gains an ignore entry commented "probably fine". Instead: fix the dependency, or file a dated VEX note with reachability reasoning and a review-by date (SE-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-053 — Merging a dependency whose install scripts nobody read.** Banned: adding or updating a package with install/postinstall hooks without reviewing what they execute. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: a PR adds a package whose postinstall downloads and runs a remote binary; the diff is approved on the version number alone. Instead: read the install scripts, record the review in the adoption check (SE-106, SE-107), then merge. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-054 — Unpinned base images.** Banned: a Dockerfile or deploy config referencing a mutable tag such as `latest` for a production base image. Defeats: DET-INF-026. Bad: `FROM node:latest`. Instead: pin by digest (`FROM node:22-bookworm-slim@sha256:<digest>`) and rebuild on the SE-110 cadence. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-055 — Known-bad dependency kept indefinitely with no decision on record.** Banned: a dependency with an unpatched critical/high CVE stays in the shipped tree release after release with no fix, VEX note, or risk acceptance. Defeats: DET-INF-025. Bad: the same critical finding appears in three consecutive release scans, acknowledged in chat each time, written down nowhere. Instead: fix it, replace it, or record a dated risk acceptance with an owner and a review-by date. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-SE-051 — CI vulnerability gate (automated).** Verifies: SE-103, SE-104. Check: CI runs `osv-scanner --lockfile=<committed lockfile>` (or `npm audit --audit-level=high` / `pip-audit` for the stack) on every PR and on the release branch. Pass: exit code 0 — no critical or high finding without an unexpired SE-104 analysis on file. Fail: merge and release are blocked. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-052 — Lockfile presence and sync (automated).** Verifies: SE-101, SE-111. Check: CI fails if no lockfile is committed, and a frozen install (`npm ci` or equivalent) succeeds without modifying it. Pass: lockfile present, in sync with the manifest, and unchanged by install. Fail: block merge; regenerate and commit the lockfile. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-053 — SBOM artifact check (automated).** Verifies: SE-102. Check: the release job emits an SBOM file (CycloneDX or SPDX) generated from the shipped manifest and attaches it to the release. Pass: SBOM exists, parses, and its component count matches the lockfile's package count. Fail: release is blocked until the SBOM is produced. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-054 — Scheduled rescan of the shipped artifact (automated).** Verifies: SE-103, SE-109. Check: a scheduled workflow (at least weekly) scans the last released manifest and final image and files an alert on any new critical or high. Pass: the schedule exists, its last run is under 8 days old, and its target is the released artifact — not the dev tree. Fail: treat as a missing control; fix the schedule before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-055 — Adoption review (manual).** Verifies: SE-106, SE-107, SE-108. Check: for every PR that adds a dependency, the PR record shows the maintenance check, the license flag, the need justification, and the install-script review. Pass: all four items recorded for every added dependency. Fail: the dependency is removed or the record is completed before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Scanner-green theater.** The scanner runs in CI but its exit code is ignored or its threshold is set so high nothing can fail; the pipeline is green while findings pile up. Catch it by checking that a deliberately vulnerable test branch actually fails G-SE-051.
- **Automation without follow-through.** Dependabot/Renovate PRs open on schedule and are never merged or rejected, so the inventory looks managed while nothing is ever patched. Catch it by counting update PRs older than the stated cadence.
- **Borrowed suppressions.** An ignore list or VEX note is copied from another project (or an older release) without re-checking reachability in this codebase. Catch it by sampling suppressions and asking for the analysis behind each.
- **Dev-tree confidence.** A "0 vulnerabilities" claim sourced from a scan that included devDependencies but never touched the production image. Catch it by asking which manifest and image the scan ran against (SE-109).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Floating range, no lockfile](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects SE-101, SE-111 (BAN-SE-051).
- [Example 2 — Muted critical vs. VEX note](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects SE-104, SE-112 (BAN-SE-052).
- [Example 3 — Unpinned base image](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects SE-110 (BAN-SE-054).

## Recall anchors

- The lockfile is the build input; resolution at install time is unreviewed by definition.
- Reachable critical blocks release; unreachable needs a dated VEX note, not a mute.
- Install scripts are code execution — read them before merge.
- Scan what ships: production manifest and final image, not the dev tree.
- Suppressions expire; update PRs get merged or rejected, never left to rot.

## Checklist

- [ ] Lockfile committed, in sync, and CI installs from it in frozen mode (SE-101, G-SE-052).
- [ ] SBOM generated for this release and stored with the artifacts (SE-102, G-SE-053).
- [ ] CI scan passes with no unexempted critical/high findings (SE-103, SE-104, G-SE-051).
- [ ] Every suppression has a finding ID, justification, and unexpired date (SE-112).
- [ ] Scheduled rescan targets the last released manifest and image (SE-109, G-SE-054).
- [ ] Update automation is configured and no update PR is older than the cadence (SE-105).
- [ ] Every newly added dependency has a recorded adoption check, including install-script review (SE-106, SE-107, SE-108, G-SE-055).
- [ ] Base images are digest-pinned and within their rebuild cadence (SE-110).

<!-- generated from skills/security/encryption/SKILL.md -->

# encryption

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D7 Security (SE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet and Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html ; Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator, https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/
- **Depends on:** secrets-management, auth-hardening
- **Feeds into:** security-audit, pci-compliance, api-security

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** choosing or reviewing how data is encrypted in transit or at rest — TLS configuration, field or file encryption, key storage, certificate lifecycle — in any application this repo builds.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is password verification parameters (use auth-hardening) or where secret values live day to day (use secrets-management); this skill owns the constructions and the transport profile, they own those surfaces.

## Rules

1. **SE-141 — Standard constructions only.** Every cipher, mode, and protocol comes from a maintained library as a standard option; no hand-designed cipher, protocol, key exchange, or obfuscation scheme ships. If the library does not offer it as a standard option, the design is wrong.
2. **SE-142 — TLS 1.2 minimum, 1.3 preferred.** The deployed TLS configuration is generated from a maintained profile (Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator, Intermediate or stricter) and the generated file is committed; TLS 1.0/1.1 and obsolete cipher suites are disabled (DET-INF-015).
3. **SE-143 — HTTP redirects, HSTS after proof.** Every HTTP request 301-redirects to HTTPS on every route including APIs; HSTS is enabled only after HTTPS is verified working on all hosts, and the decision is recorded (DET-INF-014).
4. **SE-144 — Certificates renew automatically.** Certificates are ACME-issued or provider-managed with unattended renewal proven by a dry run at setup; an expiry alert fires weeks before the expiry date as a backstop, never as the mechanism (DET-INF-016).
5. **SE-145 — AEAD at rest.** Sensitive data at rest is encrypted with an AEAD construction — AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 — through the platform or library API; unauthenticated modes and hand-assembled encrypt-then-MAC do not ship.
6. **SE-146 — Fresh random nonce per message.** Every AEAD encryption generates a new random nonce/IV from the library's CSPRNG and stores it with the ciphertext; a nonce is never constant, derived from the key alone, or reused under the same key.
7. **SE-147 — Keys come from a key store, never from code.** Encryption keys are generated and held by a KMS or platform key store; no key material appears in source, committed config, environment files in the repo, or the same store as the ciphertext it protects (DET-CODE-018).
8. **SE-148 — Envelope encryption for per-record keys.** Where individual records or tenants need their own keys, a data key encrypts the record and is itself stored encrypted under the key-store master key; master keys never leave the key store.
9. **SE-149 — Key access is logged and rotation is planned.** Every key use by the application is attributable in logs (key ID, caller, time — never key material), and each key has a recorded rotation path that re-wraps or re-encrypts without downtime.
10. **SE-150 — Passwords are hashed, never encrypted.** Passwords go through a dedicated password KDF per auth-hardening (Argon2id first choice per the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet); reversible encryption of passwords does not ship, because anyone with the key recovers every password.
11. **SE-151 — Tokens are stored hashed.** Session tokens, API reset links, and similar bearer secrets are stored as hashes and compared against the hash of the presented value, so a database leak does not hand out working tokens.
12. **SE-152 — No downgrade path.** Sensitive traffic has no plaintext fallback: a failed TLS handshake, an expired certificate, or an unreachable key store fails the operation closed — it never retries over HTTP, skips verification, or serves the data unencrypted.

## BAN list

- **BAN-SE-071 — Banned primitives and modes.** Banned: ECB mode, static or zero IVs, MD5 or SHA-1 for any security purpose, or a home-grown cipher/obfuscation routine. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Bad: `createCipheriv("aes-256-ecb", key, null)` for customer records. Instead: use an AEAD construction — `createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, randomBytes(12))` — and a current hash where a hash is the right tool. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-072 — Plaintext or unverified transport.** Banned: serving any route over HTTP without redirect, calling an internal API over `http://`, or disabling certificate verification to make a call succeed. Defeats: DET-INF-014. Bad: `fetch("http://billing.internal/charge")` because the internal cert had expired. Instead: renew the certificate, call the `https://` endpoint with verification on, and let the call fail closed until transport is sound. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-073 — Weak TLS profile or mixed content.** Banned: enabling TLS 1.0/1.1 or obsolete ciphers for compatibility, or loading any script, image, or API call over `http://` on an HTTPS page. Defeats: DET-INF-015. Bad: server profile keeps `TLSv1` enabled "for old clients" with no exception record. Instead: ship the Mozilla Intermediate profile (TLS 1.2+); a genuine legacy need gets a written exception with an expiry date, never silent acceptance. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-074 — Manually tended certificates.** Banned: a certificate installed by a one-off manual step with no auto-renewal configured and no expiry alert. Defeats: DET-INF-016. Bad: a Certbot run done once at launch; the cert expires 90 days later and the site goes down. Instead: enable the ACME client's unattended renewal (or the provider's managed certificate), prove it with a renewal dry run, and set an expiry alert weeks ahead. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-SE-075 — Keys beside the data.** Banned: an encryption key stored in source code, a committed config file, or the same database/volume as the ciphertext it protects. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: `FIELD_KEY = "9f2c…"` in `config.py`, committed next to the encrypted columns it unlocks. Instead: hold the key in the KMS or platform key store, reference it by key ID, and log every access. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-SE-071 — TLS profile scan.** Verifies: SE-142, SE-143, SE-152. Check: run `testssl.sh https://<prod-domain>` (or SSL Labs) against the deployed endpoint each release and archive the report. Pass: TLS 1.2+ only, no obsolete ciphers, HTTP 301-redirects to HTTPS, HSTS present. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-072 — Banned-primitive scan (automated).** Verifies: SE-141, SE-145. Check: `grep -rnEi "aes-[0-9]+-ecb|createCipher\(|md5|sha1|DES|RC4" src/` plus the SAST crypto ruleset in CI, and a manual read of every hit. Pass: zero hits in security-relevant code (checksums of public files with a recorded reason are the only exception). Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-073 — Certificate lifecycle check (automated).** Verifies: SE-144. Check: `echo | openssl s_client -connect <prod-domain>:443 -servername <prod-domain> 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates` and confirm the renewal mechanism (ACME timer or provider setting) and expiry alert exist. Pass: more than 30 days of validity remaining, auto-renewal configured, alert rule present. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-SE-074 — Key custody review.** Verifies: SE-147, SE-148, SE-149. Check: manual, checklist-driven — list every encryption key in the system; for each, name its key-store location, who/what can use it, its access log, and its rotation path; grep the repo for key-shaped strings as a cross-check. Pass: every key lives in a key store, separated from its ciphertext, logged, and rotatable. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Encryption theater.** Data is "encrypted at rest" by the disk or platform default while application-level secrets sit in plaintext columns. Catch it: ask which fields the application itself encrypts; if the answer is "the volume handles it," sensitive fields are unprotected against a database leak.
- **Nonce reuse by convenience.** A fixed IV constant sits at the top of the crypto module because per-message randomness "complicated the format." Catch it: search for IV/nonce literals; under GCM, one reused nonce pair breaks confidentiality of both messages.
- **Encrypting passwords "for recovery."** Passwords are reversibly encrypted so support can "look them up." Catch it: any decrypt path for a password column means a key holder — or a key thief — recovers every user's password, including ones reused elsewhere.
- **Verify-off debugging left in.** `rejectUnauthorized: false` or `verify=False` was added to get past a staging certificate error and rode along to production. Catch it: the G-SE-072 scan and a production-config read; the fix is always the certificate, never the check.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — AEAD field encryption with a fresh nonce](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects SE-145, SE-146 (BAN-SE-071).
- [Example 2 — Key held by the key store, not the code](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects SE-147 (BAN-SE-075).
- [Example 3 — HTTPS-only internal call that fails closed](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects SE-143, SE-152 (BAN-SE-072).

## Recall anchors

- Library constructions only — if it is not a standard option, the design is wrong.
- AEAD, fresh random nonce, every single message.
- Keys live in the key store, never beside the data they protect.
- Passwords are hashed; tokens are hashed; only data is encrypted.
- Renewal is automated and proven; the expiry alert is only the backstop.

## Checklist

- [ ] TLS profile is generated from the Mozilla profile and committed; scan shows TLS 1.2+ only (SE-142, G-SE-071).
- [ ] HTTP redirects to HTTPS everywhere and HSTS is on, with the decision recorded (SE-143).
- [ ] Certificate auto-renewal is configured and dry-run proven; expiry alert exists (SE-144, G-SE-073).
- [ ] At-rest encryption is AEAD with a fresh random nonce per message (SE-145, SE-146).
- [ ] Banned-primitive scan returns zero security-relevant hits (G-SE-072).
- [ ] Every key is in a key store, separated from its ciphertext, access-logged, and rotatable (SE-147–SE-149, G-SE-074).
- [ ] Passwords and stored tokens are hashed, never reversibly encrypted (SE-150, SE-151).
- [ ] No plaintext or verification-off fallback exists in any sensitive path (SE-152).
