<!-- generated from skills/qa-testing/integration-testing/SKILL.md -->

# integration-testing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Ham Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid" — https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html ; GitHub Docs, "Continuous integration" — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/continuous-integration
- **Depends on:** unit-testing, test-data
- **Feeds into:** e2e-testing, contract-testing, qa-gates

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** verifying that real components work together — the API against a real database, real migrations, real HTTP, real transaction and permission behavior — before the e2e layer spends its budget on the same defects.
- **Do NOT use when:** the behavior is one module's logic with no collaborator (unit-testing covers it), or the claim is about a full user journey in a browser (e2e-testing). Do not use this layer to re-test what the unit layer already pins; the pyramid stays narrow at the top.

## Rules

1. **QA-021 — Real database, real migrations.** The database under test is a real instance of the production engine, started by the harness (throwaway container or ephemeral schema) and built by running the project's actual migrations. A hand-maintained test schema or a different in-memory engine is a failed setup, not a shortcut.
2. **QA-022 — Real HTTP path.** Tests drive the API over real HTTP — a booted server or the framework's test client running the full middleware stack (auth, validation, error handling). Calling route handlers or services directly is a unit test wearing a costume.
3. **QA-023 — Mocks only at the system edge.** The only collaborators replaced are third parties outside the project's control (payment providers, email APIs), and they are replaced by the provider's own sandbox or a contract-verified stub. The project's own database, API, queue, and cache are never faked.
4. **QA-024 — Write, then read back elsewhere.** Every write endpoint has at least one test that performs the write and reads the result back through a different surface — a read endpoint, a second endpoint, or a direct database query. Asserting on the write response alone proves nothing about persistence.
5. **QA-025 — Each test seeds exactly what it needs.** Tests create their own records through factories or fixtures with known values and assert on those records. No test asserts on ambient or pre-existing data it did not create.
6. **QA-026 — Cleanup by construction.** Isolation comes from a fresh database, an ephemeral schema, or a transaction rolled back at test end. Cleanup by deleting rows is forbidden: a delete can remove another test's data and hides the very persistence bugs this layer exists to catch.
7. **QA-027 — Tenant and permission boundaries are tested here.** For every tenant-scoped or role-scoped entity, at least one test proves a cross-tenant or unauthorized read returns nothing (empty result, 403, or 404) and a cross-tenant write is rejected with no state change.
8. **QA-028 — Multi-write operations are atomicity-tested.** Any operation that writes more than one record has a test that forces a failure partway (invalid second write, killed constraint) and asserts that no partial state persists after the error response.
9. **QA-029 — Failure paths are integration cases.** Provider declines, dependency timeouts, and downstream 5xx responses (from the edge stub) are tested at this layer: the API must return its documented error and must not record a success state.
10. **QA-030 — Deterministic and order-independent.** The layer passes with tests shuffled and with any single test run alone. Dependence on execution order, wall-clock time, or leftover state from another test is a defect in the suite.
11. **QA-031 — The layer's runtime is budgeted.** Slow tests are tagged and reported by name. The layer's total CI runtime budget is recorded in TESTING.md, and a breach fails the job like any other threshold.
12. **QA-032 — The layer must be able to fail.** A seeded fault — one migration reverted, one write path broken — must turn the suite red. A layer that has never been observed failing is decoration, and its green checkmark certifies nothing.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-011 — Hand-written fake of your own component.** Banned: replacing the project's own database, repository layer, or API with a hand-written in-memory fake inside integration tests. Defeats: DET-FAKE-010. Bad: the admin-save test runs against a `Map`-backed fake repository, passes, and ships an admin panel whose real save writes nothing. Instead: run against the real database built by the real migrations; stub only third parties at the system edge (QA-023). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-012 — Write asserted from the response only.** Banned: a write test whose only assertion is the write call's response body or status. Defeats: DET-FAKE-016. Bad: `PATCH /profile` returns `200 {name: "New Name"}` and the test passes, while the update is applied to request state and reverts on the next read. Instead: read the record back through a different surface and assert the stored value (QA-024). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-013 — Mock-call verification as proof of persistence.** Banned: asserting that a mocked store's `save()` was called as evidence that data persisted. Defeats: DET-FAKE-003. Bad: the signup test mocks the user store, verifies the mock was invoked, and passes while production registration discards the account. Instead: register against the real store, then sign in with the new credentials in the same test and assert the session works. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-014 — Delete verified on the list only.** Banned: a delete test that checks only that the item leaves a list response. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Bad: after `DELETE /items/42` the list no longer shows 42, so the test passes — but `GET /items/42` still returns the record and search still finds it. Instead: assert the record is unreachable through every surface: list, direct read, and search. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-015 — Assertions on ambient seed data.** Banned: tests that pass because a shared seed or fixture row exists, asserting on data the test did not create. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the search test finds "Acme Corp" because the seed file inserts it; when the seed changes, the test breaks — and while it passes, it proves nothing about records the system actually writes. Instead: the test creates its own uniquely named record and asserts on that record (QA-025). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-QA-011 — Clean-room green run.** Verifies: QA-021, QA-026. Check: automated — CI destroys all test volumes (`docker compose down -v` or the stack's equivalent) and runs the layer from a clean checkout with no pre-existing database, e.g. `npm run test:integration`; the command's exit code is the verdict. Pass: exit code 0. Fail: non-zero exit blocks merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-012 — Reverted-migration negative control.** Verifies: QA-021, QA-032. Check: automated — a script reverts exactly one migration (e.g. `npm run db:migrate:undo`) against the test database and re-runs the layer. Pass: the run exits non-zero — the suite noticed the missing schema. Fail: a green run means the layer cannot detect schema drift; block merge and repair the layer before any other QA sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-013 — Write/read-back coverage.** Verifies: QA-024, QA-027. Check: automated — a script lists every write route from the API's route table or OpenAPI document and greps the integration suite for a corresponding read-back test and, for tenant-scoped entities, a cross-tenant case; uncovered routes are printed by name. Pass: zero uncovered write routes. Fail: block merge until each gap has a test or a written waiver with owner and expiry in progress.md. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-014 — Shuffled run inside the runtime budget.** Verifies: QA-030, QA-031. Check: automated — CI runs the layer with the runner's random-order flag under a hard timeout set to the TESTING.md budget, e.g. `timeout 600 npm run test:integration -- --shuffle`. Pass: exit code 0 within the timeout. Fail: non-zero exit or timeout blocks merge; the slowest tests are named in the job report. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The hand-synced test schema.** A `test-schema.sql` maintained by hand alongside the real migrations; it drifts a little each sprint, and the layer certifies a database production never runs. Catch it: search the repo for schema definitions outside the migrations folder — any hit is the tell.
- **The happy-path corridor.** Every integration test asserts a 2xx; there is no decline, no constraint violation, no cross-tenant attempt. Catch it: count the layer's non-2xx assertions; a layer with none has tested only the corridor where defects are rarest.
- **The shared kingdom fixture.** One giant seed dataset every test leans on; failures cascade across unrelated tests and nobody can say which test owns which row. Catch it: run any single test alone on an empty database — if it cannot set itself up, it lives in the kingdom.
- **The slow swamp.** The layer quietly re-tests unit-level logic at a hundred times the cost until CI takes an hour and the team moves it out of the merge gate "temporarily." Catch it: read the slowest-test report each week; anything duplicating a unit test's assertion is pushed back down the pyramid.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Write asserted from the response, corrected to read-back](examples/example-1.md) — corrects QA-024.
- [Example 2 — Hand-maintained test schema, corrected to real migrations](examples/example-2.md) — corrects QA-021.
- [Example 3 — Missing tenant boundary, corrected to a cross-tenant test](examples/example-3.md) — corrects QA-027.

## Recall anchors

- Real database, real migrations, real HTTP — mocks only at the edge.
- A write is proven by reading it back somewhere else.
- Each test seeds its own data and cleans up by construction.
- If reverting a migration doesn't turn it red, it tests nothing.
- Slow is a budget breach, not a personality trait.

## Checklist

- [ ] The test database is created by the project's real migrations on the production engine (QA-021).
- [ ] No hand-written fake stands in for the project's own database, API, queue, or cache (QA-023).
- [ ] Every write endpoint has a read-back test through a different surface (QA-024, G-QA-013).
- [ ] Every tenant-scoped entity has a cross-tenant read/write test (QA-027).
- [ ] Multi-write operations have a partial-failure atomicity test (QA-028).
- [ ] The layer passes shuffled and single-test runs inside its runtime budget (QA-030, QA-031, G-QA-014).
- [ ] The reverted-migration negative control turned the suite red (G-QA-012).
- [ ] The layer runs green from a clean checkout with no pre-existing database (G-QA-011).

<!-- generated from skills/qa-testing/load-testing/SKILL.md -->

# load-testing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Grafana k6, "Thresholds" — https://grafana.com/docs/k6/next/using-k6/thresholds/ ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, Load and performance testing element
- **Depends on:** test-strategy, test-data
- **Feeds into:** qa-gates, performance-budgets

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a release candidate must prove it holds the project's performance budgets under realistic load, a capacity question needs a measured answer, or a performance regression is suspected between releases.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is whether a feature works at all (that is e2e-testing), whether one screen feels fast in a browser audit (performance-budgets owns the budget; a Lighthouse run is not a load test), or the target is a third party's production service — never load-test what you do not own.

## Rules

1. **QA-121 — Percentiles, never averages.** Results are reported and gated on p(95), p(99), and error rate. A mean latency is never a result; a mean that hides a collapsing p99 is a failed report.
2. **QA-122 — Journey mix, not one endpoint.** The script models the real journeys — login, browse, search, checkout — in production-like proportions. A single-endpoint run is labeled a smoke run in its header and its report.
3. **QA-123 — The header declares the run.** Every script header states, before the run executes: scenario mix, data volume, target environment, and the document each threshold came from. A run whose header is filled in afterward is void.
4. **QA-124 — Production-shaped data.** Release runs execute against production-shaped data volumes. A run against an empty or fixture-sized database is a smoke run and cannot satisfy a release gate.
5. **QA-125 — Thresholds live in the budget.** Threshold values are copied from the project's performance budget / SLO documents (owned by D12). Changing a value is a reviewed change to those documents, never an edit inside the test PR.
6. **QA-126 — Thresholds before the run.** Thresholds are written into the script before execution and are part of the reviewed script. Thresholds added or adjusted after seeing results void the run.
7. **QA-127 — Staged load profile.** Every release scenario declares ramp-up, steady hold, and spike stages. Instant full load is a smoke profile, not a release scenario.
8. **QA-128 — Third parties stubbed or sandboxed.** Payment, email, and other external providers are stubbed or run in sandbox mode. A load run never sends its traffic to a real provider's production endpoints.
9. **QA-129 — The exit code is the gate.** The k6 exit code is wired into the pipeline: non-zero blocks the release. A manual override is recorded as an override, never as a pass.
10. **QA-130 — Results archived per release.** The run summary, the environment record, and the declared data volume are archived with the release, so regressions read as trends across releases instead of being rediscovered.
11. **QA-131 — Bottlenecks become defects.** Every threshold breach or bottleneck is filed as a defect with the run's evidence — percentile table and a profile — attached. "It got slow at 400 users" without a profile is not a finding.
12. **QA-132 — The environment is named.** Release runs execute against staging or a production-like environment whose configuration is recorded with the results. A run against a developer machine is a smoke run.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-061 — The toy-dataset proof.** Banned: presenting a run against an empty or fixture-sized database as release-grade load evidence. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: the release notes claim "checkout holds p(95) under 800 ms at 500 users" from a run seeded with 12 products and 3 user accounts. Instead: seed production-shaped volumes, declare the volume in the script header, and label any small-data run a smoke run that cannot satisfy the release gate. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-062 — The canned target.** Banned: hammering one static or cached page and reporting the numbers as application load results. Defeats: DET-FAKE-008. Bad: the script requests only the homepage — served from cache — and the report announces "10,000 requests/second sustained" for the whole system. Instead: drive the journey mix against the real application and data tier, and report per-journey percentiles. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-063 — The doctored green gate.** Banned: loosening a threshold, trimming the load profile, or reclassifying a failed run so the pipeline shows a pass the system never earned. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; governed by QA-125. Bad: p(95) is raised from 800 ms to 2,000 ms inside the test PR after a failing run, and the release ships on the new green check. Instead: the run fails, a defect is filed with the evidence, and any threshold change goes through review of the budget document itself. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-064 — The frozen result.** Banned: carrying performance figures from a previous release, a template, or a target document into a report as this release's measured results. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Bad: three consecutive release reports show the identical p(95) of 212 ms because the summary block is copied forward each time. Instead: every reported figure comes from the archived summary of the run it claims to describe, and the archive is linked from the report. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-QA-061 — Release load gate.** Verifies: QA-121, QA-125, QA-129. Check: automated — in CI on the release candidate, run `k6 run scripts/load/release.js`; the script carries thresholds on `http_req_duration` p(95) and p(99) and on the `http_req_failed` rate. Pass: k6 exits 0. Fail: non-zero exit blocks the release; no manual pass is recorded. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-062 — Seeded-fault threshold check.** Verifies: QA-126, QA-129. Check: automated — in a throwaway run, tighten one threshold below current measured performance (for example p(95) at 1 ms) and re-run the release script. Pass: k6 exits non-zero and the pipeline blocks. Fail: the gate machinery is broken; repair it before any release run counts. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-063 — Data-volume audit.** Verifies: QA-123, QA-124. Check: automated — a pre-run script prints the seeded row counts of the test environment and diffs them against the volumes declared in the script header and the production-shaped minimum recorded in TESTING.md. Pass: declared and seeded volumes match and meet the minimum. Fail: the run is reclassified as a smoke run and cannot satisfy G-QA-061. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-064 — Archive completeness.** Verifies: QA-130, QA-131. Check: automated — after the release run, assert the release archive contains the k6 summary output, the environment record, and a defect link for every threshold breach. Pass: all artifacts present. Fail: the release record is incomplete and is completed before sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The victory-lap rerun.** The scenario is re-run until a green result appears, and only the passing run is archived. Catch it: compare the CI run history against the archived summaries — missing failed runs are the tell.
- **The all-cache measurement.** Every request in the "application" scenario is served from cache, so the data tier is never touched and the numbers flatter it. Catch it: check the cache-hit ratio and per-journey breakdown in the run evidence; a release run shows real origin and database traffic.
- **The unprofiled verdict.** "The database is the bottleneck" asserted from latency curves alone, with no query profile or trace behind it. Catch it: ask for the profile attached to the defect (QA-131); a verdict without one is sent back.
- **The spike that never lands.** The profile declares a spike stage, but CI timeouts quietly cut the run during ramp-up, so the spike is never executed. Catch it: compare the stage durations in the run summary against the stages declared in the script.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Averages replaced by percentile thresholds](examples/example-1.md) — corrects QA-121.
- [Example 2 — A toy-database run relabeled and reseeded](examples/example-2.md) — corrects QA-124.
- [Example 3 — A loosened threshold returned to the budget](examples/example-3.md) — corrects QA-125.

## Recall anchors

- Percentiles and error rate — a mean is never a result.
- Toy data makes a smoke run, never release evidence.
- Thresholds come from the budget, before the run, or the run is void.
- The k6 exit code is the gate; an override is not a pass.
- Every breach becomes a defect with a profile attached.

## Checklist

- [ ] Script header declares scenario mix, data volume, environment, and threshold sources (QA-123).
- [ ] Data-volume audit passed: seeded volumes are production-shaped (G-QA-063).
- [ ] Thresholds match the current budget documents exactly (QA-125).
- [ ] Seeded-fault check observed k6 exiting non-zero (G-QA-062).
- [ ] Release run exited 0 on the release candidate, or the release is blocked (G-QA-061).
- [ ] Third parties were stubbed or sandboxed for the run (QA-128).
- [ ] Summary, environment record, and breach defects are archived with the release (G-QA-064).
- [ ] Report shows p(95), p(99), and error rate per journey — no averages (QA-121).

<!-- generated from skills/qa-testing/placeholder-scan/SKILL.md -->

# placeholder-scan

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** SquirrelScan content rules, "Placeholder text" — https://docs.squirrelscan.com/rules/content/placeholder-text ; VerifixScan, "Placeholder text in production" — https://www.verifixscan.com/problems/placeholder-text-in-production ; skills/detection/fake/PARAMETERS.md (DET-FAKE-001…022) and skills/detection/content/PARAMETERS.md (DET-CON-001…028) in this repo
- **Depends on:** qa-gates
- **Feeds into:** bug-triage, browser-verification, e2e-testing

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** before every release, and whenever a feature claims to work end to end — run the scan to prove no placeholder copy, stub handler, fixture data, or simulated function ships in the production build.
- **Do NOT use when:** judging whether a real function is correct (that is e2e-testing and browser-verification), or flagging a clearly labeled demo or sample — a labeled demo is honest and is never a finding. Fixes belong to the builder skill named in the DET parameter's Fix field; this skill produces the verdict, not the repair.

## Rules

1. **QA-281 — Two passes, both mandatory.** Every release runs the static pass (pattern sweep of the shipped artifact) and the dynamic pass (the DET-FAKE probe checklist against the running build). Neither pass alone clears a release.
2. **QA-282 — Scan the shipped artifact.** Scope is the production bundle, production routes, and production seed state. A clean staging demo does not clear a dirty production build. The static sweep scans rendered output, not source: run the pattern list over the built pages and shipped strings as a user receives them, never over source files — template-syntax patterns false-positive on source constructs (the `${` fingerprint matches every JavaScript template literal). Source files are in scope only for QA-291's import and bundle-content check.
3. **QA-283 — The pattern list is versioned.** The fingerprint list lives in the repo as a reviewed file. Every fake that reaches production adds its fingerprint to the static list and its probe to the dynamic checklist in the same change that fixes it.
4. **QA-284 — Static fingerprints, exact set.** The sweep covers at minimum: `lorem|ipsum|dolor sit amet`; `TODO|FIXME|XXX` and stub markers in shipped strings; unrendered template syntax (`{{`, `}}`, `${`, `[object Object]`, literal `undefined`/`NaN` outside code blocks); placeholder contacts (`example.com`, `example@`, `555-01`, `123 Main Street`); "coming soon" / "content to follow" in live fields, meta, and alt text; known template/CMS default strings for the stack in use.
5. **QA-285 — Success without a write is a blocker.** A success UI state (toast, confirmation page, "saved" indicator) with no corresponding server write in the network capture is a blocker finding by definition, filed against the matching DET-FAKE parameter — never a style note.
6. **QA-286 — Dynamic probes per interactive feature.** Each interactive feature gets, per release: the persistence test (act, reload, log in again — the change must survive), the network test (the action must produce a real request and a stored result), the wrong-password probe on auth, the decline-card probe on payment, and the fresh-account emptiness check (a new account shows empty states, not staged content).
7. **QA-287 — Seeded-fault negative control.** The scan is itself tested: a throwaway branch seeded with a stub handler and a fixture-rendered list must make the sweep exit non-zero. The control runs in CI on a schedule; a scanner that passes the seeded branch is broken and blocks releases until repaired.
8. **QA-288 — Allow-list entries expire.** Every allow-list entry names the visible label that makes the exception honest (demo banner, "sample" tag) and an expiry tied to a named release. An expired entry fails the scan like any other hit.
9. **QA-289 — Findings are defects, with provenance.** Each finding is filed in bug-triage at the severity of the DET parameter it matches (blocker for undisclosed simulation of a core function), naming the DET ID and the fingerprint or probe that caught it.
10. **QA-290 — The scan never grades its own homework.** The scan configuration is reviewed repo code. Removing or loosening a pattern requires the same waiver record as loosening any qa-gate: named owner, reason, expiry.
11. **QA-291 — Fixtures stay unreachable.** Seed and fixture files must not be imported by, bundled into, or reachable from production code paths. The sweep checks imports and bundle contents, not just visible copy.
12. **QA-292 — Placeholder media counts.** Stock or generated images presented as the real team, real customers, or real product shots are findings (DET-CON-019), as are placeholder image URLs and grey-box assets in production routes.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-141 — Lorem ipsum in the build.** Banned: any lorem ipsum or variant fragment in shipped copy, headings, or titles. Defeats: DET-CON-001. Bad: the pricing page ships with "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet" under two plan tiers. Instead: write the final plan copy from the fact sheet, or remove the section until the copy exists. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-142 — Success toast, no request.** Banned: a form or action that shows success without issuing a request or storing anything. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Bad: the contact form shows "Message sent!" while the network capture shows zero requests and no record is created. Instead: wire the form to the real endpoint and show success only after a confirmed server response. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-143 — Fixture array as the live catalog.** Banned: hardcoded fixture or seed arrays rendered as the product catalog, user list, or testimonial set. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the storefront renders a `const products = [...]` literal with invented names, prices, and five-star quotes. Instead: render from the real data source; with no data, show the designed empty state. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-144 — Placeholder contact details.** Banned: `example@` addresses, 555-01xx numbers, or template street addresses in live contact blocks, footers, or checkout help text. Defeats: DET-CON-005. Bad: the footer lists support@example.com and (555) 014-2200 on the production site. Instead: publish the real, monitored contact details, verified by a test message before release. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-145 — Timer-driven "live" indicators.** Banned: "live", "online now", viewer counts, or activity feeds driven by random timers or rotation through staged entries. Defeats: DET-FAKE-018. Bad: a "128 people viewing" badge whose number is `Math.floor(Math.random()*50)+100` on a 5-second interval. Instead: bind the indicator to the real presence/analytics source, or remove the badge. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-QA-141 — Static sweep clean.** Verifies: QA-282, QA-284, QA-291, QA-292. Check: automated — run the versioned pattern list over the rendered production output (built pages and shipped strings), e.g. `rg -i -n "lorem|ipsum|dolor sit amet|example\.com|example@|555-01|coming soon|content to follow" dist/` plus the template-syntax and stub-marker patterns from the pattern file; exclude documented code-sample contexts. Scan rendered output, not source: copy and template-syntax patterns run against the build output only (against source they false-positive, e.g. `${` in JavaScript template literals); source is examined only for QA-291's fixture-import fingerprints. Pass: exit 0 with zero unallow-listed hits. Fail: block the release; each hit is filed per QA-289. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-142 — Seeded-fault control.** Verifies: QA-287. Check: automated — on the seeded throwaway branch (one stub handler returning success, one fixture-rendered list, one lorem ipsum paragraph), run the same sweep command as G-QA-141. Pass: exit code non-zero and all three seeds reported. Fail: the scanner is treated as broken; releases block until the control passes again. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-143 — Dynamic checklist complete.** Verifies: QA-285, QA-286. Check: per release, the DET-FAKE checklist is executed against the running production build; every interactive feature has filed evidence for its persistence test and network test, plus the wrong-password, decline-card, and fresh-account probes where applicable. Pass: evidence exists for 100% of interactive features and no success-without-write observation stands. Fail: block the release; each gap or fake is filed per QA-289. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-144 — Allow-list audit.** Verifies: QA-288, QA-290. Check: automated — a script reads the allow-list file and confirms every entry names its honesty label and an expiry release that has not yet shipped. Pass: zero expired or unlabeled entries. Fail: block the release until entries are renewed with a waiver record or the exceptions are removed. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Scanner theater.** The sweep runs against the source tree while the shipped bundle is built differently, so the scan certifies an artifact nobody ships. Catch it: the gate command's target path is the build output directory, and the seeded-fault control (G-QA-142) seeds the built artifact, not just source.
- **Green by deletion.** A finding is closed by deleting its pattern from the list instead of fixing the fake. Catch it: pattern-list diffs are reviewed like gate changes (QA-290); a shrinking list with no corresponding code fix is the tell.
- **Demo creep.** A "temporary" demo mode with staged data quietly becomes the production experience, its banner removed in a redesign. Catch it: allow-list expiries (QA-288) force the demo to be re-justified or removed every release.
- **English-only fingerprints.** The pattern list covers English placeholder copy, so localized filler and template defaults in other languages sail through. Catch it: when a locale ships, its placeholder strings and CMS defaults are added to the list in the same change.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Lorem ipsum and placeholder contacts in the shipped footer](examples/example-1.md) — corrects QA-284.
- [Example 2 — A contact form whose success toast fired with no request](examples/example-2.md) — corrects QA-285.
- [Example 3 — A fixture array rendered as the live product catalog](examples/example-3.md) — corrects QA-291.

## Recall anchors

- Scan the artifact you ship, not the demo you staged.
- Success with no server write is a blocker, full stop.
- Every escaped fake leaves a fingerprint and a probe behind.
- Allow-list entries name their label and expire.
- A labeled demo is honest; an unlabeled one is a finding.

## Checklist

- [ ] Static sweep ran on the rendered production output — not source — and exited 0 (G-QA-141).
- [ ] Seeded-fault control still bites: the seeded branch exits non-zero (G-QA-142).
- [ ] Dynamic checklist evidence filed for every interactive feature (G-QA-143).
- [ ] No success UI state lacks a matching server write in the network capture (QA-285).
- [ ] Fresh-account check shows real empty states, not staged content (QA-286).
- [ ] Allow-list has no expired or unlabeled entries (G-QA-144).
- [ ] Every finding is filed as a defect with its DET ID and severity (QA-289).
- [ ] Any new fake found this release added its fingerprint and probe to the lists (QA-283).

# qa-gates

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/continuous-integration ; https://web.dev/articles/vitals
- **Depends on:** test-strategy (TESTING.md names the gates, thresholds, and cadences this skill wires)
- **Feeds into:** bug-triage (escaped defects name the gate that should have caught them), placeholder-scan (its sweep runs as a required check), all D8 layer skills (their suites are enforced here)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** defining or changing the merge/release gates; wiring required status checks and branch protection; a gate goes red and someone proposes a bypass, a threshold change, or a re-run; a flaky gate needs quarantine; a release needs its gate evidence assembled.
- **Do NOT use when:** deciding what must be proven or what the budgets are (test-strategy — this skill enforces the strategy, it does not set it); writing the tests a gate runs (the owning layer skill); triaging a defect a gate caught (bug-triage).

## Rules

1. **QA-221 — A gate is a command with an exit code.** Every automated gate is a named command whose exit code decides pass/fail; if a human must judge whether it passed, it is a review checklist item, labeled as such in TESTING.md, and never reported as an automated gate.
2. **QA-222 — Gate definitions predate the work they judge.** Gate configuration and thresholds live in files (workflow files, branch-protection config, the budget file) committed before the change they gate; a gate invented or edited inside the PR it judges does not judge that PR.
3. **QA-223 — Threshold and test changes in the same PR need a waiver.** Changing a threshold, or the tests a gate runs, in the same PR as the code that failed it requires a waiver record in the project log naming the owner, the reason, and an expiry date; without the record the PR does not merge.
4. **QA-224 — The required-checks list is single-sourced.** The branch-protection required status checks match the gate list in TESTING.md exactly; any difference between the two lists is a defect, reconciled in a reviewed change, never by quietly editing one side.
5. **QA-225 — Every gate has a witnessed failure.** When a gate is created and after any pipeline change, a seeded fault of its class (broken assertion, removed form label, shifted layout header, tightened k6 threshold) is run against it and must make it exit non-zero; a gate never seen red is unverified and is not reported as protection.
6. **QA-226 — Negative controls run on a schedule.** The seeded-fault suite runs in a named nightly job, one fault per gate class; a gate that reports green on its seeded fault is filed as a blocker defect against the gate itself, and the release is blocked until the gate bites again.
7. **QA-227 — Bypasses are logged and counted.** Every admin merge, `[skip ci]`, and manual override is recorded with who, when, and why; the bypass count is reported per release, and a rising count is itself a quality finding with a named owner.
8. **QA-228 — Quarantine is a counted, expiring state.** A flaky gate or test enters quarantine only with a named owner and an expiry date, and appears in the release's quarantine count; an expired quarantine without a fix or a justified extension blocks the release — re-running until green is not a state.
9. **QA-229 — Baselines update only through reviewed diffs.** Visual, contract, and performance baselines change only via a diff whose description names the intentional change being accepted; a bulk regenerate-all-baselines commit is rejected, because it accepts regressions sight unseen.
10. **QA-230 — A gate result is an artifact, not a claim.** Each gate run records the command, the exit code, and a link to the CI run in progress.md; "passed locally" or a green screenshot with no run behind it is not a result.
11. **QA-231 — A coverage gate must prove the tests assert.** A coverage-threshold gate runs alongside a mutation sample or seeded-fault check on the covered code (G-QA-115); a suite that stays green under seeded faults fails the gate no matter what its coverage percentage says.
12. **QA-232 — Every gate names its cadence and its job.** TESTING.md lists each gate as per-PR, merge/nightly, or per-release, with the job that runs it; a gate with no scheduled job, or a job that has not run inside its cadence, does not exist for reporting purposes.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-111 — Echo-only pipeline.** Banned: a CI pipeline whose test step is `echo ok`, a no-op script, or a suite of assertions that assert nothing, presented as a passing gate. Defeats: DET-INF-002. Bad: the merge gate shows green for six months because its only step prints "tests passed"; the figure never moves when behavior breaks. Instead: wire the gate to the real suite command, and prove it can fail with a seeded fault (QA-225) before counting it as protection. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-112 — Same-PR threshold loosening without a waiver.** Banned: lowering a threshold, widening a budget, or deleting the failing test inside the same PR that failed it, with no waiver record. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; governed by QA-223. Bad: the performance gate fails at LCP 2.9s, so the PR edits the budget to 3.5s and merges green — the bar reset to whatever the code already does. Instead: fix the code, or record a waiver with owner, reason, and expiry and review the threshold change as a standards change (QA-223). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-113 — Re-run until green.** Banned: merging after re-running a flaky gate until it happens to pass, with no quarantine entry and no fix. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the e2e gate fails three times and passes on the fourth re-run; the PR merges under a "Passed" indicator that the code never earned. Instead: quarantine the flake with owner and expiry (QA-228) or fix it; the merge waits for a green run that is not a lottery win. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-114 — Routine admin bypass.** Banned: using admin merge, `[skip ci]`, or a disabled required check as the normal path past a red gate, unlogged. Defeats: DET-INF-002. Bad: branch protection lists nine required checks, but the maintainer merges red PRs with the admin override weekly and nothing records it — enforcement exists only in the settings screenshot. Instead: fix the failure, or log the bypass with who and why and count it in the release report (QA-227). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-115 — Bulk baseline regeneration.** Banned: regenerating all visual, contract, or performance baselines in one unreviewed commit to turn a red gate green. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; governed by QA-229. Bad: a layout change breaks 40 snapshots; the fix is `update-snapshots --all`, and the regression the gate existed to surface disappears from view. Instead: update baselines through a reviewed diff whose description names the intentional change (QA-229), one cause at a time. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

The five check scripts these gates cite — `negative_controls.py`, `check_required_checks.py`, `check_gate_provenance.py`, `gate_ledger.py`, and `mutation_sample.py` — ship in this repository at `scripts/qa/` as reference implementations, each documented in its own header. A project may replace any of them with its own equivalent provided the gate's behavior is preserved exactly (same inputs, same pass/fail semantics), and the substitution is recorded in progress.md; an unrecorded or behavior-changing substitution is a gate failure, not a customization.

- **G-QA-111 — Negative-control meta-gate.** Verifies: QA-225, QA-226. Check: run the shipped runner, `scripts/qa/negative_controls.py`, in one of its two forms. Nightly form: the named nightly job runs `python3 scripts/qa/negative_controls.py --branch qa/seeded-faults`; the branch carries one seeded fault per gate class. Local form (the manifest-driven invocation, for a project without the branch — a scratch workspace, a pre-push check, a single agent): `python3 scripts/qa/negative_controls.py --project <project>` reads the project's own controls manifest (default `<project>/scripts/qa/negative-controls.json`; `--manifest` overrides the path) and runs each control against a scratch copy of the local tree — a control seeds its fault with its `apply` command, or the tree is already seeded — and each control's `check` command must exit non-zero with its fault present. Either form: the script exits non-zero if any gate reports green on its own fault (exit 1), and exit 2 is a setup error (no manifest, no controls, unusable project). The script's header documents the controls-manifest format. The runner also reports any gate declared in TESTING.md that has no negative control; that gap fails the run unless `--allow-missing` is passed, which downgrades it to a printed warning — the `--allow-missing` disposition is legitimate only for a consciously partial control set, and its use is recorded in progress.md with the uncovered gates named. Pass: exit 0 — every gate went red on its fault, and no declared gate lacks a control (or the gap is an `--allow-missing` warning recorded as above). Fail: block the release; file a blocker defect against the non-biting gate. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-112 — Required-checks diff.** Verifies: QA-224. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/check_required_checks.py` reads the branch-protection required status checks through the platform API and diffs them against the gate list parsed from TESTING.md; it exits non-zero on any difference. The script ships in this repo at `scripts/qa/check_required_checks.py`; where the platform API is unreachable it diffs against the checked-in snapshot `.github/required-checks.txt` or the workflow job definitions, and prints which source it used. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block merge; reconcile the lists in a reviewed change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-113 — Gate provenance and waiver check.** Verifies: QA-222, QA-223. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/check_gate_provenance.py` compares commit timestamps for gate-config and threshold files against the code they gate, and exits non-zero if a same-PR threshold or test change lacks a waiver entry with a named owner and an unexpired date in the project log. The script ships in this repo at `scripts/qa/check_gate_provenance.py` and evaluates the commit range `--base..HEAD`; its `--log-trace` mode also verifies that gate results recorded in progress.md trace to gate IDs defined in the skills. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block merge until the change predates the work or the waiver exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-114 — Bypass and quarantine ledger audit.** Verifies: QA-227, QA-228. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/gate_ledger.py --fail-on-expired` reads the bypass/quarantine ledger and exits non-zero if any bypass lacks who/why, any quarantine entry is expired without resolution, or the release's bypass count rose over the previous release with no linked quality finding. The script ships in this repo at `scripts/qa/gate_ledger.py`; its header documents the ledger format (default `scripts/qa/gate-ledger.json`). Pass: exit 0. Fail: block the release; resolve or formally extend each entry. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-115 — Mutation sample behind the coverage gate.** Verifies: QA-231. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/mutation_sample.py --sample 20` seeds 20 faults (or applies 20 sampled mutations) into covered production code and runs the unit suite; it exits non-zero if the suite stays green on more faults than the TESTING.md allowance. The script ships in this repo at `scripts/qa/mutation_sample.py`; its header documents the sample-config format (default `scripts/qa/mutation-sample.json`). Pass: exit 0. Fail: block the release; the hollow tests are rewritten before the coverage figure is reported again. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Gate sprawl without ownership.** A gate is added after every incident and none is ever removed, until nobody can say what each one protects; catch it by reviewing the gate list against TESTING.md each release and deleting or adopting the orphans.
- **Human judgment in gate costume.** A "gate" whose check reads "the agent confirms the page looks right" — no command, no artifact, no diff; catch it by asking for the command and its exit code, and reclassify it as a checklist item when there is none.
- **The nightly graveyard.** Expensive gates are scheduled nightly, but the job has been disabled or failing unattended for weeks, so the cadence is fictional; catch it by checking the last successful run artifact for every scheduled gate before reporting it.
- **Threshold archaeology.** A budget whose number nobody can trace to a source document, loosened so long ago that the original standard is lost; catch it by requiring every threshold to cite its budget or SLO source, and treating an unsourced number as unwritten.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A gate that had never failed](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects QA-225.
- [Example 2 — The threshold that moved with the code](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects QA-223.
- [Example 3 — Re-run until green, replaced by quarantine](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects QA-228.

## Recall anchors

- A gate is a command with an exit code, or it is a checklist item — never both stories.
- Gate files are committed before the work they judge.
- A gate never seen red is unverified.
- Bypasses and quarantines are counted, owned, and expiring — or they are hiding places.
- Baselines change by named intention, never by bulk regeneration.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every automated gate is a named command with an exit code; judgment calls are labeled checklist items (QA-221).
- [ ] Gate configuration and thresholds predate the changes they gate (QA-222).
- [ ] Any same-PR threshold or test change carries a waiver with owner, reason, and expiry (QA-223).
- [ ] Branch-protection required checks match the TESTING.md gate list exactly (QA-224).
- [ ] The nightly negative-control run is inside its cadence and every gate went red on its seeded fault (QA-225, QA-226).
- [ ] All bypasses this release are logged with who and why, and the count is reported (QA-227).
- [ ] No quarantine entry is expired without a fix or a justified extension (QA-228).
- [ ] Baseline changes this release are reviewed diffs naming the intentional change (QA-229).
- [ ] The coverage gate's latest mutation sample is on file and within allowance (QA-231).

# security-testing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG), https://owasp.github.io/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/stable/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/01-Information_Gathering/05-Review_Webpage_Content_for_Information_Leakage ; OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
- **Depends on:** integration-testing, e2e-testing
- **Feeds into:** qa-gates, bug-triage

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** A release needs security evidence: WSTG checklist execution, CI scanner triage, authorization/IDOR testing, session and authentication abuse cases — always against the project's own staging or production-like environments, or inside its own CI pipeline.
- **Do NOT use when:** The target is any system the project does not own or operate — never in scope, no exceptions. Tool selection, hardening, and fixes belong to D7 (security); penetration testing under a written engagement belongs to D7's penetration-testing skill.

## Rules

1. **QA-181 — Written scope before any test runs.** The test plan names the target environments (own staging/production-like only), the accounts and roles used, and the techniques allowed; testing outside that written scope does not start.
2. **QA-182 — WSTG checklist per release.** Each release executes the app-relevant OWASP WSTG categories (information gathering, authentication, authorization, session management, input validation, business logic) under their stable test IDs (e.g., WSTG-INFO-05), with pass/fail and evidence recorded per case.
3. **QA-183 — Skipped categories are named, with reasons.** The release record lists every WSTG category executed and every category skipped with its reason; an unlisted category is treated as not executed.
4. **QA-184 — Scanner suite in CI on every change.** Dependency, SAST, secrets, and container/config scanners run on every change; a new confirmed critical or high finding fails the pipeline with a non-zero exit.
5. **QA-185 — Every scanner result is triaged.** Each result is marked confirmed-exploitable, accepted-risk with a written note, or false-positive with the reason; raw scanner output is never the finding record.
6. **QA-186 — Authorization matrix by replay.** For every privileged endpoint, an automated test replays the request with a lower-privilege session and requires rejection (401/403); UI hiding is never accepted as evidence of enforcement.
7. **QA-187 — IDOR sweep on object access.** For every endpoint that takes an object ID, a test requests another account's object ID under a different session and requires rejection, run against own staging data only.
8. **QA-188 — Session cases per the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.** Tests verify cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), session rotation on login and privilege change, and server-side invalidation on logout.
9. **QA-189 — Authentication abuse cases pass end to end.** A wrong password is rejected (no any-password login), and a password reset is proven by logging in with the new password while the old one fails — receiving the reset email alone is not a pass.
10. **QA-190 — Findings close only by retest.** Every finding is recorded with evidence, severity, and remediation, and is retested after the fix; an unretested fix leaves the finding open.
11. **QA-191 — Business-logic abuse cases per release.** The app's core flows get manual abuse cases scanners cannot see: price/quantity tampering, step skipping, replayed submissions, and concurrent-request races, each with a recorded verdict.
12. **QA-192 — DAST only against own staging, authenticated.** Dynamic scans run against the project's staging environment with test accounts for each role; results enter the same triage queue as every other scanner (QA-185).

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-091 — Cosmetic authorization accepted as tested.** Banned: signing off authorization because a privileged button is hidden in the UI while the endpoint was never replay-tested. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: "Admin page is safe — the delete button only renders for admins." Instead: replay the delete request with a standard-user session and require 403 before sign-off (QA-186). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-092 — Reset test that stops at the email.** Banned: marking password reset tested because a reset email arrived, without proving the credential changed. Defeats: DET-FAKE-020. Bad: test asserts the inbox received a reset link and closes the case. Instead: complete the reset, then assert login with the old password fails and login with the new password succeeds (QA-189). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-093 — Security control disabled to get CI green.** Banned: suppressing a scanner rule, skipping the secrets scan, or loosening an auth check in shipped configuration so the pipeline passes. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Bad: `// nosec` added to a flagged query with no ticket or risk note. Instead: fix the finding, or record an accepted-risk note with owner and expiry and keep the control on (QA-185). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-094 — Session "verified" by a client-side flag.** Banned: treating a `loggedIn=true` value in browser storage as proof a session exists or is enforced. Defeats: DET-FAKE-002. Bad: test sets the flag, reloads, sees the dashboard, and passes session management. Instead: verify the server-issued session cookie's flags and that a protected API call without it is rejected (QA-188). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-095 — Real credentials hardcoded in test assets.** Banned: real passwords, tokens, or API keys committed in security-test fixtures, scripts, or CI configuration. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: the DAST script contains the production admin password "so it can log in." Instead: use dedicated staging test accounts whose credentials live in the CI secret store and are injected at runtime. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-QA-091 — Scanner gate.** Verifies: QA-184, QA-185. Check: `scripts/security-scan.sh` runs the dependency, SAST, secrets, and container/config scanners and exits non-zero on any new confirmed critical/high finding. Pass: exit code 0 and a triage record exists for every result. Fail: block merge/release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-092 — Authorization matrix gate.** Verifies: QA-186, QA-187. Check: `npm run test:authz` runs the privilege-replay and IDOR suites; the run exits non-zero if any privileged endpoint lacks a replay test or any replay is not rejected. Pass: exit code 0 with one replay test per privileged endpoint. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-093 — Seeded-fault negative control.** Verifies: QA-184. Check: on a scratch branch, seed one known-vulnerable dependency and remove one authorization check, then run the pipeline; both G-QA-091 and G-QA-092 must exit non-zero. Pass: both gates report red on the seeded branch. Fail: the gates are broken — fix the gates before any release relies on them. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-094 — WSTG release record gate.** Verifies: QA-182, QA-183. Check: `test -s docs/security/wstg-record.md && grep -q "Skipped:" docs/security/wstg-record.md` — the record exists, names executed categories by WSTG ID with evidence, and lists skipped categories with reasons. Pass: command exits 0. Fail: block release sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Scanner theater.** Dashboards are green and dashboards are shown, but the findings queue has not been triaged in weeks; catch it by sampling five scanner results and asking for each one's triage verdict.
- **Happy-path-only auth tests.** Every security test logs in as an admin and asserts success; no test ever asserts a rejection. Catch it by counting tests whose expected result is 401/403 — zero means the suite proves nothing.
- **Checklist photocopy.** The WSTG record is last release's file with the date changed and identical evidence links. Catch it by spot-checking one evidence artifact per category against this release's build.
- **Staging drift.** DAST and replay suites run against a staging build whose auth configuration differs from production, so green results describe a system that does not ship. Catch it by diffing the security-relevant configuration of staging and production before sign-off.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Authorization proven by replay, not by a hidden button](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects QA-186.
- [Example 2 — Scanner output triaged into a finding record](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects QA-185.
- [Example 3 — Password reset proven end to end](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects QA-189.

## Recall anchors

- Test from the attacker's seat: replay it as the low-privilege user.
- A scanner report is raw material, not a verdict — triage every line.
- Skipped is a recorded decision; silent is a gap.
- An unretested fix is an open finding.
- Own systems only — if the project does not own it, it is out of scope.

## Checklist

- [ ] Written scope names own environments, accounts, and allowed techniques (QA-181).
- [ ] WSTG record lists executed categories by ID with evidence, and skipped categories with reasons (QA-182, QA-183).
- [ ] Scanner suite ran in CI on this change and exited 0 (QA-184, G-QA-091).
- [ ] Every scanner result carries a triage verdict (QA-185).
- [ ] Privilege-replay and IDOR suites pass, one replay per privileged endpoint (QA-186, QA-187, G-QA-092).
- [ ] Session cases cover cookie flags, rotation, and logout invalidation (QA-188).
- [ ] Reset proven by login with the new password; wrong-password login rejected (QA-189).
- [ ] All fixed findings retested; seeded-fault control still turns the gates red (QA-190, G-QA-093).

# test-data

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://playwright.dev/docs/best-practices
- **Depends on:** test-strategy
- **Feeds into:** qa-gates, placeholder-scan, e2e-testing, integration-testing

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** creating, reviewing, or fixing the data any test, seed script, fixture, or demo environment runs on — factories, builders, fixtures, seed scripts, test database lifecycle, or production-shaped data requests.
- **Do NOT use when:** designing production seed/reference data itself (countries, plans, tax tables as shipped product data) — use seed-data (D5); or deciding data retention and privacy policy — use D14's privacy skills. This skill governs data manufactured for testing and demos.

## Rules

1. **QA-241 — Manufactured, never harvested.** All test data is created by code — factories, builders, or fixtures versioned with the tests that use them. No test data originates from a database export, a spreadsheet, or a manual insert.
2. **QA-242 — Tests own their data.** A test reads only data it created or explicitly loaded in its own setup. Shared mutable fixtures that tests read and write are prohibited; order dependence traced to shared data is a defect in the fixture, not in the test order.
3. **QA-243 — Valid by default.** A factory call with zero overrides produces a record that passes every validation and constraint of the real model. If a legal record needs overrides, fix the factory defaults, not the call sites.
4. **QA-244 — Deterministic generation.** Every random-looking value comes from a seeded generator whose seed is fixed in the repo or logged by the run. Wall-clock time is never read directly: dates and timestamps are computed relative to an injected clock.
5. **QA-245 — The harness owns the lifecycle.** The test database is created by the project's migrations, populated per test or per suite, and destroyed or reset by the harness afterward. No test depends on rows left behind by a previous run, and no cleanup is done by hand.
6. **QA-246 — Synthetic data is labeled synthetic, end to end.** Every seed or fixture record carries a machine-readable marker (for example an `is_seed` flag or a reserved seed email domain) that survives into API responses and screens in non-production environments. Generated people and records are never presented as real users, customers, or activity.
7. **QA-247 — The seed path refuses production.** The seed entry point checks the environment before writing anything and exits non-zero when the environment is production, unless an explicit demo flag is set — and demo-flagged seeding still writes only marker-carrying records (QA-246).
8. **QA-248 — No production data in test environments.** Production rows are never copied into test, CI, staging, or development databases — including "anonymized" copies that keep real names, emails, or phone numbers. When production shape is needed, generate the same shape synthetically; any exception is sanitized under D14's privacy rules before it leaves production.
9. **QA-249 — Fixtures contain no real personal details.** Fixture people are invented: names created for the fixture, email addresses on reserved domains (`example.com`, `example.org`), phone numbers from reserved fictional ranges. A real person's details in a fixture file are a privacy defect, not a convenience.
10. **QA-250 — Reference data comes from the shared fixtures.** Countries, plans, currencies, and other shared reference data are loaded from the same fixtures development uses. Test-local copies that can drift from the shared set are prohibited.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-121 — Production database copy as test data.** Banned: restoring a production dump (full or partial) into any test, CI, staging, or development database. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: a nightly production backup is restored into staging, so tests and demos run on real customer accounts. Instead: generate production-shaped synthetic data with factories at comparable volume, or sanitize under D14's privacy rules before any non-production use. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-122 — Seed users shipped as real customers.** Banned: seed or fixture accounts, testimonials, or activity presented in production as real users or social proof. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the seed script creates 50 "customers" with praise quotes that appear on the production homepage. Instead: keep seed accounts in development and demo environments only, behind the QA-247 environment guard, marker-carrying, and excluded from the production seed path. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-123 — Real personal details in fixtures.** Banned: real names paired with real email addresses, phone numbers, or other personal details of real people anywhere in fixture or seed files. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: a fixture user carries the developer's real Gmail address and a real customer's phone number "just for one test." Instead: invent fixture people with `example.com` addresses and reserved fictional phone numbers (QA-249). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-124 — Identical staged notifications for every account.** Banned: seeding every account with the same pre-written notification or activity feed presented as real events. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Bad: every new test and demo account starts with "John liked your post" and three scripted comments. Instead: generate notifications from real events inside the test; fresh accounts start with an empty feed, and demo notifications are labeled demo data. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-QA-121 — Isolation proof.** Verifies: QA-242, QA-245. Check: in CI, run the full suite with randomized test order, then run each test file standalone (the framework's shuffle and per-file modes). Pass: both runs fully green. Fail: block merge; the failing test's data dependencies are fixed, not reordered. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-122 — Seed/production refusal check.** Verifies: QA-247. Check: invoke the project's seed command with production environment variables set (for example `APP_ENV=production npm run db:seed`, substituting the project's actual command). Pass: the command exits non-zero and writes zero rows. Fail: block release until the guard exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-123 — Fixture personal-data scan.** Verifies: QA-246, QA-249. Check: run the placeholder-scan sweep over fixture and seed directories, including `grep -rEi '@(gmail|yahoo|hotmail|outlook|icloud)\.com' tests/ fixtures/ db/` plus a marker audit of every fixture user record. Pass: zero real-domain hits and every fixture user carries the synthetic marker. Fail: block merge; replace the data, do not allow-list it. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-124 — Determinism check.** Verifies: QA-244. Check: run the data-generating test files twice with the fixed seed and diff the generated fixture snapshots or database dumps between runs. Pass: byte-identical output. Fail: block merge until the unseeded source is seeded or clock-injected. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Override sprawl.** Every call site overrides four or five factory fields to get a legal record — the defaults are wrong and every test teaches the wrong shape. Catch it by grepping factory calls for override counts before review.
- **Calendar rot.** Fixtures hardcode dates ("expires 2025-01-01", "trial ends next week" as a literal) that silently flip test results as the calendar moves. Catch it by searching fixtures for literal dates outside the injected-clock helper.
- **The golden shared account.** One beloved login (`test@test.com`) that every test and demo depends on, whose state nobody can state. Catch it by searching tests for shared credentials or a single hardcoded user ID.
- **One-row world.** Every fixture set has exactly one to three rows, so pagination, empty states, limits, and N+1 behavior are never exercised. Catch it by checking that at least one fixture set per list-shaped feature exceeds one page of results.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Factory data instead of a production copy](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects QA-241, QA-248.
- [Example 2 — Seed script that refuses production](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects QA-247.
- [Example 3 — Labeled synthetic fixture people](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects QA-246, QA-249.

## Recall anchors

- Manufactured, deterministic, disposable — data a test did not make is data it cannot trust.
- A fresh account starts empty; a fresh database starts synthetic.
- The seed command must refuse production on its own, not by policy.
- Real people never appear in fixtures — invented names, reserved domains.
- If tests only pass in one order, the fixture is the bug.

## Checklist

- [ ] All test data is produced by factories, builders, or fixtures versioned with the tests (QA-241).
- [ ] The full suite passes with randomized order and per-file standalone runs (G-QA-121).
- [ ] Factories produce valid records with zero overrides (QA-243).
- [ ] Generators are seeded and time comes from an injected clock (QA-244).
- [ ] Every seed/fixture record carries the synthetic marker (QA-246).
- [ ] The seed command exits non-zero under production environment variables (G-QA-122).
- [ ] No production rows and no real personal details exist in any fixture or seed file (QA-248, QA-249, G-QA-123).

# test-strategy

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D8 QA & Testing (QA)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html
- **Depends on:** none (consumes the project's acceptance criteria from D1)
- **Feeds into:** unit-testing, integration-testing, e2e-testing, browser-verification, visual-regression, accessibility-testing, load-testing, chaos-testing, contract-testing, security-testing, qa-gates, test-data, bug-triage, placeholder-scan

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** starting a project, before any test suite is written; when the architecture changes materially; when a new test type is proposed; at each release, for the strategy-to-suite audit.
- **Do NOT use when:** writing or fixing an individual suite (use that layer's skill, executing against this strategy); setting merge-gate wiring or thresholds (qa-gates — this skill decides what must be proven, qa-gates wires the proof into CI).

## Rules

1. **QA-201 — One strategy document.** The strategy lives in TESTING.md at the repo root, is committed before the suites grow, and is the single place that names layers, environments, and budgets; a strategy that lives in a slide deck, wiki, or chat thread does not exist.
2. **QA-202 — Pyramid allocation in numbers.** TESTING.md states the target count or share per layer (unit / integration / e2e) and a wall-clock runtime budget per layer; "mostly unit tests" without numbers fails this rule.
3. **QA-203 — Every acceptance class maps to a layer.** Each requirement class in the project's acceptance criteria names at least one test layer that can catch its failure; a class with no layer is moved to the Accepted Risks section (QA-204), never left unmapped.
4. **QA-204 — Exclusions are written, with reasons.** TESTING.md carries an explicit Not Tested / Accepted Risks section: each entry names what is not tested, why, and who accepted the risk; silence is a gap, a written exclusion is a decision.
5. **QA-205 — E2E admission is earned.** A flow earns an e2e test by revenue or risk (signup, login, the core transaction, the top admin action); the PR adding one names the lower layer that cannot cover the case, or the test is pushed down the pyramid.
6. **QA-206 — Quality attributes are assigned, not assumed.** Visual, accessibility, load, chaos, contract, and security testing each appear in TESTING.md with an owning D8 skill, the environment they run in, and their cadence (per-PR, nightly, per-release); an attribute with no owner is untested by definition.
7. **QA-207 — Environment and cadence matrix.** TESTING.md states where each layer runs — local, CI per-PR, merge/nightly, or release pipeline; expensive gates (full-browser e2e, load, chaos) are scheduled explicitly, and "nightly" entries name the job that runs them so they cannot silently become "never."
8. **QA-208 — Flake budget is a number.** TESTING.md sets a maximum flake rate per suite; a flaky test is quarantined only as a tracked state with a named owner and an expiry date recorded in the strategy's quarantine list.
9. **QA-209 — Thresholds trace to a source document.** Every numeric threshold in the strategy (latency percentiles, error rates, Core Web Vitals budgets) cites the budget or SLO document it comes from; loosening a threshold is a reviewed change to that source document, never an edit inside a test PR.
10. **QA-210 — Every suite has a named owner.** TESTING.md lists each suite with its owning skill; a suite with no owner is adopted or deleted at the next strategy review — unowned suites are not run and not reported.
11. **QA-211 — New test types enter the strategy first.** A new kind of testing is added to TESTING.md (layer, budget, owner, cadence) in a reviewed change before its first test lands in the repo.
12. **QA-212 — Fake-functionality coverage is mapped.** For every interactive feature class in the DET-FAKE family (auth, payments, uploads, forms, counters, exports), TESTING.md names which skill runs its persistence and network probe — placeholder-scan, browser-verification, or e2e-testing — so no claimed effect goes unprobed.

## BAN list

- **BAN-QA-101 — Deck-only strategy.** Banned: presenting a strategy deck or document as the project's verification while no committed TESTING.md or running suites stand behind it. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: a "QA Strategy" slide set claims full coverage; CI runs only a build step. Instead: write TESTING.md with layers, budgets, and owners, and land the first suite it names before claiming any coverage. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-102 — Coverage percentage as proof.** Banned: reporting a coverage number (or a green dashboard) as evidence the product works, when the tests behind it assert nothing. Defeats: DET-CODE-012. Bad: "92% coverage" in the release note from tests that call functions without asserting on outputs, so the figure never moves when behavior breaks. Instead: pair every coverage claim with the layer census (G-QA-102) and seeded-fault evidence that the suites can fail. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-103 — Staged-account verification claimed as coverage.** Banned: counting manual click-throughs on a curated demo account as test coverage for a flow. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: checkout is "verified" by clicking through a seeded demo store whose data every account shares. Instead: cover the flow with an isolated automated journey that provisions its own account and data (e2e-testing), and record the demo pass as exploratory only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-QA-104 — Unnumbered budgets.** Banned: strategy language like "keep e2e small" or "suites stay fast" with no counts, runtimes, or flake ceiling. Defeats: DET-FAKE-005. Bad: TESTING.md says "a small e2e suite"; a year later it holds 400 journeys and takes three hours, with nothing ever in breach. Instead: state the e2e count ceiling, per-layer runtime budgets, and flake ceiling as numbers the census gate can check. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-QA-101 — Strategy document and mapping audit.** Verifies: QA-201, QA-203. Check: `test -f TESTING.md && python3 scripts/qa/check_strategy_map.py` — the script exits non-zero if TESTING.md is missing, contains TODO/TBD placeholders, or any acceptance-criteria class lacks a named layer or an Accepted Risks entry. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block the release; fix the map or record the risk. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-102 — Layer census within budgets.** Verifies: QA-202, QA-205, QA-210. Check: CI runs `node scripts/qa/layer-census.mjs --budgets TESTING.md --fail-on-breach`; it counts tests and wall time per layer and exits non-zero when a count, runtime, or unowned suite breaches the strategy. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block merge; push tests down the pyramid, adopt, or delete. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-103 — Accepted risks are explicit.** Verifies: QA-204. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/check_risks.py` exits non-zero if the Accepted Risks section is absent, empty, or any entry lacks a reason or a named acceptor. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block the release until every exclusion is written and owned. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-QA-104 — Flake budget and quarantine hygiene.** Verifies: QA-208. Check: `python3 scripts/qa/flake_report.py --max-rate 0.02` exits non-zero when a suite's measured flake rate exceeds the TESTING.md ceiling or any quarantined test lacks an owner or a future expiry date. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block the release; fix, extend with justification, or delete the flaky test. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Ice-cream-cone drift.** The e2e count grows every release while the unit layer stays flat, because UI tests are easier to add than to argue about; catch it in the census trend before the suite takes hours.
- **Retrofitted strategy.** TESTING.md is written after the suites exist and describes whatever was built, so it can never find a gap; catch it by checking the file's first commit predates the suites it governs.
- **Borrowed strategy.** A strategy copied from another project, with its flows, thresholds, and risks intact; catch it by sampling three entries and confirming each names this project's flows and budget documents.
- **Review theater.** The strategy is "reviewed" each release with no diff, no census output, and no decisions recorded; catch it by requiring the review to attach the G-QA-102 census result.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Mapping acceptance criteria to layers](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects QA-203.
- [Example 2 — Numbered budgets replace "small and fast"](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects QA-202.
- [Example 3 — A written exclusion with an accepted risk](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects QA-204.

## Recall anchors

- No TESTING.md, no strategy — a deck is not verification.
- Every acceptance class maps to a layer, or it is a written accepted risk.
- Budgets are numbers the census can breach, not adjectives.
- A flow earns e2e by revenue or risk, and names why lower layers cannot cover it.
- Unowned suites are adopted or deleted, never silently kept.

## Checklist

- [ ] TESTING.md exists at the repo root and predates the suites it governs (QA-201).
- [ ] Per-layer counts/shares and runtime budgets are stated as numbers (QA-202).
- [ ] Every acceptance-criteria class maps to a named layer or an Accepted Risks entry (QA-203, QA-204).
- [ ] Visual, accessibility, load, chaos, contract, and security each have an owner, environment, and cadence (QA-206).
- [ ] Each layer's environment and cadence are named, including the nightly job names (QA-207).
- [ ] Flake ceiling is set and every quarantined test has an owner and expiry (QA-208).
- [ ] Every threshold cites its source budget/SLO document (QA-209).
- [ ] DET-FAKE probe ownership is mapped for every interactive feature class (QA-212).
