<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/internal-linking/SKILL.md -->

# internal-linking

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Internal linking and sitemaps"; Google Search Central, "AI features and your website" (internal links named an AI-visibility fundamental) — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features
- **Depends on:** technical-seo, sitemaps
- **Feeds into:** content-strategy, aeo, geo

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing a site's navigation, hubs, and breadcrumbs; publishing or retiring any page; reviewing a crawl; or diagnosing a page that gets no organic or referral traffic.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which URLs exist in the sitemap file (sitemaps — the sitemap is a fallback, never the linking strategy), what a page says (copywriting, on-page-seo), or whether a URL should exist at all (content-strategy).

## Rules

1. **CO-201 — No orphan pages.** Every indexable page is linked from at least one non-sitemap page. An indexable page with zero inbound internal links is a defect, and every defect gets a named owner and a fix date.
2. **CO-202 — Shallow depth.** Every indexable page is reachable from the home page in at most 3 clicks by following links. Depth is measured on the crawl-derived link graph, never estimated.
3. **CO-203 — The brief names inbound links first.** Every new page's content brief names its planned inbound links (source page + anchor text) before the page is written. A page with no planned inbound links does not enter production.
4. **CO-204 — Anchor text describes the destination.** Anchor text names the destination page's topic, so it reads correctly out of context. "Click here", "here", and a bare "read more" are never the anchor for a content link.
5. **CO-205 — One anchor, one destination.** Identical anchor text never points to two different pages, and one destination is not linked under contradictory names. Collisions found in a crawl are renamed until each anchor maps to exactly one page.
6. **CO-206 — Link the canonical URL directly.** Internal links point at the canonical URL itself. No internal link may resolve through a redirect: if the target moved, the link is updated to the new URL in the same change.
7. **CO-207 — Critical pages earn in-content links.** Pricing, signup, and flagship content pages receive deliberate in-content links from relevant high-traffic pages. Nav or footer placement alone does not satisfy this rule.
8. **CO-208 — Retirement is one change.** When a page is retired or merged, its inbound internal links are updated or removed and its redirect is added in the same change — never in a later cleanup.
9. **CO-209 — The link graph is reviewed per release.** Every release produces a crawl-derived link graph (depth, in-degree, orphan list) and the review is recorded. A release with no graph review does not ship link or template changes.
10. **CO-210 — Hubs and breadcrumbs carry the structure.** Every section has a hub page that links its children, and every child page links back via breadcrumb or hub. No section is reachable only through site search or the sitemap.
11. **CO-211 — No broken internal links.** Every internal link resolves to a live page returning HTTP 200. A link to a 404, an error page, or an empty route is a defect with an owner, fixed like any other broken feature.
12. **CO-212 — Links are placed for readers.** A link exists because a reader at that point benefits from the destination. Link blocks, footer dumps, and pages built only to pass crawl equity to other pages are not a linking strategy.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-101 — Sitemap-only discovery.** Banned: shipping an indexable page whose only discovery path is the XML sitemap, with no inbound link from any real page. Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: the new pricing page is in sitemap.xml and returns 200, but no page on the site links to it, so neither users nor crawlers following links ever reach it. Instead: add at least one in-content inbound link from a relevant page before publish (CO-201, CO-203). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-102 — Generic anchor text.** Banned: using "click here", "here", or "read more" as the anchor text for content links. Defeats: DET-CON-006. Bad: a features page ends three sections with "To learn more, click here", "click here", and "click here", pointing at pricing, docs, and a case study. Instead: write the anchor as the destination's topic — "See pricing plans", "Read the API docs", "Read the Acme case study" (CO-204). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-103 — Anchor promises the destination doesn't keep.** Banned: anchor text naming a topic, offer, or document the destination page does not contain. Defeats: DET-CON-022. Bad: the anchor "Download the 2026 pricing PDF" links to a generic contact page with no PDF and no pricing. Instead: make the anchor describe what the destination actually delivers, or create the promised page and link that (CO-204). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-104 — Same anchor, different destinations.** Banned: one anchor string (e.g. "Our platform") linking to the product page in one place, the home page in another, and a landing page in a third. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: "Our platform" resolves to three different URLs across the blog, so readers and crawlers cannot tell which page the phrase names. Instead: assign each anchor string exactly one destination site-wide and rename the variants (CO-205). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-CO-105 — Template and staging links shipped live.** Banned: production navigation, footer, or body links still pointing at scaffold demo pages, a staging host, or placeholder routes from the site template. Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: the footer "Company" column links to the theme's demo About page on staging.example.com. Instead: repoint every shipped link at the real production page or remove it, and verify with the G-CO-102 scan before release. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-101 — Orphan and depth report.** Verifies: CO-201, CO-202, CO-210. Check: automated — crawl the production site, build the link graph, and list every indexable URL with in-degree 0 (sitemap excluded as a link source) plus every URL deeper than 3 clicks from home. Pass: zero orphans and zero pages deeper than 3 clicks. Fail: block the release; each orphan is assigned a named owner in progress.md. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-102 — Direct-target scan.** Verifies: CO-206, CO-211. Check: automated — request every internal href found by the crawl and record the status chain. Pass: 100% of internal links return HTTP 200 with no redirect hop. Fail: block shipment of the affected templates until links point at canonical URLs directly. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-103 — Anchor-text audit.** Verifies: CO-204, CO-205. Check: semi-automated — grep the rendered pages for the banned anchor strings ("click here", "here", "read more" as the complete anchor) and group all anchors by string to find one string mapping to multiple URLs; then manually read a sample of 20 in-content anchors against their destinations. Pass: zero banned anchors, zero multi-destination anchor strings, and every sampled anchor describes its destination. Fail: rework the failing anchors and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-104 — New-page inbound check.** Verifies: CO-203, CO-207. Check: manual — at publish, open each inbound link named in the page's brief and confirm it is live on the production page it was planned from, with the planned anchor text. Pass: every planned inbound link exists live at publish. Fail: do not announce or promote the page until the links are in place. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Nav-only thinking.** Assuming the main menu links everything that matters, so in-content linking is skipped and deep pages depend on two menu levels and luck. Catch it: the G-CO-101 graph shows in-degree, not menu membership — check it, not the menu.
- **The stale hub.** A hub page written at launch and never updated, so everything published since is missing from the one page meant to collect it. Catch it: diff the hub's link list against the section's current page inventory at every release.
- **Redesign amnesia.** Rebuilding navigation or templates without re-running the crawl, silently orphaning pages the old structure used to reach. Catch it: any nav or template change triggers CO-209's graph review before it ships, not after traffic drops.
- **Footer-dump compensation.** Answering "this page needs links" by adding it to a 60-link footer block nobody reads, instead of one relevant in-content link. Catch it: CO-207 asks where the in-content link lives; a footer entry is not an answer.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The pricing page only the sitemap knew about](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CO-201.
- [Example 2 — Three "click here"s, three destinations](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CO-204.
- [Example 3 — Every blog post linking through a redirect](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CO-206.

## Recall anchors

- If only the sitemap links to it, it is an orphan — and an orphan is a defect with an owner.
- Anchor text is a micro-description of the destination.
- Link the canonical URL, never the redirect.
- The brief names inbound links before the page is written.
- Retire a page and fix its links in the same change.

## Checklist

- [ ] Crawl graph generated this release: zero orphan indexable pages (G-CO-101).
- [ ] Every indexable page is within 3 clicks of home (G-CO-101).
- [ ] Every internal link returns 200 directly — no redirect hops, no 404 targets (G-CO-102).
- [ ] No "click here" / "here" / bare "read more" anchors anywhere (G-CO-103).
- [ ] No anchor string points to more than one destination (G-CO-103).
- [ ] Each new page's brief named its inbound links, and they are live at publish (G-CO-104).
- [ ] Pricing, signup, and flagship pages have in-content links from relevant high-traffic pages (CO-207).
- [ ] Any retired page had its inbound links updated and its redirect added in the same change (CO-208).

# lifecycle-email

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://support.google.com/mail/answer/14229414 ; http://braze.com/docs/user_guide/messaging/campaigns/creating_campaign ; https://www.ftc.gov/business-center/resources/can-spam-act-compliance-guide-business
- **Depends on:** fact-sheet, real-content
- **Feeds into:** growth-experiments, web-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing, editing, or auditing a behavior-triggered message program — onboarding, activation, engagement, retention, or win-back journeys across email, push, or in-app — including its authentication, consent, suppression, and measurement setup.
- **Do NOT use when:** the message is transactional (receipts, password resets, security alerts — that is D11's transactional-email skill, on its own stream), when the message is an incident or status communication (D18), or when the task is a one-off page or post (copywriting).

## Rules

1. **CO-141 — Authentication before volume.** SPF, DKIM, and an aligned DMARC record (minimum p=none) exist and verify on every sending domain before any program sends from it; no journey launches on an unauthenticated domain.
2. **CO-142 — Consent is a send-time check.** Every send verifies the profile's current opt-in status for that message type at send time; a signup-time consent memory never substitutes for the check, and an opt-out recorded anywhere suppresses everywhere for that type.
3. **CO-143 — Streams are never mixed.** Marketing journeys send only from the marketing stream and subdomain; transactional mail never carries marketing content to borrow transactional consent or deliverability, and marketing mail never rides the transactional stream.
4. **CO-144 — Every journey is fully specified.** Each journey names its lifecycle stage, entry event, exit events (stored on the user profile), conversion goal, owner, and one primary metric before it is built; an unspecified journey is not launched.
5. **CO-145 — Every journey carries a control group.** A fixed holdout of eligible users receives no journey messages, so the journey's effect on its primary metric is measured against the control, never assumed from opens or clicks alone.
6. **CO-146 — Merge fields ship with tested fallbacks.** Every personalization field has a fallback value or a fallback rendering (e.g. a greeting that works with no first name), and the fallback path is exercised in testing, not just written.
7. **CO-147 — Seed-send after every edit.** After any journey or template edit, the full sequence is sent to seed accounts on every channel it uses, and the rendered messages are read before the edit goes live.
8. **CO-148 — Suppression is part of the journey definition.** Each journey's exit and exclusion logic is event-based: win-back excludes anyone who purchased or was active inside the stage's window, and re-entry is blocked while a user is inside another conflicting journey.
9. **CO-149 — Frequency caps stop stage collisions.** A per-user cap across all journeys (per day and per week) is enforced by the sending platform, so onboarding, engagement, and win-back messages can never stack on the same user in the same window.
10. **CO-150 — Subject lines and headers are honest.** No deceptive subject lines, no fake "Re:" or "Fwd:" prefixes, no sender names implying a person or relationship that does not exist; the subject states what the message actually contains (CAN-SPAM).
11. **CO-151 — Lists are earned and sunset.** Recipients come only from the product's own opt-in capture — never purchased, rented, or scraped lists — and profiles with no engagement inside the documented sunset window are suppressed from regular sends and eventually removed.
12. **CO-152 — Unsubscribe is one click and honored fast.** Marketing mail carries one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe-Post) where the bulk-sender regime applies, every opt-out is honored within 48 hours (inside the CAN-SPAM 10-business-day legal floor), and the sending domain's spam rate is kept under 0.3%.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-071 — Unrendered merge field in production.** Banned: a live message containing raw template tokens or stringified empty values. Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: "Hi {{first_name}}, your plan renews soon" delivered to 4,000 users. Instead: give every field a tested fallback and pass the seed-send rendering test before the edit goes live (CO-146, CO-147). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-072 — Fabricated familiarity.** Banned: personalization that asserts a history, tenure, or preference the profile does not record. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: "As a loyal customer since 2019…" sent to an account created last week. Instead: render tenure and history claims only from profile fields, and omit the claim when the field is absent (CO-146). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-073 — Invented social proof in email copy.** Banned: statistics, ratings, or customer counts in a message with no source record behind them. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "Join 50,000 happy customers" in a win-back email when the business has 900 accounts. Instead: use only figures with a fact-sheet.md entry that agree everywhere they appear, or cut the claim (real-content). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-074 — Deceptive subject line.** Banned: a subject that promises an outcome, reply, or document that does not exist. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "Re: Your refund is ready" on a promotional email to users with no refund. Instead: write a subject that states the message's real content and offer (CO-150). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-075 — Behavior-blind win-back.** Banned: a generic "we miss you" journey whose audience is defined by signup date alone, with no event-based suppression. Defeats: DET-CON-006. Bad: "We miss you!" delivered to a user who purchased yesterday. Instead: define entry and suppression by events — exclude recent purchasers and active users inside the stage window (CO-148). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-CO-071 — DNS authentication check.** Verifies: CO-141. Check: automated in CI for every sending domain — `dig +short TXT example.com` shows an SPF record, `dig +short TXT selector._domainkey.example.com` returns the DKIM key, `dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com` returns a DMARC record, and the DMARC domain aligns with the From domain. Pass: all three records present and aligned. Fail: block sending from that domain. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-072 — Seed-send rendering test.** Verifies: CO-146, CO-147. Check: automated — after any journey edit, send the full sequence to seed accounts, capture the rendered messages, and scan them for unrendered tokens: `grep -E '\{\{|}}|undefined|null|NaN' rendered/` returns nothing. Pass: zero token hits on every channel. Fail: block the edit from going live. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-073 — Journey audit.** Verifies: CO-144, CO-145, CO-148, CO-149. Check: manual checklist per journey — stage, entry event, exit events, conversion goal, owner, primary metric, control group, event-based suppression, and the cross-journey frequency cap are all present in the journey definition. Pass: every field present. Fail: journey stays in draft. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-074 — Consent and deliverability check.** Verifies: CO-142, CO-151, CO-152. Check: automated pre-send audience assertion — every profile in the send list has a current opt-in record for the message type and is not on the suppression or sunset list — plus a weekly spam-rate review per sending domain. Pass: 100% of recipients verified opted-in, spam rate under 0.3%. Fail: halt the send and clean the audience. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **One automation for everyone.** A single newsletter-style sequence stands in for a lifecycle program; catch it by asking which stage each message serves — if the answer is "all of them", the program is undifferentiated and gets split by stage.
- **Set-and-forget journeys.** Journeys run for a year with no owner reading results; catch it by checking each journey's last review date against its primary metric — no review, no continued sending.
- **Open-rate as the goal.** Subjects and send times are tuned for opens while the conversion goal quietly flatlines; catch it by reading the journey's primary metric against its control group before any creative change.
- **Rescue-by-volume.** Falling engagement is answered with more messages to the same list instead of sunset and hygiene; catch it in the spam-rate trend — rising complaints with rising volume means the list, not the copy, is the problem.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Win-back journey with suppression and a tested fallback](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CO-146, CO-148.
- [Example 2 — Sending domain authenticated before the first program](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CO-141, CO-152.
- [Example 3 — Deceptive subject and invented count replaced](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CO-150, and BAN-CO-073's rule via real-content.

## Recall anchors

- Authenticate before volume: SPF, DKIM, aligned DMARC, or nothing sends.
- Consent is checked at send time, never remembered from signup.
- If it renders `{{first_name}}` to a real user, the release failed.
- Win-back excludes yesterday's buyer — by event, not by hope.
- Every journey has a holdout; unmeasured effect is assumed effect.

## Checklist

- [ ] SPF, DKIM, and aligned DMARC verify on every sending domain (CO-141, G-CO-071).
- [ ] Every journey names stage, entry/exit events, goal, owner, and primary metric (CO-144).
- [ ] Every journey has a control group and event-based suppression (CO-145, CO-148).
- [ ] Send-time opt-in check and cross-journey frequency cap are enforced (CO-142, CO-149).
- [ ] Seed-send rendering test passes with zero unrendered tokens (G-CO-072).
- [ ] One-click unsubscribe present and opt-outs honored within 48 hours (CO-152).
- [ ] No purchased or scraped addresses anywhere in the audience (CO-151).
- [ ] Every statistic or social-proof claim in copy has a fact-sheet entry (BAN-CO-073).

<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/on-page-seo/SKILL.md -->

# on-page-seo

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance ; https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies
- **Depends on:** technical-seo, fact-sheet
- **Feeds into:** aeo, geo, structured-data, internal-linking

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an indexable page is created, rewritten, or audited — assigning its search intent, writing its title, H1, heading outline, body, and meta description, or resolving two pages that compete for the same query.
- **Do NOT use when:** the problem is crawlability, indexation, canonicals, or rendering (use technical-seo), when the deliverable is structured data markup (use structured-data), or when the page is non-indexable app UI that no searcher should land on.

## Rules

1. **CO-021 — One page, one primary intent.** Every indexable page is mapped in the intent map to exactly one primary search intent drawn from real query data (Search Console or documented keyword research); a page with no mapped intent is not published as indexable.
2. **CO-022 — Metadata is written last.** The title and meta description are written from the finished page content, never from the brief or template, so both describe what the visitor actually gets.
3. **CO-023 — Unique title and description per page.** No two indexable pages share a title or a meta description, and neither is ever a template default or placeholder string.
4. **CO-024 — Titles state topic and offer plainly.** A title names the page's topic and its concrete offer in natural language a searcher would type; it contains no repeated keyword variants and no claim the page does not support.
5. **CO-025 — One H1, real heading outline.** Each page has exactly one H1 matching its primary intent, and H2/H3 headings form a true outline of the page's argument in reading order — no heading exists only to hold a keyword.
6. **CO-026 — Body satisfies the intent first.** The page's opening section answers the primary query directly with page-specific facts; supporting sections expand it. Generic filler that could sit on any competitor's page is cut.
7. **CO-027 — Descriptions promise only what the page delivers.** Every offer, price, feature, or outcome named in the meta description appears on the page itself, worded consistently with fact-sheet.md.
8. **CO-028 — Intent collisions are resolved in writing.** When a new page targets an intent an existing page owns, the intent map records the resolution before publication: merge, redirect, or a written differentiation (page-specific facts, audience, or format).
9. **CO-029 — Claims on the page are sourced or removed.** Any statistic, ranking, or superlative in title, headings, or body carries a citation on the page or in fact-sheet.md; unmeasurable superlatives ("best", "leading") are deleted, not softened.
10. **CO-030 — Intent map is re-checked quarterly.** The top indexable pages are sampled against Search Console query data each quarter; a page whose real queries no longer match its mapped intent is reassigned, merged, or rewritten.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-011 — Keyword-stuffed title.** Banned: a title that repeats keyword variants or lists services instead of stating the topic plainly. Defeats: DET-CON-022. Bad: `<title>Cheap Shoes | Best Shoes Online | Buy Shoes Sale Shoes Store</title>`. Instead: state the topic and offer once, in natural language: `<title>Running Shoes for Flat Feet — Fit Guide & Picks</title>`. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-012 — Duplicate or default metadata.** Banned: the same title or meta description on multiple pages, or template defaults shipped to production. Defeats: DET-CON-022. Bad: twelve product pages all titled "Our Products — Company" with description "Add a description here". Instead: write a unique title and description per page from its finished content (CO-022, CO-023). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-013 — Meta description advertising an absent offer.** Banned: a description that promises a discount, feature, or outcome the page does not contain. Defeats: DET-CON-022. Bad: description says "Free returns for a year" while the page and policy allow 30 days. Instead: describe only what the page delivers, consistent with fact-sheet.md (CO-027). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-014 — Scaled near-duplicate intent pages.** Banned: publishing many pages that target the same intent with swapped nouns (city, product, audience) and no page-specific substance. Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: 40 location pages identical except the city name and one stock photo. Instead: merge into one strong page, or differentiate each with real page-specific facts, audience, or format recorded in the intent map (CO-028). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-015 — Unsubstantiated superlative in title or body.** Banned: "the best", "#1", "leading" or similar claims with no cited substantiation. Defeats: DET-CON-026. Bad: H1 reads "The #1 Project Tool for Teams" with no ranking source anywhere on the site. Instead: state the verifiable fact ("Used by 4,000 teams", with the figure in fact-sheet.md) or drop the claim (CO-029). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-CO-011 — Metadata lint.** Verifies: CO-023, CO-024. Check: automated CI lint over the route inventory — extract every indexable page's `<title>` and meta description and fail on duplicates, missing values, or placeholder strings: `grep -rhoP '(?<=<title>).*?(?=</title>)' dist/ | sort | uniq -d` returns nothing, and the same for descriptions. Pass: zero duplicates, zero missing, zero defaults. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-012 — Intent map coverage.** Verifies: CO-021, CO-028. Check: diff the indexable route inventory against the intent map; every route has exactly one primary intent and every collision has a recorded resolution. Pass: 100% coverage, no unresolved collisions. Fail: block shipment of the unmapped page. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-013 — Description-to-page promise check.** Verifies: CO-022, CO-027. Check: manual sample — for each new or changed page, list every offer named in the meta description and point to the page section that delivers it. Pass: every promise located on the page and consistent with fact-sheet.md. Fail: rewrite the description before release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-014 — Heading outline check.** Verifies: CO-025. Check: automated — parse each indexable page and assert exactly one H1 and no skipped heading levels: a DOM query for `h1` returns count 1 per page. Pass: all pages conform. Fail: fix the outline and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Outline by keyword list.** Headings read as a keyword checklist rather than the page's argument; catch it by reading only the headings — if they don't summarize the page, rewrite the outline before the body.
- **Metadata written first.** Title and description drafted from the brief, then never revisited after the page changed; catch it by re-reading the finished page against its description at checklist time.
- **Intent drift by accretion.** A page gradually absorbs sections targeting other queries until it competes with three siblings; catch it in the quarterly review when its Search Console queries stop matching its mapped intent.
- **Snippet chasing.** Rewriting titles weekly in reaction to ranking wiggles, so no version is ever measured; catch it by dating every metadata change in the intent map and requiring a measurement window before the next change.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Title and description rewritten from the finished page](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CO-022, CO-023, CO-024.
- [Example 2 — Two pages, one intent, resolved by differentiation](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CO-021, CO-028.
- [Example 3 — Description promise and superlative removed](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CO-027, CO-029.

## Recall anchors

- One page, one job: one primary intent per indexable page.
- Metadata is written last, from the finished page.
- A title states the topic plainly — stuffing is a spam violation, not a technique.
- If the description promises it, the page must deliver it.
- Colliding intents are merged, redirected, or differentiated in writing.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every indexable page is in the intent map with exactly one primary intent (CO-021).
- [ ] Title and meta description were written or re-checked against the finished page (CO-022).
- [ ] Metadata lint passes: no duplicate, missing, or default titles/descriptions (G-CO-011).
- [ ] Exactly one H1 per page and headings form a real outline (CO-025, G-CO-014).
- [ ] Every offer in each description is delivered on its page and matches fact-sheet.md (CO-027).
- [ ] No unsubstantiated superlatives or unsourced statistics in titles, headings, or body (CO-029).
- [ ] Every intent collision has a written merge, redirect, or differentiation (CO-028).

<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/real-content/SKILL.md -->

# real-content

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/a-guide-to-understanding-ftc-s-4503495/ ; skills/detection/content/PARAMETERS.md (DET-CON-010…016, 019, 020, 028)
- **Depends on:** fact-sheet (D1)
- **Feeds into:** copywriting, structured-data, content-strategy, growth-experiments

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Any page, post, email, metadata set, or JSON-LD block is about to publish and contains a factual element — a testimonial, review, statistic, credential, person, price, promise, or byline. This skill is the pre-publish enforcement pass for the Real Content Rule (QB-10).
- **Do NOT use when:** Drafting copy from scratch (use copywriting, then run this pass on the result), deciding whether a claim is legal in a specific jurisdiction (route to D14 legal-privacy — this skill blocks, it does not give legal advice), or checking code-level fake functionality (use D8 placeholder-scan and the DET-FAKE parameters).

## Rules

1. **CO-121 — Classify before you publish.** Before publication, list every factual element in the piece and classify it: testimonial, review, statistic, credential, person, price, promise, or authorship. Each element is matched to its evidence — a source record the business can produce, a fact-sheet.md entry, or the live data the page renders from. An element with no match does not ship.
2. **CO-122 — The blocker list is absolute.** A fabricated testimonial (DET-CON-010), review set (DET-CON-013), third-party statistic (DET-CON-011), credential or press claim (DET-CON-012), or person (DET-CON-019) fails the entire content pass. There is no "mostly real" grade and no averaging against the elements that check out.
3. **CO-123 — First-party counters are not exempt.** A self-attested usage counter ("84 million accounts") needs a fact-sheet.md entry recording its source system and as-of date, and the same figure must appear everywhere it is used (DET-CON-011 check (b), DET-CON-015). A counter contradicted by another page is a fail; a consistent counter with no fact-sheet entry is a gap to close before publish, not a pass.
4. **CO-124 — Prices come from one source.** Every price, plan name, and billing term renders from the single pricing data source and is verified against a test checkout total before publish. A marketing page may never carry a price the checkout contradicts (DET-CON-016). Promotions carry visible dates and terms.
5. **CO-125 — No backing artifact, no promise.** Every operational promise — support hours, response times, guarantees, refund and cancellation terms — links to the policy page or documented process that makes it true (DET-CON-028). If the backing artifact does not exist, the promise is removed, not reworded.
6. **CO-126 — Bylines name real people or an honest house byline.** An individual byline requires an author page plus one independent trace (staff page, professional profile). Genuinely collective content may use an accountable team byline ("The Support Team"). An invented individual is never acceptable (DET-CON-020).
7. **CO-127 — Cut, don't soften.** An element with no evidence is deleted. It is never rescued with hedges ("up to", "as much as", "customers love us"), moved to a less prominent slot, or kept "until we get the real one." Placeholder social proof is fabrication with a deadline.
8. **CO-128 — Metadata and structured data pass the same gate.** Titles, meta descriptions, OG tags, and JSON-LD fields are factual elements under CO-121. Every JSON-LD rating, price, date, and author has a visible counterpart with an identical value, or a fact-sheet entry (DET-CON-024). Review markup exists only where real, visible reviews exist.
9. **CO-129 — A named human verifies the facts.** AI may draft and assemble evidence, but a named person checks each classified element against its source and records their name and the date in progress.md before publish. "The model wrote it" is not a verification step.
10. **CO-130 — Dated claims have owners and expiry.** Every date-bearing claim (sale end, event date, "new for <year>") carries an owner and a review-by date. Expired promotions and past events presented as current are removed or reframed as archive at the review date (DET-CON-018).
11. **CO-131 — Team imagery is real or absent.** Portraits captioned with employee names and roles are photographs of those people. Where no real photo exists, the page runs without a portrait — never a stock image or generated face in its place (DET-CON-019).
12. **CO-132 — Block and route legal questions; never improvise them.** Superlatives, guarantees, review displays, and testimonial use can be advertising-law questions. This skill blocks the element and routes the question to D14; it never clears a claim by arguing the law itself.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-061 — Invented testimonial.** Banned: a quoted endorsement from a person whose quote the business cannot produce as a source record. Defeats: DET-CON-010. Bad: "TaskBoard cut our planning time in half." — Sarah M., Marketing Manager, with no customer, email, or review behind it. Instead: publish only quotes held as source records (email, platform review, signed quote) with permission, or ship the section with no testimonial. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-062 — Unsourced third-party statistic.** Banned: a rating, market, benchmark, or comparison figure with no provenance anywhere on the domain or on file. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "Rated 4.9/5 — the fastest-growing tool in its category" with no review platform, survey, or dataset behind either number. Instead: cite the dataset or platform the figure came from, or delete the figure and describe the product plainly. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-063 — Substitute people.** Banned: a stock photograph or generated portrait captioned as a named employee, founder, or customer. Defeats: DET-CON-019. Bad: a stock headshot labeled "Amara Osei, Head of Support" on the About page. Instead: use a real photograph of the named person, or publish the name and role with no portrait. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-064 — Unbacked promise.** Banned: a present-tense operational promise with no policy or process behind it. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "24/7 support and a 30-day money-back guarantee" on the pricing page when support is email-only on weekdays and no refund policy exists. Instead: link the promise to the policy or documented process that honors it, or remove the promise and state the actual terms. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-065 — Seed people presented as real users.** Banned: demo, seed, or sample accounts, reviews, or activity shipped in production copy as real customers or demand. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the launch homepage shows a "recent signups" feed populated from the development seed data. Instead: exclude seed data from production surfaces entirely; social proof comes only from real, attributable users. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-061 — Claim-trace audit.** Verifies: CO-121, CO-123, CO-124. Check: run `python3 scripts/claim-trace.py --pages dist/ --fact-sheet fact-sheet.md` — the script extracts checkable facts (numbers, prices, dates, names) from the rendered pages and diffs them against fact-sheet.md, exiting non-zero on any unmatched or contradicted fact. Pass: exit code 0; every extracted fact traces to a fact-sheet entry. Fail: block publication; fix the copy or the stale fact-sheet side and record which was corrected. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-062 — DET-CON pre-publish scan.** Verifies: CO-122, CO-127, CO-128, CO-130. Check: run the DET-CON-001…028 checks over the rendered pages, metadata, and JSON-LD; the automatable subset runs as `python3 scripts/det-con-scan.py --pages dist/` (placeholder strings, template tokens, date extraction, JSON-LD-vs-page field diff), and the remaining parameters (010–013, 019, 020, 028) are worked as a manual checklist against the evidence register. Pass: zero blocker hits and zero unaddressed major hits. Fail: block publication — one fabricated element fails the whole pass. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-063 — Evidence register completeness.** Verifies: CO-121, CO-122, CO-126. Check: for every testimonial, review, statistic, credential, and byline in the piece, the evidence register holds a source-record reference (file path, platform URL, or fact-sheet line). Run `grep -c "source:" evidence-register.md` and compare the count against the classified element list from CO-121; then open two records at random and confirm each actually contains the claim it is cited for. Pass: counts match and both spot-checks support their claims. Fail: block publication; the unsupported element is cut under CO-127. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-064 — Named human verification.** Verifies: CO-129. Check: progress.md contains the verifier's name, the date, and the list of pages passed, entered before the publish timestamp. **Human-required:** the verifier is by definition a named human; no automated or agent-produced substitute satisfies this gate, and autonomous publication is blocked until the human entry exists. Single-agent disposition: the agent prepares the verification packet — the page list plus the G-CO-061 claim-trace and G-CO-063 evidence-register results — records this gate as human-required in progress.md, and stops at the publication step; the packet and the recorded gate state are the agent's complete deliverable for this gate. Pass: entry present and complete. Fail: block publication until a named human has done the check — an automated pass alone never satisfies this gate. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Hedge laundering.** An invented number kept alive as "up to 87% faster" or "teams save hours every week." The hedge changes the grammar, not the evidence; catch it by asking for the source record exactly as you would for the unhedged claim.
- **Evidence theater.** A citation that exists but does not contain the claim — a link to a homepage offered as proof of a rating, a study cited for a figure it never reports. Catch it by opening every cited source and finding the number on the page, which G-CO-063's spot-check samples.
- **Screenshot proof.** Accepting a screenshot of a review, dashboard, or inbox as a source record. Screenshots are producible by anyone in minutes; require the record itself — the platform URL, the exported file, the fact-sheet entry.
- **Body-only verification.** The visible copy passes, so the title tag, OG card, and JSON-LD ship unchecked — where the fabricated rating or stale price actually lives. Catch it by running G-CO-062 over metadata and markup, not just body text.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The testimonial with no customer](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CO-122 and BAN-CO-061.
- [Example 2 — The counter that disagreed with itself](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CO-123.
- [Example 3 — The promise with nothing behind it](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CO-125 and BAN-CO-064.

## Recall anchors

- No evidence, no element — cut it, don't soften it.
- One fabricated item fails the whole pass.
- First-party numbers need a fact-sheet entry too.
- No backing policy, no promise.
- Metadata and JSON-LD are claims, and they get checked like claims.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every factual element is classified and matched to evidence (CO-121).
- [ ] Zero blocker-list fabrications: testimonials, reviews, statistics, credentials, people (CO-122).
- [ ] Every first-party counter has a fact-sheet entry and agrees site-wide (CO-123).
- [ ] Every price matches the pricing source and a test checkout total (CO-124).
- [ ] Every operational promise links to its backing policy or process (CO-125).
- [ ] Every byline is a real, traceable person or an honest house byline (CO-126).
- [ ] Claim-trace audit (G-CO-061) and DET-CON scan (G-CO-062) both pass.
- [ ] A named human has verified the facts and signed progress.md (CO-129, G-CO-064).

# sitemaps

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Search Central, "Build and submit a sitemap" — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap ; Sitemaps protocol — https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html
- **Depends on:** technical-seo
- **Feeds into:** internal-linking, web-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a site launches, migrates, restructures, or changes its route or content inventory, and whenever sitemap correctness, freshness, or Search Console sitemap errors are in question. This skill owns the sitemap as a generated claim about which URLs exist and are indexable.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is whether a page should be indexable or canonical at all (technical-seo sets that contract; this skill generates against it), or how pages get discovered by users (internal-linking — the sitemap is a crawler fallback, never a linking strategy).

## Rules

1. **CO-181 — Generated, never hand-maintained.** The sitemap is a build artifact generated from the actual route and content inventory at publish time. No sitemap file is ever edited by hand; a needed change is made in the inventory or the generator, never in the output.
2. **CO-182 — Canonical entries only.** Every listed URL returns HTTP 200, is indexable (no `noindex`, no robots block), and is its own canonical. An entry is a claim that the URL is live and canonical — if any leg fails, the URL does not belong in the file.
3. **CO-183 — No dead or redirected entries.** Redirects (3xx), errors (4xx/5xx), non-canonical variants, and parameter, filter, sort, or session URLs are never listed. The sitemap names destinations, not paths to them.
4. **CO-184 — One host, one scheme, absolute URLs.** Every entry is an absolute URL on the site's single canonical host and scheme (per technical-seo CO-009). No relative URLs, no mixed www/non-www, no HTTP entries on an HTTPS site.
5. **CO-185 — Truthful lastmod.** `lastmod` is the date the page's content last changed significantly, taken from the content record — never the build or deploy timestamp. When the change date is not known, omit `lastmod` rather than invent one; engines discount sitemaps whose dates cry wolf.
6. **CO-186 — Event-driven regeneration.** The sitemap regenerates in the same build or publish event that changes the inventory: publish, unpublish, route change, redirect change. A sitemap older than the newest content change is stale by definition and is a defect, not a backlog item.
7. **CO-187 — Protocol limits.** Each sitemap file holds at most 50,000 URLs and 50 MB uncompressed, per the sitemaps protocol. Beyond either limit, split into multiple files under a sitemap index. The limit is measured on the uncompressed file, even when the served file is gzipped.
8. **CO-188 — Shard by section.** Large sites shard sitemaps by content type or section (posts, products, docs) under one sitemap index, so a broken or stale section is visible in Search Console reporting instead of diluted across one giant file.
9. **CO-189 — Count reconciliation.** After every generation, the sitemap URL count is reconciled against the route/content inventory count. Every difference has a named reason (draft, noindex by design, redirect) recorded with the build; an unexplained difference fails the release.
10. **CO-190 — Discovery wiring.** The sitemap is referenced by a `Sitemap:` line in robots.txt and submitted in Search Console. After a domain change, restructure, or index rebuild, the submission is re-verified — the file existing on the server is not evidence any engine knows about it.
11. **CO-191 — Production purity.** A staging sitemap never deploys to production, and a production sitemap never lists staging hosts or staging URLs. The sitemap host check is part of technical-seo's staging-vs-production promotion diff.
12. **CO-192 — No invented priority or changefreq.** `priority` and `changefreq` are omitted, or set truthfully per section from the actual update pattern. Values that misstate the pages (1.0 and "always" site-wide) are fabricated metadata and are never emitted to look thorough.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-091 — Dead and excluded URLs listed.** Banned: a sitemap containing URLs that return 404/410, redirect, carry `noindex`, or canonicalize to a different URL. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the launch sitemap still lists 214 URLs a year later; 96 are deleted products, 41 redirect to category pages, and 12 are `noindex` landing pages. Instead: generate from the live inventory and filter on 200 + indexable + self-canonical before writing any entry (CO-182, CO-183). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-092 — Deploy-date lastmod.** Banned: stamping every entry's `lastmod` with the build or deploy date, so unchanged pages claim to have changed on every release. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: a nightly deploy rewrites all 8,000 `lastmod` values to today's date, including a legal page untouched for two years. Instead: take `lastmod` from each content record's real change date, and omit it where that date is unknown (CO-185). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-093 — The hand-maintained sitemap.** Banned: a static `sitemap.xml` written or edited by hand — typically generated once at launch and shipped untouched ever after while the site changes around it. Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: a developer hand-adds three new pages to the XML, misses eleven others, and the file still lists the scaffold's sample page. Instead: the sitemap is generated from the route/content inventory on every publish event; hands never touch the output (CO-181, CO-186). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-094 — Variant URLs listed as pages.** Banned: listing parameter, filter, sort, session, or print variants as separate sitemap entries to inflate the URL count. Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: `/products?color=red`, `/products?sort=price`, and `/products?utm_source=newsletter` all appear as entries alongside `/products`. Instead: list only the canonical URL of each substantively distinct page (CO-183); variants canonicalize or carry `noindex` under technical-seo. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-095 — Staging URLs in the production sitemap.** Banned: a production sitemap listing staging hosts, preview URLs, or internal hostnames. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: after a rushed release, `https://staging.example.com/pricing` ships in the live sitemap and crawlers are sent to an auth-walled preview. Instead: generate against the production inventory on the canonical host only, and run the host check in the promotion diff (CO-184, CO-191). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-091 — Sitemap audit script.** Verifies: CO-182, CO-183, CO-184. Check: automated — `python3 scripts/sitemap_audit.py --sitemap https://example.com/sitemap.xml` fetches the sitemap (following the index to every shard), requests every listed URL (or a statistically sound random sample above 10,000 URLs), and asserts per URL: HTTP 200, no redirect, canonical tag equal to the listed URL, no `noindex` in meta robots or X-Robots-Tag, host and scheme equal to the canonical host. Pass: zero assertion failures. Fail: block the release; fix the inventory or generator, never the output file. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-092 — Count reconciliation.** Verifies: CO-181, CO-189. Check: automated — the build compares the generated sitemap's URL count against the route/content inventory count and writes both numbers plus a reason for every excluded inventory item (draft, noindex, redirect) to the build log. Pass: counts reconcile with every difference explained. Fail: block the release until the difference is explained. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-093 — Regeneration-on-change test.** Verifies: CO-181, CO-186. Check: automated — in the staging build, publish one test page and unpublish another, rebuild, and diff the sitemap: the published URL must appear and the unpublished URL must disappear, with no manual step. Pass: both changes reflected by the build alone. Fail: the generator is not wired to the inventory; fix before launch. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-094 — lastmod spot-check.** Verifies: CO-185. Check: automated assist — sample 25 entries carrying `lastmod` and compare each against the content record's actual last-change timestamp (CMS field or version-control history for that page's source). Pass: every sampled `lastmod` matches the record, or the entry omits `lastmod`. Fail: remove or correct the dates at the generator and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-095 — Discovery wiring check.** Verifies: CO-190, CO-191. Check: automated — fetch robots.txt and assert it contains a `Sitemap:` line naming the production sitemap index on the canonical host; fetch that URL and assert HTTP 200 and zero listed URLs on any non-production host. Pass: both assertions hold and the Search Console submission is confirmed in the project log. Fail: fix robots.txt or the generator's host configuration and re-check. Before a production environment is provisioned, this gate's disposition is a recorded provisioning waiver per the §6.3 protocol; it unblocks when the production site is deployed on its canonical host and Search Console access exists. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Ping-and-pray resubmission.** Resubmitting the same stale sitemap in Search Console hoping indexing improves, while the file still lists dead URLs. Catch it: a resubmission with no generator or inventory change since the last one fixes nothing — run G-CO-091 first.
- **Sitemap as linking strategy.** Adding an orphan page to the sitemap instead of linking it from navigation, a hub, or body content, and calling it discoverable. Catch it: if the page's only inbound reference is the sitemap, internal-linking owns the fix, not this file.
- **Count pride.** Reporting "12,000 URLs submitted" as an SEO result while a third are excluded, redirected, or dead. Catch it: the honest numbers are the reconciled count (G-CO-092) and the audit pass rate (G-CO-091), never the raw entry count.
- **The forgotten index.** Restructuring shards — renaming, merging, removing sections — without updating the sitemap index, so the index points at files that no longer exist. Catch it: after any shard change, fetch every child named in the index; a 404 child is a release defect.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The launch-day sitemap, one year later](examples/example-1.md) — corrects CO-181.
- [Example 2 — Every lastmod is the deploy date](examples/example-2.md) — corrects CO-185.
- [Example 3 — The audit: 1,200 entries, 214 bad claims](examples/example-3.md) — corrects CO-182.

## Recall anchors

- Generated from the inventory — hands never touch the output.
- Every entry is a claim: 200, indexable, self-canonical.
- lastmod is the content's change date, or it is omitted.
- Counts reconcile, or the difference has a name.
- The sitemap is a crawler fallback, not a linking strategy.

## Checklist

- [ ] Sitemap generated from the route/content inventory in this build — no hand edits (CO-181).
- [ ] Audit script passes: every listed URL returns 200, self-canonical, indexable (G-CO-091).
- [ ] Sitemap count reconciles with the inventory count; every difference explained (G-CO-092).
- [ ] Publish/unpublish test changes the sitemap with no manual step (G-CO-093).
- [ ] Sampled `lastmod` values match real content change dates (G-CO-094).
- [ ] No staging host or non-canonical URL anywhere in the file (G-CO-095).
- [ ] Each file within 50,000 URLs / 50 MB uncompressed; index current (CO-187, CO-188).
- [ ] robots.txt names the sitemap and Search Console submission is confirmed (CO-190).

<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/social-open-graph/SKILL.md -->

# social-open-graph

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** The Open Graph protocol — https://ogp.me
- **Depends on:** on-page-seo, technical-seo
- **Feeds into:** web-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a site launches, a page template is built or changed, branding changes, or a shared link previews the wrong title, description, or image. This skill owns the Open Graph and Twitter Card tags every public page emits.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what the page itself says (copywriting, on-page-seo), what its JSON-LD declares (structured-data), or whether the page is indexable (technical-seo). Never use it to promise share traffic: platforms render the tags; they do not guarantee distribution.

## Rules

1. **CO-221 — The four required properties, on every public page.** Every public page emits `og:title`, `og:type`, `og:image`, and `og:url`, plus `og:description` and `og:site_name`. A page missing any required property is a defect, not a style choice.
2. **CO-222 — og:url is the page's canonical URL.** og:url equals the canonical URL technical-seo assigns the page. A site-wide homepage og:url on interior pages is a defect (DET-CON-023).
3. **CO-223 — og:title and og:description are per-page.** Both are generated from the page's own title and topic and match what the link actually opens. Identical og:title or og:description across pages with different destinations is a defect.
4. **CO-224 — og:image is absolute and page-appropriate.** og:image is an absolute URL (never a relative path a crawler cannot resolve) pointing to an image that represents this page, at full share size — the protocol's recommended 1200×630. The homepage logo is never the og:image for every page.
5. **CO-225 — The image fallback is a compromise, not the design.** Only og:image may fall back to a site-wide default share image, and that fallback is recorded as a known compromise. og:title, og:description, and og:url never fall back to site-wide values.
6. **CO-226 — og:site_name is this site's own name.** og:site_name carries the site's current name from the fact sheet, on every page. A scaffold's or another site's name in og:site_name is a defect.
7. **CO-227 — og:type matches the content, with its properties.** Pages use the og:type that fits (website for general pages, article for posts, product for product pages), and type-specific properties are emitted where they apply — article:published_time and article:author on posts.
8. **CO-228 — Twitter Card tags mirror the OG values.** twitter:card, twitter:title, twitter:description, and twitter:image are emitted and carry the same per-page values as their OG counterparts; twitter:card is summary_large_image wherever og:image meets the large-image size. Two metadata systems describing one page never disagree.
9. **CO-229 — Tags are generated in the page template.** OG and Twitter tags are produced by the page template from the page's own data — the same source that renders the visible title and description. Hand-edited per-page tag blocks and tags pasted from a scaffold or another site are defects.
10. **CO-230 — Share images are real assets.** Every og:image URL returns HTTP 200 and serves the image the tags claim. A purpose-built share image is produced for each page type; a stretched logo, a placeholder graphic, or a stock photo presented as the product is a defect.
11. **CO-231 — No private or gated page gets public card promises.** Pages behind authentication, staging hosts, and noindex pages do not emit OG tags describing them as public content, and production tags never point at staging URLs or staging images.
12. **CO-232 — Debuggers re-run after template or branding changes.** Social platforms cache previews aggressively, so after any template, branding, or share-image change, the home, article, and product templates are re-run through the platform debuggers to force fresh scrapes. A fix that is never re-scraped is not live.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-111 — Site-wide homepage og:url.** Banned: emitting the homepage URL as og:url on every page. Defeats: DET-CON-023. Bad: `/pricing`, `/blog/setup-guide`, and `/about` all carry `<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/">`, so every share attributes to and previews as the homepage. Instead: og:url is each page's own canonical URL, generated by the template (CO-222). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-112 — One og:title and og:description for the whole site.** Banned: a single global title/description pair in the social tags regardless of destination. Defeats: DET-CON-023. Bad: every page shares with og:title "Example — Do More With Less" and the homepage description, including the changelog and a support article. Instead: og:title and og:description are generated per page from that page's title and topic (CO-223). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-113 — Homepage logo as every page's og:image.** Banned: pointing og:image at the site logo or one generic brand graphic for all pages. Defeats: DET-CON-023. Bad: a detailed pricing page and a photo-heavy case study both preview as the company logo on a white background. Instead: each page type gets a purpose-built share image representing its content; only a recorded fallback may reuse the default image (CO-224, CO-225). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-114 — Another site's identity in the tags.** Banned: og:site_name, og:title suffixes, or image URLs copied from a scaffold, theme demo, or another site and never replaced. Defeats: DET-CON-023. Bad: og:site_name reads "Acme Starter Kit" and og:image resolves on the theme vendor's domain, months after launch. Instead: site_name and branding come from this site's fact sheet, and all tag assets are served from this site's own domain (CO-226, CO-229). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-115 — Relative or broken og:image.** Banned: og:image as a relative path, a staging URL, or a URL that does not return the claimed image. Defeats: DET-CON-023. Bad: `<meta property="og:image" content="/images/share.png">` on production pages, so crawlers cannot resolve it and shares render with no image. Instead: og:image is an absolute production URL verified to return HTTP 200 with the intended image (CO-224, CO-230). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-111 — Site-wide tag dump diff.** Verifies: CO-221, CO-222, CO-223, CO-226. Check: automated — crawl every public URL, extract all OG and Twitter tags, and diff: og:url must equal the page's canonical URL, og:title/og:description must match the page's own title/topic with no cross-page duplicates across different destinations, og:site_name must equal the current brand name, and all four required properties must be present. Pass: zero mismatches. Fail: block shipment of the affected templates. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-112 — og:image resolution and size check.** Verifies: CO-224, CO-225, CO-230. Check: automated — request every distinct og:image URL; assert absolute URL, HTTP 200, image content type, and dimensions of 1200×630; flag any image reused across pages outside the recorded fallback list. No-image disposition: a page with no image assets (a text-only page) may ship with no og:image only when that absence is recorded as a deliberate disposition in progress.md, naming the page and the reason; an unrecorded absence is a failure, not a disposition. Pass: every og:image resolves at full share size and reuse matches the fallback record, and every page without one carries the recorded no-image disposition. Fail: fix the asset or the template and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-113 — Platform debugger pass.** Verifies: CO-227, CO-228, CO-232. Check: manual — run the production home, article, and product URLs through the Meta Sharing Debugger and the X/Twitter card validator; confirm the rendered preview shows the page's own title, description, and image, and re-scrape after any template or branding change. Pass: all three templates preview correctly with current branding. Fail: correct the tags and force a re-scrape before launch sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-114 — Template generation audit.** Verifies: CO-229, CO-231. Check: automated grep plus manual review — search templates and rendered output for hardcoded og: tags, foreign domains, and staging hosts; confirm tags are emitted from page data and that gated/noindex pages carry no public card tags. Pass: no hardcoded or foreign tag values found; tags trace to the page template. Fail: move generation into the template and re-run G-CO-111. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The set-and-forget card.** Tags were correct at launch, then a redesign changed titles, branding, and images while the OG tags kept describing the old site. Catch it: any template or branding change without a debugger re-run (CO-232) means the cards are stale by default.
- **Checking one page and declaring the site done.** The homepage previews perfectly, so nobody samples an article, a product page, or a deep docs page — where the template defaults actually live. Catch it: verification samples every page type, never just the homepage.
- **The plugin shrug.** A metadata plugin or framework default is installed and trusted, and its output is never read. Catch it: dump the rendered tags (G-CO-111) — if nobody has seen the actual values, they are unverified, whatever generated them.
- **Designing the share image last.** Pages ship with whatever image was nearest — a screenshot with a browser chrome edge, a logo stretched to 1200×630. Catch it: share images are named deliverables per page type (CO-230), reviewed like any other visual asset.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Every page sharing as the homepage](examples/example-1.md) — corrects CO-222.
- [Example 2 — The logo that previewed a pricing page](examples/example-2.md) — corrects CO-224.
- [Example 3 — The scaffold's name in og:site_name](examples/example-3.md) — corrects CO-226.

## Recall anchors

- og:url is the page's canonical URL — never the homepage site-wide.
- Title and description are per-page; only the image may fall back.
- og:image: absolute URL, page-appropriate, 1200×630.
- og:site_name is this site's own current name.
- Platforms cache previews — re-scrape after every template or branding change.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every public page emits og:title, og:type, og:image, og:url, og:description, and og:site_name (CO-221).
- [ ] Tag dump diff is clean: og:url equals canonical, no cross-page title/description duplicates (G-CO-111).
- [ ] Every og:image is absolute, returns 200, and is 1200×630 (G-CO-112).
- [ ] og:site_name matches the current brand name from the fact sheet (CO-226).
- [ ] Twitter Card tags mirror the OG values (CO-228).
- [ ] Home, article, and product templates pass the platform debuggers with current branding (G-CO-113).
- [ ] No hardcoded, foreign-domain, or staging values in any tag (G-CO-114).

# structured-data

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Search Central, introduction to structured data — https://developers.google.com/structured-data/ ; Schema.org vocabulary and validator — https://schema.org ; Google Search spam policies — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies
- **Depends on:** real-content (whether reviews, ratings, and claims may exist at all), fact-sheet (D1, for page-external facts)
- **Feeds into:** technical-seo, aeo, web-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a page type gains, changes, or loses JSON-LD markup; a template or data model feeding markup changes; or Search Console reports a rich-result error. This skill owns the markup contract; D3 frontend implements the templates against it.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is whether the underlying content may be published (real-content decides), what the page says (copywriting), or whether the page is crawlable (technical-seo). Never use markup to make a claim the page itself does not make.

## Rules

1. **CO-161 — Generated, never hand-written.** Every JSON-LD block is emitted by a template from the same data store that renders the visible page. No per-page hand-edited or copy-pasted blocks exist; if a value is wrong, the fix lands in the data or the template, never in one page's markup.
2. **CO-162 — Markup says only what the page shows.** Every rating, price, date, author, and availability value in JSON-LD has a visible counterpart on the same page with an identical value. A field with no visible counterpart is removed, not "completed" (DET-CON-024).
3. **CO-163 — One template per page type, kept small.** A schema type is added only when pages of that type genuinely contain the content the type describes. Marking up content the page type does not have — a recipe schema on a product page — is a defect, not ambition.
4. **CO-164 — Required properties complete.** Each template carries every property Google requires for the rich result that page type is eligible for, plus recommended properties wherever the underlying data exists. Eligibility is checked against Google's structured-data documentation per type, not assumed.
5. **CO-165 — No placeholder values, ever.** Generator defaults — "Product Name", price `0.00`, `example.com` URLs, sample organization names — are build failures. A template that cannot populate a required property from real data does not ship.
6. **CO-166 — Review markup follows real reviews.** `Review` and `aggregateRating` markup exists only on pages where real reviews are visibly rendered and have passed real-content. The markup question is never asked before the real-content question is answered.
7. **CO-167 — Prices match everywhere.** `Offer.price` and `priceValidUntil` in markup are identical to the price rendered on the page and the price charged at checkout, drawn from the same price source (DET-CON-016). A sale that ended removes the offer markup in the same change.
8. **CO-168 — JSON-LD, syntactically valid.** JSON-LD is the only format. Every block parses as valid JSON — one trailing comma invalidates the whole block — and validation runs in the build, not by eyeball.
9. **CO-169 — Dates and authors match.** `datePublished`, `dateModified`, and `author` in markup are identical to the visible byline and dates. `dateModified` changes only when the content actually changed, never on a bare redeploy.
10. **CO-170 — Change triggers revalidation.** Any template or data-model change re-runs validation on every affected page type before release. A refactor that touches rendering is presumed to touch markup until validation proves otherwise.
11. **CO-171 — Monitored after deployment.** Search Console enhancement reports are reviewed on the web-analytics cadence. A new error or invalid-item class is a defect with a named owner, not a statistic to watch.
12. **CO-172 — Page-external fields verified, not exempt.** Fields with no visible counterpart by design (e.g. an organization's founding date or logo) are verified against fact-sheet.md before the template ships, and re-verified when the fact sheet changes.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-081 — Markup-only claims.** Banned: JSON-LD stating ratings, prices, dates, or authors the visible page never shows. Defeats: DET-CON-024. Bad: a product page renders no rating, but its JSON-LD declares `aggregateRating: 4.8, reviewCount: 212`. Instead: generate the block from the page's data (CO-161); if no reviews render, no rating markup ships (CO-166). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-082 — Generator placeholders in production.** Banned: shipping JSON-LD containing scaffold values such as "Product Name", `price: 0.00`, or `https://example.com/logo.png`. Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: a pasted generator block names the product "Product Name" with price 0.00 on the live pricing page. Instead: bind every property to the page's data store and fail the build on placeholder patterns (CO-165, G-CO-083). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-083 — Fabricated review markup.** Banned: `aggregateRating` or `Review` markup without real, visible, attributable reviews behind it. Defeats: DET-CON-013. Bad: markup claims 300 five-star reviews on a page whose review section is empty because "the widget loads later". Instead: no real visible reviews, no review markup — route the reviews themselves through real-content first (CO-166). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-084 — Separately maintained markup copies.** Banned: static JSON-LD blocks stored apart from the page data and edited by hand, so markup and page drift apart over time. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: a developer updates the price in the CMS; the hard-coded JSON-LD in the template footer keeps the old price for three months. Instead: one template reads the same record the page renders (CO-161); price changes propagate in the same commit (CO-167). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-085 — Marking up hidden content.** Banned: describing in JSON-LD any content that is hidden from users on the page (display:none sections, unloaded tabs, geo-gated blocks). Defeats: DET-CON-024. Bad: FAQ markup lists eight questions, but only three are visible; five sit in a hidden div "for SEO". Instead: mark up exactly the visible set; if a question matters, show it (CO-162). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-081 — CI schema validation.** Verifies: CO-164, CO-168. Check: automated — on every build, fetch one sample URL per page type from the staging build, extract each `application/ld+json` block, parse it as JSON, and validate required properties per type against Google's rich-result requirements (Rich Results Test during development). Pass: every block parses and carries all required properties. Fail: block the build. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-082 — Markup-vs-visible diff.** Verifies: CO-162, CO-167, CO-169. Check: automated — script diffs `aggregateRating`, `price`, `datePublished`/`dateModified`, and `author` values in JSON-LD against the rendered page text for the same sample URLs. Pass: zero fields without an identical visible counterpart (page-external fields checked against fact-sheet.md per CO-172). Fail: block shipment; this gate runs the DET-CON-024 check. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-083 — Placeholder scan.** Verifies: CO-165. Check: automated — grep all emitted JSON-LD in the build output for `Product Name`, `example.com`, `example.org`, `"price": 0`, `Lorem`, and `TODO`. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block the build. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-084 — Change-triggered revalidation.** Verifies: CO-170. Check: manual with checklist — any merge touching a markup template or its data model lists the affected page types, and G-CO-081/G-CO-082 results for those types are attached to the change before release. Pass: revalidation evidence present for every affected type. Fail: hold the release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-085 — Enhancement-report review.** Verifies: CO-171. Check: manual — on the web-analytics cadence, open Search Console's rich-result enhancement reports and log new error/invalid classes with a named owner and fix date. Pass: review logged for the current cycle with no unowned error class. Fail: escalate as a defect before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Schema maximalism.** Emitting every type in the vocabulary "for coverage" — Event, JobPosting, Course — on pages that contain none of that content. Catch it: for each type on a page, point at the visible content it describes; a type with nothing to point at comes out (CO-163).
- **The copied competitor block.** Lifting a competitor's JSON-LD and swapping the brand name, importing their claims, dates, and ratings along with the structure. Catch it: every value must trace to this site's data store, never to the clipboard (CO-161).
- **Validate-once launch.** Markup validated at launch, then template refactors silently break it for months. Catch it: validation lives in CI and in the change checklist (G-CO-081, G-CO-084), not in launch memory.
- **Rich-result chasing.** Reshaping visible content to fit a markup type the page does not naturally have — inventing an FAQ section solely to earn FAQ markup. Catch it: content decisions come from copywriting and real-content; markup describes what exists, it never commissions what does not.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Rating markup with no reviews on the page](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CO-166.
- [Example 2 — The generator block that shipped with placeholders](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CO-165.
- [Example 3 — Markup price disagrees with the page and checkout](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CO-167.

## Recall anchors

- Generated from the same data that renders the page — never decorated.
- If the page doesn't show it, the markup doesn't say it.
- No real visible reviews, no rating markup.
- Placeholders are build failures, not drafts.
- Template change means revalidation, every affected type.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every JSON-LD block is template-generated from the page's own data store (CO-161).
- [ ] Every markup field has an identical visible counterpart, or a fact-sheet entry (CO-162, CO-172).
- [ ] Required properties complete for each type's rich result (G-CO-081).
- [ ] Review/aggregateRating markup exists only over real, visible reviews (CO-166).
- [ ] Markup price equals page price equals checkout price (CO-167).
- [ ] Placeholder scan returns zero hits in the build output (G-CO-083).
- [ ] Markup-vs-visible diff passes on a sample URL per page type (G-CO-082).
- [ ] Template or data-model changes carry revalidation evidence (G-CO-084).
