<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/technical-seo/SKILL.md -->

# technical-seo

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Search Central, SEO guide for developers — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/get-started-developers ; RFC 9309, Robots Exclusion Protocol — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html ; Google Search spam policies — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies ; Google Search Central, "AI features and your website" — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features ; Sitemaps protocol — https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: it audits the site's own rendered output, server responses, and robots/sitemap files — the crawl-and-index contract is checked against the site itself, not another skill's output. It feeds on-page-seo, aeo, geo, sitemaps, and web-analytics.
- **Feeds into:** on-page-seo, aeo, geo, sitemaps, web-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a site is built, migrated, redesigned, or promoted between environments, and whenever crawlability, rendering, indexation, canonicalization, or redirect behavior is in question. This skill owns the crawl-and-index contract between the site and search engines.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what a page says (copywriting, on-page-seo), what its markup declares (structured-data), or which URLs the sitemap lists (sitemaps — this skill sets the contract that skill generates against). Never use it to promise a ranking: Google documents eligibility requirements, not ranking outcomes.

## Rules

1. **CO-001 — The indexable-page contract.** Every page intended for search returns HTTP 200, carries a self-referencing canonical, and is reachable by following links from the site itself. A page failing any leg is a defect to fix, not a ranking mystery to explain.
2. **CO-002 — Server-rendered by default.** Indexable content ships as server-rendered or statically generated HTML. Client-side rendering of indexable content is an exception that must be verified under CO-003, never a default.
3. **CO-003 — Verify the rendered HTML.** JavaScript-dependent content is checked in the rendered HTML (Search Console URL Inspection or an equivalent rendered-DOM fetch), never assumed from source code, view-source, or a local build.
4. **CO-004 — robots.txt discipline.** robots.txt follows RFC 9309 syntax, is served at the host root with HTTP 200, and never blocks the CSS or JavaScript assets that rendering the pages requires. Every change to it is reviewed like a code change.
5. **CO-005 — The promotion indexability diff.** Before every production release, staging and production are diffed on robots.txt, `noindex` (meta and X-Robots-Tag), basic-auth walls, and canonical host. Any staging protection found in production is a release blocker.
6. **CO-006 — One canonical URL per page.** Each page has exactly one canonical URL, stated as an absolute URL that itself returns 200 and is indexable. Parameter, filter, sort, session, and print variants canonicalize to the base URL or carry `noindex`; they are never indexable duplicates competing with it.
7. **CO-007 — Redirect hygiene.** Permanent moves use 301 or 308. Redirects are single-hop wherever the destination is known; a chain longer than two hops is fixed at the source, not documented and left.
8. **CO-008 — Real status codes.** Missing content returns a real 404 or 410. An error page served with HTTP 200 (a soft 404) is a defect, as is redirecting every removed URL to the homepage.
9. **CO-009 — One host, one scheme.** The site canonicalizes to a single host form (www or non-www) over HTTPS. Every other host/scheme combination 301-redirects to it, and canonicals, sitemaps, and internal links use only that form.
10. **CO-010 — The sitemap contract.** The XML sitemap lists only canonical, indexable URLs that return 200, is regenerated when routes change, stays within protocol limits (50,000 URLs / 50 MB per file, sitemap index beyond that), and is referenced in robots.txt. Generation itself belongs to the sitemaps skill; this rule is the contract it must satisfy.
11. **CO-011 — Directive consistency.** robots.txt, meta robots, X-Robots-Tag, and canonicals never contradict each other on the same URL, and no CDN, firewall, or hosting rule blocks search or AI crawlers that robots.txt allows — Google names CDN/hosting-level blocking as a real eligibility failure for its AI features.
12. **CO-012 — Coverage reviewed on a cadence.** Search Console coverage and indexing reports are reviewed on a fixed cadence (monthly at minimum) and the review is logged. Every spike in excluded or error URLs is triaged to a named cause. Reports state eligibility and defects found; they never state or imply a ranking guarantee.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-001 — Staging protection shipped live.** Banned: promoting a build whose production environment still carries staging `noindex`, `Disallow: /`, a basic-auth wall, or staging-host canonicals. Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: the redesigned site launches with `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` copied from the staging template, and organic traffic falls to zero over two weeks before anyone checks. Instead: run the CO-005 promotion diff; production ships only when no staging directive survives. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-002 — Indexable duplicate URL variants.** Banned: letting parameter, filter, sort, or session URLs be indexed as separate pages with self-referencing canonicals, splitting signals across duplicates of one page. Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: `/products?color=red`, `/products?sort=price`, and `/products` are all indexed, each canonicalizing to itself. Instead: variants canonicalize to the base URL or carry `noindex` (CO-006); only substantively different pages are indexable. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-003 — Soft 404s.** Banned: serving "page not found" content with HTTP 200, or answering every deleted URL with a redirect to the homepage. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: a removed product URL returns 200 with a "this item is gone" template, so the index fills with dead pages the status code calls healthy. Instead: return a real 404/410 for gone content, and 301 only to a genuinely equivalent replacement (CO-008). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-004 — Ranking guarantees and fabricated visibility wins.** Banned: promising a ranking, traffic figure, or AI-citation outcome in any plan or report, or reporting an unadopted proposal (e.g. llms.txt, which Google states on the record it does not use) as an AI-visibility win. Defeats: DET-CON-026. Bad: the launch report claims the new llms.txt file "secures AI Overview citations" and projects a "#1 ranking within 90 days". Instead: report only what Google documents — indexed, snippet-eligible, defects fixed — and label every other claim with its evidence level or cut it. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CO-001 — Promotion indexability diff.** Verifies: CO-005, CO-004, CO-011. Check: automated — script fetches staging and production robots.txt plus the response headers and meta robots of the top route templates, and diffs directives and canonical host. Pass: zero staging protections (noindex, Disallow: /, auth wall, staging canonical) present in production. Fail: block the release. Before a production environment is provisioned, this gate's disposition is a recorded provisioning waiver per the §6.3 protocol; it unblocks when a production environment is provisioned and the release is deployed to it. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-002 — Route inventory crawl.** Verifies: CO-001, CO-006, CO-009. Check: automated — crawl the production route inventory and assert, per indexable URL: HTTP 200, self-referencing canonical in the canonical host form, no `noindex`. Pass: 100% of indexable URLs satisfy all three. Fail: block shipment of the affected routes. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-003 — Redirect and status audit.** Verifies: CO-007, CO-008. Check: automated — follow every redirect reachable from internal links and the sitemap; assert chains are ≤2 hops, permanent moves are 301/308, and a sample of deleted URLs returns 404/410, not 200 or a homepage redirect. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: fix at the source and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-004 — Rendered-content verification.** Verifies: CO-002, CO-003. Check: manual with tooling — for a sample of JavaScript-dependent templates, compare the rendered HTML (URL Inspection or rendered-DOM fetch) against the expected primary content: heading, body text, links, canonical. Pass: primary content fully present in the rendered HTML for every sampled template. Fail: treat as a rendering defect; do not ship the template. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-005 — Coverage review log.** Verifies: CO-012. Check: manual — the monthly Search Console review exists in the project log with excluded/error counts, each spike triaged to a named cause, and no ranking or traffic guarantee stated anywhere in it. Pass: log entry complete for the current month. Fail: the review is overdue; complete it before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The view-source check.** Verifying a JavaScript page by reading its source HTML and concluding the content is "there" or "missing" from an unrendered shell. Catch it: any verification note that does not name the rendered-HTML tool used is not a verification (CO-003).
- **Folklore-first fixes.** Implementing tactics with no basis in Google's documentation — meta keywords, keyword-density targets, llms.txt as a ranking lever — while documented crawl or indexation defects stay open. Catch it: ask of every task, "which Google document requires this?"; no answer, no priority.
- **Canonical roulette.** Changing the canonical host, scheme, or trailing-slash strategy repeatedly, each time without a recorded decision, so the index never settles. Catch it: the canonical form is a one-time decision under CO-009; a second change in a quarter demands a written reason.
- **The one-and-done audit.** A thorough launch audit, then silence while template refactors quietly break canonicals, directives, and status codes for months. Catch it: gates G-CO-001–G-CO-003 run per release and G-CO-005 monthly — an audit with no cadence is a snapshot, not a control.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The staging noindex that shipped to production](examples/example-1.md) — corrects CO-005.
- [Example 2 — Filter URLs indexed as duplicates](examples/example-2.md) — corrects CO-006.
- [Example 3 — The page that existed only after JavaScript](examples/example-3.md) — corrects CO-003.

## Recall anchors

- 200, self-canonical, reachable by links — or it is a defect.
- Verify the rendered HTML, never the source.
- Diff staging against production before every release.
- One canonical URL per page; variants canonicalize or noindex.
- Report eligibility and defects — never promise a ranking.

## Checklist

- [ ] Promotion indexability diff is clean: no staging directive in production (G-CO-001).
- [ ] Every indexable URL returns 200 with a self-referencing canonical (G-CO-002).
- [ ] robots.txt is RFC 9309-valid and blocks no render asset (CO-004).
- [ ] Redirect chains are ≤2 hops; permanent moves are 301/308 (G-CO-003).
- [ ] Deleted URLs return a real 404/410 — no soft 404s (CO-008).
- [ ] JavaScript-dependent templates verified in rendered HTML (G-CO-004).
- [ ] Sitemap lists only canonical, indexable, 200 URLs (CO-010).
- [ ] This month's Search Console coverage review is logged, with no ranking guarantee stated (G-CO-005).

<!-- generated from skills/seo-content/web-analytics/SKILL.md -->

# web-analytics

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D9 SEO & Content (CO)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Analytics developer documentation — https://developers.google.com/analytics ; Google Search Central, "AI features and your website" (measurement section) — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features
- **Depends on:** technical-seo, product-analytics (D12 — owner of the shared tracking plan)
- **Feeds into:** content-strategy, on-page-seo, growth-experiments

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** search and acquisition measurement is set up, audited, or reported: Search Console verification, coverage and performance review, GA4 organic landing-page analysis, and the content decisions that follow from them. This skill owns the search/acquisition slice of measurement.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is product behavior inside the app — funnels, feature usage, retention — or the event taxonomy itself: those belong to D12 (product-analytics, event-tracking). **Boundary: one shared tracking plan, two consumers.** D12 owns the plan and the event names; this skill consumes them for search reporting and never invents, renames, or duplicates an event.

## Rules

1. **CO-241 — Search and acquisition only.** This skill measures how search and acquisition channels deliver visitors: Search Console performance (queries, pages, clicks, impressions), coverage/indexing, rich-result reports, and GA4 organic landing-page behavior. Anything past the landing page is D12's slice of the shared plan.
2. **CO-242 — Every production property verified.** Search Console is verified for every production property, including domain variants, and the GA4 property is linked. An unverified property is a blind spot and is treated as a defect with an owner, not an oversight.
3. **CO-243 — The tracking plan is the contract.** Every tag and event this skill relies on is an entry in the shared tracking plan (D12-owned): name, trigger, parameters, owner. A live tag with no plan entry, or a plan entry with no live implementation, is a defect found by the G-CO-121 diff.
4. **CO-244 — Configuration is verified, never assumed.** A pasted snippet proves nothing. Each relied-on event is observed firing — in GA4 DebugView or Tag Assistant — with the plan's exact name and parameters, and the primary conversion is completed end to end in a debug session before anyone reports on it.
5. **CO-245 — Consent is respected end to end.** Where consent mode applies, analytics does not collect before the visitor's consent state allows it, and the consent configuration is verified in a fresh, no-consent session — not inferred from the banner being visible on the page.
6. **CO-246 — Fixed review cadence.** Search Console coverage and performance are reviewed monthly at minimum, and the review is logged with the actions it produced. A review that produces no briefs, refreshes, retirements, or technical fixes — and says why — is an incomplete review.
7. **CO-247 — No content decision without a citation.** Every brief, refresh, and retirement this skill informs names the query, page, or landing-page evidence behind it. "We should write about X" with no Search Console or GA4 evidence cited does not enter content-strategy's queue.
8. **CO-248 — AI-feature traffic is read where Google reports it.** Appearances in Google's AI features are reported inside Search Console's overall Performance data. They are never split out, estimated, or presented as a separate metric — no platform publishes such a number, so any standalone "AI traffic" figure is invented.
9. **CO-249 — Every reported figure reproduces from source.** Each number in a report names its platform, property, report, date range, and filters, and can be re-pulled to the same value. A figure nobody can reproduce is cut from the report, not footnoted.
10. **CO-250 — Event and tag changes go through the plan.** Changes are proposed into the shared tracking plan, keep D12's names consistent, and are debug-validated before release. No duplicate or variant spellings of an existing event are ever shipped (BAN-CO-124).
11. **CO-251 — Indexing regressions are incidents.** A spike in excluded or error URLs, or a sudden drop in indexed pages, is triaged to a named cause with an owner and a fix or an accepted-risk note — never left as an observation on a chart.
12. **CO-252 — Reports are dated and current.** Every report states its pull date, date range, and comparison convention, and its figures come from that pull. A recycled screenshot or a figure from a previous period presented as current is stale copy (BAN-CO-125).

## BAN list

- **BAN-CO-121 — Invented metrics reported as measured.** Banned: presenting any metric no platform produces — a standalone "AI Overview traffic" number, a paid "GEO score" shown as a platform metric, an estimated citation share — as measured fact in a plan or report. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: the monthly report carries a line "AI Overview visits: 1,240 (+18%)" that appears in no Search Console or GA4 report and cannot be re-pulled. Instead: report AI-feature appearances only inside overall Performance data (CO-248); label anything else with its evidence level or cut it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-122 — Measurement claimed, never configured.** Banned: announcing that analytics or conversion tracking is "set up" when the snippet is pasted but no tracking-plan entry exists and no debug session has ever verified an event firing. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the launch checklist marks "analytics done"; three months later the team discovers the signup conversion was never marked and DebugView shows no events at all. Instead: no measurement claim until the G-CO-121 plan diff is clean and a G-CO-122 debug session has completed the primary conversion. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-123 — Consent promise without the configuration.** Banned: privacy or consent copy stating that tracking starts only after consent, while tags fire on page load regardless of consent state. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the cookie policy says "we track only with your permission," but a fresh no-consent session fires the full GA4 event stream. Instead: make the firing match the promise — consent state gates collection (CO-245) and the fresh-session check in G-CO-122 proves it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-124 — Duplicate and misspelled event variants.** Banned: shipping variant spellings of one event (`sign_up`, `signup`, `SignUp`) so a single action fragments across several report rows. Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: the signup conversion is split across three event names, each showing a third of the real total, and the team debates which is "the" number. Instead: one canonical name from the shared tracking plan (CO-250); variants are removed and the change is debug-validated before release. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CO-125 — Stale figures presented as current.** Banned: reusing a previous period's screenshot, export, or headline number in a current report, including after the underlying tag has broken. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: this month's report reuses last month's traffic chart while the GA4 tag has been missing from the redesigned template for two weeks. Instead: every report is built from a fresh, dated pull (CO-252), and a broken tag is a CO-251 incident, not a quiet gap. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-CO-121 — Tracking-plan diff.** Verifies: CO-243, CO-250. Check: automated — export the live tag/event list (GTM container export or a crawl grep for measurement IDs, e.g. `grep -rhoE "G-[A-Z0-9]{6,}" dist/ | sort -u`, plus the implemented event names) and diff it against the shared tracking plan's entries. Pass: zero live tags or events missing from the plan, and zero plan entries with no live implementation. Fail: block the release until the diff is clean. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-122 — DebugView conversion and consent session.** Verifies: CO-244, CO-245. Check: manual with tooling — in a fresh browser profile, load the site with no consent given and confirm no analytics collection beyond consent-state pings; then grant consent, complete the primary conversion flow, and watch GA4 DebugView. Pass: the conversion event fires exactly once, under its plan name with its plan parameters, and nothing collected before consent. Fail: block; fix configuration and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-123 — Monthly Search Console review.** Verifies: CO-242, CO-246, CO-251. Check: manual — the review log holds an entry for the current month covering every verified property: coverage counts, performance summary, each exclusion or error spike triaged to a named cause and owner, and the actions the review produced. Pass: entry complete for the current month. Fail: the review is overdue; complete it before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CO-124 — Report reproducibility audit.** Verifies: CO-247, CO-248, CO-249, CO-252. Check: semi-automated — list every figure in the latest report; each must cite platform, property, report, and date range; re-pull a sample of at least two figures and compare values; scan the report for any standalone AI-feature metric. Pass: every sampled figure reproduces exactly and no invented metric appears. Fail: withdraw and reissue the report. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Dashboard theater.** A polished dashboard exists, so the team feels measured — but no review ever opens it and no decision ever cites it. Catch it: if this month's G-CO-123 log entry is missing, the dashboard is decoration.
- **Vanity slicing.** The review leads with whichever number rose — impressions up — while organic landing-page conversions fell, unmentioned. Catch it: every review opens with coverage health and the primary conversion, in that order; growth metrics come second.
- **Two sources of truth, averaged.** Search Console and GA4 disagree (they measure different things), so someone blends them into one comfortable number. Catch it: each metric has exactly one named source platform under CO-249; a discrepancy gets an explanation of the definitions, never an average.
- **The drifting comparison.** Comparison periods quietly change month to month — vs. last month, vs. last quarter, vs. launch — so the trend always flatters. Catch it: the comparison convention is fixed in the tracking plan; changing it is a noted plan amendment, not an editorial choice.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The "AI traffic" line nobody could reproduce](examples/example-1.md) — corrects CO-248.
- [Example 2 — The snippet that measured nothing](examples/example-2.md) — corrects CO-244.
- [Example 3 — Three names for one signup](examples/example-3.md) — corrects CO-250.

## Recall anchors

- Search and acquisition here; product events are D12's — one plan, two consumers.
- Snippet present is not configured. DebugView, or it didn't happen.
- No content decision without a citation.
- AI appearances live inside overall Performance data — never invent the split.
- A figure nobody can reproduce is a figure you cut.

## Checklist

- [ ] Search Console verified for every production property and domain variant (CO-242).
- [ ] Tracking-plan diff is clean: no live tag or event missing from the plan (G-CO-121).
- [ ] DebugView session completed the primary conversion exactly once, under its plan name (G-CO-122).
- [ ] Fresh no-consent session collects nothing before consent (CO-245).
- [ ] This month's Search Console coverage and performance review is logged, spikes triaged (G-CO-123).
- [ ] Every figure in the latest report reproduces from its cited source (G-CO-124).
- [ ] No standalone "AI traffic" or other invented metric appears in any report (CO-248).

## Department D10 — project-memory

# changelog

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 — https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ ; Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: entries are written from the project's own commit history and release diff, read directly from the repo; no other skill's output is an input. It feeds readme-writing and handover.
- **Feeds into:** readme-writing (README links the changelog), handover

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project ships anything a user can notice — a release, a deprecation, a fix — and its CHANGELOG.md must be created, updated, or cut for release.
- **Do NOT use when:** recording internal work with no user effect (that belongs in the work log or commit history), or announcing a release socially (release notes and posts are written from the changelog, not instead of it). Do not keep a second change history in GitHub Releases that can drift from CHANGELOG.md (PM-124).

## Rules

1. **PM-121 — One file, newest first.** Exactly one CHANGELOG.md at the project root. `## [Unreleased]` sits on top; released sections follow in strictly descending version order. No per-year, per-component, or per-team changelog files.
2. **PM-122 — Entries land with the change.** Every user-visible change adds its entry to Unreleased in the same change (same PR/commit) as the behavior it describes. A release is never assembled by reconstructing entries from memory at release time.
3. **PM-123 — Six categories only.** Category headings are exactly: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. No invented categories ("Misc", "Improvements", "Updates"), and an empty category is omitted, not left as a bare heading.
4. **PM-124 — One canonical history.** CHANGELOG.md is the single source of truth for change history. Release-page or store notes are generated or copied from it at release time, never maintained as a separate, editable copy.
5. **PM-125 — Written for users.** Each entry describes the effect on the user in one plain sentence: what they can now do, what behaves differently, what they must act on. Implementation details, internal codenames, and ticket IDs never appear.
6. **PM-126 — Curated, never generated.** Entries are selected and written by a human judgment pass. Merge commits and internal refactors with no user effect are omitted; one user-visible change is one entry, however many commits it took.
7. **PM-127 — The bump matches the content.** SemVer: breaking change → major, new feature → minor, fix only → patch. A release containing Removed entries or breaking Changed entries cannot ship as minor or patch; a release with Added entries is at least minor.
8. **PM-128 — Exact heading and date format.** Release headings are `## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD` with a real SemVer version and the actual release date in ISO 8601. Version labels are written the same way everywhere: no mixing of `v1.2`, `1.2`, and `Version 1.2.0`.
9. **PM-129 — No heading without a release.** A version section is created only when that version actually ships — a tag or published artifact exists for it. Planned versions live in Unreleased or the roadmap, never as empty or speculative version headings.
10. **PM-130 — The version source of truth is declared, never assumed.** The project states its version source — git tag, `package.json`, a `VERSION` file, or another stack-specific file — in the changelog header or project config. Gates read the version from that declared source only; no gate hardcodes a source.
11. **PM-131 — Every entry traces to a real change.** Each entry corresponds to a change actually merged in the release it sits under. An entry for work that was planned, reverted, or shipped in a different release is removed or moved, never left in place.
12. **PM-132 — Published sections are frozen.** After a version ships, its section is not silently edited. A factual error is corrected with a dated erratum note appended to that section, so the record shows both what was claimed and what was corrected.
13. **PM-133 — Deprecation precedes removal.** A feature appears under Deprecated at least one release before it appears under Removed, and the deprecation entry names the release in which removal is planned when that is known.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-061 — The dumped git log.** Banned: pasting raw commit output, merge commits, or commit hashes into CHANGELOG.md as entries. Defeats: DET-CON-004. Bad: "## [1.4.0] - 2026-11-02 — Merge pull request #812 from fix/typo; a3f9c1e wip; revert 'revert add export'". Instead: curate the release into user-effect entries under the six categories (PM-125, PM-126) — the export fix becomes one Fixed entry, the merge and revert noise is omitted. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-062 — Entries for changes that never shipped.** Banned: changelog entries describing features, fixes, or behavior that are not in the release — planned, reverted, or imagined. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: the 1.4.0 section announces "Added: CSV export" but the export PR was reverted before release and no export exists in 1.4.0. Instead: the entry is deleted before release; if the feature ships later, its entry lands with that release (PM-131). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-063 — The content-free entry.** Banned: entries that carry no information about what changed — "bug fixes and improvements", "various enhancements", "performance improvements" with no behavior named. Defeats: DET-CON-006. Bad: "Fixed: Bug fixes and performance improvements." Instead: name the user-visible effect: "Fixed: invoice PDFs no longer render a blank second page for multi-currency accounts." Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-064 — The phantom version heading.** Banned: a `## [X.Y.Z]` section for a version that was never tagged or published. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: CHANGELOG.md carries a polished `## [2.0.0] - 2026-10-15` section, but the project's latest tag is v1.4.0 and no 2.0.0 artifact exists anywhere. Instead: unreleased work stays under `## [Unreleased]` until the version actually ships (PM-129). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-065 — Mixed version labels.** Banned: referring to versions inconsistently across the changelog and release surfaces — `v1.2`, `1.2`, `Version 1.2.0`, `Release 12` for the same versioning scheme. Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: the changelog heads a section `## [1.2] - 2026-09-01` while the tag is `v1.2.0` and the README announces "Version 1.2". Instead: one label form everywhere — the SemVer number in brackets in the changelog, matching the declared source of truth (PM-128, PM-130). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-061 — Heading and category parser.** Verifies: PM-121, PM-123, PM-128. Check: automated — a script asserts every `## ` heading in CHANGELOG.md matches `^## \[Unreleased\]$` or `^## \[(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\] - \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$`, the captured date parses as a real calendar date, and every `### ` heading is one of Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Pass: zero non-matching headings. Fail: block the release; fix the heading or category. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-062 — Order and date sequence.** Verifies: PM-121, PM-127. Check: automated — the parser from G-PM-061 additionally asserts version headings are in strictly descending SemVer order and their dates are non-increasing down the file. Pass: no inversions. Fail: block; reorder the sections — never edit a date to make the order pass. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-063 — Version source-of-truth match.** Verifies: PM-129, PM-130. Check: automated — read the project's declared version source (per PM-130: e.g. `git describe --tags --abbrev=0` stripped of a leading `v`, or the `version` field of `package.json`, or the contents of `VERSION`) and compare it with the topmost version heading in CHANGELOG.md. Pass: the two are exactly equal. Fail: block the release; either the release was not tagged or the heading is wrong — fix whichever is false. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-064 — Bump consistency.** Verifies: PM-127. Check: automated — diff the newest section's categories against the previous version: if Removed is present or any Changed entry is marked breaking, the major number must have increased; if Added is present, at least the minor number must have increased; a patch bump may contain only Fixed and Security entries. Pass: the actual bump is at least the required level. Fail: block; renumber the release before anything ships under the wrong version. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-065 — Entry-to-change cross-check.** Verifies: PM-122, PM-131. Check: manual, sampled — pick three entries from the newest release and trace each to a merged change (PR or commit) inside that release's range; separately, if the diff since the previous tag contains user-visible changes, Unreleased must not have been empty at release time. Pass: 3 of 3 entries trace to real changes. Fail: block; remove or move every untraceable entry and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The release-day reconstruction.** Unreleased stays empty for weeks, then one person writes the whole section the night before release from memory and merged-PR titles. Catch it: check whether entries arrived in the same commits as their changes (PM-122); a single giant changelog commit at release time is the tell.
- **The marketing changelog.** Entries written as launch copy — "our most powerful release ever", superlatives, exclamation marks — instead of statements of what changed. Catch it: read an entry aloud and ask what the user can now do; if the answer is an adjective, rewrite it (PM-125).
- **The security-fix whisper.** A fix for an exploitable vulnerability is buried as an ordinary Fixed entry, so users cannot tell they must upgrade urgently. Catch it: any fix that closes a vulnerability, leak, or permission hole belongs under Security (PM-123), worded to convey urgency without disclosing exploit detail.
- **The orphaned changelog.** CHANGELOG.md exists but nothing links to it — not the README, not the release page — so it silently rots while users read stale release notes elsewhere. Catch it: the README links the changelog (readme-writing), and G-PM-063 failing after a release means the file was left behind.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Git log dump vs curated release section](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-126 / BAN-PM-061.
- [Example 2 — Phantom heading and version-source mismatch](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-129, PM-130 / BAN-PM-064.
- [Example 3 — Breaking change shipped as a patch bump](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-127 / G-PM-064.

## Recall anchors

- Entries land with the change, not at release time.
- Written for users: effect, not implementation.
- Six categories, no inventions.
- No heading without a real release behind it.
- The bump must match the content — breaking means major.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every user-visible change in this release has an entry, added in the same change as the behavior (PM-122).
- [ ] All entries sit under the six categories only, one user effect per entry (PM-123, PM-125).
- [ ] No entry describes anything that is not actually in the release (PM-131, BAN-PM-062).
- [ ] Heading format, descending order, and ISO dates verified by G-PM-061 and G-PM-062.
- [ ] Top version heading equals the declared version source of truth (PM-130, G-PM-063).
- [ ] The version bump is consistent with the categories present (PM-127, G-PM-064).
- [ ] Deprecations were announced at least one release before any removal in this release (PM-133).
- [ ] Gates G-PM-061 to G-PM-065 pass; results recorded in progress.md.

# decision-logs

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" — https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions ; MADR 4.0.0 — https://adr.github.io/madr/ ; adr-tools — https://github.com/npryce/adr-tools
- **Depends on:** project-templates (emits `docs/adr/` and DECISIONS.md)
- **Feeds into:** progress-tracking, handover, memory-retrieval

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project makes a significant, hard-to-reverse decision — stack, vendor, data model, protocol, a mandated-set change — or reverses one already recorded.
- **Do NOT use when:** the choice is trivially reversible or purely local (naming, formatting) — those belong in the work log or a commit message, not an ADR. Do not use DECISIONS.md as a second copy of the records; it is their index (PM-109).

## Rules

1. **PM-101 — One decision, one numbered file.** Each significant decision gets exactly one file in `docs/adr/`, named `NNNN-short-title.md`. Numbers are sequential and never reused; a withdrawn number stays withdrawn and is noted in DECISIONS.md.
2. **PM-102 — Written at decision time.** The record is created in the same change as the decision itself, while the context and the decider are known — never reconstructed later from chat or memory.
3. **PM-103 — Fixed structure.** Default to Nygard's five sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences. Escalate to MADR when the decision is contested, adding decision drivers, considered options with pros and cons, and a Confirmation section.
4. **PM-104 — Context is neutral fact.** Context states the forces, constraints, and evidence at play, without advocacy. Persuasion belongs in the options analysis and the Decision, never in Context.
5. **PM-105 — Decision in active voice, with a named decider.** The Decision reads "We will…" and the record names who decided (person or role) and the date. A record with no decider is incomplete.
6. **PM-106 — Consequences include the negatives.** Every record states what becomes harder, what is given up, and what risk is accepted — not only the benefits.
7. **PM-107 — Closed status lifecycle.** Status is exactly one of: proposed → accepted → deprecated, or superseded-by-ADR-NNNN. No other values, no free-text statuses.
8. **PM-108 — Accepted records are immutable except for Status.** A reversal is a new ADR that supersedes the old one and links to it; the old record's body is never edited, and its Status is updated to superseded-by-ADR-NNNN.
9. **PM-109 — DECISIONS.md is the index, not a copy.** The index lists each record's number, title, status, and link — and nothing else. Record content lives only in `docs/adr/`.
10. **PM-110 — Rejected options are recorded.** For contested decisions, each considered option is listed with why it lost. That record is what stops the decision being reopened later.
11. **PM-111 — Every fact in a record traces to evidence.** Figures, constraints, and claims in Context cite their source (a fact-sheet entry, a benchmark, a document). No number or constraint is invented to justify the choice.
12. **PM-112 — MADR records state how compliance is confirmed.** The Confirmation section names the check — a test, a review step, or a gate — that will show the decision is actually being followed.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-051 — Rewriting an accepted ADR in place.** Banned: editing the Context, Decision, or Consequences of an accepted record so the file no longer shows what was decided. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: ADR-0007 said "We will use SQLite"; after the switch to Postgres someone edits it to say Postgres, and every document citing ADR-0007 now contradicts the record. Instead: leave ADR-0007 untouched, write ADR-0019 choosing Postgres, link it, and set ADR-0007's Status to superseded-by-ADR-0019. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-052 — Invented rationale.** Banned: stating figures, benchmarks, or constraints in Context that have no source behind them. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: "Context: the current API handles only ~200 req/s" when no measurement exists and the fact sheet records no such limit. Instead: cite the measurement or fact-sheet entry, or state the limit as an unverified assumption and mark it as one. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-053 — The non-decision.** Banned: a Decision section hedged until it commits to nothing. Defeats: DET-CON-009. Bad: "We may possibly migrate to the new queue at some point if it seems beneficial." Instead: "We will migrate the notification queue to SQS by 2026-12-01; the decider is the tech lead; revisit only if the cost ceiling in ADR-0011 is exceeded." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-054 — Index as second copy.** Banned: pasting full ADR text into DECISIONS.md alongside the record in `docs/adr/`. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: DECISIONS.md carries the full text of ADR-0003; the ADR is later superseded but the index copy is not, so the project states two different current decisions. Instead: the index holds number, title, status, and link only (PM-109); readers follow the link to the single canonical record. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-055 — Reused or duplicated ADR number.** Banned: assigning a number that an earlier record already used, or two records sharing one number. Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: a deleted draft's number 0012 is given to a new record, so existing citations to "ADR-0012" now point at two different decisions. Instead: numbers are allocated once, in order, and never recycled; a withdrawn record keeps its number with Status deprecated. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PM-051 — Filename and numbering lint.** Verifies: PM-101. Check: automated — `ls docs/adr/ | grep -vE '^[0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9-]+\.md$'` must print nothing, and `ls docs/adr/ | cut -d- -f1 | sort | uniq -d` must print nothing (no duplicate numbers). Pass: zero output from both commands. Fail: block the change; renumber before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-052 — Index cross-check.** Verifies: PM-107, PM-109. Check: automated — script compares the set of files in `docs/adr/` against the links in DECISIONS.md and diffs each index status against the record's Status line. Pass: every record is indexed exactly once, every index link resolves, statuses agree. Fail: block; fix the index or the record, never both silently. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-053 — Status and section lint.** Verifies: PM-103, PM-107. Check: automated — for each record, `grep -E '^## Status' -A1` yields a value in {proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded-by-ADR-NNNN}, and the five section headings Title/Status/Context/Decision/Consequences are all present. Pass: all records conform. Fail: block; correct the status value or add the missing section. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-054 — Immutability check.** Verifies: PM-108. Check: manual-assisted (script-supported) — for each accepted record, run the project's immutability script (sketch below) with the record's file and its acceptance commit. The script walks the `git log -p --follow` hunks after acceptance, tracks the current `## ` section from diff context lines, and prints a FLAG line for every added or removed line outside the Status section. The agent then reads each flagged line in the full diff and confirms it is a genuine body edit — hunk context can omit the section heading, so the script over-reports rather than under-reports, and the human/agent judgment on the flagged lines is part of the check. Pass: no confirmed body edits to any accepted record after its acceptance commit. Fail: block; restore the original body and express the change as a new superseding ADR. Recorded in: progress.md.

  ```bash
  # scripts/adr-immutability-check.sh FILE ACCEPTANCE_COMMIT
  git log -p --follow "$2..HEAD" -- "$1" | awk '
    /^diff --git/ { section = "" }
    /^ /  { if ($0 ~ /^ ## /) section = substr($0, 2); next }
    /^[+-]/ && $0 !~ /^\+\+\+/ && $0 !~ /^---/ {
      if (section != "## Status") print "FLAG: " $0
    }'
  ```

## Anti-patterns

- **The retroactive batch.** A dozen ADRs written in one sitting at project end, "reconstructing" decisions nobody remembers making. Catch it: creation dates cluster and Context reads omniscient — real records are written one at a time, at decision time (PM-102).
- **The rubber stamp.** Every record accepted with one option and "Consequences: none." Catch it: a record with no rejected option and no negative consequence has not been thought through (PM-106, PM-110).
- **The orphan decision.** Architecture visibly changed in the code but no ADR exists. Catch it: before accepting a structural change, search DECISIONS.md for its record; no hit means the record is written first.
- **The zombie proposal.** Records sit at "proposed" for months while the team already follows them. Catch it: the index cross-check (G-PM-052) review includes aging proposals — accept them or mark them deprecated.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Reversal by supersession, not rewrite](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-108 / BAN-PM-051.
- [Example 2 — A decision that actually decides](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-105 / BAN-PM-053.
- [Example 3 — Index entry, not a second copy](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-109 / BAN-PM-054.

## Recall anchors

- One decision, one file, one number — never reused.
- Write it when you decide it, not when you remember it.
- Accepted means frozen; reversal means a new record.
- DECISIONS.md points; `docs/adr/` holds.
- Consequences include what it costs.

## Checklist

- [ ] Record created at decision time, in `docs/adr/`, with the next unused number (PM-101, PM-102).
- [ ] Five sections present; MADR escalation used if the decision was contested (PM-103).
- [ ] Decision is active voice and names the decider and date (PM-105).
- [ ] Negative consequences and rejected options are written down (PM-106, PM-110).
- [ ] Every fact in Context cites a source (PM-111).
- [ ] Status is a lifecycle value, and DECISIONS.md index entry added (PM-107, PM-109).
- [ ] Gates G-PM-051 to G-PM-054 pass; results recorded in progress.md.

# documentation-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Diátaxis — https://diataxis.fr/ ; Google developer documentation style guide, timeless documentation — https://developers.google.com/style/timeless-documentation ; Documentation checks in CI — https://datadef.io/guides/en/docs-checks-in-ci ; Documentation as code — https://sourcegraph.com/blog/documentation-as-code
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: docs are written from the product and code itself, checked against the running system; this skill sets the standards the other doc skills follow rather than consuming their output. It feeds readme-writing, runbook-writing, and changelog.
- **Feeds into:** readme-writing, runbook-writing, changelog

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** writing or revising any project documentation page — tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation — setting a project's doc standards, or reviewing docs before a release.
- **Do NOT use when:** the artifact is the README (use readme-writing), an incident procedure (runbook-writing), a decision record (decision-logs), a changelog (changelog), or marketing and site copy (D9 copywriting).

## Rules

1. **PM-021 — One page, one Diátaxis mode.** Every page is exactly one of tutorial (learning), how-to (task), reference (facts), or explanation (background), and the mode is declared in the page's front matter. A draft serving two modes is split before it ships.
2. **PM-022 — Verify before you write.** Every documented feature, flag, command, default value, and behavior is checked against the actual system — run it, or read the code/config that implements it — before the page ships. Behavior you cannot verify is not documented; it is filed as an open question.
3. **PM-023 — Name the reader need first.** Before drafting, state the reader and the job the page does for them in one line at the top of the draft. No identifiable reader need, no page.
4. **PM-024 — Docs as code.** Documentation lives in the same repository as the code it describes, in plain-text markup, reviewed in the same pull-request flow, and published on merge — never in a separate wiki or document store that drifts from the code.
5. **PM-025 — Docs ship with the code change.** A behavior change and its documentation change land in the same change. When that is impossible, a tracked doc-gap issue is filed in the same change and linked from the changed code or release notes.
6. **PM-026 — Owner and review trigger on every page.** Front matter carries `owner` and `last_reviewed`. A page is reviewed when code in its area changes or when its freshness window (a project-policy parameter) expires, whichever comes first.
7. **PM-027 — The word list governs terminology.** Product, feature, and concept names match the project word list and naming list exactly. A term not in the word list is defined at first use or not used.
8. **PM-028 — Write timelessly.** Document the current state in the present tense. "Currently", "new", "latest", and "now" never stand in for a version: version-specific facts carry the version number ("In 2.4, …") or are not stated.
9. **PM-029 — Match voice to mode.** How-tos address the reader in the imperative ("Run the migration"); tutorials guide step by step with the expected result at each step; reference pages state facts without narrative or persuasion.
10. **PM-030 — Execute every code sample.** Each command, API call, and config block in a page is run verbatim against the current system before the page ships or changes. A sample that fails is a documentation bug with the same priority as a code bug.
11. **PM-031 — One canonical page per fact.** A fact lives on exactly one page; other pages link to it instead of copying it. Duplicated passages found in review are replaced by links in the same change.
12. **PM-032 — Complete front matter or no merge.** Every page carries `mode`, `owner`, and `last_reviewed` in front matter. A page missing any field fails G-PM-011 and does not merge.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-011 — Documenting an unverified feature.** Banned: writing instructions, flags, or behaviors from a ticket, plan, or assumption without checking them against the running system. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: a how-to documents `backup --dry-run`, a flag the CLI does not have, and readers script against it. Instead: run the feature or read its implementation first (PM-022); document only what the system demonstrably does. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-012 — Scaffold and default text shipped as documentation.** Banned: publishing generator boilerplate, template prompts, or placeholder sections ("Add a description here", empty headed sections) as finished docs. Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: the setup guide ships with the template's "TODO: describe your project" paragraph under the Installation heading. Instead: write the real content for the slot or delete the section; an honest gap is a tracked issue, not filler. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-013 — Draft markers in published docs.** Banned: `TODO`, `FIXME`, "content to follow", or "coming soon" (undated) in any published page, heading, or metadata field. Defeats: DET-CON-004. Bad: the reference page for webhooks ends with "TODO: add payload examples" on the live docs site. Instead: keep markers in the repo's issue tracker; published pages contain only finished statements. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-014 — Time-anchored claims left to rot.** Banned: "new for 2026", "our latest release", or undated "coming soon" feature claims on evergreen pages. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: the concepts page still announces "New in 2024: dark mode" two major versions later. Instead: state the fact with its version ("Dark mode, added in 1.8") and let the freshness gate (G-PM-014) retire stale claims. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-015 — Model-default register in docs.** Banned: dense AI filler vocabulary (delve, tapestry, realm, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's important to note") standing in for technical content. Defeats: DET-CON-007. Bad: an explanation page opens with two paragraphs of elevated filler before naming the component it explains. Instead: cut to the subject; every paragraph names a component, mechanism, or fact the reader can check. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-011 — Structure and front-matter lint.** Verifies: PM-021, PM-026, PM-032. Check: automated — run `npx markdownlint-cli "docs/**/*.md"` and a front-matter script asserting every page has `mode`, `owner`, and `last_reviewed`; the same commands run locally as a script or in CI. Pass: exit 0 and zero pages missing a field. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-012 — Link check.** Verifies: PM-031. Check: automated — run `lychee docs/ README.md` for internal links on every change; external URLs on a scheduled run. Pass: zero broken internal links. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-013 — Style and terminology lint.** Verifies: PM-027, PM-028. Check: automated — run `vale --minAlertLevel=error docs/` with the project's word list and timeless-writing rules (flagging "currently/latest/new" as version substitutes) configured as the Vale style. Pass: zero error-level alerts. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-014 — Freshness gate.** Verifies: PM-026. Check: automated — a script reads `last_reviewed` from every page's front matter and fails any page older than the project's review window (policy parameter, set per project tier). Pass: no page past its window. Fail: block release until the page is reviewed and re-dated or the window is changed by a recorded decision. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-015 — Reader task test.** Verifies: PM-022, PM-023, PM-030. Check: manual — a reader unfamiliar with the material completes one learn, one task, and one lookup using only the docs, with no outside help. Pass: all three tasks completed; every stall is filed as a documentation bug. Fail: rework the failing pages and retest before the docs ship. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The sprawling mega-page.** One page trying to be tutorial, manual, and rationale at once, growing by accretion because splitting feels like extra work. Catch it: if you can name two reader needs on one page, split it now (PM-021).
- **The changelog dump.** Release notes or commit messages pasted in as documentation — a record of what changed, mistaken for an explanation of how things work. Catch it: if the page reads as a dated list of changes, it belongs in changelog, not the docs tree.
- **The orphan page.** A correct page that no index, navigation, or other page links to, so no reader ever finds it and it rots unreviewed. Catch it: after writing, follow your own link to the page from the docs index; if you cannot, the page is not finished.
- **Copy-paste twins.** The same procedure pasted into several pages "for convenience"; fixes land in one copy and the others become quietly wrong. Catch it: search the docs for a distinctive sentence from any procedure you edit — every hit beyond the canonical page is a link waiting to replace a copy (PM-031).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — One page, two jobs](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects PM-021.
- [Example 2 — The flag that did not exist](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects PM-022.
- [Example 3 — "New and latest" forever](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects PM-028.

## Recall anchors

- One page, one Diátaxis mode, one reader need.
- If you did not run it, do not document it.
- Docs ship with the code change — or the gap is a tracked issue.
- No "new", "latest", "currently": state the version or the fact.
- Every page: mode, owner, last_reviewed — or it does not merge.

## Checklist

- [ ] The page declares exactly one Diátaxis mode in its front matter (PM-021).
- [ ] Every documented behavior was verified against the actual system (PM-022).
- [ ] Owner and last_reviewed are set, and the review trigger is known (PM-026).
- [ ] All terms match the project word list; any new term is defined at first use (PM-027).
- [ ] No time-anchored word stands in for a version number (PM-028).
- [ ] Every code sample was executed verbatim and passed (PM-030).
- [ ] markdownlint, lychee, and Vale error-level checks pass locally (G-PM-011, G-PM-012, G-PM-013).
- [ ] The doc change ships with its code change, or a doc-gap issue is filed and linked (PM-025).

# handover

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google Cloud Blog, "How SREs find the landmines in a service" (Production Readiness Review practice) — https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/how-sres-find-the-landmines-in-a-service-cre-life-lessons ; datadef.io, docs checks in CI (freshness-gate pattern) — https://datadef.io/guides/en/docs-checks-in-ci ; Sourcegraph, "Documentation as code" — https://sourcegraph.com/blog/documentation-as-code
- **Depends on:** project-templates, progress-tracking, memory-retrieval
- **Feeds into:** none — handover is the terminal transfer step; its outputs are consumed by the receiving owner, not by another skill

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project changes hands — new owner, new maintainer, end of engagement, or the single agent's work is picked up by a different operator. handover.md is maintained during the project and finalized at transfer; this skill runs the readiness review and the acceptance test that close the transfer.
- **Do NOT use when:** recording day-to-day status (progress-tracking), writing the runbooks and postmortems that transfer (runbook-writing, postmortem-writing), or recording why decisions were made (decision-logs). This skill verifies and transfers the project's memory; it does not author it.

## Rules

1. **PM-181 — Handover is a process, not a document.** It runs as a readiness review against a checklist — mandated file set fresh and complete, architecture and failure-mode walkthroughs, landmines list, credentials path, acceptance — modeled on Google's Production Readiness Review. A file drop with no review is not a handover.
2. **PM-182 — No handover without a named accepting owner.** The receiver is a named person or role who agrees to take the project on. A transfer addressed to "the team" or to nobody has not happened.
3. **PM-183 — Acceptance is recorded, with a date.** handover.md records who accepted, in what role, on which ISO 8601 date, and what scope they accepted. Undated or unsigned acceptance does not count.
4. **PM-184 — Landmines are listed explicitly, each with evidence.** Every open risk, known fragility, and unresolved follow-up appears in the landmines list with evidence or a link to where the evidence lives. If there are none, handover.md states "no known landmines" as a finding — silence is never read as none.
5. **PM-185 — Credentials path, never credentials.** Handover materials name each system, where its secrets live (vault, provider, owner), and the procedure by which access is granted or transferred. Secret values — passwords, tokens, keys — never appear in handover.md or any transferred document.
6. **PM-186 — The memory transfers, not only the code.** Runbooks, postmortems, DECISIONS.md and the ADR set, progress.md, and the fact sheet are line items in the transfer manifest. A receiver who gets code without the project's memory has received a partial handover.
7. **PM-187 — Failure modes are walked through, not just listed.** Before sign-off, the giver walks the receiver through the architecture and the known failure modes — what breaks, how it presents, which runbook answers it. The walkthrough is recorded in handover.md with its date and participants.
8. **PM-188 — The mandated set is fresh at transfer.** Every mandated file is present and within its freshness window (a project-policy parameter, per file tier) at the transfer date. A stale runbook or a kickoff-era progress.md is refreshed or flagged as a gap before sign-off, not discovered after.
9. **PM-189 — Open work transfers with owners.** Every blocked item, postmortem follow-up, and deferred fix open at transfer is listed with its current owner, its state, and what unblocks or completes it, so nothing open depends on the giver's memory after they leave.
10. **PM-190 — The cold run is the acceptance test.** Using only the handover materials, the receiving owner deploys the project, finds the runbook for a named incident class, names the top open risks, and states who accepted the transfer and when. Any failed step is a handover gap.
11. **PM-191 — Gaps block sign-off and are recorded.** A failed cold-run step, a missing mandated file, or an unlisted landmine is written into handover.md as a gap with an owner and a fix date. Sign-off waits until gaps are closed or the accepting owner explicitly accepts them in writing in handover.md.
12. **PM-192 — handover.md is maintained during the project.** It is updated as owners, risks, and systems change, and finalized at transfer. A handover.md authored from scratch on the exit day is a defect — it will carry the author's memory gaps as the project's record.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-091 — Secret values in handover materials.** Banned: pasting passwords, API keys, tokens, or recovery codes into handover.md, a transferred doc, or the transfer message. Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: handover.md's "Access" section lists the production database password and the Stripe secret key "so the new owner can log in right away." Instead: name the system, the vault or provider where the secret lives, and the grant procedure — the receiver is given access through that procedure, never the value in a document. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-092 — The link-and-cheer handover.** Banned: a transfer consisting of a repository link and an encouraging message, with no review, no walkthrough, and no acceptance. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the giver's last message is "Repo's all yours — good luck! 🚀" and handover.md does not exist. Instead: run the readiness review (PM-181), walk the failure modes (PM-187), and close with a recorded, dated acceptance (PM-183). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-093 — Landmines by omission.** Banned: a handover whose risks section is empty, absent, or "all good" while the project's own records — progress.md blockers, postmortem follow-ups, the issue tracker — name open risks. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: handover.md says "No known issues" while a postmortem follow-up about the payment-retry defect is still open. Instead: build the landmines list from the project's records, each entry with evidence or a link; "none known" appears only as an explicit finding after that check. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-094 — The code-only transfer.** Banned: transferring the repository without the project memory — runbooks, postmortems, DECISIONS.md/ADRs, progress.md — while handover.md claims a complete transfer. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the receiver gets the code repo; the runbooks live in the giver's private notes and the decision rationale lives in a chat thread nobody exported. Instead: the memory set is a line item in the transfer manifest (PM-186) and the manifest gate (G-PM-091) fails until each item is present in the transferred repo. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-095 — The exit-day handover.** Banned: a handover.md written entirely at exit, presenting kickoff-era or from-memory content as the project's current state. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: handover.md, dated the giver's last day, describes the launch architecture — two services have since been replaced and the on-call rotation it names no longer exists. Instead: maintain handover.md during the project (PM-192); at transfer, re-verify each section against the current repo and records, and date the verification. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-091 — Mandated-file manifest and freshness check.** Verifies: PM-186, PM-188. Check: automated — a script diffs the repo's file list against the mandated set for the project type (the project-templates manifest) and asserts every memory-set item (runbooks, postmortems, DECISIONS.md, docs/adr/, progress.md, fact sheet, handover.md) is present; then for each file carrying a `last_reviewed` date or git-tracked mtime, asserts it falls within its freshness window (project-policy parameter). Pass: zero mandated files missing, zero outside their window unflagged. Fail: each miss or stale file is recorded as a handover gap (PM-191); sign-off is blocked. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-092 — Secrets scan and credentials-path check.** Verifies: PM-185. Check: automated — grep the handover materials and transfer manifest for credential patterns (high-entropy strings, `password`, `secret`, `token`, `api_key` followed by a value, private-key headers); assert zero matches, and assert handover.md has a credentials-path section naming at least one system with its secret location and grant procedure. Pass: zero secret-value matches and the path section present. Fail: remove the value, rotate the exposed secret, and re-run; sign-off is blocked until clean. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-093 — Acceptance record check.** Verifies: PM-182, PM-183. Check: automated — grep handover.md for the acceptance block: a named accepting owner (person or role), an ISO 8601 date, and the accepted scope. Pass: all three present and the date is the transfer date or later. Fail: no acceptance, no handover — the transfer stays open in progress.md. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-094 — Landmines cross-check.** Verifies: PM-184, PM-189. Check: automated assist — extract open items from progress.md (blocked entries), postmortem follow-up actions not marked closed, and any open risks in the issue tracker export; diff against the landmines list in handover.md. Pass: every open item appears in the landmines list with evidence or a link, or is explicitly closed with a date. Fail: add the missing entries and re-run; an unexplained diff blocks sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-095 — Cold-run acceptance test.** Verifies: PM-187, PM-190. Check: manual — the receiving owner, using only the handover materials and no help from the giver: (1) deploys or starts the project following the transferred docs, (2) finds the runbook for a named incident class, (3) names the top open risks from the landmines list, (4) states who accepted the transfer and on what date. Pass: 4 of 4 steps completed unaided. Fail: each failed step is recorded as a gap with an owner and fix date (PM-191); the cold run repeats after fixes before sign-off. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The component inventory.** handover.md lists what the system is made of — services, tables, pages — and nothing about how it fails, who owns it, or what is still open. Catch it: check the document against the four questions a receiver actually asks (how do I run it, what breaks, what is risky, who accepted it); an inventory answers none of them.
- **The verbal walkthrough.** The failure-mode walkthrough happened — in a call, unrecorded — so its content leaves with the giver. Catch it: handover.md must carry the walkthrough's date, participants, and the failure modes covered (PM-187); if it is not written there, it did not happen for handover purposes.
- **Acceptance by silence.** The giver sends the materials, hears nothing back, and marks the transfer complete. Catch it: the only acceptance that exists is the recorded one (PM-183); a transfer with no acceptance block is still open, however long the silence.
- **The clean-sheet risks section.** The landmines list is short and reassuring because it was written from the giver's impression, not from the project's records. Catch it: run the cross-check (G-PM-094); the list is built by diffing records, not by remembering.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A link-and-cheer transfer corrected to a recorded acceptance](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-183.
- [Example 2 — Secrets pasted into handover.md, replaced by a credentials path](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-185.
- [Example 3 — "No known issues" replaced by an evidenced landmines list](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-184.

## Recall anchors

- No named accepting owner, no handover.
- Acceptance is recorded, dated, and scoped — or it did not happen.
- Landmines are listed with evidence; silence never means none.
- Credentials path, never credentials.
- The memory transfers with the code — and the cold run proves it.

## Checklist

- [ ] Readiness review run against the mandated set; manifest and freshness gate passes (G-PM-091).
- [ ] Landmines list built from the project's records, each entry with evidence or a link (PM-184, G-PM-094).
- [ ] Credentials path names every system, secret location, and grant procedure — and the secrets scan is clean (PM-185, G-PM-092).
- [ ] Failure-mode walkthrough held and recorded with date and participants (PM-187).
- [ ] Runbooks, postmortems, DECISIONS.md/ADRs, and progress.md are in the transfer manifest (PM-186).
- [ ] Cold run passed 4 of 4, or every failed step is recorded as a gap with an owner and fix date (G-PM-095, PM-191).
- [ ] Acceptance block present in handover.md: named owner, ISO date, accepted scope (PM-183, G-PM-093).

# memory-retrieval

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Docs as code (Sourcegraph) — https://sourcegraph.com/blog/documentation-as-code ; GitHub Docs, creating a default community health file — https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/creating-a-default-community-health-file
- **Depends on:** project-templates, readme-writing, decision-logs
- **Feeds into:** handover, progress-tracking

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing or auditing how a project's own record is found again — canonical locations for facts, index pages, file and heading naming, superseded-document handling, and the tests that prove a fresh reader (or the single agent returning later) can retrieve what the project knows using only the repo.
- **Do NOT use when:** the task is writing the documents themselves (documentation-writing, readme-writing, runbook-writing own content), recording a decision (decision-logs), or transferring the project (handover — this skill supplies handover's retrieval acceptance tests, not the transfer process).

## Rules

1. **PM-161 — One canonical home per fact.** Every fact (version, database choice, price, escalation path, status) is stated in exactly one file. Every other document that needs it links to that file; it never restates the value.
2. **PM-162 — Fixed names and locations.** Mandated files use the set's fixed names and paths. A project never renames, moves, or re-extensions a mandated file to suit local taste.
3. **PM-163 — Two hops maximum.** Every mandated file is reachable from README.md or the docs index in at most two link hops. A file no index path reaches is treated as missing.
4. **PM-164 — Indexes link, never restate.** DECISIONS.md links every ADR; the README and docs index link every mandated file. An index entry is a title plus a link — copying the target's content into the index creates a second home and violates PM-161.
5. **PM-165 — Duplicates become links on sight.** When a duplicated fact is noticed, the non-canonical copy is replaced by a link to the canonical home in the same change — not filed for later cleanup.
6. **PM-166 — Superseded means marked, never silently deleted.** A replaced document stays in place with a SUPERSEDED banner naming and linking its replacement. Deleting or overwriting it without the marker is forbidden, so an old answer is always visibly old.
7. **PM-167 — Guessable terms.** File names, headings, and vocabulary follow the set's conventions and the project word list, so a searcher can guess the term that will hit (decision → DECISIONS.md and `docs/adr/`, incident → postmortem and runbook). One concept, one term, everywhere.
8. **PM-168 — Repo-only retrieval.** Retrieval must work with the repo alone: plain-text search (`grep`, `git log`) over consistently named files, plus the index pages. No hosted search service, wiki, or chat history may be a required step in finding a project fact.
9. **PM-169 — The project owns a query list.** Every project maintains `retrieval-queries.md`: at least 10 known-fact questions a newcomer would actually ask (which database, current version, on-call escalation, how to deploy), each naming the canonical file that answers it. It is created at project start and extended whenever a new class of fact appears.
10. **PM-170 — Test with the project's own questions.** The scripted known-fact search runs PM-169's list, never a generic list shipped with a template — a generic list tests the template's facts, not the project's.
11. **PM-171 — Crawl on cadence.** The orphan crawl (G-PM-081) and the known-fact search (G-PM-082) run at every release or work-cycle boundary, and their results are recorded in progress.md like any other gate.
12. **PM-172 — Change the home, then sweep.** When a fact changes, only its canonical home is edited; before the change closes, a repo-wide search for the old value returns no live copies (hits inside marked superseded documents and the changelog are the only permitted remains).

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-081 — The copied fact.** Banned: pasting a fact's value into a second document instead of linking to its canonical home. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the supported database version is stated in stack.md, the README, and a runbook; stack.md is updated and the other two keep answering with the old version. Instead: state the fact once in its canonical home and link to it from every other document (PM-161). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-082 — The vanished predecessor.** Banned: deleting or silently overwriting a superseded document so no trace of the replacement relationship remains. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: the old deployment guide is deleted when the new one lands; a month later a cached copy circulates and nobody can tell it is stale. Instead: keep the document, add a SUPERSEDED banner, and link to its replacement (PM-166). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-083 — The renamed mandated file.** Banned: giving a mandated file a project-specific name or location (`our-decisions.md`, `docs/final/ARCHITECTURE-v2.md`). Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: decisions live in `team-notes.md`, so the standard search for DECISIONS.md returns nothing and the project's rationale reads as absent. Instead: use the set's fixed name and path; put project flavor in the content, not the filename (PM-162). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-084 — The mirrored document.** Banned: copying a whole document into additional folders "for convenience" (the runbook duplicated under docs/, ops/, and the service folder). Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: three identical runbooks exist; the fix lands in one and the other two keep prescribing the broken procedure. Instead: keep one canonical document and link to it from each place that needs it (PM-161, PM-165). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PM-081 — Orphan crawl.** Verifies: PM-163, PM-164. Check: automated — starting at README.md and the docs index, follow Markdown links to depth 2 and diff the reached set against the mandated file manifest: `grep -rhoE '\]\([^)]+\.md\)' README.md docs/ | sort -u`, compared with the manifest list. Pass: every mandated file is reached; zero orphans. Fail: block shipment until the file is linked or the manifest is corrected. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-082 — Known-fact search test.** Verifies: PM-169, PM-170. Check: automated — for each row of `retrieval-queries.md`, run `grep -ril '<query term>' --include='*.md' .` and confirm the row's named canonical file appears among the hits. Pass: 10 of 10 queries return their canonical file. Fail: fix naming, headings, or the canonical home — never edit the query list to match a broken layout. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-083 — Duplicate-value sweep.** Verifies: PM-161, PM-172. Check: automated — sample five load-bearing facts from their canonical homes (current version, database, escalation path, deploy command, support promise) and `grep -rn '<value>' --include='*.md' .`; each value must appear definitionally in exactly one file, elsewhere only inside links, the changelog, or marked superseded documents. Pass: no live second home for any sampled fact. Fail: replace the copies with links (PM-165) and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-084 — Superseded-marker check.** Verifies: PM-166. Check: automated — every file the index or DECISIONS.md marks superseded carries a SUPERSEDED banner linking its replacement: `grep -L 'SUPERSEDED' <superseded files>` returns nothing; `git log --diff-filter=D --name-only` shows no mandated document deleted without a superseding entry. Pass: both checks clean. Fail: restore and mark the document before shipping. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-085 — Fresh-reader retrieval test.** Verifies: PM-167, PM-168. Check: manual — a reader or agent with no prior project context answers five questions drawn from `retrieval-queries.md` using only the repo (no asking the author, no chat history), timed. Pass: all five answered correctly from canonical files within the project's agreed time budget. Fail: each miss is a retrieval defect — fix the index, name, or canonical home, then retest. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Index rot.** The index pages exist and pass a glance, but still list the file set as it stood at kickoff — new mandated files were added and never linked. Catch it: diff index link targets against the manifest (G-PM-081), not against last month's index.
- **Synonym scatter.** The same concept is filed under different terms in different documents — deploy, release, ship, rollout — so any single search term misses copies. Catch it: search each concept by its word-list term only; any hit under a synonym is a PM-167 defect.
- **Deep nesting.** Mandated files are buried under project-specific subfolders (`docs/final/v2/real/`), so paths cannot be guessed and two-hop reachability quietly breaks. Catch it: if you cannot predict a mandated file's path from the convention, the layout is wrong.
- **The chat-only answer.** A retrieval question gets answered from conversation memory, everyone moves on, and the repo still cannot answer it. Catch it: if a human or agent had to ask, the repo failed — land the fix in the files, not just in the reply.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The database version in three places](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-161.
- [Example 2 — The deployment guide that vanished](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-166.
- [Example 3 — The template's retrieval test](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-169.

## Recall anchors

- One fact, one home; everything else is a link.
- If it is not reachable in two hops, it does not exist.
- Mark superseded — never silently delete.
- Test retrieval with the project's own questions.
- If grep cannot find it, the project does not know it.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every sampled fact has exactly one canonical home; all other mentions are links (PM-161, G-PM-083).
- [ ] All mandated files use the set's fixed names and paths (PM-162).
- [ ] Orphan crawl passes: zero mandated files unreachable within two hops (G-PM-081).
- [ ] `retrieval-queries.md` exists with ≥10 project questions, each naming its canonical file (PM-169).
- [ ] Known-fact search test passes 10/10 against the project's own list (G-PM-082).
- [ ] Every superseded document carries a SUPERSEDED banner linking its replacement (PM-166, G-PM-084).
- [ ] Fresh-reader test passed and recorded in progress.md (G-PM-085).

---
