# postmortem-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google SRE Workbook, "Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure" — https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/ ; Atlassian, "Incident postmortems" — https://www.atlassian.com/incident-management/handbook/postmortems
- **Depends on:** runbook-writing (the runbook used in the incident is an input and a link target), progress-tracking (incidents and postmortems are recorded there)
- **Feeds into:** progress-tracking, handover, runbook-writing (lessons learned update the runbook that failed)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an incident meets one of the project's configured postmortem triggers (PM-081) — user-visible downtime, data loss, manual on-call intervention, or a severity at or above the project's mandatory threshold.
- **Do NOT use when:** the event was a routine deployment, a caught-in-testing defect, or a near-miss below every trigger — those get a work-log or runbook note, not a postmortem. Do not use it to assign personal blame; that is the failure this skill exists to prevent (BAN-PM-041).

## Rules

1. **PM-081 — Triggers are configured parameters, never hardcoded.** The project sets its own trigger thresholds — severity levels, downtime minutes, data-loss classes — in its project files before incidents happen. Google SRE's triggers (user-visible downtime, data loss, on-call manual intervention) and Atlassian's (severity 1–2 mandatory) are worked examples to start from, not universal values; a small project copies the shape and sets its own numbers.
2. **PM-082 — Blameless by construction.** People are referred to by role ("the on-call engineer", "the deployer"), never named as a cause. Every cause is framed as a system or process property: what the system allowed, lacked, or failed to signal.
3. **PM-083 — Fixed structure, all sections present.** Every postmortem carries, in order: Summary, Impact, Timeline, Contributing causes, Mitigation, Follow-up actions. A missing section is an incomplete postmortem, not a stylistic choice.
4. **PM-084 — The timeline is built from records, never memory.** Each timeline entry carries a timestamp and its source (alert log, deploy log, monitoring graph, chat log). An event whose time cannot be sourced is marked "time unverified" — it is never given a plausible-looking time.
5. **PM-085 — Impact is measured, not estimated.** Duration, scope (users, requests, data affected), and severity come from monitoring and incident records. A figure with no record behind it is stated as unknown, not rounded into existence.
6. **PM-086 — Causes are contributing and multiple.** The analysis names every contributing system/process factor, plural. A single "root cause" line that stops at the triggering event — and any analysis that ends at "human error" — is incomplete: the question is always what made that action possible and its effect undetected.
7. **PM-087 — Every follow-up action has an owner, a due date, and a tracking ID.** Owner is a named person or role, the due date is an ISO date, and the tracking ID points at the project's tracker. An action missing any of the three does not count as an action and blocks closure.
8. **PM-088 — A named owner drives it to closure.** One named postmortem owner (by role) drives drafting, review, and approval. The postmortem closes only when every preventive action is filed in the tracker and tracked — writing the document is not closure.
9. **PM-089 — Review includes a blameless-language pass by a non-participant.** Someone not involved in the incident reviews the draft specifically for blame framing, memory-sourced timeline entries, and unsupported figures, before the postmortem is published.
10. **PM-090 — Published where the team can find it, and linked.** The finished postmortem lives in the project's postmortem location (repo or docs index) and is linked from progress.md and from the runbook for that incident class.
11. **PM-091 — Corrections are appended, never silently rewritten.** If a fact in a published postmortem turns out wrong, a dated correction note is appended stating what changed and why. The original text is not edited to look as if it was always right.
12. **PM-092 — Lessons reach the runbook.** Any procedure gap the incident exposed is fixed in the relevant runbook in the same change that closes the postmortem, or filed as a follow-up action under PM-087.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-041 — Naming a person as the cause.** Banned: any sentence that makes an individual the cause of the incident ("the outage happened because Alex deployed without checking"). Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: "Root cause: Priya restarted the wrong service." — a claim the logs contradict: the system offered two identically named services and no confirmation step. Instead: "Contributing cause: the admin console listed two services under the same display name and the restart action required no confirmation; the on-call engineer (role) selected the staging entry." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-042 — Timeline from memory.** Banned: timeline entries with timestamps reconstructed from recollection or rounded to plausible times, with no log source. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: "14:05 — team noticed errors; 14:20 — rollback started" written the next day from memory, when the alert log shows first alert 13:47 and rollback 14:31. Instead: every entry cites its source — "13:47 — alert fired (alert log #A-2214); 14:31 — rollback initiated (deploy log)". Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-043 — "Be more careful" actions.** Banned: follow-up actions that are exhortations or intentions — "be more careful", "double-check next time", "pay more attention" — or any action with no owner, due date, or tracking ID. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "Action: engineers will be more careful with migrations. Owner: team." Instead: "Action: add a pre-migration dry-run check to the deploy pipeline. Owner: platform lead. Due: 2026-12-05. Tracker: OPS-118." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-044 — Invented impact figures.** Banned: impact numbers with no monitoring or incident record behind them ("about 10,000 users were affected", "roughly two hours of downtime") presented as findings. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: "Impact: ~5,000 users, ~3 hours" in a postmortem whose monitoring shows 41 minutes and no user-count query was ever run. Instead: "Impact: 41 minutes of elevated errors (monitoring, incident window 13:47–14:28); affected-user count not measured — recorded as unknown." Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-045 — The single root cause that stops at the trigger.** Banned: a Contributing causes section with one line naming the triggering event or a person's action as "the root cause", with no system or process factors. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: "Root cause: a bad config was deployed." — contradicted by the postmortem's own timeline, which shows the config passed a validator that did not check that field. Instead: list each contributing factor: the field was unvalidated, staging did not mirror the production value, and the deploy had no canary stage. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PM-041 — Section completeness check.** Verifies: PM-083. Check: automated — `grep -cE '^## (Summary|Impact|Timeline|Contributing causes|Mitigation|Follow-up actions)' postmortem-<incident>.md` returns 6. Pass: all six sections present. Fail: block publication; add the missing section. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-042 — Action-row completeness check.** Verifies: PM-087. Check: automated — parse the Follow-up actions table and assert every row has non-empty Action, Owner, Due date (matching `^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$`), and Tracking ID fields, e.g. `awk -F'|' 'NR>2 && NF>5 && ($3=="" || $4=="" || $5=="" || $6=="") {print "incomplete action row:", NR}' postmortem-<incident>.md` prints nothing. Pass: zero incomplete rows. Fail: block closure until each action is owned, dated, and tracked. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-043 — Blame and vagueness lint.** Verifies: PM-082, PM-086, PM-087. Check: automated plus manual — `grep -inE 'be more careful|double-check next time|pay more attention|root cause: (a |the )?(human|operator|engineer)' postmortem-<incident>.md` prints nothing, and the PM-089 non-participant reviewer signs off that no person is named as a cause. Pass: no lint hits and reviewer sign-off recorded. Fail: rewrite the flagged passages as system/process causes before publication. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-044 — Timeline sourcing and linkage check.** Verifies: PM-084, PM-090. Check: automated — every Timeline row carries a source marker (log, alert, or record reference) or the words "time unverified", and `grep -l 'postmortem-<incident>' progress.md <runbook>.md` lists both files. Pass: all entries sourced or marked, both links present. Fail: block publication; source the entries from the logs and add the links. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The sanitized timeline.** Detection and response gaps are quietly smoothed over: the 25 minutes between first alert and first responder vanish, so the timeline reads as instant response. Catch it: diff the timeline against the alert log — any gap with no entry is a gap to explain, not to hide.
- **The orphaned actions.** Actions are filed at closure, then never looked at again; due dates pass silently and the same incident recurs. Catch it: closure (PM-088) means the tracker owns the actions — review open postmortem actions wherever the project reviews its tracker, not only when writing the next postmortem.
- **The copy-paste postmortem.** Causes and actions are boilerplate reused across incidents ("add more monitoring", "improve communication") regardless of what actually failed. Catch it: if an action sentence could be pasted into a different incident unchanged, it describes nothing about this one.
- **The victory lap.** Three paragraphs celebrate the heroic fix; the causes section is one line and prevention is an afterthought. Catch it: compare section lengths — when Mitigation dwarfs Contributing causes and Follow-up actions combined, the document is a story, not an analysis.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Blame line rewritten as a system cause](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-082 / BAN-PM-041.
- [Example 2 — Memory timeline replaced by a log-sourced timeline](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-084 / BAN-PM-042.
- [Example 3 — "Be more careful" replaced by an owned, dated, tracked action](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-087 / BAN-PM-043.

## Recall anchors

- Blame the system that allowed it, never the person who did it.
- Timeline from logs, or mark it unverified — never from memory.
- Causes are plural; "human error" is where analysis starts, not ends.
- No owner, no due date, no tracking ID — no action.
- Closed means the preventive actions are tracked, not that the document is written.

## Checklist

- [ ] Incident met a configured trigger, and the trigger values came from the project's own settings (PM-081).
- [ ] All six sections present: Summary, Impact, Timeline, Contributing causes, Mitigation, Follow-up actions (PM-083).
- [ ] People appear by role only; every cause is a system or process property (PM-082).
- [ ] Every timeline entry is timestamped with its log source, or marked "time unverified" (PM-084).
- [ ] Impact figures come from monitoring/incident records; unmeasured values are stated as unknown (PM-085).
- [ ] Every follow-up action has an owner, an ISO due date, and a tracking ID (PM-087).
- [ ] Non-participant blameless review passed, postmortem published and linked from progress.md and the runbook (PM-089, PM-090).
- [ ] Gates G-PM-041 to G-PM-044 pass; results recorded in progress.md.

# progress-tracking

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** datadef.io, docs checks in CI (freshness-gate pattern) — https://datadef.io/guides/en/docs-checks-in-ci ; Sourcegraph, "Documentation as code" — https://sourcegraph.com/blog/documentation-as-code
- **Depends on:** project-templates, decision-logs
- **Feeds into:** handover, memory-retrieval, postmortem-writing

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** any work starts, changes state, blocks, or finishes on a project — progress.md is updated as part of that work, and every gate result from every skill is recorded here. Anyone asking "where does this project stand?" is answered from this file.
- **Do NOT use when:** recording history or rationale — effort narration belongs in the work log and git, decisions belong in DECISIONS.md via decision-logs, incident analysis belongs in postmortem-writing. progress.md holds current verified state only.

## Rules

1. **PM-141 — One status of record.** progress.md is the project's single status file. Status maintained in chat, a dashboard, or a README section instead is merged into progress.md or deleted.
2. **PM-142 — Verified state only.** An item is marked done only when its gate result is recorded in progress.md. Attempted, drafted, or "should work" is in progress — never done.
3. **PM-143 — Gate results land here.** Every gate run, from every skill loaded for the work, records its result in progress.md: gate ID, pass or fail, date. A gate with no recorded result is treated as never run.
4. **PM-144 — Every entry is dated.** Each status entry carries an ISO 8601 date. An undated entry is treated as stale: re-verify it or remove it at the next update.
5. **PM-145 — Done names the artifact.** Every done item names or links what was produced. A done claim whose artifact cannot be found in the repo is not done.
6. **PM-146 — Updated with the work.** progress.md is updated in the same change as the work it reports. A separate status-update commit made later is a process defect.
7. **PM-147 — Blocked is a triple.** A blocked item names the blocker, the blocker's owner, and the condition that unblocks it. "Waiting" alone is not a status.
8. **PM-148 — Four states only.** Entries are done, in progress, blocked, or next. No other status vocabulary: "almost done", "wrapping up", and "90%" are not states.
9. **PM-149 — State, not effort.** progress.md reports state. Hours spent, difficulty, and history belong in the work log and git history, never in the status file.
10. **PM-150 — Decisions and incidents link out.** A decision made during the work is appended to DECISIONS.md via decision-logs and linked from progress.md; an incident links its postmortem. progress.md is never the only copy of either.
11. **PM-151 — Next is concrete.** The Next section names the upcoming actions, each with an owner. An empty Next while unfinished work exists is a defect.
12. **PM-152 — Stale entries are resolved, not carried.** At each update, entries older than the current work cycle are re-verified against the deliverable, then corrected or deleted — never silently carried forward.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-071 — Done on attempt.** Banned: marking an item done because the work was attempted or drafted, with no gate result recorded. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: "Auth flow — done" while the auth gate never ran and the flow accepts a wrong password. Instead: run the gate, record its result with gate ID and date, and only then mark the item done. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-072 — The invented percentage.** Banned: progress figures ("80% complete", "frontend 90% done") with no counted list of items behind them. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: a status report claims the frontend is 90% done with no inventory of frontend items anywhere. Instead: report counts over a named item list ("14 of 16 screens pass their gates"), or report states with no percentage. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-073 — The kickoff fossil.** Banned: progress.md entries that predate the current work cycle presented as current status. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: progress.md still says "scaffolding in progress" three releases after launch because nobody touched it since kickoff. Instead: update the file in the same change as the work; re-verify or delete stale entries at every update. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-074 — Template status shipped.** Banned: generator boilerplate or placeholder text ("Project status — TODO", "coming soon") surviving in a shipped progress.md. Defeats: DET-CON-004. Bad: the scaffold's "Status: TODO" line is still the first line of progress.md in a released repo. Instead: replace boilerplate with dated, verified entries at project start, or delete the placeholder line. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-PM-075 — The bare "blocked".** Banned: a blocked entry naming no blocker, no owner, and no unblocking condition. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "Blocked: waiting on API keys" — nobody can act on it, and nobody is named who could. Instead: record the triple — what blocks, who owns the blocker, what unblocks it — plus a re-check date. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-071 — Freshness gate.** Verifies: PM-144, PM-146. Check: automated — `git log -1 --format=%cs -- progress.md` must fall within the current work cycle (project policy window, default 7 days while work is active), and a grep confirms every entry line carries an ISO date. Pass: both conditions true. Fail: all status is treated as stale; update progress.md before any status report leaves the project. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-072 — Done-artifact check.** Verifies: PM-142, PM-145. Check: automated — extract the file paths and links named by done entries and assert each exists (`test -f` for paths, link resolution for URLs). Pass: every done item's artifact exists. Fail: the item reverts to in progress until the artifact exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-073 — Gate-result completeness.** Verifies: PM-143. Check: automated — collect the gate IDs recorded in progress.md and diff them against the gate IDs of the skills loaded for the current work. Pass: every loaded skill's gates appear with a pass/fail result and a date. Fail: block the status report; run the missing gates or record why they do not apply. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-074 — Sampled truth audit.** Verifies: PM-142, PM-152. Check: manual — sample three entries (one done, one in progress, one blocked) and confirm each against the actual deliverable, the named blocker owner, and the repo state. Pass: 3 of 3 match reality. Fail: correct the file and re-audit the full entry list. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The victory lap.** progress.md narrates effort — "long week wrestling with the build" — instead of state. Catch it: scan for effort language; a status entry is a dated fact about an item, nothing else (PM-149).
- **The parallel status.** The real status lives in chat messages or a separate dashboard while progress.md quietly rots. Catch it: ask where a newcomer would look; if the honest answer is not progress.md, merge the rival and delete it (PM-141).
- **Zombie next steps.** The Next section lists items already finished or abandoned long ago, so nobody trusts it. Catch it: at every update, each Next item is promoted, re-dated with an owner, or deleted (PM-151, PM-152).
- **The silent unblock.** The blocker cleared days ago but the entry still says blocked, so readers route around finished work. Catch it: blocked entries carry re-check dates; an entry past its re-check date is tested against its unblocking condition before anything else is updated.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Done on attempt, corrected to done on gate result](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-142.
- [Example 2 — A bare "blocked" rewritten as a triple](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-147.
- [Example 3 — A kickoff-fossil progress.md re-verified entry by entry](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-152.

## Recall anchors

- Done means a gate result is recorded — not attempted, recorded.
- Every entry dated; undated is stale.
- Done names the artifact; no artifact, no done.
- Blocked is a triple: blocker, owner, unblocking condition.
- Update progress.md in the same change as the work.

## Checklist

- [ ] progress.md updated in the same change as the work it reports (PM-146).
- [ ] Every done item has its gate result recorded, with gate ID and date (PM-143).
- [ ] Every done item names or links an artifact that exists (G-PM-072).
- [ ] No undated entries; stale entries re-verified or removed (PM-144, PM-152).
- [ ] Every blocked item names blocker, owner, and unblocking condition (PM-147).
- [ ] No percentage appears without a counted item list behind it (BAN-PM-072).
- [ ] Decisions appended to DECISIONS.md and incidents linked to their postmortems (PM-150).

---

# project-templates

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/creating-a-template-repository ; https://simonwillison.net/2021/Aug/28/dynamic-github-repository-templates/ ; https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/creating-a-default-community-health-file
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: this skill owns the scaffold itself; its input is the mandated project file set defined in this repo, not another skill's output — every project starts here. It feeds readme-writing, documentation-writing, progress-tracking, and handover.
- **Feeds into:** readme-writing, documentation-writing, progress-tracking, handover

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a new project repository is being created, the mandated file set changes, or the project template itself is being revised. This skill owns the scaffold every project starts from.
- **Do NOT use when:** the project already exists and only its content needs work (use the owning skill — readme-writing, changelog, decision-logs), or when backfilling one missing file by hand would leave the template unchanged (fix the template, then regenerate).

## Rules

1. **PM-001 — Full mandated set, or a recorded exception.** Generation emits the full extended mandated set for the project type (the Appendix A files plus the D-006 additions: LICENSE, CODEOWNERS, `docs/adr/`, issue and PR templates, .gitignore, dependabot.yml). Every file not emitted is listed in the generation record as not-applicable with a reason. A file is never silently absent.
2. **PM-002 — Templates carry variables, not content.** Template files contain structure, headings, fill-in prompts, and substitution tokens (`{{project_name}}`, `{{owner}}`, stack choices) — nothing else. A token is a variable to be replaced at generation time, never prose to be read.
3. **PM-003 — No invented facts, ever.** No template ships a name, metric, date, contact detail, testimonial, team member, or capability claim as sample content. Where a real project would state a fact, the template carries a prompt naming where the fact comes from (fact-sheet.md, the owner's input) — never a plausible invention.
4. **PM-004 — Empty sections stay honestly empty.** A section with no real content yet keeps its heading and its fill-in prompt, and nothing more. Filler prose written to make a section look finished is a defect, even when it is generic.
5. **PM-005 — Conditional files fire on triggers only.** CONTENT_METADATA, PAYMENT_SECURITY, and CLONE_DESIGN_SYSTEM are emitted only when the project type triggers them (content publishing, payments, a clone build). A condition stated in the owning playbook (for example, a step marked "if paid", or a recorded stack choice the file depends on) is a trigger for this rule: when the condition does not hold, the file is recorded not-applicable in the generation record with the condition as the reason. Where the owning playbook has not yet defined the trigger, the gap is recorded in the generation record — the drafter does not guess the classification.
6. **PM-006 — Generation is one reproducible command.** A fresh project is produced by running a generator (cookiecutter-style, Jinja + `cookiecutter.json`, or any equivalent) against the versioned template. Generation means producing exactly the file set listed in the project type's shipped manifest, `templates/mandated-manifest-<type>.txt` — the manifest is the normative artifact: where a generator's output and the manifest disagree, the manifest governs and the generator is fixed. GitHub template repositories copy structure but substitute no variables, so they are never the whole mechanism. Hand-assembling the file set is not generation. This repository ships a reference generator for exactly this contract — `python3 scripts/generate-project.py --type <type> --target <dir>` emits the manifest's file set (the template file where `templates/` carries one, an honest empty-section scaffold otherwise) and prints the manifest diff result; any equivalent generator satisfies the rule the same way.
7. **PM-007 — Output is never hand-patched.** A defect found in a generated project is fixed in the template and the project is regenerated, or the fix is recorded as a deliberate project-level divergence. Editing only the output guarantees the next project inherits the defect.
8. **PM-008 — The template is versioned and changelogged.** The template carries a semantic version and a changelog entry per change, like a product. A version with no changelog entry does not ship.
9. **PM-009 — Mandated-set changes are decisions first.** Any change that adds, removes, or renames a mandated file is recorded in the decision log before the template ships it. The template never drifts ahead of the recorded set.
10. **PM-010 — Public projects get the community files.** CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SUPPORT, and GOVERNANCE are emitted when the project is public, on top of GitHub's recognized community-profile floor (README, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY). For a private project they are recorded not-applicable under PM-001, not forgotten. SECURITY in that floor is a single file with two named sections — vulnerability reporting (how to report) and the project's security design — never two separate files with the same name.
11. **PM-011 — Generated output passes the gates from the first commit.** A generated project passes markdownlint and the link checks with zero errors before its first commit. "We'll lint it later" is how unlinted scaffolds become permanent.
12. **PM-012 — Every template change is self-tested.** Before a template change merges, a sample project is regenerated from it and gates G-PM-001 to G-PM-003 are run against the output. An untested template change does not merge.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-001 — Invented social proof baked into the template.** Banned: template output containing sample testimonials, user counts, ratings, or press mentions presented as the project's own. Defeats: DET-CON-010. Bad: the generated README opens with "Trusted by 10,000+ teams" and two named-customer quotes the new project has never had. Instead: the README carries the heading and a prompt — "List real customers only, each with a producible source record (see real-content)" (PM-003). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-002 — Scaffold boilerplate shipped as project content.** Banned: generator or theme defaults surviving into the shipped files — a scaffold README describing the template itself, "Hello world!" posts, "Add a description here". Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: the new project's README explains how to use the template repository instead of what the project is. Instead: every default string is replaced by project structure and prompts at generation time, or the file is not emitted (PM-002). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-003 — Unreplaced substitution tokens in shipped files.** Banned: `{{project_name}}`, `{{owner}}`, or any `{{ }}` token visible in a committed project file. Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: the shipped CONTRIBUTING.md is titled "Contributing to {{project_name}}" because generation ran without the variable set. Instead: generation fails unless every declared variable has a value, and gate G-PM-002 scans the output before the first commit. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-004 — Compliance furniture without the process.** Banned: emitting a conditional file that asserts a practice the project does not run — above all a PAYMENT_SECURITY.md describing controls that do not exist. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: a project with no payment flow ships a payment-security file claiming encrypted card handling and audit reviews. Instead: conditional files fire only on their real trigger (PM-005) and describe only processes that exist. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-005 — Draft markers left in generated files.** Banned: TODO, FIXME, or "content to follow" strings in any generated file's fields, headings, or metadata. Defeats: DET-CON-004. Bad: the generated SUPPORT.md ships with "TODO: add the real support email" as its contact section. Instead: an unknown value is an unfilled variable that blocks generation, or a fill-in prompt that names the missing fact (PM-002, PM-004). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-001 — Manifest diff.** Verifies: PM-001, PM-005, PM-010. Check (automated): generate a fresh project into a scratch directory and run `diff <(cd <output> && find . -type f | sort) <repo>/templates/mandated-manifest-<type>.txt` — the manifest shipped in this repository's `templates/` directory, never a locally reconstructed copy. Scope: this is a generation-time (step-0) check; files that later playbook steps mandate (for example performance-budget.json, PRIVACY_REGISTER.md, the CI workflow) are expected additions recorded in progress.md, and when the diff is re-run later they are matched against those step records — they are not diff violations. Pass: zero differences, or every difference matched by a not-applicable entry with a reason in the generation record. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-002 — Unreplaced-token and marker scan.** Verifies: PM-002, PM-003. Check (automated): `grep -rn '{{' <output>/` and `grep -rn 'TODO\|FIXME' <output>/` — both must return nothing. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block shipment; fix the template or the variable set, never the output alone. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-003 — Lint parity on generated output.** Verifies: PM-011. Check (automated): run `markdownlint <output>/**/*.md` on the freshly generated tree, using the starter configuration shipped with the mandated set (`templates/.markdownlint.json`, emitted into every generated project as `./.markdownlint.json`; DECISIONS D-017) unless the project has recorded its own documentation configuration in its decision log. Where markdownlint is not available in the agent's environment, the fallback is a documented manual style check of the generated Markdown against that same rule set — heading hierarchy, list and table structure, link syntax — with the check and its result recorded in progress.md; the automated run remains required wherever the tool exists. Pass: exit 0, zero errors, before the first commit (under the fallback: a recorded manual check with zero findings). Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-004 — Exception register review.** Verifies: PM-001, PM-009. Check (manual): read the generation record for the new project; every absent mandated file has a stated reason, and every mandated-set change the template embodies has a decision-log entry that predates the template version. Pass: zero unexplained absences and zero unlogged set changes. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Template drift.** A fix is made inside one generated project and never lands in the template, so every later project re-inherits the defect. Catch it by asking of any project-level doc fix: "is this already in the template?"
- **Copy-the-last-project scaffolding.** The new repo is cloned from a previous project and find-replaced, inheriting that project's facts, decisions, and risks as silent defaults. Catch it: any file whose content names a source other than the template version and the new project's own inputs is suspect.
- **Vague prompts.** Fill-in prompts like "write something about the project" invite the generator to guess. Catch it: a prompt must name the fact it wants and where that fact lives; a prompt that names neither is rewritten before the template ships.
- **Manifest by memory.** Checking the emitted file set against what the author remembers the mandated set to be. Catch it: the manifest is a file in the template repo, and gate G-PM-001 diffs against that file — never against recollection.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The README that arrived with customers](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects PM-003.
- [Example 2 — The security file nobody missed](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects PM-001.
- [Example 3 — Tokens and TODOs in the first commit](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects PM-002.

## Recall anchors

- Full set, or a recorded reason — never a silent gap.
- Structure and prompts ship; facts never do.
- An empty section is honest; a filled-looking one may not be.
- Fix the template, regenerate — never patch the output.
- Conditional files fire on real triggers only.

## Checklist

- [ ] Manifest diff is clean, or every absence has a recorded reason (PM-001, G-PM-001).
- [ ] No template file contains an invented name, metric, testimonial, or date (PM-003).
- [ ] Token and marker scan returns zero hits on the generated output (G-PM-002).
- [ ] Conditional files match the project type's triggers; undefined triggers are recorded as gaps (PM-005).
- [ ] Public projects include CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SUPPORT, and GOVERNANCE (PM-010).
- [ ] markdownlint passes on the generated tree before the first commit — or, where the tool is absent, the manual style check against the starter configuration is recorded (PM-011, G-PM-003).
- [ ] Template version bumped and changelogged; mandated-set changes have a prior decision-log entry (PM-008, PM-009).

# readme-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/creating-a-default-community-health-file ; https://sourcegraph.com/blog/documentation-as-code
- **Depends on:** project-templates
- **Feeds into:** documentation-writing, handover

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** creating a project README, replacing scaffold output at project start, or changing anything the README states — what the project is, its status, its version, or how to run it.
- **Do NOT use when:** writing the depth the README points to — tutorials, how-tos, and reference belong to documentation-writing; operating procedures belong to runbook-writing. The README is the front door and index, never the manual.

## Rules

1. **PM-041 — Fixed front-door order.** The README carries, in this order: project name, one line stating what it is, who it is for, current status with a date, the quickstart, and a link index into the doc set (ARCHITECTURE, runbook, CHANGELOG, DECISIONS). A section that fits none of these moves behind a link.
2. **PM-042 — No boilerplate survives.** Every line of generator or template output (framework welcome text, default badges, placeholder sections) is replaced with project content or deleted before the README first ships; "we will fill this in later" is not a shipped state.
3. **PM-043 — Quickstart executed verbatim.** Every quickstart command is run exactly as written, in order, in a clean checkout, before the README ships and after any change to it. A command that fails, or needs a step the README omits, is a README bug fixed in the README or the project — never explained away.
4. **PM-044 — Badges report real systems only.** A badge is present only if it is generated by a live system: CI status from the actual pipeline, version from the project's version source of truth, coverage from the actual test run. Hand-written or static shields claiming a state nobody measured are prohibited.
5. **PM-045 — Link, never duplicate.** Each mandated file is linked exactly once from the index; its content is never copied into the README. Every fact has one canonical home, and the README's copy of a fact is a link to that home.
6. **PM-046 — Every claim verified against the system.** Features, commands, flags, ports, and requirements named in the README are checked against the actual project before shipping. A feature that does not exist yet is labeled with its planned status and date, or omitted.
7. **PM-047 — Status is dated and current.** The status line carries an ISO 8601 date and is re-verified whenever the README changes; a stated version must equal the version source of truth (git tag or package version). An undated status is treated as stale.
8. **PM-048 — One-sitting length.** The README is short enough to read in one sitting; when a draft grows past what a new reader can scan in a few minutes, the overflow moves into the doc set and the README keeps the link.
9. **PM-049 — Shortest path to running.** The quickstart is the minimum sequence from clone to a running project, with prerequisites (runtime versions, required services, env files) listed before the first command — never discovered mid-sequence.
10. **PM-050 — README changes ride with the change.** Any change that alters what the README states (a renamed command, a new prerequisite, a status change) updates the README in the same change; a merged change that leaves the README wrong is incomplete.
11. **PM-051 — Every link resolves.** Relative links point at files that exist in the repo; external links are checked with the link checker. A link to a planned-but-absent file is removed until the file exists.
12. **PM-052 — Names match the record.** The project name, product names, and terminology are spelled exactly as in the project's fact sheet and word list, in the title, body, and badge URLs alike.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-021 — Scaffold README shipped.** Banned: publishing the generator's default README (framework welcome text, "getting started" boilerplate, sample badges) as the project's front door. Defeats: DET-CON-002. Bad: the repo ships the Vite default README — "This template provides a minimal setup to get React working in Vite" — for a client billing tool. Instead: replace or delete every scaffold line at project start (PM-042); the first shipped README is written for this project. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-022 — Decorative badges.** Banned: static or hand-made badges asserting build status, coverage, or version that no live system produced. Defeats: DET-CON-012. Bad: a green "build: passing" shield pasted from shields.io into a repo with no CI configured. Instead: wire the badge to the real pipeline's badge URL, or remove it until the system exists (PM-044). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-023 — Untested quickstart.** Banned: shipping quickstart commands that were written from memory and never executed in a clean checkout. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the README says `npm run dev` but the package defines only `start`; the README and the project contradict each other on the first command a reader runs. Instead: run every command verbatim in a clean checkout and fix the mismatch at its source before shipping (PM-043). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-024 — Features that do not exist.** Banned: describing planned, imagined, or removed features in the README as current capability. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: "Exports reports to PDF and Slack" in the feature list of a project with no export code and no Slack integration. Instead: verify each named feature against the running system (PM-046); label planned work as planned, with a date, or cut it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-025 — Fossil status line.** Banned: a status or version statement left standing after it stops being true ("currently in alpha", a version two releases old, a roadmap dated last year). Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: the README announces "v0.2 — early alpha, expect breaking changes" while the repo is tagged v1.4. Instead: date the status, re-verify it on every README change, and match the version source of truth (PM-047). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-PM-021 — Quickstart execution.** Verifies: PM-043, PM-049. Check: automated — in a clean clone, run the project's `scripts/readme-quickstart-check.sh`, which extracts the fenced shell blocks under the README's quickstart heading and executes them in order. Pass: every command exits 0 and the final state is the running project. Fail: block shipment; fix the README or the project. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-022 — Boilerplate and marker scan.** Verifies: PM-042. Check: automated — `grep -niE 'create-react-app|create vite|this template provides|getting started with .* framework|TODO|FIXME|lorem|description here' README.md` plus a diff of the README's first heading against the scaffold default. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block shipment until each hit is replaced or deleted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-023 — Link integrity.** Verifies: PM-045, PM-051. Check: automated — `lychee README.md` for all links, and a manifest check that each mandated file for the project type appears as a link target. Pass: zero broken links and every mandated file linked exactly once. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-024 — Fresh-reader test.** Verifies: PM-041, PM-048. Check: manual — a reader who has never seen the project reads the README once and states what the project is, who it is for, its current status, and the exact steps to run it. Pass: all four answers correct from the README alone. Fail: rewrite the failing section and re-test. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The link farm with no door.** An index of links and nothing else — no statement of what the project is or who it serves. Catch it: cover the links; if the remaining text cannot answer "what is this?", PM-041 has failed even though every link works.
- **The screenshot hero.** A banner image or demo GIF carrying the explanation while the text says nothing checkable. Catch it: read the README with images disabled; every claim must survive in text.
- **The buried quickstart.** Forty lines of philosophy, architecture, and history before the first runnable command. Catch it: the quickstart must appear before any section a first-time reader does not need to run the project.
- **The changelog dump.** Release history pasted into the README to make it look maintained, duplicating CHANGELOG.md until the two disagree. Catch it: history lives in CHANGELOG.md; the README links to it (PM-045).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Scaffold README replaced by a front door](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-042, PM-041.
- [Example 2 — The quickstart that never ran](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-043.
- [Example 3 — Fake badges and a copied manual](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-044, PM-045.

## Recall anchors

- Front door and index — never the manual.
- If a command is printed, it was run, verbatim, in a clean checkout.
- A badge is a report from a live system or it is deleted.
- Every fact lives in one file; the README holds the link.
- Undated status is stale status.

## Checklist

- [ ] Sections follow the PM-041 order: what, who, dated status, quickstart, link index.
- [ ] No scaffold or template text remains (G-PM-022 clean).
- [ ] Quickstart executed verbatim in a clean checkout, all exit 0 (G-PM-021).
- [ ] Every badge is generated by a real system; version matches the source of truth (PM-044, PM-047).
- [ ] Every mandated file linked exactly once; no content duplicated from them (G-PM-023).
- [ ] Every named feature, command, and requirement verified against the actual project (PM-046).
- [ ] Fresh-reader test passed and recorded (G-PM-024).

# runbook-writing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D10 Project & Memory (PM)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PagerDuty, "What is a Runbook?" (Limoncelli's runbook sections) — https://www.pagerduty.com/resources/automation/learn/what-is-a-runbook/ ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md Appendix A, runbook.md row (Google SRE practice)
- **Depends on:** documentation-writing
- **Feeds into:** postmortem-writing, handover, incident-response

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an incident class recurs, an alert fires, or a procedure (deploy rollback, failover, certificate renewal, data backfill) must be executable by whoever is on call — including someone who did not build the system, at 3 a.m., under pressure.
- **Do NOT use when:** the document explains how the system works (that is documentation-writing / explanation), records a past incident (postmortem-writing), or is a one-off task never expected to repeat. A runbook is a procedure to execute, not a narrative to read.

## Rules

1. **PM-061 — One runbook, one incident class.** Each runbook covers exactly one alert, symptom, or repeated procedure. Two failure modes in one file get two files, each named for its trigger.
2. **PM-062 — Fixed section order.** Every runbook carries, in order: service overview, trigger/symptom, prerequisites, numbered steps, escalation, verification. No section is omitted; an inapplicable section states why.
3. **PM-063 — Steps are actions with expected results.** Each step is one action — an exact command or a concrete UI action — followed by the output or state that confirms it worked. A step with no expected result is unfinished.
4. **PM-064 — Branch on difference.** Where a step's output can differ, the runbook states what to do in each case ("if the pod does not appear, go to step 9"). The executor never has to guess which branch reality took.
5. **PM-065 — Exact, runnable values.** Commands are copy-paste runnable against the real system: real hostnames, real service names, real flags. Placeholder tokens (`<host>`, `your-server`, `example.com`) never survive into a shipped runbook.
6. **PM-066 — Prerequisites up front.** Access required, where credentials live (the vault or system name — never the secret values), tools to install, and the dashboards to open are all listed before step 1, never discovered mid-incident.
7. **PM-067 — The alert links here.** Every alert this runbook serves links to the runbook file, and the runbook's trigger section names that alert or symptom verbatim, so the path from page to procedure is one click and unambiguous.
8. **PM-068 — Escalation names a role.** The escalation path names a role (e.g. "database on-call"), how to reach it, and the condition or time threshold that triggers escalation. A person's name may appear additionally, never instead.
9. **PM-069 — Verification closes the runbook.** The final step is an observable check that proves resolution — a health endpoint returning 200, the alert cleared, a real user action succeeding — not the absence of error messages.
10. **PM-070 — Same-change updates.** A runbook is updated in the same change as any incident that used it and exposed an error, and after any change to the procedure it describes. A runbook known to be wrong is fixed or withdrawn that day, not left for the next incident.
11. **PM-071 — Written for the stranger.** The runbook must be executable by a competent engineer who did not build the system and has never seen this incident. Every term, system, and "usual" step is spelled out or linked.
12. **PM-072 — Reference generic process, never copy it.** Incident-wide process (declare the incident, open the timeline, notify stakeholders) is linked to the one canonical process document, not pasted into each runbook where copies drift apart.

## BAN list

- **BAN-PM-031 — The filler step.** Banned: a step that gestures at the work instead of specifying it ("check the database and fix any issues"). Defeats: DET-CON-006. Bad: step 3 reads "Investigate the connection pool and resolve the problem." Instead: give the exact query, the healthy output range, and the action for each outcome (PM-063, PM-064). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-032 — Placeholder values shipped.** Banned: unreplaced template values in commands, hosts, or contacts (`<your-db-host>`, `TODO: add command`, `admin@example.com`). Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: the failover step runs `psql -h <db-host>` and the on-call must hunt for the hostname mid-incident. Instead: ship the real hostname, or the exact command that retrieves it (PM-065). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-033 — Person-only escalation.** Banned: an escalation path that names only an individual ("call Dave") with no role, channel, or fallback. Defeats: DET-CON-005. Bad: Dave left the company in March; the runbook still routes a page-down incident to his phone. Instead: escalate to the owning role via the paging tool, with the time threshold stated (PM-068). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-034 — The stale runbook.** Banned: shipping or keeping a runbook whose commands, hosts, or thresholds no longer match the system, past its `last_reviewed` date. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: the rollback runbook targets a cluster decommissioned two releases ago; the review date is eight months old. Instead: re-verify against the live system and update `last_reviewed`, or withdraw the runbook (PM-070). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-PM-035 — Resolution declared without verification.** Banned: ending a runbook at the fix ("restart the service and close the ticket") with no step that proves the user-visible problem is gone. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the service restarts cleanly, the ticket closes, and checkout is still failing for users. Instead: end with the observable verification check and its pass value (PM-069). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-PM-031 — Structure check.** Verifies: PM-061, PM-062, PM-063. Check: automated — script asserts each runbook file contains the six PM-062 section headings in order, and that every numbered step is followed by an "Expected:" line. Pass: all runbooks conform. Fail: block the change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-032 — Placeholder scan.** Verifies: PM-065, PM-066. Check: automated — `grep -rnE '<[a-z-]+>|TODO|FIXME|example\.com|your-[a-z]+|localhost' runbooks/` returns no hits outside explicitly marked illustrative blocks. Pass: zero hits. Fail: block the change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-033 — Freshness gate.** Verifies: PM-070. Check: automated — compare each runbook's `last_reviewed` front matter against the project's review window (a project policy parameter; default 90 days). Pass: every runbook is inside its window. Fail: block release until re-verified or withdrawn. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-034 — Link check.** Verifies: PM-066, PM-067. Check: automated — run lychee over the runbooks directory; every dashboard, tool, and alert link resolves. Pass: zero broken links. Fail: fix or remove the link before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-PM-035 — Cold-run drill.** Verifies: PM-063, PM-064, PM-071. Check: manual — someone other than the author executes the runbook in a drill or tabletop exercise and completes it without asking the author a single question. Pass: completed unaided; every hesitation is filed as a runbook fix. Fail: revise and re-drill. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The war story.** The runbook narrates one past incident ("On 14 May the cache filled because…") instead of giving a reusable procedure. Catch it: dates and past tense in the steps; rewrite each anecdote into the action it taught.
- **The screenshot procedure.** Steps exist only as UI screenshots, unsearchable and silently wrong after the next UI release. Catch it: search the file for its own key commands — if the text is not in the file, neither is the procedure.
- **The expert's shorthand.** "Bounce the usual box and clear the queue like last time." Catch it: any step the author cannot expand into PM-063 form on demand fails PM-071; the cold-run drill (G-PM-035) exposes it.
- **The twin runbooks.** One copy in the repo, one in a wiki, each edited independently. Catch it: search both locations for the procedure's name; one canonical file survives, the other becomes a link (PM-072's rule applied to the runbook itself).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Narrative steps rewritten as actions with expected results](examples/example-1.md) — corrects PM-063.
- [Example 2 — Person-only escalation replaced by role escalation and verification](examples/example-2.md) — corrects PM-068.
- [Example 3 — Placeholder commands and missing prerequisites made executable](examples/example-3.md) — corrects PM-066.

## Recall anchors

- Steps are actions with expected results — never explanations.
- Prerequisites before step 1; nothing is discovered mid-incident.
- Escalate to a role, not a person.
- The runbook ends by proving the fix, not by performing it.
- If an incident exposed an error, the fix lands in the same change.

## Checklist

- [ ] Sections present in order: overview, trigger, prerequisites, steps, escalation, verification (G-PM-031).
- [ ] Every step has an exact command or action and an "Expected:" result (PM-063).
- [ ] Every step whose output can differ carries a branch (PM-064).
- [ ] Placeholder scan is clean: no `<tokens>`, TODOs, or example values (G-PM-032).
- [ ] Prerequisites list access, credential locations (never values), tools, dashboards (PM-066).
- [ ] Escalation names a role, a channel, and a time threshold (PM-068).
- [ ] Final step is an observable verification with a pass value (PM-069).
- [ ] `last_reviewed` is inside the review window; cold-run drill passed or scheduled (G-PM-033, G-PM-035).

## Department D11 — integrations-payments

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/api-keys-management/SKILL.md -->

# api-keys-management

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "API keys" (publishable, secret, and restricted keys) — https://docs.stripe.com/keys ; Stripe, "Create restricted API keys" — https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys
- **Depends on:** secrets-management (D7 owns compromise-response depth)
- **Feeds into:** third-party-apis, webhooks, sdk-embeddables

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project issues, stores, rotates, or revokes credentials: provider secret keys it consumes, webhook signing secrets, or API keys it issues to its own customers. Credentials are inventory with a lifecycle, not strings in a config file.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is how a provider call is made (third-party-apis owns the adapter and its auth usage), how a webhook signature is verified (webhooks owns receiving mechanics; this skill owns the signing secret's lifecycle), or incident response beyond the first rotation (secrets-management in D7).

## Rules

1. **IN-201 — Keys live in secret storage, never in the repo.** Every credential is read at runtime from the environment or a secret manager. The repository carries only `.env.example` with obvious dummy placeholders (`sk_live_EXAMPLE`), and a real `.env` file is gitignored and never committed.
2. **IN-202 — Secret keys are server-side only.** A provider secret key is used only in server code. The browser or mobile client receives only keys the provider designed to be public (publishable keys) or a short-lived, narrowly scoped token minted server-side per session.
3. **IN-203 — One key per environment and purpose, least-privilege scope.** Keys are issued per environment (test, live) and per purpose (billing worker, reporting job), using restricted keys with the smallest permission set the provider offers wherever the provider supports them. A key's scope is written in the register (IN-211).
4. **IN-204 — Test and live credentials never mix.** Test and live keys are different keys held in different stores. A test key resolved in production configuration, or a live key in a development or CI environment, is a launch blocker.
5. **IN-205 — Keys you issue are shown once and stored hashed.** A customer API key's full value is displayed exactly once, at creation. At rest you store only a keyed hash of the value plus a non-secret prefix (e.g. `pk_live_9f3…`) that identifies the key in dashboards and logs without being usable as a credential.
6. **IN-206 — Every key is individually revocable.** Each key can be revoked on its own, without touching any other key, and revocation takes effect immediately. There is no shared "master key" whose revocation would be an outage, because there is no shared master key (IN-203).
7. **IN-207 — Rotation runs on a schedule and on suspicion, with overlap.** Each key carries a rotation date in the register. Rotation issues the replacement, deploys it, confirms the integration is green, and only then revokes the old key — overlap makes rotation routine instead of an outage.
8. **IN-208 — A found key is a leaked key: rotate first.** A key value appearing in a commit, a built bundle, a log, a screenshot, or a ticket is treated as compromised: rotate it before investigating how it got there. Deleting the line does not unpublish git history; history is leaked forever.
9. **IN-209 — Webhook signing secrets are keys.** Each webhook endpoint has its own signing secret, stored like any other credential, listed in the register, and rotatable without changing the endpoint URL. One secret shared across endpoints and providers is a defect.
10. **IN-210 — Key values are never logged.** Logs, error reports, analytics events, and support tickets record at most the key's prefix or last four characters. Redaction is applied at the logging layer, not left to each call site's memory.
11. **IN-211 — The key register is the inventory of record.** Every key has one register entry: provider, purpose, scope, environment, storage location, owner, and last rotation date. A key found in a store with no register entry is an orphan: it is revoked, not adopted.
12. **IN-212 — A client-visible key is never authorization.** Publishable keys shipped to the client are domain- or referrer-restricted where the provider allows, and the server still verifies every privileged outcome itself. Anything the client can read is public by definition, whatever its name.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-101 — The secret key in the client bundle.** Banned: embedding a provider secret key in frontend or mobile code that ships to users. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: the web app calls the provider with `sk_live_51H…` bundled into its JavaScript, so every visitor's browser downloads a full-access credential. Instead: the secret key stays in server-side secret storage (IN-201); the client gets the publishable key or a per-session scoped token (IN-202). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-102 — The committed credential.** Banned: a real key, password, or token as a literal in source, tests, or a committed config or `.env` file. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: `.env` with the live payment key is committed "temporarily" and cloned by every fork and CI cache from then on. Instead: the repo carries `.env.example` with dummy placeholders only; real values live in the secret store (IN-201). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-103 — Least privilege in name only.** Banned: claiming scoped credentials while every service, environment, and teammate uses the same single unrestricted key. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: the register says "restricted billing key," but the billing worker, the reporting cron, and a developer's laptop all authenticate with the account's one full-access secret key. Instead: issue per-purpose restricted keys and record each scope in the register (IN-203, IN-211). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-104 — The key in the logs.** Banned: writing a full key value to logs, error reports, or debug output, including "temporary" request logging that captures authorization headers. Defeats: DET-CODE-029. Bad: a debug middleware logs every outbound request header, and the provider secret key sits in searchable log storage readable by the whole team. Instead: redact credentials at the logging layer and log only the prefix (IN-210). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-105 — Delete-the-line incident response.** Banned: responding to a leaked key by only removing it from the code or rewriting the visible file, while the same key stays active. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: the key is scrubbed from the repo in a follow-up commit, the ticket is closed, and the unchanged key still authenticates a month later — every clone made in between kept a copy. Instead: rotate first, then clean up; the old value is revoked before the incident is closed (IN-208). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-101 — Secret scan.** Verifies: IN-201, IN-202. Check: automated — run a gitleaks-class secret scanner over the repository, the full git history, and the built client bundle and mobile package; assert the report is empty. Pass: zero findings (obvious placeholders such as `sk_live_EXAMPLE` in `.env.example` are allowlisted by value, not by path). Fail: block shipment and treat any real hit as a leak under IN-208. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-102 — Environment separation check.** Verifies: IN-204. Check: automated — script resolves the credential identifiers the production configuration points at and asserts every one is a live key from the production store, and that development/CI configuration resolves only test keys. Pass: no test identifier in production scope and no live identifier outside it. Fail: block the release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-103 — Register audit.** Verifies: IN-203, IN-211. Check: automated — script lists the keys present in each secret store and diffs them against the key register. Pass: every stored key has a register entry with purpose, scope, owner, and rotation date, and every register entry resolves to a stored key. Fail: orphan keys are revoked and the audit re-run before release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-104 — Rotation drill.** Verifies: IN-207, IN-211. Check: manual with evidence — rotate one staging credential end-to-end using only the register's instructions: issue replacement, deploy, confirm the integration is green, revoke the old key. Pass: the integration never errors and the old key is rejected afterward. Fail: fix the register or the procedure and repeat. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-105 — Revocation test.** Verifies: IN-206. Check: automated — create a throwaway key in the provider's test mode, confirm it authenticates, revoke it, and assert the provider now rejects it while a second key for the same account still works. Pass: revoked key rejected, sibling key unaffected. Fail: block shipment of any flow that issues keys. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Rotation theater.** A fresh key is issued on schedule and deployed, but the old one is never revoked "just in case," so every rotation adds a live credential instead of replacing one. Catch it: after any rotation, count active keys per purpose in the register audit (G-IN-103); the count must not grow.
- **The realistic placeholder.** `.env.example` ships with a value copied from a real key "so the format looks right," and someone later points staging at production with it. Catch it: placeholders are obviously fake (`sk_live_EXAMPLE`); the secret scan allowlists only those exact dummy values (G-IN-101).
- **The unnamed key.** The provider dashboard fills with keys labeled by creation date alone, and nobody can say which service breaks if one is revoked — so none ever are. Catch it: a key whose purpose cannot be stated in one sentence fails the register audit (IN-211).
- **Production keys on laptops.** Developers copy the live key into local `.env` files to "test the real thing," spreading the most powerful credential to the least controlled machines. Catch it: live keys exist only in the production store (IN-204); local work runs on test keys, and the environment separation check (G-IN-102) proves it.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Moving a secret key out of the client bundle](examples/example-1.md) — corrects IN-202.
- [Example 2 — Replacing a committed .env with secret-store references](examples/example-2.md) — corrects IN-201.
- [Example 3 — Issuing a customer API key: shown once, stored hashed](examples/example-3.md) — corrects IN-205.

## Recall anchors

- If it shipped to a client, it is public — whatever its name.
- A found key is a leaked key: rotate first, investigate second.
- One key per environment and purpose, scoped as small as the provider allows.
- Shown once, stored hashed, identified by prefix.
- No register entry, no key: orphans are revoked, not adopted.

## Checklist

- [ ] All credentials resolve from secret storage; the repo holds only dummy placeholders (IN-201, G-IN-101).
- [ ] No secret key appears in the built client bundle or mobile package (IN-202, G-IN-101).
- [ ] Test and live keys are separate keys in separate stores, verified by the separation check (IN-204, G-IN-102).
- [ ] Every key has a register entry with purpose, scope, owner, and rotation date (IN-211, G-IN-103).
- [ ] Issued customer keys are shown once and stored only as hash + prefix (IN-205).
- [ ] A throwaway key revokes cleanly without affecting sibling keys (IN-206, G-IN-105).
- [ ] The staging rotation drill passed using only the register's instructions (IN-207, G-IN-104).
- [ ] Logs and error reports contain prefixes only, never full key values (IN-210).

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/dunning/SKILL.md -->

# dunning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Automate payment retries" — https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/smart-retries ; Stripe, "Automatic collection" — https://docs.stripe.com/invoicing/automatic-collection
- **Depends on:** subscriptions, webhooks, transactional-email
- **Feeds into:** subscriptions, refunds-disputes

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a recurring charge fails and the product must recover the payment — retries, customer notices, grace period, and the end state — without surprising the customer or improvising access. This skill owns the failed-payment sequence from first decline to resolution.
- **Do NOT use when:** the failure is a first purchase (payments), the customer is voluntarily canceling (subscriptions), or money is moving back to the customer (refunds-disputes). Do not use it to design prices or plan terms; dunning executes the terms the product already published.

## Rules

1. **IN-081 — Dunning is one configured sequence.** Retries, customer contact, grace window, and end state are defined once, in provider and product configuration, before the first failure. A failure handled by ad-hoc support action or an engineer's judgment call is a defect in the sequence, not a rescue.
2. **IN-082 — The first failure notifies the customer the same day.** The first declined renewal sends a failed-payment email that day carrying a hosted payment-update link. Silent retrying burns the window in which a card update is most likely; the customer learns of the failure from the product, never from losing access.
3. **IN-083 — Retries are smart, finite, and configured.** The provider's smart retry machinery is enabled where offered, or a custom schedule is set, sized to the product's billing period. (Stripe's documented new-account default — up to 8 retries within 2 weeks, checked 2026-11-21 — is a starting configuration to review, not a law.) An unbounded or inherited-by-accident retry schedule is a finding.
4. **IN-084 — Hard declines exit retries immediately.** A hard decline (stolen card, closed account, do-not-honor) leaves the retry sequence at once and enters the contact layer; retrying it is cost without chance. Soft declines stay in the retry schedule.
5. **IN-085 — Card-updater features are enabled where offered.** Provider card-updater and network-token features are turned on, so reissued and replaced cards retry against current credentials — many "failures" are reissued cards, not unwilling customers.
6. **IN-086 — The payment-update path works and writes to the provider.** The update link lands on a hosted, login-light page (signed link, no full re-login gauntlet); submitting a new card stores it at the provider, and a successful update triggers an immediate retry rather than waiting for the next scheduled one.
7. **IN-087 — One past_due access rule, written and uniform.** During the grace window the product grants exactly one of full access, read-only access, or no access — stated in the published terms and enforced identically by every entitlement check. No page, endpoint, or export improvises its own variant.
8. **IN-088 — Dunning copy states facts and only real consequences.** Every notice names the amount, what happens next, and the deadline. Copy never threatens an action the sequence will not actually take — no deletion warnings on a sequence that pauses, no "final notice" that is not final.
9. **IN-089 — The sequence ends in exactly one configured state.** At the end of the window the subscription is canceled, marked unpaid, or paused — the one outcome chosen per product — executed at the provider, mirrored locally, and communicated to the customer with what it means for their access and data.
10. **IN-090 — Contact stops the moment payment succeeds.** A successful retry or card update halts the sequence immediately: no further reminders, no lingering banner, mirror back to active. A "your payment failed" email arriving after a successful charge is a sequence bug.
11. **IN-091 — Recovery is measured and reconciled.** The recovery rate (recovered ÷ failed renewals) is reported per period and reconciled against the provider's failed and recovered counts; involuntary churn is reported separately from voluntary cancellation, never blended into one churn number.
12. **IN-092 — Every dunning surface reads the mirrored state.** The banner, the emails, and the billing page all render from the mirrored provider subscription state (subscriptions, IN-021). No surface computes its own "days overdue" or paid status from local dates.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-041 — Silent retries.** Banned: a retry sequence that runs for days with no customer notice, so the first signal of a failed renewal is the end state. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Bad: the provider retries for two weeks, every attempt declines, the subscription is canceled, and the customer's first email is "your account has been closed" — the recovery window was spent in silence. Instead: the first failure notifies the customer the same day with a working update link (IN-082). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-042 — The update link that updates nothing.** Banned: a payment-update page that accepts a new card but never stores it at the provider, so retries keep hitting the old declined card. Defeats: DET-FAKE-016. Bad: the customer updates their card twice, gets a "Card updated" toast each time, and is canceled anyway because the form wrote to a local table the billing flow never reads. Instead: the hosted update writes the new payment method to the provider and triggers an immediate retry against it (IN-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-043 — Threat copy the sequence will not perform.** Banned: dunning notices claiming a consequence — deletion, legal action, a deadline — that the configured sequence does not actually carry out. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: three emails warn "your data will be permanently deleted on Friday," while the configured end state is pause with data retained; the state the copy claims never exists. Instead: copy states the amount, the real next step, and the real deadline (IN-088). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-044 — The UI-only access cut.** Banned: ending dunning by hiding the app behind a paywall screen while the API, exports, or shared links still serve the account — or the reverse, a banner claiming access is cut while nothing enforces it. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: the web app shows "subscription ended," but the mobile API keeps returning full data because only the frontend checks the flag. Instead: the end state changes entitlement at the one mirrored-state check every surface reads (IN-087, IN-092). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-045 — Locally "recovered" revenue.** Banned: marking a past_due subscription paid or active in local state — by support edit, admin toggle, or a retry stub — without a confirmed charge at the provider. Defeats: DET-FAKE-006. Bad: an admin "mark recovered" button flips the row to active so the dashboard looks healthy; no charge ever succeeded, and the customer is never billed again because the mirror says active. Instead: recovery exists only when the provider confirms the charge and the webhook converges the mirror (IN-090, IN-092). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-041 — Decline-card test-clock walk.** Verifies: IN-082, IN-083, IN-087, IN-089. Check: automated — in test mode with a provider test clock, run a renewal against a test decline card and advance the clock through the configured window; assert in order: the first-failure email fires the same day with a working update link, retries occur on the configured schedule, the past_due banner shows, the grace access rule holds, and the sequence lands in the one configured end state. Pass: every step occurs as configured. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-042 — Mid-sequence recovery stop test.** Verifies: IN-086, IN-090. Check: automated — fail a renewal in test mode, advance the clock into the sequence, then update the card through the hosted update link; assert an immediate retry runs against the new card, succeeds, the mirror returns to active, and no further dunning notice is sent afterward. Pass: recovery is immediate and contact stops. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-043 — Hard-decline exit test.** Verifies: IN-084. Check: automated — run a renewal against a provider test card that returns a hard decline and inspect the resulting schedule. Pass: zero further retry attempts are scheduled and the contact layer is entered on the first failure. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-044 — Recovery-report reconciliation.** Verifies: IN-091. Check: automated — generate the period recovery report and diff recovered and failed counts against the provider's invoice outcomes for the same period. Pass: counts match exactly and involuntary churn is reported as its own line. Fail: block the report; the metric is part of the feature. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Retry-forever configuration.** The schedule is copied from a tutorial or left at a default nobody chose, and declines retry until the provider gives up on its own. Catch it: open the configuration and read the actual retry count and window; if nobody can say why those numbers, the schedule was never designed (IN-083).
- **Email-only dunning.** Notices go out by email while the product itself shows nothing, so a customer who misses the email discovers the failure at the access cut. Catch it: sign in as a past_due test user — if no banner or billing-page state is visible in-product, the contact layer has one channel too few.
- **Copy drift toward menace.** Each rewrite of the dunning emails sounds tougher than the sequence behind it, because tougher "feels" more effective. Catch it: read every consequence the copy names and point to the configuration line that performs it; an unmatched consequence is a BAN-IN-043 hit, not a style choice.
- **The sympathetic extension.** Support quietly extends grace for loud customers by editing dates, so identical failures get different treatment and the end state stops meaning anything. Catch it: sample past_due rows and compare time-to-end-state; variance with no configured reason is improvisation (IN-087).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The two silent weeks](examples/example-1.md) — corrects IN-082.
- [Example 2 — The update link that saved nothing](examples/example-2.md) — corrects IN-086.
- [Example 3 — Four pages, four grace periods](examples/example-3.md) — corrects IN-087.

## Recall anchors

- First failure, same-day email, working update link.
- Smart retries, finite window, hard declines exit at once.
- One grace rule, one end state — both written in the terms.
- Copy threatens only what the sequence actually does.
- Recovery is a reconciled number, not a feeling.

## Checklist

- [ ] Retry machinery enabled and the schedule explicitly configured for this product (IN-083).
- [ ] Card-updater / network-token features enabled where the provider offers them (IN-085).
- [ ] Decline-card test-clock walk passes end to end (G-IN-041).
- [ ] Mid-sequence card update recovers immediately and stops all contact (G-IN-042).
- [ ] Hard declines schedule zero retries (G-IN-043).
- [ ] The past_due access rule is in the published terms and enforced by the one entitlement check (IN-087).
- [ ] Every dunning notice's stated consequence exists in the configured sequence (IN-088).
- [ ] Recovery report reconciles against provider counts, involuntary churn on its own line (G-IN-044).
