# subscriptions

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Subscription invoices" — https://docs.stripe.com/billing/invoices/subscription ; Stripe, "Use free trial periods on subscriptions" — https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/trials/free-trials ; Stripe, "Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint" — https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks
- **Depends on:** payments, webhooks
- **Feeds into:** dunning, refunds-disputes, invoicing-tax

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product sells recurring access — trials, renewals, plan changes, pauses, cancellation — and the entitlement a user sees must match what the payment provider will actually charge. This skill owns the subscription lifecycle as mirrored from the provider.
- **Do NOT use when:** the charge is one-off (payments), the work is recovering a failed renewal (dunning), or money is moving back to the customer (refunds-disputes). Do not use it to design pricing; prices come from the catalog the billing configuration mirrors.

## Rules

1. **IN-021 — The provider state machine is the model.** Local subscription status mirrors the provider lifecycle (trialing, active, past_due, canceled/unpaid). Every local transition is driven by an invoice or subscription webhook event or a verified server-side API read — nothing else moves state.
2. **IN-022 — No local timers.** No local clock, cron job, client flag, or stored date ever grants, extends, or revokes access. A date field is display data; the provider event is the transition.
3. **IN-023 — Every row carries the provider truth.** Each subscription row stores the provider subscription ID, provider customer ID, current status, and current period end. Entitlement logic never infers state from payment history, signup date, or plan name.
4. **IN-024 — Trial terms are shown before signup.** Trial length, whether a payment method is required upfront, the price at conversion, and the conversion date appear on the signup surface. A trial converts only on those terms; terms that differ at charge time from terms shown at signup are a defect.
5. **IN-025 — Trial-end behavior is configured, never inherited.** For each plan, the missing-payment-method outcome at trial end (invoice, pause, or cancel) and the with-card outcome are set explicitly in the provider configuration. Provider defaults left in place are a finding.
6. **IN-026 — No surprise conversion.** A trial-will-end warning reaches the customer before conversion (driven by the provider's trial-will-end event where offered), naming the amount and the date. A first charge the customer could not see coming is a defect, not a conversion.
7. **IN-027 — Cancellation is a provider state change.** Cancel writes to the provider, the local mirror converges to the returned state, and the customer receives a confirmation stating what access remains and until when. Whether cancellation takes effect at period end or immediately is a per-plan configured choice, stated before the customer confirms.
8. **IN-028 — Cancellation is as easy as signup.** The cancel path lives in the same channel as signup, takes no more steps than signup, and requires no call, chat, or retention gauntlet. This is the ROSCA / FTC Act Section 5 line: a negative-option offer whose cancellation is materially harder than its enrollment is an unfair-practice risk, independent of any single rule.
9. **IN-029 — Plan changes declare their arithmetic first.** Before the customer confirms an upgrade, downgrade, or interval switch, the UI states the proration behavior and the effective date. The change is executed at the provider and mirrored; it is never simulated locally and "synced later."
10. **IN-030 — One entitlement rule, read from the mirror.** Every surface — web, API, email, export — decides access by reading the same mirrored subscription state, including the one written past_due access rule handed to dunning. No page improvises its own access check.
11. **IN-031 — Reconciliation repairs missed events.** A periodic sync re-reads live subscriptions from the provider and repairs any local row whose status or period end has drifted. Webhooks are assumed losable; drift found by a customer is a defect in this sync, not bad luck.
12. **IN-032 — Mutations are idempotent and server-side.** Create, plan change, pause, resume, and cancel are executed server-side with an idempotency key derived from the business operation, so a double-click, retry, or replayed request produces exactly one effect.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-011 — The UI-only cancel.** Banned: a cancel button that hides the subscription in the UI while the provider keeps billing, or that revokes access the provider still shows as paid. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Bad: "Cancel" sets `hidden=true` on the local row; the customer is charged again at renewal and the support inbox finds out first. Instead: cancel at the provider, converge the mirror to the returned state, and confirm to the customer what remains and until when (IN-027). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-012 — The timer entitlement.** Banned: granting, extending, or revoking access from a local clock, a `trialEndsAt` comparison, or a client-side plan flag. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: middleware reads `localStorage.plan === "pro"` and a `setTimeout` ends trials in the browser; editing storage grants Pro, and paying customers lose access when the tab's clock is wrong. Instead: entitlements read the mirrored provider state only (IN-022, IN-030). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-013 — Status ahead of the provider.** Banned: any surface displaying a subscription state the provider has not reached — "Pro active" rendered on signup success, "canceled" shown before the provider confirms. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the success page announces "Your Pro plan is active" while the subscription object was never created because the webhook failed; the dashboard and the invoice disagree for a week. Instead: render state from the mirror, which moves only on provider events or verified reads (IN-021). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-014 — The phantom plan change.** Banned: applying an upgrade or downgrade in local state only, so it shows in the app but never reaches the provider and reverts or double-charges at renewal. Defeats: DET-FAKE-016. Bad: the settings page switches the user to the annual plan locally; at renewal the provider charges the old monthly price and the "change" silently disappears. Instead: execute the change at the provider with proration stated up front, then mirror the result (IN-029). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-015 — The subscription that exists only in your database.** Banned: marking a customer subscribed — plan, welcome email, unlocked features — without a subscription object existing at the provider. Defeats: DET-FAKE-006. Bad: trial signup inserts a local row with status `trialing` and unlocks Pro; no provider subscription was created, so nothing ever converts, renews, or can be canceled. Instead: create the subscription at the provider first; the local row is its mirror and carries its ID (IN-023). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-011 — Test-clock lifecycle walk.** Verifies: IN-021, IN-025, IN-026. Check: automated — in test mode with a provider test clock, create a trialing subscription, advance the clock, and assert in order: the trial-will-end warning is sent, the conversion charge matches the terms shown at signup, a decline card moves the mirror to past_due, and a card update returns it to active. Pass: every transition lands in the configured local state. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-012 — Missed-webhook drill.** Verifies: IN-031. Check: automated — disable the webhook endpoint for one renewal cycle in test mode, let the renewal happen, re-enable the endpoint, and run the reconciliation sync. Pass: the sync repairs the mirror to the provider's state with no manual edit. Fail: block shipment; the sync is part of the feature, not an enhancement. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-013 — Cancel-path verification.** Verifies: IN-027, IN-028. Check: automated plus timed walkthrough — script a cancellation in test mode and assert the provider state, the local mirror, the confirmation message, and the entitlement at period end all agree; then walk signup and cancel side by side and count steps. Pass: all four records agree and cancel takes no more steps than signup. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-014 — Trial-terms surface diff.** Verifies: IN-024, IN-025. Check: automated — extract the trial length, card requirement, conversion price, and trial-end behavior from the signup surface and diff them against the provider product/price and subscription configuration. Pass: zero differences, and both card and no-card trial-end outcomes are explicitly configured. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The second state machine.** A local status enum grows values the provider never emits ("grace," "pending-cancel," "vip") until nobody can say which system is right. Catch it: list local statuses next to provider statuses; any local value with no provider counterpart is deleted or demoted to a display label.
- **Webhook-only faith.** The mirror is trusted because "webhooks are reliable," and no reconciliation job exists in the repo. Catch it: search the codebase for the periodic provider re-read; if the only writer of subscription state is the webhook handler, drift is a matter of time (IN-031).
- **Retention-maze creep.** The cancel flow gains one small step per quarter — a survey, an offer modal, a "talk to us" screen — each harmless alone. Catch it: re-run the G-IN-013 step count after any cancel-flow change; growth in steps is a finding even when cancel still works.
- **Proration surprise.** Plan changes ship with the provider's default proration because nobody chose one, and the first upgraded customer is charged an amount no screen ever showed. Catch it: if the confirm screen cannot state the amount and effective date, the proration behavior was never configured (IN-029).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The cancel button that only hid the row](examples/example-1.md) — corrects IN-027.
- [Example 2 — A browser timer replaced by the provider lifecycle](examples/example-2.md) — corrects IN-022.
- [Example 3 — The missed webhook the reconciliation sync repaired](examples/example-3.md) — corrects IN-031.

## Recall anchors

- The provider's state machine is the only state machine.
- No local timer ever grants, extends, or revokes access.
- Trials convert only on the terms shown at signup.
- Cancel at the provider, confirm to the customer, same steps as signup.
- Webhooks get missed; the reconciliation sync is not optional.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every subscription row carries provider subscription ID, status, and period end (IN-023).
- [ ] Trial-end behavior is explicitly configured for card and no-card cases (G-IN-014).
- [ ] Signup surface trial terms diff clean against the provider configuration (G-IN-014).
- [ ] Test-clock lifecycle walk passes end to end (G-IN-011).
- [ ] Missed-webhook drill: the sync repairs the mirror unaided (G-IN-012).
- [ ] Cancel verified at provider, mirror, confirmation, and entitlement — in no more steps than signup (G-IN-013).
- [ ] Plan-change screens state proration and effective date before confirmation (IN-029).
- [ ] All entitlement checks read the one mirrored state (IN-030).

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/third-party-apis/SKILL.md -->

# third-party-apis

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microsoft Learn, Azure Architecture Center, "Circuit Breaker Pattern" — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker ; Stripe, "Idempotent requests" — https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- **Depends on:** api-keys-management
- **Feeds into:** payments, subscriptions, webhooks, transactional-email, sms, oauth-sso

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product calls any external provider API — payments, email, SMS, maps, search, AI models, data feeds — whether adding a new integration or changing an existing one. This skill owns the wrapper every outbound call passes through.
- **Do NOT use when:** the call is to the project's own backend (api-building, D4), or the work is the provider-specific money/message semantics of a single flow (payments, webhooks, sms own those; this skill owns the shared calling discipline underneath them). Provider-specific facts live in the integration's dated annex, never in this skill.

## Rules

1. **IN-181 — One adapter per provider.** Each provider sits behind a single internal adapter module that speaks the provider's API and exposes the project's own domain interface. No provider SDK type, response object, or error shape appears outside the adapter; replacing the provider is a one-module change.
2. **IN-182 — Every call carries a timeout.** Every outbound call sets an explicit connect timeout and read timeout, sized to the caller's latency budget and recorded in the adapter's configuration. A call with no timeout is a defect, even if it has never hung yet.
3. **IN-183 — Retries are bounded and safe.** Transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a configured maximum. A non-idempotent operation is retried only when it carries an idempotency key derived from the business operation; without a key it is attempted once.
4. **IN-184 — Circuit breaker per provider.** Repeated provider failures trip a circuit breaker for that provider; while open, calls fail fast into the degradation path instead of queueing behind a dead dependency. The breaker half-opens on a timer to probe recovery.
5. **IN-185 — Responses are validated before use.** Every provider response is checked against the adapter's expected schema (required fields, types, value ranges) before any field reaches domain code. A response that fails validation is an integration error, never data.
6. **IN-186 — Outage is a visible state, never empty data.** When a provider is down or a call fails after retries, the product shows its designed degradation: an explicit unavailable/stale state naming the affected feature. A provider failure is never rendered as an empty list, zero count, or "no results" — the user's data did not disappear.
7. **IN-187 — Rate limits are respected by design.** The adapter tracks the provider's documented limits (token bucket or queue where volume warrants) and treats a 429 as a backoff signal, honoring Retry-After when present. Client code never retries a 429 immediately.
8. **IN-188 — Credentials stay server-side.** Provider secret keys live in secret storage, are scoped per environment, and are used only by server-side code. The browser receives only keys the provider designed to be public, or short-lived scoped tokens the server mints. No secret appears in the client bundle, the repo, or logs.
9. **IN-189 — Contract drift alerts.** Schema-validation failures (IN-185) are logged and alerted as integration incidents, because providers change response shapes without changing version numbers. A rising validation-failure rate is treated as provider drift until proven otherwise.
10. **IN-190 — The degradation statement ships with the integration.** Every integration has a written statement, kept with its annex: what the product does when this provider is slow, down, or returning errors — which features degrade, what the user sees, and what is queued for later. No statement, no launch.
11. **IN-191 — Raw traffic is logged, secrets redacted.** Requests and responses are logged at the adapter (method, endpoint, status, latency, provider request ID) with credentials and personal data redacted, so a dispute or incident can be reconstructed from logs alone.
12. **IN-192 — Done means tested against failure.** An integration is complete only after it passes the sandbox contract suite and the failure drills (G-IN-091–G-IN-094) in staging. "It worked once in development" is not a completion state.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-091 — Fixture fallback sold as live.** Banned: shipping a code path that returns canned, hardcoded, or sample data when the provider call fails, times out, or was never wired up — presented to the user as the provider's real response. Defeats: DET-FAKE-009. Bad: the "AI summarizer" catches provider errors and returns one of three rotating template paragraphs; users cannot tell the model was never reached. Instead: call the provider through the adapter and surface failure per IN-186; a fallback is allowed only when it is labeled as a fallback in the UI. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-092 — Outage rendered as empty.** Banned: mapping a provider timeout, 5xx, or open circuit breaker to an empty list, zero count, or "nothing here yet" state. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the provider's outage makes the orders page show "You have no orders" for every customer for an hour. Instead: render the degradation state from the integration's statement (IN-190) — feature unavailable, data intact, retry offered. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-093 — Swallowed errors serving stale as current.** Banned: catching provider errors and silently returning cached or default data with no staleness marker, so figures freeze while the UI claims they are live. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Bad: the exchange-rate widget has shown the same rate for three days because every failed fetch falls back to the first cached value. Instead: serve cached data only with a visible "as of <time>" label, or fail into the degradation state. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-094 — Success claimed before provider confirmation.** Banned: telling the user an external action succeeded (ticket created, message sent, record synced) when the request was merely dispatched, or after it failed. Defeats: DET-FAKE-010. Bad: the UI toasts "Support ticket created" on submit; the helpdesk provider rejected the call, and no ticket exists. Instead: confirm from the provider's response (or its later status callback) before claiming the effect; a pending state is shown as pending. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-095 — First page presented as the whole dataset.** Banned: fetching one page of a provider's paginated results and rendering it as the complete list, with counts, filters, or totals computed from that page alone. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: the catalog imports the provider's first 100 items and reports "100 products" while the provider holds 4,000. Instead: paginate to completion or query server-side, and derive every count from the same full query as the results. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-091 — Sandbox contract suite.** Verifies: IN-181, IN-185. Check: automated — run the adapter's contract tests against the provider's sandbox/test environment (or replayed recorded fixtures where no sandbox exists), asserting request shape, auth, pagination, and response parsing for every operation the product uses. Pass: every contract test green. Fail: block the integration change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-092 — Dead-endpoint and latency drill.** Verifies: IN-182, IN-184, IN-186. Check: automated — in staging, point the adapter at a dead URL (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:9`) and at a fault-injection endpoint that sleeps past the read timeout; assert each affected feature answers within its latency budget with the degradation state from its statement, and that no screen renders an empty/zero state for existing data. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-093 — Failure-injection retry audit.** Verifies: IN-183, IN-187. Check: automated — route the adapter through a fault proxy returning, in sequence, 500, 429 with Retry-After, and a dropped connection; assert retry count never exceeds the configured maximum, backoff intervals grow, the 429 waits at least the Retry-After interval, and a non-idempotent operation without an idempotency key is attempted exactly once. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-094 — Malformed-response fixture suite.** Verifies: IN-185, IN-189. Check: automated — replay recorded provider fixtures mutated to be malformed (missing fields, wrong types, truncated body, error payload with HTTP 200) through the adapter; assert every one is rejected by schema validation, none reaches domain code, and a drift alert is emitted per case. Pass: all fixtures rejected and alerted. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-095 — Secret scan.** Verifies: IN-188. Check: automated — scan the repository and the built frontend bundle for provider key patterns (e.g. `grep -rE "(sk_live|sk_test|AKIA|ghp_)[A-Za-z0-9_]+" build/ src/` plus the project's secret-scanner in CI). Pass: zero findings. Fail: block shipment and rotate any key found. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **SDK confetti.** Provider SDK calls sprinkled through pages, handlers, and components, each with its own error handling. Catch it: grep the codebase for the provider's SDK import — every hit outside the adapter module is a violation of IN-181 waiting to hurt.
- **The infinite spinner.** A loading state with no timeout behind it, so a hung provider call becomes a permanently spinning page. Catch it: any loading UI whose underlying call lacks a configured read timeout (IN-182).
- **Copy-paste integration.** A second provider integrated by cloning the first provider's calls into feature code instead of writing its adapter. Catch it: two providers' base URLs or auth headers appearing in the same feature file.
- **Happy-path annex.** An integration annex that documents requests and success responses but no error shapes, limits, or outage behavior. Catch it: an annex with no error table and no degradation statement fails IN-190 on sight.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — An outage shown as "no orders" corrected to a degradation state](examples/example-1.md) — corrects IN-186.
- [Example 2 — Scattered provider calls consolidated behind an adapter](examples/example-2.md) — corrects IN-181.
- [Example 3 — An unbounded, retry-everything call given timeouts and safe retries](examples/example-3.md) — corrects IN-182, IN-183.

## Recall anchors

- One provider, one adapter — SDK types never escape it.
- No timeout, no call.
- Retry only what is idempotent or keyed, with backoff and a cap.
- An outage is a visible state — never empty data.
- Validate the response before a single field is used.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every provider call passes through its adapter; no SDK types leak into domain code (IN-181).
- [ ] Connect and read timeouts are configured for every outbound call (IN-182).
- [ ] Retries are bounded with backoff and jitter; non-idempotent retries carry idempotency keys (IN-183).
- [ ] Circuit breaker and degradation statement exist for this provider (IN-184, IN-190).
- [ ] Responses are schema-validated before use, and validation failures alert (IN-185, IN-189).
- [ ] Failure states render as unavailable/stale — never as empty lists or zero counts (IN-186).
- [ ] No provider secret appears in the repo, the client bundle, or logs (G-IN-095).
- [ ] Sandbox contract suite and failure drills pass in staging (G-IN-091–G-IN-094).

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/transactional-email/SKILL.md -->

# transactional-email

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Amazon SES, "Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES" — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email-authentication-dmarc.html ; RFC 7208 (SPF) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208 ; RFC 6376 (DKIM) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376 ; RFC 7489 (DMARC) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489 ; RFC 8058 (one-click unsubscribe) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8058
- **Depends on:** webhooks (provider delivery, bounce, and complaint events), api-keys-management (provider credentials)
- **Feeds into:** payments (receipts), subscriptions (billing notices), dunning (failed-payment mail), backend-auth (verification and reset mail)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product sends mail a user is waiting for because of something they just did — receipts, email verification, password resets, account and security notices, order and billing confirmations.
- **Do NOT use when:** the message is marketing or lifecycle mail — onboarding sequences, win-back, newsletters, promotional content of any kind. That is D9's lifecycle-email skill, sent on a separate stream under its own consent rules. This skill owns transactional streams only; the boundary is crossed deliberately, in a design decision, never by drift.

## Rules

1. **IN-121 — Authenticate the sending domain before the first send.** The dedicated sending subdomain publishes SPF and DKIM records aligned with the visible From: domain, plus a DMARC record that starts at `p=none` monitoring and progresses to enforcement. Alignment is proven in the `Authentication-Results` header of a real test send, not assumed from DNS records existing.
2. **IN-122 — Transactional and marketing mail use separate subdomains and streams.** A marketing reputation problem must never be able to take password resets down with it; no configuration shares a stream between the two.
3. **IN-123 — Send through a provider, as a background job.** The request handler enqueues a message with a template ID and its data; a worker sends via the email provider. No mail is sent inline in a web request, and none leaves from the app server's own SMTP.
4. **IN-124 — "Email sent" means provider-accepted, with the message ID stored.** The UI may claim a message was sent only after the provider accepts it and the returned message ID is written to the message row. Anything earlier is "sending," and a failed enqueue is an error the user sees.
5. **IN-125 — Delivery outcomes are recorded per message.** Provider delivered / bounced / complaint events return by webhook and are stored against the message row, so "did the reset email arrive" is a database query, never a guess or a support shrug.
6. **IN-126 — Bounces and complaints suppress automatically.** A hard bounce or a spam complaint adds the address to the suppression list inside the send path; no later send to that address leaves until the suppression is deliberately cleared. Re-mailing a hard-bounced address damages the domain for every user.
7. **IN-127 — Templates are versioned in the repo and ship with a plain-text part.** Every transactional template names the action it confirms or requests, the expiry where one applies, and the "this wasn't you" path. Template changes go through the same review as code.
8. **IN-128 — Templates render with tested fallbacks.** Every variable has a defined fallback for missing data; a rendered message never contains a raw template token, an empty gap, or the word "undefined". A seed-send with full and with empty data proves this before a template ships.
9. **IN-129 — Codes and links are single-use, expiring, and rate-limited.** Verification codes and reset links work once, expire on a stated clock, and are rate-limited at both send and confirm. D7 owns the security depth; this skill owns that the mechanism exists and is wired to the real send.
10. **IN-130 — Receipts and confirmations render from the stored, provider-confirmed record.** Amounts, items, and references in a receipt email come from the payment record the provider confirmed — never from template sample data, client-submitted values, or a recomputation that can drift.
11. **IN-131 — Transactional templates carry no marketing content.** No promotional block, cross-sell, or engagement bait in a transactional template: it reclassifies the stream, breaks the consent boundary with lifecycle-email, and trains filters to treat resets as bulk mail.
12. **IN-132 — A promised email that never arrives is a product defect.** Any flow that tells a user to check their inbox is verified end-to-end for arrival before launch, and failed sends retry with backoff into a visible dead-letter state — a silently dropped send is a defect, not an acceptable loss.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-061 — Reset toast with nothing behind it.** Banned: showing "Reset link sent" while no provider is called and no token exists. Defeats: DET-FAKE-020. Bad: the forgot-password handler renders a success toast and writes nothing; no email ever leaves. Instead: enqueue a real send through the authenticated provider carrying a single-use, expiring token, and store the message ID (IN-123, IN-124, IN-129). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-062 — The staged "we emailed you" state.** Banned: notification or account state claiming an email was sent when the send is a stub, a log line, or a fixture. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Bad: signup marks the account "verification email sent" while the mailer is a console-log stub left from development. Instead: the state is set only from the provider-acceptance record, and delivery advances only from provider events (IN-124, IN-125). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-063 — "Delivered" copied from the send response.** Banned: marking a message delivered because the provider's send API returned success. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the message row flips to `delivered` in the same call that enqueues it; bounces are never seen because nobody reads the events. Instead: acceptance records `accepted` with the message ID; only a provider delivery event records `delivered`, and bounce/complaint events record their own states (IN-125). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-064 — Receipt email rendered from sample data.** Banned: a receipt or invoice email whose amounts or items come from template placeholders or example data rather than the confirmed charge. Defeats: DET-FAKE-019. Bad: the receipt template ships with a hardcoded "$49.00 — Pro plan" body that real customers receive after paying a different amount. Instead: render every figure from the stored provider-confirmed payment record (IN-130). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-065 — Verification that verifies nothing.** Banned: an email-verification step that accepts any code, or marks the address verified without the code check passing. Defeats: DET-FAKE-003. Bad: the confirm endpoint accepts any six digits so testers can get through, and the shortcut ships. Instead: the code is server-issued, single-use, and expiring; the account stays in a pending state until the real check passes (IN-129). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-061 — Authentication check.** Verifies: IN-121, IN-122. Check: automated — query DNS (`dig +short TXT <sending-subdomain>`, the DKIM selector record, and `dig +short TXT _dmarc.<sending-subdomain>`), then send a test message and assert its `Authentication-Results` header shows SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passing and aligned with the visible From: domain, on a subdomain separate from the marketing stream. Pass: all three pass and align. Fail: block launch; no transactional mail ships from an unauthenticated domain. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no production sending domain or provider account exists yet, the DNS queries and header assertions run against a simulated sending setup — a test domain whose DNS records the project controls, configured exactly as the production subdomain will be, with the test send routed through it; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, verification against the production sending domain remains required before launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-062 — Seed-send token scan.** Verifies: IN-127, IN-128. Check: automated — send every transactional template to seed inboxes twice, once with complete data and once with empty optional data, and grep the rendered text and HTML parts for `{{`, `}}`, `undefined`, and `null`. Pass: zero unrendered tokens or placeholder artifacts in any rendering. Fail: block the template release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-063 — Bounce and suppression drill.** Verifies: IN-125, IN-126. Check: automated — send to the provider's bounce-simulator address; assert the message row records the bounce event and the address appears on the suppression list; then attempt a second send to the same address and assert the send path refuses it. Pass: bounce recorded, address suppressed, second send blocked. Fail: block launch. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-064 — End-to-end arrival test.** Verifies: IN-123, IN-124, IN-132. Check: automated in staging — complete the signup and password-reset flows; assert a message row exists with a provider message ID and reaches the delivered state via provider events, and that completing the reset actually changes the credential (the old password fails, the new one works). Pass: both flows arrive and the reset takes effect. Fail: block launch. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account exists yet, a local simulated provider — a mail double that issues provider-style message IDs, emits delivery events, and captures the messages — stands in for the provider and both flows are verified against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the arrival test against the real provider remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).

## Anti-patterns

- **The fire-and-forget send.** The provider is called and its return value thrown away, so failures are invisible until a user complains. Catch it: search for send calls whose message ID is never stored.
- **The "just this once" promo block.** A marketing paragraph sneaks into a receipt for one campaign and quietly reclassifies the stream. Catch it: diff transactional templates at review and question any sentence that sells rather than confirms.
- **The console-log mailbox in production.** The development stub transport survives into the production config. Catch it: the launch checklist names the active transport explicitly; "log" or "noop" is a stop.
- **The invisible retry loop.** The worker retries a failing send forever with no cap, no dead-letter, and no alert. Catch it: queue configuration with no maximum attempts or dead-letter destination is unfinished work.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The reset email that was never sent](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects IN-124.
- [Example 2 — "Delivered" copied from the send response](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects IN-125.
- [Example 3 — The receipt with sample totals](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects IN-130.

## Recall anchors

- "Sent" means the provider accepted it and you stored the ID.
- Delivered is an event, not an assumption.
- SPF, DKIM, DMARC — aligned, or it lands in spam.
- Transactional and marketing never share a stream.
- A promised email that never arrives is a product defect.

## Checklist

- [ ] SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verified passing and aligned on a real test send (G-IN-061).
- [ ] Transactional and marketing mail are on separate subdomains and streams (IN-122).
- [ ] Every send goes through the queue and stores its provider message ID (IN-123, IN-124).
- [ ] Delivered, bounce, and complaint events are stored against each message row (IN-125).
- [ ] Hard bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically in the send path (IN-126).
- [ ] Seed-sends with full and empty data show zero unrendered template tokens (G-IN-062).
- [ ] Signup and password-reset flows verified end-to-end for arrival in staging (G-IN-064).

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/webhooks/SKILL.md -->

# webhooks

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint" — https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Webhooks"
- **Depends on:** payments, api-keys-management
- **Feeds into:** subscriptions, refunds-disputes, dunning, transactional-email

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project receives provider events (payments, subscriptions, disputes, delivery status) or sends events to customers: endpoint design, signature verification, deduplication, processing, replay, and delivery logging.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what an event means for money state (payments and subscriptions own the semantics; this skill owns receiving and processing mechanics), or the transport is a general job queue with no provider signature or delivery contract (D4 queues-jobs owns transport mechanics).

## Rules

1. **IN-101 — Verify the signature over the raw body, before parsing.** The endpoint reads the exact bytes received and verifies the provider signature with the provider's library before any JSON parsing or body-parsing middleware touches the route. A parsed-and-reserialized body fails verification and is the most common self-inflicted outage.
2. **IN-102 — Reject and log every failed verification.** A request with a missing, invalid, or stale signature (outside the provider's timestamp tolerance — Stripe's libraries default to five minutes, the replay defense) is rejected with an error status, logged with its source, and changes no state. The endpoint is public by design; the signature is the only authentication.
3. **IN-103 — Persist before you acknowledge.** On successful verification, insert the event into an events table and only then return 2xx. The 2xx is a promise that the event is durably stored, never a claim that it has been processed.
4. **IN-104 — Deduplication is a database constraint, not a check.** The events table carries a unique constraint on the provider event ID; a duplicate delivery collides on insert and is acknowledged as already-received. An application-level "look up, then insert" is a race (DET-CODE-030), not deduplication.
5. **IN-105 — Process asynchronously, never in the request.** The request handler verifies, stores, and returns; a worker processes from the queue. No provider call, email send, or multi-table write happens inside the webhook request — slow handlers time out, and timeouts are what trigger duplicate retries.
6. **IN-106 — Handlers converge state; they never increment it.** A handler sets the mirror to the event's state ("set subscription status to `past_due`"), so a duplicate, a retry, or a replay of the same event is a no-op. A handler that adds, counts, or appends per delivery double-applies on the provider's normal at-least-once delivery.
7. **IN-107 — Assume unordered delivery.** Events arrive out of order; a handler never trusts arrival order or an older event over newer state. Where the event's object state matters, re-read the current object from the provider API and converge the mirror to that, so a late `created` event cannot resurrect a canceled subscription.
8. **IN-108 — Reconcile before fulfilling.** A signed event is necessary but not sufficient: before any fulfillment or entitlement change, the event is checked against the expected local record — account, amount, currency, and state must all match. A verified event naming the wrong amount fulfills nothing and is logged for review.
9. **IN-109 — Recover missed events with a periodic provider-state sync.** A scheduled job re-reads the provider state for active objects (subscriptions, open invoices, recent payments) and repairs the mirror where it has drifted. Webhooks get missed — endpoints go down, deliveries exhaust retries — and the sync is what makes the mirror converge anyway.
10. **IN-110 — Every delivery and outcome is logged, and failures are replayable.** Each event row records receipt time, verification result, processing outcome, and attempt count; a failed processing keeps the event and retries or dead-letters it for manual replay, never drops it. Events that arrived while the endpoint or worker was down are recovered by provider resend or event re-fetch, and the replay path is tested, not assumed.
11. **IN-111 — The signing secret is a credential.** Each endpoint has its own signing secret, held in the project's secret store (never in source, config files committed to the repo, or logs), and rotatable without a code change. D7 secrets-management owns compromise response; this skill owns the per-endpoint register entry.
12. **IN-112 — Outbound webhooks follow the same discipline.** Events sent to customers are signed with a per-endpoint secret the customer can rotate, retried with backoff over days (not minutes), logged per attempt with the response received, and exposed in a delivery-status view with a customer-triggered replay. An outbound event with no delivery record is a claim, not a notification.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-051 — The trusted POST.** Banned: a webhook endpoint that acts on any POST claiming an event ("payment succeeded") without signature verification. Defeats: DET-FAKE-006. Bad: `POST /webhooks/stripe` with a hand-written JSON body marks an order paid and grants access — no charge exists anywhere, and anyone who finds the URL can mint paid orders. Instead: verify the signature over the raw body first (IN-101) and reject failures (IN-102). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-052 — Check-then-insert deduplication.** Banned: deduplicating by reading for an existing event row and inserting if absent. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Bad: two concurrent duplicate deliveries both read "not found," both insert, and the customer is granted twice and emailed twice. Instead: a unique constraint on the provider event ID makes the duplicate collide safely (IN-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-053 — The incrementing handler.** Banned: handlers that advance state per delivery — incrementing a counter, appending a credit, counting retries as renewals. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the provider retries a `payment_succeeded` event once and the customer's balance is credited twice; the dashboard now reports money that never moved. Instead: handlers set the mirror to the event's state, so redelivery is a no-op (IN-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-054 — The swallowed processing failure.** Banned: catching a handler exception, returning 2xx anyway, and discarding the event. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Bad: the fulfillment write throws, the catch block logs "ok," the provider sees success and never retries, and the paid customer silently gets nothing. Instead: the stored event keeps a failed outcome, retries or dead-letters, and is replayable (IN-110); the failure is visible, not absorbed. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-055 — The committed signing secret.** Banned: a webhook signing secret hardcoded in source or committed in a config file. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: `WEBHOOK_SECRET = "whsec_..."` sits in the repo, so anyone with read access can forge perfectly signed events and defeat IN-101 entirely. Instead: the secret lives in the secret store, one per endpoint, rotatable without a deploy (IN-111). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-051 — Forgery test.** Verifies: IN-101, IN-102. Check: automated — POST a correctly shaped payment event to the endpoint with an invalid signature (and a second with a valid signature over a tampered body), then query the affected order. Pass: both requests are rejected with an error status and the order state is unchanged. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account exists yet, the endpoint is configured with a local simulated provider's signing secret and both forgery cases are exercised against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the run with a real provider-issued signing secret remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-052 — Duplicate-delivery test.** Verifies: IN-104, IN-106. Check: automated — deliver the same real event twice through provider tooling (resend from the provider dashboard or CLI) and assert one event row, one state transition, and one side effect (one grant, one email). Pass: exactly one effect from two deliveries, including under concurrent delivery. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account or provider tooling exists yet, a local simulated provider — a provider double that delivers validly signed events and resends the same event on demand — stands in for the provider and this check runs against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the run through the real provider's tooling remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-053 — Backlog replay test.** Verifies: IN-105, IN-109, IN-110. Check: automated — stop the worker, deliver a sequence of events (including an out-of-order pair), restart the worker, then run the provider-state sync. Pass: the mirror converges to the provider's current state, every event has a recorded outcome, and no effect is doubled. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-054 — Reconciliation-before-fulfillment test.** Verifies: IN-108. Check: automated — in test mode, deliver a validly signed event whose amount does not match the expected order, and assert nothing is fulfilled and the mismatch is logged. Pass: zero fulfillment, one logged mismatch. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-055 — Signing-secret scan.** Verifies: IN-111. Check: automated — grep the repository and committed config for signing-secret literals and provider secret prefixes (e.g. `whsec_`) and assert the endpoint reads its secret from the secret store at runtime. Pass: zero literals in the repo. Fail: block shipment and rotate the exposed secret. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The success redirect as a webhook substitute.** "We don't need webhooks; the success page tells us it worked." Catch it: search for entitlement or order-state writes triggered by a browser return URL — that path trusts the client completely (payments IN-005); webhooks verified under IN-101 are the only event source.
- **Verify-after-parse.** The signature check runs, but on the framework's parsed-then-reserialized JSON, so it fails intermittently and someone proposes "just skipping verification when it fails." Catch it: any code path where a verification failure can fall through to processing — the raw-body route must bypass body-parsing middleware entirely (IN-101).
- **The 200-always endpoint.** The handler returns 2xx before storing anything "to keep the provider happy," so a crash after the response loses the event permanently. Catch it: kill the process between response and insert in a drill — if the event is gone, the ack lied (IN-103).
- **Retry-blind outbound sending.** Customer webhooks are fired once, synchronously, inside the customer's triggering request, with no attempt log. Catch it: ask for the delivery record of one specific event; if none exists, delivery status is being asserted, not tracked (IN-112).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Replacing a trusted POST with signature verification over the raw body](examples/example-1.md) — corrects IN-101.
- [Example 2 — Replacing check-then-insert with a unique constraint and a converging handler](examples/example-2.md) — corrects IN-104.
- [Example 3 — Replacing in-request processing with persist, acknowledge, and queue](examples/example-3.md) — corrects IN-105.

## Recall anchors

- Verify the signature over the raw bytes — before parsing, every time.
- Store first, acknowledge second, process third — never in the request.
- Duplicates and disorder are normal delivery, not errors; converge, don't count.
- A signed event still has to match the order before it fulfills anything.
- Missed events are certain; the periodic sync is what makes the mirror true.

## Checklist

- [ ] Signature verified over the raw body before any parsing middleware (IN-101, G-IN-051).
- [ ] Failed verifications are rejected and logged with no state change (IN-102).
- [ ] The event is durably stored before the 2xx is returned (IN-103).
- [ ] A unique constraint on the provider event ID enforces deduplication (IN-104, G-IN-052).
- [ ] Handlers set state, never increment it, and tolerate out-of-order arrival (IN-106, IN-107).
- [ ] Fulfillment reconciles account, amount, currency, and state first (IN-108, G-IN-054).
- [ ] The periodic provider-state sync runs and the replay path is tested (IN-109, IN-110, G-IN-053).
- [ ] Signing secrets are per-endpoint, in the secret store, and absent from the repo (IN-111, G-IN-055).

# alerting

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Google, *The Site Reliability Workbook*, "Alerting on SLOs" — https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/ ; Google, *Site Reliability Engineering*, "Monitoring Distributed Systems" — https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Alerting"
- **Depends on:** monitoring (owns the signals and SLOs this policy alerts on)
- **Feeds into:** incident-response (D6 — consumes the pages this policy fires)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** defining or changing alert policy for a project: which conditions page, at what threshold, at what severity tier, with what payload, and how alert quality is reviewed over time.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is on-call mechanics — rotations, escalation execution, incident command, postmortems (incident-response, D6, owns those; this skill's policy is what D6's mechanics execute), infrastructure saturation plumbing (D6 consumes this policy for its hosts; D12 sets the policy), or which signals exist at all (monitoring owns signal coverage; this skill alerts on the signals monitoring provides).

## Rules

1. **AN-121 — Boundary: D12 owns policy, D6 owns mechanics.** This skill decides what pages, at what threshold, and with what signal quality. D6 owns the on-call rotation, the escalation execution, and the incident response the page triggers. Neither side silently redefines the other's half: a threshold change is a policy change here; a rotation change is a mechanics change there.
2. **AN-122 — Page on symptoms, never on causes alone.** Pages fire on what users experience: error-budget burn against a user-facing SLO, or a failed synthetic check on a critical flow. CPU, disk, memory, or a single host are causes — they are ticket or dashboard material unless they are themselves the user-visible symptom.
3. **AN-123 — Thresholds are derived from the error budget.** Paging alerts use the Workbook's multi-window, multi-burn-rate form. For a 99.9% SLO over a 30-day window: page at burn rate 14.4 over 1h/5m windows (2% of budget consumed), page at 6 over 6h/30m (5%), ticket at 1 over 3d/6h (10%); in each paging pair the short window is 1/12 of the long window and proves the burn is still happening. For any other SLO target or window, recompute the rates from the same budget-consumption logic — never copy these numbers onto a different SLO.
4. **AN-124 — Three severity tiers, honestly assigned.** Every alert is exactly one of: page (a human acts now), ticket (a human acts in working hours), or dashboard-only (informational, never routed as an alert). Anything burning slower than the paging rates in AN-123 is a ticket; "page everything to be safe" is a policy failure, not caution.
5. **AN-125 — Every page is actionable at the hour it fires.** The person paged must be able to do something that changes the outcome. If the correct response is "wait" or "ignore", the alert is reclassified to a lower tier, re-thresholded, or deleted — it is not endured.
6. **AN-126 — Complete payload or it does not ship.** Every alert carries: what is broken, the user impact, the runbook link, the dashboard link, and the escalation path. A paging alert without a runbook link does not ship.
7. **AN-127 — Every alert has a named owner.** Each alert rule names its owning team or person in the alert configuration itself. An ownerless alert is a defect: nobody is responsible for its threshold, its runbook, or its retirement.
8. **AN-128 — Routing is verified, not assumed.** Pages route through the alert manager with deduplication and grouping to the current on-call, never to a hardcoded individual or a channel nobody watches. A business-hours product may route to a monitored team inbox instead of a pager only where a named human demonstrably receives and acts on it.
9. **AN-129 — Silence is time-boxed and recorded.** Every silence or inhibition carries a reason and an expiry. An expired silence still in effect, or a silence with no expiry, is a defect; a permanently muted alert is fixed or deleted, never left pretending to protect anything.
10. **AN-130 — Alert quality is measured and pruned.** Track pages per period and the share that required action. On the review cadence, any alert that fired repeatedly with no action taken is fixed, demoted a tier, or deleted; a falling action share triggers an alert-review task, not greater tolerance for noise.
11. **AN-131 — Missing data is itself an alert.** If the metrics pipeline, an exporter, or the external synthetic check stops reporting, a dead-man's-switch alert fires through an independent path. "No data" never reads as "zero errors", and an external check on the public endpoints feeds the same paging path as internal alerts, so a total host or network failure still pages someone.
12. **AN-132 — Low-traffic mode is explicit.** Where request volume is too low for a burn rate to be meaningful, the policy says so and switches to longer windows, ticket-only tiers, and synthetic-check pages on critical flows. A threshold that can never fire, or that fires on ordinary noise, is a defect either way.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-061 — Alerts that reach nobody.** Banned: alert rules firing into an unmonitored channel, an unused chat room, a former team member's address, or no rule existing at all for downtime or error burn. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: the error-rate alert posts to a Slack channel the team archived last quarter; a two-hour outage is discovered from user complaints. Instead: route pages through the alert manager to the current on-call and prove receipt with the G-AN-062 fire drill. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-062 — Cause-threshold paging.** Banned: a paging alert on a raw cause threshold — "CPU > 80% for 1 minute" — while the user-facing error rate has no alert of its own. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the pager fires on every deploy's CPU spike and stays silent through an afternoon of checkout 500s, because nothing alerts on the golden signals. Instead: page on SLO burn rate per AN-123; chart and ticket causes under monitoring. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-063 — A page with no way to act.** Banned: shipping a paging alert with no runbook link, no dashboard link, or no stated user impact, so the person paged starts from a blank page at 3 a.m. Defeats: DET-INF-029. Bad: "ALERT: latency high" arrives with a metric name and nothing else; the responder improvises while the incident clock runs. Instead: attach what is broken, user impact, runbook link, dashboard link, and escalation path per AN-126 — the G-AN-063 lint blocks anything less. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-064 — The permanent mute.** Banned: silencing a noisy alert indefinitely — no expiry, no ticket, no threshold fix — instead of repairing or deleting it. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: a flapping disk alert is muted "until we get to it" in March; in November the disk fills during a launch and nothing pages. Instead: time-box the silence with a reason and a linked fix task per AN-129, or delete the alert at the AN-130 review. Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AN-065 — Blind when the pipeline dies.** Banned: an alerting setup with no dead-man's switch and no external check, so a dead metrics pipeline, dead host, or dead network path presents as a quiet, healthy system. Defeats: DET-INF-028. Bad: the monitoring VM fails at midnight; every internal check dies with it and the team learns of the outage from social media. Instead: an independent external synthetic check plus an absence-of-data alert per AN-131, both feeding the paging path. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AN-061 — Alert rules check.** Verifies: AN-123. Check: automated — run `promtool check rules` (or the alerting platform's equivalent validator) over the alert rule files in CI on every change to them. Pass: the validator exits 0 and every paging rule's windows and burn rates match the values derived for its SLO in the policy document. Fail: block the change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-062 — Fire drill.** Verifies: AN-126, AN-128. Check: automated in staging — stop a staging service (or fire the test alert) and time the result. Pass: a page reaches the current on-call channel within the documented time, deduplicated, carrying the runbook link and dashboard link. Fail: block shipment of the alert configuration; fix routing before any production reliance on it. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-063 — Alert-config lint.** Verifies: AN-124, AN-126, AN-127. Check: automated — lint the alert configuration and assert every paging alert has a runbook link, a dashboard link, a stated user impact, a severity tier, and a named owner. Pass: zero paging alerts missing any field. Fail: block the change; the alert does not ship incomplete. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-064 — Inventory audit.** Verifies: AN-129, AN-130. Check: automated — a scheduled report lists alerts with no runbook link, silences past their expiry, and alerts that fired three or more times in the period with no linked incident or action. Pass: the list is empty, or every listed item has a fix, demote, or delete task from the review. Fail: each unresolved item is recorded as a defect. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-065 — Dead-man's-switch test.** Verifies: AN-131. Check: automated in staging — halt the metrics exporter/pipeline for the staging service. Pass: the absence-of-data alert fires within the documented window through the independent path, and the external synthetic check still reports. Fail: block reliance on the alerting setup until absence alerts as reliably as presence. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The deploy metronome.** An alert fires on every deploy and is acknowledged on reflex, so the one time it means something it is acked too. Catch it: the G-AN-064 audit's fired-with-no-action list — if a deploy-shaped pattern is on it, the alert is measuring deploys, not health.
- **The hero's phone number.** Escalation works because one named person's personal device is the real target, whatever the rotation says. Catch it: run the fire drill with that person unreachable; if the page dies with them, routing was never real (AN-128).
- **Threshold folklore.** Numbers like "80% for 1 minute" copied from a tutorial, with no SLO and no budget fraction behind them. Catch it: ask of any threshold, "which SLO, and what share of its budget does this consume?" — no answer, no alert (AN-123).
- **Dashboard theater.** Forty charts glow green in a tab nobody opens while no alert exists for the same signals — monitoring as decoration. Catch it: if a signal matters enough to chart, its burn has a tier under AN-124; if it does not, the chart is the decoration.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The CPU page that fired on every deploy](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-122.
- [Example 2 — The alert that posted to a dead channel](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-128.
- [Example 3 — The alert muted since March](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-129.

## Recall anchors

- Page on symptoms and burn rate; causes get tickets and dashboards.
- Thresholds are derived from the error budget, never copied.
- No runbook link, no page — incomplete alerts do not ship.
- Silence has an expiry; a permanent mute is a deleted alert lying.
- Missing data pages too: quiet is not the same as healthy.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every paging alert derives from a named SLO with budget-derived windows and burn rates (AN-123).
- [ ] No page fires on a cause alone; causes are ticketed or charted (AN-122).
- [ ] Every paging alert carries impact, runbook link, dashboard link, escalation path, and a named owner (G-AN-063).
- [ ] Fire drill reached the current on-call within the documented time (G-AN-062).
- [ ] All silences carry a reason and an unexpired time box (AN-129).
- [ ] The inventory audit is clean, or every noisy alert has a fix/demote/delete task (G-AN-064).
- [ ] Dead-man's switch and external check verified in staging (G-AN-065).
- [ ] Low-traffic services run the explicit low-traffic mode, not silent thresholds (AN-132).

# apm

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenTelemetry, "Observability primer" — https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/ ; Google, *Site Reliability Engineering*, "Monitoring Distributed Systems" — https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
- **Depends on:** logging, monitoring
- **Feeds into:** performance-optimization, dashboards, error-tracking

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** instrumenting a service for application performance monitoring: choosing and configuring tracing, setting the sampling strategy, propagating trace context across services, queues, and jobs, building per-service performance views (throughput, error rate, duration percentiles, top endpoints, downstream dependencies), or diagnosing a slow endpoint or database call from traces.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is browser-side, real-user performance — LCP, INP, and CLS field metrics, per-template vitals, and lab reproduction. **core-web-vitals owns the browser-side field metrics; this skill owns server-side application tracing** — spans, slow endpoints, and database time — and the two meet only where a trace explains what the server contributed to a page load. Host and platform telemetry belong to D6; SLI/SLO definitions and metric-label policy belong to monitoring; this skill consumes both.

## Rules

1. **AN-181 — One instrumentation standard: OpenTelemetry.** Every service is instrumented with OpenTelemetry libraries and OTel semantic conventions for span names and attributes, exported through a collector to the project's backend. A service instrumented with a proprietary one-off agent is recorded as a correlation break and a migration debt, not as an acceptable variation.
2. **AN-182 — One trace ID from edge to database.** Trace context propagates across every boundary a request crosses — inbound HTTP, outbound HTTP, message queues, and background jobs, whose payloads carry the trace context explicitly. The same trace ID appears on every span and on the request's log lines (logging owns the log format; this skill owns the shared ID), so one production request can be reconstructed end to end and pivoted from span to logs without SSH or new code.
3. **AN-183 — Sampling is a written decision.** The repo records the sampling strategy with its reason: the head-based baseline rate, what is always kept (errors and slow outliers, via tail sampling at the collector where volume justifies it), and what the blind spot costs. "Whatever the default was" is not a strategy; a sampler that can discard the only trace of an incident has failed its purpose.
4. **AN-184 — Rich detail lives on spans, never in metric labels.** Span attributes carry the high-cardinality detail traces exist for — endpoint, query shape, downstream target, result status. User IDs, request IDs, and full URLs never leak from spans into metric labels; monitoring's cardinality budget applies unchanged (AN-107).
5. **AN-185 — No secrets or personal data in span attributes.** Span attributes and span events never carry passwords, tokens, authorization headers, card numbers, emails, or free-text user input. Attribute keys come from the semantic conventions or a reviewed project list; a trace backend is a data store, and whatever lands in a span is retained like one.
6. **AN-186 — Instrumentation coverage is inventoried.** Every service and every async path is listed in the repo as instrumented or explicitly not instrumented, with the gap's owner named. "No trace" during an incident must be a known, recorded gap — never a surprise discovered mid-investigation.
7. **AN-187 — Per-service views are built from the traces.** Each instrumented service has a standard view built from its telemetry: throughput, error rate, duration percentiles (p50/p95/p99, never averages), top endpoints by traffic and by duration, and its downstream dependencies with their share of its latency. A slow endpoint is identified from this view, not from anecdote.
8. **AN-188 — A latency claim without a trace is an opinion.** No statement about where time goes — in a review, a postmortem, or an optimization proposal — stands unless it names the trace evidence behind it: the service, endpoint, and span breakdown (self time versus downstream time, database time shown separately). Claims are restated from percentile data over a stated window, not from a single hand-picked trace.
9. **AN-189 — Exemplars link spikes to traces.** Latency metrics carry exemplars where the backend supports them, so a p99 spike on a chart opens the actual slow traces behind it. Where exemplars are unsupported, the view links the chart's time window and filters into the trace search — a spike nobody can descend into is decoration.
10. **AN-190 — Database time is its own span.** Database calls appear as child spans with the operation and target recorded (never the literal parameter values), so an endpoint's duration decomposes into application time, database time, and downstream-call time. An endpoint whose duration is one opaque span is uninstrumented where it matters most.
11. **AN-191 — Critical paths get manual spans where automation goes blind.** Where automatic instrumentation misses the work that matters — a queue consumer's processing body, a batch loop, a cache layer — explicit manual spans are added with semantic-convention names. The test is behavioral: the primary flow's trace shows every hop it actually took.
12. **AN-192 — Trace retention is stated, like sampling.** The repo records how long traces are retained and what the sampling-plus-retention combination makes unanswerable (for example, last month's rare error on a low-traffic endpoint). Performance comparisons across releases use windows inside retention; a comparison the telemetry cannot support is reported as unmeasurable, not estimated.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-091 — One-off proprietary instrumentation.** Banned: instrumenting a service with a vendor-specific agent or hand-rolled timing calls while the rest of the system uses OpenTelemetry, so its spans join no shared trace. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the payments service ships a proprietary agent; during a checkout incident every other service's trace stops at its door, and its own data sits in a separate console nobody can correlate. Instead: instrument with OpenTelemetry and semantic conventions, exported through the same collector as every other service (AN-181). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-092 — Trace context dropped at the queue.** Banned: enqueueing a job or message without the trace context, so the consumer starts an unrelated trace and the request's story ends at the exact boundary where the incident lives. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: the order request traces cleanly to `enqueue confirmation-email`, but the job that times out and double-charges runs under a fresh ID; the two halves are never connected. Instead: carry the trace context in the job payload and continue the originating trace in the consumer (AN-182). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-093 — The default sampler as the strategy.** Banned: shipping whatever sampling the library defaulted to, with no written decision, so errors and slow outliers are sampled away at the same rate as routine traffic. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: a 1-in-1,000 default keeps almost nothing; the one checkout failure mode that matters occurs eleven times in a week and leaves zero traces. Instead: record a baseline rate and always keep errors and slow requests, with tail sampling at the collector where volume justifies it (AN-183). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-094 — Identifiers as metric labels via APM.** Banned: promoting span attributes such as user ID, request ID, or full URL into metric labels because the APM view made it one click. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: a `user_id` label on the duration metric explodes series count, the metrics store saturates and drops data, and every golden-signal dashboard gaps during the incident the labels were meant to explain. Instead: keep identifiers on spans and log fields, where high cardinality is their purpose (AN-184). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AN-095 — Secrets and personal data in span attributes.** Banned: attaching credentials, tokens, emails, or raw user input as span attributes or span events. Defeats: DET-INF-021. Bad: a debugging pass adds the full request body to every span; the trace backend now retains customer emails and a password-reset token, searchable by anyone with dashboard access. Instead: record operation, target, and status attributes from the reviewed list only (AN-185). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AN-091 — Trace-completeness test.** Verifies: AN-182, AN-186, AN-191. Check: automated — drive a synthetic request through the primary flow in staging (sign-in, the core action, checkout where one exists) and fetch its trace from the backend API; assert a span exists for every service and every async hop the flow touches, all under one trace ID. Pass: zero missing spans. Fail: block; the flow is unobservable where it matters. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-092 — Queue propagation test.** Verifies: AN-182. Check: automated — in staging, perform the action that enqueues the primary background job, then query the backend for the job consumer's spans; assert they carry the originating request's trace ID, not a fresh one. Pass: the consumer's spans join the originating trace. Fail: block the change that touched the enqueue or consume path. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-093 — Coverage inventory check.** Verifies: AN-186. Check: automated — diff the instrumentation inventory in the repo against the service registry, including async paths. Pass: every service and async path is listed as instrumented or explicitly not, with an owner on each gap. Fail: an unlisted service is a release defect. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-094 — Always-kept sampling test.** Verifies: AN-183. Check: automated — with the production sampling configuration applied in staging, drive a forced error response and a deliberately slow request on the primary flow, then query the backend for both traces. Pass: both traces are present despite the baseline rate. Fail: block; the sampler can discard the next incident. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-095 — Span-to-log pivot test.** Verifies: AN-182, AN-187. Check: automated — take the trace from G-AN-091, extract its trace ID, and query the central log store for that ID; assert entries exist from every service the trace touched, and that the service's standard view renders throughput, error rate, and duration percentiles from the same window. Pass: the pivot resolves for every service and the view renders. Fail: the correlation chain is declared broken until fixed. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The three-console observability story.** Metrics in one tool, logs in another, a tracing trial in a third, with no shared ID between them — sold internally as "we have observability". Catch it: run the behavioral test — reconstruct one request end to end; if you open a second console and start guessing, it fails (AN-182).
- **The single opaque span.** The endpoint's trace is one long bar with no children: no database span, no downstream calls, so "the endpoint is slow" is all anyone can ever say. Catch it: if the trace cannot decompose duration into app, database, and downstream time, instrumentation is unfinished (AN-190).
- **Cherry-picked trace as proof.** One slow trace pasted into a review thread presented as the endpoint's latency profile. Catch it: ask for the percentile over a stated window with the trace as illustration, never as the dataset (AN-188).
- **Instrumenting only the happy path.** Spans wrap successful operations while error branches, retries, and fallback paths emit nothing — so traces are plentiful exactly when nothing is wrong. Catch it: force the error path in staging and read its trace before signing off coverage (G-AN-094).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The trace that ended at the queue](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-182.
- [Example 2 — The default sampler that threw away the incident](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-183.
- [Example 3 — The 200 ms claim with no trace behind it](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-188.

## Recall anchors

- One trace ID, edge to database — or the story ends where the incident lives.
- Sampling is a written decision; errors and slow requests are always kept.
- Detail belongs on spans; labels stay low-cardinality.
- A latency claim without a trace behind it is an opinion.
- Browser vitals belong to core-web-vitals; spans and database time belong here.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every service is instrumented with OpenTelemetry and semantic conventions (AN-181).
- [ ] Trace-completeness test passes: every service and async hop on the primary flow under one trace ID (G-AN-091).
- [ ] Queue propagation test passes: consumer spans join the originating trace (G-AN-092).
- [ ] Sampling strategy is written in the repo, and the always-kept test passes for an error and a slow request (AN-183, G-AN-094).
- [ ] Coverage inventory matches the service registry, gaps owned (G-AN-093).
- [ ] No secrets or personal data in span attributes; no identifiers promoted to metric labels (AN-184, AN-185).
- [ ] Span-to-log pivot resolves for every service on the primary flow (G-AN-095).
- [ ] Retention window is recorded, and no performance claim cites data outside it (AN-192).
