<!-- generated from skills/analytics-observability/core-web-vitals/SKILL.md -->

# core-web-vitals

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** web.dev, "Web Vitals" — https://web.dev/articles/vitals ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Performance budgets"
- **Depends on:** product-analytics (owns the RUM collection pipeline and consent gating), performance-budgets (owns the numeric budget file and CI enforcement)
- **Feeds into:** performance-optimization (owns the fix loop), dashboards, alerting

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** measuring, reporting, or fixing a web product's Core Web Vitals — setting up real-user monitoring, reading a field report, deciding whether a template passes, or diagnosing a failing LCP, INP, or CLS.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is the numeric budget file or its CI assertions (performance-budgets owns budgets; this skill owns the field verdict the budgets mirror), the hands-on optimization change itself (performance-optimization owns the fix loop; D3/D4/D5 own implementation), or synthetic load testing of APIs (D8 load-testing owns test craft).

## Rules

1. **AN-221 — Field data is the verdict.** A template's Core Web Vitals status is its real-user field data at the 75th percentile over a rolling 28-day window, against the web.dev thresholds: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1. Lab data diagnoses; it never overrules a failing field score and is never reported as the user experience.
2. **AN-222 — Report per template and per device class.** Field results are reported for each key page template (home, listing, detail, checkout, app shell — the project's template inventory), separately for mobile and desktop. No site-wide blended figure is published; the average of a fast homepage and a slow checkout is a lie about both.
3. **AN-223 — All three must be good to pass.** A template passes only when LCP, INP, and CLS are all in the "good" band at p75. Two good vitals do not compensate for one poor one, and a template's status names the failing vital, not just "slow."
4. **AN-224 — Every key template is instrumented.** Real-user monitoring (the web-vitals library or the platform's RUM) collects LCP, INP, and CLS on every template in the inventory, tagged with template, device class, and country. A template with no field data is reported as unmeasured — never as passing.
5. **AN-225 — Reproduce in the lab before fixing.** For each failing template, a throttled lab run (a mid-tier mobile device profile on a throttled network, not the office desktop) reproduces the failure mode before optimization work begins. No reproduction, no fix attempt: a lab run that cannot reproduce the field failure is evidence the diagnosis is wrong.
6. **AN-226 — Decompose the metric before fixing it.** Diagnosis names the dominant subpart: LCP decomposes into time to first byte, resource load delay, resource load duration, and element render delay; INP into the long tasks blocking the main thread; CLS into the specific elements that shift. Fixes target the dominant subpart, never "the metric" in the abstract.
7. **AN-227 — INP is the responsiveness vital.** Budgets, reports, and fixes are written against INP, which replaced FID as the responsiveness vital on March 12, 2024. No document, budget, or dashboard tracks FID as a current vital; a stale FID reference is a defect to remove, not a metric to report.
8. **AN-228 — CLS fixes are structural.** Width and height (or aspect-ratio space) are reserved for images, embeds, ads, and async slots before they load. Content is never injected above existing rendered content except in direct response to user input within the same interaction.
9. **AN-229 — The LCP element is named and prioritized per template.** Each template's report names its LCP element. That resource is prioritized — discoverable in the initial HTML, not lazy-loaded, not behind a client-side render chain — and hero media is sized to the template's budget, not shipped at source weight.
10. **AN-230 — Every fix is verified in the field.** A fix ships with the field window that will judge it: the template's p75 is re-read over the following 28-day window (or the shorter stated window once enough visits accumulate). A fix that does not move field p75 is reverted or reworked, not celebrated on the strength of its lab run.
11. **AN-231 — Low-traffic templates report "insufficient data."** When a template lacks the visits to form a meaningful p75, the report says so and judges it on the lab-plus-RUM hybrid: throttled lab runs plus whatever field samples exist, over a longer window. Thresholds never silently pass — or fail — on noise.
12. **AN-232 — Breaches become tracked defects.** The field report runs on a recorded cadence. Any template outside "good" opens a defect naming the template, the failing vital, and its p75; the defect closes only on field evidence under AN-230, not on a lab screenshot.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-111 — Lab score as the verdict.** Banned: reporting a Lighthouse score or a desktop lab timing as the product's Core Web Vitals result, in a status report, README, or sales page. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the launch report announces "Performance: 98" from one desktop Lighthouse run on the office connection while field mobile LCP p75 is 4.6 s. Instead: report field p75 per template and device class against the AN-221 thresholds; cite lab runs only as diagnosis. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-112 — Homepage-only measurement.** Banned: measuring, optimizing, or quoting vitals for the homepage alone while the templates users actually convert on go unmeasured. Defeats: DET-VIS-044. Bad: the homepage is tuned to a 1.8 s LCP for the launch screenshot; the checkout template — never instrumented — runs a 5 s LCP for a month. Instead: instrument and report every template in the inventory (AN-222, AN-224) before quoting any vitals figure. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-113 — The site-wide blended number.** Banned: publishing one averaged vitals figure for the whole site, blending templates and device classes into a single passing score. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: "Average LCP 2.3 s — good" across the site, computed over a homepage that takes 90% of traffic, while the mobile product page sits at 4.1 s. Instead: publish the per-template, per-device-class table (AN-222); the worst key template is the headline, not the mean. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-114 — Unbudgeted hero payload.** Banned: shipping hero media at source weight — a multi-megabyte autoplay video or uncompressed banner image — because it "looked fine" on a fast connection. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: a 4 MB hero video ships; on the office fiber it paints instantly, on real mobile networks it is the LCP element at 6 s. Instead: size hero media to the template budget, compress and poster-frame video, and verify under the throttled lab profile (AN-225, AN-229). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-115 — Late injection above rendered content.** Banned: inserting banners, cookie notices, promo bars, or async embeds above already-rendered content so the page jumps under the reader's finger. Defeats: DET-VIS-039. Bad: a promo bar loads two seconds after first paint and pushes the article — and the button the user was tapping — down by its full height; CLS p75 is 0.31. Instead: reserve the slot's space before render or overlay without reflowing content (AN-228). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AN-111 — Field report check.** Verifies: AN-221, AN-222, AN-223. Check: automated — a scheduled job queries the RUM store for the trailing 28 days and emits, per template in the inventory and per device class, the p75 of LCP, INP, and CLS against the thresholds (LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1). Pass: every key template is "good" on all three vitals, or carries an open defect under AN-232. Fail: block any release note or status report that claims performance health; open the defects. Before a production environment is provisioned, this gate's disposition is a recorded provisioning waiver per the §6.3 protocol; it unblocks when the production site is live, real-user monitoring is collecting field data, and the first 28-day window has matured. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-112 — RUM integrity check.** Verifies: AN-224, AN-231. Check: automated — for each template, compare RUM beacon volume to pageview volume for the same window; flag any template whose beacon ratio falls below the project's stated coverage floor, and mark templates below the p75 sample floor as "insufficient data." Pass: every key template is either measured at or above the floor or explicitly reported unmeasured/insufficient. Fail: block the field report from marking that template passing. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-113 — Lab reproduction and template lab run.** Verifies: AN-225, AN-226, AN-229. Check: automated — run Lighthouse CI (`lhci autorun`) against a staging build for every key template under the throttled mobile profile, asserting the budget file's LCP and CLS values on the median of multiple runs; for each field-failing template, confirm the lab run reproduces the failing vital and the report names its dominant subpart. Pass: all key templates are lab-run, and every field failure has a reproduction plus a named subpart. Fail: block optimization work on unreproduced failures. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-114 — Threshold and vital currency check.** Verifies: AN-221, AN-227. Check: automated — grep the repo's budgets, reports, and dashboards for "FID" as a tracked vital and for threshold values; assert the only responsiveness vital is INP and the asserted thresholds read LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1. Pass: zero FID references as a current vital and thresholds match. Fail: block the change until the stale vital or threshold is corrected. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-115 — Field verification of fixes.** Verifies: AN-230. Check: automated — for each closed vitals defect, pull the template's field p75 for the post-fix window and compare it with the pre-fix p75 recorded on the defect. Pass: the failing vital moved into "good," or the defect is reopened as reverted/reworked with the reason recorded. Fail: the defect cannot close on lab evidence alone. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Score chasing.** Reloading the lab tool with different settings, extensions disabled, or a faster profile until a green number appears, then screenshotting that run. Catch it: ask which field window the claim rests on — if the answer is a lab run, it is not a result (AN-221).
- **Optimizing the metric in the abstract.** "Improve LCP" work that compresses everything a little instead of decomposing the failing template first. Catch it: require the named dominant subpart (AN-226) before any fix is scheduled.
- **The quiet template.** Attention and fixes concentrate on the homepage because it is the demo surface, while a low-traffic template fails unnoticed. Catch it: read the field report's worst row first, not its first row (AN-222).
- **Premature celebration.** A fix announced as done the day it merges, weeks before field data can judge it. Catch it: every fix names its judging window up front (AN-230); until that window reads, the status is "awaiting field verdict."

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The 4 MB hero video that "looked fine on the office connection"](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-221.
- [Example 2 — "Average LCP 2.3 s" while mobile checkout failed](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-222.
- [Example 3 — The promo bar that pushed the page under the reader's finger](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-228.

## Recall anchors

- Field is the verdict; lab is the flashlight.
- Per template, per device class — never one blended number.
- All three good, or the template is failing.
- Unmeasured is not passing.
- A fix is done when field p75 moves, not when it merges.

## Checklist

- [ ] Field p75 for LCP, INP, and CLS is reported per key template, mobile and desktop separately, over the rolling 28-day window (G-AN-111).
- [ ] Every key template is instrumented, or explicitly reported unmeasured / insufficient data (G-AN-112).
- [ ] Every field-failing template has a throttled lab reproduction and a named dominant subpart (G-AN-113).
- [ ] No budget, report, or dashboard tracks FID; thresholds read LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 (G-AN-114).
- [ ] Each template's LCP element is named, prioritized, and sized to budget (AN-229).
- [ ] Images, embeds, and async slots reserve their space before load; nothing injects above rendered content (AN-228).
- [ ] Every closed vitals defect closed on post-fix field evidence, not a lab run (G-AN-115).
- [ ] Every template outside "good" has an open tracked defect naming the failing vital and its p75 (AN-232).

# dashboards

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Monitoring" ; Google, *Site Reliability Engineering*, "Monitoring Distributed Systems" — https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
- **Depends on:** monitoring (owns the signals), product-analytics (owns the product metrics rendered)
- **Feeds into:** alerting, incident-response (D6), performance-optimization

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building, changing, or reviewing any dashboard — product overview, per-service golden-signal view, or incident view — and when deciding whether a panel earns its place on one.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which signals exist or how they are collected (monitoring owns the signals; this skill owns their presentation), what a product metric means (product-metrics, D1, owns definitions; product-analytics owns measurement), or infrastructure saturation telemetry itself (D6 owns hosts and clusters; this skill consumes that telemetry, never redefines it).

## Rules

1. **AN-141 — Dashboards are code.** Every dashboard is defined in the repo (provisioning JSON or the platform equivalent), reviewed in the same change process as code, and deployed from the repo to every environment. A dashboard that exists only in a web console does not exist for this skill's purposes.
2. **AN-142 — Every panel answers a named question.** Each panel states the question it answers and the decision or action its reading triggers. A panel nobody can state the question for is removed in the same change that notices it.
3. **AN-143 — Query and definition are visible.** Every panel exposes the query or expression that produces it and names the metric definition it renders (from the metrics document or the service's SLI definitions). A number whose computation cannot be inspected from the dashboard is not trusted and not shipped.
4. **AN-144 — Computed from live records only.** Every figure is computed from the live event stream, metrics store, or underlying records at read time (or at the panel's stated aggregation cadence under AN-145). No panel renders a constant, a fixture, a typed-in value, or a value copied from an earlier reading.
5. **AN-145 — Refresh cadence is stated and honest.** Each panel or dashboard states how fresh its data is: the aggregation interval and the expected lag. The word "live" or "real-time" appears only on panels whose data is actually current within the stated lag; a periodically aggregated panel is labeled with its period.
6. **AN-146 — One golden-signal template, every service.** Per-service dashboards are generated from a single template covering latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. A new service gets its dashboard by instantiation, not by hand-drawing; a service with no generated instance is a coverage defect.
7. **AN-147 — Percentiles, never averages.** Latency panels show percentile bands (p50/p95/p99 at minimum) with successful and failed requests charted separately. Error panels show both rate and count. No panel presents a mean latency as its headline figure.
8. **AN-148 — Units, thresholds, and windows on every panel.** Each panel shows its units, an SLO or threshold line where one exists, and a default time window appropriate to its question (an incident panel defaults to hours, a capacity panel to weeks). A panel the reader must mentally rescale or re-window before it means anything is unfinished.
9. **AN-149 — Annotations are on by default.** Deploy markers and incident markers are overlaid on every service dashboard. A graph that forces the reader to reconstruct "what changed" from memory or another tool fails this rule.
10. **AN-150 — Three layers, kept separate.** Dashboards live in exactly one layer: the product overview (D1's metrics, from product-analytics), the per-service golden-signal view (AN-146), or the incident view (the service dashboard annotated per AN-149, arranged for diagnosis). Product figures are not mixed into service panels, and service internals do not crowd the overview.
11. **AN-151 — A stale or empty panel is a surfaced defect.** When a panel's query returns no data for its stated window, the dashboard shows that state explicitly and the gap is logged as a defect against the data source. A silently blank panel that a reader can mistake for "zero" or "healthy" is a failure of this skill, not of the reader.
12. **AN-152 — Pruning is part of maintenance.** On the dashboard review cadence recorded in progress.md, every panel is re-asked the AN-142 question. Panels with no named question, no reader, or no decision are deleted; the deletion is recorded with the reason.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-071 — Frozen figures.** Banned: a panel whose value comes from a constant, fixture, seeded sample data, or a hand-typed number instead of a query over live records. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Bad: the overview's "Revenue today" panel is a text card reading "$4,820", typed at launch; it reads $4,820 every day for a quarter. Instead: the panel runs the revenue query against live records, with its definition visible per AN-143. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-072 — Console-only dashboards.** Banned: a dashboard created or edited only in the web console, with no corresponding definition in the repo — or a production dashboard hand-edited until it drifts from the repo version. Defeats: DET-INF-024. Bad: during an incident someone fixes the error panel in the console; three months later a redeploy from the repo silently restores the broken panel. Instead: every change lands in the repo definition first and deploys from it (AN-141). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-073 — Fake "live" panels.** Banned: labeling a panel "live" or "real-time" when its data is a periodic aggregate, a cached snapshot, or a client-side timer animating values no query produced. Defeats: DET-FAKE-018. Bad: the "live visitors" widget increments on a random timer while the analytics pipeline batches hourly; support quotes its number to a customer as current. Instead: label the panel with its true aggregation period and lag per AN-145, or wire it to the actual stream before using the word "live". Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-074 — Averages as the latency story.** Banned: a latency panel or alert whose headline figure is a mean, with no percentile view, so the tail users actually feel is invisible. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the service dashboard shows "avg latency 120 ms" and stays green while p99 sits at 4 s and the slowest decile of checkouts times out. Instead: chart p50/p95/p99 bands with success and error latency separate (AN-147). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-075 — The tutorial dashboard.** Banned: shipping the platform's sample or tutorial dashboard — host CPU, memory, a homepage ping — as the service's monitoring view while the user-facing endpoints and their error rates are unmeasured. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: the "production dashboard" charts VM CPU for a service whose checkout endpoint returns unmeasured 500s for two days. Instead: instantiate the golden-signal template (AN-146) so the service's latency, traffic, errors, and saturation are the default view. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AN-071 — Data-change movement test.** Verifies: AN-144. Check: automated — in a test environment, create one record a chosen panel counts (one completed order, one signup), wait exactly one stated refresh cycle (AN-145), and re-read the panel; then delete the record and re-read after another cycle. Pass: the figure moves by exactly +1, then exactly −1. Fail: block the dashboard's release; the panel is treated as a frozen-figure defect under BAN-AN-071. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-072 — Provisioning and drift check.** Verifies: AN-141. Check: automated — deploy all dashboard definitions from the repo to a scratch instance and load each one; then export the production dashboards and diff them against the repo versions. Pass: every dashboard renders with zero datasource errors, and the production diff is empty. Fail: block shipment; reconcile the drift into the repo before release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-073 — Template coverage check.** Verifies: AN-146. Check: automated — list every service in the service registry and assert each has a dashboard instance generated from the golden-signal template with all four signal groups present. Pass: coverage is 100%. Fail: generate the missing instances before the service's next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-074 — Panel completeness lint.** Verifies: AN-142, AN-143, AN-145, AN-148. Check: automated — lint the dashboard definitions in the repo: every panel carries a question/decision note, a query, a named metric definition, units, a stated refresh cadence, and (where an SLO exists) a threshold line. Pass: zero panels missing any required field. Fail: block the dashboard change until the fields are present. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-075 — Freshness check.** Verifies: AN-151. Check: automated — query every panel on the product overview and each service dashboard for its stated window (last 24 hours for the overview) and assert each returns data or an explicit no-data state that is logged as a defect. Pass: no panel is silently blank. Fail: open a defect against the data source before the dashboard is cited in any report. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The wallboard museum.** Forty panels accumulate because adding is free and deleting feels risky; nobody reads past the first row and the three panels that matter drown. Catch it: at review, ask each panel when it last changed a decision — silence is a deletion vote (AN-152).
- **Screenshot status reports.** A static export of a dashboard is pasted into a report and quoted for weeks after the data moved on. Catch it: link the live dashboard and state the reading time; a figure with no "as of" is a screenshot, not a status.
- **Green-by-construction thresholds.** Threshold lines set so wide the panel can never turn red, because a red panel once caused an uncomfortable meeting. Catch it: compare each threshold against the SLO it claims to represent; a threshold looser than the SLO is decoration (AN-148).
- **One window for everything.** Every panel defaults to the same 30-day window, so today's outage is averaged into invisibility on the incident view. Catch it: check the default window against the panel's layer — incident panels default to hours (AN-148, AN-150).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The revenue panel that read the same number for a quarter](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-144.
- [Example 2 — The incident fix that lived only in the console](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-141.
- [Example 3 — "Average latency 120 ms" while the tail timed out](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-147.

## Recall anchors

- If it isn't in the repo, it isn't a dashboard.
- Every panel: a named question, a visible query, a stated cadence.
- A figure that cannot move when the data moves is not a metric.
- Percentiles or it didn't happen — averages hide the tail.
- A panel nobody can name the decision for gets deleted.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every dashboard is defined in the repo and deploys from it with zero drift (G-AN-072).
- [ ] The data-change test moved a panel figure by exactly the known amount (G-AN-071).
- [ ] Every service in the registry has a golden-signal instance from the one template (G-AN-073).
- [ ] Every panel names its question, decision, query, definition, units, and refresh cadence (G-AN-074).
- [ ] Latency panels show percentile bands; no mean is a headline figure (AN-147).
- [ ] Deploy and incident annotations are on for every service dashboard (AN-149).
- [ ] No panel is silently blank; every no-data state is logged as a defect (G-AN-075).
- [ ] Panels with no named question or decision were deleted at this review, with reasons recorded (AN-152).

<!-- generated from skills/analytics-observability/error-tracking/SKILL.md -->

# error-tracking

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenTelemetry, "Observability primer" — https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/ ; OWASP, *Logging Cheat Sheet* — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Error handling" and "Logging"
- **Depends on:** logging
- **Feeds into:** alerting, monitoring, dashboards

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** setting up or changing how unhandled errors are captured, grouped, scrubbed, triaged, and read at release time — for any client or server surface whose failures someone must learn about from the system, not from user complaints.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is application log format, levels, or shipping (logging owns those; this skill consumes the correlation ID logging guarantees), alert routing and burn-rate policy (alerting owns the page; this skill owns the issues alerts point at), or fixing the defect itself (the owning department's skill fixes it; this skill makes sure it is seen, owned, and verified gone).

## Rules

1. **AN-161 — Every unhandled error is captured in the tracker.** Client and server unhandled errors are captured by the dedicated error tracker (Sentry is the reference implementation) at the boundary where they surface. An error users can hit that exists only in a log file — or nowhere — is a defect in the error handling itself, not a gap to note.
2. **AN-162 — Every event carries its context.** Each captured event carries a readable stack trace, the release version, the environment, and the request's trace/correlation ID, so an issue pivots straight into the logs and traces for the same request (per the OpenTelemetry correlation model). An event missing release or correlation ID is incomplete and fails G-AN-081.
3. **AN-163 — Context is scrubbed before it leaves.** A before-send scrubber with a denylist in the repo strips passwords, tokens, authorization headers, session IDs, card numbers, and direct personal identifiers from event payloads, breadcrumbs, and attached request data before transmission — enforcement lives in the scrubber, never in developer memory (OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet). Obvious placeholders only in examples and tests.
4. **AN-164 — Source maps ship with the release.** Source maps (and server symbolication inputs) are uploaded to the tracker as a step of the release pipeline. A release that ships without its maps uploaded is an incomplete release, because every stack from it is undebuggable minified offsets.
5. **AN-165 — Release and environment tags are mandatory.** Every event is tagged with the exact release and environment that produced it; untagged events cannot be attributed to a deploy, counted in release health, or recognized as regressions, and are treated as a capture defect.
6. **AN-166 — Grouping is curated.** Fingerprint rules merge one root cause into one issue and split distinct causes that share a generic message. A tracker where one bug appears as hundreds of issues gets ignored, which is the same as having no tracker; grouping rules are reviewed whenever issue volume jumps.
7. **AN-167 — Expected errors are not issues.** Handled, user-facing errors by design — validation failures, 404s for genuinely missing resources, denied permissions — are logged or counted as metrics, never captured as tracker issues. The tracker is reserved for defects; noise in it is how real defects get missed.
8. **AN-168 — Every issue has a named owner and a triage cadence.** New issues are assigned to a named owner within the project's stated triage window, and the tracker is triaged on that cadence whether or not anyone feels like it. An error nobody owns is a bug that ships twice; a tracker installed but never triaged is decoration.
9. **AN-169 — Priority follows user impact.** Issues are ranked by affected users and by whether the flow is revenue- or trust-critical, not by raw event count alone: a rare failure on the payment path outranks a frequent failure on a settings page.
10. **AN-170 — Regressions reopen, they do not restart.** A resolved issue whose error recurs in a newer release is flagged by the tracker as a regression of the original issue — with its history and owner — and pages or tickets by user impact. A regression silently opened as a brand-new issue loses the record that it was already "fixed" once.
11. **AN-171 — Release health is read at every deploy.** Crash-free sessions and crash-free users per release are checked after each deploy against the project's stated threshold; a release below threshold triggers a rollback or hotfix decision, recorded — not a hope that the numbers recover.
12. **AN-172 — Tracker configuration lives in the repo.** The SDK configuration, scrubbing denylist, fingerprint rules, and alert rules are versioned configuration in the repo, changed by reviewed commits. Setup that exists only in the tracker vendor's console does not exist for the next agent.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-081 — Swallowed errors.** Banned: empty catch blocks, caught-and-discarded exceptions, or a failure path that reports success — any pattern where an error happens and no system records it. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: a failed payment throws, the catch block is empty, the user sees "Success," and the team learns about the lost orders from complaints a week later. Instead: let unhandled errors reach the tracker with stack and correlation ID, and show the user an honest failure state (AN-161, AN-162). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-082 — "The logs probably have it."** Banned: relying on log text as the error record — no dedicated tracker, no grouping, no release tags — so finding one bug means grepping raw output and counting occurrences by hand. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: after a bad deploy, the only way to know what broke is to SSH in and read container output that the next redeploy will erase. Instead: capture errors in the tracker, grouped into issues with readable stacks and release tags (AN-161, AN-164, AN-165). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-083 — Stack traces served to users.** Banned: rendering raw exceptions, stack traces, SQL, or file paths in the user-facing error response while the same failure is captured nowhere server-side. Defeats: DET-INF-021. Bad: a 500 page shows the full framework stack trace with internal paths, and the tracker has no record of the error at all. Instead: return a generic error response with a correlation ID the user can quote, and capture the full detail in the tracker under that same ID (AN-161, AN-162). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-084 — The ownerless tracker.** Banned: a tracker that is installed and capturing, but whose new-issue alerts route to an unmonitored inbox or channel and whose issues have no named owner or triage cadence. Defeats: DET-INF-012. Bad: the tracker holds 300 unassigned issues, the alert email goes to a mailbox nobody opens, and a checkout defect runs for a month. Instead: route new-issue and regression alerts to the monitored on-call channel and assign every issue an owner within the triage window (AN-168, AN-170). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AN-081 — Synthetic-error capture test.** Verifies: AN-161, AN-162, AN-165. Check: automated — in staging, trigger one known client error and one known server error through the test hooks; within 60 seconds query the tracker. Pass: each error appears exactly once, grouped as a single issue, with a de-minified stack naming real source lines, the correct release and environment tags, and a correlation ID that resolves to entries in the central log store. Fail: block the release; fix capture, maps, or tagging and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-082 — Source-map upload check.** Verifies: AN-164. Check: automated — CI asserts the release pipeline's source-map upload step ran for the release being deployed and the uploaded artifact set matches the build output. Pass: upload step succeeded for this exact release. Fail: block the deploy; the release is incomplete. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-083 — Scrub canary test.** Verifies: AN-163. Check: automated — in staging, trigger an error from a request carrying the canary values `CANARY-PASSWORD-EXAMPLE` and `CANARY-TOKEN-EXAMPLE`, then search the resulting tracker event (payload, breadcrumbs, request data) for both strings. Pass: zero occurrences anywhere in the event. Fail: block shipment; fix the denylist or scrubber and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-084 — Regression drill.** Verifies: AN-170. Check: in staging, mark a known synthetic issue resolved, reintroduce its error, and inspect the tracker. Pass: the original issue is flagged as a regression with its history intact, not opened as a new issue, and the regression alert reaches the monitored channel. Fail: fix fingerprinting and regression settings before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-085 — Triage and ownership audit.** Verifies: AN-168, AN-169. Check: automated-assisted — list every unresolved issue older than the project's triage window and every issue with no named owner. Pass: zero unowned issues and zero issues past the triage window without a recorded priority decision (impact-ranked per AN-169). Fail: triage before the next deploy; an audit that keeps failing is a BAN-AN-084 defect. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The 400-issue bug.** One root cause fragments into hundreds of issues because grouping was never curated, so the board reads as chaos and gets abandoned. Catch it: sort by event count — if the top events share a stack shape, the fingerprint rules are the defect (AN-166).
- **Resolve-and-forget.** Issues are marked resolved with no linked fix or release, so "resolved" means "we stopped looking" and the regression, when it comes, surprises everyone. Catch it: sample resolved issues — each should name the release that fixed it (AN-170, AN-171).
- **Count-chasing.** The board is worked top-down by raw event count, so the loudest cosmetic error gets fixed while a rare payment failure waits. Catch it: if the priority order cannot be explained in affected users and flow criticality, it is count order, not impact order (AN-169).
- **The muted tracker.** Ignore and snooze rules grow until the tracker goes quiet — not because the product improved, but because the team tuned the alarm off. Catch it: a sudden drop in new issues after a rule change is a signal about the rules, not about the code.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The payment failure that displayed "Success"](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-161.
- [Example 2 — The release nobody could debug](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-164, AN-165.
- [Example 3 — The error event that carried a password](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-163.

## Recall anchors

- If users can hit it, it is a tracked issue with a readable stack.
- Release tag and correlation ID on every event, or it cannot be used.
- The scrubber strips secrets; developers never have to remember to.
- An unowned error is a bug that ships twice.
- Release health is read at the deploy, not after the complaints.

## Checklist

- [ ] Unhandled client and server errors reach the tracker; no empty catch blocks or success-on-failure paths remain (BAN-AN-081).
- [ ] The synthetic-error test passes: grouped once, de-minified stack, release tag, correlation ID resolving in the log store (G-AN-081).
- [ ] The source-map upload step ran for this release and is asserted in CI (G-AN-082).
- [ ] The scrub canary test returns zero hits in the tracker event (G-AN-083).
- [ ] Expected errors (validation, by-design 404s) are metrics or logs, not tracker issues (AN-167).
- [ ] Every issue has a named owner within the triage window, prioritized by user impact (G-AN-085).
- [ ] The regression drill flags a reintroduced error as a regression, not a new issue (G-AN-084).
- [ ] Release health (crash-free sessions/users) is checked against threshold at this deploy (AN-171).

# event-tracking

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Twilio Segment, "Naming conventions: why you need them for clean data" — https://www.twilio.com/en-us/resource-center/naming-conventions-for-clean-data ; Segment documentation, "Data Collection Best Practices" (tracking plan guidance) — https://segment-docs.netlify.app/docs/protocols/tracking-plan/best-practices/
- **Depends on:** product-analytics
- **Feeds into:** product-analytics, experimentation-platform, revenue-analytics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** adding, renaming, or removing an analytics event; writing or changing instrumentation code; reviewing a funnel or report that looks wrong; setting up validation for a new analytics platform.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which metrics the product should report (product-metrics, D1; measurement setup is product-analytics), what an experiment's result means (experimentation-platform), or whether revenue figures reconcile (revenue-analytics). This skill owns the event taxonomy as a contract, not the conclusions drawn from it.

## Rules

1. **AN-021 — The plan precedes the code.** The tracking plan is a versioned file in the repo recording, per event: name, properties with types, required/optional status, owner, and the question the event answers. No event is emitted that is not in the plan; adding an event means editing the plan first, in the same change.
2. **AN-022 — One naming convention, enforced mechanically.** Events are Object-Action in past tense under one casing standard, and properties under one casing standard, chosen once and never varied (Segment's reference: Title Case events such as "Order Completed", snake_case properties). A name that deviates from the convention is a defect even if it is spelled correctly.
3. **AN-023 — No dynamic values in event names.** An event name contains no product names, IDs, prices, search terms, or user data. The varying value goes in a property; one event per value turns one report row into hundreds and fragments every funnel built on it.
4. **AN-024 — Property keys are fixed by the plan.** The property set of an event is exactly the set the plan declares, with the declared types. Keys are never generated from data (no key per product, per error message, or per user), and a property that arrives with the wrong type is a violation, not a variant.
5. **AN-025 — Name the outcome, not the widget.** Events record what the user accomplished ("Order Completed", "Subscription Started"), not which control they touched ("Checkout Button Clicked"). Outcome names survive redesigns and count successes; widget names count clicks that may have failed.
6. **AN-026 — No personal data in events.** Event names and property values carry no emails, personal names, phone numbers, or free text that can contain personal data. People are referenced by opaque IDs only. Consent and retention rules themselves are D14's; this rule is their enforcement point in the event stream.
7. **AN-027 — Every event has an owner and a question.** An event with no named owner, or whose plan entry cannot state the decision it informs, is not added. Prefer fewer, well-shaped events with rich properties over an event per button.
8. **AN-028 — Emit only through the wrapper.** Application code emits events through one typed wrapper (generated from the plan or checked against it), never through raw platform calls scattered across the codebase. The wrapper is the single point where names and property shapes can be enforced.
9. **AN-029 — Validate in the debug view before release.** Before a release ships, the primary flows are run in a test session and every expected event is confirmed in the platform's debug or realtime view: correct name, correct properties, correct types, fired once. An event first seen in production data was never validated.
10. **AN-030 — No firing before consent state.** Non-essential events do not fire until the visitor's consent state is known, and never fire when consent is denied. Consent state is recorded with the session so reports can state their coverage honestly (rules: D14 cookie-consent, privacy-laws).
11. **AN-031 — Renaming is a breaking change.** Renaming or removing an event ships with a plan version bump, a migration note naming the reports and funnels it affects, and a deprecation window in which the change is announced. A silent rename splits history into two incomparable series.
12. **AN-032 — Sweep production for violations.** On a fixed cadence, recent production events are checked against the plan: any emitted name absent from the plan, and any property shape violating it, is filed as a defect with an owner. A non-empty violation list is a bug in the pipeline, not a curiosity.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-011 — Event-name variants.** Banned: two or more live spellings or casings of one event ("Signup Completed", "SignUp Completed", "signed_up"). Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: a redesign ships `signed_up` alongside the existing "Signup Completed", and the activation funnel silently halves. Instead: one canonical name per event, emitted only through the AN-028 wrapper and checked by the AN-022 lint. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-012 — Personal data in event properties.** Banned: property values carrying emails, names, or free-text user input (e.g. `user_email: "a@b.com"`, `search_query` holding typed personal text). Defeats: DET-CON-003. Bad: a "Support Requested" event ships the user's typed message, email included, into the analytics store. Instead: reference the person by opaque ID and keep content in the system of record; properties carry IDs, categories, and counts only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-013 — Validation that never gates.** Banned: a tracking-plan lint or schema check that runs as an advisory warning while merges and releases proceed on failure. Defeats: DET-INF-002. Bad: CI prints "3 unplanned events" on every build for a quarter; nobody reads it, and the taxonomy rots anyway. Instead: the lint is a required check — an unplanned event or wrong-typed property fails the build (G-AN-011). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-014 — Silent renames and removals.** Banned: renaming, repurposing, or deleting an event in code without a plan version bump and migration note. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: "Trial Started" is repurposed to fire at payment instead of signup; the dashboard contradicts last quarter's report and nobody can say when it changed. Instead: follow AN-031 — bump the plan version, write the migration note, announce the deprecation window. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AN-011 — Tracking-plan lint.** Verifies: AN-021, AN-022, AN-024. Check: automated — CI runs the plan validator over the build's emitted-event manifest (or the wrapper's schema) against `tracking-plan` in the repo, e.g. `node scripts/validate-tracking-plan.js --plan analytics/tracking-plan.json --src src/`; any event absent from the plan, any name breaking the casing convention, and any property with a wrong type exits non-zero. Pass: validator exits 0 as a required status check. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-012 — Debug-view validation.** Verifies: AN-025, AN-029. Check: manual with tooling — before release, run the primary conversion and retention flows in a test session with the platform's debug/realtime view open; confirm each planned event appears once, with the planned name, properties, and types. Pass: every expected event observed exactly as planned. Fail: block the release; fix instrumentation and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-013 — Plan-diff review.** Verifies: AN-031. Check: automated plus review — a CI script diffs `tracking-plan` on the change; any removed or renamed event without a plan version bump and a migration-note file in the same change exits non-zero. Pass: no unplanned removals; every breaking change carries its bump and note. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-014 — Production violation sweep.** Verifies: AN-023, AN-026, AN-032. Check: automated — a scheduled job lists distinct event names and property keys received in the last 7 days and diffs them against the plan, e.g. `node scripts/audit-live-events.js --plan analytics/tracking-plan.json --days 7`; output is the violation list. Pass: the list is empty. Fail: file each violation as a defect with an owner before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The pageview-only strategy.** The snippet is installed, automatic pageviews are counted, and the team calls it tracking. Catch it: ask which business question the instrumentation answers; if the answer is a pageview chart, no planned event exists yet (AN-021).
- **Event-per-button sprawl.** Every control gets its own event, so the taxonomy has hundreds of names and no outcomes. Catch it: count events that name a widget instead of an accomplishment (AN-025) and fold them into one outcome event with a property.
- **Instrumenting to the dashboard.** Events are added because a chart someone wants needs a field, with no plan entry, owner, or question. Catch it: any event whose plan entry cannot state its decision is removed or justified (AN-027).
- **Fixing it in the report.** Analysts merge variants with report-side aliases and filters instead of fixing emission. Catch it: an alias table in a reporting tool is a symptom; the fix belongs in the wrapper and the plan, and the sweep (G-AN-014) will keep finding the variants until it lands.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — One signup, three event names](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-022.
- [Example 2 — The product name inside the event name](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-023.
- [Example 3 — The email address riding in a property](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-026.

## Recall anchors

- Plan first, code second — no event exists outside the plan.
- One event, one spelling, forever; a rename is a breaking change.
- Values go in properties; names stay fixed.
- Name the outcome, not the widget.
- If the lint cannot fail the build, it is decoration.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every emitted event is in the tracking plan with properties, types, owner, and question (AN-021, AN-027).
- [ ] All names follow the single casing convention; no variants exist (AN-022).
- [ ] No event name contains a dynamic value; no property key is generated from data (AN-023, AN-024).
- [ ] No personal data appears in any event name or property value (AN-026).
- [ ] All emission goes through the typed wrapper (AN-028).
- [ ] Primary flows were run and every event confirmed in the debug view (G-AN-012).
- [ ] The plan lint is a required, passing CI check (G-AN-011).
- [ ] Any rename or removal carries a version bump and migration note (AN-031, G-AN-013).

<!-- generated from skills/analytics-observability/experimentation-platform/SKILL.md -->

# experimentation-platform

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Growth experimentation" ; Optimizely, experimentation strategy documentation — https://docs.optimizely.com/experimentation-strategy/docs/take-action-based-on-the-results-of-an-experiment
- **Depends on:** event-tracking (exposure and outcome events ride the shared tracking plan), product-analytics
- **Feeds into:** growth-experiments (D9 — consumes the result payloads this platform emits), dashboards

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or changing the experimentation infrastructure itself: the assignment function, exposure logging, experiment configuration, sample-ratio-mismatch (SRM) health checks, and the analysis job that produces a result.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is program discipline — which experiments to run, hypothesis quality, cadence, or the experiment register. Those belong to growth-experiments (D9). This skill owns the machinery (assignment, exposure, health checks); D9 owns the program and keeps the register. A result this platform emits is an input to D9's record, never a substitute for it.

## Rules

1. **AN-041 — Assignment is a deterministic hash.** A unit's variant is computed as a hash of experiment ID + unit ID (usually user ID), bucketed against the configured split. The same inputs always yield the same variant — across sessions, devices, and deploys — and the computation is reproducible in a test.
2. **AN-042 — Assignment is server-verifiable and identical everywhere.** One assignment implementation serves every surface; there is no second client-side bucketing that can disagree with it. Any surface that cannot call the shared function does not run the experiment.
3. **AN-043 — Exposure is logged at assignment time.** The moment a unit is assigned and the variant is actually served, an exposure event (experiment ID, variant, unit ID, timestamp) is written as a durable event into the same analytics stream as the outcome events — not into request logs, not into a side table nobody reconciles.
4. **AN-044 — Exposure is never reconstructed.** Exposure counts come only from AN-043 events. Rebuilding exposure after the fact from pageviews, sessions, or variant-render logs is forbidden: a pageview proves a page rendered, not that a unit was assigned and served a variant.
5. **AN-045 — Pre-registration lives in the experiment config.** Before launch, the versioned experiment config records: hypothesis, exactly one primary metric, guardrail metrics, minimum runtime and sample size, the traffic split, the bot/internal-traffic filtering rules, and the decision rule. The platform refuses to activate an experiment whose config lacks any field.
6. **AN-046 — SRM is a stop condition, enforced by the analysis job.** The analysis job computes a chi-squared check of observed exposure counts against the configured split before producing any result. While the check fails at the significance threshold recorded in the config, the job renders no verdict — it reports the mismatch and the experiment is treated as broken (bucketing, logging, or filtering) until the cause is found.
7. **AN-047 — No peeking-based decisions.** Results unlock at the pre-registered horizon, or the config names a sequential / always-valid method in advance. The platform exposes no "current winner" readout that invites an early stop; a run stopped early for a peeked lead is emitted as invalid, not as a result.
8. **AN-048 — Minimum runtime is one full business cycle.** The pre-registered minimum runtime is at least one complete business cycle for the surface under test (weekday/weekend pattern included), regardless of how quickly the sample size is reached.
9. **AN-049 — One surface, one active experiment — or explicit layers.** Experiments touching the same surface are mutually exclusive by assignment layer: a unit enters at most one of them, enforced by the assignment function, never by hoping the audiences do not overlap.
10. **AN-050 — A leaked or flipped assignment invalidates the run.** If any unit's variant can change mid-run — a salt change, a split edit, a second bucketing path, a config push that rehashes — the affected data is discarded and the run is emitted as invalid with the cause recorded. Contaminated data is never "interpreted with caution."
11. **AN-051 — Filtering rules are pre-registered and symmetric.** Bot, internal-user, and QA exclusions are declared in the config before launch (AN-045) and applied by the pipeline identically to every variant. Post-hoc exclusions invented after seeing results are forbidden; a needed new filter ends the run and starts a new experiment.
12. **AN-052 — Conclusion emits a complete result payload.** When a run ends — horizon reached, stopped, or invalidated — the platform emits one payload: experiment ID, pre-registration reference, primary-metric result with confidence interval, guardrail outcomes, final SRM status, runtime, and the ship/kill/invalid outcome. D9's growth-experiments files this payload in the register, including for losers and inconclusive runs; an experiment that ends without a payload is a platform defect.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-021 — Random or per-request assignment.** Banned: bucketing with a random draw, a timestamp, or any input that can give the same unit different variants on different requests. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the client calls `Math.random() < 0.5 ? 'A' : 'B'` on each page load; a user sees the new checkout on Monday and the old one on Tuesday, and support screenshots contradict each other. Instead: assign by deterministic hash of experiment ID + unit ID per AN-041. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-022 — A verdict rendered while SRM fails.** Banned: an analysis job or dashboard that displays a winner, an effect size, or a ship recommendation for an experiment whose SRM check is failing — the health check exists on paper but never actually gates the output. Defeats: DET-INF-002. Bad: the results page shows "B +4.2%, significant" above a red SRM warning the team has learned to ignore. Instead: the job refuses to render a verdict while SRM fails, per AN-046; only the mismatch and its investigation are reported. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-023 — The peeked "winner."** Banned: stopping an experiment before its pre-registered horizon because a variant is "winning," then reporting the lead as the experiment's result. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: at day two, variant B leads on a secondary metric; the test is stopped, and the launch note claims a measured conversion lift that no valid analysis produced. Instead: run to the horizon or the pre-declared sequential method (AN-047); an early stop is emitted as invalid under AN-050/AN-052, never as a lift. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-024 — Exposure kept only in ephemeral logs.** Banned: recording assignment or exposure only in server console output, request logs, or any store that rotates, restarts away, or is never reconciled against assignment counts. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: the variant each user saw is knowable only from application stdout, which the platform rotated after 24 hours; by analysis day, exposure is unrecoverable and is quietly estimated. Instead: emit a durable exposure event at assignment time per AN-043, reconciled by G-AN-023. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-025 — Mid-run split or salt edits.** Banned: changing the traffic split, the variant set, the targeting, or the hash salt of a running experiment while continuing to pool its data. Defeats: DET-CON-011. Bad: traffic is raised from 10% to 50% and the salt rotated in week two to "balance the arms"; the pooled report presents one experiment where two different assignments ran. Instead: stop the run, emit its payload (AN-052), and start a new experiment ID with the new configuration. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AN-021 — Assignment determinism test.** Verifies: AN-041, AN-042. Check: automated — hash a fixed set of 10,000 recorded unit IDs twice, in two separate processes simulating different sessions, and diff the variant maps; also assert the observed split matches the configured split within the tolerance stated in the test. Pass: the two maps are identical for 100% of units. Fail: block the experiment launch; the assignment function is fixed and the test re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-022 — SRM gate in the analysis job.** Verifies: AN-046. Check: automated — run the analysis job against the live exposure counts; it computes the chi-squared statistic of observed vs. expected counts per variant and compares it with the config's threshold. Pass: the job renders a verdict only when the check passes, and a forced test with skewed fixture counts renders no verdict. Fail: block any result publication; investigate bucketing, logging, or filtering before reading anything. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-023 — Exposure-completeness reconciliation.** Verifies: AN-043, AN-044. Check: automated — reconcile exposure-event counts against assignment counts per variant over the run window. Pass: the gap is within the tolerance recorded in the experiment config, and every counted exposure traces to an AN-043 event (zero reconstructed exposures). Fail: results are computed on partial data — publication is blocked until the gap is explained or the run is emitted as invalid. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-024 — Pre-registration completeness check.** Verifies: AN-045, AN-048, AN-051. Check: automated — schema-validate the experiment config at activation: hypothesis, one primary metric, guardrails, minimum runtime ≥ one business cycle, minimum sample, split, filtering rules, and decision rule all present. Pass: activation succeeds only with every field present. Fail: activation is refused; the missing field is added to the config, never supplied verbally. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-025 — Conclusion payload audit.** Verifies: AN-050, AN-052. Check: list every experiment whose run ended in the period; for each, confirm exactly one result payload exists containing the primary-metric result with confidence interval, final SRM status, and a ship/kill/invalid outcome. Pass: 100% of ended experiments have a complete payload, losers and invalid runs included. Fail: the missing payload is emitted before the next experiment launches on that surface. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Render-then-assign flicker.** Assignment is deterministic but evaluated in the browser after first paint, so users watch the control render, then swap to the variant. Catch it: if a variant change is visible as a flash, assignment is happening too late — it belongs in the server response or the first evaluation, and the exposure event must mark what was actually served (AN-043).
- **The significance thermometer.** A dashboard shows a live p-value or "percent to significance" that the team watches daily, so the fixed-horizon rule exists in the config and nowhere else. Catch it: if anyone can quote today's leader, AN-047 is already being violated in spirit — hide interim effect readouts; health (SRM, exposure counts) is the only live view.
- **Salt-shuffling to "fix" imbalance.** When arms look uneven, someone rotates the hash salt or nudges the split to even them out, quietly restarting assignment for everyone. Catch it: any mid-run config touch is BAN-AN-025; imbalance is an SRM investigation (AN-046), not a tuning knob.
- **Guardrail theater.** Guardrail metrics are named in the config but the results view shows only the primary metric, so a conversion win that doubled error rates ships unread. Catch it: if the payload (AN-052) can be read without its guardrail section, the view is wrong, not the data.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Coin-flip bucketing becomes a deterministic hash](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-041.
- [Example 2 — The verdict that shipped over a failing SRM check](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-046.
- [Example 3 — Exposure rebuilt from pageviews becomes exposure at assignment](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-043.

## Recall anchors

- Hash of experiment + unit decides the variant — never chance, never the clock.
- Exposure is an event written when the variant is served, or it did not happen.
- SRM failing means the experiment is broken; no verdict renders until it passes.
- Peeked, flipped, or re-salted data is discarded, not interpreted.
- D12 builds the machinery; D9 runs the program and keeps the register.

## Checklist

- [ ] Assignment is a deterministic hash of experiment ID + unit ID, one implementation for all surfaces (AN-041, AN-042).
- [ ] Determinism test passes: 10,000 unit IDs, two runs, identical variant maps (G-AN-021).
- [ ] Exposure events fire at assignment time into the shared analytics stream (AN-043).
- [ ] Experiment config is pre-registered and complete; activation refuses missing fields (AN-045, G-AN-024).
- [ ] Minimum runtime covers at least one full business cycle (AN-048).
- [ ] Analysis job renders no verdict while the SRM check fails (AN-046, G-AN-022).
- [ ] Exposure counts reconcile with assignment counts within the config's tolerance (G-AN-023).
- [ ] Every ended experiment — win, loss, inconclusive, invalid — has exactly one complete result payload for D9's register (AN-052, G-AN-025).

<!-- generated from skills/analytics-observability/logging/SKILL.md -->

# logging

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D12 Analytics & Observability (AN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP, *Logging Cheat Sheet* — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html ; OpenTelemetry, "Observability primer" — https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/ ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Logging"
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: log format, field set, and redaction rules are defined against the application's own code and the events it emits, inspected directly; this is the base layer the rest of D12 reads from. It feeds monitoring, alerting, error-tracking, and apm.
- **Feeds into:** monitoring, alerting, error-tracking, apm

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** setting up or changing how an application logs: the log format and field set, correlation IDs, levels, redaction, shipping to a central store, or retention — for any service whose behavior someone will need to reconstruct later.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is infrastructure or platform telemetry — hosts, clusters, networks, the deploy pipeline, infra saturation, or the mechanics of being on call (D6 owns those; this skill consumes D6's telemetry, never redefines it). This skill owns the application-signal discipline: what the application itself records, in what shape, and how long it is kept. Alert policy on top of logs is alerting's; the SLOs logs serve are D12 policy, the paging plumbing is D6's.

## Rules

1. **AN-081 — One logger, one format.** Every service logs through the shared logger, which emits single-line JSON with the fixed field set: timestamp (UTC, ISO 8601), level, service, environment, trace ID, request ID, message, plus structured context fields. A line missing a standard field is a defect, not a style choice.
2. **AN-082 — Boundary: application signals here, infrastructure with D6.** This skill defines what the application logs and how those logs are shaped, shipped, and retained. Host, cluster, and platform logs, the collector's infrastructure, and on-call mechanics belong to D6; where an incident needs both, the trace ID (AN-083) is the join, and neither side redefines the other's signals.
3. **AN-083 — Correlation ID on every request-scoped line.** A trace/request ID is generated or accepted at ingress and propagated across every service, queue, and background-job boundary the request crosses. A log line that cannot be tied to its request is of forensic value only by luck.
4. **AN-084 — Levels are a contract.** `error` means a human may need to act; `warn` means degraded but handled; `info` means a business-significant event; `debug` is detail for active diagnosis. Debug logging is off by default in production and is raised per service, temporarily, with the raise recorded.
5. **AN-085 — Secrets and personal data are never logged.** Passwords, tokens, authorization headers, session IDs, card numbers, and direct personal identifiers are redacted by the logger's field denylist before a line is written — enforcement lives in the logger, never in developer memory (OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet). The denylist is configuration in the repo, reviewed like code.
6. **AN-086 — Log the event, not the data dump.** Log lines carry named context fields (order ID, status, duration, outcome), never serialized request bodies, whole objects, or full payloads: a dump leaks whatever the object happens to contain and buries the fact that matters.
7. **AN-087 — Logs ship off the host.** Logs are shipped by a collector or shipper to a central, searchable store; a file on the host or container stdout is transport, never the record — containers are ephemeral, so local logs are lost logs. Retention is tiered (hot search window, then archive, then deletion) on the schedule D14's rules set.
8. **AN-088 — No raw console logging in production paths.** Free-text `console.log`-style calls in server production paths are a lint failure with a count of zero; all production logging goes through the shared logger so the field set, redaction, and shipping of AN-081/085/087 always apply.
9. **AN-089 — An error is logged once, as an error.** A failure is logged at the boundary that handles it, at `error` level, with its stack and correlation ID, and captured by error-tracking. Empty catch blocks and failures logged at `info` or `warn` so dashboards stay green are defects: the error signal must be able to tell the truth.
10. **AN-090 — Log volume is a budget.** Noisy success-path logging at scale is a defect: it buries errors and bills like them. High-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, request IDs) belong in log fields, where they are searchable — never in metric labels, which is monitoring's rule and this skill's hand-off.
11. **AN-091 — Retention and deletion reach the log store.** The retention schedule is written down per environment, and a deletion request that covers logs is executed against the central store and its archives, with the execution recorded; "the vendor probably handles it" is not a retention policy (the rules are D14's; this skill implements them for logs).
12. **AN-092 — Logging configuration lives in the repo.** The field set, level defaults, denylist, and retention tiers are versioned configuration, changed by reviewed commits. A logging change that exists only in a vendor console does not exist for the next agent.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AN-041 — Logs that die with the container.** Banned: application logs written only to a local file or host stdout, never shipped, so a restart or redeploy erases the only record of what the service did. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: after a redeploy, the team debugs a payment failure from memory because the previous container's logs vanished with it. Instead: ship every line through the collector to the central store before the work is called done (AN-087). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-042 — Secrets or personal data in log lines.** Banned: logging credentials, tokens, authorization headers, card data, or personal identifiers — in a field, in a dumped object, or in an error message — whether the store is local or central. Defeats: DET-INF-021. Bad: a login handler logs the submitted form, and the central store accumulates every user's password in searchable plain text. Instead: redact by the logger's denylist (AN-085) and log identifiers and outcomes, never values (AN-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-043 — Swallowed or downgraded errors.** Banned: empty catch blocks, or logging a real failure at `info`/`warn` (or as "handled") so error rates and dashboards read healthy while users hit failures. Defeats: DET-INF-011. Bad: a checkout exception is caught, logged as `info: "checkout note"`, and discarded; the errors golden signal reads zero during an outage users are reporting. Instead: log the failure once at `error` with stack and correlation ID and let error-tracking capture it (AN-089). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AN-044 — The debug firehose left on.** Banned: shipping or leaving a service at debug/trace verbosity in production, so log volume saturates disk or the central store and drowns the error signal. Defeats: DET-INF-027. Bad: a debug flag set during an incident is never reverted; three weeks later the log volume has tripled, retention silently shrank, and the disk-full alert is the first symptom. Instead: debug is off by default, raised per service for a bounded time, and reverted with the incident (AN-084, AN-090). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-AN-041 — Production-path logging lint.** Verifies: AN-081, AN-088. Check: automated — run the repo lint/grep suite over server production paths (e.g. `grep -rnE "console\.(log|debug)|print\(" src/ --include="*.ts" --include="*.js"` outside test and logging-module files, plus a schema spot-check that logger call sites pass the standard field set). Pass: zero raw console calls and zero missing-field call sites. Fail: block the release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-042 — Redaction canary test.** Verifies: AN-085, AN-086. Check: automated — in staging, submit a request carrying the canary values `CANARY-PASSWORD-EXAMPLE` and `CANARY-TOKEN-EXAMPLE` through the login and one authenticated flow, then search the central log store for both strings. Pass: zero occurrences in any field, message, or stack. Fail: block shipment; fix the denylist or the call site and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-043 — Schema validation of shipped lines.** Verifies: AN-081. Check: automated — sample the most recent 1,000 lines per service from the central store and validate each against the field-set schema (required keys present, timestamp parses as ISO 8601 UTC, level in the allowed set). Pass: 100% of sampled lines validate. Fail: block the release for the failing service. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-044 — Trace-join test.** Verifies: AN-083, AN-089. Check: pick one failed request from the error tracker, take its trace ID, and query the central store for that ID in every service the request touched. Pass: each service returns entries under the same trace ID, including the `error` line with its stack. Fail: fix propagation at the silent boundary before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AN-045 — Restart persistence test.** Verifies: AN-087, AN-091. Check: automated-assisted — note a marker log line in a non-production instance, restart or redeploy the instance, then query the central store for the marker and confirm the configured retention settings on the store match the written schedule. Pass: the pre-restart line is still queryable and retention matches the schedule. Fail: treat as a BAN-AN-041 defect and block promotion. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The data-dump line.** Logging the whole request or object "just in case," so the one field that matters hides inside two kilobytes of noise — and whatever sensitive value the object carried ships with it. Catch it: if a line cannot be read at a glance, it is a dump, not an event (AN-086).
- **Log-and-throw at every layer.** Each layer logs the same exception and rethrows, so one failure becomes five `error` lines and every count of errors is inflated. Catch it: search one trace ID — the failure should appear exactly once, at the handling boundary (AN-089).
- **Prose messages.** Log text written as full sentences with values interpolated ("User 42 failed to check out because…") instead of a stable message plus fields, so nothing can be grouped, counted, or alerted on. Catch it: if the same event cannot be found with one exact-match search, it was written as prose.
- **Localhost observability.** Logging verified only against a developer machine's console, where every line looks fine, while the deployed service's format, shipping, and retention were never exercised. Catch it: any logging claim not backed by a query against the central store is unverified (G-AN-043, G-AN-045).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Console breadcrumbs become structured logs](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AN-081, AN-088.
- [Example 2 — The login handler that logged passwords](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AN-085.
- [Example 3 — The failure no one could reconstruct](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AN-083, AN-087.

## Recall anchors

- One logger, one JSON field set — no exceptions in production paths.
- Every line carries its trace ID, or it cannot be used.
- The logger redacts; developers never have to remember to.
- Error means a human may need to act — never log a failure as less.
- If it is not in the central store, it did not happen.

## Checklist

- [ ] All production logging goes through the shared logger; the raw-console lint count is zero (G-AN-041).
- [ ] Every request-scoped line carries trace and request IDs across services and jobs (AN-083).
- [ ] The denylist covers passwords, tokens, authorization headers, session IDs, and card numbers, and lives in the repo (AN-085).
- [ ] The redaction canary test returns zero hits in the central store (G-AN-042).
- [ ] Sampled shipped lines validate 100% against the field-set schema (G-AN-043).
- [ ] A failed request's trace ID returns entries from every service it touched (G-AN-044).
- [ ] Logs survive a restart in the central store, and retention matches the written schedule (G-AN-045).
- [ ] Debug verbosity is off in production, or raised per service with a recorded revert (AN-084).
