# rtl-layouts

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** "Internationalization Best Practices: Handling Right-to-left Scripts in HTML", W3C — https://www.w3.org/International/geo/html-tech/tech-bidi.html ; CSS Logical Properties and Values, W3C (via MDN) — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_logical_properties_and_values
- **Depends on:** internationalization (supplies correct `lang`/`dir` metadata and flexible containers)
- **Feeds into:** localization-workflow (RTL renders are part of its in-context review), wcag (mirrored focus order and reading order feed conformance)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Building or reviewing any layout that must serve a right-to-left locale (Arabic, Urdu, Persian, Hebrew) — setting document direction, writing directional CSS, deciding which icons and components flip, isolating embedded LTR content, and running the per-script RTL visual QA pass.
- **Do NOT use when:** Extracting strings, wiring ICU/`Intl` formatting, or setting `lang` (internationalization), running the translation pipeline and its review states (localization-workflow), or judging general WCAG conformance (wcag, accessibility-audit).

## Rules

1. **AC-161 — Direction is declared on the root, never faked or inferred.** Every RTL locale is served with `dir="rtl"` on the document root element, set from the locale's metadata. Direction is never inferred from `lang` by hand-rolled code, never guessed from text content, and never simulated by transforming an LTR layout.
2. **AC-162 — Directional layout uses CSS logical properties only.** Spacing, positioning, borders, radii, and alignment are written as `margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline`, `inset-inline-start`, `border-start-start-radius`, `text-align: start`, and their siblings, so one stylesheet serves both directions and flipping `dir` flips the layout. A physical directional property in component code is a defect.
3. **AC-163 — Flexbox and grid are left to follow direction.** Flex rows and grid inline axes already run in the inline direction; no `row-reverse`, manual `order` shuffling, or direction-detection JavaScript is added to compensate for physical CSS elsewhere — the physical CSS is fixed instead.
4. **AC-164 — What mirrors is decided once, in the design system.** Navigation order, breadcrumb order, progress indicators, pagination, back/forward chevrons, directional flow diagrams, and media-player progress follow the inline direction. The flip/no-flip decision for every icon and component class lives in one design-system list, not in per-screen judgment calls.
5. **AC-165 — Semantic direction never flips.** Clocks and time representations, chart and graph axes tied to data conventions, logos and brand marks, phone keypads, and the media content itself (photos, video) are never mirrored. Play icons are decided once in the tokens per AC-164, not per screen.
6. **AC-166 — Embedded opposite-direction runs are isolated.** An English product name, number, price, or code fragment inside an RTL sentence is wrapped in `<bdi>`, an inline element with an explicit `dir`, or Unicode isolate characters (U+2066–U+2069), so the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm places numbers and punctuation on the correct side.
7. **AC-167 — Inherently LTR content stays LTR.** Code blocks, URLs, email addresses, and phone numbers inside an RTL page render with `dir="ltr"` (and `unicode-bidi: isolate` where they sit inside RTL text), so they read and select in their native order.
8. **AC-168 — Scroll regions, carousels, and sliders start at inline-start.** Horizontal scroll regions begin scrolled to the inline-start edge, carousel advance follows the inline direction, slider value increases toward inline-end, and the scrollbar sits where the platform places it for the document direction — none of these is hard-coded to the left.
9. **AC-169 — Text truncation and alignment follow the logical end.** Body text aligns to `start`; truncation clips at the logical end of the line with the ellipsis there. A deliberate exception (centered display type, justified legal text) is recorded in the design system, not improvised per component.
10. **AC-170 — Numbers and dates are formatted, never hand-reversed.** Digits use the locale's CLDR numbering system as decided per locale, and dates render through `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for the RTL locale. A date or number string is never reversed, reordered, or re-punctuated by string manipulation to "look RTL".
11. **AC-171 — RTL QA is per script, with real text.** Each target script is checked with real content in that script: Arabic (Naskh) passing does not certify Urdu — Nastaliq has far taller line boxes, so line-height, clipping, and truncation are verified separately for Nastaliq, and again for Persian and Hebrew where targeted.
12. **AC-172 — Charts, maps, and diagrams are individually reviewed in RTL.** No chart, map, or annotated diagram ships in an RTL locale until a human has reviewed its RTL render: axis and legend order, label placement, and annotation direction are checked against the data conventions in AC-165.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-081 — Physical directional CSS in component code.** Banned: `margin-left`, `padding-right`, `left: 0`, `float: left`, `text-align: right` used to position or align layout in a component. Defeats: DET-UX-023. Bad: the checkout summary is placed with `margin-left: auto` and `left`-positioned step icons; under `dir="rtl"` the summary overlaps the form and the primary pay button is pushed out of the usable flow. Instead: the same layout in logical properties (`margin-inline-start: auto`, `inset-inline-start: 0`, `text-align: start`) mirrors automatically when `dir` flips. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-082 — Mirroring faked with transforms.** Banned: `transform: scaleX(-1)` (or a flipped duplicate stylesheet) applied to a container or page to simulate RTL. Defeats: DET-VIS-037. Bad: a wrapper flips the settings page visually, but text renders mirrored-glyph by glyph in screenshots, focus order still runs left-to-right, and embedded images and logos are flipped too — the layout was collapsed into place, not adapted. Instead: set `dir="rtl"` on the root and build on logical properties (AC-161, AC-162) so content, focus order, and reading order all follow direction. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-083 — Un-isolated embedded LTR run in RTL text.** Banned: interpolating a Latin-script product name, number, or price directly into an RTL string with no `<bdi>`, inline `dir`, or Unicode isolate. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Bad: "Order Pro Max 12 today" inside an Arabic sentence renders with the "12" and the trailing punctuation jumped to the wrong side of the product name, so the offer text is garbled at reading size. Instead: the interpolated value is isolated — `<bdi>Pro Max 12</bdi>` — so the bidi algorithm orders the sentence around it correctly. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-084 — Blanket-flipping icons and media.** Banned: a global rule such as `[dir="rtl"] svg { transform: scaleX(-1) }` or flipping every icon, logo, and image in RTL. Defeats: DET-UX-015. Bad: the same clock icon that reads correctly in LTR now runs counter-clockwise, the logo is mirrored, and a play glyph flips on one screen but not another because a component opted out ad hoc — the same element behaves differently across screens. Instead: only the directional icons on the design-system flip list (AC-164) flip, via a named utility or token; semantic icons, logos, and media never do (AC-165). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-085 — Fixed line-height or height tuned to Latin/Arabic text shipped for Nastaliq.** Banned: shipping an Urdu (or any new-script) locale with line-height, fixed-height headings, or single-line truncation carried over from the LTR or Arabic build without a per-script render check. Defeats: DET-VIS-039. Bad: card titles get a fixed 1.2 line-height and a fixed hero height from the English design; Nastaliq ascenders and descenders are clipped in every heading — the fixed height clips the script itself. Instead: line-height and container heights are verified per script with real Urdu text (AC-171) and fixed heights on text containers are removed or raised until nothing clips. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-081 — Physical-property scan.** Verifies: AC-162, AC-163. Check: run stylelint with a logical-properties rule set (e.g. `stylelint-use-logical-spec` / `liberty/use-logical-spec`) over all component CSS, plus `grep -rnE "(margin|padding)-(left|right)|(^|[^-])(left|right)\s*:|float:\s*(left|right)|text-align:\s*(left|right)" src/ --include='*.css'` as a backstop. Pass: zero findings outside the recorded exception list (e.g. print stylesheets). Fail: block shipment; convert each finding to its logical equivalent and re-run. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-082 — RTL render pass.** Verifies: AC-161, AC-164, AC-168, AC-169. Check: with the browser/Playwright, load every key template in an RTL locale and assert `document.documentElement.dir === "rtl"`, `document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= window.innerWidth` (no page-level horizontal overflow), and screenshot each template beside its LTR counterpart for the human diff review. Pass: all assertions hold and a reviewer has signed the LTR/RTL screenshot diff set, including icon flips and scroll-region start positions. Fail: block shipment for that locale; fix and re-render. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-083 — Bidi test-string check.** Verifies: AC-166, AC-167, AC-170. Check: render the agreed bidi test set — mixed Arabic/English/number strings, a price with currency, a phone number, a URL, and a code snippet — on the data-dense screens (product, checkout, account) and inspect each render against the expected ordering recorded in the test file. Pass: every test string renders with numbers, punctuation, and embedded LTR runs on the correct side, and code/URL/phone render LTR. Fail: block shipment; add or fix the isolation and re-render. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-084 — Per-script visual QA.** Verifies: AC-171, AC-172. Check: for each targeted script beyond the first RTL script (Urdu/Nastaliq, Persian, Hebrew as applicable), screenshot the key templates with real content in that script; a reviewer checks line-height, clipping, truncation direction, and every chart/map/diagram render individually. Pass: signed checklist per script with zero clipped or overflowing text blocks and every chart reviewed. Fail: block shipment for that locale only; the Arabic pass does not substitute. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-085 — Icon flip-list conformance.** Verifies: AC-164, AC-165. Check: diff the set of icons flipped in the RTL render (from the G-AC-082 screenshots) against the design-system flip list; grep the codebase for blanket flip rules (`scaleX(-1)` on icon or container selectors). Pass: flipped set matches the list exactly and no blanket flip rule exists. Fail: block shipment; correct the icon utility or the list — in the design system, not per screen. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The Arabic-pasted LTR page.** `dir="rtl"` is set and the words are Arabic, but the layout still runs on physical CSS, so columns, icons, and scroll regions stay in LTR positions — an LTR page with Arabic pasted in. Catch it in the G-AC-082 side-by-side screenshots, not by reading the markup.
- **The pseudo-RTL shortcut.** QA tests a mechanically flipped or pseudo-locale build and signs off, so real bidi ordering and Nastaliq shaping defects survive to production. Catch it by requiring real text in the real script for G-AC-083 and G-AC-084 — pseudo-RTL catches flips, never shaping.
- **The one-off flip.** A developer flips a single icon or component inline "for the Arabic page," outside the design-system list, so the next screen — or the next locale — makes the opposite choice. Catch it at G-AC-085: any flip not traceable to the list is rework.
- **The reversed string.** A date, price, or tracking number is reversed character-by-character in code to "look right" in RTL, corrupting the value for copy-paste, screen readers, and search. Catch it by selecting and copying rendered values during the G-AC-083 pass — a correct render copies in logical order.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Physical CSS converted to logical properties](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AC-162, AC-163.
- [Example 2 — Transform mirroring replaced by `dir="rtl"`, and blanket icon flip replaced by the flip list](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AC-161, AC-164, AC-165.
- [Example 3 — Un-isolated product name and price isolated with `<bdi>`](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AC-166, AC-167.

## Recall anchors

- Flip the document, not the stylesheet: `dir="rtl"` plus logical properties, and mirroring is automatic.
- Physical left/right in a component is a defect, not a style choice.
- Directional icons flip; clocks, charts, logos, and media never do — the list lives in the design system.
- Isolate every embedded run: numbers, names, code, and URLs keep their own direction inside RTL text.
- Arabic passing does not certify Urdu — Nastaliq gets its own visual QA.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every RTL locale serves `dir="rtl"` on the root from locale metadata; no transform-based mirroring exists anywhere.
- [ ] G-AC-081 physical-property scan is clean outside the recorded exception list.
- [ ] G-AC-082 RTL render pass: correct `dir`, zero page-level horizontal overflow, screenshot diff set human-reviewed.
- [ ] Icon and component flips match the design-system flip list exactly — G-AC-085; clocks, charts, logos, and media unflipped.
- [ ] Bidi test strings render with correct ordering on data-dense screens, and code/URLs/phone numbers render LTR — G-AC-083.
- [ ] Scroll regions, carousels, and sliders start at inline-start and advance in the inline direction.
- [ ] Each additional script (Urdu/Nastaliq, Persian, Hebrew) has its own signed visual QA, including every chart and map — G-AC-084.

# screen-readers

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG), W3C — https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/ ; WCAG 2.2, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- **Depends on:** wcag (name/role/value and status-message criteria), accessibility-audit (its smoke-test pass consumes this skill's matrix)
- **Feeds into:** accessibility-testing, keyboard-accessibility, inclusive-copy

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Building or reviewing anything a screen-reader user must operate or understand — forms, custom widgets, dynamic updates, data tables, navigation — and when running the screen-reader test pass for a release.
- **Do NOT use when:** The defect is purely visual (contrast, focus visibility — wcag / keyboard-accessibility), the question is which law applies (accessibility-law), or the work is a full conformance evaluation (accessibility-audit runs this skill's test matrix as one of its passes).

## Rules

1. **AC-041 — Native semantics first; ARIA is the last resort.** Use the native HTML element for every control and structure (`<button>`, `<nav>`, `<table>`, `<label>`). Add ARIA only where no native element expresses the widget, per the first rule of ARIA use: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA. A role bolted onto a `<div>` is a defect until the full APG pattern (AC-046) is implemented.
2. **AC-042 — Every interactive element has an accessible name that matches its visible label.** The computed accessible name must contain the visible text label (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name), so speech-input and screen-reader users refer to the same control by the same words. Icon-only controls get a name from `aria-label` or visually hidden text that states the action ("Close dialog", not "X").
3. **AC-043 — Headings are a navigation outline, not font sizing.** Headings nest in logical order without skipped levels, each heading text describes the section it opens, and visual size is set with CSS. Screen-reader users navigate by the heading list; an outline that reads as nonsense is a failed page even if it looks right.
4. **AC-044 — Landmarks are few and labeled when repeated.** One `<main>`, one `<nav>` per navigation region; when a landmark type repeats (two `<nav>`s, multiple `<section>`s with `aria-label`), each instance carries a distinct accessible name so the landmark list is usable.
5. **AC-045 — Images: real alt text or empty alt, never a file name.** Informative images get alt text conveying the information the image carries in context; purely decorative images get `alt=""` so they are skipped. File names ("IMG_2043.jpg"), "image", and redundant phrases ("image of") fail this rule.
6. **AC-046 — Custom widgets implement the APG pattern exactly or are replaced.** A custom tabs, menu, combobox, or grid ships with the APG roles, states, properties, and full keyboard model for that pattern — all of it, not the visible half. If the team cannot implement the whole pattern, the widget is rebuilt on native elements.
7. **AC-047 — Dynamic changes are announced by live regions, politely by default.** Status changes (save confirmations, cart totals, step changes, toasts) go through an `aria-live="polite"` region (WCAG 4.1.3); `assertive` is reserved for errors that block the current task. Announcements never move focus — the user hears the change and stays where they are.
8. **AC-048 — Reading order and focus order match the visual order.** DOM order is the single source of sequence: content reads in the same order it is seen, and no CSS (`order`, absolute positioning, grid placement) reorders meaning visually without the DOM agreeing. Multi-column visual layouts built from a scrambled DOM fail this rule.
9. **AC-049 — Data tables use real table semantics with header association.** Data tables are `<table>` markup with `<th>` header cells and `scope` (or `headers`/`id` for complex tables), so a cell is announced with its row and column headers. Layout tables and div-grids presenting tabular data are prohibited; a genuine grid widget follows the APG grid pattern instead.
10. **AC-050 — Language is declared so pronunciation is right.** The document carries a correct BCP 47 `lang`, and any in-page language change is wrapped with its own `lang` (WCAG 3.1.1, 3.1.2). A screen reader pronouncing French text with English rules is a markup defect, not a user problem.
11. **AC-051 — Test in a fixed screen-reader matrix, navigating the way users navigate.** The project fixes its matrix in writing (department default: NVDA + Chrome and JAWS + Chrome on Windows, VoiceOver + Safari on macOS and iOS, TalkBack + Chrome on Android) and records the combinations and date per journey. Testers move by headings, landmarks, link lists, and form-control lists — not only by linear reading — because that is how screen-reader users actually navigate. Untested combinations are stated residual risk, never implied coverage.
12. **AC-052 — Form state is programmatic, not visual.** Required fields expose their required state, invalid fields set `aria-invalid="true"`, and each field's error text and instructions are associated with `aria-describedby`, so the error is announced with the field when the user reaches it — not painted red somewhere on the page.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-021 — Clickable divs and spans as controls.** Banned: `<div>`/`<span>` elements with click handlers acting as buttons, links, or tabs, with no role, accessible name, or keyboard path. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Bad: `<div class="tab" onclick="showPanel(2)">Billing</div>` — focus never reaches it and a screen reader announces nothing. Instead: use a native `<button>` (or the full APG tabs pattern with `role="tablist"`, arrow-key model, and `aria-selected`). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-022 — Placeholder text as the only label.** Banned: form fields labeled only by placeholder text that vanishes on typing. Defeats: DET-UX-022. Bad: `<input placeholder="Email address">` with no `<label>` — the field announces unreliably and is unidentifiable once filled. Instead: give every field a persistent visible `<label>` (or `aria-label` where a visible label is genuinely impossible) and let the placeholder show a format example only. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-023 — Silent dynamic changes.** Banned: content that changes on screen — success toasts, totals, step indicators, filtered results — with no live-region announcement, so the change exists only visually. Defeats: DET-UX-011. Bad: clicking "Save" shows a green toast for three seconds; a screen-reader user hears nothing and cannot tell the save happened. Instead: route the confirmation through an `aria-live="polite"` status region that announces "Profile saved" without moving focus (AC-047). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-024 — Focus dropped to the document top.** Banned: closing a dialog, submitting a form, or changing views in a way that resets focus and the reading position to the top of the document (or nowhere). Defeats: DET-UX-017. Bad: after dismissing a settings dialog, the screen-reader user is returned to the page header and must re-navigate to where they were. Instead: return focus to the control that opened the dialog, and on view change move focus to the new view's heading (AC-048). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-025 — Errors announced visually only.** Banned: validation errors shown as red borders or a distant error banner while the field itself carries no programmatic error state or associated message. Defeats: DET-UX-005. Bad: a banner at the top reads "2 errors" and the card-number field is outlined in red; at the field, the screen reader announces only "Card number, edit text". Instead: set `aria-invalid="true"` on the field and associate the specific error text with `aria-describedby`, with a polite/assertive announcement per AC-047 and AC-052. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-021 — Automated name/role scan in CI.** Verifies: AC-041, AC-042, AC-045, AC-052. Check: run `npx @axe-core/cli <each key URL> --tags wcag2a,wcag2aa,wcag22aa` in CI (or the project's axe-core job) and fail the build on `button-name`, `link-name`, `label`, `image-alt`, and `aria-required-attr` violations. Pass: zero violations of those rules on every key template. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-022 — Accessibility-tree name/role assertion.** Verifies: AC-042, AC-044, AC-049. Check: scripted pass over the rendered accessibility tree of each key page (e.g. Playwright's accessibility snapshot): assert every interactive node has a non-empty accessible name and a valid role, repeated landmarks have distinct names, and every data-table cell resolves to at least one header. Pass: zero unnamed interactive nodes, zero unlabeled repeated landmarks, zero headerless data cells. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-023 — Screen-reader smoke pass on primary journeys.** Verifies: AC-043, AC-048, AC-051. Check: manual pass — execute each primary journey in at least one desktop (NVDA + Chrome) and one mobile (VoiceOver + Safari or TalkBack + Chrome) combination from the project's fixed matrix, navigating by headings, landmarks, and form controls; log pass/fail per journey with the AT/browser versions and date. Pass: every primary journey completable end to end in both combinations, with names, roles, and order as designed. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-024 — Live-region announcement test.** Verifies: AC-047, AC-052. Check: with a screen reader running, trigger each dynamic change in the primary journeys (save, add-to-cart, step advance, a blocking validation error, a failed submit) and record what is announced and where focus sits afterward. Pass: every change is announced by the correct live region and focus never moves on a status announcement. Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-025 — Heading and landmark outline review.** Verifies: AC-043, AC-044. Check: extract the heading outline and landmark list for each key template (headings-map tool or the screen reader's headings/landmarks dialogs during G-AC-023) and read them as a standalone table of contents. Pass: the outline alone describes the page's structure accurately, with no skipped levels and no heading whose text is styling noise ("Welcome!", "Section 2"). Fail: block release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **ARIA wallpaper.** Sprinkling roles and labels over broken markup — `role="button"` on a div with no keyboard handler, `aria-label` on a non-interactive wrapper — until the code *mentions* accessibility everywhere and provides it nowhere. Catch it by asking, for every ARIA attribute, what a screen reader does differently because it exists (AC-041).
- **Linear-read testing only.** Testing by tabbing or reading top to bottom once, then declaring the page screen-reader friendly — while the heading list is garbage and the link list is forty "click here"s. Catch it by navigating one journey using only the headings dialog and the form-controls list (AC-051).
- **One-combination claim.** Testing in NVDA alone and writing "screen-reader accessible" in the release notes. Combinations differ, especially on custom widgets and live regions. Catch it by checking the claim against the project's fixed matrix and its recorded test dates (AC-051).
- **Visually hidden text dumps.** Stuffing paragraphs of screen-reader-only text onto a page to compensate for visible copy that makes no sense — doubling maintenance and announcing a different product than sighted users see. Catch it by comparing the announced content against the visible content: they must say the same thing (inclusive-copy owns the copy fix).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Div tab bar vs. native buttons with names](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AC-041.
- [Example 2 — Silent save toast vs. polite live region](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AC-047.
- [Example 3 — Styled text vs. a real heading outline](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AC-043.

## Recall anchors

- Native element first; ARIA only where HTML runs out.
- No name, no control — if it can't be announced, it doesn't exist.
- Headings are the table of contents; write them like one.
- Changes speak politely; only blocking errors interrupt.
- DOM order is reading order — never let CSS tell a different story.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every interactive element has an accessible name containing its visible label (AC-042).
- [ ] No clickable div/span controls remain; custom widgets implement the full APG pattern (AC-041, AC-046).
- [ ] Heading outline reads as an accurate table of contents with no skipped levels (AC-043, G-AC-025).
- [ ] All informative images have real alt text; decorative images have `alt=""` (AC-045).
- [ ] Every dynamic change is announced by a live region without moving focus (AC-047, G-AC-024).
- [ ] Form errors are programmatic: `aria-invalid` plus `aria-describedby` error text (AC-052).
- [ ] Primary journeys passed in one desktop and one mobile matrix combination, versions and date recorded (AC-051, G-AC-023).

# wcag

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D13 Accessibility & i18n (AC)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** WCAG 2.2, W3C — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ ; "What's New in WCAG 2.2", W3C WAI — https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/new-in-22/
- **Depends on:** none (this skill fixes the conformance target every other D13 skill builds or tests against)
- **Feeds into:** accessibility-audit, keyboard-accessibility, screen-readers, accessibility-law, reduced-motion, inclusive-copy

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** Building or changing any interface that must conform — this skill is the conformance discipline itself: how each WCAG criterion is met by construction in design tokens, markup, and interaction code, at the project's fixed target of WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
- **Do NOT use when:** Running an evaluation and producing findings (that is accessibility-audit — it audits against the target this skill sets), mapping laws to a pinned version (accessibility-law), or deep work owned by a sibling skill (keyboard-accessibility, screen-readers, reduced-motion). This skill states the criteria-level requirements those skills implement in detail.

## Rules

1. **AC-021 — Fix the target in writing before build.** Every project records its target as "WCAG 2.2 Level AA" in its project files before interface work starts. Where a contract or law pins an older version (EN 301 549/EAA pins 2.1 AA; Section 508 pins 2.0 AA), the pin is recorded alongside; building to 2.2 AA satisfies the older pins in almost every case, because 2.2 only removes the obsolete 4.1.1 Parsing. Claims are always stated against a named version and level — never bare "WCAG compliant."
2. **AC-022 — Contrast floors, computed from the actual palette.** Normal text ≥4.5:1 (1.4.3); large text ≥3:1 (1.4.3); UI component boundaries and meaningful graphics ≥3:1 against adjacent colors (1.4.11). Ratios are computed from the real token values and re-checked in every state (hover, focus, disabled-looking, placeholder, error) — never eyeballed from a design mock.
3. **AC-023 — Color is never the only carrier of meaning (1.4.1).** Every state or distinction shown in color (error, success, required, chart series, selected) is paired with a redundant cue: text, icon, pattern, or position. If a screen still reads correctly in grayscale, this rule passes.
4. **AC-024 — Focus is visible and never fully hidden.** Every interactive element shows a visible focus indicator (2.4.7), and a focused component is never entirely obscured by author-created content such as sticky headers, cookie banners, or chat widgets (2.4.11). Sticky chrome ships with `scroll-margin` (or equivalent) sized so focused elements clear it.
5. **AC-025 — Pointer targets meet the size floor.** Targets are at least 24×24 CSS px, or have equivalent spacing so a 24px circle centered on the target does not overlap another target (2.5.8). Where space allows, the design target stays in the 44px class; the 2.5.8 floor is a minimum, not a goal.
6. **AC-026 — Everything is keyboard-operable, in logical order, with no traps.** All functionality works by keyboard alone (2.1.1); focus can always move on or out of every component (2.1.2); focus order follows the visual and reading order (2.4.3) with no positive `tabindex` values. Custom widgets follow the sibling keyboard-accessibility skill's APG models.
7. **AC-027 — Name, role, and value are programmatic; status is announced.** Every component exposes its name, role, value, and state to assistive technology (4.1.2) — native HTML elements first, ARIA only where HTML has no equivalent. Status messages (toasts, result counts, save confirmations) are announced via live regions without moving focus (4.1.3).
8. **AC-028 — Text alternatives and persistent labels.** Informative images carry real alt text and decorative images carry `alt=""` (1.1.1) — never a file name. Every form field has a persistent, programmatically associated visible label (1.3.1, 3.3.2); a placeholder may show a format example only. A control's accessible name matches or contains its visible label (2.5.3).
9. **AC-029 — The 2.2 interaction additions are built in.** Every dragging movement has a single-pointer alternative that needs no path-based gesture (2.5.7). Authentication offers a path with no cognitive-function test as the only option — no memorized codes, puzzles, or blocked paste (3.3.8).
10. **AC-030 — Help is consistent and entry is never redundant.** Help mechanisms (contact link, chat, help page) appear in the same relative order on every page that has them (3.2.6). Information the user already gave in the same process is pre-filled or selectable, never re-typed, except where re-entry is essential or security-required (3.3.7).
11. **AC-031 — Conformance is inherited from the design system.** Design tokens are mapped to the criteria they satisfy: each text/background pair to 1.4.3/1.4.11, each target-size token to 2.5.8, each focus style to 2.4.7/2.4.11. A component built entirely from mapped tokens inherits its conformance; a token change re-triggers the mapping check for every criterion that token serves.
12. **AC-032 — Claims are per criterion, per full page, per complete process.** Conformance applies to full pages and complete processes (a checkout fails if step 3 fails), using only accessibility-supported technologies, with non-interference from any non-conforming content on the page. Results are reported per criterion — never as a blanket claim that a page or product "is accessible."

## BAN list

- **BAN-AC-011 — Focus outline removed for looks.** Banned: `outline: none` (or an equivalent reset) on interactive elements with no equal-or-better focus indicator replacing it. Defeats: DET-UX-018. Bad: global reset `*:focus { outline: none; }` shipped because outlines "looked messy" in review. Instead: keep a designed `:focus-visible` indicator on every interactive element, styled from the mapped focus token (AC-024, AC-031). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-012 — Color-only state.** Banned: conveying error, success, required, or selection state by color change alone, with no text, icon, or position cue. Defeats: DET-UX-021. Bad: invalid fields get a red border only; in grayscale the form gives no hint which fields failed. Instead: pair every color signal with a redundant cue — an error icon plus a text message naming the problem (AC-023). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-013 — Placeholder as the only label.** Banned: a form field whose sole label is placeholder text that disappears on input. Defeats: DET-UX-022. Bad: checkout fields labeled only by placeholders ("Card number", "Expiry"), unlabeled once filled and unnamed to screen readers. Instead: give every field a persistent visible `<label>`; use the placeholder, if at all, for a format example such as "MM / YY" (AC-028). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AC-014 — Sub-floor pointer targets.** Banned: shipping standalone interactive targets smaller than 24×24 CSS px without the 2.5.8 spacing exception. Defeats: DET-UX-019. Bad: 16×16 px icon buttons packed edge-to-edge in a data-table row, including a delete action. Instead: size targets to at least 24×24 CSS px (44px class where space allows) or space them so the 24px circles do not overlap (AC-025). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AC-015 — Overlay widget claimed as conformance.** Banned: installing a third-party "accessibility overlay" or toolbar and treating any criterion as met because of it, instead of fixing the underlying code. Defeats: DET-NONE — no DET parameter names this signal; pattern owned by this skill. Bad: low-contrast controls left at 2.6:1 with a note that "the overlay's contrast button resolves 1.4.3." Instead: fix the code and tokens so the criterion is met by construction and verified by the gates below; an overlay changes nothing about the rendered page for users who never open it. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AC-011 — Palette contrast computed by script.** Verifies: AC-022, AC-031. Check: run the project contrast script (e.g. `node scripts/check-contrast.mjs design-tokens.json`), which parses every text/background and component-boundary token pair — including hover, focus, placeholder, and error states — and computes the WCAG ratio from the actual hex values. Pass: every normal-text pair ≥4.5:1, every large-text and non-text pair ≥3:1, zero pairs skipped. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-012 — Automated criterion rules pass in CI.** Verifies: AC-027, AC-028. Check: run axe-core in CI over the changed screens (`npx @axe-core/cli <changed URLs>` or the project CI job) and confirm the rules mapped to 4.1.2, 1.1.1, and label criteria report zero violations. Manual form (tool-form substitution): where no browser or axe-core runtime is available, perform the G-AC-015 criterion checklist by hand for the criteria mapped to 4.1.2, 1.1.1, and labels — inspect each changed screen's name/role/value exposure (AC-027), text alternatives, and label association (AC-028) in the accessibility tree and the source — and record it in progress.md as a tool-form substitution for this gate; the automated run remains required wherever tooling exists. Pass: zero violations on the mapped rule set (automated) or zero unmet criteria under the manual form. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-013 — Focus spot-verification on changed screens.** Verifies: AC-024, AC-026. Check: manual pass — Tab through every changed screen; at each stop confirm the indicator is visible and not entirely covered by sticky headers, banners, or widgets; confirm focus enters and leaves every component (no trap) in reading order. Pass: every stop identifiable, none obscured, none trapped. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-014 — Target sizes measured.** Verifies: AC-025. Check: measure the rendered bounding boxes of all standalone interactive elements on changed screens (DevTools or a Playwright bounding-box script). Pass: every target ≥24×24 CSS px, or its 24px centered circle overlaps no other target. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AC-015 — Per-release criterion checklist for changed screens.** Verifies: AC-021, AC-032. Check: open the release checklist; for each changed screen, confirm every criterion its changes touch is marked met / not met with the verifying method named (script, CI, or manual pass). Pass: zero unmarked affected criteria, and the target line still reads "WCAG 2.2 Level AA" (or the recorded pinned version). Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Criterion cherry-picking.** Declaring "AA" because the easy criteria pass while an untested one (focus order, live regions) was never checked. Catch it by requiring every claim to name its criterion and method (AC-032) — an unexamined criterion is an unmade claim.
- **Single-viewport conformance.** Checking criteria only at desktop width, so 400% reflow, zoom, and small-viewport target spacing are never exercised. Catch it by spot-checking changed screens at 320 CSS px width and 200%/400% zoom before sign-off.
- **ARIA wallpaper.** Bolting roles and `aria-*` attributes onto broken markup to make a scanner quiet down, instead of switching to the native element that carries the semantics for free. Catch it by asking, for every ARIA attribute in review: "what native element or attribute does this replace, and why can't we use it?" (AC-027).
- **Stale token map.** A palette or focus-style token changes, but the token-to-criterion map is not updated, so inherited conformance silently stops being true. Catch it by diffing token changes against the map in review; any unmapped token change reopens G-AC-011.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Eyeballed contrast vs. computed token pairs](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AC-022.
- [Example 2 — Focus buried under a sticky header vs. visible, unobscured focus](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AC-024.
- [Example 3 — Drag-only reordering vs. single-pointer alternative](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AC-029.

## Recall anchors

- Target is named: WCAG 2.2 AA, in writing, before build.
- Contrast is computed from real tokens — never eyeballed.
- Focus visible, focus never fully hidden.
- 24×24 minimum; 44 is the design habit.
- Conformance is per criterion, by construction — never by overlay.

## Checklist

- [ ] Project files record the target "WCAG 2.2 Level AA" plus any law/contract pin (AC-021).
- [ ] Contrast script passes on all token pairs in all states (G-AC-011).
- [ ] No state is carried by color alone anywhere in the changed screens (AC-023).
- [ ] Keyboard walk of changed screens: visible focus at every stop, none obscured, none trapped (G-AC-013).
- [ ] All targets measured at ≥24×24 CSS px or spacing-equivalent (G-AC-014).
- [ ] Every field has a persistent label; every informative image has real alt text (AC-028).
- [ ] Drag actions have a single-pointer alternative; login has a non-cognitive-test path (AC-029).
- [ ] Release checklist marks every affected criterion with its verifying method (G-AC-015).

# age-requirements

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D14 Legal & Privacy (LG)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng ; https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/privacy-security/childrens-privacy
- **Depends on:** privacy-laws, audit-trails
- **Feeds into:** dsar-handling, legal-documents, compliance-audit

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product is child-directed, is likely to be accessed by children, or may acquire child users in any market; building or changing the age screen, the parental-consent flow, the under-age removal path, or the per-market age table; a market is added where an age regime applies.
- **Do NOT use when:** the product decision itself is open — whether to serve children at all, which verification vendor is proportionate for a children's product, or a contested parental-rights call. Children's products are an escalation stop (LG-151): this skill builds the gate and the records; qualified counsel confirms the regime choices.

## Rules

1. **LG-141 — The threshold is per-market configuration, never a constant.** A table in the project legal file maps each market to its regime, minimum age, accepted verification method, source, last-verified date, and review date (GDPR Article 8: 16 by default, member states may lower to not below 13; UK 13; US COPPA: under 13 with verifiable parental consent). Code reads the table; adding a market means adding a verified row first.
2. **LG-142 — The gate runs before collection.** Where a service is child-directed or child users are expected, the age screen runs before any personal data is collected beyond what the gate itself needs; an under-threshold result stops the signup, not a later step of it.
3. **LG-143 — The age screen is neutral.** No pre-filled or defaulted adult date, no "Are you over X?" one-tap-through on a child-directed service, no copy, ordering, or visual emphasis that coaches a passing answer. The screen asks for the date of birth (or the regime's neutral equivalent) and computes the determination.
4. **LG-144 — Under-threshold means routed or blocked, never waved through.** An under-threshold user is routed to the parental-consent flow where the regime provides one, or blocked where none exists. After a failed determination, changing the entered date in the same session is locked or flagged per the market row — retry-until-pass is a defect, not a UX choice.
5. **LG-145 — Parental consent is verifiable and recorded.** Consent is captured by a method the regime accepts (COPPA: signed form, payment-card transaction with notice, trained-staff call/video, government-ID check with prompt deletion, knowledge-based authentication; GDPR Article 8(2): reasonable efforts to verify parental authorisation) and stored as a consent record — method, timestamp, scope, child account — in the audit trail. A lone "I am the parent" checkbox is not a method.
6. **LG-146 — Store the determination, not the birthday.** The record kept is the threshold determination, its basis (market row, method), and its date. A full date of birth is stored only where a registered purpose in the data map requires it; age-gate data carries its own retention limit and is deleted when the determination no longer needs to be demonstrable.
7. **LG-147 — Age data is never reused.** Data collected for the gate or for parental consent is never used for marketing, profiling, ad targeting, or product analytics. It exists for the determination and its demonstration, and for nothing else.
8. **LG-148 — Actual knowledge applies retroactively.** When the product learns an existing user is under-threshold (support contact, report, content signals), that account enters the same flow as a fresh under-threshold signup: parental consent obtained, or the account is removed. Time on the platform grandfathers nothing.
9. **LG-149 — Parents hold working rights.** A parent can review the child's data, withdraw consent, and demand deletion through the dsar-handling flows, with the same clocks and records as any other request; withdrawal stops the processing the consent justified.
10. **LG-150 — Removal is a defined, executed path.** An under-age account without valid consent is suspended on discovery, then deleted per the retention schedule across primary stores, indexes, analytics, and processors — deletion verified by a residue check, never by hiding the profile.
11. **LG-151 — Design codes and teen laws are register entries, and children escalate.** Regimes beyond the consent age (e.g. the UK Age Appropriate Design Code, US state teen-privacy laws) are rows in the obligations register, flagged as variance and reviewed — not silently ignored. Launching or materially changing a children's product stops for qualified counsel before build, per privacy-laws LG-011.
12. **LG-152 — Every row is dated and sourced.** A market row past its review date is treated as unverified: the threshold it states cannot be relied on until re-verified against the national rule in force at that date. National ages change by statute; the table is the only place they live.

## BAN list

- **BAN-LG-071 — The cosmetic age gate.** Banned: an age control that does not gate — a self-declaration checkbox or "confirm your age" button on a child-directed service whose answer is never checked, never stored, and blocks nothing. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Bad: signup shows "I confirm I am 13 or older" with a pre-ticked box; unchecking it still creates the account, and no record of the answer exists. Instead: run a neutral age screen before collection, compute the determination from the market row, and store the determination (LG-142, LG-143, LG-146). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-072 — One hardcoded age for every market.** Banned: a single age constant in code or copy applied to all markets regardless of the per-market regime. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: `MIN_AGE = 13` ships globally; German users are admitted at 13 although the German Article 8 age is 16, and nobody notices because the number looks plausible. Instead: read every threshold from the dated, sourced market table (LG-141, LG-152). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-073 — The recorded lie: age_verified without verification.** Banned: setting an `age_verified` (or equivalent) flag, or telling parents/regulators that age is verified, when the flow performed no verification step. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the account record carries `age_verified: true` because the user clicked "Yes" on a prompt; the privacy notice states "we verify the age of all users." Instead: the flag is set only by a completed determination or parental-consent flow, and the notice describes the method actually used (LG-143, LG-145). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-074 — The birthday kept and spent.** Banned: retaining full dates of birth collected at the gate beyond the determination's need, or reusing gate data for birthday marketing, targeting, or profiling. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: the notice says birth dates are collected "only to check your age"; the full date is stored permanently and feeds a birthday-discount campaign segment. Instead: store the determination and its basis, delete the raw date per its retention limit, and never route gate data to marketing (LG-146, LG-147). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-075 — The child-safety promise with no removal process.** Banned: publishing "children under X cannot use this service" (or equivalent) while no discovery, suspension, and deletion path for under-age accounts exists behind the claim. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the terms bar under-13s; a parent reports an 11-year-old's account and support replies that they "cannot verify ages," leaving the account live. Instead: ship the actual-knowledge flow — suspend, seek parental consent or delete, verify by residue check — before the promise is printed (LG-148, LG-150). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-LG-071 — Age-flow test suite.** Verifies: LG-141, LG-142, LG-144. Check (automated): scripted signups run per market row in staging — a test user below the row's threshold must be blocked or routed to the parental-consent flow and must not reach account creation or any age-restricted feature; a test user at the threshold proceeds. Pass: every market row behaves as configured. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-072 — Consent-record assertion.** Verifies: LG-145. Check (automated): completing the parental-consent flow in staging asserts a stored consent record with method, timestamp, and scope; completing an under-threshold signup with no consent record on file must be impossible — the test attempts it directly against the account-creation endpoint. Pass: record exists for the consented account; the unconsented creation is rejected. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-073 — Configuration and freshness scan.** Verifies: LG-141, LG-152. Check (automated): `grep` the codebase and copy for hardcoded age thresholds (numeric age constants outside the market-table module) and scan the market table for rows past their review date. Pass: zero hardcoded thresholds, zero stale rows. Fail: block shipment — thresholds move into the table and stale rows are re-verified first. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-074 — Minimisation and removal drill.** Verifies: LG-146, LG-148, LG-150. Check (automated): seed a test under-age account, trigger the actual-knowledge path, and run removal; afterwards residue queries across the database, search index, and admin views return nothing for the test subject, and the account store holds no full date of birth for determination-only accounts. Pass: zero residue, determination-only storage confirmed. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-075 — Neutrality and escalation review.** Verifies: LG-143, LG-149, LG-151. Check (manual): read the live age screen against the neutrality rules (no defaults, no coaching, no retry-until-pass), walk a parental review/withdrawal/deletion request through dsar-handling end to end, and confirm the children's-product escalation to counsel is recorded for this product or the stop condition is absent in writing. Pass: all three hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The gate at the checkout.** The age screen sits at payment or first posting instead of signup, so an under-age user's data has been collected and profiled for weeks before the gate fires. Catch it by tracing which personal data exists before the gate step in the flow; anything beyond the gate's own input means the gate is in the wrong place.
- **"Not child-directed" as a permanent fact.** The product was declared general-audience once and the declaration is never revisited while the audience visibly fills with children. Catch it by sampling support tickets, reports, and content signals for age evidence; a rising count is actual knowledge arriving, whether or not anyone files it.
- **One screen, every locale, wrong dates.** A single English age screen with one date format serves all markets, so day/month order flips determinations for real users. Catch it by running the gate in each shipped locale with a boundary date (e.g. 05/06) and confirming the computed determination matches the intended reading.
- **Verification maximalism.** Every user is sent through ID-document verification because it feels safest, although the regime accepts a lighter method for the risk at hand. Catch it in design review: the method per market row must be the least-data method the regime accepts, and any heavier method needs a recorded reason.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The checkbox that gated nothing](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects LG-142, LG-143.
- [Example 2 — One age for the whole world](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects LG-141.
- [Example 3 — The under-age account support found](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects LG-148, LG-150.

## Recall anchors

- The threshold is a table row, never a constant.
- The gate runs before collection, and it actually gates.
- A neutral screen asks; it never coaches.
- Store the determination, not the birthday.
- Discovered under-age means consent or deletion — never grandfathered.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every served market has a dated, sourced age-table row with regime, threshold, and method (LG-141, LG-152, G-LG-073).
- [ ] The age screen runs before personal-data collection and blocks or routes under-threshold users (LG-142, LG-144, G-LG-071).
- [ ] The screen is neutral: no pre-filled dates, no coaching, no retry-until-pass (LG-143, G-LG-075).
- [ ] Parental consent uses a regime-accepted method and is stored as a consent record (LG-145, G-LG-072).
- [ ] Only the determination is stored; gate data is retention-limited and never reused (LG-146, LG-147, G-LG-074).
- [ ] The actual-knowledge path suspends and removes under-age accounts, verified by residue check (LG-148, LG-150, G-LG-074).
- [ ] Parental review, withdrawal, and deletion work through dsar-handling (LG-149, G-LG-075).
- [ ] Design-code and teen-law variance is registered, and the children's-product counsel escalation is recorded (LG-151, G-LG-075).

# audit-trails

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D14 Legal & Privacy (LG)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng/ ; https://cppa.ca.gov/regulations/pdf/20230329_final_regs_text.pdf
- **Depends on:** privacy-laws, logging
- **Feeds into:** compliance-audit, dsar-handling, cookie-consent, legal-documents, clone-ethics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or reviewing the record of regulated actions — consent grants and withdrawals, policy acceptances, DSAR lifecycle events, data exports, refunds and billing adjustments, admin access to personal data, permission changes, and D14 rights/authorization decisions — including the trail store's integrity, access control, and retention.
- **Do NOT use when:** the record is application telemetry — request logs, error traces, performance metrics (that is D12's logging skill; this skill owns only the compliance-grade record of who did what to regulated data and systems), or the question is whether an action was lawful in the first place (derive that in privacy-laws; the trail records the basis, it does not create it). This skill is implementation guidance, not legal advice.

## Rules

1. **LG-161 — The regulated-action inventory is explicit.** The project file lists every action type that must write a trail entry — at minimum: consent grant/withdrawal, policy acceptance, DSAR receipt/extension/delivery/refusal/closure, data export, refund and billing adjustment, admin access to personal data, permission or role change, and each D14 rights/authorization decision (including clone-ethics records). An action type not on the list is a coverage gap to close, not an exemption.
2. **LG-162 — The entry is written in the same flow as the action.** The trail entry is created inside the transaction or service call that performs the action, so the action cannot complete without its entry. An action that "happened but has no entry" is treated as not having validly happened, and the flow surfaces the failure instead of proceeding silently.
3. **LG-163 — Every entry is complete.** Each entry carries: actor (user, admin, or system process, with role), action, subject/target (whose data or which record), trusted timestamp, and the basis reference — the document version accepted, the consent scope granted, the register row or rule the decision applied, and the approver where one exists. An entry missing any field fails G-LG-081.
4. **LG-164 — Entries are append-only.** No entry is ever edited or deleted in place. A correction is a new entry that references the original entry's ID, states what was wrong, and carries its own actor and timestamp; both entries remain readable.
5. **LG-165 — The store is tamper-evident.** Entries are protected by append-only storage plus hash-chaining (each entry's hash covers the previous entry's hash) or WORM storage where the risk warrants; the application role holds no UPDATE or DELETE grant on the trail store. Integrity is verified on a schedule under G-LG-083, not assumed.
6. **LG-166 — Timestamps come from a trusted server clock.** Entry times are written by the server at the moment of the action. A client-supplied time (from a browser, a form, or an imported record) is stored, if at all, as a labeled claim field — never as the entry's timestamp.
7. **LG-167 — The basis is recorded, not just the outcome.** A decision entry names the rule, register row, or approval it rests on (for example "rights decision: replace, approved per clone-ethics record REF-EXAMPLE-04"). An outcome with no basis is an incomplete entry and fails audit sampling.
8. **LG-168 — Access to the trail is itself trailed.** Reading, searching, or exporting the trail writes a trail entry naming the reader and the query scope. Trail read access is limited to the named roles in the project file; the trail is never exposed through a general admin screen or an unauthenticated endpoint.
9. **LG-169 — The trail has its own retention schedule.** Each entry category is retained for the period its obligation specifies in the project file (for example, CCPA request records at least 24 months; consent records for as long as the processing they justify continues, plus the limitation period the register names) and purged on schedule — never earlier, and never kept indefinitely by default.
10. **LG-170 — The trail is personal data and is treated as such.** The trail sits inside the data inventory with access control and minimisation applied: entries record references and identifiers needed for accountability, not copies of the underlying personal data. How a DSAR reaches the trail, and how erasure interacts with trail retention duties, is resolved per regime in the project file — never improvised per request.
11. **LG-171 — Trail health is reviewed on a cadence.** On the schedule compliance-audit sets, a reviewer samples entries against real actions (a refund in the billing system, a closed DSAR, a consent withdrawal) and confirms each has a complete, correctly based entry; every gap becomes a finding with an owner and a remediation date.
12. **LG-172 — No claim outruns the trail.** Product copy, sales material, and audit answers may claim only the recording the trail actually performs ("every refund is logged with actor and reason" only if refunds are on the LG-161 inventory and pass G-LG-081). A claim with no passing gate behind it is removed, not softened.

## BAN list

- **BAN-LG-081 — Trail kept in ephemeral logs.** Banned: regulated actions recorded only in application console output, a rotating log file, or an analytics event stream that ages out — anywhere the record can vanish with a restart or a retention default. Defeats: DET-INF-013. Bad: consent withdrawals are visible via `console.log("consent withdrawn", userId)` and unrecoverable after the host's 7-day log rotation. Instead: write the entry to the append-only trail store in the same flow as the action, under LG-162 and LG-165. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-082 — History edited in place.** Banned: UPDATE or DELETE statements against existing trail entries — to fix a typo, reassign an actor, tidy a timestamp, or remove an embarrassing decision. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: an admin runs `UPDATE audit_log SET actor = 'system' WHERE id = 1042` so a manual refund looks automated. Instead: leave the original untouched and append a correction entry referencing it, under LG-164. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-083 — Trail readable by anyone, reads unrecorded.** Banned: a trail viewer, export, or API route available to all staff accounts (or worse, unauthenticated), whose reads write no entry — so the most sensitive metadata in the product can be browsed invisibly. Defeats: DET-INF-021. Bad: `/admin/audit` renders for every support login and logs nothing when opened. Instead: restrict reads to the named roles and trail every read under LG-168. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-084 — Backfilled trail presented as contemporaneous.** Banned: reconstructing entries after the fact — from tickets, chat, or memory — and storing them with the action's original date as if they were written when the action happened. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: after an incident, a week of admin data accesses is "rebuilt" into the trail with last week's timestamps. Instead: record the reconstruction honestly — entries carry the true write time, name the source they were reconstructed from, and the gap itself is filed as a finding under LG-171. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-085 — Retention shorter than the recorded schedule.** Banned: a purge job, storage tier, or vendor default that deletes trail categories before the period the project file records for them — for example request records destroyed at 90 days where the applicable regime's row requires at least 24 months. Defeats: DET-CON-015. Bad: the privacy notice promises request records are kept for two years while the trail store's lifecycle policy expires them in a quarter. Instead: set purge rules per category from the schedule under LG-169 and verify them under G-LG-085. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-LG-081 — Action-coverage test.** Verifies: LG-161, LG-162, LG-163, LG-167. Check (automated): in staging, perform each action type on the LG-161 inventory — accept a policy version, grant and withdraw consent, file/extend/deliver/close a DSAR, export data, issue a refund, open a subject's record as an admin, change a permission, record a rights decision — then query the trail and assert exactly one complete entry per action with actor, action, subject, server timestamp, and basis reference populated. Pass: zero missing or incomplete entries. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-082 — Tamper test.** Verifies: LG-164, LG-165. Check (automated): in a staging copy of the trail, (a) attempt UPDATE and DELETE on an existing entry using the application role's credentials — both must be denied; (b) modify one historical entry's field directly at the storage layer, then run the integrity verification — the modification must be detected and located. Pass: writes denied and the planted modification flagged. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-083 — Integrity verification job.** Verifies: LG-165. Check (automated): a scheduled job recomputes the hash chain (or verifies WORM attestations) across the full trail and reports any gap, break, or sequence anomaly; the job's own result is filed with its run date. Pass: chain verifies end to end with zero anomalies. Fail: block shipment and raise an incident — a broken chain is treated as a security event, not a data-quality note. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-084 — Trail-access audit.** Verifies: LG-168, LG-170. Check (automated + manual): open the trail viewer and run a search and an export as an authorized role, and attempt the same as an unauthorized role; assert the authorized reads each produced a trail entry naming reader and scope, the unauthorized attempts were refused, and the current role list matches the project file. Pass: all reads trailed, all unauthorized access refused, role list exact. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-085 — Retention conformance check.** Verifies: LG-169. Check (automated): for each entry category, compare the oldest surviving entry's age and the store's purge configuration against the schedule in the project file; assert no category is purged before its recorded period and every category has a purge rule. Pass: zero early purges and zero categories without a rule. Fail: block shipment until configuration matches the schedule. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Audit theater.** A beautiful trail dashboard exists, but half the regulated actions never write to it because they were built before the trail was. Catch it by picking three real actions from the last week — not from the inventory document — and searching for their entries.
- **The log that logs everything except decisions.** Technical events are captured in detail while approvals, refusals, and rights calls live in chat threads. Catch it by sampling decision-type entries specifically; they are the ones an auditor asks for first.
- **One giant retention.** Every category is set to "keep forever" to avoid thinking about schedules — which quietly turns the trail into an unbounded personal-data store. Catch it by checking whether any category has a purge rule that has ever actually run.
- **Timestamps that agree too well.** Entries for a messy real-world process all land on round hours or in perfect sequence days later — the signature of backfill. Catch it by plotting entry write times against the actions they claim to record.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The refund nobody recorded](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects LG-162, LG-163.
- [Example 2 — The entry that got "fixed"](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects LG-164, LG-165.
- [Example 3 — The trail everyone could read](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects LG-168.

## Recall anchors

- If it is not in the trail, it did not validly happen.
- Append-only: corrections are new entries, never edits.
- The trail records the basis, not just the outcome.
- Reading the trail is a trailed act.
- D12 logs the machine; this trail answers for the humans and the system acting on regulated data.

## Checklist

- [ ] The LG-161 inventory lists every regulated action type, including rights/authorization decisions (LG-161).
- [ ] Entries are written in the same flow as the action and are complete: actor, action, subject, timestamp, basis (LG-162, LG-163, LG-167, G-LG-081).
- [ ] The store denies UPDATE/DELETE to the application role and the tamper test detects a planted edit (LG-164, LG-165, G-LG-082).
- [ ] The integrity verification job runs on schedule and its results are filed (LG-165, G-LG-083).
- [ ] Timestamps are server-written; client times, if kept, are labeled claims (LG-166).
- [ ] Trail reads are role-restricted and themselves trailed (LG-168, G-LG-084).
- [ ] Every category has a retention period and a working purge rule matching the project file (LG-169, G-LG-085).
- [ ] The trail is in the data inventory, minimised, with per-regime DSAR/erasure treatment recorded (LG-170).
