# licensing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D14 Legal & Privacy (LG)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://spdx.org/licenses/ ; https://choosealicense.com/
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: license checks read the actual license texts of the dependencies, fonts, images, and datasets being added — primary legal sources, not another skill's output. Its verdicts feed compliance-audit and legal-documents.
- **Feeds into:** compliance-audit, legal-documents

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** adding any dependency, font, image, dataset, or copied snippet; vendoring third-party code; preparing a release (SBOM and notices); choosing or changing the project's own LICENSE; reviewing whether an asset's terms permit the intended use, including transfer to a client or a rebuild.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is a contested rights call — disputed ownership, a license whose terms are ambiguous for the intended use, a takedown or infringement claim. This skill records provenance and applies the written tier policy; it never interprets a license for a contested case or gives legal advice (LG-112).

## Rules

1. **LG-101 — Every component is inventoried.** Every shipped component — library, font, image, dataset, copied snippet — has an inventory row recording its name, version, origin, and license as an SPDX License List identifier (e.g. `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, `GPL-3.0-only`), so policy is machine-checkable instead of name-matching prose. A component with no row does not ship.
2. **LG-102 — Provenance is recorded at adoption time.** The inventory row is written when the component is adopted: where it came from, where its license text lives, and the adoption date. An asset whose provenance cannot be established is treated as unlicensed until proven otherwise.
3. **LG-103 — "No license found" is forbidden-tier.** Absence of a license is not permission: default copyright means all rights reserved. A component with no license found is replaced, or the rights holder's written permission is obtained and filed with the inventory row.
4. **LG-104 — Tiers are set per distribution model.** The project's written license policy defines three tiers — allowed (permissive), review (weak or file-level copyleft), forbidden without a written exception (strong/network copyleft in a distribution model it infects, non-commercial terms, no license found) — separately for each way the product ships (hosted service vs. distributed artifact). The same library can be allowed in one model and forbidden in the other; the tier is decided against the actual model, never in the abstract.
5. **LG-105 — Review-tier items get a named decision.** Every review-tier component carries a recorded decision: the decider's name, the date, the distribution model considered, and the reasoning. An undecided review-tier component does not ship.
6. **LG-106 — Exceptions are written and expire.** A forbidden-tier exception names the component, the reason, the approver, and a review date. An exception past its review date is void until re-approved; a verbal exception does not exist.
7. **LG-107 — Vendored code keeps its license files.** Vendored code, fonts, and assets keep their license and copyright files intact in the tree. Stripping them is a defect found by scan (G-LG-054), not a cleanup step.
8. **LG-108 — Notices are generated, never hand-written.** Attribution is discharged by a notices file generated from the inventory and shipped with the product; where a license triggers a copyleft source-offer duty, the offer is implemented as a real download or disclosure of the corresponding source, not a link to upstream. A notices entry with no inventory row, or a shipped component with no notices entry, is a defect.
9. **LG-109 — An SBOM is emitted per release.** Each release emits an SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX format) from the build, and the SBOM, the inventory, and the notices file are diffed against each other (G-LG-052). The OpenChain ISO/IEC 5230 program elements are the reference for what the compliance program contains.
10. **LG-110 — Licensing is a CI property.** Adding or upgrading a component re-runs the scan and inventory update in the same change. Licensing is never a launch-week audit reconstructed from memory.
11. **LG-111 — The project's own LICENSE is chosen deliberately.** At project creation a LICENSE is selected deliberately (Choose a License is the selection aid), names this project and its rights holder, and matches the intended distribution. No LICENSE file means nobody — including future collaborators — has permission to use the code.
12. **LG-112 — Transferability is checked; contested calls escalate.** Before an asset ships in client work or a rebuild, its terms are checked for transferability (e.g. stock and font licenses that do not transfer). Where the rights position is ambiguous or contested, work on that asset stops and the call goes to qualified counsel with the inventory record attached.

## BAN list

- **BAN-LG-051 — Vendored material shipped with its license files stripped.** Banned: dropping vendored code, a font, or an asset into the tree with its LICENSE, COPYING, or copyright notices deleted. Defeats: DET-CON-020. Bad: a charting library is vendored under `vendor/`; its LICENSE and copyright header are removed "to keep the folder clean," leaving code in the product with no attribution or terms. Instead: keep the license and copyright files with the vendored copy and add the inventory row (LG-101, LG-107). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-052 — "Fully licensed" claimed with no inventory behind it.** Banned: stating in product copy, a client deliverable, or a store listing that all assets or components are licensed or rights-cleared when no inventory and tier record exists to prove it. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the delivery report says "all imagery fully licensed"; half the photos came from a bulk download with no rights record. Instead: make the claim only for what the inventory covers, component by component, or do not make it (LG-101, LG-102). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-053 — A LICENSE file that names another project.** Banned: copying a LICENSE from a tutorial, template, or another repository so the shipped file names the wrong project or rights holder. Defeats: DET-CON-017. Bad: the repo's LICENSE reads "Copyright (c) 2023 Example Tutorial App" while the product is a client storefront under a different name and owner. Instead: choose the license deliberately for this project and put this project's name and rights holder in it (LG-111). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-054 — A component shipped because "no license" was read as "free to use."** Banned: shipping a library, snippet, font, or dataset for which no license was found, on the reasoning that public availability implies permission. Defeats: DET-CON-020. Bad: a utility snippet copied from a personal blog with no license statement is pasted into the codebase and shipped in two releases. Instead: treat no-license-found as forbidden-tier — replace the component or file the rights holder's written permission (LG-103). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-055 — Notices or license claims that contradict the inventory.** Banned: publishing a notices file, attribution page, or compliance claim (e.g. "OpenChain conformant") that the inventory and scan results do not support, or leaving a generated notices file stale after components change. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: the shipped notices list twelve components; the release contains nineteen, including a copyleft library whose source-offer duty nobody implemented. Instead: regenerate notices from the inventory at release and implement triggered duties as real disclosures (LG-108, LG-109). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-LG-051 — CI license scan.** Verifies: LG-101, LG-103, LG-104. Check (automated): run a source-level scan (ScanCode Toolkit) plus the ecosystem metadata checker (`license-checker`, `pip-licenses`, or `cargo-deny`) over the full tree, including vendored directories; compare every detected SPDX identifier against the policy tiers for the target distribution model. Pass: no forbidden-tier identifier, no unlisted identifier, and no component detected that lacks an inventory row. Fail: block the build. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-052 — SBOM–inventory–notices diff.** Verifies: LG-108, LG-109. Check (automated): emit the release SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) and diff its component set against the inventory and the generated notices file. Pass: the three sets are identical. Fail: block shipment until the missing row or notices entry exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-053 — Provenance completeness lint.** Verifies: LG-101, LG-102. Check (automated): lint the inventory — every row must carry a non-empty SPDX identifier, origin, license-text location, and adoption date; a row marked "unknown" in any field fails. Pass: zero incomplete rows. Fail: block shipment; the component is provenanced, replaced, or removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-054 — Vendored-file integrity scan.** Verifies: LG-107. Check (automated): for every vendored directory, assert a LICENSE/COPYING/NOTICE file (or the upstream license text recorded in the inventory) is present and non-empty. Pass: every vendored component retains its license material. Fail: block shipment and restore the files from upstream. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-055 — Decision and exception register review.** Verifies: LG-105, LG-106, LG-112. Check (manual): read the decision register — every review-tier component in the inventory has a named decision with reasoning; every exception names component, reason, approver, and a review date that has not passed; every client/rebuild asset has a recorded transferability check or an escalation entry. Pass: all three hold in writing. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Launch-week license audit.** The inventory is assembled once, just before release, from memory and folder names. Catch it by comparing inventory adoption dates against commit history; rows all dated in the same week as the release were reconstructed, not recorded (LG-102).
- **Metadata-only trust.** The check reads package-manager license fields and calls the tree clean, while vendored files, fonts, and pasted snippets — exactly what metadata misses — go unscanned. Catch it by asking what the scan covered; a scan with no source-level pass over `vendor/` and asset folders is incomplete (G-LG-051).
- **Tier by vibe.** A component is waved through because its license "looks like MIT" from its name or README badge, without reading the actual license text or recording an SPDX identifier. Catch it in review: no SPDX ID and no license-text location in the row means the tier was guessed (LG-101).
- **Exception amnesia.** A forbidden-tier component was "agreed in a call" months ago; nothing is written and nobody remembers the terms. Catch it by asking for the exception record; if it cannot be produced, the exception does not exist (LG-106).

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The snippet with no license](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects LG-103.
- [Example 2 — The font folder with its license deleted](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects LG-107.
- [Example 3 — The copyleft library nobody tiered](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects LG-104.

## Recall anchors

- No license found means no permission — default copyright applies.
- Unknown provenance is unlicensed until proven otherwise.
- Every component: SPDX ID, origin, tier — recorded when adopted, not at launch.
- Notices are generated from the inventory, never hand-written.
- Tier follows the distribution model: the same library can be allowed hosted and forbidden shipped.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every shipped component has an inventory row with SPDX identifier, origin, and adoption date (LG-101, LG-102, G-LG-053).
- [ ] No component with no license found is shipped without filed written permission (LG-103, BAN-LG-054).
- [ ] Every review-tier component has a named, reasoned decision; every exception is written and in date (LG-105, LG-106, G-LG-055).
- [ ] Vendored code and assets retain their license and copyright files (LG-107, G-LG-054).
- [ ] The release SBOM, inventory, and shipped notices diff clean (LG-108, LG-109, G-LG-052).
- [ ] The CI license scan passes for the target distribution model (LG-104, G-LG-051).
- [ ] The project's own LICENSE names this project, and client/rebuild assets have a transferability check or escalation on record (LG-111, LG-112).

# privacy-laws

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D14 Legal & Privacy (LG)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng ; https://cy.ico.org.uk/for-organisations/advice-and-services/audits/data-protection-audit-framework/toolkits/accountability/records-of-processing-and-lawful-basis/
- **Depends on:** fact-sheet
- **Feeds into:** legal-documents, cookie-consent, dsar-handling, data-residency, compliance-audit

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product enters a market, adds a feature, data category, user type, or processor; building or re-verifying the obligations register, the data map (RoPA), the lawful-basis register, or the retention schedule; deciding whether a processing purpose may be built at all.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question needs a legal decision — novel processing, children's, health, finance, or biometric data, a contested rights call, regulator contact. This skill produces engineering artifacts for qualified counsel to confirm; it never gives legal advice and never declares a product compliant (LG-011).

## Rules

1. **LG-001 — Register before features.** Before build, enumerate markets served × data categories processed × user types in the obligations register; each cell records the governing regime, the obligations it creates, and the product requirement satisfying each. A market or feature with no register row does not ship.
2. **LG-002 — The register is data, not prose.** Register rows carry: market, regime, obligation, requirement, owner, lawful basis, last-verified date, review date. If coverage cannot be checked mechanically from the table, the register is an essay and fails.
3. **LG-003 — Lawful basis per purpose.** Every processing purpose has a recorded lawful basis (GDPR Article 6, or the applicable regime's equivalent permission) assigned per purpose, never per product, before the purpose is built.
4. **LG-004 — The data map is the source.** Every personal-data category in the data map (RoPA) has a purpose, a lawful basis, and a retention period; the register derives from the data map, and the two never disagree silently — a mismatch is a defect in one of them.
5. **LG-005 — Minimisation at the schema level.** A form field, column, or event property with no registered purpose is removed from the form and schema, not excused in policy prose.
6. **LG-006 — Triggers are tested, not assumed.** DPIA triggers (GDPR Article 35) and DPO/representative triggers (Articles 37–39) are tested explicitly for each product and the outcome recorded, including "not triggered, because…" with the reasoning.
7. **LG-007 — Retention is a schedule, not an intention.** Every data category has a retention period in the register and a deletion or anonymisation mechanism that actually runs; "kept as long as needed" is not a retention period.
8. **LG-008 — Variance is stated, never averaged.** Where regimes conflict (e.g. a retention duty against an erasure right), the conflict is logged in the register and escalated to counsel; nobody resolves it by picking the convenient rule.
9. **LG-009 — Every legal statement is dated and sourced.** Each register row names its source and last-verified date; a row past its review date is treated as unverified and blocks reliance until re-verified.
10. **LG-010 — Scope is explicit.** Deep profiles ship for GDPR and CCPA/CPRA only. Every other regime is a register-format entry marked "register before serving"; no output implies coverage the register does not contain.
11. **LG-011 — Escalation stops are hard stops.** Children's products, health/finance data, biometric processing, novel processing, contested rights calls, and any regulator contact stop the work: the output is the artifact set plus "this needs qualified counsel." The skill never declares a product "GDPR compliant" or equivalent.
12. **LG-012 — Change re-derives the register.** A new market, feature, processor, data category, or user type triggers a register update before release; the register is re-run on change, not on an annual ritual.

## BAN list

- **BAN-LG-001 — Compliance claimed without a tested process.** Banned: publishing "GDPR compliant", "fully compliant", or an equivalent badge in marketing, docs, or the product when no tested control supports the exact wording. Defeats: DET-CON-012. Bad: the pricing page carries a "100% GDPR Compliant" badge; the register has no DSAR flow and no retention schedule behind it. Instead: publish only what a dated audit artifact proves, worded as what was tested, when, and against what (LG-011). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-002 — Privacy artifacts copied from another product.** Banned: a data map, register, or notice derived from a template or another product's documents instead of this product's own inventory. Defeats: DET-CON-014. Bad: the data map lists "patient records" copied from a healthcare template while omitting the analytics identifiers this product actually stores. Instead: derive every row from this product's data map and feature list (LG-001, LG-004). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-003 — Erasure on paper, hiding in the product.** Banned: recording an erasure right or retention limit in the register while the implemented flow only hides the profile or flags the record and keeps the data reachable. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Bad: the register promises erasure within one month; "Delete account" sets `hidden = true` and the record still appears in admin search and exports. Instead: implement erasure against the stores the register names, verified by a residue check (LG-007). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-004 — Rights promised with no process behind them.** Banned: a privacy notice or register that promises access, erasure, or objection rights while no working intake and handling flow exists. Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: the notice says "email us to delete your data"; the address is unmonitored and no request has ever been actioned or logged. Instead: ship the intake channel, the clock, and the handling flow first, then write the promise (LG-001). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-LG-005 — Regime values hardcoded as eternal constants.** Banned: baking a consent age, a response clock, or an adequacy status into code or copy as an undated constant with no source or review date. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: the signup flow hardcodes "age 16" for every market and the help page states a response deadline copied when the register was first drafted. Instead: keep every such value in the dated, sourced register table and read it as per-market configuration (LG-009). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-LG-001 — Register coverage check.** Verifies: LG-001, LG-003. Check (automated): script the register against product config and the data map — every market in config and every processing purpose in the data map must have a register row with non-empty regime, lawful-basis, and owner fields. Pass: zero uncovered markets or purposes. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-002 — Data-map completeness check.** Verifies: LG-004, LG-005, LG-007. Check (automated): every data-map row asserts a stated purpose, lawful basis, and retention period; every personal-data field found in schemas and forms (`grep` the schema/form definitions against the data map's category list) maps to a data-map row. Pass: no category missing a basis or retention, no unmapped field. Fail: block shipment — the unmapped field is removed or registered first. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-003 — Review-date lint.** Verifies: LG-009. Check (automated): scan the register for rows whose review date is earlier than today. Pass: zero stale rows. Fail: block reliance on the stale rows until re-verified against their sources; the compliance-audit checklist stays open meanwhile. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-004 — Processor tripwire.** Verifies: LG-012. Check (automated): diff the dependency/SDK list and third-party endpoints in the build against the register's processor rows. Pass: every processor in the build has a register row. Fail: block shipment — a new analytics or processor SDK with no row is unregistered processing. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-LG-005 — Trigger and escalation review.** Verifies: LG-006, LG-008, LG-011. Check (manual): read the register's trigger section and conflict log — every DPIA/DPO trigger test has a recorded outcome, every regime conflict has an escalation entry, and every LG-011 stop condition is either absent (with the check recorded) or escalated to counsel. Pass: all three hold in writing. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Launch-week register.** The register is written after the features exist, describing whatever was built instead of constraining it. Catch it by comparing register row dates against feature commit dates; rows that postdate their features were paperwork, not engineering.
- **One-regime copy-paste.** GDPR rows are duplicated for every market with the regime name swapped. Catch it by sampling a non-GDPR row and asking which of its obligations actually differ; if none do, the row was never derived.
- **Aspirational register.** Rows describe the processing the team intends someday, not the processing running today. Catch it by tracing one row to the live schema and one live field back to a row; either direction failing means the register is fiction in one direction.
- **Verified by confidence.** A reviewer bumps a row's last-verified date because "nothing changed" without opening the source. Catch it in review: a re-verification names what was compared against the source text, or the date does not move.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The purpose with no lawful basis](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects LG-003.
- [Example 2 — The compliant badge](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects LG-011.
- [Example 3 — The field collected just in case](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects LG-005.

## Recall anchors

- No register row, no ship: markets and purposes are enumerated before build.
- Lawful basis is per purpose, never per product.
- A field with no purpose is deleted, not policy-washed.
- Conflicts are logged and escalated, never averaged away.
- This skill builds artifacts for counsel; it never declares compliance.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every market, feature, and user type has a register row (LG-001, G-LG-001).
- [ ] Every processing purpose has a recorded lawful basis (LG-003).
- [ ] Every data-map category states purpose, lawful basis, and retention period (LG-004, LG-007, G-LG-002).
- [ ] No form or schema field lacks a registered purpose (LG-005).
- [ ] DPIA and DPO trigger tests recorded, including negative outcomes (LG-006, G-LG-005).
- [ ] No register row is past its review date (LG-009, G-LG-003).
- [ ] No LG-011 stop condition is un-escalated; no public compliance claim lacks a tested control (LG-011, BAN-LG-001).

## Department D15 — developer-experience

<!-- generated from skills/developer-experience/code-generation/SKILL.md -->

# code-generation

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenAPI Generator overview and workflow — https://nordicapis.com/introduction-to-openapi-generator/ ; OpenAPI Generator usage in practice — https://apidog.com/blog/openapi-generator-5/ ; OpenAPI Specification v3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0
- **Depends on:** dependency-management, dev-environment
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** code is produced mechanically from a machine-readable source — an OpenAPI description (clients, server stubs, types), a database schema (ORM models), or project templates (scaffolding) — and whenever generated output already in the repo changes.
- **Do NOT use when:** the code is written by hand, however repetitive it feels; hand-written code belongs to its owning skill. Do not use generation to produce a finished-looking feature: a generated scaffold is a starting shape, not an implementation.

## Rules

1. **DX-041 — Named source of truth.** Every generated artifact traces to one machine-readable source committed in the repo — an OpenAPI description, a schema, or a template set. The generation command and its source are recorded in the project config; output with no named source is deleted, not adopted.
2. **DX-042 — Never hand-edit output.** A change to generated code is made in the source or the template, then regenerated. A hand edit in a generated file is a defect, even if the edit itself is correct.
3. **DX-043 — Generated header.** Every generated file carries the standard header naming the generator, the generator version, and the source file it was generated from. A file in a generated directory without the header is flagged, not assumed hand-written.
4. **DX-044 — Generator pinned.** The generator and its exact version are declared in the dependency manifest and lockfile like any other dependency. Generating with an unpinned or locally different generator version is not permitted.
5. **DX-045 — Deterministic regeneration.** The same source plus the same generator version produces byte-identical output on any machine. Generators that embed timestamps, absolute paths, or unordered iteration are configured or wrapped until the output is stable.
6. **DX-046 — One output rule, stated.** Generated output is either committed (so a source change shows as an output diff in review) or built fresh in CI and never committed. The project states which rule applies; a mixture of both is drift waiting to happen.
7. **DX-047 — Source reviewed like code.** The spec or schema change goes through the same review as a code change. Generation is never a route for an unreviewed API or data-model change to enter the codebase disguised as a mechanical update.
8. **DX-048 — Generated code passes every gate.** Generated code is linted, type-checked, and tested by the same pipeline as hand-written code. "Generated" is not an exemption from any project gate.
9. **DX-049 — Scaffolds fail loudly.** A generated stub that is not yet implemented throws an explicit not-implemented error or carries a failing test. It never returns canned data that callers or UI can mistake for real behavior.
10. **DX-050 — Template overrides are minimal and documented.** Custom templates are versioned with the project. Where a stock template is overridden, the override is as small as possible and the reason is recorded next to the template.
11. **DX-051 — Regeneration runs in CI.** CI regenerates from the committed source and diffs against the committed output (where output is committed). Any difference fails the build; drift is never merged and fixed later.
12. **DX-052 — Hand-written logic lives outside generated files.** Custom behavior goes in files the generator never overwrites — separate modules, registered hooks, or the generator's documented extension points. If no extension point exists, wrap the generated code; do not fork it by editing it.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-021 — The hand-edited generated file.** Banned: editing generated output directly instead of changing the source or template and regenerating. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: a developer patches a validation rule inside the generated API client; the next regeneration silently reverts it, and the client and server disagree until a user hits the bug. Instead: change the OpenAPI description or the template, regenerate, and commit source and output together. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-022 — The unmarked generated file.** Banned: generated output shipped without the generated-file header naming generator, version, and source. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Bad: a generated parser lands with no header; review flags it as copy-paste duplication and a god function, and a later editor "cleans it up" by hand. Instead: configure the generator to emit the standard header on every file, and fail the header scan (G-DX-023) on any file missing it. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-023 — The canned-data stub.** Banned: a generated endpoint or function that returns sample data, an empty success, or a hardcoded result while callers and UI treat the feature as working. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: the generated `listInvoices` stub returns two sample invoices; the billing page ships displaying them as the customer's real records. Instead: leave the stub throwing an explicit not-implemented error until the real implementation replaces it (DX-049). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-024 — The unpinned generator.** Banned: generating from a globally installed, latest, or otherwise unrecorded generator version. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: two developers regenerate the same spec a week apart and get different output because one's generator updated; the diff is noise and the real change is unreviewable. Instead: pin the generator and its version in the manifest and lockfile (DX-044) and generate only through the project's recorded command. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-025 — The gate-exempt generated directory.** Banned: excluding generated code from lint, type checking, or tests "because it is generated." Defeats: DET-CODE-004. Bad: the generated client calls a method the API library does not have; with type checking disabled for that directory, the hallucinated call reaches production and fails at runtime. Instead: run the full pipeline over generated code like any other code (DX-048); fix failures at the source or template. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-021 — Drift check.** Verifies: DX-042, DX-045, DX-051. Check: automated — in CI, regenerate from the committed source into a temporary directory (`<generate command> --output /tmp/regen`) and run `diff -r /tmp/regen <generated dir>`; also run `git status --porcelain <generated dir>` after a local regeneration. Pass: zero differences. Fail: block the merge; the fix is made in the source or template, never by committing the drift. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-022 — Determinism check.** Verifies: DX-044, DX-045. Check: automated — run the recorded generation command twice in clean checkouts and compare `find <generated dir> -type f -exec sha256sum {} +` output between the runs. Pass: identical hash lists. Fail: block; find and remove the nondeterminism (timestamp, path, ordering) before any output is committed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-023 — Header scan.** Verifies: DX-043. Check: automated — `grep -rL "<generated-header marker>" <generated dir>` returns no files, and a grep for manual-edit markers in generated files returns nothing. Pass: every generated file carries the header naming generator, version, and source. Fail: block; regenerate with the header configured. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-024 — Full pipeline over generated code.** Verifies: DX-048. Check: automated — run the project's lint, type check, and test suite with no exclusion for generated directories. Pass: all three pass. Fail: block; the correction goes into the source or template and is regenerated, not patched in the output. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-025 — Stub honesty check.** Verifies: DX-049. Check: automated plus spot check — grep generated stubs for canned return bodies (literal arrays/objects returned from operations with no implementation), and exercise one unimplemented generated endpoint. Pass: every unimplemented operation throws an explicit not-implemented error; no generated stub returns sample data as if real. Fail: block the feature from being presented as working until implemented. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The quiet regeneration.** Output is regenerated as a side effect of an unrelated change, producing a huge mechanical diff nobody reviews. Catch it: if a diff touches generated files whose source did not change, stop — that is drift or a generator-version change, and it gets its own commit and explanation.
- **Template fork drift.** A stock template is copied into the project "temporarily" and then edited for months, until upgrading the generator means re-applying a fork nobody understands. Catch it: diff project templates against the stock versions; every difference beyond the documented overrides (DX-050) is removed or documented.
- **Generation as architecture.** New modules are added to the spec mainly because generating them is easy, so the API grows surfaces nobody needs. Catch it: review the source diff first (DX-047) and ask what consumer each new operation serves before looking at the output at all.
- **The almost-generated file.** A file starts as generated output, is copied elsewhere, and is then hand-maintained — two versions of the same logic, one stale. Catch it: search for near-duplicates of generated files outside the generated directory; the copy is deleted or replaced by an import.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A hand-edited client, fixed at the source](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DX-042.
- [Example 2 — A canned-data stub made honest](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DX-049.
- [Example 3 — Nondeterministic output from an unpinned generator](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DX-044, DX-045.

## Recall anchors

- Edit the source, never the output.
- Same source, same generator, same bytes — on any machine.
- If it is generated, it is marked, pinned, and gated.
- A stub that lies is worse than a stub that throws.
- Drift in CI is a failed build, not a follow-up task.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every generated artifact names its committed source of truth (DX-041).
- [ ] Generator and version are pinned in the manifest and lockfile (DX-044).
- [ ] Drift check passes: regeneration matches committed output exactly (G-DX-021).
- [ ] Determinism check passes: two clean regenerations are byte-identical (G-DX-022).
- [ ] Every generated file carries the standard header (G-DX-023).
- [ ] Lint, type check, and tests pass with no generated-directory exclusions (G-DX-024).
- [ ] No unimplemented stub returns canned data; stubs throw not-implemented (G-DX-025).
- [ ] Template overrides are minimal, versioned, and documented (DX-050).

# dependency-management

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Dependabot version updates — https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-supply-chain/secure-your-dependencies/configure-version-updates ; Renovate npm manager and lockfile maintenance — https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/manager/npm/
- **Depends on:** dev-environment (toolchain pins the installs run under), tech-debt (debt register holds stale-update reasons)
- **Feeds into:** dependency-safety (D7 — receives routed advisories), versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** adding, updating, pinning, or removing a dependency; configuring update automation; reviewing a change that touches the manifest or the lockfile.
- **Do NOT use when:** responding to a published vulnerability or a compromised package — that is D7's dependency-safety, which owns advisory triage, patch SLAs, and incident response. This skill owns the everyday discipline of choosing, pinning, and updating dependencies; it routes advisories to D7 and never runs a parallel security process.

## Rules

1. **DX-061 — The lockfile is committed and canonical.** The lockfile is version-controlled next to the manifest. A change that edits one without the other is incomplete and does not merge.
2. **DX-062 — Installs are frozen and reproducible.** Local setup and CI install from the lockfile in frozen mode (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, or the ecosystem equivalent). An install that modifies the lockfile is a failed install, not a fix.
3. **DX-063 — Every new direct dependency is justified in one line.** The change description states what the package does, why the standard library and the existing dependencies do not cover it, and its maintenance status. No justification, no merge.
4. **DX-064 — Update automation is configured in the repo.** A committed `.github/dependabot.yml` or `renovate.json` drives updates: minor and patch grouped, majors individual, security updates ungrouped and immediate. The config validates against its schema.
5. **DX-065 — Updates land in small, reviewed batches.** Grouped minor/patch updates merge as small batches; a major update is its own change. A single change never bumps many unrelated packages at once.
6. **DX-066 — Read the changelog before a major update.** The change description names the breaking changes from the release notes and the code changes they required. "Tests pass" alone is not a major-update review.
7. **DX-067 — Version ranges are deliberate.** Applications pin exact versions. Caret ranges appear only in published libraries where the ecosystem convention makes them the consumer contract. Wildcard ranges are prohibited (BAN-DX-032).
8. **DX-068 — No stale update without a recorded reason.** No update PR or report entry stays unaddressed past the project's stated window (default 30 days) unless the debt register records why and when it will be taken.
9. **DX-069 — Dead and duplicate dependencies are removed.** A package nothing imports is deleted from the manifest in the same change that removed its last use; two packages serving one job collapse to one. Removal is part of the work, not a later cleanup.
10. **DX-070 — The manifest stays coherent.** Every manifest entry is imported, or its build/plugin role is documented in the manifest's config; every import resolves to a declared entry. Transitive packages are never imported directly.
11. **DX-071 — Advisories route to D7, currency stays here.** Audit findings are handed to dependency-safety for triage and patching priority; this skill's job is only to keep versions current enough that D7's patches are small. Never sit on a known advisory because "the update is scheduled."
12. **DX-072 — An update merges only on a green suite.** The full test suite passes in CI on the updated tree, installed frozen from the updated lockfile, before any update change merges.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-031 — Uncommitted or casually regenerated lockfile.** Banned: deleting the lockfile and regenerating it inside an unrelated change, or leaving it out of version control. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: a feature PR deletes `package-lock.json` and commits a fresh one, silently moving 40 transitive versions. Instead: regenerate the lockfile only in a dedicated update change whose diff is the review. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-032 — Wildcard or `latest` version ranges.** Banned: `"*"`, `latest`, or an open range in any manifest entry. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `"axios": "*"` installs whatever exists on the day of the build. Instead: pin the exact version for applications; use a caret range only for a published library per DX-067. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-033 — Manifest and lockfile changed out of step.** Banned: a change that edits the manifest without the lockfile, or the lockfile without the manifest. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `package.json` gains a dependency; the lockfile is "fixed later," so CI and the author's machine resolve different trees. Instead: generate both in the same local install and commit them together (DX-061). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-034 — Duplicate libraries for one job.** Banned: two packages serving the same purpose in one codebase (two date libraries, two HTTP clients, two validation libraries). Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `moment` is added to a project already using `dayjs` because one snippet online used it. Instead: use the package already in the tree; if the new one is genuinely better, migrate fully and remove the old in the same change. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-035 — Hand-edited lockfile.** Banned: editing lockfile entries by hand to force a version, instead of changing the manifest and letting the package manager resolve. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: a version string inside `package-lock.json` is edited to silence a conflict; the next install rewrites it and the build changes. Instead: express the constraint in the manifest (pin, override field) and regenerate the lockfile with the package manager. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-031 — Frozen-lockfile install.** Verifies: DX-061, DX-062. Check: in a clean CI checkout run `npm ci` (or the ecosystem frozen equivalent), then `git status --porcelain`. Pass: install exits 0 and the lockfile shows no modification. Fail: block merge; the manifest/lockfile pair is regenerated and recommitted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-032 — Production audit threshold.** Verifies: DX-071. Check: run `npm audit --production` / `pip-audit` / ecosystem equivalent in CI. Pass: no high or critical advisories in production dependencies; any finding is logged and routed to D7 dependency-safety the same day. Fail: block release until D7 triages. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-033 — Update-bot config present and valid.** Verifies: DX-064. Check: assert `.github/dependabot.yml` or `renovate.json` exists and validate it (`npx renovate-config-validator` or the Dependabot schema check). Pass: file present, schema-valid, majors ungrouped, security updates ungrouped. Fail: block; add or fix the config before further dependency work. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-034 — Stale-dependency report.** Verifies: DX-065, DX-068. Check: run `npm outdated` (or equivalent) and list direct dependencies more than one major behind, or with an update unaddressed past the 30-day window. Pass: the list is empty, or every entry has a debt-register reason with a take-by date. Fail: warn and register the items before the next feature change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-035 — Manifest coherence scan.** Verifies: DX-069, DX-070. Check: run `npx depcheck` (or equivalent) and diff the import list against the manifest. Pass: no unused and no missing dependencies, except build/plugin packages documented in config. Fail: block; remove or declare before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Dependency as first resort.** A package is added for a ten-line job the standard library already does. Catch it at the DX-063 justification line: if it cannot name why the platform fails, the package does not enter.
- **Phantom transitive imports.** Code imports a package that only arrives transitively through another dependency; it breaks without warning when the parent updates. Catch it with G-DX-035 and by asking of every import: is this declared by us?
- **The update snowball.** Update PRs are ignored for months until dozens of majors, some breaking, must land together under time pressure. Catch it by watching the G-DX-034 report trend, not its snapshot.
- **Manifest copied from another project.** A new project starts by pasting a familiar manifest wholesale, inheriting packages nothing will import. Catch it at the first coherence scan: every entry must trace to a use in this project.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — A second date library for one snippet](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-063, DX-069.
- [Example 2 — Wildcard range and a regenerated lockfile](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-061, DX-067.
- [Example 3 — One giant "update everything" change](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-065, DX-066.

## Recall anchors

- The manifest is the intent; the lockfile is the truth.
- Every dependency is inventory: justified, pinned, pruned.
- Majors land one at a time, changelog in hand.
- Security response belongs to D7; currency belongs here.
- If nothing imports it, it does not stay.

## Checklist

- [ ] Lockfile committed, and a frozen install leaves it unchanged (G-DX-031).
- [ ] Every new direct dependency carries its one-line justification (DX-063).
- [ ] Update-bot config exists, validates, and keeps majors and security updates ungrouped (G-DX-033).
- [ ] No update is past the stale window without a debt-register reason (G-DX-034).
- [ ] Coherence scan is clean: nothing unused, nothing missing, no transitive imports (G-DX-035).
- [ ] Major updates landed individually with their breaking changes named (DX-065, DX-066).
- [ ] Full suite green on the updated tree before merge (DX-072).

# dev-environment

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://containers.dev/implementors/json_reference/ ; https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/ ; https://12factor.net/config
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: setup is derived from the project's own repo (its manifests, version pins, and environment variables) so a fresh machine can run it; it is a starting-point skill and consumes no other skill's output. It feeds monorepo-tooling and dependency-management.
- **Feeds into:** monorepo-tooling, dependency-management

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project is created or handed over; a new machine, container, or CI runner must reach a running app; setup instructions, tool versions, or environment variables are being written or changed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which versions to bump in an existing dependency set (use dependency-management), how releases are numbered (use versioning), or how production is deployed (use D6 deployment skills) — this skill covers the local development environment only.

## Rules

1. **DX-001 — One bootstrap command.** Exactly one documented command (e.g. `make setup`, `npm run setup`, or `mise install` plus the install step) takes a clean clone to a running app with the test suite passing. Any second manual step is a defect in the setup, not a README footnote.
2. **DX-002 — One pin file.** Every runtime and CLI tool version is declared exactly once, in one committed pin file (`mise.toml`, `.tool-versions`, or the ecosystem equivalent). No other file restates a tool version.
3. **DX-003 — Exact pins, never "latest".** The pin file and dependency manifests carry exact versions for tools and application dependencies. Floating references (`latest`, `*`, unpinned "current LTS") are not permitted anywhere in setup instructions or config.
4. **DX-004 — Lockfile committed, installs frozen.** The dependency lockfile is committed, and local and CI installs run in frozen/CI mode (`npm ci`, `--frozen-lockfile`, or equivalent) so an install never silently rewrites the resolved set.
5. **DX-005 — `.env.example` is complete.** Every variable the code reads appears in `.env.example` with a placeholder value and a one-line purpose note. A variable read by code but missing from the example file is a defect.
6. **DX-006 — Placeholders only.** Example files contain only obviously non-functional values (`change-me`, `sk_test_...`, reserved example hosts). No real secret, token, or connection string appears in any committed file, example or otherwise.
7. **DX-007 — Config fails fast.** The app validates required configuration at startup and exits non-zero, naming each missing or malformed variable. There is no silent fallback to a default environment, host, or credential.
8. **DX-008 — Setup is idempotent.** Running the bootstrap command a second time changes nothing and breaks nothing: no duplicate installs, no clobbered local config, no appended duplicates in generated files.
9. **DX-009 — CI runs the same pins.** CI installs the toolchain from the same pin file and the dependencies from the same lockfile as a laptop. A CI-only version override is drift, treated as a defect under DX-002.
10. **DX-010 — Services are declared, not hand-started.** When the app needs backing services (database, cache, queue), they are declared in `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` and/or a compose file committed with the project, and the bootstrap starts them. "Start Postgres locally first" is not a setup step.
11. **DX-011 — Config comes from the environment.** Per-deploy values arrive as environment variables (Twelve-Factor Factor III), strictly separate from code. Code contains no `if (environment === "prod")` branches selecting hardcoded URLs, hosts, or credentials.
12. **DX-012 — README references, never restates.** The README names the bootstrap command and links the pin file and `.env.example`. It restates no version numbers and no variable lists, so there is exactly one place each can drift from.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-001 — Real secret in an example or config file.** Banned: a working API key, password, or connection string committed in `.env.example`, a config sample, or source. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: `.env.example` ships with the project's live Stripe key copied from the dashboard "so the demo works." Instead: placeholder values only, per DX-006. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-002 — Floating tool versions.** Banned: setup instructions or manifests that install `latest`, a wildcard range, or an unpinned "current LTS" for any runtime or CLI tool. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: the README says "install Node (latest LTS) and the newest Docker." Instead: pin the exact version in the pin file and install from it, per DX-002 and DX-003. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-003 — Setup steps outside the bootstrap.** Banned: any required setup step that lives only in a wiki, chat message, or a human's memory instead of the bootstrap command. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: after cloning, a new developer must "ask in chat for the extra step" that creates the local storage bucket. Instead: fold the step into the bootstrap command, per DX-001. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-004 — Silent default to production.** Banned: a fallback that points the app at a production host, database, or credential when a configuration variable is unset. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Bad: `DATABASE_URL` defaults to the production database URL when the variable is missing, so a misconfigured laptop writes to prod. Instead: no default for environment-selecting variables; fail fast naming the variable, per DX-007. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-005 — A committed real `.env` file.** Banned: committing a `.env` (or equivalent) containing real values, or leaving it out of `.gitignore`. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Bad: `.env` with the real database password is tracked in git "temporarily" and never removed from history. Instead: commit `.env.example` with placeholders only and gitignore the real file, per DX-005 and DX-006. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-001 — Fresh-clone bootstrap test.** Verifies: DX-001, DX-008, DX-010. Check (automated): in a clean container or VM, `git clone <repo> test-clone && cd test-clone && <bootstrap command>`, then run the test suite and the app's health check; run the bootstrap a second time and repeat. Pass: app starts, tests pass, second run changes nothing, and zero undocumented steps were needed. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-002 — Example-file secret scan.** Verifies: DX-006. Check (automated): run a secret scanner (gitleaks or equivalent) over the tree, plus `git grep -nE "sk_live|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY" -- .env.example "*.example" "*.sample"` must return nothing. Pass: zero hits and every example value is an obvious placeholder. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-003 — Pin singularity and CI parity check.** Verifies: DX-002, DX-003, DX-009, DX-012. Check (automated): the pin file exists; `grep -rniE "latest" README.md docs/ <setup files>` returns no install instruction using it; CI configuration references the pin file and frozen install mode rather than naming its own tool versions. Pass: one pin file, referenced by CI, no floating versions anywhere. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-004 — Environment-variable coverage check.** Verifies: DX-005. Check (automated): extract variable names read by the code (e.g. `grep -rhoE "process\.env\.[A-Z_]+|os\.environ\[\"[A-Z_]+\"\]" src/`), extract keys from `.env.example`, and diff. Pass: zero variables missing from `.env.example`, and every entry has a purpose note. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-005 — Fail-fast startup check.** Verifies: DX-007, DX-011. Check (automated): start the app with one required variable unset, then with it set to a malformed value. Pass: both runs exit non-zero with an error naming the variable; no run silently connects to a default environment. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Bootstrap that "mostly works."** The setup script prints warnings, skips failed steps, and exits 0, leaving a half-built environment that fails later in confusing ways. Catch it by checking the bootstrap's exit code on an induced failure — it must be non-zero.
- **Pin file present but bypassed.** The pin file exists, but developers actually run globally installed tools and only CI uses the pins, so version bugs surface at release time. Catch it by asking what `which <tool>` resolves to in a fresh shell after bootstrap — it must be the pinned install.
- **`.env.example` updated "later."** New variables land in code during feature work while the example file waits for a cleanup pass that never comes. Catch it by running G-DX-004 on every change that touches configuration reads, not only at release.
- **Warm-machine timing.** Setup is declared "fast" based on the author's machine with warm caches and pre-installed tools. Catch it by timing only the clean-container run from G-DX-001 and recording that number.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The nine-step README](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-001, DX-002.
- [Example 2 — The example file with a real key](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-005, DX-006, DX-007.
- [Example 3 — CI on a different Node](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-003, DX-009.

## Recall anchors

- One command from clone to running — a second manual step is a defect.
- Versions live in one pin file; docs reference it, never restate it.
- Examples hold placeholders; real secrets live nowhere in git.
- Missing config fails fast and names the variable — never defaults to prod.
- If it only works on your machine, the gate has failed, not the machine.

## Checklist

- [ ] One bootstrap command reaches a running app with tests green from a clean clone (DX-001, G-DX-001).
- [ ] Every tool version pinned exactly once in one committed pin file; no `latest` anywhere (DX-002, DX-003, G-DX-003).
- [ ] Lockfile committed; installs run frozen/CI mode locally and in CI (DX-004).
- [ ] `.env.example` lists every variable the code reads, with placeholder value and purpose note (DX-005, G-DX-004).
- [ ] Secret scan over examples and tree returns zero real credentials (DX-006, G-DX-002).
- [ ] App fails fast, naming any missing or malformed required variable (DX-007, G-DX-005).
- [ ] Bootstrap run twice in the clean test with no change on the second run (DX-008, G-DX-001).
- [ ] CI installs from the same pin file and lockfile as a laptop (DX-009, G-DX-003).
- [ ] Backing services declared in devcontainer/compose and started by the bootstrap (DX-010).

<!-- generated from skills/developer-experience/legacy-migration/SKILL.md -->

# legacy-migration

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://kindatechnical.com/software-engineering/large-scale-change-strangler-branch-abstraction.html ; https://microservices.io/post/refactoring/2023/06/21/strangler-fig-application-pattern-incremental-modernization-to-services.md.html ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html
- **Depends on:** tech-debt
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, versioning

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a working legacy system, module, or data shape must be replaced — a framework swap, a service extraction, a store or API migration — and the old behavior must keep serving users while the new one is built.
- **Do NOT use when:** the change preserves behavior inside one implementation with no old/new coexistence (use refactoring), the code is being deleted with no replacement (just delete it, with a decision-log entry), or the "legacy" system has no users yet (rewrite freely; there is nothing to migrate).

## Rules

1. **DX-121 — The plan is slices, seams, and rollbacks.** Every migration plan names its slices (one capability at a time), the seam for each slice (routing facade, abstraction layer, or expand–migrate–contract for data/API shapes), and the rollback for each step. A plan whose migration is one big step is rejected before work starts.
2. **DX-122 — Characterization tests pin behavior before anything moves.** Before a slice is touched, tests are written against the legacy implementation recording what it actually does today — including its quirks and error behavior — on production-shaped cases. The replacement is built to pass these tests, not to match a spec written from memory.
3. **DX-123 — The seam goes in first.** The facade, router, or abstraction layer is introduced and deployed with all traffic still flowing to the legacy implementation before any new implementation exists. A seam that only appears together with the new code cannot be rolled back independently and is not a seam.
4. **DX-124 — Legacy stays deployable and is the fallback.** The legacy implementation remains buildable, deployable, and monitored for the whole coexistence period. It is never edited into a half-migrated state, and no migration step may leave the project with only the new path working.
5. **DX-125 — Parallel run with compared outputs before cutover.** Before a slice's traffic flips, the new implementation runs against the same recorded production-shaped inputs as the legacy one (shadow calls, replayed requests, or dual execution) and the outputs are diffed. Every diff is either fixed or recorded as an intended behavior change with a decider named. Cutover on untested equivalence is a guess.
6. **DX-126 — Cutover is per slice and reversible in one change.** Traffic flips slice by slice through the routing seam (route rule or toggle), never all slices at once. Flipping back to legacy is a single configuration change, rehearsed in staging before the first production flip.
7. **DX-127 — Data migration is rehearsed and reversible, or its point of no return is explicit.** Every data move is first run against a copy of production-shaped data with row counts and checksums compared. The migration is reversible until a stated point of no return; a verified backup is taken at that point, and the point is named in the plan before the rehearsal, not discovered during it.
8. **DX-128 — No new features on scheduled legacy paths.** Once a slice is scheduled for migration, its legacy implementation receives fixes only. A feature that must land before the slice migrates is built in the new implementation, or the schedule is formally changed — building it in legacy "just this once" moves the target forever.
9. **DX-129 — Coexistence has an end date.** The plan states the date or release by which coexistence ends and the legacy path is eliminated. "Both systems for now" with no end date is not a stage of the plan; it is how migrations fail.
10. **DX-130 — Elimination is a separate, later step.** The legacy path is deleted only after its replacement has carried real production traffic for the soak period named in the plan, as its own reviewed change — never in the same change as the cutover, and never on cutover day.
11. **DX-131 — Shape changes use Parallel Change.** A breaking data or API shape change goes expand (new shape added alongside old, both written) → migrate (readers and writers moved, old shape still valid) → contract (old shape removed). No step breaks a reader that has not yet migrated.
12. **DX-132 — Migration state is recorded as it changes.** Each slice's stage (seamed, built, parallel-running, cut over, eliminated) and its current routing are recorded in the migration plan and progress.md at the moment they change. The routing table in production and the plan's stated stage must agree; disagreement is a defect found by G-DX-062, not a documentation nit.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-061 — Big-bang cutover.** Banned: freezing the legacy system, rewriting it wholesale, and switching everything over in one release. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: the store is rebuilt over a month behind a feature freeze and launched in one deploy; the first production bug has no partial rollback, only the whole old system or the whole new one. Instead: slice the migration behind a routing seam and flip one capability at a time (DX-121, DX-123, DX-126). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-062 — Legacy deleted at cutover.** Banned: removing, undeploying, or letting the legacy implementation rot in the same change that flips traffic to its replacement, leaving dead references and no fallback. Defeats: DET-CODE-002. Bad: the cutover PR deletes the old billing module and its routes; a defect found on day two cannot be rolled back because the fallback no longer builds. Instead: keep legacy deployable through the soak period and delete it in a separate elimination step (DX-124, DX-130). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-063 — New features built into a scheduled legacy path.** Banned: implementing new behavior in a legacy implementation whose slice is already scheduled, so the feature exists only in code about to be replaced and must be built twice. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Bad: a discount feature is added to the legacy checkout "because the migration is still weeks away"; the replacement team re-implements it from scratch and the two versions diverge. Instead: build it in the new implementation, or formally reschedule the slice (DX-128). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-064 — Migration with no characterization tests.** Banned: replacing a legacy path whose current behavior is pinned by no tests, so "equivalent" is asserted from reading the code or from the original spec. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Bad: the pricing engine is reimplemented from its README; production reveals rounding and edge-case behavior the README never mentioned, one invoice at a time. Instead: write characterization tests against the running legacy behavior first and build the replacement to pass them (DX-122). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-065 — Legacy kept as commented-out code after elimination.** Banned: leaving the removed implementation commented out, copied into a `legacy/` folder inside the shipped code, or otherwise retained in the working tree "just in case" after the eliminate step. Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Bad: 900 lines of the old search implementation sit commented above its replacement, still indexed, still confusing every reader and search. Instead: delete it — version control is the archive — and record the elimination in the plan (DX-130, DX-132). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-061 — Parity suite on both implementations (automated).** Verifies: DX-122, DX-125. Check: run the slice's characterization/parity suite twice, once per implementation — `IMPL=legacy npm run test:parity -- <slice>` and `IMPL=new npm run test:parity -- <slice>` (or the project's equivalent recorded in the plan) — over the recorded production-shaped case set. Pass: exit 0 on both runs, and every output diff between the two runs is either zero or listed in the plan as an intended change with a named decider. Fail: block cutover for that slice. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-062 — Route audit (automated).** Verifies: DX-126, DX-132. Check: dump the facade/router's effective routing table and diff it against the migration plan's stated current stage: every route the plan marks "cut over" points at the new implementation, every other route at legacy, with no unlisted routes. Pass: empty diff. Fail: block shipment; reconcile the table or the plan before proceeding. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-063 — Rollback drill (automated/staging).** Verifies: DX-124, DX-126. Check: in staging, flip the slice's routing back to legacy using only the documented single configuration change, then run the primary-flow smoke tests against the legacy path. Pass: smoke tests green on legacy with no code change and no redeploy of the new implementation. Fail: block the production cutover — a rollback that has never been executed is assumed not to exist. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-064 — Post-elimination dead-reference sweep (automated).** Verifies: DX-130. Check: after an eliminate step, `grep -rn '<removed module/endpoint name>' --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=node_modules .` over source, config, and routing, plus a full build and test run. Pass: no references outside the migration plan and changelog; build and tests green. Fail: block shipment until references are removed or the elimination is reverted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-065 — Plan completeness review (manual).** Verifies: DX-121, DX-127, DX-129. Check: before the first slice is built, read the migration plan and confirm every slice names its seam, its rollback, its data point-of-no-return and backup (or "no data change"), and that the plan carries a coexistence end date. Pass: all fields present for all slices. Fail: block the start of migration work; a plan missing a rollback or an end date is not yet a plan. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Seam theater.** A facade exists on paper but callers still reach the legacy code directly in a dozen places, so flipping the route changes nothing for most traffic. Catch it before cutover by grepping for direct references to the legacy module outside the seam — the seam must be the only door.
- **Parity by eyeball.** The parallel run happens, someone scrolls the outputs, declares them "basically the same," and the diffs are never enumerated. Catch it by requiring the diff list as a file in the plan: if it is not written down, the comparison did not happen.
- **The permanent pilot.** One easy slice migrates, the announcement declares victory, and the remaining slices quietly never schedule — coexistence becomes the architecture. Catch it at each review by comparing slices eliminated against the plan's end date (DX-129), not against slices started.
- **Rollback by redeploy.** "We can always roll back" means checking out the old release and redeploying everything, untested, under incident pressure. Catch it with G-DX-063: if rollback is not a configuration flip that has been drilled, it is a hope, not a rollback.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The one-release rewrite plan](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-121.
- [Example 2 — Cutover on a README](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-122, DX-125.
- [Example 3 — Deleted on cutover day](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-124, DX-130.

## Recall anchors

- Slice it behind a seam, or do not start.
- Pin the behavior before you move it — tests first, replacement second.
- Legacy is the fallback until the replacement has carried real traffic.
- Cutover is a routing flip; rollback is the same flip, backwards, already drilled.
- Coexistence without an end date is the failure mode, not a stage.

## Checklist

- [ ] The plan names every slice, its seam, and its rollback; no single-step plan (DX-121, G-DX-065).
- [ ] Characterization tests pass against the legacy implementation before the replacement is built (DX-122).
- [ ] The seam is deployed with all traffic still on legacy before new code lands behind it (DX-123).
- [ ] Parity suite passes on both implementations; every diff is fixed or recorded as intended (DX-125, G-DX-061).
- [ ] The rollback flip has been drilled in staging for this slice (DX-126, G-DX-063).
- [ ] Data moves are rehearsed on a copy; the point of no return and its backup are named (DX-127).
- [ ] No new features were added to scheduled legacy paths during this work (DX-128).
- [ ] The plan's coexistence end date stands, slice stages are recorded, and elimination is scheduled as its own later change (DX-129, DX-130, DX-132).

<!-- generated from skills/developer-experience/monorepo-tooling/SKILL.md -->

# monorepo-tooling

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Turborepo concepts and pipeline practice — https://www.devtoolsguide.com/turborepo-monorepo-guide/ ; mise dev tools (task/tool layer at repo root) — https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/
- **Depends on:** dev-environment, dependency-management
- **Feeds into:** versioning, ci-cd

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project has two or more deployables (web app plus API, worker, or second app) or a package genuinely shared by more than one of them, and the operator wants shared code and atomic cross-package changes in one repository.
- **Do NOT use when:** the project is a single app with no shared package — a plain single-package repo (or separate repos per deployable) is the honest default. Do not scaffold a monorepo for a landing page, and do not use this skill to split one app into packages that only exist to look architectural.

## Rules

1. **DX-021 — Stated trigger, recorded.** A monorepo is created only when the trigger holds: 2+ deployables, or one package consumed by 2+ deployables. The reason is recorded in the project's stack file or an ADR before scaffolding. No trigger, no monorepo.
2. **DX-022 — One lockfile, at the root.** Exactly one lockfile exists, at the repository root, committed. CI installs from it frozen; a package-level lockfile or an install that modifies the root lockfile is a defect.
3. **DX-023 — Declared internal dependencies only.** Every internal package a package uses is declared in that package's manifest. The task graph (build/lint/test order) is derived from those declarations by the task runner — never from a hand-maintained build-order list or script sequence.
4. **DX-024 — Entry points, not reach-across.** A package imports another package only through its declared package name and public entry point (or declared export subpaths). Relative imports that cross a package boundary are forbidden.
5. **DX-025 — Acyclic, tool-enforced boundaries.** The package dependency graph has no cycles, and boundary rules (allowed dependency directions, entry-point-only imports) are enforced by lint or graph tooling in CI — not by convention or review memory.
6. **DX-026 — Every task declares outputs.** Each build/test task in the pipeline config declares its outputs. A task that cannot declare outputs is marked uncacheable in the config with the reason written next to it.
7. **DX-027 — Cache keys cover all inputs.** Cache keys include the lockfile hash and every environment variable the task reads. A cache hit after any input changed is a correctness bug to be fixed in the key, never a speedup to be celebrated.
8. **DX-028 — Shared configs live in config packages.** TypeScript, lint, and test-preset configs live in internal config packages and are extended or referenced by each package. Config files are never copy-pasted per package.
9. **DX-029 — Root scripts are the only entry points.** `build`, `lint`, `test`, and `dev` run from the root and fan out through the task graph. Documentation names only root scripts; per-package scripts are implementation detail.
10. **DX-030 — One versioning model, chosen up front.** The repo states its model before the first release: independent per-package versioning (Changesets-style) or one fixed version for the whole repo. The two are never mixed by accident; internal dependency ranges follow the chosen model.
11. **DX-031 — Affected-only CI for changes.** Pull-request CI builds and tests only the changed packages and their dependents (affected/filter run). A change to a shared package automatically pulls every dependent into the run. The full pipeline runs on merge to the main branch.
12. **DX-032 — Deliberate internal ranges.** Internal dependencies use the workspace protocol (or the ecosystem equivalent) so local packages link locally. No internal or external dependency is declared with `*` or `latest`.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-011 — Reach-across imports.** Banned: importing another package's source by relative path (`../../api/src/db/client`) instead of its declared entry point. Defeats: DET-CODE-014. Bad: `apps/web` imports `../../packages/api/src/internal/session.ts`, so the API package cannot move a file without breaking the web build. Instead: declare `@repo/api` in the web package's manifest and import the exported entry point. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-012 — Copy-pasted shared configs.** Banned: duplicating `tsconfig`, ESLint, or test-preset files into every package and editing the copies separately. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: five packages carry five near-identical `tsconfig.base.json` copies; one gets `strict: true`, the others silently do not. Instead: one internal config package (e.g. `@repo/tsconfig`) that every package extends. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-013 — Undeclared internal dependency.** Banned: importing an internal package that is not declared in the importing package's manifest, relying on hoisting to make it resolve. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `packages/ui` imports `@repo/utils` with no manifest entry; the build passes by hoisting luck and breaks under a stricter linker, and the task graph omits the edge so `ui` is not rebuilt when `utils` changes. Instead: declare every internal import in the manifest so the graph edge exists. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-014 — Wildcard and latest ranges.** Banned: `*` or `latest` as a version range for any dependency, internal or external. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `"@repo/utils": "*"` and `"react": "latest"` in two manifests, so two installs a week apart produce different trees under the same lockfile discipline. Instead: workspace protocol for internal packages and the project's deliberate range policy for external ones, resolved by the single root lockfile. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-015 — Monorepo without a trigger.** Banned: scaffolding workspaces, a task runner, and shared packages for a single deployable with no shared package. Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: a marketing landing page ships as a four-package monorepo with a task graph, a remote cache, and one app. Instead: a plain single-package repo; adopt this skill when a second deployable or a genuinely shared package appears. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-011 — Double-run cache verification.** Verifies: DX-026, DX-027. Check: automated — from a clean checkout, run the full root pipeline twice (`turbo run build test` or the Nx equivalent); hash all declared outputs after each run and `diff` the two hash lists. Pass: the second run reports cache hits for every unchanged package and the outputs are byte-identical. Fail: block shipment; fix the task's declared outputs or cache inputs. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-012 — Affected-only rebuild test.** Verifies: DX-023, DX-031. Check: automated — in a scratch clone, touch one file in a leaf package and run the CI affected command (e.g. `turbo run build --filter=...HEAD^` or `nx affected`); then touch one file in a shared package and repeat. Pass: the first run builds only the leaf and its dependents, and the second run includes every dependent of the shared package. Fail: block shipment; the graph is missing a declared edge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-013 — Boundary and cycle check.** Verifies: DX-024, DX-025. Check: automated — run the boundary lint/graph check in CI (e.g. the task runner's graph validation plus `grep -rn "from '\.\./" packages/*/src apps/*/src` excluding same-package relative imports), and a cycle detector over the package graph. Pass: zero cross-boundary relative imports and zero cycles. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-014 — Single-lockfile frozen install.** Verifies: DX-022, DX-032. Check: automated — `find . -name "*lock*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` (ecosystem equivalent) returns exactly one lockfile at the root; then a frozen install (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` or equivalent) succeeds and `git status` shows the lockfile unmodified. Pass: one lockfile, frozen install clean. Fail: block the merge. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The dumping-ground shared package.** A `utils` or `shared` package that every package depends on and into which unrelated helpers are thrown, so any leaf change rebuilds the world. Catch it: list the shared package's dependents and its export count; unrelated domains in one package means split it by domain.
- **Cache-hit triumphalism.** Reporting a high cache-hit rate as a performance win while never verifying that hit outputs match a clean build. Catch it: if G-DX-011's byte-identical check has not run since the pipeline config last changed, the hit rate proves nothing.
- **External version drift inside the repo.** Two packages resolving different major versions of the same external library, so the "shared" platform behaves differently per package. Catch it: run the package manager's dedupe/why report; duplicate majors of one library need a recorded reason or a single aligned range.
- **Root script swamp.** Dozens of root scripts that duplicate package scripts with slight variations (`build:web:fast`, `build:web:ci`) until nobody knows the real entry point. Catch it: if a root script does not fan out through the task graph, delete it or move it into the owning package.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Reach-across import replaced by a declared dependency](examples/example-1.md) — corrects DX-023, DX-024.
- [Example 2 — Copy-pasted configs replaced by one config package](examples/example-2.md) — corrects DX-028.
- [Example 3 — Hand-ordered build script replaced by a task graph with honest caching](examples/example-3.md) — corrects DX-023, DX-026, DX-027.

## Recall anchors

- No trigger, no monorepo.
- One repo, one lockfile, one version policy.
- If it is imported, it is declared; the graph comes from the manifests.
- Entry points only — never reach across a boundary.
- A cache hit on changed inputs is a bug, not a speedup.

## Checklist

- [ ] The monorepo trigger is recorded and still holds (DX-021).
- [ ] Exactly one lockfile, at the root, and the frozen install leaves it untouched (G-DX-014).
- [ ] Every internal import is declared in the importing package's manifest (DX-023).
- [ ] Zero cross-boundary relative imports and zero package cycles (G-DX-013).
- [ ] Every task declares outputs, or is marked uncacheable with a reason (DX-026).
- [ ] Double-run check passed: cache hits with byte-identical outputs (G-DX-011).
- [ ] Affected-only run rebuilds a shared package's dependents (G-DX-012).
- [ ] Shared configs come from config packages; no copy-pasted config files (DX-028).
- [ ] The versioning model is stated and internal ranges follow it (DX-030, DX-032).
