# refactoring

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://martinfowler.com/articles/workflowsOfRefactoring/fallback.html ; https://deepwiki.com/gmoral/Books/7.3-refactoring:-improving-the-design-of-existing-code
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: restructuring decisions are made from the code under change itself, read directly, with behavior pinned by the project's existing tests; no other skill's output is an input. It feeds legacy-migration and tech-debt.
- **Feeds into:** legacy-migration, tech-debt

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** code must be restructured — duplication removed, names clarified, a function decomposed, coupling reduced — to make a coming feature or fix easy, or while reading unfamiliar code (comprehension refactoring); the work changes internal structure only.
- **Do NOT use when:** observable behavior must change (that is a feature or fix change, committed separately), a whole system or module is being replaced (use legacy-migration), or the goal is measurable performance improvement (benchmarked performance work, its own change type).
- **Cross-reference:** the commented-out-code pattern banned here as BAN-DX-054 is also banned as standing debt in tech-debt (BAN-DX-042); the two entries cover the same pattern in different moments.

## Rules

1. **DX-101 — Behavior is the contract.** A refactoring leaves observable behavior identical: same outputs, API responses, persisted data, side effects, and error behavior for every input. Any change that alters observable behavior is not a refactoring — it is reclassified, renamed, and reviewed as the feature, fix, or rewrite it actually is.
2. **DX-102 — Safety net before structure.** The full relevant test suite is run and green before the first structural step. Where the area lacks tests, the first step is characterization tests that pin current behavior — including its quirks — and they land in their own preceding commit before any restructuring begins.
3. **DX-103 — Two hats, never both.** While refactoring, no features are added and no bugs are fixed; while adding features, no opportunistic restructuring is folded in. Switching hats is explicit: the refactoring commits and the behavior commits are separate, so each can be reviewed and reverted on its own.
4. **DX-104 — Small, named steps.** Each step is one named transformation from the refactoring catalog (Extract Function, Inline Variable, Change Function Declaration, Rename, Move, …), small enough that the suite runs between steps. A step too big to describe with one catalog name is split before it is committed.
5. **DX-105 — Red means stop and back up.** If the suite goes red mid-refactoring, work stops and the last step is undone or corrected; the suite is never pushed through, and the failure is never "fixed" by adjusting the code's behavior or the test. Two consecutive red steps mean the step size is too large — halve it.
6. **DX-106 — Tests are read-only during a refactoring.** No test file is added to, edited, or deleted inside a refactoring change (characterization tests under DX-102 land before it, separately). A test that appears to need changing is evidence the change alters behavior: stop and reclassify under DX-101.
7. **DX-107 — Refactor toward a named pressure.** Every refactoring change states the design pressure it answers — duplication, coupling, unclear names, runaway complexity — in its description. "Cleaner," "nicer," or "more modern" is not a pressure and does not justify a change.
8. **DX-108 — Rule of Three for abstractions.** A shared abstraction is extracted only when the same logic or shape appears for the third time. The first occurrence is written plainly; the second is duplicated deliberately and noted; the third triggers the extraction.
9. **DX-109 — The public surface does not move.** Exported symbols, API routes, and contracts are byte-identical before and after a refactoring. A change that must alter the public surface uses legacy-migration techniques (branch by abstraction, parallel change), not a refactoring commit.
10. **DX-110 — Preparatory refactoring precedes the feature.** When a feature is hard to add because of the code's shape, the order is: first make the change easy (refactoring commits, suite green), then make the easy change (feature commits). The two phases are never interleaved in one commit.
11. **DX-111 — Performance work is not refactoring.** An optimization changes a measurable quality, so it is benchmarked before and after, states its target metric, and is labeled as its own change type. It is never smuggled in under a "refactor" label, where its behavior risk would escape review.
12. **DX-112 — Replaced code is deleted in the same change.** Once an extraction or move lands, the superseded implementation is deleted — not commented out, not kept "just in case." Version control is the archive; anything worth remembering about the old shape goes to the changelog or decision log.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-051 — Tests edited to fit the refactor.** Banned: modifying, weakening, or deleting a test inside a refactoring change so the suite passes against restructured code. Defeats: DET-CODE-012. Bad: the extracted pricing function rounds differently, so the assertion is relaxed from `toBe(19.99)` to `toBeCloseTo(20)` and the PR is labeled "refactor." Instead: the failing test is proof of a behavior change — restore the exact behavior, or split the rounding change out as its own fix commit with its own test change (DX-101, DX-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-052 — Big-bang rewrite committed as a "refactor."** Banned: replacing a module in one unreviewable diff — hundreds of lines changed at once — under a refactoring label. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: a 900-line PR titled "refactor checkout" rewrites the module wholesale; no reviewer can separate structure from behavior, and revert means losing everything. Instead: decompose the work into named catalog steps, one commit each, suite green between steps; if the module truly needs replacement, run it as legacy-migration (DX-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-053 — Speculative abstraction for a single use.** Banned: extracting a generic framework, strategy layer, or configuration-driven engine around logic that exists exactly once, "for future flexibility." Defeats: DET-CODE-015. Bad: one discount calculation is wrapped in a `RuleEngine` with pluggable strategies because "other discount types are coming." Instead: write the single case plainly; extract only at the third real occurrence (DX-108). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-DX-054 — Old implementation left commented out.** Banned: keeping the superseded code as a commented block above or below its replacement "in case we need it." Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Bad: 70 lines of the old tax function sit commented out over the new one for two releases, rotting against APIs that no longer exist. Instead: delete it in the same change — git history recovers it exactly — and note the replacement in the changelog (DX-112). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-055 — Restructuring untested code with no net.** Banned: beginning structural changes in an area with no test coverage and no characterization tests, on the strength of reading the code carefully. Defeats: DET-CODE-013. Bad: the legacy billing module has zero tests; the agent restructures it over a day and reports "behavior preserved" because nothing visibly broke in manual spot-checks. Instead: pin current behavior with characterization tests first, in their own commit, then refactor under them (DX-102). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-051 — Suite-green invariant (automated).** Verifies: DX-101, DX-102, DX-105. Check: run the project's full test suite on the base commit and on the refactoring branch (`<test-command>` per stack.md, e.g. `npm test`); compare results, and list modified test files: `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD -- '*test*' '*spec*' 'tests/'`. Pass: identical pass/fail sets on both runs and zero test files modified. Fail: block shipment; the change is reclassified or the behavior restored. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-052 — Public surface diff (automated).** Verifies: DX-109. Check: diff the exported surface between base and branch — for a library, the generated type/symbol listing; for an API, the OpenAPI contract (`git diff <base>...HEAD -- openapi.yaml` or the project's contract snapshot). Pass: the surface diff is empty. Fail: block shipment; move the surface change to legacy-migration (branch by abstraction / parallel change). Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-053 — Commit separation audit (automated).** Verifies: DX-103, DX-110. Check: `git log --format='%h %s' <base>..HEAD` — every commit in the change is a single-type change (`refactor:` commits contain no behavior change; no `feat:`/`fix:` commit is interleaved inside the refactoring range), and per-commit size stays reviewable: `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD` shows no single commit rewriting a whole module. Pass: clean separation, no mixed commits. Fail: block shipment; split the commits and resubmit. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-054 — Characterization-first ordering (automated).** Verifies: DX-102. Check: for any module the change restructures that lacked coverage at base, `git log --format='%h %s' --reverse <base>..HEAD -- <module>` shows a test-only commit adding characterization tests for that module before the first structural commit touching it. Pass: ordering holds for every previously untested module. Fail: block shipment; write and land the characterization tests first. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-055 — Deletion and step review (manual).** Verifies: DX-104, DX-112. Check: read the full diff; confirm each commit maps to one named catalog transformation, every superseded implementation is deleted (search the diff and the resulting files for large commented-out blocks), and the change description names the design pressure answered (DX-107). Pass: all three confirmed. Fail: warn once; on repeat, block shipment and split or complete the deletion. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Boy-scout sprawl.** "Leave it cleaner than you found it" applied to every file a feature happens to touch, until a two-file feature ships as a forty-file diff nobody can review. Catch it by counting files outside the change's stated scope before committing — sprawl is visible in `git status`, not in intentions.
- **Perpetual preparation.** Preparatory refactoring that never arrives at the feature: the code is made "easy to change" week after week while the change itself is never made. Catch it by checking the plan — if a preparatory phase has no feature commit scheduled directly after it, the preparation is the project, and it stops.
- **Rename churn.** Names changed to match personal taste, then changed again next quarter by the next reader, generating history noise and merge conflicts with zero comprehension gain. Catch it by asking what a new reader would misunderstand about the current name; if the answer is "nothing," the rename is churn.
- **Refactoring during a freeze.** Structural work started while a release is stabilizing or an incident is open, when every diff should be minimal and behavior-focused. Catch it on the calendar, not in the code: if the team is in freeze or firefighting, the refactoring waits.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Extract Function under a green suite](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-104, DX-102.
- [Example 2 — The behavior change hiding in a "refactor"](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-101, DX-103, DX-106.
- [Example 3 — Characterization tests before touching legacy billing](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-102.

## Recall anchors

- Refactoring changes structure, never behavior — anything else gets a new name.
- No net, no refactoring: characterization tests come first.
- Two hats: never refactor and change behavior in the same commit.
- Red suite means back up one step — never push through, never edit the test.
- Extract at the third occurrence, delete the old code in the same change.

## Checklist

- [ ] Full suite was green on the base commit before the first structural step (DX-102, G-DX-051).
- [ ] Previously untested areas got characterization tests in a preceding, separate commit (DX-102, G-DX-054).
- [ ] No test file is modified anywhere in this change (DX-106, G-DX-051).
- [ ] Every commit is a single named transformation; no feature or fix is mixed in (DX-103, DX-104, G-DX-053).
- [ ] Public surface diff (symbols / OpenAPI) is empty (DX-109, G-DX-052).
- [ ] The change description names the design pressure answered (DX-107).
- [ ] No abstraction was extracted before its third occurrence (DX-108).
- [ ] All superseded code is deleted, none commented out (DX-112, G-DX-055).
- [ ] Suite result after the change matches the base run exactly, recorded in progress.md (G-DX-051).

# tech-debt

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://learningloop.io/glossary/technical-debt ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/workflowsOfRefactoring/fallback.html ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html
- **Depends on:** none — standalone: the debt register is built from shortcuts, workarounds, and TODO/FIXME markers found in the project's own codebase, inspected directly; it records debt rather than consuming another skill's output. It feeds refactoring and legacy-migration.
- **Feeds into:** refactoring, legacy-migration

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a shortcut, workaround, duplication, or stale toggle is being introduced or discovered; TODO/FIXME markers exist in the codebase; a release or iteration plan is being drawn up and repayment capacity must be allocated; the debt register is due its review.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work is the repayment itself (use refactoring for behavior-preserving cleanup, legacy-migration for replacing a system in slices), or the item is a defect in current behavior rather than a known shortcut (track it as a bug, not debt).
- **Cross-reference:** the commented-out-code pattern banned here as BAN-DX-042 is also banned at refactor time in refactoring (BAN-DX-054); the two entries cover the same pattern in different moments.

## Rules

1. **DX-081 — One register, one record.** Every known item of technical debt is a numbered entry (DEBT-NNN) in the project's single debt register, `docs/tech-debt.md`. Debt known only from chat, memory, or code comments is not recorded debt — it is invisible debt, and invisible debt is never scheduled.
2. **DX-082 — Complete fields at birth.** Every entry carries, from the moment it is created: location (file/module), Fowler quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent × prudent/reckless), the interest it charges, a named owner, a repayment trigger (a date, or the next feature/release touching that area), and the date incurred. An entry missing any field is incomplete and fails G-DX-042.
3. **DX-083 — Deliberate debt is registered in the same change that incurs it.** A shortcut taken on purpose gets its register entry in the same pull request that merges the shortcut. Registering it "later" is how deliberate debt becomes inadvertent.
4. **DX-084 — Deliberate + reckless is not a permitted category.** A shortcut with no repayment trigger and no plan is not debt, it is an unmade decision: the review blocks it, or the scope is cut until the work can be done properly.
5. **DX-085 — Interest is stated concretely.** The interest field names the work the debt slows or the risk it creates, in observable terms ("every billing change requires the same edit in three duplicated places"). "Code is messy," "needs cleanup," and similar phrases are not interest statements and are rejected at review.
6. **DX-086 — Code markers must reference the register.** Every `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`, or `XXX` comment carries a register reference, e.g. `TODO(DEBT-123): …`. A marker with no reference is either fixed in place, converted into a register entry with a reference, or deleted in the same change that touches it. Core functionality is never deferred to a marker — a marker may only defer minor, already-working-around items.
7. **DX-087 — Temporary means an expiry.** Every workaround and hack carries its repayment trigger as its expiry. When a trigger fires (the date passes, or work touches the area), repayment is scheduled into the next plan — the trigger firing is the scheduling event, not a reminder to update the date.
8. **DX-088 — Inadvertent debt is logged as a defect to schedule.** Debt discovered while reading or changing code (reckless shortcuts, rotted patterns, undocumented workarounds) is entered in the register the day it is found, classified inadvertent, and scheduled like a defect. It is neither silently fixed opportunistically inside an unrelated change nor noted and forgotten.
9. **DX-089 — Repayment is a standing capacity slice.** Each iteration or release plan reserves a stated slice of capacity for repayment (the project names its figure, e.g. one item or a fixed share of the plan) before new feature work is allocated. Repayment is never negotiated item-by-item against features at planning time.
10. **DX-090 — Closure requires a merged change.** An entry is closed only by a merged change that removes the debt, and the closure records the date and the change reference. Editing an entry away, or deciding it "no longer matters," is not closure; an item the project consciously accepts permanently is reclassified as a recorded accepted-risk decision, with the decider named.
11. **DX-091 — The register is reviewed on a cadence and reported.** The register is reviewed at least once per release (or monthly, whichever is sooner): triggers checked against today, owners confirmed live, expired items scheduled. The open-item count and the age of the oldest open item are reported in progress.md like any other project metric.
12. **DX-092 — Stale flags are a debt class.** Every feature flag/toggle is a register entry (or register-listed) with an owner and a removal trigger, classified by its toggle type (release, experiment, ops, permissioning). A flag whose trigger has passed is debt in default and is scheduled for removal before new flags are added in the same area.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-041 — Bare TODO/FIXME marker.** Banned: a `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`, or `XXX` comment with no register reference, owner, or trigger. Defeats: DET-CODE-011. Bad: `// TODO: add validation later` above the checkout form handler, merged and forgotten. Instead: fix it now, or create the register entry and write `// TODO(DEBT-123): validate postcode format — see register` (DX-086). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-042 — Commented-out code kept as memory.** Banned: leaving a superseded implementation commented out "in case we need it" instead of deleting it and, if the reason matters, recording the decision in the register or decision log. Defeats: DET-CODE-010. Bad: 60 lines of the old pricing function commented out above its replacement for three releases. Instead: delete it — version control is the archive — and note the replacement in the changelog (DX-090). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-043 — Duplication merged as the permanent solution, off-register.** Banned: copy-pasting logic into a second or third location and merging it with no register entry recording the duplication and its consolidation trigger. Defeats: DET-CODE-007. Bad: the tax calculation pasted into checkout, invoice, and refund code, described in review as "fine for now," with nothing recorded. Instead: either extract the shared function now, or register the duplication as deliberate + prudent debt with the trigger "next change to any copy" (DX-083, DX-085). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-044 — Register entry deleted to close it.** Banned: removing or rewriting a register entry so the debt disappears from the record without a merged fix. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: a cleanup commit deletes DEBT-009 ("old, probably fine") and the duplicated logic it described ships for another year. Instead: close entries only under DX-090 — merged change reference recorded, or a named accepted-risk reclassification. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-045 — Stub shipped as done, gap relabeled "debt" off-register.** Banned: presenting a placeholder or stub as the finished feature and calling the missing behavior "technical debt" without a register entry. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Bad: the export button downloads a hardcoded sample file; the missing real export is described in the handover as "a bit of debt." Instead: the feature is not done — either implement it, or ship it visibly incomplete with the gap registered, triggered, and owned (DX-082, DX-083). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-041 — Marker-reference lint (automated).** Verifies: DX-086. Check: `grep -rnE '\b(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\b' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git . | grep -vE '(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX)\(DEBT-[0-9]+\)' | grep -vE '(samples|templates|examples|docs|locales)/'` — instructional fill-in prompts in copy-and-edit templates are excluded per DET-CODE-011. Pass: no output (every marker carries a register reference). Fail: block shipment until each hit is fixed, registered, or deleted. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-042 — Register completeness check (automated).** Verifies: DX-081, DX-082. Check: parse the register table in `docs/tech-debt.md` (columns: ID, location, quadrant, interest, owner, trigger, incurred) and assert no cell is empty: `awk -F'|' 'NR>2 {for(i=2;i<=8;i++) if($i ~ /^[[:space:]]*$/) {print "incomplete:", $2; bad=1}} END {exit bad}' docs/tech-debt.md`. Pass: exit 0. Fail: block shipment; complete the fields before merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-043 — Cross-reference and expiry check (automated).** Verifies: DX-086, DX-087. Check: extract register IDs from code (`grep -rhoE 'DEBT-[0-9]+' --exclude-dir=.git . | sort -u`) and from the register's ID column; `comm` the two lists — code references with no register entry, and register entries with no code reference where a location is in code, are reported; entries whose trigger date is past are listed. Pass: zero dangling references; past-trigger entries appear on the next plan. Fail: block shipment on dangling references; warn on past triggers until scheduled. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-044 — Register audit (manual).** Verifies: DX-088, DX-091. Check: at the release/monthly review, sample at least five open entries (or all, if fewer): confirm each owner is still the right owner, each trigger is in the future or scheduled, and each interest statement still describes reality; record open count and oldest-item age in progress.md. Pass: every sampled entry verified and metrics recorded. Fail: warn; correct entries and re-run before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-045 — Closure audit (manual).** Verifies: DX-090. Check: list every entry closed since the last release; for each, open the recorded change reference and confirm the merged change actually removes the debt at the entry's location; diff the register against its previous version (`git log -p docs/tech-debt.md`) and confirm no entry vanished without a closure record. Pass: zero unexplained closures or deletions. Fail: block shipment; restore the entry or record a proper closure. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Invisible interest.** Entries whose interest field says "messy" or "tech debt" — nothing can be weighed against feature work, so the item loses every planning argument forever. Catch it by reading the interest field aloud: if no concrete work is named as slower or riskier, the entry is not finished.
- **Register graveyard.** Entries are written faithfully at birth and never reviewed; triggers pass, owners move on, and the register becomes a museum. Catch it at each cadence review by listing entries whose trigger date is already past — a growing list means the review is theater.
- **Amnesty by rewrite.** A big refactor or rewrite is declared to "clear the tech debt," and the register is zeroed without mapping which entries the change actually closed. Catch it by requiring per-entry closure references (G-DX-045) — a rewrite closes only the entries it names and demonstrably removes.
- **Interest paid forever, principal never.** The same duplicated or awkward area is worked around change after change — the team pays the interest monthly — while its entry stays "low priority." Catch it by counting touches: if an entry's location has been edited repeatedly since the entry was created, its trigger has effectively fired; schedule the principal.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The bare TODO](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-086, DX-082.
- [Example 2 — The deliberate shortcut, registered](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-083, DX-085.
- [Example 3 — The entry that vanished](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-090.

## Recall anchors

- If it is not in the register, it is not scheduled — it is invisible.
- Deliberate debt is registered in the same change that incurs it.
- "Temporary" without a trigger and an owner is permanent.
- Interest is concrete work slowed or risk created — never "messy."
- Entries close by merged changes, never by editing the register.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every new shortcut from this change has a register entry created in the same change (DX-083).
- [ ] Every entry has location, quadrant, concrete interest, owner, trigger, and incurred date (DX-082, G-DX-042).
- [ ] No deliberate + reckless item was merged — blocked or scope cut (DX-084).
- [ ] Marker lint passes: every TODO/FIXME/HACK carries a DEBT reference (DX-086, G-DX-041).
- [ ] No core functionality is deferred to a code marker (DX-086).
- [ ] Inadvertent debt found during this work is logged and scheduled (DX-088).
- [ ] This plan reserves its standing repayment slice before feature allocation (DX-089).
- [ ] Closures since the last release each cite a merged change; register metrics are in progress.md (DX-090, DX-091, G-DX-045).

# versioning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D15 Developer Experience (DX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://semver.org/ ; https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/ ; https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/
- **Depends on:** changelog
- **Feeds into:** dependency-management

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** cutting any release of a library, package, API, or deployed app; choosing the next version number; deprecating or removing a public feature; withdrawing a bad release; setting up a project's release process.
- **Do NOT use when:** versioning an HTTP API's URL/contract scheme itself (use api-versioning in D2 — this skill supplies the SemVer contract and deprecation window it builds on), or recording what changed in prose (use changelog in D10 — this skill governs the number, the tag, and their consistency).

## Rules

1. **DX-141 — SemVer 2.0.0 is the public contract.** Every published package, library, and API carries a version of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with SemVer precedence rules: MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for backward-compatible functionality, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. No other numbering scheme (dates, codenames, "final") is used for the same artifact.
2. **DX-142 — One source of truth for the version.** The version string lives in exactly one place — the package manifest or the git tag, as the project declares — and every other appearance (docs, banners, generated files, `--version` output) is read or generated from that source. No file is hand-edited to "also" update the version.
3. **DX-143 — The bump is derived, not chosen.** The next bump is computed from the Conventional Commits in the range since the last release tag: any `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer or `!` → MAJOR; else any `feat:` → MINOR; else PATCH. The highest signal wins, and the release notes state the derivation. A bump that disagrees with the derivation is a defect.
4. **DX-144 — Breaking changes force a major bump and a migration note.** Any incompatible change to the public API — removed or renamed symbols, changed signatures, changed defaults or behavior consumers rely on — ships only under a new MAJOR version, and its changelog entry carries a migration note saying what consumers must change. There is no "small breaking change" exception.
5. **DX-145 — Deprecation precedes removal.** A public feature is marked deprecated in at least one MINOR release (libraries/APIs) before it is removed in a MAJOR release, announced in the changelog's Deprecated section with the replacement named. Removal without a prior deprecation release is a process failure, not a shortcut.
6. **DX-146 — Pre-1.0 is an explicit, declared state.** While the major version is 0, the project states in its README that anything may change; within 0.x, incompatible changes bump MINOR and compatible features bump PATCH. Version 1.0.0 is cut when the public API becomes a real commitment consumers are invited to depend on — not when the code feels old enough.
7. **DX-147 — Pre-release and build metadata follow the SemVer grammar.** Pre-release suffixes are dot-separated identifiers (`1.0.0-alpha.1`, `1.0.0-rc.2`) with no leading zeros in numeric identifiers; build metadata (`+build.5`) never affects precedence and is never the only difference between two published artifacts. Invented suffixes outside the grammar (`-final`, `-new`, `-v2`) are invalid versions.
8. **DX-148 — A released version is immutable.** Once a version is tagged and published, its code and artifacts are never modified, re-tagged, or republished. A fix ships as a new PATCH version. If the tag must move because the release was cut in error before publication, that fact is recorded in progress.md with the reason — after publication, never.
9. **DX-149 — A release is a consistent triple.** Each release produces, in one release commit: a git tag `vX.Y.Z`, the manifest version set to the identical string (without the `v`), and the top CHANGELOG version heading with the same number and an ISO 8601 date. If any of the three disagrees, the release is not done.
10. **DX-150 — The changelog is the consumer record of versions.** Releases move entries from `[Unreleased]` into a new version section, grouped by the six Keep a Changelog types (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security), written for consumers — what changed for them — with breaking changes marked in place. Entries are added under `[Unreleased]` as work lands, not reconstructed from memory at release time.
11. **DX-151 — Yanked releases stay in history, marked.** A withdrawn release is marked `[YANKED]` in the changelog with the date and reason, and its tag remains. Deleting the section, the tag, or the artifact record so the version "never happened" destroys the trace consumers need when they are pinned to it.
12. **DX-152 — Deployed apps version for traceability.** A deployed web app still tags every production deployment and keeps the changelog; its version is an internal traceability device (deployment → tag → exact commit), so bump rules may relax but DX-148 and DX-149 do not. Every bug report and incident note cites the deployed version or tag it was observed on.

## BAN list

- **BAN-DX-071 — Silent re-tag or republish.** Banned: moving a version tag to a different commit, or replacing a published artifact, so the same version number names different code. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: the 2.3.1 tag is force-moved to include a late fix; users who installed "2.3.1" yesterday run different code from users who install it today. Instead: publish the fix as 2.3.2 with its own tag and changelog entry (DX-148). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-072 — Breaking change under a minor or patch bump.** Banned: shipping an incompatible API change while bumping only MINOR or PATCH, because the change "feels small." Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: `getUser(id)` changes its return shape in 1.4.1, a patch release; every consumer's manifest promised compatibility the content does not have. Instead: bump MAJOR and write the migration note (DX-144). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-073 — Version hand-edited in several places.** Banned: updating the version by editing the manifest, a source constant, and the docs independently, so the copies can disagree. Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Bad: manifest says 3.0.0, the app banner still renders 2.9.4 from a hardcoded string, and support cannot tell which build a user runs. Instead: keep one source of truth and generate or read every other display from it (DX-142). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-074 — Non-SemVer release identity.** Banned: releasing under an identity that is not a valid SemVer version — `latest`, `final`, `1.0`, `2.0-new`, or a date — for a versioned artifact. Defeats: DET-CODE-028. Bad: the download page offers "app-final-v2.zip" and the manifest says `"version": "1.0"`. Instead: assign the next derived SemVer version and tag it (DX-141, DX-143, DX-147). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-DX-075 — Erasing a withdrawn release.** Banned: deleting a yanked version's changelog section, tag, or release record instead of marking it withdrawn. Defeats: DET-CODE-031. Bad: after a broken 4.1.0 is pulled, its changelog section is deleted; consumers pinned to 4.1.0 find no record it ever existed or why it vanished. Instead: mark it `[YANKED]` with the date and reason, tag intact (DX-151). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-DX-071 — Version triple equality (automated).** Verifies: DX-142, DX-149. Check: extract the manifest version (`node -p "require('./package.json').version"` or the ecosystem equivalent), the newest tag (`git describe --tags --abbrev=0`), and the top CHANGELOG version heading; assert all three are the identical version string. Pass: exact match. Fail: block shipment; fix the out-of-line copy from the source of truth, never by editing all three by hand. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-072 — Bump derivation check (automated).** Verifies: DX-143. Check: run commit lint (commitlint with the Conventional Commits config) over `git log <last-tag>..HEAD`, compute the derived bump from the commit types, and compare it with the bump actually taken between the last tag and the candidate version. Pass: lint clean and derived bump equals actual bump. Fail: block shipment; either correct the version or correct the commit record — never ship a number the history does not justify. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-073 — Breaking-change / major-bump check (automated).** Verifies: DX-144. Check: diff the public contract against the last release (OpenAPI diff for APIs, exported-symbol diff for libraries); if the diff reports a breaking change, assert the candidate version's MAJOR is exactly one greater and MINOR/PATCH are zero. Pass: no breaking change, or major bumped. Fail: block shipment until the bump is corrected and the migration note exists. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-074 — Immutability and grammar check (automated).** Verifies: DX-147, DX-148. Check: validate the candidate version against the official SemVer regular expression from semver.org, and confirm every existing release tag still points at the commit recorded for it at its release (compare `git rev-parse vX.Y.Z^{commit}` against the release record in progress.md). Pass: version is valid SemVer and no tag has moved. Fail: block shipment; a moved tag is restored or the change is shipped as a new version. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-DX-075 — Release record review (manual).** Verifies: DX-145, DX-150, DX-151. Check: read the new changelog section as a consumer: entries grouped by the six types, breaking changes marked with migration notes, anything removed was announced as Deprecated at least one minor release earlier, and any withdrawn release in the period is marked `[YANKED]` with a reason. Pass: all four hold. Fail: warn and complete the record before the next release; a missing prior deprecation blocks the removal itself. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Version inflation.** Major versions bumped for marketing ("Version 10!") or minor versions used as a progress diary, until the number carries no compatibility information and consumers stop trusting it. Catch it by asking what the derived bump (G-DX-072) says — if the release story and the commit history tell different stories, the number is decoration.
- **Release-time changelog archaeology.** The changelog is written the night of the release by scrolling the commit log and guessing what mattered; consumer-visible changes are missed and internal refactors are presented as features. Catch it by checking `[Unreleased]` during ordinary work: an empty section mid-cycle means entries are not being written as work lands.
- **The eternal 0.x.** A package with real external consumers stays at 0.x for years because 1.0.0 "feels like a commitment" — which it is, and avoiding it does not remove the dependence, only the contract. Catch it at release review: if consumers exist and the API has been stable across several minors, the 1.0.0 question belongs on the record.
- **Version by environment.** Dev, staging, and production quietly run different builds under the same version label, so a bug "fixed in 2.3.0" reproduces in production. Catch it by tying every deployment to its tag (DX-152) and comparing the deployed tag, not the label, when a report comes in.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The breaking patch](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects DX-144, DX-143.
- [Example 2 — Three versions of the version](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects DX-142, DX-149.
- [Example 3 — The hotfix that rewrote history](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects DX-148, DX-151.

## Recall anchors

- The version is a contract, not a mood: derive the bump from the commits.
- One source of truth — tag, manifest, and changelog are the same string or the release is not done.
- Breaking change means major bump plus a migration note. No exceptions for "small" breaks.
- Published means immutable: fixes ship as a new version, never a moved tag.
- Yanked is marked, never erased.

## Checklist

- [ ] The candidate version is valid SemVer, including any pre-release/build suffixes (DX-141, DX-147, G-DX-074).
- [ ] The bump matches the derivation from the commit range since the last tag (DX-143, G-DX-072).
- [ ] Any breaking change has a major bump and a migration note in the changelog (DX-144, G-DX-073).
- [ ] Anything removed was deprecated at least one minor release earlier (DX-145, G-DX-075).
- [ ] Tag, manifest, and changelog heading are the identical version string (DX-149, G-DX-071).
- [ ] No existing tag moved and no published artifact was replaced (DX-148, G-DX-074).
- [ ] The changelog section is grouped by the six types and written for consumers (DX-150).
- [ ] Any withdrawn release is marked `[YANKED]` with a reason, not deleted (DX-151).

# asset-harvesting

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D16 Cloning & Replication (CL)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://github.com/iipc/warc-specifications/blob/master/specifications/warc-format/warc-1.1/index.md ; https://webrecorder.net/blog/2021-02-22-introducing-browsertrix-crawler/
- **Depends on:** clone-ethics (D14 gate), site-discovery, page-inventory, licensing (D14)
- **Feeds into:** page-reconstruction, fidelity-verification, design-extraction

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** An authorized rebuild needs the target's asset inventory — images, media, fonts, documents, icons — captured with provenance so each asset can be reused, recreated, or replaced on a recorded rights basis.
- **Do NOT use when:** No D14 authorization record exists (stop; clone-ethics gates first), when the need is design values rather than files (design-extraction), or to stock a general asset library from a site (out of scope; harvest only what in-scope pages reference).

## Rules

1. **CL-061 — Authorization precedes harvesting.** No asset is fetched before the D14 clone-ethics authorization record exists and predates the first harvest log entry.
2. **CL-062 — Harvest the full in-scope surface.** Extract asset URLs from HTML, CSS, JS, and network logs for every page in page-inventory; a file the live site no longer serves is recovered from an archived capture or recorded as unrecoverable, never silently skipped.
3. **CL-063 — Manifest before workspace.** Every harvested asset gets a manifest row — source URL, capture date, checksum, rights decision — before the file enters the rebuild workspace; a file with no row does not exist for the build.
4. **CL-064 — Four verdicts only.** Each manifest row carries exactly one rights decision: `owned`, `licensed`, `recreate`, or `replace`. An undecided asset is treated as `replace` until a decision is recorded.
5. **CL-065 — Archive-grade capture.** Captures are stored as WARC records (ISO 28500) with full request/response provenance, via a browser-driven archiver (e.g. Browsertrix Crawler) for JS-heavy pages; where WARC tooling is impractical, the fallback is a HAR plus checksum manifest, and the choice is recorded.
6. **CL-066 — Only owned/licensed ship as-is.** Assets decided `recreate` or `replace` are rebuilt or substituted before build; the harvested original never enters the ship folders in harvested form.
7. **CL-067 — Licensed needs a license record.** A `licensed` verdict cites the license — holder, scope, and transferability to this rebuild checked. Even on the client's own site, third-party stock and font licenses govern; "the client uses it" is not a license record.
8. **CL-068 — Trademarks are logged, never reused.** Logos, wordmarks, and brand artwork are recorded in the manifest with verdict `replace` and their placement noted, so reconstruction knows what the operator's own mark must substitute; they are never harvested into the rebuild's assets.
9. **CL-069 — Fonts are assets.** A harvested font file ships only after its license permits the rebuild's use (embedding/redistribution terms checked); an unlicensed font goes to design-extraction as a substitution record, not into the build.
10. **CL-070 — Never hotlink.** The deliverable references only local, manifest-covered asset files; no built page, stylesheet, or script URL points at the source domain.
11. **CL-071 — Respectful, lawful capture.** The harvester sends an identifying user-agent, obeys robots.txt Disallow rules, and respects rate limits; assets are never pulled from behind a login or paywall by bypass — gated assets are recorded as gated.
12. **CL-072 — Provenance survives the source.** The WARC record and checksum remain the evidence after the live site changes or vanishes; a harvested file whose checksum no longer matches its capture record is re-captured or dropped, never quietly kept.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CL-031 — Manifest-less shipment.** Banned: an asset file entering the rebuild with no manifest row or no rights decision. Defeats: DET-CRWL-007. Bad: `hero.jpg` is copied from the crawl folder into `src/assets/` because the build needs it today. Instead: create the manifest row (source URL, capture date, checksum, verdict) first; the file moves only after the row exists. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-032 — Silent reuse of protected media.** Banned: shipping a harvested photograph, illustration, font, or copy file unchanged without an `owned`/`licensed` verdict. Defeats: DET-CRWL-009. Bad: the target's product photo library is bulk-downloaded and ships as the rebuild's gallery. Instead: record verdict `recreate` or `replace` and shoot, license, or substitute the operator's own media before build. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-033 — Hotlinking the source CDN.** Banned: the deliverable loading any asset from the source site's domain at runtime. Defeats: DET-CRWL-015. Bad: the rebuild's `<img src="https://target.example/media/banner.jpg">` works until the original site redesigns, then breaks. Instead: ship a local file with a manifest row and a reuse verdict, or a recorded replacement. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-034 — Bypass harvesting.** Banned: pulling asset files from behind a login or paywall using borrowed credentials or an access workaround. Defeats: DET-CRWL-008. Bad: a customer's login is used to download the members-only media kit "for completeness." Instead: record those assets as gated; obtain them only through access the client legitimately provisions. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-035 — Robots-blind bulk harvest.** Banned: crawling asset paths robots.txt disallows, or fetching at rates that burden the target, to complete the inventory. Defeats: DET-CRWL-014. Bad: the harvester ignores the `/media/` Disallow and pulls 4,000 files overnight. Instead: obey the Disallow set, log disallowed paths as excluded, and throttle to the recorded crawl rate. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CL-031 — Manifest completeness (automated).** Verifies: CL-063, CL-064. Check: script walks the rebuild's asset folders and asserts every file has a manifest row with source URL, capture date, checksum, and one of the four verdicts. Pass: zero orphan files, zero verdict-less rows. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — manifest rows record origin “original creation” in place of source URL and capture date; checksum, verdict, and zero-orphan bars unchanged; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-032 — Checksum spot-check (automated).** Verifies: CL-065, CL-072. Check: recompute checksums for a random 10% sample (minimum 10 files) of harvested assets and compare against their WARC records and manifest rows. Pass: 100% match. Fail: block shipment; mismatched files are re-captured or dropped. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: NOT APPLICABLE — no WARC records exist because nothing was harvested; on-disk checksum integrity is asserted by G-CL-031 (adapted); see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-033 — Hotlink scan (automated).** Verifies: CL-070. Check: `grep -rE "https?://(www\.)?<source-domain>" dist/` over built HTML, CSS, and JS, filtered to asset references (img, srcset, url(), font, media). Pass: zero hits. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: NOT APPLICABLE — no source domain exists; every shipped asset is a local file in the G-CL-031 manifest, so hotlinking is structurally excluded; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-034 — Verdict enforcement audit (automated).** Verifies: CL-066, CL-067, CL-068. Check: script asserts no file whose manifest verdict is `recreate`, `replace`, or undecided exists in the ship asset folders in harvested form, and every `licensed` row cites a license record (holder, scope, transferability). Pass: zero violations. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — harvested form is evidenced by the manifest's origin field plus the zero-fetch crawl log; the licensed-row citation check runs unchanged; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-035 — Access compliance check (automated).** Verifies: CL-061, CL-071. Check: grep the harvest log against the target's robots.txt Disallow set and against the gated-URL list from site-discovery; confirm the authorization record's timestamp predates the first log entry. Pass: zero disallowed or gated fetches; authorization predates harvest. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the robots/gated grep runs against the zero-fetch harvest log; the authorization-predates-work half runs unchanged; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.

## Anti-patterns

- **Folder-dump harvest.** Everything lands in one folder with names like `img_final2.png`, and provenance is reconstructed later from memory. Catch it: any file not created through the manifest-first flow (CL-063) is suspect until its row exists.
- **Screenshot-substitute assets.** A screenshot crop stands in for a missing image file because it "looks the same." Catch it: shipped media must be real files with checksums in the manifest, never crops of a capture.
- **Verdict drift.** An asset marked `replace` early quietly becomes the shipped hero image under deadline pressure. Catch it: run the verdict audit (G-CL-034) at ship time, not at harvest time.
- **Whole-library sweep.** The entire media library is harvested "just in case," far beyond what in-scope pages reference, inflating rights exposure. Catch it: every manifest row names the in-scope page that references the asset; rows that name none are out of scope.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Photo library shipped vs. recreate verdict](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CL-066, BAN-CL-032.
- [Example 2 — Hotlinked banner vs. local licensed file](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CL-070, BAN-CL-033.
- [Example 3 — Logo in the asset folder vs. logged replacement](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CL-068, BAN-CL-032.

## Recall anchors

- No manifest row, no file — provenance is recorded at capture, not reconstructed.
- Four verdicts only; undecided means replace.
- Only owned/licensed ship as-is; everything else is recreated or replaced.
- Trademarks and logos are logged for replacement, never harvested for reuse.
- Never hotlink, never bypass, never outrun robots.txt.

## Checklist

- [ ] D14 authorization record exists and predates the first harvest log entry (CL-061).
- [ ] Asset URLs extracted from HTML, CSS, JS, and network logs for every in-scope page (CL-062).
- [ ] Every file in the rebuild's asset folders has a manifest row with source URL, capture date, checksum, and verdict (G-CL-031).
- [ ] Captures stored as WARC records, or the HAR fallback choice recorded (CL-065).
- [ ] Every `licensed` verdict cites a license record with transferability checked (CL-067).
- [ ] No `recreate`/`replace`/undecided asset ships in harvested form (G-CL-034).
- [ ] Built output contains zero references to the source domain (G-CL-033).
- [ ] Harvest log shows zero robots-disallowed or gated fetches (G-CL-035).

# behavior-cloning

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D16 Cloning & Replication (CL)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots ; https://webrecorder.net/browsertrix/
- **Depends on:** clone-ethics, page-inventory
- **Feeds into:** page-reconstruction, fidelity-verification

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** an authorized replication engagement has a signed-off page inventory and the target's interactive behavior — forms, modals, filters, routing, validation, animations — must be specified from observation so the rebuild can be re-implemented in original code and accepted against the same recordings.
- **Do NOT use when:** no D14 clone-ethics authorization record exists (run clone-ethics first; this skill refuses to start), the task is page structure or styling (page-inventory, design-extraction), reconstructing pages that cannot be observed (page-reconstruction, which consumes this skill's `unobserved` records), or verifying a finished rebuild (fidelity-verification).

## Rules

1. **CL-081 — Authorization precedes the first recording.** No interaction is recorded, scripted, or replayed on the target before the project's clone-ethics authorization record exists, is dated, names the target and the recording scope, and predates the first recording log entry. Recording tooling checks for the record and fails closed when it is absent or out of scope.
2. **CL-082 — Behavior is specified as executable tests, not prose.** Every in-scope flow is recorded as a scripted interaction (Playwright test scripts are the working format): the clicks and inputs, the expected state change after each step, and the network responses behind it. A flow described only in prose impressions is treated as uncloned.
3. **CL-083 — Every spec records trigger, action, and observed result.** Each interaction spec names its trigger (control, input), the action performed, the observed state change, and any network request the behavior depends on. Only what the recording shows may be written; an expected result the agent did not observe is not part of the spec.
4. **CL-084 — Re-implementation is original code; the target's code is never copied.** Behavior is rebuilt from the observation specs in the project's own code. The target's scripts, bundles, or styles are never copied, deobfuscated, decompiled, or adapted into the rebuild — similarity of behavior is the goal, never similarity of source.
5. **CL-085 — Unobservable interactions are recorded as unobserved, never invented.** Any interaction the operator cannot legitimately observe — behind a login or paywall the operator does not hold, or in a state that cannot be reached — is entered in the behavior record as `unobserved` with the reason. It is never filled in from generic patterns, competitor sites, or plausibility, and it passes to page-reconstruction labeled as such.
6. **CL-086 — Recording uses only the operator's own provisioned accounts.** Where a flow needs an account, the client provisions a test account for the engagement, or the agent registers its own where the target permits. The site owner's, an employee's, or any real user's credentials are never used, borrowed, or replayed from a captured session.
7. **CL-087 — Test data is synthetic, and recordings carry no real personal data.** All inputs used in recordings are fabricated test values. If a recording incidentally captures real users' personal data (names, emails, order details visible in an account view), that data is scrubbed from the recording before it is stored, and the scrub is noted in the recording log.
8. **CL-088 — The evidence set is frozen at inventory sign-off.** The recordings and specs are frozen when the inventory is signed off, and the frozen set is what the rebuild is accepted against. If the source changes afterward, the change is recorded as drift with a date; frozen tests are never silently re-recorded to match.
9. **CL-089 — Coverage spans the whole inventoried interaction surface.** Menus, forms and their validation messages, modals, filters and sorting, search, client-side routing, animation triggers, and error and empty states are all in scope: every interaction listed in the page inventory gets a spec or an `unobserved` record — none is skipped silently.
10. **CL-090 — Content surfaced by behavior is replaced, not transcribed.** Form mechanics, flow order, and validation behavior are functional and may be recreated; the target's marketing copy, help text, error-message wording beyond functional necessity, and branded assets are replaced with the operator's own content, never transcribed verbatim into the rebuild.
11. **CL-091 — Observed timing and edge cases are part of the spec.** Where the recording shows them, the spec records debounce and delay behavior, double-submit handling, invalid-input responses, and slow- or failed-response states. An edge case that was not exercised is listed as unexercised, not assumed.
12. **CL-092 — The frozen suite accepts the rebuild unmodified.** The recorded interaction suite runs against the rebuild unchanged as its acceptance test; development continues until the same scripts pass. Editing, weakening, or deleting a test to make the rebuild pass falsifies the result and is treated as a failed acceptance.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CL-041 — Working by screenshot.** Banned: declaring an interactive element or flow "working" or "cloned" from its appearance in screenshots without executing it. Defeats: DET-CRWL-013. Bad: the rebuild report marks the checkout "behavior verified" because the button looks right; nobody clicked it, and the source's submit actually validates stock before charging. Instead: record every flow as an executable interaction test and let the coverage gate (G-CL-042) refuse any flow without one, under CL-082. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-042 — The target's code in the rebuild.** Banned: copying, deobfuscating, or adapting the target's JavaScript, bundles, or stylesheets into the rebuild to reproduce behavior. Defeats: DET-CRWL-009. Bad: the source's minified filter widget is deobfuscated and pasted into the rebuild because "rebuilding it would take a week". Instead: specify the filter's observed behavior (inputs, state changes, network calls) and re-implement it in original code, under CL-084. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-043 — Invented gated behavior.** Banned: writing a behavior spec for a flow behind a login or paywall the operator cannot legitimately access and presenting it as observed behavior. Defeats: DET-CRWL-002. Bad: the members' billing flow is specced from a competitor's flow and the operator's expectations, and the record lists it as "recorded from source". Instead: enter the flow as `unobserved` with the access reason and hand it to page-reconstruction labeled as such, under CL-085. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-044 — Real credentials, real people's data.** Banned: recording with the site owner's or any real user's credentials, replaying a captured real session, or storing recordings that contain real users' personal data. Defeats: DET-CRWL-008. Bad: the client shares the admin login "to save time", and the recordings capture real customer names and orders that ship with the project files. Instead: use only provisioned test accounts and synthetic data, and scrub any incidental personal data before storage, under CL-086 and CL-087. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-045 — The success toast accepted as behavior.** Banned: treating a success message, toast, or redirect as proof a flow works, without verifying the state change or network effect behind it. Defeats: DET-CRWL-004. Bad: the source's contact form shows "Message sent!" on submit, the spec records "form sends message", and the rebuild clones the toast — while the source in fact posts to a CRM the clone never reproduces. Instead: record the network request and resulting state change as the behavior; where no effect can be verified, say so in the spec, under CL-083. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CL-041 — Authorization and account pre-flight check.** Verifies: CL-081, CL-086. Check (automated): before recording starts, a script asserts the clone-ethics authorization record exists, is dated, covers behavior recording on the target, and its commit timestamp predates the run; the recording plan lists only provisioned test accounts. Pass: record complete and pre-committed, accounts provisioned. Fail: recording refuses to start (fail closed). Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — no recording or test accounts exist; the check asserts the authorization record predates the first behavior spec and covers pattern-reference specification; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-042 — Behavior-spec coverage check.** Verifies: CL-082, CL-085, CL-089. Check (automated): diff the page inventory's interaction list against the behavior record; every inventoried interaction must have either an executable spec naming trigger, action, and expected result, or an `unobserved` entry with a reason. Pass: the diff is empty. Fail: block; behavior-cloning is incomplete until every interaction is specced or honestly recorded as unobserved. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the diff runs against the pattern inventory's interaction list, and specs are marked designed-from-pattern; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-043 — Frozen-suite acceptance run.** Verifies: CL-088, CL-092. Check (automated): the recorded interaction suite runs in CI against the rebuild, with the test files hash-matched to the frozen evidence set so any edit is detected. Pass: every in-scope test passes unmodified. Fail: block delivery; failures are fixed in the rebuild, never in the tests. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the frozen set is the pattern-derived spec suite frozen at spec sign-off instead of at recording; hash-matching runs unchanged; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-044 — Recording hygiene scan.** Verifies: CL-084, CL-087, CL-090. Check (automated): scan the stored recordings, specs, and rebuild source for (a) real-looking personal data patterns, (b) verbatim strings from the target's marketing and help copy beyond functional labels, and (c) target-origin code fingerprints (bundle banners, distinctive minified identifiers). Pass: zero hits in all three scans. Fail: block; offending material is scrubbed or rewritten and the finding is logged. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the copy and fingerprint scans compare against the pattern inventory's protected-items list, there being no target copy or code; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-045 — Full click-through sign-off.** Verifies: CL-083, CL-091. Check (manual): a reviewer clicks through the complete inventoried flow list on the rebuild, comparing each step's state change, validation message, and edge-case behavior against its spec, including at least one invalid-input and one double-submit case per form. Pass: every flow matches its spec or the mismatch is filed as a defect. Fail: block sign-off until mismatches are fixed or the spec is corrected from a new authorized recording. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Prose impressions.** The behavior record reads "the checkout felt standard, filters worked normally" — impressions that no gate can run and no builder can implement from. Catch it by requiring every flow to exist as an executable test file before it counts as recorded (G-CL-042).
- **Happy-path-only recording.** Every form is recorded with valid data and every flow ends in success, so validation, error, and empty states are discovered for the first time in the rebuild. Catch it by checking each form's spec list for at least one invalid-input recording before sign-off.
- **Spec drift by paraphrase.** Mid-build, specs get "clarified" from memory in chat instead of replayed from the frozen recordings, and the rebuild quietly diverges. Catch it by treating the frozen recording, never a paraphrase, as the only source a spec may be corrected from.
- **Drift denial.** The source site changes mid-engagement, the frozen tests start failing against the source itself, and the team assumes the rebuild is at fault. Catch it by replaying a failing test against the source first; if it fails there too, record drift under CL-088 instead of reworking the rebuild.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — "Verified" from the screenshot](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CL-082, CL-083.
- [Example 2 — The billing flow nobody could see](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CL-085.
- [Example 3 — The borrowed filter widget](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CL-084.

## Recall anchors

- No authorization record, no first click — recording fails closed.
- If it has no executable test, it is not cloned.
- Record what you observed; label what you could not as unobserved.
- Recreate the behavior, never copy the code or the copy.
- The frozen suite judges the rebuild — tests are never edited to pass.

## Checklist

- [ ] The clone-ethics authorization record is committed, covers behavior recording, and predates the first recording (CL-081, G-CL-041).
- [ ] Every inventoried interaction has an executable spec or an `unobserved` record with a reason (CL-082, CL-085, CL-089, G-CL-042).
- [ ] Every spec names trigger, action, observed state change, and network dependency — nothing unobserved is written as fact (CL-083, CL-091).
- [ ] The rebuild's behavior is re-implemented in original code; no target code, deobfuscated or otherwise, is present (CL-084, G-CL-044).
- [ ] Only provisioned test accounts and synthetic data were used; recordings are scrubbed of real personal data (CL-086, CL-087, G-CL-044).
- [ ] The evidence set is frozen at inventory sign-off and any source change since is logged as drift (CL-088).
- [ ] The frozen suite passes against the rebuild unmodified, hashes matching the frozen set (CL-092, G-CL-043).
- [ ] A full manual click-through, including invalid-input and double-submit cases, is signed off against the specs (G-CL-045).

# design-extraction

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D16 Cloning & Replication (CL)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.w3.org/community/reports/design-tokens/CG-FINAL-format-20251028/ ; https://backlight.dev/docs/style-dictionary
- **Depends on:** clone-ethics (D14 gate), site-discovery, page-inventory
- **Feeds into:** page-reconstruction, fidelity-verification

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** An authorized rebuild needs the target's design system — tokens for color, type, spacing, radii, shadows, breakpoints, and component states — sampled from the live or archived source.
- **Do NOT use when:** No D14 authorization record exists (stop; clone-ethics gates first), when only one page's appearance is needed (record it in page-inventory instead), or to capture the target's branding for reuse (never; see BAN-CL-024).

## Rules

1. **CL-041 — Authorization precedes sampling.** No computed style is sampled before the D14 clone-ethics authorization record exists and predates the first sampling log entry.
2. **CL-042 — Sample the system, not a page.** Sample computed styles across at least one page per template from page-inventory, never from a single page; a token set built from one page is a trace, not a system.
3. **CL-043 — Sample every interactive state.** For each interactive component, sample default, hover, focus, disabled, and error states; a state that cannot be reached within authorization is recorded as unsampled, never invented.
4. **CL-044 — Tokens are measurements only.** Each token records a measured value (hex/rgb, px/rem, font stack, weight, shadow, radius, breakpoint) traced to at least one sampled element's page, selector, and state.
5. **CL-045 — Cluster near-identical values.** Raw values within a recorded tolerance (e.g. spacing within 1px, colors within one hex step per channel) collapse into one token; the token file keeps the cluster's sample count so distributions stay visible.
6. **CL-046 — Type is a scale, not a list.** Record the full font stack, every sampled font-size/line-height/weight pairing, and the ratio pattern between steps; a flat list of sizes with no scale fails the extraction.
7. **CL-047 — Breakpoints are sampled, not assumed.** Record each media-query breakpoint found in the source's CSS or observed by resizing; never substitute framework defaults (768/1024) for measured values.
8. **CL-048 — Export in DTCG format.** The token file uses the W3C Design Tokens format (`$value`, `$type`, groups, aliases) and is the single source the rebuild consumes.
9. **CL-049 — Compile, never retype.** CSS variables and JS constants are generated from the token file with Style Dictionary or an equivalent compiler; no token value is hand-typed into a page stylesheet.
10. **CL-050 — Font substitution is a recorded decision.** If a sampled font is commercial and unlicensed for the rebuild, the token file names the substitute and the accepted visual delta in a substitution record; silent substitution is a defect.
11. **CL-051 — Branding is flagged, never tokenized.** The target's logo, wordmarks, brand artwork, and copy strings are recorded in a replace-list for the operator's own assets; they never appear as token values or rebuild assets.
12. **CL-052 — Sampling obeys crawl rules.** Sampling uses authorized/public pages only, honors robots.txt, identifies the agent, and never bypasses a login or paywall to capture a gated state.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CL-021 — Invented palette.** Banned: publishing tokens whose values were guessed or "close enough" rather than sampled. Defeats: DET-CRWL-018. Bad: the rebuild uses #2563eb because the source "looked like Tailwind blue." Instead: sample the element's computed `color`/`background-color` and tokenize the returned value. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-022 — Hardcoded values in the rebuild.** Banned: hex, px, or font-stack literals in page CSS that exist in no token. Defeats: DET-VIS-043. Bad: one template ships `border-radius: 10px` typed inline while the token says 8px. Instead: reference the compiled variable generated from the token file. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-023 — Silent font substitution.** Banned: swapping an unlicensed source font for a similar-looking one with no record. Defeats: DET-VIS-011. Bad: the rebuild quietly uses Inter where the source used a commercial grotesque. Instead: add a substitution record naming the source font, the substitute, and the accepted delta. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-024 — Tokenized branding.** Banned: capturing the target's logo, wordmark, brand artwork, or copy as tokens or reusable assets. Defeats: DET-CRWL-009. Bad: the source's logo SVG is saved into the rebuild's asset folder "as a token." Instead: log the logo on the replace-list with its measured size and placement; the operator supplies their own mark. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CL-025 — Gated-state capture by bypass.** Banned: sampling styles behind a login or paywall using borrowed credentials or an access workaround. Defeats: DET-CRWL-014. Bad: a shared customer login is used to sample the dashboard theme. Instead: record gated states as unsampled, or sample only through access the client legitimately provisions. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CL-021 — Token traceability diff (automated).** Verifies: CL-044, CL-045. Check: script re-samples computed styles from the recorded source pages/states and diffs every token value against the samples; any token with no matching sample (within its cluster tolerance) fails. Pass: 100% of tokens trace to ≥1 sample. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: NOT APPLICABLE — tokens are authored, not extracted, so no source samples exist; token discipline is gated by G-CL-022 and G-CL-025 (adapted); see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-022 — Orphan-value scan (automated).** Verifies: CL-049. Check: `grep -rE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}|font-family:'` run against the built CSS output (e.g. `dist/assets/*.css`, adjusted to the project's actual output layout) and compare every hit against the compiled token output; any value present in no token fails. The gate record must name the actual path scanned, so the scan never runs vacuously against a path the project does not produce. Pass: zero orphan values. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CL-023 — State coverage check (automated).** Verifies: CL-043. Check: script asserts every interactive component in the extraction log has entries for default/hover/focus/disabled/error or an explicit "unsampled — reason" record. Pass: no state silently missing. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the component list checked is the pattern inventory's, and unsampled records read as designed-state records from the design record; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-024 — Replace-list completeness (manual).** Verifies: CL-051. Check: review the extraction output for logo, wordmark, artwork, and copy items; each must appear on the replace-list and none in the token file or asset folders. Pass: replace-list covers all branding found; token file contains measurements only. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the review runs over the pattern inventory and the build's asset folders, and the replace-list is the inventory's protected-items list; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.
- **G-CL-025 — Token-only render (manual).** Verifies: CL-042, CL-048. Check: render one page per template using only the compiled token file, side by side with the source capture; check palette, type scale, spacing rhythm, radii, and states. Pass: no systematic drift; per-value differences trace to a substitution record. Fail: rework extraction. Recorded in: progress.md. Pattern-reference mode: ADAPTED — the token-only render runs, compared against the pattern inventory's recorded design characteristics, not a source capture; see the pattern-reference disposition table in the clone-rebuild playbook.

## Anti-patterns

- **Homepage-only extraction.** Sampling stops at the home page because it "represents the brand"; interior templates quietly drift. Catch it: compare the sampled page list against page-inventory's template list before exporting.
- **Single-sample spacing.** One measured margin becomes "the spacing scale." Catch it: a spacing token with sample count 1 is a suspicion, not a scale — sample more pages.
- **Screenshot eyeballing.** Values are read off a screenshot with a color picker instead of computed styles, baking in compression and scaling error. Catch it: every token must name the element it was computed from.
- **State blindness.** Only the default state is sampled, so hover/focus/error styling is invented during the rebuild. Catch it: run the state coverage check before calling extraction done.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Guessed palette vs. sampled tokens](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CL-044, BAN-CL-021.
- [Example 2 — Inline radius vs. compiled token](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CL-049, BAN-CL-022.
- [Example 3 — Logo as asset vs. replace-list entry](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CL-051, BAN-CL-024.

## Recall anchors

- Sample the system across templates and states, never one page.
- Every token traces to a computed style — no sample, no token.
- Compile from the token file; never retype a value.
- Branding goes on the replace-list, never in the token file.
- Unlicensed font? Record the substitution and the delta.

## Checklist

- [ ] D14 authorization record exists and predates the first sampling entry (CL-041).
- [ ] At least one page per inventory template was sampled (CL-042).
- [ ] All five states sampled or explicitly recorded unsampled per component (CL-043).
- [ ] Token file is valid DTCG format and every token traces to a sample (CL-048, G-CL-021).
- [ ] Built CSS contains zero values absent from the token file (G-CL-022).
- [ ] Every font substitution has a record naming the accepted delta (CL-050).
- [ ] Replace-list covers all logos, wordmarks, artwork, and copy found (CL-051).
- [ ] Token-only render checked against source captures for one page per template (G-CL-025).
