# recommendations

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D17 AI Features (AI)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://cloud.google.com/retail/docs/predict
- **Depends on:** embeddings-search
- **Feeds into:** ai-evaluation, ai-observability

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a surface suggests items to a user from their behavior or from catalog signals — "for you" rails, related-items lists, next-item suggestions — or when an existing recommender's candidates, ranking, fallback, or labels are being added or changed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the task is ranked results for an explicit query (use search-relevance), retrieving documents for a prompt (use rag-retrieval), or computing the embeddings used for content similarity (use embeddings-search). This skill owns what gets recommended, in what order, and under what label — not search, retrieval, or the embedding pipeline.

## Rules

1. **AI-101 — Events before algorithms.** Views, clicks, purchases, and dismissals are logged from launch in one defined schema — user ID, item ID, event type, surface, timestamp, request ID. A recommender with no event stream cannot learn and must not claim to personalize.
2. **AI-102 — Fixed pipeline order.** Serving runs candidate generation, then the hard exclusion filter (AI-103), then ranking, then the response. No stage is skipped, reordered, or merged into another.
3. **AI-103 — Exclusion filtering is deterministic code.** Already-purchased or consumed items, out-of-stock or unavailable items, and items the user is ineligible for are removed by code after candidate generation. Filtering is never delegated to a model or a prompt instruction.
4. **AI-104 — Availability is rechecked at serve time.** Availability and eligibility are verified when the response is built, or read from a cache with a stated TTL. An item that became unavailable after candidate generation is dropped and the slot is backfilled from the remaining filtered candidates.
5. **AI-105 — Every segment has a defined fallback.** Cold-start and low-signal users receive the documented popularity/quality fallback. An empty recommendation slot is a defect, never a shipped state.
6. **AI-106 — Labels tell the truth.** Fallback content is labeled for what it is — "Popular right now", "New in" — and the labels "Recommended for you" / "Picked for you" are used only for lists computed from that user's own signals.
7. **AI-107 — Personalized means computed from the user's signals.** The served list is a function of the user's events and the documented ranking logic. Two users with different histories must be able to receive different lists; identical output for different histories is a failed surface.
8. **AI-108 — Ranking logic is documented and matches production.** Candidate sources, signals, and their order or weights are written down in the serving configuration or a document it references. Behavior nobody can read in the config does not ship.
9. **AI-109 — Every response is logged with its version.** Each served response records the request ID, model/config version, personalized-or-fallback flag, and the item IDs served, so quality can be attributed to a version and a bad version can be rolled back.
10. **AI-110 — Reasons are real and correctable.** Each rail or item carries the true reason it was chosen, taken from the ranking signals that actually fired ("Because you bought X"). Users can dismiss an item or mark "not interested", and the correction changes future output.
11. **AI-111 — Business boosts are explicit configuration.** Boosts and sponsored placements are named entries in the serving config, visible to anyone reviewing it — never hard-coded promotions hidden in code — and boosted items still pass the exclusion filter (AI-103).
12. **AI-112 — Feedback closes the loop.** Impressions, clicks, purchases, and dismissals on recommendations are logged against the serving request ID (AI-109), so the next ranking can learn from them and ai-evaluation can measure whether it did.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AI-051 — One static list under a "For you" label.** Banned: a "Recommended for you" rail that renders the same hard-coded or globally fixed list to every visitor regardless of history. Defeats: DET-FAKE-009. Bad: the home page "Picked for you" rail renders the same six product IDs from a constant array for logged-in users with years of history and for anonymous visitors alike. Instead: compute the list from the user's events (AI-101, AI-107), or serve the fallback under its honest label (AI-105, AI-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AI-052 — Cosmetic exclusion filter.** Banned: exclusion that exists on paper but not in the serving path — purchased or out-of-stock items keep being recommended because filtering is a prompt hint, a UI-side hide, or code that never runs. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: the prompt tells the model "avoid items the user owns", and the boots the user bought last week are recommended again, next to a sold-out jacket. Instead: remove owned, consumed, unavailable, and ineligible items in deterministic code after candidate generation, rechecked at serve time (AI-103, AI-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AI-053 — Fabricated recommendation reasons.** Banned: reason text that does not come from a signal that actually fired — template strings like "Because you loved X" attached to items the user never viewed, bought, or rated. Defeats: DET-FAKE-009. Bad: every card in the rail prints "Because you bought the trail shoes" because the template hard-codes it, including for users who have never bought anything. Instead: generate the reason from the logged ranking signal for that item, and omit the reason when no signal fired (AI-110, AI-109). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AI-054 — Hidden hard-coded promotion.** Banned: a specific product or seller boosted inside a personalized rail by a hard-coded rule in code, with no entry in the serving config and no disclosure. Defeats: DET-FAKE-009. Bad: a developer adds `if (item.id === 4417) score *= 3` before launch; the item tops every user's "For you" rail and nobody reviewing the config can see why. Instead: declare the boost as a named config entry, disclose it where the surface requires, and keep it behind the exclusion filter (AI-111, AI-108). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AI-055 — Seed or demo items in a production rail.** Banned: recommendations drawn from seed, fixture, or demo catalog data presented to real users as purchasable products. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the "More like this" rail recommends three seed products with placeholder images that have no product page and cannot be bought. Instead: generate candidates only from the live catalog, and keep demo data behind a visibly labeled demo mode (AI-102). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AI-051 — Two-user divergence test.** Verifies: AI-107, AI-101. Check (automated): seed two test users through the event API — user A with views and purchases of trail-running items, user B with views and purchases of baking items — then call the recommendations endpoint for each and compare the top-10 item ID lists. Pass: the two lists are not identical. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-052 — Exclusion sweep.** Verifies: AI-103, AI-104. Check (automated): for a test user, mark one item purchased and set one item out of stock, then request recommendations 20 times (or exhaust the candidate pool) and assert neither item ID appears in any response. Pass: zero appearances across all responses. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-053 — Cold-start fallback test.** Verifies: AI-105, AI-106. Check (automated): create a fresh user with no events, call the recommendations endpoint, and assert (a) the response is non-empty, (b) the items match the documented fallback configuration, and (c) the returned surface label is the fallback label, not "For you". Pass: all three assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-054 — Serving-log completeness check.** Verifies: AI-109, AI-110, AI-112. Check (automated): make one recommendations request, then query the serving log by that request ID and assert the record carries model/config version, personalized-or-fallback flag, served item IDs, and a reason code per item. Pass: all fields present. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-055 — Boost and ranking config audit.** Verifies: AI-111, AI-108. Check (manual): serve recommendations to a neutral test user, list every item whose position is explained by a boost, and confirm each one has a named entry in the serving config and that the documented ranking logic matches the config. Pass: no undeclared boosts; document and config agree. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Popularity echo.** The ranking over-weights global popularity, so "personalized" lists quietly converge on the same bestsellers for everyone. Catch it in the serving logs: if the overlap between different users' lists keeps climbing, the personal signals are being drowned out — before a reviewer has to notice.
- **Frozen fallback.** The "Popular right now" fallback is a snapshot taken at launch and never refreshed, so it recommends last season's items forever. Catch it by checking the fallback's source: it must be a live query or a config with a refresh date, not a pasted list.
- **Reason drift.** A ranking change ships, but the UI's reason templates still describe the old signals, so explanations stop matching why items were chosen. Catch it by sampling served reasons against the logged reason codes (G-AI-054) after every ranking change.
- **Duplicate slot stuffing.** The same item is placed in several rails on one page to fill space, making a thin catalog look deep. Catch it with a render check that deduplicates item IDs across all recommendation responses on the page.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The "Picked for you" rail that showed everyone the same six products](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AI-106, AI-107 (BAN-AI-051).
- [Example 2 — Recommended again: the boots you already bought](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AI-103 (BAN-AI-052).
- [Example 3 — The new user who got a blank rail](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AI-105, AI-106.

## Recall anchors

- Events first: no event stream, no personalization claim.
- Filter in code, after candidates — never in a prompt.
- Fallback exists for every segment, and it wears its own label.
- "For you" is a promise: the list must differ by history.
- Log the version with every response, or quality is a rumor.

## Checklist

- [ ] Views, clicks, purchases, and dismissals are logged in the defined event schema from launch (AI-101).
- [ ] Serving runs candidates → exclusion filter → ranking → response, with no stage skipped (AI-102).
- [ ] Purchased, consumed, out-of-stock, and ineligible items never appear in any response; the exclusion sweep passes (AI-103, AI-104, G-AI-052).
- [ ] Two test users with different histories receive different lists (AI-107, G-AI-051).
- [ ] A cold-start user receives the documented fallback, non-empty and labeled as fallback — never "For you" (AI-105, AI-106, G-AI-053).
- [ ] Every response is logged with model/config version, fallback flag, item IDs, and reason codes; feedback events join on the request ID (AI-109, AI-112, G-AI-054).
- [ ] Each item's displayed reason comes from a signal that actually fired, and dismiss / "not interested" corrections change future output (AI-110).
- [ ] All boosts are named serving-config entries; no hard-coded promotion exists in code (AI-111, G-AI-055).

<!-- generated from skills/ai-features/search-relevance/SKILL.md -->

# search-relevance

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D17 AI Features (AI)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://cloud.google.com/generative-ai-app-builder/docs/custom-ranking ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/generative-ai-app-builder/docs/ranking
- **Depends on:** embeddings-search
- **Feeds into:** ai-evaluation, ai-observability

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or tuning a search feature whose results are ranked — candidate retrieval, ranking signals and weights, filters and sorting, zero-result handling — or when a ranking change, boost, or reranker is proposed.
- **Do NOT use when:** the task is indexing and embedding the corpus (use embeddings-search), answering questions from retrieved documents (use rag-retrieval), or ranking a personalized recommendation feed (use recommendations). This skill owns the relevance of query-driven search results.

## Rules

1. **AI-121 — Ranking is tuned against a maintained judged query set.** The set holds real queries drawn from query logs, each with graded relevance labels for its expected results. It is versioned in the repo, and it — not opinion — is the baseline every tuning decision is measured against.
2. **AI-122 — No ranking change ships without an offline NDCG comparison.** Before release, the candidate ranking is scored against the current ranking on the judged set (AI-121) and NDCG@10 for both is recorded in the change. A regression blocks the release.
3. **AI-123 — The judged set grows from real query logs.** Each review cycle, zero-result queries and reformulated queries (the user immediately searched again in different words) are triaged: labeled and added to the set, or fixed and recorded as fixed.
4. **AI-124 — Zero-result rate is a monitored metric with a named owner.** Every zero-result search is logged with its query and active filters. The owner reviews the log on the recorded cycle and fixes causes — missing synonyms, unhandled spelling variants, indexing gaps — at the cause, not per complaint.
5. **AI-125 — Fixes target the query class, never one query.** A change must improve the class of queries that share the failure (a synonym group, a field-weight problem, an indexing gap). A boost, pin, or special case that helps exactly one query string is forbidden.
6. **AI-126 — A zero-result search returns an honest recovery state.** The state says that nothing matched, shows the active query and filters, and offers a working path: clear or loosen filters, corrected spelling, or the closest broader category. A blank area is never the answer.
7. **AI-127 — Filters never silently contradict the query.** Active filters are always visible, result counts are computed by the same query that produces the results, and when a filter combination excludes everything the query itself would match, the UI says so and offers to remove the conflicting filter.
8. **AI-128 — Paid and boosted placement is labeled and kept honest.** Sponsored or business-boosted results carry a visible label and are visually distinguishable from organic results. Payment never changes the organic ranking order while the surface presents that order as relevance.
9. **AI-129 — Sort labels say what the sort does.** The default order may be labeled "Relevance" only when it is produced by the ranking signals (AI-132). An order by date, price, or popularity is labeled by that field, never dressed up as relevance.
10. **AI-130 — Any LLM reranker carries a latency and cost budget.** The reranker runs under a recorded per-query latency budget and cost budget, with a timeout that falls back to the non-LLM ranking. A reranker with no budget or no fallback is forbidden.
11. **AI-131 — Search queries the real index over the real dataset.** Queries reach a server-side index over the full catalog or corpus; a record added through the product becomes findable without a redeploy. Filtering a small client-side array and presenting it as the catalog is forbidden.
12. **AI-132 — Ranking signals are explicit, weighted configuration.** The signals (semantic relevance, keyword match, freshness, popularity, document fields, business rules) and their weights live in one versioned ranking configuration. Scattered hard-coded boosts in feature code are forbidden.

## BAN list

- **BAN-AI-061 — Search with canned results.** Banned: every query returning the same fixture list, or results filtered client-side from a small hard-coded array presented as the catalog. Defeats: DET-FAKE-008. Bad: searching "invoice export", "zzzqqq", and a term from a record created a minute ago all return the same eight products. Instead: query the server index over the real dataset so contents and counts vary with the query and the data (AI-131). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AI-062 — Sort and filter controls that only rearrange a fixture.** Banned: sort, filter, and pagination controls that reorder one small hard-coded set while counts and pages claim a larger dataset. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: "Sort by relevance" and "Sort by newest" return the same twelve items in slightly different orders, and page 2 repeats page 1. Instead: execute filtering, sorting, and pagination against the real dataset with counts derived from the same query (AI-127, AI-131). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-AI-063 — Blank zero-result state.** Banned: a search that matches nothing renders an empty container with no explanation. Defeats: DET-UX-009. Bad: a misspelled query leaves a white gap under the search box; the user cannot tell whether search is broken, loading, or genuinely empty. Instead: render the recovery state — what matched nothing, the active constraints, and the next action (AI-126). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AI-064 — Filter dead end with invisible constraints.** Banned: a filter combination returning zero results while the active filters are hidden and no clear-or-adjust action exists. Defeats: DET-UX-025. Bad: three facets are still applied from an earlier session; every new search returns nothing and the page offers no way to see or remove them. Instead: show active filters on the results view and offer one-action clear/broaden whenever results are empty (AI-126, AI-127). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-AI-065 — Paid placement disguised as relevance.** Banned: sponsored or boosted items inserted into the organic order, unlabeled, so payment reads as relevance. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: a vendor's product sits at position 1 for unrelated queries under a "Best match" heading, with no label and no entry in the ranking configuration. Instead: label boosted placement visibly, keep it distinguishable from the organic order, and record every boost in the ranking configuration (AI-128, AI-132). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-AI-061 — Offline NDCG regression gate.** Verifies: AI-121, AI-122. Check (automated): run the project's eval script, e.g. `python3 scripts/search_eval.py --judged search/judged-queries.json --candidate candidate --baseline current`, which prints NDCG@10 for both rankings. Pass: candidate NDCG@10 is at or above the baseline, and both scores are recorded in the change. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-062 — Zero-result audit.** Verifies: AI-123, AI-124. Check (automated): run the zero-result report over the period's query log, e.g. `python3 scripts/zero_result_report.py --log search-queries.log`, which prints the zero-result rate and the untriaged zero-result queries. Pass: the rate is at or below the recorded threshold and every listed query is either added to the judged set with labels or recorded as fixed with its cause. Fail: block shipment of the ranking release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-063 — Findability and honesty probe.** Verifies: AI-131. Check (automated): create a record containing a unique marker term through the product's normal write path, search the marker, then search a gibberish string. Pass: the marker search returns the new record with no redeploy, and the gibberish search returns the honest zero-result state (AI-126). Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-064 — Filter recovery walk.** Verifies: AI-126, AI-127. Check (manual): in the running product, run a nonsense search, then apply a filter combination that excludes everything the query matches. Pass: both cases show what matched nothing, display the active query and filters, and offer a working clear/broaden action; counts shown equal the results the same query returns. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-AI-065 — Placement and label audit.** Verifies: AI-128, AI-129, AI-132. Check (automated + manual): diff the ranking configuration for the release — every boost or pin must appear there with a reason — then inspect the rendered results for a boosted query. Pass: no boost exists outside the configuration, every boosted item carries its label in the UI, and the default sort is labeled "Relevance" only when produced by the configured signals. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **The manager's query.** One stakeholder searches once, dislikes the order, and the team starts tuning to that single anecdote. Catch it by asking which judged-set queries the change improves — if the answer names one person's search, it is AI-125 failing in conversation before it fails in code.
- **Freshness creep.** A "small" change makes results effectively sort by date, and within a month the default order is a changelog wearing a "Relevance" label. Catch it by checking the recorded NDCG delta and the effective signal weights in the ranking configuration at each release.
- **Synonym whack-a-mole.** Each zero-result complaint gets its own one-off synonym until the table is an unmaintainable list of individual grievances. Catch it in the zero-result report: fixes should cluster into classes (spelling, indexing gaps, missing fields), not accumulate as singletons.
- **Reranker by vibes.** An LLM reranker is added because it "feels smarter," with no judged-set score, latency measurement, or timeout behavior recorded. Catch it by asking for its G-AI-061 scores and its budget line — if neither exists, it is decoration, not ranking.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The same eight results for every query](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects AI-131 (BAN-AI-061).
- [Example 2 — The manager's pinned product](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects AI-122, AI-125, AI-132 (BAN-AI-065).
- [Example 3 — The zero-result dead end](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects AI-124, AI-126, AI-127 (BAN-AI-064).

## Recall anchors

- No judged set, no tuning — opinion is not a baseline.
- Every ranking change records its NDCG delta.
- Zero results are logged, owned, and fixed at the cause.
- Fix the query class, never the one query.
- Boosted is labeled, or it does not ship.

## Checklist

- [ ] The judged query set is versioned, built from real queries with graded labels, and grew this cycle from zero-result and reformulated queries (AI-121, AI-123).
- [ ] The release records candidate vs. baseline NDCG@10 and shows no regression (AI-122, G-AI-061).
- [ ] The zero-result rate is reported, at or below threshold, with an owner and every untriaged query resolved (AI-124, G-AI-062).
- [ ] A newly created record is findable by search without a redeploy, and gibberish returns the honest empty state (AI-131, G-AI-063).
- [ ] Zero-result and impossible-filter states explain themselves, show active constraints, and offer a working recovery action (AI-126, AI-127, G-AI-064).
- [ ] All boosts live in the ranking configuration with reasons; boosted items are labeled in the UI; sort labels name the actual sort (AI-128, AI-129, AI-132, G-AI-065).
- [ ] Any LLM reranker has a recorded latency and cost budget and a tested timeout fallback to the non-LLM ranking (AI-130).

## Department D18 — customer-experience

<!-- generated from skills/customer-experience/activation-metrics/SKILL.md -->

# activation-metrics

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D18 Customer Experience (CX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Amplitude, "Driving product engagement by obsessing over activation" — https://amplitude.com/blog/getting-started-activation
- **Depends on:** event-tracking
- **Feeds into:** user-onboarding, trial-conversion, growth-experiments

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** defining or changing the activation event, setting an activation target, building or auditing an activation dashboard or funnel report, diagnosing onboarding drop-off or funnel drop-off (where users abandon before first value, and why), or aiming onboarding at a measurable first-value moment.
- **Do NOT use when:** building the analytics pipeline, event instrumentation, or dashboard tooling itself — D12 (analytics-observability) owns the platform. This skill defines which activation events, windows, and thresholds D18 reads from that platform; it does not operate the platform.

## Rules

1. **CX-081 — Boundary: definitions here, platform in D12.** D12 owns event pipelines, storage, and dashboard tooling. This skill owns the activation definition — the event, the window, and the thresholds — that every D18 surface reads from the platform. A platform or dashboard change never silently changes the metric.
2. **CX-082 — One event.** Activation is exactly one defined event: the first action by which a user receives the product's core value. If a small set is unavoidable, the set carries one shared written definition and is reported as one metric, never as several competing ones.
3. **CX-083 — Signup is not activation.** Account creation, email verification, and profile completion are never the activation event. They are funnel steps before it.
4. **CX-084 — The written definition matches the instrumented event.** The event name in the written definition is identical to the event name in the tracking plan, and the event demonstrably fires in a test session. A definition naming an event that does not exist or does not fire is void.
5. **CX-085 — Every rate carries its window.** Each reported activation rate states its window (e.g., within the first session, within 7 days of signup). A rate published without a window is not a metric and is not reported.
6. **CX-086 — Validated against retention on own data.** The definition is validated by cohort analysis on this product's data: users who complete the event within the window retain better at a stated horizon (e.g., day 30) than users who do not. Before any validation run, the definition records the minimum retention delta and the horizon in advance; validation passes only when the measured delta meets that pre-recorded threshold. An unvalidated definition is labeled a hypothesis everywhere it appears.
7. **CX-087 — Thresholds come from the product's own baseline.** Activation targets and alert thresholds are computed from this product's measured baseline and recorded with that computation. No target is set from an external benchmark, article, or another product's published rate.
8. **CX-088 — Borrowed milestones are hypotheses only.** Another product's famous activation milestone may be tested as a candidate event under CX-086. It is never adopted as the definition or the target before it passes validation on this product's data.
9. **CX-089 — One definition everywhere.** Product, marketing, CX, and data surfaces report the same event, the same window, and the same cohort rule. No surface reports a local variant; a needed change goes through CX-091 and applies everywhere at once.
10. **CX-090 — The denominator is the signup cohort.** The activation rate is activated users divided by the signup cohort of the stated period. It is never computed over "active users," sessions, or any base that excludes the users who never activated.
11. **CX-091 — Revalidation triggers.** The definition is re-validated under CX-086 whenever the core value action, the packaging, or the target segment changes materially, and any change to the event or window is dated and annotated on every trend report so old and new definitions are never spliced into one line.
12. **CX-092 — Reported counts reconcile with raw events.** Every published activation count and rate must reconcile with an independent computation from raw events for the same cohort and period. A discrepancy blocks reporting until it is explained and fixed at the source.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CX-041 — Signup relabeled as activation.** Banned: counting account creation as the activation event in any dashboard, report, or claim. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Bad: the dashboard reports "activation rate: 100%" because every signup is counted as activated, so real value actions never move the figure. Instead: count only the defined core-value event within its window over the signup cohort (CX-082, CX-083, CX-090). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-042 — The borrowed milestone.** Banned: adopting another product's famous activation milestone, or its published activation rate, as this product's definition or target. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Bad: activation is defined as "invited three teammates" because a famous collaboration tool uses it, while this product's solo users receive core value without ever inviting anyone — the metric never moves when value is delivered. Instead: treat the milestone as a hypothesis and validate it against this product's retention data before adopting it (CX-086, CX-088). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-043 — Seed and test accounts in the cohort.** Banned: including seed, demo, staff, or test accounts in activation cohorts or counts. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: the launch-week activation rate is computed over a cohort in which a third of the "users" are the team's seeded demo accounts, all of which performed the activation event during setup. Instead: exclude flagged non-customer accounts from the cohort at query time and state the exclusion in the report (CX-090, CX-092). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-044 — The scripted live counter.** Banned: a "live activations" or "users activated today" indicator driven by a timer, a random increment, or any source other than the real event stream. Defeats: DET-FAKE-018. Bad: the marketing page shows an activations-today counter that ticks up every few seconds overnight, when no signups are occurring. Instead: compute the indicator from the real event stream with its refresh period labeled, or remove it (CX-092). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-045 — Segment counts that cannot reconcile.** Banned: publishing activation breakdowns (by plan, channel, or segment) whose counts are produced from a fixed summary that does not match the underlying event query. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Bad: the by-channel activation counts sum to 1,240 while the headline rate for the same period is computed over 1,180 signups, and nobody can say which is right. Instead: derive every breakdown from the same raw-event query as the headline figure and assert the segments sum to it (CX-092). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CX-041 — Funnel reconciliation.** Verifies: CX-089, CX-090, CX-092. Check: automated — a scheduled query independently computes the previous month's signup-cohort activation rate from raw events and diffs it against the dashboard figure for the same cohort and window. Pass: the figures match exactly, or differ only by a stated rounding rule recorded with the definition. Fail: block external reporting of the metric until reconciled. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-042 — Definition-consistency check.** Verifies: CX-082, CX-084. Check: automated — a script asserts the event name in the written definition exists verbatim in the tracking plan and fires at least once in an instrumented test session. Pass: name matches and the event fires. Fail: block shipment of any surface reporting activation. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-043 — Cohort validation run.** Verifies: CX-086, CX-088. Check: scheduled query plus manual review — first confirm the definition records a minimum retention delta and horizon set before the run; then compute the stated-horizon retention of the activated cohort vs. the non-activated cohort from raw events on this product's data. Pass: the measured retention delta meets or exceeds the pre-recorded minimum delta at the recorded horizon, and the result, threshold, horizon, and date are recorded with the definition. Fail: the definition is downgraded to "hypothesis" in every surface until a candidate event passes. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-044 — Threshold provenance audit.** Verifies: CX-087. Check: manual — for every activation target or alert threshold in dashboards, docs, and decks, trace the number to a recorded baseline computation on this product's data. Pass: every number traces to an own-data baseline. Fail: any number traceable only to an external source is removed or replaced before the report ships. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-045 — Revalidation and change control.** Verifies: CX-089, CX-091. Check: manual — on any change to the core value action, packaging, or target segment, confirm a revalidation run (G-CX-043) is scheduled; on any definition change, confirm the change date is annotated on every trend report. Pass: revalidation scheduled and annotations present. Fail: trend reporting freezes at the last consistently defined period. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Window shopping.** Quietly widening the window (7 days to 30 days) so the rate rises, without restating historical figures under the new window. Catch it: any window change appears in the definition's dated change log and history is recomputed or the trend line is broken visibly at the change.
- **Denominator shopping.** Reporting activation as a share of "active users" in the periods when the honest signup-cohort rate looks bad. Catch it: the denominator is named next to every rate; if it is not the signup cohort, the figure is not the activation rate.
- **Event stuffing.** Adding more events to the activation set until the rate looks healthy, instead of testing which single event predicts retention. Catch it: every candidate event must face the CX-086 retention comparison on its own before joining the set.
- **Validation theater.** Running the cohort comparison once at launch and treating the definition as permanently proven while the product changes around it. Catch it: the definition records its last validation date and the triggers in CX-091; a stale date means the metric is reported as unvalidated.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Replacing "signed up" with a validated activation event](examples/example-1.md) — corrects CX-082, CX-083.
- [Example 2 — Reconciling a dashboard rate against raw events](examples/example-2.md) — corrects CX-092.
- [Example 3 — Replacing a copied benchmark target with an own-baseline target](examples/example-3.md) — corrects CX-087, CX-088.

## Recall anchors

- Activation is the first value received — never the signup.
- One event, one window, one definition, everywhere.
- A rate without a window is not a metric.
- Thresholds come from your own baseline, never a benchmark.
- If the dashboard and the raw events disagree, the dashboard is wrong until proven otherwise.

## Checklist

- [ ] The activation event is one named core-value action, defined in writing (CX-082).
- [ ] Signup and account-setup steps are excluded from the event (CX-083).
- [ ] The written event name matches the tracking plan and fires in a test session (G-CX-042).
- [ ] Every reported rate states its window and its signup-cohort denominator (CX-085, CX-090).
- [ ] The definition has a recorded, dated retention validation on this product's data (G-CX-043).
- [ ] Every target traces to an own-data baseline computation (G-CX-044).
- [ ] Dashboard figures reconcile with an independent raw-event computation (G-CX-041).
- [ ] Revalidation triggers and definition-change annotations are in place (G-CX-045).

# churn-prevention

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D18 Customer Experience (CX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://docs.recurly.com/recurly-engage/docs/cancel-save ; https://docs.stripe.com/billing/revenue-recovery/smart-retries ; https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/P214800%20Dark%20Patterns%20Report%209.14.2022%20-%20FINAL.pdf
- **Depends on:** subscriptions, dunning
- **Feeds into:** feedback-loops, trial-conversion

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or auditing a cancellation flow, exit survey, or save offer; configuring dunning, payment retries, or card updates; reviewing churn reasons and save outcomes; writing any copy on the cancel or win-back path.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work is trial terms and trial-end behavior (use trial-conversion — its cancellation step follows this skill's rules), subscription plan mechanics (use D11 subscriptions), or general feedback collection outside the exit moment (use feedback-loops).

## Rules

1. **CX-141 — Two churn kinds, two logs.** Voluntary churn (user cancels) and involuntary churn (payment failure) are tracked separately; every event records its kind, the stated reason or failure cause, any offer shown, and the outcome. A single blended churn number is not a reviewable record.
2. **CX-142 — Cancel in-product, in the same medium.** Cancellation is completable inside the product, in the same medium as signup, in no more steps than signup took. No path may require emailing support, calling, or waiting for a human to process the request (ROSCA's simple-cancellation duty; the FTC dark-patterns report names obstruction an enforcement target).
3. **CX-143 — One question, one offer, one confirmation.** The cancel flow contains at most: one optional exit-reason question, at most one save offer matched to that reason, and one final confirmation. No second save screen appears after the offer is declined.
4. **CX-144 — Offers matched to the stated reason.** The offer follows the reason: pause for low usage, downgrade or discount for price, support escalation for a defect or unmet need. An accepted offer is applied in the billing system in the same session, and the confirmation shows the new state.
5. **CX-145 — Decline is plain and one step.** The decline control is labeled in plain words ("Cancel my subscription"), styled no less visibly than the accept control, and never carries confirmshaming copy ("No, I don't want to save money"). One decline action completes the flow.
6. **CX-146 — Declining completes the cancellation.** When the offer is declined, cancellation takes effect immediately: the confirmation states the access end date and any final charge, and no charge is taken after that date. A cancellation that needs a later manual step is not complete.
7. **CX-147 — Exit feedback is product feedback.** Stated reasons are reviewed on a fixed cadence by a named owner, recurring reasons route to the product backlog or support with the originating records linked, and fixes are announced back to affected users where a channel exists. Reasons nobody reads are not collected.
8. **CX-148 — At-risk signals trigger help, not pressure.** Usage-drop or failed-payment signals trigger an offer of assistance — a check-in, a help article, a support path — never scare copy, fake deadlines, or loss-framed warnings the product cannot substantiate.
9. **CX-149 — Dunning runs before any non-payment cancellation.** Failed payments trigger, in the billing platform: smart retries, automatic card-account updates where the network offers them, and dunning emails containing a working payment-update link. All three run before an account is cancelled for non-payment.
10. **CX-150 — Non-payment cancellation is announced in advance.** An account is cancelled for non-payment only after the dunning sequence (CX-149) completes, and the user is told the exact end date before it arrives. No account ends silently mid-cycle.
11. **CX-151 — Save rate never justifies friction.** The save rate is reported alongside cancellation-completion rate and post-cancel complaints. Adding any step, screen, or delay to the cancel flow is forbidden unless the friction audit (G-CX-072) still passes and the reason is recorded; a step added to lift the save rate is removed.
12. **CX-152 — The billing state is the truth.** After confirmation, the billing system shows the subscription cancelled (or paused/downgraded, if an offer was accepted) with exactly the end date the confirmation stated. Any disagreement between the UI state and the billing state is a defect, found by G-CX-073, not by a charged user.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CX-071 — Phantom cancellation.** Banned: a cancel flow that displays "Your subscription is cancelled" while the subscription stays active in billing and the next charge is taken. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Bad: the user cancels, sees a confirmation screen, and is charged again on the renewal date because the cancel handler only hid the plan banner. Instead: complete the cancellation in the billing system in the same session and state the real end date (CX-146, CX-152). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-072 — Cancel path that submits nowhere.** Banned: the only cancellation route is a "request cancellation" form or email link whose submission creates no billing change and no tracked task. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Bad: Settings links to a form reading "Tell us why you're leaving and we'll process your cancellation"; submissions land in an unmonitored inbox and renewals continue. Instead: cancel self-serve in-product (CX-142); the reason question is optional and inside that flow (CX-143). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-073 — Confirmation state that lies.** Banned: a confirmation screen or email stating an access end date or "no further charges" that the billing system does not honor. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the confirmation says "Access until March 31 — this was your final charge," but the subscription record still shows auto-renew on and an invoice is generated April 1. Instead: generate the confirmation from the billing record after the state change lands, and verify the two agree (CX-152, G-CX-073). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-074 — Save offer that doesn't stick.** Banned: an accepted pause or downgrade that displays as applied but silently reverts, so the next cycle bills the original plan at the original price. Defeats: DET-FAKE-016. Bad: the user accepts a two-month pause, sees "Paused until June," and is charged in May because the pause was stored only in UI state. Instead: apply the offer as a billing-system state change and show the resulting plan, price, and resume date from that record (CX-144). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-075 — Fake urgency on the save offer.** Banned: a countdown timer, expiring-offer clock, or "only today" deadline on a save offer that resets, restarts, or is not enforced by any real expiry. Defeats: DET-FAKE-018. Bad: the save screen shows "This 30% offer expires in 09:59" on every visit, indefinitely. Instead: show the offer's real terms with no timer, or a deadline the billing system actually enforces (CX-144, CX-148). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CX-071 — Cancel-flow walkthrough per reason.** Verifies: CX-143, CX-144, CX-146. Check (automated): as a test subscriber, run the cancel flow once per exit reason and assert: exactly one reason question and at most one offer appear; the offer matches the stated reason; accepting it changes the billing record to the offered state in the same session; declining completes the cancellation immediately; the reason, offer, and outcome are written to the churn log. Pass: every assertion true for every reason. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-072 — Friction audit.** Verifies: CX-142, CX-151. Check (automated): scripted click-count of signup vs. cancellation from the same starting surface, plus a check that the cancel path never leaves the product or requires a message to support. Pass: cancel steps ≤ signup steps, completed entirely in-product. Fail: block shipment until steps are removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-073 — Post-cancel billing state test.** Verifies: CX-146, CX-152. Check (automated): cancel a test subscription, then query the billing system and assert: status is cancelled, the end date equals the date on the confirmation, and with a test clock advanced past that date, no further invoice is generated. Pass: all three assertions true. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-074 — Dunning sequence test.** Verifies: CX-149, CX-150. Check (automated): in billing test mode, fail a test payment and assert: retries are attempted, a card-update attempt or request fires, dunning emails send with a payment-update link that resolves, the account stays active through the sequence, and cancellation — with advance notice naming the end date — happens only after the sequence completes. Pass: every stage fires in order. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-075 — Churn-log review audit.** Verifies: CX-141, CX-147, CX-151. Check: sample the last 30 days of churn events and assert each records kind (voluntary/involuntary), reason or failure cause, offer shown, and outcome; confirm a review record exists for the period naming the owner and any reason routed to the backlog. Pass: complete records and a current review. Fail: warn; two consecutive failures block the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Save-rate worship.** The team celebrates a rising save rate while post-cancel complaints and chargebacks climb — retention by exhaustion. Catch it by reading the save rate only next to the completion rate and complaint count (CX-151); if they move in opposite directions, the flow got worse, not better.
- **Reason-blind roadmap.** Exit reasons are collected faithfully and never opened, so the top fixable reason ships in no release. Catch it at the review cadence: if no reason has been routed anywhere in a full cycle, the survey is decoration and the review (CX-147) is not happening.
- **Win-back barrage.** A cancelled user gets a sequence of escalating win-back emails after choosing to leave. Catch it by capping post-cancel contact at one message and checking the suppression list actually excludes completed cancellations.
- **Pause preselected.** The save screen pre-checks "Pause instead" so a user who clicks through quickly pauses rather than cancels, then is charged at resume. Catch it by requiring the user's explicit selection — no option on the cancel path starts pre-chosen.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The cancel button that went nowhere](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CX-142, CX-143 (BAN-CX-072).
- [Example 2 — One discount popup for every reason](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CX-144, CX-145 (BAN-CX-075).
- [Example 3 — The failed card that silently ended the account](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CX-149, CX-150.

## Recall anchors

- Cancel takes no more steps than signup — ever.
- One question, one matched offer, one confirmation.
- Declining the offer is the cancellation completing, not a detour.
- A trapped customer is a liability, not a save.
- Failed payment is a billing problem to fix before it is a churn event.

## Checklist

- [ ] Cancellation completes in-product, in the same medium, in ≤ signup steps (CX-142, G-CX-072).
- [ ] Flow is one optional reason question, at most one matched offer, one confirmation (CX-143, G-CX-071).
- [ ] Every offer matches its stated reason and applies in billing when accepted (CX-144, G-CX-071).
- [ ] Decline is plain, one step, free of confirmshaming, and completes the cancellation (CX-145, CX-146).
- [ ] Confirmation end date and final charge match the billing record exactly (CX-152, G-CX-073).
- [ ] Dunning — retries, card updates, linked emails — runs before any non-payment cancellation, with advance notice (CX-149, CX-150, G-CX-074).
- [ ] Voluntary and involuntary churn logged separately with reason, offer, and outcome (CX-141, G-CX-075).
- [ ] Exit reasons reviewed on cadence and routed to the backlog by a named owner (CX-147, G-CX-075).

# feedback-loops

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D18 Customer Experience (CX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://www.intercom.com/help/en/articles/5256662-how-your-nps-survey-responses-make-intercom-better
- **Depends on:** support-ticketing
- **Feeds into:** user-onboarding, activation-metrics

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** launching or auditing any feedback channel — post-resolution CSAT, lifecycle NPS, in-product ratings, feature-request paths; setting survey triggers, frequency caps, and ownership; reporting scores; announcing shipped changes back to the users who requested them.
- **Do NOT use when:** the request is a support issue needing resolution (use support-ticketing — its post-resolution survey is configured here), product usage measurement (use activation-metrics / D12 analytics), or one-off research interviews, which are scheduled conversations, not instrumented surveys.

## Rules

1. **CX-121 — Defined trigger moments only.** Every survey fires at a defined lifecycle moment — after a support resolution, after onboarding completes, at a set account-age interval — recorded in the survey's configuration. A survey with no defined trigger does not launch.
2. **CX-122 — Context is captured with the response.** Every response records the user or account, the triggering event, the product area, and the timestamp at the moment of the experience. A score stored without its context is not actionable and counts as a configuration defect.
3. **CX-123 — Responses attach to the record.** Scores and comments attach to the user or account record in the feedback system. Responses stored only in a detached spreadsheet or export that no workflow reads are treated as not collected.
4. **CX-124 — Frequency caps across all surveys.** A per-user frequency cap is enforced across every live survey combined: a user inside the cooldown window is not re-prompted by any survey. No survey fires on every page load or every session.
5. **CX-125 — Named owner and cadence before launch.** Every survey names an owner and a fixed review cadence in its configuration before it goes live. The owner reviews new responses on that cadence; the last-reviewed date is recorded.
6. **CX-126 — Neutral wording, equal effort both ways.** Survey questions are worded neutrally and every response option — including the most negative — is equally visible and equally easy to submit. Prompts timed or phrased to catch only satisfied users are prohibited (see BAN-CX-063).
7. **CX-127 — Detractors get a human path.** A low score or a comment describing a problem creates a follow-up task for the owning team, and the respondent is told how a human will reach them. Collecting detractor pain with no response path is worse than not asking.
8. **CX-128 — Themes route to the backlog, linked.** Recurring themes from review are entered in the product backlog with the originating responses linked, so any shipped fix can be traced back to the feedback that caused it.
9. **CX-129 — The loop closes visibly.** When a change requested through feedback ships, the users who requested it are notified that it shipped and what changed. An announcement is sent only for changes that actually shipped.
10. **CX-130 — Scores reported with counts and segment.** Every reported score is published with its response count, time window, and segment. A bare average with no count or segment is not a reportable figure.
11. **CX-131 — No unsourced score claims.** A survey score appears in marketing or product copy only if it is real, current, and produced by this feedback system, cited with its count and window (CX-130). Scores from a removed or unowned survey are never quoted.
12. **CX-132 — Unowned surveys are removed.** A survey whose owner leaves, whose cadence lapses, or whose responses nobody reviews is paused or removed within one cadence cycle. A survey nobody reads does not keep running.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CX-061 — Survey that submits nowhere.** Banned: a feedback form or survey whose responses persist to no reviewed system — discarded, or exported to a spreadsheet nobody opens — while the UI thanks the user. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Bad: an NPS popup stores responses in a shared spreadsheet last opened at launch and shows "Thanks!" on submit. Instead: persist responses on the user/account record in the feedback system with a named owner and cadence (CX-123, CX-125), or remove the survey. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-062 — Receipt that lies.** Banned: showing a success state ("Thanks — your feedback helps us improve!") before, or regardless of, the response actually being stored. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Bad: the survey widget displays its thank-you panel on button click while the submission request fails silently in the background. Instead: show the confirmation only after the store is acknowledged; a failed submission surfaces an error and a retry (CX-123). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-063 — Rigged rating harvest.** Banned: prompts designed to manufacture positive ratings — asking only after a success moment with the negative path hidden, pre-selecting the top score, or wording that shames a low rating. Defeats: DET-FAKE-014. Bad: a "Rate your experience" prompt appears only after a completed purchase, pre-fills five stars, and routes one-star taps to a dead-end page. Instead: ask at defined moments with neutral wording and every option equally submittable (CX-121, CX-126). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-064 — Detractor dead end.** Banned: collecting a low score or problem report with no follow-up task, queue, or human response path behind it. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Bad: a CSAT survey asks "What went wrong?" after bad resolutions; the comments are stored but no ticket, task, or owner ever sees them. Instead: route low scores to a follow-up task for the owning team and tell the respondent a human will reach them (CX-127). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-065 — Loop-closure theater.** Banned: announcing "You asked, we shipped" (or equivalent) for a change that did not ship, or notifying users who never requested it while the actual requesters hear nothing. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Bad: a release email claims a top-requested feature was added based on feedback; the feature is a settings toggle rename, and the users who filed the requests receive no notification. Instead: announce only shipped changes, linked to their originating responses, to the users who requested them (CX-128, CX-129). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-CX-061 — End-to-end submission trace.** Verifies: CX-121, CX-122, CX-123, CX-124, CX-127. Check (automated): using the survey tool's test mode, trigger each live survey as a test user at its defined moment and submit a low score with a unique marker comment; assert the response lands on the test user's record with its context (trigger event, product area, timestamp), the marker appears in the owning team's review queue, a detractor follow-up task is created, and an immediate second trigger is blocked by the frequency cap. Run on launch and on every survey-config change. Pass: every assertion true for every survey. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-062 — Ownership and cadence audit.** Verifies: CX-125, CX-132. Check (automated): export the configuration of every live survey and assert each lists a named owner, a review cadence, and a last-reviewed date within one cadence cycle of today. Pass: zero live surveys missing an owner, cadence, or current review date. Fail: block shipment of new surveys; pause any lapsed survey until ownership is restored. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-063 — Loop-closure audit.** Verifies: CX-128, CX-129. Check: sample the changes announced as feedback-driven in the review period; for each, assert a backlog item exists linking the originating responses, the change is present in the shipped product, and the announcement was sent to the users who requested it. Pass: every sampled announcement traces to linked feedback and a real shipped change, with requesters notified. Fail: warn; correct or retract the announcement and record the gap. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-064 — Score reporting integrity check.** Verifies: CX-130, CX-131. Check (automated): recompute every published score from the raw responses in the feedback system and diff against the published figure; grep marketing and product copy for score claims and assert each carries its response count, window, and segment and matches the recomputation. Pass: every published figure matches its raw data and carries count, window, and segment. Fail: block shipment of the copy until corrected. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-065 — Detractor follow-up test.** Verifies: CX-127. Check (automated): submit a detractor score with a problem comment through each survey's test mode and assert a follow-up task is created in the owning team's queue, assigned to a named human, with the respondent's contact path attached. Pass: a task exists for every survey tested. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Survey sprawl.** Each team launches its own prompt until users are asked something on every visit and response rates collapse. Catch it by counting live surveys and total prompts per user per month against the shared cap (CX-124) — the fix is consolidation, not another survey.
- **Score watching without reading.** The team tracks the average moving up or down but nobody reads the comments, where the actionable content lives. Catch it at review: a cadence meeting with no verbatim responses on the agenda has become a dashboard ritual.
- **Cherry-picked verbatims.** Only glowing comments are quoted in decks and copy while detractor themes stay buried. Catch it by requiring every internal report to pair quoted praise with the period's top detractor theme.
- **Asking again because the first answer was ignored.** A new survey re-asks a question a previous survey already answered, because its responses were never routed anywhere. Catch it by searching existing feedback for the theme before approving a new survey on it.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — The NPS popup nobody read](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CX-123, CX-124, CX-125 (BAN-CX-061).
- [Example 2 — The detractor who heard nothing](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CX-127 (BAN-CX-064).
- [Example 3 — Closing the loop for real](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CX-128, CX-129, CX-130 (BAN-CX-065).

## Recall anchors

- A survey nobody reviews is removed, not left running.
- Feedback attaches to the user record, never to a spreadsheet.
- Caps are per user, across every survey combined.
- Low scores create work for a human, not just a number.
- The loop closes when the requester is told it shipped.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every survey fires at a defined lifecycle moment, recorded in its configuration (CX-121, G-CX-061).
- [ ] Responses land on the user/account record with trigger, area, and timestamp context (CX-122, CX-123, G-CX-061).
- [ ] The shared per-user frequency cap blocks re-prompts across all surveys (CX-124, G-CX-061).
- [ ] Every live survey has a named owner, a cadence, and a current last-reviewed date (CX-125, G-CX-062).
- [ ] Wording is neutral and every score is equally easy to submit (CX-126).
- [ ] A detractor submission creates an assigned human follow-up task (CX-127, G-CX-065).
- [ ] Shipped feedback-driven changes link their originating responses and notify the requesters (CX-128, CX-129, G-CX-063).
- [ ] Every published score matches its raw data and carries count, window, and segment (CX-130, CX-131, G-CX-064).

# help-center

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D18 Customer Experience (CX)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408846795674-Getting-started-with-your-help-center ; https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408883389338
- **Depends on:** support-ticketing
- **Feeds into:** in-app-chat, user-onboarding

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** building or maintaining a help center — choosing its structure, writing or revising articles, configuring search, or running the review cycle that keeps articles matched to the current product.
- **Do NOT use when:** answering an individual customer's request (use support-ticketing / in-app-chat), writing marketing or landing-page copy (use copywriting), or documenting internal procedures for staff (use runbook-writing).

## Rules

1. **CX-041 — Real questions only.** An article is published only because a real, recurring customer question exists behind it (from tickets, chat transcripts, or search logs); no article is written to fill out a category or to make the center look complete at launch.
2. **CX-042 — One problem per article.** Each article solves exactly one problem end to end; a second problem gets its own article, cross-linked, never appended.
3. **CX-043 — Customer-language structure.** The hierarchy is category → section → article, at most three levels deep, and category and article names use the words customers use in tickets, not internal team, feature-code, or org-chart names.
4. **CX-044 — Steps match the current UI.** Every step names the exact label, button, or menu item as it appears in the current released UI; an article whose steps cannot be followed verbatim on the live product is unpublished or fixed before release.
5. **CX-045 — Review date on every article.** Each article carries a last-verified date; a UI release that changes a covered flow puts the affected articles into re-verification or archival in the same release cycle.
6. **CX-046 — Search tested with real phrasing.** Help search is tested with the actual phrasing customers used in tickets and prior searches, not with article titles; a query a customer would plausibly type must return the article that answers it.
7. **CX-047 — Zero-result searches are work items.** Search queries that return no result are logged and reviewed on the review cycle; repeated zero-result queries become a new article, a retitle, or added search terms — they are never ignored.
8. **CX-048 — Every article ends at a human.** Each article ends with a working path to human support (ticket form, chat, or email that actually creates a ticket per support-ticketing); an article with a dead end is not finished.
9. **CX-049 — Promises are linked, never restated.** Articles never state response times, support hours, or availability in their own text; they link to the single configured support-expectations page, so the promise exists in exactly one place.
10. **CX-050 — Reachable and resolving.** Every article is reachable without authentication unless it genuinely requires an account, and every link in every article resolves; a broken link found by the crawl gate is fixed or the article is pulled.
11. **CX-051 — Screenshots show the real, current UI.** Screenshots are captured from the current released product with sample data; a screenshot from an older UI version, a design mock, or another product is replaced before publication.
12. **CX-052 — Archive, don't abandon.** An article for a removed or changed feature is archived or rewritten in the release that changes the feature; the center never keeps live instructions for behavior the product no longer has.

## BAN list

- **BAN-CX-021 — Placeholder or filler articles.** Banned: publishing "coming soon," lorem ipsum, or generic launch-day FAQ articles with no real question behind them. Defeats: DET-CON-001. Bad: a "Getting started" article reading "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet — content coming soon!" Instead: publish only articles written from real recurring questions, and leave the category unpublished until its first real article exists. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-022 — AI-spun articles about features that do not exist.** Banned: generating articles in bulk for features, settings, or integrations the product does not have. Defeats: DET-CON-025. Bad: twenty near-identical articles describing an "Advanced reporting" module that was never built. Instead: write one article per real question about shipped behavior, verified against the live product. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-023 — Stale steps and old-UI screenshots.** Banned: leaving live instructions or screenshots from a previous UI version after the flow changed. Defeats: DET-CON-018. Bad: an article saying "Click Settings → Billing in the left sidebar" with a screenshot of the old layout, months after billing moved to a top-level page. Instead: re-verify steps and recapture screenshots in the release that changes the flow, or archive the article. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-024 — Restated support promises.** Banned: writing response-time or availability promises into article text ("We reply within 4 hours!"). Defeats: DET-CON-028. Bad: an article footer promising a 4-hour reply while the configured support hours deliver next-business-day replies. Instead: link to the single configured support-expectations page and state no promise in the article itself. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-CX-025 — Generic filler answers.** Banned: articles that gesture at help without solving the problem ("Simply adjust your settings to fix this issue"). Defeats: DET-CON-006. Bad: "To resolve sync problems, just update your preferences and it should work seamlessly." Instead: give the exact steps, in order, with the current UI labels, ending in the human-support path. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-CX-021 — Top-questions walkthrough.** Verifies: CX-041, CX-046, CX-050. Check: take the five most common real support questions; as an unauthenticated visitor, answer each using only help-center search; assert the correct article is found and every link in it resolves. Pass: 5/5 questions answered from search alone. Fail: block the release; fix search terms, titles, or links first. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-022 — UI-label and link audit (automated).** Verifies: CX-044, CX-050, CX-051. Check: run a link-check crawl over the whole center (`linkchecker` or the platform's built-in broken-link report) and diff every bolded UI label quoted in article steps against the current release's label inventory. Pass: zero broken links, zero labels absent from the current UI. Fail: block publication of the affected articles. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-023 — Zero-result search review.** Verifies: CX-047. Check: export the help-search zero-result report for the review period; confirm each repeated query (≥3 occurrences) has a resulting action — new article, retitle, or added search terms — logged in progress.md. Pass: no repeated zero-result query unactioned. Fail: schedule the articles before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-024 — Human-path check.** Verifies: CX-048. Check: open every published article and follow its end-of-article support path in a test session; assert it reaches a form, chat, or address that creates a ticket. Pass: 100% of articles end at a working human path. Fail: block; repair or unpublish the dead-ended articles. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-CX-025 — Stale-article sweep.** Verifies: CX-045, CX-052. Check: list all articles whose last-verified date predates the latest UI release touching their flow; assert each is re-verified (date updated after a live walkthrough) or archived. Pass: zero live articles stale past a flow-changing release. Fail: archive the stale articles until re-verified. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Anti-patterns

- **Mirror-of-the-app navigation.** The category tree copies the product's internal module names and admin structure, so customers must already know the product to find help. Catch it: try finding an article using only the words from the ticket that prompted it.
- **Screenshot walls.** Articles that are mostly annotated screenshots with almost no text — unsearchable, untranslatable, and silently wrong after any redesign. Catch it: if deleting the images leaves no followable steps, the article fails CX-044 in spirit.
- **The orphan launch set.** A batch of articles written once at launch and never revisited while the product changes around them. Catch it: sort by last-verified date; a long untouched tail is the pattern, caught by G-CX-025 only if someone runs it.
- **Deflection-first framing.** Articles written to keep users away from support ("Before contacting us, try everything below") rather than to solve the problem. Catch it: read the first line — if it argues instead of answering, rewrite it.
- **Duplicate answers drifting apart.** The same question answered in two articles that slowly diverge after edits. Catch it: search the center for the question's key phrase; more than one live answer means merge and redirect.

## Examples

- [Example 1 — Stale steps after a UI move](examples/example-1.md) — violates/corrects CX-044.
- [Example 2 — Article born from a zero-result search](examples/example-2.md) — violates/corrects CX-047.
- [Example 3 — Promise restated in an article footer](examples/example-3.md) — violates/corrects CX-049.

## Recall anchors

- No real question, no article.
- Steps a stranger can follow verbatim on today's UI, or it doesn't ship.
- A failed search is a work order, not a dead end.
- Every article ends at a human.
- Promises live in one configured place — link, never restate.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every new article traces to a real recurring question (CX-041).
- [ ] Article and category names use customer wording, hierarchy ≤3 levels (CX-043).
- [ ] Steps followed verbatim on the live product; screenshots current (CX-044, CX-051).
- [ ] Last-verified date set on every touched article (CX-045).
- [ ] Search tested with real customer phrasing, not titles (CX-046).
- [ ] Zero-result report reviewed and repeated queries actioned (CX-047).
- [ ] End-of-article human path followed and working (CX-048).
- [ ] No response-time or availability promise written into article text (CX-049).
